TUESDAY, APRIL 4, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

The committee met at 10:20 a.m., in room 2172, Rayburn House

Office  

The committee meets this morning in executive session to begin the hearings on H.R. 7099 to further amend the Foreign Assistance 

Act of 1961. 

Our witnesses this morning are the Honorable Leonard Unger, Deputy Assistant Secretary, Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs,

Department of State, and the Honorable Rutherford M. Poats, Assistant Administrator for Far East, Agency for International

Development. 

Mr. Unger and Mr. Poats, both of you have prepared statements. 

If you wish, I would be glad to have you deliver your statements and then we will direct our questions to you both. 

Mr. Unger.

STATEMENT OF HON. LEONARD UNGER, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRETARY, BUREAU OF EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS, DEPARTMENT OF STATE 

Mr. UNGER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and committee members

It is an honor and a pleasure to appear before this distinguished committee today to talk about developments in Vietnam. I am happy that my report has significant elements of progress and promise. 

I do not intend to paint for you a rosy-glowed picture of things to come in Vietnam because the enemy is still tough and determined, the war is difficult and complex, and the road ahead to political and economic stability-and to peace still long and rocky. Nevertheless, I can point to many accomplishments over the past year and to prospects for the future in Vietnam which appear brighter today than they have for a long time.

The recent Guam conference provided an opportunity for a current top-level review of the situation across the board. The conference was not the occasion for major new decisions, but obviously the information exchanged there and the discussions held will influence our Government's thinking and actions in the weeks and months ahead. 

I might say that many of the things that I will be mentioning here were subjects of discussion at Guam. I have not planned to make a specific review of what occurred at Guam, but many of these things were subjects for discussion at that time. 1

1967 

In the military field, Vietnamese, American, and other free world forces clearly have the initiative. They are keeping unrelenting pressure on the enemy, whose weekly casualties have reached a punishing rate and whose members are rallying to the Government in numbers which must be alarming to their leadership. Last week alone, enemy deaths were over 2,700, ralliers to the Government side from the Vietcong have come in at over 1,000 per week for over a montha rate well more than double the weekly average for 1966. Even the most secret and heretofore inaccessible base areas of the enemy are no longer immune from devastating and sustained-attacks.

In the field of revolutionary development, or pacification, the organization, planning, and implementation of both the Vietnamese and U.S. Government are more effective, with concrete results beginning to appear. We are getting increasing numbers of reports of the destruction or damage done to the basic Vietcong infrastructure in several areas.

This results from better coordination and integration of a very complex effort, particularly as between the civil and military aspects, from better training, and better motivation and growing confidence both on the part of government cadres and the people in the countryside whose lives they are trying to make more secure and productive. 

Mr. Poats will undoubtedly talk at greater length on this particular program. 

In the economic field, less than a year ago we were gravely concerned at the risks of runaway inflation which could have destroyed the very basis for political and even military progress. Today, thanks to vigorous stabilization measures taken last summer by the Vietnamese Government and to our support, particularly through the import program, the risks of runaway inflation have virtually disappeared. 

There are still inflationary pressures, and additional measures will be needed to cope with them, but the situation is definitely manageable. 

In the political field progress has been most remarkable and heartening, and in this progress lies the ultimate key to the problem of Vietnam. For this reason, I would like to devote a large portion of my statement today to internal political developments.

POLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS 

The two most salient political facts of South Vietnam today are: (1) The present Government has been in power for 21 months and has brought greater stability and continuity to South Vietnam than did any predecessor government since the fall of the Diem regime; and (2) the present Government, 6 months after coming to power, set a course toward constitutional representative government which has been steadfastly and faithfully adhered to both in its timetable and in its direction.

It is useful to review how far down the road of political progress the Vietnamese Government has come in order to gain perspective on the present and on the future. Politically, 1966 was a year of preparation and stage-setting in South Vietnam; 1967 is a year of realization and fruition. If political progress continues throughout this year as now anticipated, it could have a major bearing on the course of the conflict.

3 

STEPS TOWARD REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNMENT 

On January 15, 1966, Prime Minister Ky announced his Government's intention to set in process a transition to constitutional representative government to be completed by the end of 1967. On April 

14, following the general thrust of the recommendation of the Ñational Political Congress, a body representing all non-Communist groupings in South Vietnam, Chief of State Thieu issued a decree calling for the election of a constituent assembly in September to prepare a draft constitution. 

Meanwhile, in response partly to widespread political pressures and partly to its own instincts and desires, the military Directorate took steps to augment civilian participation in the Government of that day. In June the Directorate itself was expanded by the addition of 10 prominent civilians to the 10 generals serving as members. In 

July, the Directorate established a consultative body called the People's Army Council, consisting of 59 civilians and 20 military officers.

In preparation for the Constituent Assembly elections, the Election Law Drafting Committee, composed of 32 representatives of all major non-Communist groups in Vietnam, was assigned the task of preparing the election regulations and procedures. Campaigns were conducted by 532 candidates for the 117 Constituent Assembly seats in 

August and early September.

On election day, September 11, 4.3 million voters went to the polls. 

The figure represented 81 percent of the 5.3 million registered electorate, and over 50 percent of the estimated 8.25 million population of voting age. The size of the turnout was a major rebuff to the intensive Vietcong effort to prevent voting through propaganda and intimidation and even terror.

This election was the first major milestone on the road to representative government. It was the first national election in 3 years, and is generally considered to be the fairest and freest national election ever held in Vietnam. Moreover, it was no mean accomplishment in the midst of a brutal war.

The Constituent Assembly convened on September 27 to undertake its assigned task of completing a draft constitution within 6 months. All non-Communist ethnic, religious, and regional groupings in South Vietnam were represented in the Assembly, with the exception of the militant Buddhist elements which had boycotted the election.

After electing its Chairman, the respected patriot and former Chief of State, Mr. Phan Khac Suu, and other officers, the Constituent 

Assembly organized itself into bloc affiliations and designated a drafting committee. A separate committee traveled about the countryside to obtain local views on desired constitutional provisions. 

On January 11, 1967, the Assembly opened debate on the text proposed by the drafting committee. The revised draft was approved unanimously on March 18 by the 102 delegates present. On March 

19 the Directorate approved the proposed Constitution and transmitted it to the Armed Forces Council, parent body of the Directorate. 

The Armed Forces Council approved the Constitution on March 27, and General Thieu promulgated the document on April 1. It is now the law of the land, and represents the second major milestone on the road to representative government.

1967 MAIN PROVISIONS OF THE CONSTITUTION 

The form of government ordained in the Constitution is a modified presidential system. It calls for a popularly elected President and 

Vice President, a Prime Minister appointed by and responsible to the President, and a popularly elected bicameral legislature. Executive power is clearly vested in the President, but is tempered by a system of checks and balances.

Reflecting concern over possible recurrence of past abuses of executive powers, the National Assembly is empowered to exercise two principal checks upon the Executive. It can override a Presidential veto of a bill by an absolute majority of the total membership of both houses. It can also recommend Presidential removal of any or all Cabinet Ministers, including the Prime Minister, by two-thirds majority of total Assembly membership; if the President demurs, this recommendation is binding if subsequently readopted by a threequarters majority of the total membership.

Judicial power is vested in a supreme court, with inferior courts to be established by legislation. There are also special institutions, such as an inspectorate to investigate official behavior, a special court to try high officials, an armed forces council to present the military viewpoint to the President, and other advisory councils for ethnic minority, cultural, and economic affairs.

The Constitution makes extensive provision for civil rights and social welfare. These are guarantees of due process of law, including habeas corpus, counsel, public trial with presumption of innocence, and immunity from unlawful search, seizure, and self-incrimination. 

Other provisions bestow and protect the freedoms of religion, assembly, association, expression, and "overt, nonviolent" political activity, including political opposition within the democratic system. 

On the other hand, Communist propaganda and activities are prohibited. Among portions of the Constitution dealing with social welfare are statements adopting as public policy the promotion of free public education, full employment, trade union activity, social security, public welfare, land reform, and a sign of cultural innovationbasing marriage upon "mutual consent, equality, and cooperation." 

These are the governmental regulations that have been adopted prior to the elections scheduled for early this fall. 

GOVERNMENTAL ARRANGEMENTS UNTIL THE FALL ELECTIONS 

Elections for President and Vice President and for the upper house are scheduled for September 1. Elections for the lower house are planned for October 1. The Constitution provides for interim governing arrangements for the preelection period. Until the first President assumes office the present Directorate will function as the national executive. The Constituent Assembly will remain in existence to draft laws for the elections, the registration and activities of political parties, and press regulations.

In addition, the Constituent Assembly will supervise the conducting of elections and certify the winners. When the President assumes office, replacing the Directorate, the Constituent Assembly will acquire full legislative powers until installation of the newly elected 

National Assembly approximately 1 month later. (Discussion off the record.)

5 LO 

REVOLUTIONARY DEVELOPMENT 

Let me now turn to a brief discussion of the revolutionary development, or pacification, program. I would like to touch on the program as it relates to the political organization and development of rural Vietnam.

It is now almost a cliche to say that revolutionary development, or pacification, is the key program, behind the vital military shield, for resolving the conflict in Vietnam and that it has been the most frustrating and slow moving of all programs in Vietnam. These statements are true because the program deals essentially with the loyalties and commitments of men, and it is not an easy thing to turn people into supporters of the Government when they have been intimidated and terrorized by the Vietcong for years, and when they have hardly had a Government in the past which was able to protect them and enhance their well-being.

What is more, it is in this area that the Vietnamese themselves must take the lead and find solutions to the basic problems, though we can and do help with supplies and equipment and advice. Neither have the political turbulence and change which have marked much of the past 3 or 4 years in South Vietnam been conducive to the development or execution in orderly fashion of such a long-term program. 

Results to date have not been dramatic and the Vietcong infrastructure and the guerrilla war continue to present grave problems. 

There has, however, been encouraging progress in the past year and the groundwork has been laid for more significant and more rapid progress this year and in the future. 

I refer (1) to the continuous process of testing and improving the concept of how revolutionary development should work and the development of tests to measure what is being accomplished; (2) to the development of increasing numbers of trained and motivated revolutionary development teams; (3) to agreement on ways to coordinate plans and operations between the Regular Armed Forces, the paramilitary forces, the police forces, and the civilian workers; (4) to important decisions on the priority to be accorded revolutionary development in terms of money, supplies, and trained manpower, which has meant, for instance, that half of the maneuver battalions of the South Vietnamese Regular Army are being devoted to missions in support of revolutionary development; (5) to the encouraging political development on both the national and local scene; and (6) to progress in improving the economic and social lot of the people in the countryside through land reform, agricultural programs, health assistance, the building of schools, and the provision of textbooks, and the construction of wells, dams, roads, and bridges. 

All of these elements about which I am sure Mr. Poats will be speaking undoubtedly in more detail, are part of the revolutionary development program and the accomplishments of the past years should lay the groundwork for more dramatic progress in the future. 

The credit for these developments should go to the Vietnamese under the leadership of Lieutenant General Thang, the Minister of Revolutionary Development, but we have provided considerable support to the program. We have also taken important steps to reorganize our own efforts in support of revolutionary development.

1967 

We have unified the civilian elements of our mission in Saigon working on revolutionary development programs in an Office of Civil Operations with sole responsibility and direction over all American civilians working in the field. Our efforts and advice should therefore be more effective and more coordinated than in the past I might add parenthetically that one indicator, albeit a disturbing one, of the growing impact of the revolutionary development teams on the rural population is the growing number of Vietcong attacks against the revolutionary development teams. The number of such attacks in March surpassed the number of such attacks in the 2 previous months combined. 

MODERNIZATION OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT 

The targets of the revolutionary development program—the villages and hamlets of rural South Vietnam-contain the two lowest echelons of government. In the last decade the traditional autonomy of the villages and their component hamlets has been eroded by two factors: Vietcong politicomilitary activity and centralization of local government affairs by the Saigon authorities. 

Local elections have been suspended for some years because of insecure conditions, and centrally appointed officials came to exercise more and more direct authority at local levels. As the Vietnamese 

Government prepared plans for its current pacification effort, called "Revolutionary Development," officials became increasingly aware that revitalization of local self-government was indispensable in the task of winning the commitment of the population to the national cause. Thus organization of elections in hamlets and villages, with subsequent training in governmental techniques for those elected, became a significant portion of the field work performed by the new 

59-man revolutionary development teams.

Last October at the Manila Conference the Vietnamese Govern ment representatives declared that in recognition of the necessity to strengthen the democratic process at the local level, village and hamlet elections would be held in early 1967. A series of Government decrees issued in December completely revised the structure and functioning of local government. 

These decrees provide for popularly elected village councils, which will choose the village chief from among their membership, and for popularly elected hamlet chiefs, with elected deputy chiefs in hamlets having more than 3,000 residents. Moreover, village and hamlet officials will enjoy generally unrestricted exercise of a wide range of new powers. For example, only village budgets or programs in excess of 1 million piasters (about $8,500) need have prior approval by the 

Central Government. 

Elections for village councilors, who number between 6 and 12, depending on village size, have been set for the 5 Sundays this month, and they began on April 2. Hamlet elections will take place on the 

Sundays between May 14 and June 11, inclusive. Elections will be held in localities where security is adequate for the protection of candidates and voters, as well as for the officials themselves, once they have been elected.

Designation of localities to hold elections follows certain specified criteria of the revolutionary development program. Thus of approximately 2,500 villages in Vietnam, 1,004 will hold elections this spring.

7 About 205 more will probably hold elections in the summer, by which time these villages are expected to satisfy revolutionary development security criteria.

Of approximately 11,250 hamlets in Vietnam, 4,578 will hold elections this spring and about 1,500 are expected to do so later during the summer. As revolutionary development programs progress throughout the remainder of this year, more villages and hamlets will qualify for and hold elections. The proportion of the total population eligible to participate in these elections will be greater than the proportion of localities holding elections to the total number of localities because densely populated areas are generally under Government control, while contested areas and those under Vietcong control are often sparsely populated. 

New, representative leadership at the local level will emerge by these elections of approximately 13,000 local officials this spring and approximately 3,300 more during the summer. Furnishing adequate security to induce candidacies, prevent intimidation of voters and harassment of the polling by the Vietcong, and protect the new public officials will constitute a major drain upon Vietnamese resources throughout the year. The successful implementation of these local elections will constitute the third major milestone on the road to representative government in South Vietnam.

Let me summarize here our initial reporting on the elections Sunday, which were the first of the five scheduled weekly elections for village councilors. Elections were held in 219 villages with 615,000 registered voters. There were 2,718 candidates seeking 1,962 council positions; on the average, there were 12 candidates for nine positions at stake.

This relatively low ratio of candidates to positions reflects in part the depletion of resident local manpower by both Vietcong depredations and Government service requirements. Available returns from the 33 Provinces involved in this first stage indicate that 80.5 percent of the registered voters cast ballots. Vietcong antielection activity was reported relatively light despite reports of three candidates killed and 13 kidnapped by the Vietcong. Thus far the voter turnout seems to compare favorably to the high levels set in the September 11 

Constituent Assembly election. 

I would like to mention another program which is not on the record here because it is a program that is still in process of formulation although it has been publicly mentioned by the Vietnamese Government at Manila and was also discussed at the Guam meeting. This is the program that comes under the heading of national reconciliation. It is a program designed to create an atmosphere in which dissident Vietcong, Vietcong who are discouraged, whose morale is low, who have come to realize they are in a losing situation, can feel that they can come safely over to the Government side and will be accepted, will have a chance for work and will have their ordinary civil rights restored to them.

This is a program, as I say, which the Government has been in the process of formulating for some time. Some aspects of it in fact havbeen in operation already for a good time. That is what is called the 

Chieu Hoi program, the program of defectors and ralliers which I mentioned earlier. The present proposal is to put forward a wellintegrated, appealing, and effective kind of program which, hopefully,

1967 

со will reduce the number of military people which the Vietnamese and we and others are obliged to fight in South Vietnam and to lure people over, persuade them they have a chance to come over safely and join the Government side. Hopefully, this program will be announced in the next few weeks.

I have dwelt on these political developments at length because they hold major potential for the future, and because they have not really been covered comprehensively by the press. Let me hasten to add that I cannot confidently predict a smooth path ahead-the present accomplishments were not achieved without political stress and strain, and as personalities become engaged in competition for elective office, more rough terrain may well be encountered. 

What we are talking about is a transition to a new political power structure and balance foreshadowing an important shift away from political power vested totally in the military to a significant increase in civilian participation in the governing process and the power structure in essence, the creation of a military-civilian partnership in governing. This shift may not be accomplished smoothly, but when you consider how far toward representative government the Vietnamese have come since January 1966, the feat has indeed been remarkable.

Finally I would like to turn to the search for peace and discuss some U.S. actions in this field. The United States has vigorously and unremittingly pressed the search for honorable settlement, using both direct and indirect approaches, and official as well as unofficial channels. Basically, as President Johnson said in his Nashville speech 

March 15, "The road to peace could go from deeds to discussions, or it could start with discussions and move to deeds. We are ready to take either route or to move on both." 

The United States therefore- (1) Is ready at any time for discussions of the Vietnam problem or any related matter, with any government or governments, if there is any reason to believe it would advance the cause of peace. (2) Believes that the Geneva accords of 1954 and 1962 could serve as the central elements of a peaceful settlement. (3) Has stated it wants no bases in southeast Asia and does not wish to retain U.S. troops in Vietnam after peace is assured. (4) Has pledged at Manila, together with its allies, to withdraw its forces not later than 6 months after the other side withdraws its forces to the north, ceases its infiltration, and the level of violence thus subsides. (5) Has emphasized that we would much prefer to use our resources for the economic reconstruction of southeast Asia, including North Vietnam, rather than war, and that peace could permit North Vietnam to participate in a regional effort to which we would be prepared to contribute at least $1 billion. (6) Stands ready to advance toward a mutual reduction of hostilities, without prior agreement. We would take note of any deescalation on the ground and would respond accordingly. (7) Has three times, three major times, I might say, stopped the bombing of North Vietnam to discover whether there might be some constructive reaction from the other side-in May 1965 for 5 days, in December 1965 to January 1966 for 37 days, and in February 1967 for 5 days.

9 

What has been Hanoi's response? North Vietnam's leaders have consistently rebuffed our own initiatives and those of others and have rejected any terms for either talks or settlement other than their own. 

I call your attention to the press accounts on Sunday of captured documents showing both a cynical disregard for negotiations and the classic Communist tactic of using negotiations to achieve its political and military objectives.

There is an excerpt from documents which were found in the Junction City operation, including a speech given in April 1966 to the Fourth Congress of the Central Office of South Vietnam, that is the Vietcong's North Vietnam headquarters. It is a speech by 

General Vinh and it is of particular interest, and I will furnish copies for the record. It is illustrative of the Vietcong, and North Vietnamese attitude, on this general subject. 

I might read just one paragraph which has particular bearing on the question of cease-fire. This is General Vinh speaking, saying:

Depending on the situation prevailing at the time we will impose conditions. 

For example the puppet forces By which he means the South Vietnamese forcesmust be concentrated in barracks, must not repress the people, must not carry out espionage activities, must not herd the people into strategic hamlets and concentration centers, and the American troops must be stationed at the wharves. 

This is his recipe for a cease-fire and I think you can read for his reference to the people, you can read the organs of the Vietcong, their various military, paramilitary, and political organs. 

In other words, the cease-fire, in effect, hands the country over to those organs.

Before then, he had been a member of the Committee for Supervision of the South from 1954 to 1956. Fighting and Negotiating

The resolution of the Party's 11th conference clearly stated that in the process of achieving success, a situation where fighting and negotiations are conducted simultaneously may arise. At present, the situation is not yet ripe for negotiations. Fighting while negotiating is aimed at opening another front with a view to making the puppet army more disintegrated, stimulating and developing the enemy's internal contradictions, and, thereby, making him more isolated in order to deprive him of the propaganda weapons, isolate him further, and make a number of people who misunderstand the Americans clearly see their nature. 

In a war between a powerful country which wages aggression and a weak country, as long as we have not yet acquired adequate strength a situation where fighting and negotiations are conducted simultaneously does not exist. Fighting continues until the emergence of a situation where both sides are fighting indecisively. Then, a situation where fighting and negotiations are conducted simultaneously may emerge. In fighting while negotiating, the side which fights more

1967 

strongly will compell the adversary to accept its conditions. Considering the comparative balance of forces, the war proceeds through the following stages: 

The fighting stage. 

The stage of fighting while negotiating. 

Negotiations and signing of agreements.

Whether or not the war will resume after the conclusion of agreements depends upon the comparative balance of forces. If we are capable of dominating the adversary, the war will not break out again, and conversely. Therefore, fighting while negotiating also represents a principled step in the evolution of the war. 

Thus, a situation where fighting and negotiations are conducted simultaneously will unmistakably emerge. In our anti-French resistance, there were also times when fighting and negotiations were conducted simultaneously. The same situation had emerged in China.

At present, there are three viewpoints with regard to war and peace. 

The Americans find it necessary to negotiate, but negotiate from a strong position, partly because they have deceitful motives, and partly because the situation has compelled them to negotiate. Yet, they want us to make concessions to them.

A number of countries want us to enter into negotiations, any form of negotiations so that a big war does not break out and that the war can be endedregardless of the interests of Vietnam. Some other countries wonder whether we can defeat the Americans, and if not, we should enter into negotiations. (Most of these countries are nationalist countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.) A number of East European socialist countries hold the view that conditions do prevail, and are ripe for achieving success. (The Americans would withdraw their troops, and we will continue the struggle to achieve total success.) 

These socialist countries also posed a number of conditions: cessation of the bombing of the North; gradual withdrawal of U.S. troops from the South. 

China holds the view that conditions for negotiations are not yet ripe, not until a few years from now, and, even worse, seven years from now. In the meantime, we should continue fighting to bog down the enemy, and should wait until a number of socialist countries acquire adequate conditions for strengthening their main force troops to launch a strong, all-out, and rapid offensive, using all types of weapons and heeding no borders. What we should do in the South today is to try restrain the enemy and make him bogged down, waiting until China has built strong forces to launch an all-out offensive. 

Our policy: to continue fighting until a certain time when we can fight and negotiate at the same time.

This is also a fighting method: repulsing the enemy step by step, and achieving decisive success.

The Party Central Committee entrusts the Politburo with the task of deciding on the time for negotiations.

The problem of choosing the opportunity and deciding to negotiate: 

Basing ourselves upon the actual situation in the South. 

Considering the opinions of the friendly countries which have provided us with quite a large volume of assistance, in order to gain their maximum support. 

The future situation may lead to negotiations. Yet, even if there are negotiations, they are conducted simultaneously with fighting. While negotiating, we will continue fighting the enemy more vigorously. (It is possible that the North conducts negotiations while the South continues fighting, and that the South also participates in the negotiations while continuing to fight). Those who are in charge of conducting negotiations negotiate and those in charge of fighting continue fighting, because the decisive factor lies in the battlefield. The enemy wants us to stop fighting to his advantage. But we have to fight. Therefore, the enemy also fights. We must fight to win great victories with which to compel the enemy to accept our conditions. If we stop fighting (at that stage), no considerable success can be achieved in negotiations. If we conduct negotiations while fighting vigorously, we can also take advantage of the opportunity to step up the political struggle, military proselyting, and activities in the cities. Thus, we will take advantage of the opportunity offered by the negotiations to step up further our military attacks, political struggle, and military proselyting. At present, the Americans have put forth deceitful arguments. Therefore, we must put forth conditions to prove that we fight for the aspirations and interests of the people, and, thereby, to win the support of various countries. 

If the enemy wants to negotiate, he must accept a number of conditions, such as, to permanently cease their war of destruction against the North, withdraw

11 his troops from the South, and dismantle his military bases. The failure to pose the above conditions is tantamount to implicitly accepting the Americans' presence in the South.

Depending on the situation prevailing at the time, we will impose conditions. 

For example, the puppet forces must be concentrated in barracks, must not repress the people, must not carry out espionage activities, must allow the people to move about freely or choose their places of residence, must not herd the people into strategic hamlets and concentration centers; the American troops must be stationed at the wharfs.

The basic situation prevailing in the South for the past years requires that we attack the enemy more vigorously. This front involves millions of people. While attacking, we must concentrate all our forces on fighting the enemy. 

Mr. UNGER. In effect, Hanoi has: (1) Turned down or ignored our proposal for unconditional talks. (2) Rejected all overtures for mutual deescalation, including 

President Johnson's February 8 letter to Ho Chi Minh, proposing a halt in bombing the north and in troop buildup if Hanoi would give assurances that infiltration by land and sea had ceased. (3) Held to its four points as the basis for settlement-a condition which, under point 3, would be tantamount to guaranteeing Hanoi's instrument, the National Liberation Front, a dominant position in South Vietnam's political life. Such a demand is neither consistent with the Geneva accords nor with the right of self-determination. Hanoi has refused to consider reformulations of point 3 which would eliminate the reference to the NLF and would stress the right of the South Vietnamese people to settle their own affairs without outside interference. (4) Demanded that the United States recognize and deal with the NLF as the sole genuine representative of the South Vietnamese people-a condition which, again, is both contrary to the Geneva accords and unrealistic in the light of the widespread and growing repudiation of the front in the south. 

Here I might note that over 60 countries recognize the Government of South Vietnam, while no government recognizes the 

NLF as a government. (5) Sought to trade a permanent and unconditional bombing halt in return for not very precise offers of talks. As Secretary 

Rusk said on February 9, Hanoi "must not expect us to stop our military action by bombing while they continue their military action by invasion." (6) Used the 37-day pause of December 1965 to January 1966 and the 5-day Tet pause of February 1967 to move down men and supplies for new combat operations in South Vietnam, while rejecting any constructive response to our efforts to get talks started. 

What is Hanoi's position? Hanoi's action in making public the

Johnson-Ho exchange of letters remains difficult to explain, for in the non-Communist world reaction has generally favored the President's obviously sincere effort to move forward toward talks and deescalation, and has deplored the harsh and categorical tone of Ho's rejection of the offer. Although it is unfortunate that this exchange, as well as U Thant's recent initiative, have not been kept private, they illustrate the great multiplicity and variety of contacts which there have been, and the monotonous response of Hanoi running throughout. 77-470-67-pt. 1-2

1967 

I might comment here on this point. You are aware of many, many references to contacts that have been made, some of which have been clearly identified and described in full when they have been published; others of which have remained private, and our thought has been that they should remain so because only in private do we believe there is a chance to make progress in this kind of contact and discussion.

But the two sets of documents that have been made public I think are rather generally illustrative of the kind of proposals that have been put forward and the kind of response that has been received from Hanoi in almost every instance. Those instances where this has not been the kind of response, there simply has been no answer at all. 

Briefly, then, what is our outlook? Although the prospects for moving ahead toward a settlement appear bleak in light of Hanoi's actions and statements, we shall persevere in showing the other side that: (1) The cost of continuing aggression is prohibitively high; (2) Political stability and development of representative institutions in the south will continue and cannot be interrupted by threat or violence; and (3) We remain ready to use innumerable avenues of communication to negotiate an honorable settlement. We do not seek the unconditional surrender of North Vietnam; what we do seek is to assure for the people of South Vietnam the right to decide their own political destiny, free of force.

STATEMENT OF HON. RUTHERFORD M. POATS, ASSISTANT AD- MINISTRATOR FOR FAR EAST, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. POATS. Mr. Chairman, we appreciate this opportunity to report on current developments in our nonmilitary efforts to help the people of South Vietnam build a viable and secure nation. Mr. 

Unger has discussed the political aspects of this effort. I propose to summarize the current and proposed AID program and role in this unprecedented wartime effort to achieve rapid nation building and relieve human suffering.

Our economic assistance program in Vietnam is the largest, most intensive, most urgent, most operational in the history of AID. Its support is essential to the effective military defense of South Vietnam. 

But it is more than this, because all who know the problems in Vietnam know that military action alone cannot win the war or assure peace. 

It is, therefore, engaged with the government and people at all levels in constructive work to improve public services, expand the pace of achieving social justice, and relieve wartime dislocations. These efforts are at the heart of what President Johnson calls "the other war" in Vietnam.

The AID program can best be described if divided somewhat arbitrarily into four principal components or tasks. They are: (1) Maintaining economic stability, which includes financing of commercial imports (and the similar food for peace import program) and assisting the Vietnamese Government in improving

13 revenue collection and working out economic policies to cope with the wartime economic strains. (2) Revolutionary development, which comprises a complex of immediate impact measures to consolidate and expand popular support of and participation in government especially at the village and hamlet level. (3) Alleviating the economic and social consequences of military operations. These activities include relief and resettlement of wartime refugees, direct medical care of civilians, assistance to defectors from the Vietcong, and logistic operations required by the war situation. (4) Expanding the economy in secure areas and preparing now for long-term, social, and economic development. We are putting a greater proportion of our aid into long-term investments in already secure areas and where projects of a lasting developmental nature can be identified for immediate action.

STABILIZATION THE FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION 

We expect AID commercial import financing for economic stabilization to decline from $398 million in fiscal year 1966 to less than $285 million in fiscal year 1967, including fertilizer [security deletion]. 

This reduction has made possible increased AID project assistance in revolutionary development, medical and refugee care, and longer term development.

The threat of runaway inflation was blocked in the second half of 1966. Prices held relatively stable from the month after devaluation in June 1966 to early 1967. The Saigon cost-of-living index for working class families, which had risen 73 percent between June 1965 and

1967 

June 1966, leveled off after an initial 21-percent reaction to devaluation and rose only 4 percent between July and December. 

Prices of food and certain other goods recently pushed upward again, partly under pressure of the lunar new year buying season and partly due to a sharp increase in rice prices stimulated by false fears of shortages. This rice price push now has been checked and possibly reversed by increased imports. 

Our aid and joint policies have spared Vietnam the disastrous inflation which Korea suffered during its war. In the first year of the 

Korean conflict retail prices in Pusan rose by more than 7%½ times, and before the war was over prices were more than 24 times higher than in early 1950.

Imports rising rapidly in response to rising buying power have made this relatively great success in Vietnam possible. Their effectiveness as a tool of stabilization was increased by the sharp devaluation of the piaster and reforms in import procedures last summer.

Expanding imports, of both commercial goods and project aid, required radical expansion of the capacity of the Saigon port and several lesser ports. During November 1965, 196,000 short tons of cargo were discharged at Saigon. In July 1966, the monthly total was 

374,000 tons. In January 1967, 354,000 tons were discharged; by next November, we expect the discharge capacity will reach 630,000 tons. In order to achive this increase, the physical port facilities have been urgently expanded; U.S. military port units were assigned to both advisory and operational roles, and police, customs and other staffs were greatly increased. Congestion will remain a serious problem for the next several months, however, as the flood of military and civilian goods continues to grow. 

This surge of goods, economic and military supplies of all sorts, has brought with it enormous problems of management, distribution, and control. As in other war-disrupted economies in the past, thievery and corrupt diversion bave been serious problems. We estimated losses in Vietnam of AID-financed goods at an annual rate of 5 to 6 percent in the latter part of 1966. We believe these losses are being reduced now by measures taken as rapidly as staff could be put on the job to execute them. Some of these control measures are: 

Placing the U.S. Army's 4th Terminal Command in operational control of handling almost all AID project commodities from discharge at the ship to the appropriate Vietnamese Government warehouse in the Saigon area;

Assignment of the U.S. Army's 125th Terminal Company as an advisory unit with the Vietnamese port director and his staff; 

Increasing the U.S. AID mission's American audit staff from 

17 to 34 resulting in a much larger current audit program than previously;

The development of an automated arrival accounting system for AID-financed commercial imports, designed to follow imports from the license application to the delivery of commodities to the importer; 

Stationing of a U.S. Bureau of Customs advisory team-now 

17 men-in Saigon port to assist the Vietnamese Customs Office in improving its procedures while spot-checking 10 to 20 percent of all AID-financed commercial imports;

15 The recent decision to prepare and help install uniform documentation systems in Vietnamese Government agencies and to assign U.S. logistics advisers in provincial and regional warehouses as soon as possible. U.S. AID controllers, now stationed in all regions, will use the new commodity control documents as a basis for their surveys of the commodity flow from the ports through the provincial warehouses to the project sites.

REVOLUTIONARY DEVELOPMENT 

The revolutionary development program in its narrow sense is the successor to a series of hamlet pacification programs, each of which had its accomplishments and its lessons, but all of which failed in their overall goal of establishing bridges of understanding and commitment between the rural population and the Government. The new program attempts to deal honestly with the errors and omissions of the past. It recognizes that commitment and development cannot take place without the assurance of sustained physical security. It knows that the Vietnamese civilian teams which are now working in the villages cannot establish meaningful local security and self-government, promote social and economic development without extensive training, without the proper attitudes and without remaining among the village people for many months. It recognizes the need for funds and for dynamic leadership and for the full support of the Central Government. Revolutionary development has all of these advantages over its predecessors. Still, its progress has been slow. 

Progress is, however, being made, and it should accelerate steadily this year, as more Vietnamese, United States, and Korean manpower is focused on this crucial process of hamlet by hamlet recovery of the countryside and as our military operations deny the guerrillas support from main force Communist units. There are now 30,000 trained revolutionary development workers, most of whom are working in teams assigned to hamlets designated in joint military-civil pacification/revolutionary development plans. In 1966, a net of 444 hamlets and nearly 1 million people were secured and given renewed Government services. In 1967, plans which now appear conservative call for securing or consolidating about 1,100 hamlets. This process seems likely to gain momentum as elected government comes to hamlets and villages this spring and to the nation as a whole this fall. By the end of 1967, there will be 50,000 such R. & D. workers in over 

800 teams, capable of carrying out the revolutionary development program in some 2,000 hamlets over a year's time. 

Social and economic development are key elements of this truly revolutionary development. În 1966 alone over 5,700 "self-help" projects had been constructed by the people of those villages and hamlets with the assistance of revolutionary development workers, local Vietnamese officials or AID provincial and technical representatives.

About 3,600 of these projects received AID/Government of Vietnam commodity or other funding support-over 2,000 were built or financed by the people without funding or material assistance. Examples of these projects are schools, markets, village wells, clinics, roads and bridges. Nearly 2,000 self-help hamlet classrooms were built during 1966, using AID supplies-in many cases bringing the

1967 

beginnings of education to the hamlet for the first time; another 2,100 were built by the Government. Over 3,000 elementary teachers were trained and assigned to hamlet schools. Since 1965, some 9 million elementary school textbooks have been produced and distributed with AID assistance. Large quantities of improved seeds, demonstration fertilizer, fish fingerlings, pesticides, and other supplies were distributed. Three major rural electric cooperatives are being built and some 

60 villages and hamlets are getting their own diesel generators. Small irrigation works were built or expanded, town water supply systems built, land titles issued, farmers' and fishermen's associations or cooperatives organized or assisted, 300 rural health workers are being trained to man dispensaries in the villages. 

Land reform, including sale of Government-owned land to tillers, protection of tenants against high rents and uncertainty of tenure, and prohibition of landlord collection of back rents following restoration of Government control, is an important part of the revolutionary development concept. The Prime Minister and his Ministers for Revolutionary Development and Agriculture support land reform and have made several constructive moves to accelerate its tempo. 

Neither they nor we are satisfied with the pace and impact of the program. 

The first requirement is to execute more vigorously the reasonably good existing land reform laws and decrees. [Security deletion.J 

In judging what should and can be done, we must deal with these realities: Practically all of the nearly 1 million acres of arable land owned by the Government under earlier land-acquisition programs and not yet resold is occupied by farm families; some pay rent to local governments on this land, some squat on it without rent or taxes. The delta, where most of the good Government-owned land is located or where more radical land-expropriation and resale measures would have their greatest impact, is widely infested by armed guerrillas. Government land reform technicians cannot get to much of it safely. The professional staff of the Government's land administration agency is very small. Prior to the coming village council elections, there has been no legally constituted village body in much of the country to which to delegate land administration. The political importance of the landowner is not limited to Saigon absentee landlords; in the villages, resident landlords often represent essential leadership talents needed to pull together stronger local administration.

Despite these limitations, more can and must be done. A research firm employed by AID is working with the Vietnamese in gathering better detailed information. A pilot project in accelerated execution of land reform, including aerial mapping and special credit facilities, is being conducted with our help in a secure delta Province, An Giang. 

The revolutionary development worker teams are being trained to tell the villagers their rights under land reform laws and decrees and report violations of these rights. The Vietnamese Government is now rapidly issuing 100,000 formal titles confirming ownership of land sold earlier to villagers. Expansion of the staff of the land administration agency and delegation of functions to local governments is being considered. We hope this process will be accelerated by the coming elections.

17 Our public safety program equips, helps train, and advises the expanding civil police forces. Security of the villages, like the cities today, will gradually become the responsibility of civil police, whose strength has been increased from 33,500 at the end of 1964 to over 63,000 on January 31, 1967. By December of this year, we expect a police force strength at over 73,000.

The AID public safety program provides advisory services and equipment for the Vietnamese National Police, including the new police field forces. One important police function is the "resources control" effort to reduce Vietcong access to critical goods. As of 

February 1, 1967, almost 700 checkpoints were being manned by police throughout the country. Since late 1964, this resources control program has resulted in the arrest of 15,000 known or suspected Vietcong, and in the confiscation of more than 8,500 tons of food, medicine, firearms, and other equipment and supplies. The family census program, designed to detect and prevent the infiltration and movement of Vietcong, has registered almost 1,700,000 families and issued nearly 7,400,000 national identity cards. AID funding of these public safety projects in fiscal year 1967 will approximate $30.4 million. It will be more in fiscal year 1968. [Security deletion.] 

The great bulk of AID's technical assistance activities in such fields as agriculture, education, and public administration is included in this program component we classify as revolutionary development. 

Funding for support of projects in this sector will rise from $88 million in fiscal year 1967 to over $100 million in fiscal year 1968. 

WAR RELIEF AND SUPPORT 

Hostilities in a war of this kind bear very heavily on the civilian population. We are doing what we can as rapidly as we can to alleviate the inevitable suffering.

During the past 2 years, U.S. aid to the Vietnamese civilian health program has increased from $5 million annually to nearly $50 million. 

Most of the supplies and equipment of provincial hospitals and local clinics and aid stations have been provided by AID. Ministry of 

Health/AID medical supply operations are overcoming very difficult logistic management problems, though spot shortages still occur. 

About 1,200 free world medical specialists are operating throughout Vietnam, including 25 provincial teams from the United States and 

18 from other countries: Korea, China (Taiwan), the Philippines,

New Zealand, Great Britain, Australia, Spain, Iran, and Switzerland. 

These specialists are organized into teams of 14 to 16 membersdoctors, nurses, and laboratory technicians-working in provincial hospitals, supplied and equipped by AID and the Vietnamese Government. They are supplemented continuously by 32 individual volunteer American physicians serving 60-day tours in Vietnam under

American Medical Association-AID auspices. More than 150,000 patients per month are currently being treated in hospitals and clinics by these 43 medical teams.

With the help of Dr. Howard Rusk and AID financial assistance, the Vietnamese National Rehabilitation Center is now fitting prosthetic devices at the rate of 500 per month. Priority is given to war casualties, of whom many are victims of Vietcong terror tactics.

1967 

The amputees, once they are mobile again, are returned to their homes by planes accompanied by Americans who volunteer their services. 

Both the direct medical care and the general health programs will be expanded in fiscal year 1968. The Defense Department and AID 

now are urgently considering means of further improving medical care of civilian war casualties. 

One of the most promising war-related programs is the "Chieu Hoi" or "open arms" program of inviting Vietcong to accept amnesty and rally to the Government's support. This is a distinctly Vietnamese effort in which AID and USIA assistance is small but growing. 

Increasing defection by Vietcong troops and civil cadre brings nearer the end of the Communist insurgency and reveals convincingly the disillusionment eating away at VČ morale. In 1966 there were over 

20,000 defections; almost double the number in the preceding year. year. Starting in the last week of February 1967 and continuing through the first 3 weeks of March, the latest reporting period, there were over 1,000 defections each week, bringing the total for 

1967, as of March 18, to over 8,500.

Refugee movements away from Vietcong-dominated villages continue at a pace faster than resettlement. By March 1, 874,000 refugees were in camps or other recognized shelters and 915,000 had been resettled or returned to their villages. AID and the voluntary charitable agencies provide food, clothing, housing materials, school materials and equipment, skills training, and agricultural help. 

Funding for war-support and relief activities will amount to $64 million in fiscal year 1967, [security deletion] with a further increase in fiscal year 1968, with major expansion in direct medical assistance, Chieu Hoi support, and refugee relief and resettlement. 

Long-range development is the sector where AID has traditionally sought to concentrate its efforts in other countries. We are starting to shift more emphasis to lasting investment in Vietnam as the course of the war permits. This policy reflects the United States confidence in the outcome of the war and interest in speeding South Vietnam's achievement of postwar self-support. The Vietnamese Government also is setting aside funds to finance postwar development. 

Though an AID-financed contract with David Lilianthal's Develop ment & Resources Corp., a joint Vietnamese-United States longrange development planning effort has been instituted in an attempt to foresee and be prepared to cope with economic and social development problems when political and military efforts bring hostilities to an end.

In addition to this careful and complex planning for the future, AID is now engaged in insitution building and resource development projects in many fields which will be expanded in fiscal year 1968. 

These include institutional and system development activities in education, agriculture, health, labor, public works, and the business of government itself from the hamlet to the Prime Minister's office. 

We and the Vietnamese Government have agreed on an initial list of development projects which should go ahead this year if found feasible. These include expansion of power generation and distribution and other urban development projects for Saigon, industrial projects, housing and warehouse programs, inland waterway improvements, quarry development, and road reconstruction.

19 Funding for long-term development was earlier estimated at $32.7 million in fiscal year 1967; it now is likely to be considerably larger in both fiscal year 1967 and fiscal year 1968. This will be made possible by further reduction in the financing of commercial imports. 

[Security deletion.] MANAGEMENT AND STAFFING 

The means of directing and managing this most urgent and most extensive of AID programs has itself undergone important changes in the past year.

The Office of Civil Operations (OCO) was established in December 1966 for the purpose of integrating all U.S. civilian programs and people working in the rural areas of Vietnam. 

OCO is not a separate civil agency. Rather, it combines under single management the field elements of the existing civil assistance programs of AID, CIA, and USIA. Its personnel are drawn from these agencies, the U.S. Embassy and the U.S. military forces. Under 

OCO, a single U.S. senior civilian is responsible for all civilian operations in each province and region. This is providing streamlined command and communications channels, a common program philosophy and direction and a single point of coordination with the Vietnamese Government and the U.S. military. Technical, logistic and personnel support, program review and accountability for AID funds and staff remain with the AID mission director. 

The management of the program in Washington has also been changed and we are now in the process of establishing a Bureau of Vietnam Affairs which will combine into one organizational unit almost all of the AID functions concerned with the Vietnam program. 

We expect the benefits of this reorganization to be reflected in better management and increased efficiency. 

Personnel. The staff of the AID mission, including the OCO elements, has been rapidly expanded during the last year to meet the demands of the enlarged project program and to better manage AID supplies. It will continue to expand through fiscal years 1967 and 

1968. On January 1, 1966, we had, by normal AID standards, a huge staff: 630 direct-hire AID employees in Vietnam, 59 from other U.S.

Government agencies, and 134 employees under contracts with private American institutions-a total of 823 American employees. In addition, there were 1,330 Vietnamese and 248 nationals of other countries on our payroll.

On January 31 of this year, the direct-hire figure had reached 

1,295, participating personnel from other U.S. agencies stood at 89, and U.S. contract personnel numbered 283-a total of 1,667 Americans onboard in Vietnam, plus over 2,000 Vietnamese and 623 nationals of other countries. We expect to have over 1,600 direct-hire employees in Vietnam by June 30, 1967, and over 2,000 by June 20, 1968, with further large increases in personnel from other U.S. agencies and Asian countries. Some of the major components of these figures are agriculture, where we had 80 early this year and expect to have over 200 by June; field operations, which should reach 400 by this June and 500 by June 1968; and public health, which should rise from about 200 now to about 400 by June 1968. 

In order to meet these extraordinary requirements, AID launched an intensive recruitment program in October 1965. So far, we have

1967 

conducted 23 major and 65 lesser campaigns in metropolitan areas throughout this country. Over 80,000 inquiries have been received, about 12,000 promising applicants screened, and over 1,200 new employees hired since the beginning of the program. Many of these are now serving in Vietnam; others are in training or on their way to replace our veterans or to fill new positions. 

We recruit personnel who are already professionally qualified in their technical areas, but we must provide both long-term training in the Vietnamese language, specialized training in selected areas, and short-term orientation and adaptive training for Vietnamese conditions. At present, a total of 173 employees is undergoing long-term training, most of them in the fields of health, agriculture, and area development. During fiscal year 1968, we expect to train 272 additional personnel, plus about 500 in short courses. Our area development, public administration, and education training is concentrated at the University of Hawaii; agriculture in Florida; and health in a variety of U.S. hospitals and universities. We are starting a new language and area training program in support of the Office of Civil Operations this month at the Foreign Service Institute in Washington. 

This program will train an additional 400 long- and short-termers during the year.

A special note should be made of our fruitful and expanding relationships with other U.S. Government agencies. Their help has been indispensable to the AID program. These include the Department of Defense, the Department of Agriculture, the U.S. Public Health 

Service, the Bureau of the Census, the Bureau of Customs, the Federal 

Aviation Agency, the Internal Revenue Service, and others. Under the recently negotiated agreement with the Department of Agriculture, that agency is to furnish 97 specialists in irrigation, agronomy, credit and cooperatives, foresty, agricultural economics, extension services, and other areas. There are 57 employees now serving in Vietnam or in preparatory training under this agreement. 

In closing, I would like to reemphasize the interdependence of our military and civil efforts in Vietnam. Our progress in achieving the goals of the "other war" depends on the course of the "shooting" war, for we and the Vietnamese can only work for the present and build for the future where there is physical security. But in another sense, the course of the shooting war is dependent on the success of the "other war," for only if we and the Vietnamese succeed in our civil work for today and tomorrow can there be a nation that will reject Vietcong rule, fight for its life; and win a real chance at freedom.

If I may ask, Mr. Chairman, one or two questions of Mr. Poats. 

The keystone of our program in Vietnam is pacification. You have given a very glowing report. What progress has there been in surveying and plotting the land holdings, confirming titles, and transferring ownership? The last time I was there there had been a determination to go forward, but not one thing had been accomplished to make this a reality. How much has been accomplished? How much of the public-owned land is plotted?

Mr. POATS. Under the Diem government the major landowners were reduced to a holding of 250 acres, plus a small amount for burial grounds, and so forth; 2.6 million acres of land were expropriated.

About 1.6 million areas of this is occupied by 260,000 farm families and about another million acres of it is classed as abandoned or nonarable. The 260,000 occupants have received or will receive title to their land. Between 1956 and 1960, 116,000 received provincial titles to 615,000 acres. The remainder are farming Government land under a variety of arrangements under policies adopted in 1964 and 1965. They will receive titles as conditions permit. 

I mentioned that the Vietnamese Chief of State has been involved in confirming titles to those buyers who had conditional titles in the past. The major problem, as I said, is to execute this reasonably good start at a land reform. No one is saying that this is the ideal program or there shouldn't ultimately be further distribution of land. We are saying the first job is to execute the existing program. It includes, in addition to providing titles to people who have already bought the land, the sale of Government-held lands in secure areas as soon as the professional people can get there and make the calculation of exact metes and bounds of the property and can arrange the transfer of title and set up the schedule for 12-year repayment. This is going very slowly, partly because of the insecurity of the areas in which most of this land is located, partly because of the difficulty of ousting squatters from this land who are farming it without paying any rent at all, and partly for the reason that there is a very limited staff of professional people in the land administration agency to carry out the program. 

One of the criteria that General Thang has in his hamlet program is the undertaking and execution of existing land reform. The evolutionary development teams include persons trained to some extent in the execution of land reform, primarily to bring the word on what are the rights of the people and bring back to the authorities what is being done. Beyond that, you have in the new village council scheme an

1967 

administrative committee, one of whose members is a land administration agent who is responsible for executing land reform in each village. In the villages of central Vietnam a change has been made from the system of auction rental of land to the highest bidder to one of fixed rents based on preference criteria: Preference for a war veteran's family, for a war veteran, and so on. 

This program is being executed now in most villages; I don't know how thoroughly or how effectively. A number of steps are on the way. 

As I mentioned, we are carrying out a pilot program in An Giang Province to show how the job can be done properly and most efficiently with modern methods in an area of security. We are experimenting with this program in order to provide a pattern for doing it throughout the country wherever security exists.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Ambassador Unger, you mentioned several times in your statement that the revolutionary development program is the key to resolving the conflict in Vietnam. Then you went on to describe presumably significant developments in the area of local elections, village and hamlet elections. I wonder why you consider these elections so significant if as a practical matter there are barely enough candidates to fill the jobs. Why does this give anybody a great sense of participation and commitment that he wouldn't have if his leaders were chosen by other methods? 

Mr. UNGER. In the first place, I think the two things go together. 

Local government that is increasingly freely chosen and elected. I think that goes closely together with the revolutionary development program. The basic objective of the revolutionary development program is to bring the people and their government closer together to 

---

1967 

give the people a reason to believe that this is a government that is acting in their interest and deserves their support. 

One of the reasons of course that could be a persuader in such a process is that the villagers feel that they have now more of a voice in their local affairs than they have had. The paucity of candidates, even though there are more than you might have expected given the situation of the countryside, is something that I think is a transitory factor. I think as these elections proceed in succeeding years there will be more candidates and a fuller development of the democratic process.

I think even today the fact that people who have not had any such governmental institutions will now have them and they will be selecting them themselves, I think this is a considerable forward step. The village is quite a traditional factor in Vietnam's life and when the village council came to an end, I have always understood this was quite a backward step as far as the villagers were concerned in their attitude about the Government. 

Therefore it has been felt important to get the institutions back into operation.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I assume by what you say on page 11 of your statement that centrally appointed officials exercising more and more direct authority at local levels is an adverse development. Why is this so, since the revolutionary development program is an attempt to bring local government closer to the Central Government? There is confusion in my own mind as to what the aim is. Are we trying to develop that sense of nationhood that we heard about 4 or 5 years ago under the strategic hamlet program, a sense of the importance of central direction? Or do we want to encourage a sense of the importance of the local government as opposed to the Central Government?

Mr. UNGER. Sir, I would say we are trying to do both. We are certainly trying to build the sense of nationhood. But I think the analogy let's say in our own country is clear. We feel certain things are for local decision, that some things will mean more if decided by the people locally. Other things must be done on a broader scale. 

In Vietnam that would be in the district and in Saigon. Obviously the resources that are available to the Central Government are greater. 

On certain matters that have been traditionally the decision of the village and hamlet, we feel there is more, let's say more vitality there if these people are making their own decisions at that level. We don't feel these are things that interfere with the nation-building process.

I think they support and strengthen it. I think it is more a matter of division among the various fields. The presence of the Government in many of the forms that is present in the village is intended to help, to help with education, to help with agriculture, even to help with the development of local administration. But at least as another factor in local government, the Vietnamese feel there should be these local elected bodies as well, and elected officials. 

Mr. Burleson.

Mr. BURLESON.  

From your replies, Mr. Ambassador, I take it you are rather optimistic about the ability of the South Vietnamese people through

29 democratic processes to eventually govern themselves. However, I note in your statement you said there were rough roads ahead in dealing with the elective process. As I get it you are rather optimistic in their ability to govern themselves, though they have never had experience? 

Mr. UNGER. You are correct. I think the record of action over the last year supports the idea (a) that they wish it because the people as a whole have supported the steps that have been taken I think rather remarkably, and (b) that the Government has the capacity to organize this kind of a move toward constitutional and representative government.

The only thing I would say is that I think it would be a mistake to expect the kind of government that they develop to be like oursand now I am not speaking so much of the words that are used in the Constitution as the real institutions and the way they work. This is something that they are going to have to figure out for themselves. 

This is going to be something that will be peculiarly Vietnamese and will not be like our system, and maybe not like anybody else's system.

What they have done is at least pledge themselves to some of the fundamentals of a representative government and a government under a constitution and a government that does in fact rule for the benefit of its people. Beyond that when it comes to the question of just how the President will relate to the Prime Minister, and both of them to the legislature and so on, I think we can only guess. The statistics on that, on the success of that program, are rather startling. The numbers of people who did return under this program run roughly like this: In 1964, 5,000; 1965, 11,000; 1966 it rose to 

20,000. This was the year in which the facilities and the organization of the program were considerably improved and in which the Vietnamese Government had taken a much more active interest in it to promote this whole effort. 

The peak month earlier had been 2,200 that had returned in February of 1966. Since about October of 1966 this number of returnees has been climbing very steadily. So that it rose to 2,500 at the close of the year, rose to 3,000 in February and while we do not yet have complete March statistics, we believe it will be 4,500 or perhaps 5,000. It has risen so that it is going on a weekly basis now of well over a thousand whereas, as I noted, in 1964 the entire program for the entire year brought in only 5,000.

This is that kind of a program to try to reduce the military problem that we face, to try to reduce the number of Vietcong that are going to be facing Americans fighting in Vietnam by bringing these people over by various kinds of persuasion. 

I think it can be demonstrated that this is working well. We would like it to work a lot better. We and the Vietnamese Government are working closely to keep improving this process.

 POSSIBLE DUPLICATION OF RESEARCH EFFORTS 

Research funded by AID falls into two general categories: (1) research applicable to several countries and financed from funds available under Section 241 of the Foreign Assistance Act, and (2) research carried out specifically for a single country, the greater part of which is financed from country program funds. 

All central research activities are checked for possible duplication with research activities underway, completed or planned by the AID regional bureaus for a region or for specific countries. Proposed projects are also checked with other 

AID offices and with other government and non-government entities. Checks for duplication are specifically made by the Department of State's External Research Staff of the Bureau of Intelligence and Research. 

In addition, since 1962, AID has had an externally constituted committee known as the Research Advisory Committee (RAC) composed of 17 eminent scientists appointed by the Administrator. This committee meets four or five times a year to review all research proposals, and advise on possible duplication and on the quality of the proposed research. 

Before reaching RAC, each project is subjected to an internal checking process for possible duplication, relevance to AID's specific problems and the soundness of the design. This review is carried out by either the Technical Assistance and 

Research Council (TARC), established by the administration in 1963, or the 

Economic Research Advisory Committee (ERAC). 

For Vietnam specifically, research is now being carried on by the Development and Resources Corporation to develop the basis for an overall, unified development plan. A small Office of Research and Evaluation has been established to to collate existing research material and assist the Mission to establish a much needed research and reference library. A working agreement with ARPA (Advanced Research Projects Administration) has been arranged which will assure the coordination of AID and ARPA research activities in the field. clearinghouse activity to insure full knowledge of research being planned or carried out under all auspices will be established. To prevent duplication with the Department of Defense in engineering planning or feasibility studies, our engineers are in almost daily contact with the Army Corps of Engineers and the Navy Facilities Engineering Command. They are also in touch regularly with the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for

1967 

Installations and Logistics which coordinates engineering and construction activities for the three services. Our engineers do not themselves know of any duplication of research or feasibility study activities nor do the above mentioned engineering offices of the military services. There are, however, many instances of fruitful coordination and sharing of information and conclusions between these various offices. There is, for example, the excellent use made by the army engineers of the more than a dozen port studies made about a year ago under the AID contract with Daniel, Mann, Johnson, Mendenhall, in developing plans for port expansion for military purposes.

(The information follows:) DETAILS ON PROPOSED NATURE OF THE BICAMERAL LEGISLATURE UNDER THE NEW VIETNAMESE CONSTITUTION 

The bicameral legislature provided for in the new Vietnamese Constitution is to consist of a Lower House of between 100 and 200 members and an Upper House of 30 to 60 members. Members of the Lower House will be elected from separate constituencies no larger than a province and must be at least 25 years of age. Candidates for the Upper House must be 30 years of age or older and will be elected at large, by list voting, with each list including from one-third to onesixth of the total membership of the Upper House. Lower House members are to serve four year terms and Upper House members six year terms. Re-election for both is possible. Members of the National Assembly, as the two Houses will be called, will enjoy traditional rights and immunities with regard to arrest and prosecution.

Among the powers of the Assembly included in the Constitution are: vote legislation; ratify treaties and international agreements; determine declarations of war and holding of peace talks; and controlling the Government in the carrying

35 out of national policy. By a two-thirds majority of both Houses the Assembly can recommend the dismissal of any member of the Cabinet, and by a three-fourths vote can make such a recommendation binding on the President. The Assembly can also request a member of the Executive Branch to appear before it to answer questions regarding the execution of Government policy. By a combined majority vote it can override a presidential veto of legislation. In the legislative process, the Lower House can override an Upper House position on legislation which it has submitted to the Upper House only by a two-thirds majority vote. Two regular annual sessions of ninety days each are prescribed for each House, starting in April and October. Extraordinary sessions may also be convened. 

The Chairman of the Upper House is designated as next in line for succession to the Presidency following the Vice President. The Upper House is to exercise the right of confirmation of Presidential appointments of Chiefs of Diplomatic Missions and Rectors of Universities. The National Assembly as a whole must ratify or reject presidential decrees declaring states of emergency or curfew. 

Together with the President, the Assembly plays a role in the appointment of Supreme Court justices. The Assembly also plays a major role in impeachment proceedings against high Government officials, including the President, Vice President, and Prime Minister. The Assembly is to choose one-third the membership of the independent Inspectorate. Finally, a two-thirds majority of the 

Assembly must be obtained for constitutional amendments.
