Mr. DERWINSKI. I have two brief questions. You made reference, sir, to the corruption in the docks in Saigon which we know to have been quite a problem. What is the basic root of this corruption? 

Is it anything organized and tangible, or is it just the philosophy and the moral attitude of the public? 

Mr. POATS. I think the problem consists first of plain theft by needy people. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. In other words, unorganized?

Mr. POATS. Unorganized in any large sense. There may be small bands involved. Secondly, theft organized for the purpose of evading payment of customs duties, in which goods are stolen at the behest of the owner of the goods as a means of smuggling. Third, corruption in the sense of understating the value of goods and distorting documents to escape full payment of customs duties. And fourth, a willingness on the part of some stevedoring organizations to accept or demand bonus payments for movement of goods. 

These sound like a catalog of complete rottenness, but in fact the volume of these items, these particular forms of sins are, as I said, declining and they will decline to the degree that there is no economic incentive in it and the risk cost of doing it is too high. One of the causes of theft in the port has been the excessive accumulation of goods in the port where control of the commodities is difficult. Also, there are all sorts of new barge owners operating in the area. 

Another factor has been the sudden economic distress of the importer who placed his orders at a time when the piaster was valued at 60 to the dollar. Later, he was hit with a devaluation which was made retroactive on orders already placed. He suddenly had to cough up twice that amount of piasters, plus his customs duties and so on. 

This has made it difficult for him to finance the movement of these goods into the marketplace and he has therefore left more goods in the port area, and particularly in the barges, than is healthy. In some U.S. ports in order to deal with the problem of theft, very elaborate modern systems have been arranged to keep goods out of any open storage and out of the reach of anyone except a handful of port employees. This is impossible in a port such as we have in Saigon.

37 We think it is improving. We don't think there is any national attitude that can't be altered by changing the economic circumstances and by improving enforcement. The police have been greatly expanded to give that enforcement. The Prime Minister seems to have the right approach to it. The problem is one of administration. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. One last question. You mentioned the attempt to increase the use of fertilizer. Is there any basic objection that the 

Vietnamese farmer has to using commercial fertilizer? Have you run into any local taboos- Mr. POATS. No, it is quickly accepted as a sound investment by the 

Vietnamese farmer. A great increase in demand has resulted from this, particularly in vegetable farming. The resistance in rice farming stems largely from the lower paddy price for the rice that existed in the past than existed in some other fields such as vegetable or melon raising.

The present fertilizer program provides for about $42.5 million of fertilizer procurement by AID, of which $2.5 million is for demonstration projects in local gift programs, to stimulate the interest in fertilizer and its use, and about $40 million for sale through the Agricultural Development Bank to co-ops, farmers unions, and private distributors, at a fixed price through the rest of this planting year. 

That program will be at the level of about 330,000 tons, which is about one-third higher, I believe, than last year. We are quite confident there is demand for that greatly expanded program.

If we are going to succeed in pacification programs in South Vietnam, we need some people on the order of the Peace Corps of various ages and practical competences who have operated successfully in our cities or small towns. This will permit operations at the level of the people, as such applicants over the years in the United States have given people service in towns and villages, and have community action know-how.

I have therefore, through the years, I would say to the gentleman from Illinois, objected to the policy of AID recruitment with emphasis on these high-level, highly educated people, with high urban background that are then sent out to do this pacification work. 

Mr. O'HARA. One of the pleasures of serving on this committee is being in the company of my good and wise friend from Pennsylvania. 

Mr. FULTON. I certainly appreciate the friendship.

In the statement there is comment on the South Vietnam manpower being depleted and therefore few candidates for election to local offices. 

Don't the women vote in South Vietnam and run for office too? 

Mr. UNGER. Yes, sir; they certainly do.

Mr. FULTON. I think we should broaden the word "manpower" to "womanpower" too. I have a friend of mine, a private U.S. citizen, who has just made a trip around the world for 90 days, and she happens to be a woman. She can go to Vietnam. Why can't the wives of these U.S. officials now go to Vietnam? They could help too. Why don't we use the wives of our U.S. personnel in our South 

Vietnam programs? Would you please put a statement on such possibility in the record?

41 

WHY CAN'T THE WIVES OF U.S. Government EmplOYEES BE SENT TO VIETNAM TO HELP? 

The dependents of U.S. officials, both military and civilian, were evacuated from Vietnam in February 1965 after Vietcong attacks on U.S. installations and the United States began bombing North Vietnam. As the President said at the time, women and children don't belong in a war zone. The dependents of all U.S. officials and employees of direct contractors of the U.S. Government have since then been excluded from Vietnam, except for visits from time to time of the wives of the most senior U.S. officials and for visits by wives on special occasions such as Christmas, when because of truces the danger to them is lessened. 

The chief reason for keeping dependents out of Vietnam is obviously the question of their safety. Terrorist incidents occur daily throughout the countryin Saigon, in other cities, and in the countryside. Much of this terror is indiscriminate and much of it is purposely aimed at civilians and particularly Americans. 

We do not believe we should expose American women and children to unnecessary dangers. Other reasons for excluding them from Vietnam include the shortage of housing and the inflationary impact of additional spending on the Vietnamese economy.

The United States is able to direct its officials and direct-hire contractors not to bring their wives to Vietnam. While it is not able to prevent private U.S. citizens from traveling to Vietnam, we do caution those we know are planning to go there about the dangers they may encounter.

We recognize the morale and other problems caused by the exclusion of dependents from Vietnam and the separation of families. We are also very much aware of the important contribution wives can make toward the accomplishment of our goals in Vietnam. Our policy on wives in Vietnam is reviewed regularly in the light of the current security situation and other factors bearing on that policy. When it becomes possible to modify the policy we will do so. We hope this time will come soon; meanwhile we are taking all possible steps to reduce the hardships which the present policy inevitably entails. 

Mr. FULTON. One other question.

I believe the time has come on policy when we should make a distinction between guerrilla warfare against military personnel, and crimes such as assassination and kidnaping and injuring of people who are in villages either in a capacity as civil administrators, civil officials, or just plain ordinary villagers. That to me is a crime and should no longer be treated as warfare where we declare certain areas as now South Vietnam Government held and pacified. Such areas should no longer be open to this kind of guerrilla warfare. 

I believe that the United States and South Vietnam, with our allies, need a series of policy declarations that when there is an area pacified, the South Vietnamese local government set up, then any attacks against that government are dealt with as crimes within the Government of South Vietnam, not as part of guerrilla warfare. 

These areas are entitled to as much protection and safe passage as the citizens of Hanoi.

Until this action is taken and law enforced, including the trial and execution of murderers of unarmed officials, villagers, women, and children, as South Vietnam did in the case of the profiteer, we will have the war going on in every one of these little villages. Why does our policy not need this change?

I have one particular complaint, and that is the South Vietnamese Government is not enforcing its own draft laws. If they enforced the South Vietnamese draft laws there would be less able-bodied young South Vietnamese willing recruits for the Vietcong. Also we should firm up on some procedures that prevent South Vietnamese troops from, I will call it defecting, from their armed services, we would then close a big hole, as desertion rates are high, too high in

1967 

the South Vietnamese forces. If the South Vietnamese Government would go through the country and actually draft able-bodied people who might later become Vietcong, the Vietcong wouldn't have the source of the manpower. 

These people don't all have to be fighting personnel as there are many more support people required. 

Thank you very much.

I vield back the balance of my time.

NON-U.S. PARTICIPATION IN VIETNAM NATION BUILDING Free World Assistance Program (FWA) 

Thirty-one nations (Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, Costa Rica, Denmark, Ecuador, Germany, Greece, Guatemala, Honduras, Iran,

Italy, Japan, Korea, Laos, Liberia, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Netherlands, New 

Zealand, Philippines, Spain, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, United Kingdom,

Uruguay, Venezuela) are assisting Vietnam in one way or another under the free world assistance program. These nations furnish all kinds of materials and services needed in Vietnam, such as medical supplies, hospital equipment, refugee relief supplies, school and hospital construction, and so forth. It is anticipated that these 31 countries will increase their contributions in 1967 and also that the program will grow in numbers of contributors. In addition to these 31 countries, there are 6 other nations whose assistance to Vietnam does not technically come under the FWA program. Their help, nonetheless, is a valued contribution, as in the case of the 350 French teachers and roughly 150 French technicians who continue to work on long-term cultural and technical assistance programs. There is also a small number of U.N. technical personnel working in Vietnam to carry out the 37 technical assistance programs being implemented there in such fields as soil survey, labor administration, and telecommunications. 

The details of this assistance are set forth below-"Free World Assistance to Vietnam".

Free World Assistance Civilians in Vietnam (FWA) 

There are about 500 civilians from 13 nations (Australia, Canada, Republic of 

China, Germany, Iran, Italy, Japan, Korea, Netherlands New Zealand, Philippines, Spain, and the United Kingdom) working in the FWA program in Vietnam. These civilians are engaged in a variety of useful activities such as teachers, doctors, agricultural advisers, engineers, and other technical personnel. 77-470-67-pt. 14

1967 

It is anticipated that some Asian and European and possibly other countries will enlarge the number of their civilians working in the FWA program in Vietnam in 1967. 

Other Civilians 

There are in Vietnam today about 15,000 civilians from 27 countries other than the United States working in a private capacity for contractors and as employees of various United States and Vietnam Government agencies. While these civilians are not part of the FWA program, they nevertheless are doing their share in carrying the burden of the overall effort in Vietnam. The Philippines and Korea have supplied the great majority of these people.

Mr. FINDLEY. Can you tell us what the status of press freedom in 

South Vietnam is?

Mr. UNGER. I would say press freedom there is as free as it is in other countries in that part of the world, and certainly freer than in some of the other countries there. They have of course addressed themselves to this in their constitution and they have put in some pretty specific clauses about the press information which we can provide to you.

Mr. FINDLEY. Can the citizens of South Vietnam find a variety of political viewpoint in print in the local language?

Mr. UNGER. Yes, they can. Their situation is the situation of a country at war, and there is certainly some censorship. But statements either by their own people or statements by, let's say, foreign journalists, foreign officials, are carried in their press regularly. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Does the Government of South Vietnam impose a military censorship on the local newspapers to any degree? 

Mr. UNGER. I believe it is not a military censorship but a censorship by the Ministry 

Mr. FINDLEY. There is a censorship? 

Mr. UNGER. There is a censorship. This is a censorship which has been imposed at times and lifted. I am not sure that I could tell you as of this moment precisely what its status is. 

At the time, for example, when there was a good deal of internal difficulty, rioting and so on, in the spring of 1966, I think some of the censorship was imposed at least in certain areas. That censorship I believe has now been lifted.

Mr. FINDLEY. Is there any promising development of a multiparty system in South Vietnam, a political party system?

Mr. UNGER. There has not been very much development of that sort to date that is at least open and generally discussed. Our impression is that a lot of people are concerned with the need for some kind of organization to get ready for the elections that are coming. 

They can't really participate in this if there isn't some kind of effective grouping.

Mr. FINDLEY. Is General Ky identified with a party that has a name?

Mr. UNGER. He is not. There are rather small parties, not typical of the kind of political party that we know, that still exist from an earlier period. On the larger picture these have not appeared. 

One of the jobs that the Constituent Assembly has to do between now and election time is to put out a political party law which will

1967 

make it clear in the first place that political parties are permitted to organize and then to prescribe how they can operate. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Getting back to the graduates of colleges or universities of agriculture, will you put in the record the number of AID persons on a direct-hire basis in South Vietnam who are in that category? 

 AID EMPLOYEES WITH AGRICULTURAL DEGREES 

The most recent report showing the university degrees of all direct-hire AID employees is dated September 30, 1966. That report shows 32 direct-hire employees in Vietnam with college or university degrees in the field of Agriculture, or 3 percent of the direct-hire employees in Vietnam at that time. 

For the present purpose, AID has checked the college degrees of the direct-hire employees who have been appointed for projects in the field of agriculture between 

September 30, 1966, and March 31, 1967. That review of new employees for agricultural programs shows 13 new direct-hires with college or university degrees in agriculture. It is reasonable to assume that there have been other new directhire appointments with such degrees assigned to other programs, since AID seeks personnel with an agricultural background for many of its rural activities. 

Under the Participating Agency Agreement with the U.S. Department of 

Agriculture, there have been 57 appointments, of which 47 hold degrees in agriculture. 

Mr. FINDLEY. What is the trend in the food deficit situation in 

South Vietnam? It is quite clearly a food deficit area now. Is the trend up or down?

Mr. POATS. The trend is toward increasing deficits in rice and increasing production in vegetables, pork, chickens, and some fruits. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Do you have any statistics 

Mr. POATS. I have the gross figures on rice available. We expect that Vietnam will need to import in calendar 1967 just to maintain present security stocks, about 700,000 tons of rice. 

In addition, there will be produced in the delta, in excess of delta requirements and sold in the deficit areas of the country-Saigon and points north-a bit over 200,000 tons. 

This compares with the situation in 1963 in which Vietnam was an exporter of about 300,000 tons of rice. 

Mr. FINDLEY. What do you look for in the year following?

Mr. POATS. We look for, if the war continues and is particularly heightened in the delta, a further reduction in acreage under cultivation in rice, a further increase in the acreage in cultivation in vegetables and soybeans, and a further increase in the population in the deficit areas who are not engaged in farming and who are therefore dependent on the delta crop and on imports. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. FINDLEY. Can you tell us anything about the birth rate in 

South Vietnam? Is that static or up or down?

Mr. POATS. The population growth rate has been estimated at between 2.2 to 3.2 percent, which is of course high, but lower than some other developing countries. We use the figure 2.8 percent in this presentation to Congress.

Mr. FINDLEY. Is the death rate from nonmilitary events going down?

Mr. POATS. Yes, probably very much so. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Sharply?

51 Mr. POATS. Because of the expansion of medical services throughout the country, which of course may be a temporary phenomenon introduced by us and other free world countries. 

Mr. FINDLEY. If you could put some data on that in the record I would appreciate it. 

 IMPACT OF MEDICAL Programs on the DEATH RATE IN VIETNAM 

There is little hard data on the impact of medical programs on the death rate. 

It has been impossible to conduct during the war the kind of census which would produce this data. Health programs have been greatly expanded in the last year and the number of Vietnamese served by provincial hospitals, including outpatient clinical teams, has risen from 30,000 monthly to over 150,000 monthly. 

Voluntary agencies and U.S. and Vietnamese military medical personnel provide additional health services to civilians. We assume this rapid extension of health services is making a considerable impact on the death rate. One measure of earlier progress in lowering the death rate is the decline in reported infant mortality (children who die before age 1). The 1964 UN Demographic Yearbook shows a steady decline since 1961: 1960. 1961.

Mr. MONAGAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Poats, I noted with great interest the change in the emphasis of this program compared to what it has been in the past, particularly in the reduction in the import of commodities, and what I believe you call financial imports. This seems to me to be quite significant. 

Ordinarily this would mean an increase in the supply or a decrease in the demand. At least there apparently has been some change in the degree of restriction in this operation. What is the cause for the change?

Mr. POATS. What I meant to make clear, Mr. Monagan, is that while we are reducing our financing of commercial imports the Vietnamese Government through its national bank is increasing its financing of commercial imports. 

We have just sold Vietnam 300,000 tons of U.S. rice under the Public Law 480 program but at 100 percent U.S. Government retention of the piaster proceeds, which relieves the U.S. Government of having to buy piasters for the military contractor construction and maintenance operations in the country. This is made possible by increased 

Vietnamese earnings of dollars.

In the same way they are increasing their financing of general commerical imports. So the total volume of imports should not decline but the proportion borne by the U.S. Government should decline. 

Mr. MONAGAN. In other words, the problem is comparably as great but we are not directly or indirectly financing that portion that you say will be financed through private South Vietnamese sources?

1967 

Mr. POATS. That is correct. We are reducing the amount we are financing. They are increasing the amount they are financing. 

The total should remain roughly the same, although lately there has been a sharp dropoff of demand for imports as represented by the license applications. This results from the very large pipeline of imports built up last spring and summer. 

Mr. MONAGAN. With reference to the import licenses, one of the recommendations of the Moss committee was that there could be more influence exercised by the U.S. Government and U.S. agencies over the issuance of these licenses by the Government of South Vietnam and also in the supervision of the activities of the licensees after the licenses had been granted. What has been the experience in this area since the time that the report was made? 

Mr. POATS. We have attempted to gather information on which we could sensibly advise the Vietnamese Government or the Vietnamese importers of the stock status including pipeline in shipment and in procurement. We have gathered that information in a number of fields.

Recently we advised them we thought they were overordering on paper supplies. We recently advised them they were overordering on some pharmaceuticals. We have set up consolidated procurement of a number of large bulky items and are running that through the 

General Services Administration and shipping on Military Sea Trans port Service vessels. Here again by having consolidated package control over particular shipments, we are better able to control the timing and movement of the cargo and relieve the congestion problem. 

In general, we hold to the view that neither we nor the Vietnamese Government, and I would say any government anywhere, has the wisdom to interfere with the determination by businessmen of what level of procurement they wish to undertake with their own money to maintain stocks and to estimate demand for goods. 

Many governments have tried this. Some try it to a degree through control of credit available to different enterprises or different sectors of the economy. This is usually unsuccessful. We think there is a tremendous opportunity for corruption in a program of case-by-case, license-by-license determination by government of whether this much should be bought or not. 

Mr. MONAGAN. As I recall it, one of the criticisms was that these merchants were importing large stocks of a certain item and then holding them in this rising market and period of shortages in order to make a profit later on. The point was made that some pressure should be used to make them move these stocks within a specific period of time.

Mr. POATS. Yes, we were particularly concerned about holding goods in inventory in the port. That is an area in which we are moving very hard-to get these goods out of the port area and into private warehouses. This is limited by the shortage of available private warehouses, many of which have been commandeered by the military forces and by other elements of the Government. 

Of course, the whole volume of commercial imports is so much larger than the economy was geared for. As to the attempt to speculate by excessive inventory buildups in advance that has happened. 

This is one of the problems of the importer community right now.

53 They have a lot of their money tied up in inventories. They are paying bank credit rates. They are paying high warehousing charges. 

The cost of these goods is exactly double what they thought when they started this speculative import licensing operation. It is that sort of penalty of the market which we think is a lot more effective in deterring speculation than any amount of government control in that kind of society.

Mr. MONAGAN. I was glad to see the specific figures on the increase in the number of customs inspectors and controllers and accountants. 

Knowing that there has been an increase we can feel sure there will be greater supervision and that a lot of these bad practices will be automatically eliminated. 

Mr. POATS. Yes, and the Vietnamese customs operation has been increased to 1,200 employees in the Saigon port alone. The Americans working with them and the determination on the part of the port director to cut down and prevent abuses has I think improved the chances that the next month's report will show a reduced smuggling activity.

Mr. MONAGAN. There is a reference in your statement to the land reform program. Is that a basic problem in Vietnam and is it comparable to what we know to be the case, for instance in Latin America, Mr. POATS. I think it is quite different. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Let me ask, who owns the land involved?

Mr. POATS. The major land-owning class was broken up by the 

Diem land reform of the late 1950's. Many of the landlords now are villagers. They own a piece and rent a piece of land. Much of the land that I mentioned as expropriated by the Government in the past has not yet been resold to potential tiller owners. This land is being used throughout the country wherever it is arable. 

The problem is not so much the extreme disparity of holdings, of the big landowners interested in maintaining the rural status quo as you have in Latin America. It is more a matter of demonstrating to the people that a socially desirable program will be enforced and that the Government's laws and promises will be carried out. This is the weakness of the program today. 

Mr. MONAGAN. It is somewhat different than the problem we know in these other places.

Mr. POATS. Yes. I think the bigger problem there is enforcing the legal ceiling on the actual rentals paid by tenants as opposed to the issue of landownership.

Mr. MONAGAN. They have taken a very substantial step in a progressive direction?

Mr. POATS. They have taken a number of steps. The administrative enforcement is limited by staff, security, and by some local resistance to change. Those are the problems.

 INFORMATION ON MILITANT BUDDHIST ELEMENTS 

Vietnam's political, religious, and ethnic composition is highly diverse. For example, there are an estimated 1.5 million Catholics, more than 1 million Cao 

Dai, perhaps 750,000 ethnic tribespeople who are largely animists, over half a

1967 

million ethnic Cambodians who are Theravada Buddhists, over 1 million Chinese with their own Buddhist organizations, and between 1 and 2 million Hoa Hao. Most of the remainder of South Vietnam's 15-16 million population reflect a mixture Buddhist, Confucian, Taoist, and ancestor-worship beliefs. 

The largest Buddhist organization is believed to have up to 1.5 million members. Known as the Unified Buddhist Association (UBA), this organization has suffered periodically from factionalization within its ranks and is presently divided into two major factions, one of which is headed by Northern refugee bonze-Thich Tam Chau-who is the leader of many of the UBA adherents in the Saigon area, and the other of which is led by Thich Tri Quang whose following is located primarily in the area of Central Vietnam particularly Hue and Da Nang. Tri Quang's faction, which has become regarded as the "militant faction", at present enjoys little support for its political objectives outside of its loyal following in several major cities in the center, although in its campaign against former President Diem in 1963 it enjoyed general support from a number of key segments of the body politic. 

Mr. TAFT. It could be so interpreted, I think.

Mr. MONAGAN. Last spring there was a substantial revision in the rate of exchange. As I recall it, it might have been 33% percent change in the rate at which Vietnamese importers could take dollar credit.

In your judgment, has it proved to be the fact that this adoption of a rate that was more related to reality than the prior one has worked our favorably or otherwise?

Mr. POATS. It has worked out very favorably. It has reduced the opportunity for abuses of the import privilege. It has almost doubled the cost of foreign exchange to an importer and therefore increased the cost to the importer of foreign goods. Consequently, it has shrunk the demand for goods. It has reduced the profit margin in the import business because the demand simply was not great enough to absorb the increased exchange rate cost. 77-470-67—pt. 1- -5

1967 

It has been rough on the importers, has caused them considerable anguish. But we think it was a correct rate and it had precisely the effect calculated by the IMF and U.S. mission. 

Mr. MONAGAN. What is the rate now and what is the free market rate if you want to call it that?

Mr. POATS. The exchange rate for trade transactions is 118 piasters to the dollar. This is in effect a 38-piaster surcharge on top of an 80to-1 official rate; the 80-to-1 official rate applies to official conversion of piasters for foreign exchange for such purposes as government accounts. The black market rate, which of course is a rate based on a rather thin supply of dollars in the market, is about 170 to 173 to the dollar as opposed to 118. This rate did not rise after the devaluation, rather it fell. The degree of disparity between these two rates depends substantially upon the enforcement of foreign exchange regulations applying to United States and other foreign personnel in Vietnam. U.S. personnel are operating now, as you know, with military payment certificates, and it is illegal to trade foreign exchange or instruments in Vietnam, but some of this does occur. 

It is those illicit transactions with foreign hard currency that supply the black market. To the extent that we can tighten up on this illicit use of dollars the black market is likely to go up. The

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM S. GAUD, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. GAUD. Thank you. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee.

It is a pleasure to appear again before this committee, this time to discuss the foreign aid legislation and proposed program for the coming fiscal year.

In 2 months, we will observe the 20th anniversary of the Marshall plan. Since that time two decades ago, the United States has conducted a variety of aid programs addressed to a variety of problems. 

These range from the reconstruction of Europe to the provision of security aid to vulnerable countries on the edge of the Communist world to the strengthening of the poorer countries through development. All these programs have had a vital and common objectivethe security of the United States.

When I say that foreign aid is vital to our security, I am not talking only about the security-oriented supporting assistance which we furnish to Vietnam, the Dominican Republic and other countries directly threatened by economic or political chaos. I am talking about the bulk of our program, which is development aid. 

Secretary of Defense McNamara put it bluntly in his address last year before the American Society of Newspaper Editors in Montreal: 

Security is not military hardware-though it may include it. Security is not military force-though it may involve it. Security is not traditional military activity-though it may encompass it. 61

1967 

What is security, then? "Security," said the Secretary of Defense, "is development." 22 The corollary is that underdevelopment means insecurity-insecurity for the people of the poorer lands and insecurity for us. Virtually all the internationally significant outbreaks of violence in the sixties took place in less developed countries. 

Unless the poorer countries make some progress toward a better life for their people, we can expect explosions of violence to continue. 

Through the AID program we are working to stimulate the poorer nations to concentrate their energy and resources on development and to help them toward a more abundant life. It is in our interest and theirs to direct the forces of change toward development and away from violence. Development-economic growth, social reform, and political progress-is essential if we are to achieve a world at peace. 

Since we began to include substantial development assistance in our economic aid programs a decade ago, we have learned a lot about how to help a country develop faster and how to make our aid more effective. We have had to, for the focus of our efforts has shifted in that period until today development has become our main business. Vietnam aside, we no longer have to spend the bulk of our funds to shore up a large number of countries on the verge of economic or political instability or maintaining armed strength beyond their own capacities. 

Supporting assistance has been terminated completely in 24 countries since 1960. In money terms, supporting assistance programs, other than for Vietnam, have dropped from $653 million in fiscal year 1961 to $195 million in fiscal year 1968. As a result, supporting assistance has become a small fraction of the AID program in Latin American, the Near East, south Asia, and Africa. The chart below shows the distribution of AID funds by region.

65 The objective of our development aid is to help recipients progress to the point of self-sustaining growth, when they can finance their own future development without resort to external aid on concessional terms.

We have already seen several countries reach this point. A number of countries which used to receive substantial amounts of assistance from AID-countries such as Taiwan, Greece, Israel, and Iran-are now receiving very little or none at all, because they are economically on their way.

There are a number of other countries which have not yet reached the point where they no longer need our help, but in which we can see the end of the tunnel. A good example is Korea. Less than 15 years ago, there were imposing obstacles to progress in Korea. Korea needed to maintain a large standing army, which consumed a sizable portion of the Korean budget, and still does. There was a serious lack of managerial talent. You will recall that the Koreans had little experience in running their Government and business affairs until after the Japanese withdrew in 1945. Moreover, Korean population density was high and growing while the natural resource base was poor. Korea is a mountainous country with few mineral resources, where less than a quarter of the land is arable. 

Few would have dared to predict that in 10 or 15 years Korea would emerge as one of the most energetic and successful of the lessdeveloped countries. Inflation has been checked. Stabilization programs are proceeding successfully. The Government has more than doubled domestic revenues in the last 3 years and has budgeted its funds wisely. 

In the last 10 years Gross national product has risen 91 percent. 

Per capita GNP has risen 45 percent. 

Industrial production is up 216 percent. 

Electric power production is up 252 percent. 

Agricultural production is up 82 percent.

Exports have increased 10 times. (The relevant charts follow :)

KOREA 1956 1957 1958 1959 1960 1961 1962 1963 1954 1965 1966 ([u] As a result of this growth Korea has been able to put more and more of its own resources into development and we have been able to begin reducing our economic aid levels.

The Koreans have set a target in the early 1970's when they propose to achieve agricultural self-sufficiency and economywide self-sustaining growth. They may not make it as soon as they plan-political and world conditions beyond their control may slow the pace. But we are doing what we can to help them succeed and are impressed by the progress they have made so far. 

So we have reached a point where many recipient countries no longer need short-term security assistance, and where we have been in the

67 development business long enough to see more and more countries, like Korea, moving toward self-sustaining growth in the coming decade.

We have enough experience behind us to believe we are on the right track. We have enough expérience to know we can get results. We see recipients devoting themselves to serious development programs and taking necessary self-help measures. We increasingly see that development does, in practice, improve the conditions which spawn unrest and violence.

But there is no such thing as instant development. We still have a long, hard task ahead of us. That is why we are proposing that the 

Congress authorize all our activities for 2 years, as a sign of congressional recognition that the foreign aid program is in our national interest, that the program does occupy an established place in our overall foreign policy, that there is a long-term job to do, and that we are prepared to follow through where we so wisely have begun. 

Certain parts of the AID program-development loans and the Alliance for Progress have traditionally been authorized for more than 1 year. These two programs are now authorized through fiscal year 

1969. A 2-year authorization for other AID programs would bring them into line with development loan and Alliance authorizations. 

A 2-year cycle of authorizations for the entire program would provide each Congress with an opportunity to review the aid program in the light of changing world circumstances, while demonstrating our dedication to the task of long-term development. Appropriations, of course, would continue to be made annually. And we would present our off-year programs to this committee in whatever form or degree of detail the committee desired.

The legislation before you reflects our concern with the job ahead as well as the experience which has shaped the program over the last several years. It clarifies and highlights the objectives and techniques of today's foreign aid program, emphasizing the soundest ways to work for development. I have already mentioned one of these concentrating our aid in major countries with good development prospects. Others are concentrating our aid in the important areas of agriculture, education, and health; coordinating our aid with that of other donors in consortia, consultative groups, multidoor projects, and other multilateral arrangements; doing everything we can to persuade other developed countries to contribute their fair share of the costs of development; and encouraging and supporting regional institutions, projects, and other activities that make for more efficient use of scarce resources. 

I would like to discuss with you now three particular aspects of today's AID program-self-help, the war on hunger, and the use of private resources in development. Self-help Self-help is not a new idea. We have always known that sustained development is impossible unless a country devotes its own energy and resources to the effort. But self-help has evolved from an idea and a policy into a fundamental and pervasive feature of the AID program. The legislation before you stresses the importance of selfhelp by specifying criteria to be taken into account in furnishing de-

1967 

velopment aid and by authorizing the President to create a National Advisory Committee on Self-Help, composed of independent experts and leading citizens, to report each year to the President and the Congress on the effectiveness of recipient countries' self-help efforts and the role of AID in promoting self-help. 

We stimulate self-help in a variety of ways, depending on the circumstances of the individual country-its needs, its resources, its political situation, the volume and kind of aid we propose to provide and other similar factors. Sometimes, especially on smaller projects, we require only that the recipient government contribute a fair share of the costs of the project. For larger project loans, we usually require more. For instance, a loan to the Bolivian Mining Bank to finance expansion and modernization of the private mining industry was not agreed to until the Bolivian Government had undertaken a major reform of the country's mining code, a reorganization of the bank, and the passage and enforcement of new mineral export tax laws to encourage investment in mining. Today, the new code is in effect, the new tax law has been passed, and the required reorganization is being carried out. 

In Afghanistan, before disbursing a highway loan, we required the Afghan Government to create a national highway maintenance department, as it had become obvious that previous AID-sponsored highway projects had not been kept in good repair. 

In other cases, particularly where large program loans are made, we insist on broad measures, such as fiscal and monetary reform, exchange reform, tax reform, import liberalization, increased government investment in development, or other steps that may affect the whole economy.

A recent $10 million program loan to Korea, for example, committed the Korean Government to five quantified financial targets-(1) improved budgeting, (2) better foreign exchange management, (3) restraint on the issuance of private sector credit, (4) increased domestic revenue collection and (5) higher domestic savings. Half the loan was to be released in each of two quarters if Korean performance in each quarter was up to the prescribed standards. The Koreans met the conditions.

Similarly, program loans for Tunisia in this fiscal year and fiscal year 1968 will be conditioned on Tunisian adherence to IMF/IBRD stabilization measures, including restricting investment to available resources, controlling the use of suppliers' credits, curtailing expenditures to provide an operating budget surplus, controlling release of counterpart funds to eliminate inflationary effect, improving the management and operations of state enterprises and continuing IMF-set credit ceilings.

Self-help measures in each case will be tailored to the kind and amount of aid we provide. We will expect all countries receiving our aid to recognize the basic obstacles blocking their own progress and will require of them-each in the ways most appropriate for it—a sincere and sustained effort to overcome these obstacles. 

War on hunger

One of the overriding facts of today's world is that although total food production generally has been increasing, population growth

69 rates have been rising so fast that per capita food production has dropped. Still, apart from areas temporarily suffering from drought or other natural disasters, the world does not, today, face a major food shortage. World food production is still adequate to prevent mass starvation, and the United States, Canada and other countries have the capacity to increase food production to meet the needs of less developed countries for a while longer. 

But in the long run, the developed nations will simply not be able to meet these rising food needs from their increased agricultural production-nor would we consider it sensible to supply food indefinitely from excess stocks. As the new Food for Peace Act makes clear, the world's growing need for food must ultimately be met largely by the less developed countries themselves, through their own self-help efforts.

They must work to change traditional attitudes which prevent increases in food production, build fertilizer plants, shift their development plans to place more stress on agriculture, and take dozens of other steps to encourage greater food output. 

The job will take time, and there is no time to lose. If these countries do not produce more food: 

We will see famines and more malnutrition Social and political unrest will spread-unlike their ancestors, people today will not resign themselves to silent suffering and starvation;

Economic and social development will be stifled; and 

Our chances of a peaceful future will be greatly diminished. 

By concentrating our efforts on helping the less developed countries increase their agricultural output, therefore, we are accomplishing several aims simultaneously. We are helping prevent starvation and malnutrition, slowing the spread of violence born of hunger, contributing to long-range development and promoting peace. 

In order to give added emphasis to the war on hunger and to help achieve a proper balance among food, family planning, nutrition and agricultural development assistance, a central staff office devoted to all aspects of the war on hunger has been created in AID. 

The new office will lead and coordinate our attack on starvation and malnutrition in the less developed countries, which is the highest priority we have. Our proposed fiscal year 1968 program includes $668 million-compared to an estimated $504 million in fiscal year 1967-to help the poorer nations increase their food production. Additional funds will support family planning and nutrition activities. 

Most less developed countries can and must increase their food output. Few can do so significantly by putting more land under cultivation. Most must therefore increase the productivity of land already under cultivation if higher and better per capita food consumption is to be achieved. This means:

More and better agricultural material and equipment, such as improved seed, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation equipment, farm tools and other agricultural inputs;

More and better storage and distribution systems for food, including farm-to-market roads;

Research to devise the proper seed varieties, the best fertilizer mixtures, the most efficient pesticides and the most effective irri-

70€ 

 1967 

gation methods for all the various soil and climate conditions throughout the world;

Extension services to inform farmers of new agricultural inputs and educate them in their use;

Credit through rural development banks or other institutions to permit farmers to take advantage of fertilizer, pesticides, new seeds, irrigation and equipment;

Reasonable farm prices and relatively cheap agricultural inputs, to provide a profit incentive which will induce the farmer to take some risks by adopting new methods; 

Land reform, which will enable a farmer to invest in land without fear of loss because his tenure is unsure; 

Access to consumer goods, so that a farmer who produces more and earns more can benefit by a real increase in living standards for himself and his family; and 

Adequate levels of trained manpower and efficient institutions capable of administering such programs. 

The job of transforming traditional agriculture to increase productivity depends largely on the efforts of the less developed countries themselves. Their policies and actions will determine whether they make a go of it or not. But we can still play a crucial role in this complex process.

Our help not only supplies essential skills and commodities which are not otherwise available, but serves as well as an incentive to recipient countries to take the self-help measures required to step up their food production.

We provide this help in a variety of ways, using a number of different instruments, such as development loans, technical assistance, supporting assistance, private investment surveys and investment guarantees, research and direct food aid. 

Program loans-dollar-repayable development loans used to buy U.S. goods are well suited to help finance agricultural development. 

They pay for key agricultural inputs such as fertilizer, seeds, and pesticides, and the raw materials to manufacture these inputs. They finance, too, spare parts for tractors and other farm equipment and for plants which manufacture farm equipment, fertilizer and other essential products. Program loans for agriculture will run about $300 million in fiscal year 1968-up from $150 million in fiscal year 1967. 

Conditioned as they are on broad self-help measures by the recipient country, program loans can be used to encourage general social and economic policies affecting agricultural development such as farm prices, increased Government investment in agriculture, and liberalization of restrictions on importing goods which will help increase food output.

India is a good example of a country where we use program loans to promote changes in policies affecting food supply. India intends to put almost a quarter of total planned investment into agriculture during the next 5 years-a substantial and urgently needed increase. 

Changes in pricing policy will provide greater incentive for the farmer. 

The Government has also undertaken to make available more agricultural inputs such as fertilizer.

Fertilizer imports and marketing arrangements have been liberalized, and domestic fertilizer production is being increased. Five fer-

71 tilizer plants in the private sector have recently been approved, three of which are already under construction. Plans for four others are well advanced. Two fertilizer plants owned by the Government are also being built. In addition, an estimated $155 million of the fiscal year 1968 program loan to India will be used to finance imports from the United States of fertilizer, raw materials for fertilizer production, and other agricultural inputs.

Project loans-another type of dollar-repayable development loans finance specific agricultural development projects such as fertilizer plants, credit institutions, rural cooperatives, adaptive research and training institutions, irrigation projects, food storage and marketing facilities, land reclamation, livestock development, farm-to-market roads, and agricultural schools and colleges. 

For example, a major program for irrigation, land reclamation and salinity control in Pakistan is being financed by project loans. The availability and proper use of water has played a major role in West Pakistan's 5.5-percent annual increase in agricultural production. A proposed loan will cover the dollar cost of procurement and installation of 1,550 tube wells and pumps in an area of about a million acres. 

The self-help measures on which we condition project loans enable us to insure that certain reforms related to the project be carried out before the loan is signed or the funds are disbursed, that the recipient contribute funds or facilities to the project, and that the project be operated in specified ways.

Sector loans, a recent innvoation in AID programing, are development loans which have characteristics of both project and program loans. A sector loan is designed to help finance a general development plan in a specific sector such as agriculture, and is conditioned on policy commitments and institutional reforms related to that sector. This approach will give us the flexibility to reduce or suspend assistance in the particular sectors where self-help conditions are not being met. 

The technical assistance program makes U.S. skills and technical knowledge available to less developed countries. It provides training, in the United States and overseas, for qualified people from countries where technical training is at best in short supply-people who are then able to conduct agricultural research and extension activities, organize and operate credit institutions, and develop and carry out social and economic policies related to agriculture. 

AID's technical assistance programs also help teach farmers more productive farming techniques. In Pakistan, for example, an intensified agricultural extension effort, which emphasizes farmer self-help efforts, has enabled many farmers almost to triple their rice production in 3 years. This approach has been extended to seven districts of East Pakistan. Our proposed technical assistance projects in agriculture for fiscal year 1968 total $78 million. 

AID's expanded research efforts in agriculture are also financed with technical assistance funds. We have negotiated or are negotiating a number of research contracts designed to improve food production techniques and develop new knowledge on tropical agriculture. 

Other research projects deal with a wide range of topics such as mechanized farming, the use of sorghum as human food, livestock diseases, vegetable production, large-scale farming methods, village processing of food products, and the use of systems analysis to improve agricultural productivity.

1967 

In a number of countries, supporting assistance is also used for agricultural projects and programs. In the Dominican Republic, for example, a fiscal year 1968 supporting assistance loan will help finance investment in the agricultural sector. Agricultural programs in South 

Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos will also be financed with supporting assistance funds.

AID's private investment insurance and guarantee programs and private investment surveys also play a key role in the war on hunger. 

We recognize the absolute necessity to involve U.S. private enterprise more deeply, more actively, and more broadly if the war on hunger is to be successful. We are making greater use of our incentive programs to encourage private investment in war on hunger activities. 

In the last 9 months we have authorized extended risk guarantees for major fertilizer complexes in India and Brazil involving investments totaling $140 million. Further, 33 surveys of agri-business projects involving total planned private investment of $315 million are underway. 

Public Law 480 food aid, although not funded through the Foreign Assistance Act, also plays a major role in the war on hunger by supplying food resources to the less developed countries, by stimulating recipient countries through self-help requirements to adopt measures conducive to increased agricultural production, and by food-for-work programs, which feed people working on such agricultural development projects as irrigation, land drainage, construction of wells, health centers, homes and schools for farmers, and farm-to-market roads. 

Nutrition is also receiving increased attention under the war on hunger. The quality of food, as well as the quantity, is important. 

Relatively few people die of starvation, but millions are stunted by malnutrition and die of diseases caused by lack of proper nourishment. 

It is also clear that people who are weakened by malnutrition will not have the spark and energy needed to do the work of development. We have a number of programs in this area. For example: 

AID contributed some $3 million in 1966 to blend and add vitamins and minerals to 92 million pounds of high-protein cornsoya-milk food supplement, shipped to 83 countries for use in maternal and child feeding programs. 

Under the high protein commercial food studies program, AID is helping private food processing companies to produce highprotein foods to improve nutrition in less developed countries. 

AID will assist in market surveys and product testing, while private U.S. companies will be responsible for developing the products.

AID is taking an active role in cooperation with other U.S. agencies in determining the best way to make fish protein concentrate available in less developed countries. 

In addition to the effort to increase agricultural production and improve nutrition, the war on hunger includes assistance to family planning.

Family planning programs in less developed countries, and AID's activities in the family planning field, reflect a growing worldwide concern over the social and economic consequences of rapid population growth. For no matter how successful the world is in increasing agricultural productivity, the time is sure to come when there will not be enough food if present population trends continue.

73 AID policy in the family planning field is clear. Family planning is a matter of great delicacy, and we do not feel it is appropriate to make the existence of a family planning program a condition of assistance. But family planning is also a matter of great urgency, and we will provide aid to those countries which have voluntary family planning programs which allow for individual freedom of choice. 

In accordance with this policy, we are providing help in family planning to a number of countries. We are also supporting several research and training programs at such institutions as the University of California, the University of Notre Dame, Johns Hopkins University, the Columbia Institute for Social Development, and the University of Hawaii.

Progress has been too slow. Many governments lack a full appreciation of the enormous impact of fast-growing populations on the life of their people-not only on their food supply but on their entire development effort. As a result, many countries have not yet faced up to the need to deal with the problem, or have not pushed forward vigorously with well-planned programs. 

We at

In these countries the basic obstacle to progress in family planning is not so much a lack of capital as it is a lack of awareness. 

AID plan to do more than we have in the past to awaken other governments to a full realization of the true nature of the population problem. And as more and more countries adopt sound programs, they will find us ready to provide the assistance they need to carry their programs out.

In summary, Mr. Chairman, this is the role that AID is playing in the war on hunger. I consider that we have no higher priority than to do everything we can today to see that tomorrow the world will continue to be able to feed itself and that the balance between food and mouths will be maintained.

Private resources for development Another effective way of speeding up development-one of the most effective, in fact-is to mobilize the resources and energy of the private sector, both in the United States and in the less developed countries. 

AID helps bring the creative force of private initiative into the development process in three basic ways. 

1. Our programs are designed to stimulate the private sector in recipient countries. For example, a program loan may make available 

U.S. spare parts, fertilizer, raw materials, or capital equipment to thousands of businessmen and farmers and, at the same time, be conditioned on basic reforms in import and licensing procedures which will make it easier for private enterprise to obtain needed imports. 

A project loan may finance the infusion of U.S. skills and equipment which help provide the transport, power, and communications required for the expansion of private sector activity. 

Project loans to intermediate credit institutions open up to businessmen and farmers previously nonexistent sources of long-term capital vital to private sector growth.

Technical assistance may be used for such diverse projects as to help industry expand exports through better quality control, to set up a productivity and investment center, to help draft comprehensive capital markets legislation, or to develop a modern graduate school of business administration.

1967 

2. U.S. private enterprise both contributes to and benefits from our regular assistance programs. AID financed over $1.1 billion worth of U.S. commodities in fiscal year 1966. This included exports from all 50 States. We expect 97 percent of our commodity expenditures to be made in the United States in fiscal year 1968. 

We also draw heavily on the technical skills of private U.S. groups. 

Believing that the vast pool of private, nongovernmental technical resources available in this country should be tapped to the greatest possible extent, we had outstanding on December 31, 1966, 1,378 technical service contracts with private U.S. organizations, valued at over a billion dollars. Two hundred seventy of these contracts, worth about $220 million, were held by 124 U.S. colleges and universities for research, surveys, training, and technical assistance. 

To insure the greatest participation of the private sector in our regular programs, I have recently issued an Agency-wide policy determination which gives priority to private businesses and groups in helping us meet the needs of the less developed countries. This means that to carry out AID-financed activities we will look first to the private community to obtain skilled personnel, next to other Federal, State, or local government agencies, and last to our own direct-hire personnel. 

The directive also reaffirms AID's policy of encouraging U.S. private investment that would further development and attempting to obtain private U.S. financing before agreeing to fund a project. 

Which brings me to the third way in which we bring private enterprise into play in the overall development effort. 

3. In recent years, there has been a growing awareness, both within 

AID and outside it, of the importance of AID's role in generating greater participation in development by U.S. business and private nonprofit organizations. Accordingly, the President announced in his foreign aid message the creation of an Office of Private Resources in AID, responsible for the encouragement, support, stimulation, and coordination of the already widespread activities of the U.S. private sector and the achievement of even greater private participation in and contribution to development. 

The new office will provide a central point of contact for both profit and nonprofit organizations, will administer AID's private investment incentive programs, and will be charged with developing new means to increase participation of nonprofit groups in development activities. 

Within the Office of Private Resources we are planning to establish a Private Investment Center specifically designed to meet the needs of potential U.S. investors in the less developed countries. The Center will provide a single point of contact in AID for U.S. investors. 

Under the Center we will consolidate various programs of assistance to investors, most of which are familiar to you. 

Herbert Salzman, who recently joined AÏD as Assistant Administrator for Development Finance and Private Enterprise, and who will head the new Office of Private Resources, will discuss these programs in detail when he testifies before the committee. But I would like just to mention these private enterprise programs briefly this morning.

Our preinvestment services make available to potential investors detailed information, including a central reference index of in-

75 vestment opportunities which we have supplied to 47,500 organizations, firms, and individuals. 

Through our investment survey prorgam, we share the cost of surveying potential investments in less developed countries. 

Our specific risk guarantee program, now instituted in 78 countries, protects investors against the political risks of expropriation, inconvertibility, and damage due to war, revolution, and insurrection.

We have developed a new equity guarantee program providing "all risk" coverage of up to 50 percent of loss of equity or of equity-like investment.

Through our extended risk guarantee program, we protect 75 percent of investments against loss for any reason, other than commercially insurable risks, not due to the fraud or misconduct of the investor.

Our housing guarantee programs provide up to 100-percent coverage of loan investments in housing projects. 

Under the "Cooley loan" program we make local currency loans to U.S. firms and their affiliates. We also make direct dollar loans to private U.S. and local ventures. Dollar and local currency loans are also available to U.S. business abroad through intermediate credit institutions established with AID assistance. 

The Office of Private Resources will not only assist U.S. business through the Private Investment Center; it will also stimulate broader participation in development by private nonprofit groups, such as the 

International Executive Service Corps.

In addition, we are now considering a loan to a U.S. private investment corporation which would channel capital investment to the African private sector. The AID loan would provide seed capital to attract additional funds from major U.S. financial institutions. 

We hope the newly formed International Private Investment Advisory Council will help us find new ways to help increase private investment in less developed countries. The Council, established as a result of an amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act last year, includes as members the National Association of Manufacturers, the 

U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the Committee for Economic Devel opment, the National Foreign Trade Council, the U.S. Council of the 

International Chamber of Commerce, and the National Industrial 

Conference Board.

We expect that these AID programs and activites to support and stimulate private enterprise and initiative both here and abroad will continue to increase in size and in scope. The Office of Private Resources will be working actively to provide centralized, efficient service to private businesses and nonprofit groups, and we will continue to do our best to involve the private sector more effectively in the tasks of development.

Mr. Chairman, I have discussed in summary form a few of the features-self-help, the war on hunger and private resources in development that characterize the AID program today. I strongly recommend this program to you. It is right for the United States to strengthen less developed countries and help them achieve a better life for their people. It is also essential to our own national interest. for peace in the world is not possible unless we do. 77-470-67-pt. 1- -6

Where does the other 20 percent go?

Mr. GAUD. Our projected program for 1968 includes AID programs to 66 countries, not including 7 others in Africa, which will have available what we call self-help funds, a fund which is made available to the Ambassador from our appropriation and is used for small projects, small local projects. 

Chairman MORGAN. On page 5 you list eight countries particularly in the development loan program which are to receive 82 percent of the development loan fund requested for fiscal year 1968. 

How many other countries are involved in the development loan program for fiscal 1968, and does the number go above the limitation to 10 countries which was written into the foreign assistance bill last year?

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. For 1968 we are now planning development loans to a total of 22 countries, which is considerably above the limitation of 10 in last year's act. As you will recall, that provision of the act provided that if the President found it in the national interest he

77 could go above the number of 10. For fiscal year 1967 the President made a determination increasing the number to 29. Nineteen of these are in Africa, 10 of them outside Africa. The bill which we have submitted to the Congress this year contains no provisions for limiting the number of countries. We are, as I say, hoping and planning on the assumption of making loans to 22 countries next year. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gaud, I imagine that the determination to give development loans to 19 countries over the limitation specified in the act was not favorably received on the other side of the Capitol. 

Mr. GAUD. When the President submitted his determination to the 

Congress, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee asked me to come up and testify on the determination. You are quite right, there was some dissatisfaction expressed with the fact that the President had been so liberal, as it were. As I see it the law is quite clear. The authority is given to the President to act in the national interest, and he did so.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gaud, one thing that disturbs me about the economic assistance programs is the fact that last year the President's request was approximately $2,468 million. And the appropriation was for $2,143 million. This year you come back with a request for $2.5 billion for economic aid. The total foreign aid package is larger than for 1967, even though the Executive this year is attempting to move all military assistance for some of the countries in southeast 

Asia over into the DOD budget. You are putting back in the economic request more than the amount you have reduced military aid by transferring part of the military program to the Defense Department budget. Is there sufficient need to justify an increase in the economic request for the fiscal year 1968 by approximately $400 million more than was available for fiscal 1967? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. We feel very strongly that the request which we have submitted for economic aid this year-of $2.530 billion, as you say-is all urgently needed. We have submitted what we believe to be an extremely tight budget. We have budgeted very carefully. It is very little larger than our request last year.

As you point out, it is roughly $400 million larger than the appropriation for economic aid last year. There is one very significant difference between the situation in 1967 and the situation in 1968. You will remember that because of the war which broke out between India and Pakistan in the fall of 1965, we cut off new aid to India and Pakistan for some time. Aid was renewed to those two countries late in fiscal year 1966. The result was that as a practical matter some $320 million worth of loans to India and Pakistan which were authorized late in fiscal year 1966 in effect went to meet some of the requirements of fiscal year 1967. The change in cycle by virtue of our cutting off aid had that effect.

There will be no similar situation existing next year in fiscal year 1968. So that while the figure of $2.530 billion seems much larger than the figure of $2.143 billion appropriated in fiscal 1967, the fact of the matter is that there will be almost the same amount of money available if this full amount which we are asking is appropriated. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gaud, I know this is not in your shop because you are primarily concerned with the economic part of the aid program, but one thing that alarms me is the way somebody in

the executive branch, and I suppose it comes primarily from the military aid people, keeps whittling away at the military assistance part of this program by transferring to the Defense Department. I regard military aid as an important aspect of our foreign policy and feel strongly that the Committee on Foreign Affairs should continue to have jurisdiction over military assistance. 

I remember the day that we authorized $1,900 million for military assistance. Last year the military assistanct for South Vietnam was moved over to the DOD budget.

This year they transfer another important segment of military assistance to the DOD budget.

If the foreign aid program lives for 2 or 3 years more, military assistance will be related more to the interests of the Department of Defense than to the implementation of our foreign policy. 

Mr. GAUD. There are two separate factors which are responsible for the very considerable decline in the amount of military assistance, to which you have referred, over the last few years. One which I think is a very healthy situation is that the requirements for military assistance as we see them are decreasing. 

We are giving military assistance to fewer countries, we are giving it in smaller amounts to those which we are still giving it to, and I think this is something which we all applaud and approve. This is a healthy sign.

The other factor is well let's call it unhealthy-the transfer last year of military assistance for Vietnam and the proposed transfer this year of military assistance for Laos and Thailand. The theory here is that the aid program should not be financing a hot war, that the requirements which are needed for Vietnam, for Thailand and Laos are really military requirements, war requirements, not military assistance requirements.

It does not seem appropriate to us in the administration, and this is as true of the State Department as it is of the Defense Department, to finance a shooting war out of the aid program. Therefore we have suggested this transfer.

Your testimony, Mr. Gaud, dwells at length on the factor of selfhelp by nations receiving U.S. foreign aid. 81 of development aid through multilateral organizations-I think the figure was 85 percent-what good are these self-help criteria? They would affect only 15 percent of our developmental aid, would they not?

Mr. GAUD. No, sir. I am afraid there is a misunderstanding there. 

Perhaps the proposed legislation isn't as clear as it should be. Here is the provision that I think you are referring to:

It is the sense of Congress that in the implementation of the policies of this section not less than 85 percent of all Development Loan assistance furnished under this Title shall be furnished for multilateral and regional programs. 

We did not mean by that, and we don't mean by that that 85 percent of our loan funds should go through multilateral institutions such as the World Bank. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I am very happy to have that statement.

Mr. GAUD. What we mean is that 85 percent of our loan funds should be disbursed in concert with other aid givers through consortia, through consultative groups through other types of regional programs. 

We in the executive branch draw a very sharp distinction between dispensing aid through a multilateral institution and dispensing aid in what might be called a multilateral framework or a multilateral context. We think it is very important to work with other aid givers, to work with the IBRD, to work with the IMF, to work with other countries that are giving aid to the same country in which we are interested. 

This means greater efficiency. It means agreement on what the country ought to do to make better use of aid. There is less chance of their playing off one aid-giver against another. It makes for greater efficiency, greater coordination and as we see it, quicker results. It makes for more burden-sharing. We believe in encouraging this to the extent we can. We are not suggesting at all that the funds which will be authorized under this act be spent through a multilateral institution.

83 closely with the Inter-American Development Bank. The other regional banks, such as the African Development Bank and the Asian 

Development Bank, haven't made any loans yet. So we really only are talking about the IBRD, the IDA, and the IDB. Mr. ADAIR. My final question, how is that coordination maintained? 

How do you maintain the liaison?

Mr. GAUD. With the Export-Import Bank? 

Mr. ADAIR. With any of these other agencies. Is there an established office in each of the agencies for this purpose? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes. There are a variety of ways in which this happens.

There are people in AID's central staff who are charged directly with the responsibility for liaison. But more important than that really is the fact that all of these organizations which we are discussing are set up in the same way. Each has its India desk, each has its Latin 

American section, each has its African bureau. The people working on India in all these organizations get together all the time and know what the other fellow is doing. Of course, another factor which makes this coordination much easier than it might otherwise seem has been the increasing number of countries to which we give aid through consortia or through consultative groups. As I have already indicated here something like 85 percent of our development loans today are made to countries which are either getting their aid through a consortium or under a consultative group. 

Now, the World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, ourselves, IDA, we are all represented in these consortia and in these consultative groups. 

There is one other focus for coordination and that is the National Advisory Council which is an agency in the executive branch to which every loan in which the United States is involved has to go for approval of its terms regardless of what agency is making it. 

Then, too, as far as AID is concerned we make our loans only after the Administrator has had a recommendation from the Development 

Loan Committee. The membership of the Development Loan Com mittee consists of myself, a representative of the State Department, a representative of the Secretary of the Treasury, the Eximbank, a representative of the Department of Commerce, and one or two other agencies. The Treasury Department, as you know, is the chief U.S. representative to the World Bank and the IDB. Harold Linder, of the Eximbank, sits on this Committee. So these other executive branch agencies which have responsibility for these other organizations have a look at all of the loans that I make.

89 and also some minor ones. Presumably you are attempting to respond to the congressional feeling that there should be such concentration? 

Mr. GAUD. It is also our feeling, Mr. Frelinghuysen. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. But you differ over the congressional limitation. I might say that I am not enthusiastic about this rigid ceiling myself. You do feel there should be room for moderate amounts of aid to other countries, in addition to the concentrated effort in a relatively few countries?

Mr. GAUD. That is right. We feel we should put our major effort into a relatively few countries which are capable of getting results in development. There are a great many other countries such as the 

African countries, for example, in which, as we see it, it is important to carry on educational programs, agricultural programs, manpower training and that sort of business and it doesn't make any sense from the standpoint of the United States to just cut out Africa. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. You are doing that in technical cooperation as 

I understand it? You just said you were planning to cut African countries out.

Mr. GAUD. What we propose to do is shift to the extent that we possibly can, shift our programs in these small countries in Africa from bilateral programs to multilateral or regional programs. Put more of our efforts into regional projects, try and persuade the World Bank to do more in Africa, assist the African Development Bank to get going and to make some funds available to it, the whole theory being to promote regionalism in Africa. There are many small countries which standing alone do not have good development prospects. We want to do everything we can to pull these countries together. At the same time there are some 10 countries in Africa in which, if we had our way, we would continue to carry on full fledged aid programs where we think the possibility of development justifies it, although increasingly within a multilateral framework. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Are your plans for 1968 in response to a congressional mandate, rather than what you think is appropriate? 

Mr. GAUD. That isn't really so. Our aid policy toward Africa was determined in large part from certain recommendations of the Korry report. Ambassador Korry, our Ambassador to Ethiopia, last year led a group which studied our aid policy in Africa. He came up with some very specific recommendations, that we should concentrate more on fewer countries in Africa, we should spend more of our efforts in trying to promote regionalism and the like and the thrust of his report which came out before the Senate adopted a bill fixing the number of countries the thrust of his report moves in the direction of reducing the number of bilateral aid programs we have in Africa in favor of regional and multilateral programs. That report was a major factor in our decision to change our policy.
