 SOVIET ECONOMIC AID-TERMS AND METHOD OF REPAYMENT 

Most U.S.S.R. aid agreements with the less developed countries contain terms of 2.5 percent interest and 12 years for repayment of principal after completion of project. Repayment generally is to be made in exports of the recipient country. 

Recently, the U.S.S.R. has also extended trade credits for imports of machinery and equipment which carry somewhat shorter amortization periods and slightly higher interest terms; e.g., 8 to 10 years for repayment and 3 to 4 percent interest. 

These credits are also repayable in exports.

 REVIEW OF HOUSING GUARANTEE PROGRAM LATIN AMERICA 

Section 224 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended through 1964, provided authority to guarantee $250 million in U.S. investments in pilot demonstration projects in Latin America. This program was over-subscribed, and no new applications were taken between May 1964 and April 1966. At the close of the May 1964 application period, 118 applications totaling over $500 million had been received.

As of December 31, 1966: 

Thirty-seven projects in 14 countries covering 36.583 houses and $200 million in guarantees had been authorized. Thirteen of these projects, comprising 11,740 units, were under construction and 3 projects comprising 4,090 units were completed. The sponsors of the three completed projects were the American Institute for Free Labor Development (Mexico), Appollo 

Industries (Peru) and Rahmani Construction Corporation (Venezuela). 

Thirteen projects for 9,160 units and $40,000,000 in guarantees were under review.

The 1965 Foreign Assistance Act increased the available guarantee authority to $400 million, and provided four new institutional programs: 

Credit Institutions Program. 

Lower Income Program. 

Free Labor Union and Cooperative Program. 

Local Participation Program. 

One hundred twenty-three applications for $600 million in guarantees for these institutional programs were received between April 1966 and September 

15, 1966, the closing date for applications. Twenty-one of these applications

103 have been either withdrawn or canceled; the remaining 102 are being subjected to competitive review.

The 1966 Foreign Assistance Act again increased the available guarantee authority to $450 million and provided that $300 million of the $450 million should be for pilot demonstration projects. AID is currently drafting guidelines and an announcement to the public will be issued shortly. 

The President's Committee on Balance of Payments has limited the original pilot demonstration program to $240 million and the institutional program to $100 million. Also, the pilot demonstration program of 1967 has been limited to $33 million.

OTHER AREAS Section 221 (b)(2) of the Foreign Assistance Act includes authority for housing guarantees in areas other than Latin America. The total extended risk guarantee authority provided in the 1966 Act, $160 million is reserved solely for housing guarantees.

Sixteen applications for $73 million in guarantees have been received. Six of these applications were subsequently withdrawn; six are under review; and four for $20 million in guarantees and 3,583 units have been authorized. Three of the four projects for which guarantees have been authorized are under construction. The sponsors of these projects are United Builders Ltd. (Taiwan), Intercontinental Housing (Thailand) and Maissons Carnoy (Tunisia). Con struction on the fourth project is sponsored by Development Corporation International in Ethiopia, and is expected to start shortly. 

The Balance of Payments Committee has limited the housing guarantee program in areas other than Latin America to $50 million. 

Mr. GALLAGHER. Could you comment, since this again seems one of the problems, what effects this years aid program would have on the balance-of-payments question?

Mr. GAUD. This program has a relatively small impact on the balance-of-payments situation today. Roughly 85 to 87 percent of all our funds will be spent in the United States. The gross impact, the total amount of funds spent overseas is something like $319 million against which we will have repayments of loans of $212 million, meaning the net impact will be $107 million. It is pretty hard to get that much lower because that includes payments that we make to the United Nations, it includes payments made by our employees overseas out of their salaries, it includes disbursements under contracts which were entered into some years back before we started tying our aid, one or two other things of this sort. 

We have come pretty close to the irreducible minimum in terms of the impact on the balance of payments. We won't be able to go much further. What we are trying to do is use our aid program to the extent we possibly can to persuade and induce the recipients of our aid to spend more and more of their own foreign exchange, their own free funds, in the United States.

We are having some success on this. So that we are trying, to the extent that we can, to use the aid program as a vehicle toward improving our balance of payments in indirect ways. This is possible in some countries. It is not at all possible in others.

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Thank you. I should like to refer back to the first year in which I testified before this committee in support of the military assistance program. At that time, the Congress appropriated almost a billion two hundred million dollars in new obligation authority, excluding $400 million for five programs, one of which has since been transferred, and four of which have been proposed for transfer, to the regular Defense budget. That was for fiscal year 

1962. Today, we are asking $596 million for continuing support of the program which, despite reductions in scope and changes in composition during the interim, remains a key instrument of our national security and foreign policy. For those country programs remaining in the fiscal year 1968 proposal, the reduction has been more than 50 percent over the 6-year period. This is the result of a sustained and concerted effort to streamline military assistance and to sharpen the program's focus on primary objectives. 

TRANSFER PROGRAMS 

A major step this year, related to the scope of the program, but not counted as a saving in the fiscal year 1968 figure I have just 109

1967 

given you, is the removal from MAP of programs totaling $242 million which are not directly related to its basic purpose. I shall first address these proposed transfers.

The military assistance program was not designed to support forces actually engaged in combat operations, but rather to equip and train forces and provide stocks of combat consumables essential for the initial defense phase. For this reason the administration last year proposed the transfer of support for South Vietnamese forces and the direct and related costs of other free world forces engaged with us in Vietnam from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget. That transfer, which was approved by the Congress, has greatly facilitated logistics management in South Vietnam, and has relieved the military assistance program, worldwide, of the constant risk of crippling raids on resources caused by the large and unpredictable combat demands in Vietnam.

For fiscal year 1968, similar considerations underlie the proposed transfer of support for the Lao and Thai forces from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget. Laos is engaged in a war to defend itself against North Vietnamese aggression working through the instrument of the Pathet Lao, and to prevent the use of Lao territory by the North Vietnamese to infiltrate personnel and supplies into South Vietnam. Laotian forces are now constantly engaged in combat operations closely associated with the free world effort in Vietnam. Their requirements are large, especially for ammunition and light aircraft; and, being combat-related, they are subject to frequent change.

Thailand too is an integral part of the Vietnam war effort. Indeed, Thailand has agreed to commit more than 2,000 troops to South Vietnam in support of the free world effort there. Access to Thai bases is of great importance to the United States; and the great majority of the almost 35,000 U.S. military personnel in Thailand are there in support of that effort. The outcome of the Vietnam war is of vital concern to Thailand, which is situated just across the Mekong from Laos and the infiltration trails. As you know, Peking and 

Hanoi are continuing their campaign to foment insurgency in Thailand. 

Unanticipated increases in Lao and Thai requirements, stemming from changes in the overall military situation in southeast Asia, have in the past had to be financed by reducing grant programs to other important countries of the free world. Such shifts in the allocation of limited assets (most notably to meet rising Vietnam requirements in 1965) have greatly complicated management of the total program. 

They have also caused understandable concern on the part of the other MAP recipients whose programs were adversely affected. The proposed transfers will remedy this situation; at the same time they will simplify the logistical management in southeast Asia. If the 

Congress approves this proposal, all unexpended balances of fiscal year 1967 and prior-year military assistance programs for Laos and Thailand will be transferred to the accounts of the military departments as of July 1, 1967.

Two other transfers from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget are also proposed by the administration. The first involves the NATO infrastructure program, which provides for

111 the construction and maintenance of facilities needed by the United States and other NATO forces in Europe. The second involves the international military headquarters program, which supports the integrated command structures of NATO, CENTO, and SEATO. 

These programs are not military assistance. They represent the U.S. share of the total costs of two international endeavors; they go to the support of U.S. forces and, therefore, are more appropriately financed by the regular Defense budget.

All four of the transfers we propose to make in fiscal year 1968 reflect a continuing effort to provide military assistance on an increasingly selective basis, in order to attain those specific objectives of U.S. military strategy and foreign policy for which MAP is the best available instrument.

BASIC CRITERIA 

In consonance with this effort, we are applying to our military assistance planning five basic criteria:

The first is that each program should relate very directly to important U.S. security and foreign policy interests, and should contribute to the optimum politico-military approach to the threat faced by the recipient country.

The second is that aid should be responsive to changes in our interests and in the threat, external or internal. 

The third is that precautions must be taken to reduce the chances, however remote, that assistance may be put to unintended purposes, such as regional conflicts or the support of undemocratic regimes. 

The fourth is that grant aid should be terminated, and essential military equipment provided thereafter on a sales basis, with credits as necessary, when a recipient country has developed the ability to bear its own defense burden.

The fifth, but not least, is that, at a time when the conflict in Vietnam makes major claim on our total national assets, we must concentrate assets on programs which are not merely desirable, but indispensable.

There is, of course, nothing new about the essentials of these criteria. 

The differences between the thrust of our fiscal year 1968 effort and that of recent years are those of emphasis rather than of principle. 

The program I am presenting to you today represents the carefully considered and highly selective allocation of funds required to make effective use of military assistance in those cases where MAP can better serve the national interest than any other available military, political, or economic instrument.

FUNDS REQUESTED 

The total program proposed for 1968 (total obligational authority plus MAP assets) is $688 million, for which $596 million in new obligational authority is being requested. I believe there is no foreseeable way of accommodating a cut in these amounts without doing serious damage to our security interests. One-time accretions, such as occurred in fiscal year 1967, cannot be counted upon to cushion the impact of any reductions in new obligational authority. It is, for example, unrealistic to expect a repetition of the program adjustments in recoup-

1967 

ments and reappropriations such as those which released for use in fiscal year 1967 some $54 million more than the original estimate of $110 million. As you know, this substantial sum, available for prioryear suspended and undelivered balances, plus $53.8 million in additional assets accruing in connection with a change in logistic policy, augmented our new obligational authority in fiscal year 1967. Without them, we could not have lived within the reduced fiscal year 1967 new obligational authority figure without decimating the program. 

There is, as I say, no prospect of any comparable accretions in fiscal year 1968. Neither do I foresee any likelihood of reduced requirements for military assistance during the coming year. 

This being the case, I don't hesitate to state my conviction that the future effectiveness of the military assistance program as an instrument of national defense and of U.S. foreign policy depends upon authorization and appropriation of the amount requested by the administration for the coming year.

ALLOCATIONS 

About three-quarters of the proposed total is allocated to five nations adjacent to the U.S.S.R. and Red China where military assistance contributes directly to strengthening their ability to defend themselves against the threat of aggression by Communist neighbors. These countries are Greece, Turkey, Iran, China, and Korea. Their MAPsupported forces are vitally important to our forward strategy for free world common defense.

The remaining fourth of the program is divided between grant assistance for all other recipient countries, on the one hand, and funds required for credit assistance and nonregional expenses, on the other. 

Less than one-fifth of our anticipated total obligational authority for fiscal year 1968 is allocated to grant programs for countries which are not directly exposed to the threat of aggression by Communist neighbors. The fact that these latter programs are, nevertheless, important to the attainment of specific U.S. objectives will, I believe, emerge as 

I proceed to a region-by-region summary of our proposals for the coming year.

FAR EAST 

The situation in Vietnam and our relations with Red China are the pivots of military assistance planning for the Far East. Although one result of the internal upheaval in Mainland China has been a temporary reduction in Chinese interest in the outside world, there has been no diminution in that regime's support of the insurgency against Vietnam and Thailand. The potential for Red Chinese aggression against peripheral nations remains real and cannot be discounted in our global defense planning.

A continuing major objective of military assistance in the Far East is, therefore, to enable independent nations on the fringes of the Chinese land mass to protect their own security by participating in the strategic containment of the regime in Peking. U.S. power and purpose are, of course, indispensable ingredients in such containment; but MAP-supported forces of countries directly exposed to the threat are manning the forward defense line against the expansion of Red

113 Chinese influence in Asia. For this reason, more than 88 percent of the $282.1 million to be allocated to the Far East area in fiscal year 

1968 will be used to strengthen the military capabilities of two na tions-the Republics of China and Korea. 

The Republic of China continues to be threatened by Peking's plans. 

Our security commitment to the defense of Taiwan and the Pescadores remains essential to the survival of the Nationalist Chinese regime, and so do its own efforts. Although that regime has been increasingly successful in improving its military logistics system, maintaining its equipment, and bearing an increasing share of its own defense costs, we will have to continue to supply Taiwan with certain types of military equipment which cannot be produced locally or which are beyond its present means to purchase. Provision of grant assistance remains essential, for example, to insure the maintenance of effective air and naval forces, which constitute the first line of defense for an island 

100 miles from the Chinese mainland.

The proposed program of grant aid, therefore, continues to be essential to our self-interest, as well as to the free world posture in that area.

As you know, the Republic of Korea is directly participating in the Vietnam war a fact of major importance to itself, the area and the United States. Some 46,000 capable Korean troops, including two full combat divisions, are now in Vietnam fighting side by side with our own forces and the South Vietnamese. This contribution attests to the value of our past assistance, both economic and military. Korea is also continuing to develop politically and is playing an expanding role in regional cooperation. The Korean economy is making impressive progress. There remains, however, a requirement for considerable grant aid to South Korea because the military threat from North Korea has not been removed. Recurring North Korean violations in the demilitarized zone, in which the United States and South Korea have suffered casualties, attest to continued North Korean militancy. Moreover, the Red Chinese capability for reintroducing forces into the Korean peninsula cannot be ignored. U.S. forces in Korea, together with our substantial program of military assistance, remain vital to the security of Korea and to general stability in that part of the Pacific area.

As the Vietnam conflict progresses, we have relied increasingly on U.S. bases and facilities in the Philippines. In this regard, we have received excellent support from President Marcos. He is taking steps to deal with the nation's domestic problems, including internal security. 

Like President Park of Korea, he has taken a strong interest in regional security matters. He hosted the Manila Conference. Under his leadership the Philippine Government has sent an engineering construction battalion with supporting security troops, totaling 2,000 men, to Vietnam. The support we provide to the Philippine armed forces through military assistance is thus clearly in our national interest and is consistent with the importance of that country's role in the regional defense efforts of the Pacific area.

1967 NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA 

The Near and Middle East remains of strategic significance to the United States because the area is a political, military, and economic crossroads, and because the flow of Middle East oil is vital to the West. 

We, accordingly, have a large stake in the area's stability and steady development. We also have a strong interest in maintaining our alliance relationships with Greece, Turkey, and Iran, for these three countries stand between the Soviet Union and the warm water ports and oil resources of the Middle East. 

Our substantial military assistance to Greece, Turkey, and Iran over the past two decades has been a major factor in deterring Soviet aggression against these countries and in erecting barriers against subversion. 

We propose to allocate some 97 percent of the $233.9 million in military assistance for the entire region to these three key countries. 

Greece has been heavily dependent upon military assistance for its equipment needs since World War II. The program is responsible for the effective and relatively modern Greek forces which now contribute substantially to the NATO deterrent on the southeast flank. 

MAP has provided modern aircraft, weapons, ships and the educational and technical base to support them. 

Greece has made a determined effort to procure or to produce locally articles previously provided as military assistance. This has permitted the termination (in 1966) of commercial consumable support; but the Greek armed forces still remain dependent upon MAP for major items of military hardware.

Accordingly, the proposed fiscal year 1968 program for Greece is designed to provide the equipment essential for operating requirements and for vitally needed modernization of the ground forces in the areas of tactical mobility, artillery and communications. Secondary emphasis is to be placed on continued modernization of the air force and the navy.

Military assistance has also enabled Turkey to develop strong and relatively modern armed forces which help to block Soviet expansion southward. Like Greece, Turkey has improved its in-country production to the extent that MAP support for commercial consumables was terminated during fiscal year 1967. 

The proposed program for fiscal year 1968, therefore, seeks to meet the urgent need for modernization of ground forces by providing trucks, tanks, artillery, armed personnel carriers, and communications equipment. These items are beyond the capability of Turkey to produce or procure.

Secondary emphasis is to be placed on continued modernization of the air force and navy.

The military assistance program has helped to promote Iranian stability and security, and has fostered Iran's economic and political development in directions compatible with U.S. interests. 

Our present grant assistance commitment to Iran will be completed in fiscal year 1969; and we have been effecting a progressive shift from grant aid to cash and credit sales since 1964, assisted materially by the steady growth of Iran's oil revenues. 

The U.S.S.R. has continued its efforts to extend its influence in the 

Arab world by means of military and economic aid. Since 1955, the

115 Soviet Union has provided substantial quantities of military equipment to the United Arab Republic (UAR), Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. 

The United States has sought to avoid becoming a principal military supplier for any of these Middle Eastern countries; but Soviet action has forced us to supply certain defensive weapons to selected countries in the area, including Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and 

Jordan. 

Except for a small portion of the Jordan program, this has been on a sales basis. In each instance, we have sought, in consultation with other countries, to supply only the minimum amounts necessary to meet the legitimate needs of the recipient and to prevent dangerous imbalances in the area.

At the request of Jordan, the United States agreed in December to provide certain supplementary items of military equipment to strengthen the defensive capability and the morale of the Jordanian armed forces following the unfortunate Israeli retaliatory raid at Sammu. 

A substantial portion of this equipment was airlifted to Jordan. 

With stability now hopefully restored, we expect the fiscal year 1968 program to be of modest proportions. 

Apart from Greece, Turkey, Iran, and Jordan, grant assistance planned for countries in the Near East-south Asian area in fiscal year 1968 is limited to modest amounts for training. 

As you know, the United States halted all military shipments to India and Pakistan in September 1965, as a consequence of the outbreak of hostilities in the subcontinent. Since then, no grant military assistance has been provided to either country; and none is proposed for fiscal year 1968.

The undelivered balances to these countries, as mentioned earlier, were recaptured and used to complement the fiscal year 1967 new obligational authority for other country programs. Since February 

1966, we have permitted these countries to make limited cash and credit purchases of nonlethal military equipment previously supplied under MAP. 

At this point, I would make a passing comment on the great value we attach to the continuing contribution of the United Kingdom toward maintaining peace and stability in the whole broad area east of Suez. British forces in the Middle East and in the Far East have performed invaluable services over the past years, and their continued presence contributes significantly to peacekeeping and security. 

EUROPE 

Fiscal year 1967 marked the virtual termination of the once massive military assistance program for Western Europe. For the most part, European countries are now capable of meeting their military needs from resources generated by their own revitalized economies. 

Former European recipients of U.S. grant aid now satisfy a large percentage of their military requirements by purchases from the United States and through weapons-producing consortia within NATO in which U.S. companies participate. These arrangements make an important contribution to the U.S. international balanceof-payments problem.

1967 

Because of these past successes, military assistance to Western Europe in fiscal year 1968 will be limited to small programs for Spain and Portugal.

AFRICA 

The military assistance programs for Africa are quite limited, amounting to a total of $31.2 million in fiscal year 1968. The amount earmarked for equipment is well within the $25 million ceiling set by the Foreign Assistance Act. 

The material programs for northern Africa are designed to further stability in the Maghreb. There has been a substantial flow of Soviet arms to Algeria in recent years. We have responded by agreeing to provide very limited amounts of military assistance to Algeria's neighbors. In this way, while avoiding an unnecessary arms race, we have assisted in the development of modest defensive forces that will contribute to stability and thus to a sense of security essential to economic and social progress. 

The program for Ethiopia refiects a relationship of mutual cooperation that has existed for some years. The main purpose of our grant aid to Ethiopia is to provide a firm basis for peace and stability within Ethiopian borders as that country continues its program of economic development.

The remaining equipment programs are for the Congo and Liberia. 

In the Congo, our program continues to supplement the efforts of Belgium and other countries to make the Congolese forces capable of maintaining internal order. The rebellion of 1964-65 has been brought under control, but the seeds of dissidence remain; and there will be a continuing need for effective Congolese security forces. The program for Liberia is intended to improve the ability of the Liberian National Guard to carry its responsibility for maintaining order, and also to carry out civic action programs useful to Liberia's economic development.

No materiel will be programed next year for Senegal, Mali, and Guinea. These programs, begun in earlier years, were designed to equip and train engineer construction units for civic action work. We have now been able to provide the equipment needed by these units and, accordingly, the programs are being terminated. 

In addition to the foregoing, we propose to provide training in the United States for limited numbers of African military personnal. 

This training will increase their technical skills, and will also provide an opportunity for them to examine at firsthand our open society and our political institutions.

LATIN AMERICA 

In Latin America, the primary goal of the United States is to promote the social, economic, and political development of each nation so that their people can live in peaceful prosperous societies. 

While progress is being made, that goal is far from achieved. Social tensions, unequal distribution of land and wealth, unstable economies, and the lack of broadly based political structures create a prospect of continuing instability in many parts of Latin America. The answer to these and other associated problems, if one is to be found, lies in the Alliance for Progress, to which we and our Latin American friends

117 are devoting large resources. But the goals of the Alliance can be achieved only within a framework of law and order. 

Our military assistance programs for Latin America thus continue to be directed to the support of internal security and civic action measures. We have sought, with considerable success, to avoid diversion of Latin American resources to the creation or support of unnecessarily large or sophisticated military forces. Our purposes have been to insure that their limited resources are applied to social and economic objectives, and to forestall a regional arms race. While our fiscal year 1967 military assistance programs for Latin America total about $55 million, our programs for economic assistance, by way of contrast, total more than 15 times that amount. 

It is highly unlikely that any Latin American country will soon face a direct military attack from any nation outside the hemisphere, or from Cuba. The principal threat to Latin America takes the form of materiel and leadership support for internal subversion and insurgency, sometimes imported. The Cuban Government, for example, has trained about 5,000 young people from various parts of Latin America in revolutionary ideology, terrorism, and guerrilla warfare. The 

Communist Tri-Continental Conference, held in Havana in January 1966 established a permanent organization to provide support for socalled national liberation movements, particularly those which had already reached the fighting stage. The Communist parties in Latin 

America increasingly stress the creation of broad popular "antiimperialist" fronts. They continue their efforts to penetrate student and other intellectual groups, to control organized labor, and to organize the peasants.

The need to counter these threats by appropriate means is the basis upon which the fiscal year 1968 military assistance programs for Latin American countries are predicated. More specifically, the primary objective in Latin America is to aid, where necessary, in the continued development of indigenous military and paramilitary forces capable of providing, in conjunction with police and other security forces, the needed domestic security. A secondary objective is to increase the ability of Latin American armed forces to perform effective civic action.

In support of these objectives, we propose to allocate $45.5 million in grant aid to Latin America in fiscal year 1968. Of this total, $13 million will be used for training. Within the legislative ceiling of $85 million established last year on the value of military assistance and sales (other than training) to Latin America, therefore, $32.5 million is programed for grant aid equipment and related services; $52.5 million is allocated for cash or credit sales and for the value or ships transferred under ship loan legislation. 

Our continuing effort to hold down Latin American defense forces and expenditures accounts for the fact that the major component of the grant program ($34.7 million, or 76 percent) is for internal security, with emphasis on communications, mobility and training. Another $3.9 million (or 9 percent of the total grant program) is allocated for equipment and training directly associated with civic action. The remaining $6.9 million (or 15 percent of the total) is earmarked for supply operations, regional activities, and other articles and services.

1967 

The grant program will provide no tanks, artillery, fighter aircraft, or combat ships. The emphasis is on vehicles and helicopters for internal mobility, communications equipment for better coordination of in-country security efforts, and spare parts for maintenance of existing inventories.

The program includes training for Latin American military personnel at U.S. schools and in the Canal Zone. In addition to developing military skills, such training continues the close and valuable relationship between United States and Latin American military personnel. 

FOREIGN MILITARY SALES 

During the past 6 years (fiscal years 1962-66) we have progressively developed a program of foreign military sales. This program was originally authorized by the Mutual Defense Assistance Act of 1949 which provided for reimbursable aid; and the authorization was continued in the Mutual Security Acts of 1951 and 1954, and in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended. 

The objectives of the foreign military sales program were established in 1962. They are: (1) to promote the defensive strength of our allies, consistent with U.S. political and economic objectives; (2) to promote the concept of cooperative logistics and equipment standardization with our allies; (3) to offset a substantial part of the dollar outflow resulting from essential U.S. military deployments abroad. 

Over the 6-year period since 1962, military sales, including sales orders, have amounted to $11.1 billion. Five countries (Germany, Italy, United Kingdom, Australia, and Japan) account for $8 billion of this amount, and $2 billion more is attributable to 15 other industrial countries.

Thus, total military sales to the nonindustrialized countries of the Near East, south Asia, Africa, and Latin America represented about $1 billion, or 9 percent, and of this amount, nearly $800 million was attributable to six countries (Iran, Saudi Arabia, Israel, India, Jordan, and Venezuela).

It appears that there continue to be misunderstandings concerning the scope and character of our military sales program. As indicated, over 90 percent of the sales have been made to the highly industrialized countries of Europe and the Far East; and even in those cases, U.S. sales represent only moderate percentages of the total military purchases made by those countries. For example, seven NATO countries are estimated to have spent $26.7 billion during this period, of which $5.9 billion (or 22 percent), represented orders placed in the 

United States.

Similarly, the three major Far Eastern countries (Japan, New Zealand, and Australia) are estimated to have spent $2.8 billion over the same period for major military equipment, of which about $900 million (or 32 percent), represented purchases in the United States. 

It is true that the mix of U.S. military grant aid and credit sales has changed in recent years. In the 1950's, the grant program far exceeded the sales program. At the present time, the ratio is 3 to 2 in favor of sales. But since 1961, the total of the two programs has been remarkably stable, hovering around $3 billion per year; and it appears that the aggregate figure for fiscal year 1967 will be approximately $2.5 billion.

119 The shift is attributable almost entirely to natural economic developments. It has been our purpose for 20 years to strengthen our friends and allies against serious military threats, both external and internal. Since the end of World War II, we have provided billions of dollars of grant military assistance to meet important considerations of U.S. national security. In recent years, the economic advance of many countries has enabled them to assume an increasingly larger responsibility for their own defense costs. This development is reflected in the decline of U.S. military grants and the increase of U.S. military sales. It is consistent with urgings by the Congress. A year ago, the President gave formal recognition to this transition by stating in his message to the Congress on military assistance that "we will shift our military aid program from grant aid to sales whenever possible—and without jeopardizing our security interests or progress of economic development." This remains our policy. 

Let me say just a word about the policy review machinery that governs our foreign military sales. Every military sale made is either consonant with overall policy established by the Department of State, or is specifically subjected to a careful and thorough review within the U.S. Government before a negotiation is instituted. The review is concerned with the military legitimacy of the requirements, the recipient's ability to pay, the potential effect on peace or stability in the area, and other foreign policy considerations.

It is conducted at very high levels of Government, and approval is not given until a positive determination has been made that, balance of payments considerations aside, the sale is in our best national interest.

The U.S. Government is seriously interested in damping down regional tensions and slowing down the pace of arms expenditures. At the same time, we must be concerned with our national strategic interests, to which selective sales of military equipment sometimes make a contribution. Our motivation in such sales has, accordingly, been to assist in deterring an external threat, to help meet an internal security problem, or to contribute to regional stability. 

In many cases, we have successfully reduced or postponed the supply of arms desired by the recipient or, as a condition of the sale, have obtained agreements limiting the diversion of national resources for military purposes. We have, I believe, made extraordinary efforts to dissuade developing nations from overspending on military items. 

As you know, the United States has a serious balance-of-payments problem which responsible officials cannot ignore. Military sales do contribute to an amelioration of our balance-of-payments situation, but we insist that they do so within the framework of the rather stringent sales criteria we have adopted. 

For example, (1) we will not sell military equipment to a foreign country which we believe it cannot afford; (2) we will not ask a foreign country to buy anything which in its judgment, or in ours, is not needed for its armed forces; and (3) we will not ask any foreign country to purchase anything from us which it can buy cheaper or better elsewhere.

Sales operations for each year are financed from a combination of repayments and new obligational authority. For fiscal year 1968, we estimate a requirement of $120.6 million to run the program. We

1967 

anticipate that $55 million of this amount will come from repayments on earlier sales, $5.6 million from a reduction in required reserves owing to repayments, and $60 million in new obligational authority. 

We estimate that this money will be able to finance a program of about $300 million; but the precise total will depend, of course, on the outcome of particular negotiations, and on political factors which are always examined in closest detail. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Although, as I point out each year, my responsibilities do not include planning for or administering supporting assistance, I want once again to express my conviction that such assistance is an integral part of our total effort to promote free world peace and progress. 

I, therefore, consider it appropriate to advocate favorable legislative action on the administration's $745 million fiscal year 1968 request for supporting assistance which will be presented by the Agency for International Development. The use to which AID plans to put that amount of new obligational authority clearly reveals the important role played by supporting assistance in complementing military programs in developing areas where internal security and economic progress are interdependent. Some 90 percent of the $745 million total will be allocated to four countries where the need is most obviously urgent-Vietnam, Korea, Laos, and Thailand-and where our military programs are of the greatest importance. 

CONCLUSION 

The most productive possible use of every dollar appropriated for the military assistance program remains a primary objective. I have satisfied myself that the proposals I have been discussing this morning represent as direct an approach as can be devised to this objective in fiscal year 1968. Every element of the program we propose has met our carefully established criteria and is designed to generate maximum security benefits at minimum cost. I know of no element which can be removed or substantially reduced without serious jeopardy to our national defense and foreign policy interests. I therefore urgently recommend that this committee report favorably on the administration's authorization request for the proposed fiscal year 1968 military assistance program.

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: I welcome this opportunity to appear before you in support of the Military Assistance Program for the Fiscal Year 1968. I consider this program to be an integral part of our national military strategy and I feel a personal responsibility to support it. 

The Military Assistance Program has been drastically cut in recent years and this reduction is a matter of serious concern to the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 

We wholeheartedly support the premise that MAP recipient nations should, whenever possible, increase their contributions toward the development and maintenance of effective military forces, and in our opinion, they have done this. 

However, we consider that it is also in the national interest of the United States to continue to assist them so that excessive amounts of their budgets may not be devoted to military forces to the detriment of essential economic and social re- In our opinion, the goal of stable governments oriented to economic and social progress can best be achieved in the environment of security that our Military Assistance Program is designed to develop. Our concept of military assistance further recognizes that the attainment of the security necessary for social and economic progress in the Free World cannot be achieved by the efforts of any single nation, or even by a small group of nations. Security can only be gained through broad mutual effort. form programs. 

The Fiscal Year 1968 Military Assistance Program reflects the best judgment of the country team, the unified commanders, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Office of the Secretary of Defense. The development of this program takes into consideration an assessment of the enemy threat; the strategic objectives of the United States as reflected in the Joint Strategic Objectives Plan; the international political, economic, and military conditions which affect our objectives; and the impact of the continuing hostilities in Vietnam on the probable availability of military assistance funds. It reflects the absolute minimum assistance considered necessary for those countries that are of particular importance to our security, and to those military forces within those countries that bear a particular complementary relation to our own forces. 

The Joint 

Chiefs of Staff are continually aware of the interlocking relationships that exist between our national military programs and those of military assistance. I am certain that this committee also evaluates this relationship in their review of the military assistance program. 

The current level of appropriations does not provide for the previously planned replacement of much of the equipment that is rapidly becoming obsolescent. and that demands continually increasing funds for maintenance. The deferment of this force improvement becomes more of risk because of the steady improvement in the quality of equipment of the forces of the Soviet Union, Communist China, and other Communist-controlled nations. Fully cognizant of the fact that considerations other than military, such as our ultimate political and economic objectives for the various areas, must be weighed in determining the minimum level of the annual military assistance program, we are convinced that reductions below the current level are not justified by the military situation facing the United States and its Free World allies today and in the near term.

Approximately three-quarters of this year's program will be in support of the forces of those countries on the periphery of the great communist land areas. These funds will assist the Republic of China, Korea, Greece, Iran, and 

Turkey to maintain almost two million men under arms in collective defense of security interests that we share with them. If we had to replace any part of this force with our own men, the proportionate cost would be considerably more than that of the military assistance furnished. These peripheral countries are contributing a substantial portion of their budgets to the support of their armed forces; however, none has the capability of assuming full support of its forces. Further reduction of our assistance to these forward defense countries could be misinterpreted by the recipient nations as a lessening of U.S. interest in their security and encourage the communist powers to initiate actions to occupy the power vacuums that could result. The consequences would be a weakening or dissolving of the mutual security arrangements the United States has with these countries, and thus, a reduction of U.S. security. 

Approximately 50% of the small remaining balance of this program is for the assistance required by the Latin American countries. The grant aid program is not designed to encourage the acquisition of sophisticated or prestige

1967 

type armament. A portion of these limited funds assists such civic action efforts as the building of roads and schools, projects which have a direct and favorable impact on the economic and social programs of the countries. The 

MAP for Latin America contributes to achievement of the objectives of the Alliance for Progress. The countries of Latin America are at an important stage in their development, and it is in the best interests of this nation to assist them in establishing the stabilized conditions necessary to attain a higher standard of living.

The balance of the program is in support of those countries wherein the United States has special interests and specific obligations. The Joint Chiefs of Staff are in full agreement that the Military Assistance Program for FY 68 reflects the bare minimum in military aid that is required to further our national interests and the security of the Free World.

Mr. MAILLIARD. May I ask one question on the administration of the program. When you are talking about military sales, what is the procedure? Does a special section of the Defense Department act as an intermediary between a purchaser and the source or do you deal directly with the source with the consent of the- Secretary MCNAMARA. It varies. But generally a special section of the Defense Department acts as an adviser or consultant to the nation making the procurement because, in many cases, the nation is uncertain as to what to procure-whether it should be rifles or trucks or aircraft or tanks and will ask for counsel and advice from the Defense Department.

In other cases, after it has decided what to procure, it faces serious problems with respect to financing the sale and may, in some cases, request credit assistance. In other cases, it has no means of actually making effective contact with commercial sources. It has, in effect, no purchasing agents skilled in the procurement of military equipment.

So our Department, after appropriate consultation with State and other elements of the Government, provides whatever services are necessary to meet the objectives of the procuring country.

Rather than wait until the deal is consummated, they will usually discuss the matter with us very early in the transaction.

Mr. Selden.

Mr. SELDEN.  

Mr. Secretary, if the views of those who oppose this legislation were to prevail, and this program were to be eliminated, would it then be necessary to add additional funds to the military budget, and if so, how much?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think that would be one alternative we should consider. In certain areas in the world, it would be one we could undertake. In other cases, I think it would be impossible by any reasonable amount of expenditure to so strengthen our forces as to offset the failure to support other forces in the free world through the military aid program.

The result would be that we would either be forced to change our political commitments, or suffer substantial additional military risk because we were facing the potential threat of aggression and fulfillment of commitments without adequate means to meet them. 

Mr. SELDEN. Would you also say, however, that the cost would be considerably more?

Mr. SELDEN. Then you would not consider a vote to eliminate this program an economy vote?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Quite the contrary. Even in the cases where we could substitute U.S. forces for foreign forces, the cost would far exceed the small amount we are asking for in this program.

Mr. Secretary, following up on one or two questions that Congressman Mailliard asked, as I remember last year there was no opposition from the Defense Department in connection with a limitation on grants of military equipment to Latin America, but there was some concern as far as the limitation on sales.

137 

Secretary MCNAMARA. That is true. 

Mr. SELDEN. Has your position changed on that?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Let me say this. I think we can live within the total of $85 million for both grant and sales. I may prove wrong.

Secretary MCNAMARA. When we face those decisions, we invariably tend in choosing to force them to buy from foreign sources. This has happened in the past year. It is one reason that we are able to live within the $85 million, and why I think we can live within it in the future. We don't want to sell them equipment they don't need. 

Mr. SELDEN. Would it be advisable to have limits on certain military equipment?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. If they decide at Punta del Este this week not to buy some. Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. 

Mr. SELDEN. Do you feel there has been substantial improvement in the internal security programs of the different countries of Latin America? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think there has been. They have faced some serious guerrilla threats in several countries and they have increased their capability for facing those threats. (The prepared statement of Admiral Heinz is as follows:) STATEMENT OF VICE ADMIRAL L. C. HEINZ, U.S. NAVY, DIRECTOR OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE, ON THE FISCAL YEAR 1968 MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: Once again, it is my responsibility to appear before this Committee and report in some detail on the current status of the Military Assistance Program and the Administration's request for fiscal year 1968 authorization and appropriations. Secretary McNamara has already presented to you, in broad outline, the proposed program and the considerations upon which it is based. I therefore propose to review briefly the major changes which have been made in the current year program since it was submitted to you last year, and then discuss our proposals for fiscal year 1968 as set forth in the Congressional Presentation Document which you have before you. 

There are three major points I would address regarding the implementation of the fiscal year 1967 program. First, the Congress directed that military assistance, other than training in the United States, could not be furnished to more than forty countries. We have complied with this limitation by not implementing certain proposed country programs and by reducing others to CONUS training only, eliminating material support and overseas training. The details of the individual country changes made to remain within the 40 country limitation are shown on pages 20-25 of the Congressional Presentation Document. 

Secondly, the Congress placed a limitation of $85 million on total military assistance and sales (other than training) to American Republics. To comply with this provision of the law, and in view of the decreased appropriation for military assistance in 1967, we have reduced originally proposed grant aid and sales programs to the combined total authorized. Grant aid was reduced [security deletion] from the amount originally allocated to the area, with major reductions in the five largest individual country programs [security deletion]. 

Credit sales are also being limited, and cash sales, mainly of spare parts and training ammunition, carefully controlled. The allocation of our assistance to 

Latin America, including both grant aid and sales, is shown on page 90 of the 

Congressional Presentation Document. 

149

1967 

Third, there became available to MAP in 1967 some additional resources that were not anticipated at the time of our presentation last year, which counterbalanced to some extent the reduced appropriation and the increased requirements in the Far East associated with the conflict in Vietnam. These additional resources consisted of two major items. The first resulted from the decision to cancel suspended and undelivered balances for Pakistan and India, except for equipment being provided India for the border road program in Nepal. 

This decision made an additonal $43.1 million in recoupments available for application to other countries in the FY 1967 program. The second item resulted from a change in logistic support policies, stemming from the war in Vietnam. 

MAP had in the past provided funds to the Army and Air Force for stockage of spare parts and other items required for equipment in use in MAP-supported armed forces but no longer in use in our own services. With the assumption by the military departments of support of free world forces in Vietnam, a situation was created wherein both the military departments and MAP were funding stockage of support items for equipment previously peculiar to MAP. Accordingly, the 

Secretary of Defense changed the logistic support policy, and assigned to the military departments responsibility for stockage of logistic support for all military equipments items, whether in the military systems or for grant aid. 

The total funding previously provided by MAP to the Army and Air Force for procurement and stockage of MAP owned logistic support items was $53.8 million. With the change in policy, this equity in material was transferred to the 

Departments of the Army and Air Force; and equal credits for the withdrawal of spare parts were made available to MAP, with such credits to be used in FY 1967. Since no funding was involved, this had the effect of increasing MAP assets to be applied to the program in FY 1967 by $53.8 million. 

To complete this report, I would mention briefly individual country changes. 

The major increases were in the Far East, where there were program increases amounting to almost [security deletion]. Although we did not propose any program for Indonesia a year ago, the favorable turn of events in that country has presented an unforeseen requirement to manifest United States support of the new government by providing in FY 1967 modest assistance to the civic action programs of the Indonesian military.

The augmentation of those Far East area country programs, in response to increased requirements associated with the conflict in Vietnam and the change for the better in Indonesia, is cleary consistent with our national security and foreign policy interests at a time and place where those interests are very much at stake. To facilitate that augmentation within the limits of reduced fund availability, there was a [security deletion] million reduction in the program for the 

In Africa, the net total FY 1967 allocation rose by $1.4 million. There was a $2 million increase to the program for [security deletion] pursuant to a Presidential Determination, and designed to promote a more stable situation in the North African area. This was partially offset by other minor decreases. 

With respect to the Near East-South Asia region, the major change was the cancellation of programs for India and Pakistan. The only significant increase in this area was that [security deletion] resulted from the crisis in November 1966 and the consequent need to provide a significant and immediate augmenta tion of [security deletion] defense capabilities [security deletion]. 

In Europe, there was a decrease [security deletion] reflecting reductions in all four country programs-Norway, Denmark, Portugal and Spain. Our commitments to Norway and Denmark have now been completely funded-Denmark in FY 1966 and Norway in FY 1967; and we no longer have any programs for these countries.

I have already mentioned the reduction [security deletion] in Latin American programs, mainly in those for the larger countries.

FAR EAST 

With the proposed transfer to the regular Defense budget of responsibility for funding the military support requirements of Laos and Thailand, the main thrust of the MAP effort in the Far East area is toward support of the self and common defense capabilities of the Republics of China and Korea. 

The largest individual country program we propose for FY 1968 is that for the Republic of Korea, in the amount of [security deletion] million. This amount is required to enable the Republic of Korea to maintain in Korea the combat-ready posture of its armed forces for deterrence and defense, while continuing major troop deployments to South Vietnam. In military terms, the threat to South 

Korea remains approximately the same as in the past. Infiltration efforts from 

North Korea continue, and vigilance to counter them cannot be relaxed. It is necessary that we maintain in Korea a powerful and effective deterrent to Communist attack. This requires force improvement [security deletion] particularly in the air force and army, replacement of [security deletion] equipment, improved capabilities for air defense, strengthened counter-infiltration capabilities and improved mobility of forces. The FY 1968 program is designed with these purposes in mind. Major items being provided include [security deletion] communications equipment, engineering equipment and training ammunition. The program in the overall is balanced to meet the needs of maintaining those Korean forces which, together with United States forces stationed in Korea, constitute the deterrent required there.

NEAR EAST-SOUTH ASIA 

Because of the strategic importance of the Near East and South Asia to the United States, military assistance amounting to almost $6 billion has been allocated to countries in the area since the beginning of the program in 1950. Our still vital security interests throughout the region are the basis upon which we propose an FY 1968 area program totaling $234 million most [security deleted] of that amount will go to three key forward defense countries, each of which is very directly exposed to potential aggression by well-equipped and trained Communist military forces.

Two of these countries-Greece and Turkey-account for only 13% of the NATO population, but provide almost one-third of the NATO land forces. Their defense capabilities are therefore a vitally important deterrent to attack along NATO's southern flank. They make an equally important contribution to the common defense of the entire area [security deletion] by having granted the 

United States vital overflight rights [security deletion]. 

The capability of Greece to meet the Communist threat depends in great measure upon United States assistance, which provides practically all investment type military equipment. Greece has, however, made a concerted effort to procure or to produce locally some articles previously provided by MAP. Her principal efforts have been in commercial consumable support, supply of which was terminated by the United States in 1966, in-country ammunition production, rehabilitation of vehicles, and ship construction and overhaul. The proposed [security deletion]

153 million FY 1968 program for Greece is designed to cover minimum modernization and operating requirements of the Greek Armed Forces. It will provide urgently needed modernization of the ground forces in the areas of tactical mobility, artillery and communications. Secondary emphasis is on continued modernization of the air force and minor modernization of naval units. We have, over the past year, emphasized long-range planning with the Greeks, based upon the most realistic estimate possible of total resources that will be available for defense. 

[Security deletion.] The FY 1968 program supports this planning. 

Turkey's defense problems are compounded by extensive land and sea frontiers with her Communist neighbors. Since Turkish armed forces, augmented as required by other NATO forces, have the responsibility for defending NATO's southeast flank against a Soviet-supported offensive, the country's military capability is of major importance to United States security. As with Greece, Turkey in the past year has made substantial progress toward realistic long-range defense planning, and priorities for force improvement have been developed. The most urgent requirement is for modernization in the ground forces, which need increased mobility and firepower. Navy effectiveness is limited by obsolescence, but has been improved by the recent delivery of two destroyers authorized by ship loan legislation. Air force capability also has been improved through the delivery of F-5 aircraft. Substantial progress in in-country production made it possible to terminate MAP support for commercial consumables with the FY 1967 program. Major in-country defense production accomplishments through that year include ammunition production, petroleum refining, vehicle assembly, overhaul of submarines and in-country naval construction. Still, much remains to be done. 

The proposed FY 1968 program amounts to [security deletion] million. Its emphasis is placed on modernization of ground forces in tactical mobility [security deletion]. Secondary emphasis is on continued modernization of the air force

LATIN AMERICA 

Since Secretary McNamara has already discussed quite fully both the basic rationale for and general thrust of our military assistance effort to Latin America, I shall proceed directly to a more specific and detailed account of the individual country programs we propose for that area in FY 1968. 

More than half of the total $45.5 million allocation to Latin America will go to the five major countries of Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru. 

Military assistance to Latin America is subject to two major legislative restrictions. I believe that it is appropriate to recapitulate the manner in which our proposals for FY 1968 comply with both the letter of the law and the intent of the Congress. Within the $85 million ceiling established last year on value of military assistance and sales (other than training), $52 million is allocated for sales of various kinds, and $32.5 million for grant aid. The difference between this $32.5 million grant aid figure and the total proposed grant aid program of $45.5 million is the $13 million earmarked for grant aid training which is not covered by the $85 million ceiling.

Threefifths of the total amount allocated to the area will be used to furnish improved mobility in internal security operations. Another quarter will provide communications and engineer equipment, with the remainder going for various items, including spare parts. This equipment will strengthen the countries' capabilities for internal security, and is patently not the sophisticated or "prestige-type" equipment which could lead to increased defense expenditures or contribute to any type of an area arms race.

CREDIT ASSISTANCE AND NONREGIONAL COSTS 

With completion of the regional and selective country review of our grant aid proposals for FY 1968, there remains the allocation for credit assistance and some $30 million allocated for nonregional costs. 

We propose to allocate $60 million of new obligational authority to credit assistance in FY 1968. The basic purpose of the credit assistance program is essentially the same as that of the grant program-to promote the defensive strength of allied and friendly nations in support of our overall foreign policy objectives.

In the nonregional portion of the program, the largest single item is $21.4 million for administrative expenses. Although the decrease of almost $2 million in this item represents administrative expenses associated with programs we pro-

157 pose to transfer to the regular Defense budget, the fact that there is no net increase in the balance is the result of our continuing effort to offset rising civilian personnel salaries and increased administrative costs by reducing both the number of personnel engaged in the MAP operation worldwide and administrative support to the minimum consistent with efficient program management. 

Other nonregional costs are associated with weapons production assistance to NATO multilateral organizations undertaking production of United States weapons and weapons systems; operation of the Military Assistance Institute; and reimbursement to the State Department for administrative support. 

Gentlemen, this completes my formal presentation of a program which I believe is sound in concept and content.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Admiral. 

Admiral, on page 25 of the book, fourth line from the bottom, it appears that the aid program for fiscal 1967 was reduced by $62,225,000

1967 

because items adding up to this total were transferred from "Military assistance" to the Defense Department budget. The explanation in the book is rather technical.

Would you explain, Admiral, what happened, and why this was done? 

Admiral HEINZ. Yes, sir. In prior years, MAP funded the stockage of spare parts for equipment provided to allied forces for which the U.S. services had no need to stock spare parts. This is equipment which is no longer in use in the U.S. forces.

Over the period of the years of 1961 to 1966, we had allocated some $53.8 million to the stockage of such spare parts. With the transfer of the Vietnam program to service funding, the services then took on the responsibility for supplying spare parts to forces in Vietnam for equipment which previously had been peculiar to MAP. 

The result was that both MAP and the services were funding stockages of the same type of spare parts. As a result of this situation, the 

Secretary of Defense changed the logistics support policy and said that henceforth the services would bear the responsibility for stockage of spare parts for all inventories, both MAP and service. As a result, the stockage that was MAP owned was turned over to the services. They in turn gave MAP a credit, for use in 1967, which could be applied to spare parts in the service inventories.

It was a release of funds to MAP in fiscal year 1967 that had previously been tied up in spare parts. It was not a service funding of MAP, rather it was the services getting the MAP equity and giving us a drawdown in fiscal year 1967. This accounts for $54 million of the increase.

There were two other items involved. One that we had not anticipated was [security deletion].

There were other minor increases totaling about $2 million, which 

I won't go into in detail.

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, I recently read in the press about the trouble in Bolivia. In this morning's papers there is a report that six or seven military personnel have been assigned to this operation, and the Ambassador, according to the press reports I have read, has been trying to obtain military hardware in order to combat guerrilla operations down there for some time.

Apparently there are some helicopters and other essential military hardware being assigned to Bolivia now. Is that guerrilla operation in 

Bolivia getting out of control of the Bolivian authorities? 

Admiral HEINZ. No, sir; it is not getting out of control. [Security deletion.] The original estimates of the guerrilla forces were from 

200 to 400. We think now the best estimate is perhaps 100. Two helicopters are being delivered to Bolivia at the present time. 

It so happens that these were two helicopters already programed in MAP some time ago, and they are not in response to this current threat. The Bolivian forces do need better training to handle a threat of this type. There is no question about that. 

They have requested expanded training in Bolivia. It is correct that we are sending a few instructors down there. We have not flooded them with equipment. We have given them some combat rations. 

Chairman MORGAN. Is it true, Admiral, that the helicopter has become a very useful instrument in fighting against guerrillas including its usefulness in getting the wounded out?

Admiral HEINZ. It is one of the most useful instruments that we have in the total inventory for guerrilla warfare. An example is shown in Latin America where you can get a number of troops up

1967 

into the hills where guerrillas usually hide out in a very short time, whereas it would take them days and sometimes weeks to get up there by land where there are no roads.

169 Mr. BROOMFIELD. On the broader spectrum of military sales, a few years ago I sponsored an amendment I am not sure if it is still operative pertaining to the sales or grants in military sales to be used solely for internal security. What protection do we have under the military sales program to assure us that what we do sell to certain countries will be used solely for internal security? 

Admiral HEINZ. I don't know that internal security only is a restriction on military sales. Defense is the major restriction on military sales. Each time we make a sale of military equipment, we have an agreement that that equipment will not be transferred to a third country without our permission.

We have an agreement it will be used for defense only, and I think that these agreements have been lived up to. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. But if a country has the money to buy military sales that is about the only provision required, as long as they can pay for it. If there are problems of credit, then we come in as far as restricting what we feel they can use adequately, isn't that true? 

Admiral HEINZ. It isn't a question of selling them everything they ask for. We do not do this by a long shot. We do have a relatively liberal free sales policy, for example, to NATO partners, because there we have common planning and we know how they propose to use the equipment. To other countries, we sell perhaps only one-third of what they request to buy from us.

As you are well aware, we have a very tight control on sales to Latin America. We could have sold more to Latin America than we have. 

We do not sell all that we can in areas such as Latin America, Africa, or the Near East.

There are other countries we are making sales to; for example, Japan. Here we know what they are going to use the equipment for. 

We know it is of a defensive character. There is a large segment of our sales to Japan which is for air defense installations. 

Our sales to India and Pakistan have been very carefully controlled and have been limited to nonlethal equipment. [Security deletion.]

At the same time we have sold at reduced prices such items as M-48 tanks, which are several years old. We have made offers, for example, to sell F-86 aircraft, which are about 20 years old, but which are supportable for at least 5 or 6 more years.

Mr. WHALLEY. On the newer equipment, do we get the price of our cost, or do we sell it to them for reduced prices? 

Admiral HEINZ. No, sir; the contracts are based upon the full cost, including recoupment of the administrative costs of the sales transaction. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Is our aid to Greece and Turkey affected by their difficulty on Cyprus?

173 Admiral HEINZ. No; it is not. There is, of course, the continuing problem of Cyprus, but our aid to Greece and Turkey has been and is based upon the continuing NATO effort. We are continuing our aid and we hopefully anticipate the Cyprus conflict can be settled by peaceful means.
