(The following memorandum has been supplied for the record by the Department of Defense:) EXPLANATION OF AMENDMENTS PROPOSED BY THE EXECUTIVE BRANCH TO PART II (MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM) OF THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1961, AS AMENDED REORGANIZATION OF STATUTORY PROVISIONS 

Most of the amendments proposed by the Executive Branch to part II of the Act are technical in nature and are designed to delineate more clearly those provisions which apply to the military assistance program and those provisions which apply to the military sales program. They are intended as a forward step in clarifying the scope of these programs. 

Circumstances of history, in particular the clearly weakened economic conditions of most countries following World War II, forced on the United States the role of major armament supplier to the free world. During the decade of the 

1950s, the United States met the legitimate armament needs of its friends primarily through a major grant aid program. By the latter part of the decade, however, many of these countries had become prosperous again, enabling them to produce more of their own arms or buy them abroad. 

In terms of total value, US military exports in the 10 year period, FY 19621971 are not expected to be measurably higher than in the decade, FY 1952–1961; the big change will be in the shift in the way these exports are financed-from grant aid in the '50s to military sales in the '60s. By FY 1961, grant aid had declined from an average annual level of $2 billion-plus during the 1950s to about $1.5 billion. Since FY 1961 this downward trend has continued as grant aid declined both absolutely and relatively. Whereas in FY 1961 there were $2 of grant aid for every dollar of military sales to foreign recipients, by FY 1966 the ratio had been reversed. 

In view of this shift in emphasis from grant aid to sales-a shift called for by the Congress in section 506(c) of the Act-it appears desirable at this time to recodify the statutory provisions applicable to the grant aid and sales programs so as to delineate those provisions applicable to both programs and those provisions applicable only to grant aid or to sales. Under the present Act, for example, the general authority for grant aid and for reimbursable transactions (i.e., sales, exchanges, leases, and guaranties) are commingled in one sectionsection 503. Other provisions affecting these authorities are scattered through the remainder of part II of the Act in various sections. Hence, the uninformed reader of part II can be led astray in seeking to ascertain the authority governing particular kinds of transactions. The guaranty authority is illustrative of this, part of the authority being contained in section 503 (e) of the Act and part in section 509 (b) of the Act. Similarly, restrictions on grant aid to Latin America are found not only in section 511 of the Act but also in section 505(b) of the 

Act. 

To reorganize the statutory provisions into a clearer form is, accordingly, the primary purpose of the technical amendments proposed by the Executive Branch. As a result of this reorganization, part II is divided into three chapters. 

Chapter 1 sets forth the policy governing military assistance and sales and the terms which govern the utilization of defense articles and defense services granted or sold under part II. Chapter 2 consists of the substantive provisions of the military assistance program. Chapter 3 sets forth the substantive provisions of the foreign military sales program, which comprises cash sales, credit sales, guaranties, exchanges, and leases. 

---

1967 SUBBSTANTIVE AMENDMENTS 

The remaining amendments proposed by the Executive Branch to part II of the Act would accomplish the following substantive changes. 

1. Two Year Authorization for Appropriations and "Draw-down" Authority 

Sections 201 (c) and (j) of the bill authorize MAP appropriations for the fiscal years 1968 and 1969 and extends for the same period the authority to draw-down defense stocks to meet emergencies. A two-year authorization would evidence 

Congressional recognition that military assistance is in our national interest, that the program does occupy an established place in our overall foreign policy, and that there is a long-term security job to do. 

Certain parts of the AID program-development loans and the Alliance for Progress have traditionally been authorized for more than one year. These two programs are now authorized through FY 1969, and two-year authorizations are also being requested for other AID programs. A two-year authorization for military assistance would bring it into line with the economic assistance programs, and provide each new Congress with an opportunity to review military assistance in the light of changing world circumstances. Approprations, of course, would continue to be made annually, and the Executive Branch would present the off-year programs to the Committee on Foreign Affairs in whatever form or degree of detail the Committee desired. 

2. Transfer of MAP for Laos and Thailand, Infrastructure, and International 

Military Headquarters from Foreign Assistance Act to DOD Legislation 

The miiltary assistance program was not designed to support forces actually engaged in combat operations, but rather to equip forces and provide stocks of combat consumables essential to initial defense against overt aggression. For this reason, it was proposed last year to transfer the support of South Vietnamese and other free world forces engaged in the defense of the Republic of Vietnam from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget. That change, which was approved by the Congress, has facilitated the effective management of both our logistics resources in South Vietnam and of the military assistance program world-wide.

This year, similar considerations underlie the proposed transfer in FY 1968 of the miiltary assistance support costs of the Lao and Thai forces from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget. Laotian forces are heavily engaged in combat operations closely associated with the free world effort in 

Vietnam; and their requirements, especially for ammunition and light aircraft, are largely combat-related and are subject to further change. United States access to Thai bases is vital for United States aircraft operating against North Vietnam, and the Thai Government will soon be sending some of its ground forces to fight beside our own and other free world forces in South Vietnam. 

Two other transfers from the military assistance program to the regular Defense budget are also proposed in section 201(b)(2) and (3) of the bill. The first involves the NATO Infrastructure Program which provides for the construction and maintenance of facilities needed by NATO forces in Europe, including those committed to NATO by the United States and deployed throughout the NATO area. The second involves the International Military Headquarters 

Program which supports the integrated command structures of NATO, CENTO and SEATO. These programs, which represent the United States' share of the total costs of the two endeavors, are principally related to the support of our own forces and should properly be financed in the regular Defense budget. 

3. Elimination of 40 Country Restriction on MAP 

The 40 country restriction which section 504 (a) of the Act imposes upon MAP is removed by section 201(c) of the bill in order to permit the President to conduct U.S. foreign policy with an adequate degree of flexibility. While it is the goal of the Executive Branch to reduce the number of recipient countries as rapidly as practicable without jeopardizing our security, a fixed ceiling on the number of countries which can be given military assistance is an arbitrary restriction on the President's ability to respond quickly to changing world requirements.

189 

4. Exchanges

Section 201 (i) (4) (B) of the bill adds an optional way of carrying out barter transactions, which does not involve MAP funding. Under sections 503 (a) and 

509 (a) of the Act (which are continued in being by section 201(i) (1), (2), (3), and (4)(A) of the bill as new sections 527(a) and (b)), MAP funds may be used to procure defense articles and defense servies for barter with friendly foreign countries for other defense articles and defense services. The defense articles and defense services received in exchange may be used to carry out part II or may be transferred to any United States Government agency. In some cases, barter transactions have been carried out under this authority solely in furtherance of part II of the Act. In other cases, barter transactions under this authority have had the dual purpose of further part II of the Act and also of acquiring defense articles and defense services from other countries to meet the requirements of our own armed forces. In the latter kind of transactions, the MAP appropriation account is, under existing law, not reimbursed by the applicable military function appropriation until the items received as exchange are delivered to the Military Departments. The new authority propsed by section 201 (i) (4) (B) would enable such transactions to be carried out without prefunding by MAP, and this would avoid tying up and temporarily diverting MAP funds from other program uses. 

5. Credit Sales 

Section 201 (p), which re-enacts that part of section 503 (a) of the Act relating to general authority for credit sales as subsections (a) and (b) of a new section 524, also adds a new credit sales authority as subsection (b)(3) of section 524. This subsection, which would further the intent of Congress as expressed elsewhere in the Act to utilize private channels, where possible, in carrying out programs under the Act, authorizes the purchases of promissory notes issued by a foreign country to a commercial supplier which has sold defense articles and services directly to the country. 

In some cases, friendly foreign governments may, for political and/or economic reasons, desire to deal directly with the U.S. private supplier or lending institution rather than with U.S. Government agencies. This new authority-like the existing sales authority-would be used only when it is in the U.S. national interest that such sales be made. Under this subsection, DOD would, with respect to approved sales, arrange in advance with U.S. suppliers to acquire from them promissory notes issued by foreign countries and either hold these or dispose of them, in whole or in part, to appropriate financial institutions. It should be noted that enactment of this subsection would not have the effect of increasing the funds available for financing credit sales or the total volume of sales which could legally be financed by such funds; it would only provide an additional optional means of utilizing available funds to carry out approved programs for the assumption by friendly countries of a larger share of the burden of their own defense.

STATEMENT OF ADM. U. S. G. SHARP, U.S. NAVY, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, PACIFIC 

Admiral SHARP. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a pleasure to appear before this distinguished committee for the third time. I greatly appreciate the opportunity. My comments today will relate the Pacific command military assistance program to the strategic situation in the Far East-particularly in southeast Asia-and emphasize the manner in which this particular program is an integral part of our total effort to meet the Communist challenge. 

There are three main factors that comprise the backdrop of the military assistance program: 

First, the Communist threat.

Second, the posture of those friendly and allied forces assisted by the United States. 

Third, the war in southeast Asia.

Today, I will address each of these factors separately, and will start with the threat.

The aggressive, militant nature of Asian Communist power continues and this remains our basic problem. Communist China is the primary military threat with manpower being their greatest assetover 2,600,000 in their armed forces.

It is apparent that the Communists' confrontation with the United States has focused increasingly on Vietnam. Here, the North Vietnamese are attempting to extend their control over all of Vietnam, testing the feasibility of the so-called wars of national liberation, a strategy championed by the Chinese. The success or failure of the 

Communists' use of revolutionary warfare to take over other nations 191

1967 

will be determined in southeast Asia. Today, the ultimate success of this strategy must appear doubtful, even to the Chinese. 

At the same time, China has allocated a substantial portion of her scarce resources to the development of nuclear weapons. This priority has been implemented at a time when the country is experiencing internal difficulties. While these weapons offer no present threat to the continental United States, they could in time be used in the Far East as regional blackmail to enhance Peking's prestige and as a threat to our forces in the Western Pacific.

We depend on our allies in the Western Pacific to complement U.S. military power. With the exception of Japan, the economies of our Asian allies severely limit the resources they can devote to the maintenance and modernization of their forces. Their capabilities depend heavily on U.S. assistance. The United States must provide the major air and naval forces. On the other hand, the manpower our allies can make available for ground forces is an equally essential ingredient. The combat divisions of the Republics of Korea and 

China, which are supported by the military assistance program, are among the most effective allied forces in the Pacific area. 

With reference to Korea, we remember that, officially, the Korean war is not over. We are under an armistice which is frequently broken by North Korean armed forays and the infiltration of agents. The 

North Korean Army and Air Force are deployed in such a manner that an attack into South Korea could be initiated with a minimum of advance warning. Additionally, the Chinese Communists could reinforce the North Koreans with substantial ground and air support. 

Facing this threat, we must maintain effective Korean and United 

States forces in Korea. 

For fiscal year 1968 the military assistance program will provide some improvements for the South Korean forces. Included in these improvements are aircraft for the air force; firepower, mobility, and communications for the army and marines; and an improved antiinfiltration capability for the navy.

I should like to emphasize one key point with reference to the previous MAP programs in Korea. As you know, approximately 46,000 troops and five ships of the Republic of Korea are on duty in Vietnam. 

The major organizations are two infantry divisions and a marine brigade, all of which have performed exceptionally well. These troops, which were previously MAP supported, are well-equipped, have proven to be well-trained, and are doing a professional job. I would say that the results achieved by these forces in combat testify dramatically to the ultimate value of the military assistance program. 

The Japanese Self-Defense Forces, primarily as a result of military assistance given in past years, are now capable of maintaining internal security, providing security for United States and Japanese bases and, in coordination with U.S. forces, assisting in the defense of 

Japan. However, the Japanese recognize that further improvements in defense capabilities are used. The recently approved third defense buildup plan will provide a significant improvement in air defense and antisubmarine forces over the next 5 years. 

The United States has a major interest in the execution of Japanese defense buildup plans. First, as the Japanese defensive posture improves, the demand on U.S. forces decreases; and second, it is in the

193 interest of the United States and Japan that our forces be logistically compatible and mutually supporting. 

The Republic of China Armed Forces, with a strength of approximately 600,000, present a formidable force in deterring a Chinese Communist invasion of Taiwan and the Penghus, and cause the Chicom's to station considerable ground forces on the mainland opposite Taiwan. The Republic of China is a major link in our defensive strategy. Its bases, airfields, harbors, and early warning capabilities are valuable in supporting our own requirements. The Republic of 

China's contribution of highly professional teams in agriculture, psychological warfare, electric power, and surgery supports the Government of Vietnam's nation building effort. 

Improved capabilities for the Republic of China forces continue to be programed in the areas of surveillance and detection radars. The 

Republic of China's purchase through foreign military sales of aircraft, to establish a barrier patrol in and about the contiguous waters of the Taiwan Straits, will provide better observation of Chinese Communist ship and aircraft movements.

The Republic of China Air Force continues to improve its air defense capability by conversion of the outdated F-86F squadrons to F-5 tactical fighter squadrons. Airlift capablity will be improved. The navy shows an improvement through acquisition of additional ships; also, the ship rehabilitation and conversion programs, fostered under foreign military sales and cost sharing, will give improved capabilities.

The Republic of China forces have made significant strides in the area of self-sufficiency. They now perform major overhaul of virtually all types of aircraft, vehicles, ships, engines, and a wide range of lesser equipment. Production capabilities at the factories and arsenals of the combined service forces include co-production of military general purpose vehicles, manufacture of small caliber ammunition, and other significant self-help projects. 

Before discussing the Philippines and the other MAP-supported nations of southeast Asia, a few thoughts on the value of SEATO to U.S. interests and objectives in southeast Asia are appropriate. 

During the past year, the value of the SEATO framework has been dramatically underscored. It has provided the indispensable constitutional base on which all five of the Pacific members of the alliance have provided forces to assist South Vietnam. During the same year the Australians tripled their forces in South Vietnam. New Zealand contributes a combat unit. The Philippine Civic Action Group, com posed of security and construction troops, arrived in Vietnam. Thailand is operating two C-123 aircraft, a patrol craft, and an LST.

Looking beyond Vietnam it is clear the entire thrust of southeast Asia regional cooperation will depend upon a secure and stable area. It is difficult to perceive how, in the short term, this security might be provided solely by indigenous military efforts. Accordingly, SEATO will continue to play an important part in providing southeast Asia with the essential framework for needed security. 

Turning to the Philippines-maintenance of a free and increasingly prosperous Republic of the Philippines is clearly in our national interest.

1967 

When President Marcos took office at the end of 1965, he assumed the leadership of a country beset by grave problems. President Marcos is conscientiously attempting to deal with these problems and is making headway. He is concentrating on law enforcement, tax collection, antismuggling, increased rice production and civic action programs to improve the living conditions of the people. Upon taking office, President Marcos announced his intention to reorganize an engineer construction group to provide a total of 10 engineer construction battalions within his armed forces. When consistent with their military mission, he intends to use these battalions on such projects as building roads, bridges, and schools and constructing irrigation and sanitation systems. The United States has agreed to provide materiel to fill out the equipment of five of these battalions by June 30 of this year. 

The military assistance program for the Philippines will assist in developing forces for the maintenance of internal security. Considerable effort is being expended on improving the supply and maintenance capability of the Philippine Armed Forces. A significant example is the initiation of in-country overhaul of Philippine Navy ships. This will result in more effective use of military assistance funds.

In Indonesia the long, corrosive years of the Sukarno regime finally came to a climax in the violent upheaval on October 1, 1965. Since the People's Provisional Consultative Assembly in March of 1967 

officially placed the reigns of government in the hands of General Suharto, it now appears that Indonesia is firmly committed to constructive political and economic objectives. Only the Indonesians can solve those problems, but sympathetic and understanding free world support will greatly facilitate their doing so, and their remaining a free nation.

Turning to Thailand, we find a country which wholeheartedly supports U.S. Government policies in southeast Asia. This is evidenced by its public statements and by our continued use of Thailand's bases and facilities to support our operations in North Vietnam. 

During the past year there has been an escalation in Communist subversive activity in Thailand. Communist China and North Vietnam direct, train, and provide assistance to the Communist insurgent groups in Thailand's northeast. There is Communist subversive activity along the Thai-Malaysian border and attempts to penetrate the hill tribes in the north. In the face of these threats, the Thais have moved to strengthen their security forces in these critical areas. Communist guerrillas, supported by China and North Vietnam, can be expected to accelerate their activity in Thailand. The United States should continue to render assistance to enable the Thais to cope with these threats.

Next, a look at Laos. In this country the Pathet Lao and North 

Vietnamese units continue to attack the Government forces. Also, the Communists are using the eastern panhandle of Laos to provide North Vietnamese support and reinforcement to the Vietcong as well as for infiltration into Thailand. Consistent with our obligations under the 1962 Geneva accords, the United States, at the request of the neutral Government of Laos, should continue to provide assistance to that Government in its efforts to resist the attempt of indigenous and North Vietnamese Communists to take over the country.

195 Finally, I want to speak about the war in Vietnam because of its relationship with and effect upon all of southeast Asia. 

During 1966, we deployed to South Vietnam a balanced and effective military force for the conduct of the war for Vietnam. Successful spoiling operations forced the enemy to revert to defensive employment of his main force units. These operations have been instrumental in successful efforts to prevent a military takeover of South Vietnam by the Communists. Nevertheless, a capable and resourceful enemy is continuing to engage in overt warfare in South Vietnam. 

The strategy for the conduct of the war for Vietnam embraces three interdependent undertakings which together constitute an integrated concept for the conduct of the war. The undertakings are to:

Take the war to the enemy in North Vietnam by unremitting but selective application of U.S. air and naval power. 

Seek out and destroy Communist forces and infrastructure in 

South Vietnam by offensive military operations.

Extend the secure areas of South Vietnam by coordinated civil-military operations and assist the revolutionary development program of the Government of South Vietnam in building an independent, viable, free society.

In taking the war to the enemy in the North we have a twofold objective. Our attacks on war supporting activities, combined with the interdiction effort, are designed to increase the pressure on Hanoi and to convince them that this unsuccessful aggression is becoming so costly that it is not rational to continue. 

There is a tendency, unfortunately, to consider that the only objective of our air campaign is to stop infiltration, and then to say that it is not succeeding because infiltration continues. However, the fact is that our air campaign has forced Hanoi into intensive countermeasures in an attempt to mitigate its effects. An extensive and relatively sophisticated air defense system has been developed. The military began dispersing activities and installations, and digging in. 

Military forces were diverted to reconstruction tasks, which took them away from their regular functions. Reconstructing lines of communication became a national task. They have used prefabricated bridges laid at night and removed during the day. They have constructed road bypasses at vulnerable intersections. Ferries, fords and even underwater causeways have been built. Human portage was recruited by the tens of thousands. Material was moved by shuttling from rail to road to inland waterways to trucks to human back. Special camouflage techniques have been used. All in all, it has been a tremendous effort, at a huge cost.

In this regard, you recall the Communist activity during the TET truce in early February and immediately thereafter. For 5 days and nights the Communists, employing numerous ships and trucks, moved about 25,000 tons of supplies into the area north of the DMŹ. The enemy's carefully planned and skillfully executed TET resupply operations brought out clearly that our air and naval interdiction efforts have been very successful, holding the flow of supplies down to a fraction of what it could be in the absence of these efforts. 

To summarize, it is essential that we continue to apply our overwhelming air and sea power in a manner that will conclusively demon-

1967 

strate to Hanoi the price to be paid for continued aggression in South Vietnam. 

In South Vietnam we have been able to take the initiative against enemy main force units. However, the enemy can disengage many of these units almost at will by returning to his sanctuaries beyond South Vietnamese borders where our ground forces cannot search him out, thus pacing the ground war to his advantage. During 1967 General 

Westmoreland plans operations designed to defeat the Vietcong/North Vietnamese Army main force units, destroy the enemy's base areas and resources, and drive him into the sparsely populated areas where food is scarce. Concurrently, he will strive to locate, interdict and destroy the enemy's ground and water lines of communication in South Vietnam, and to root out the Communist infrastructure. The course upon which he has embarked in South Vietnam is a sound one. 

It would be an oversimplification to suggest that the enemy has reverted to tactical guerrilla action as his primary mode of operation. 

But he realizes that he cannot defeat and eject the United States/free world military forces by large unit operations and that he is vulnerable, particularly when concentrated, to our air, artillery, and tactical mobility. However, the Vietcong/North Vietnamese Army main forces are still dangerous. It is likely that they are avoiding major contact, using their sanctuaries, fighting defensively when forced to do so and attempting to rebuild and reinforce for operations at an opportune time. Tactical guerrilla warfare probably will be intensified without fragmenting main force units or discarding plans for their buildup and use. The enemy probably will attempt to keep up his present rate of infiltration in order to counter our buildup and to replace his losses. His strategy hinges on prolonging the war and out- 

Îasting our determination to see the job done. 

There are encouraging signs of progress and we believe that we may be approaching the point when enemy total losses from all causes may be exceeding his gains. Losses include the increasing number of returnees from the Chieu Hoi program as well as battle casualties. 

Recruitment into the Vietcong ranks has become more difficult. Today our free world ground forces move against enemy base areas that were inaccessible in the past. Thus, there is a basis for cautious optimism concerning our military offensive campaign.

The third facet of our strategy involves the Government of Vietnam's revolutionary development program and the support given to it by the United States and other free world governments. 

Despite many efforts, the 1966 national revolutionary development program moved slowly. There were setbacks, frustrations, and resistance. It was apparent in 1966 that the people of the hamlets, subject to the ebb and flow of war for many years, were generally reluctant to commit themselves.

However, we inaugurated 1967 with a sharpening of the focus on this activity. 1967 plans and directives for the first time specifically task major military forces to support revolutionary development. 

To facilitate support of the 1967 program, U.S. Government agencies in Vietnam-civil and military-have tailored their organizations more effectively to address revolutionary development. Continued refinements are expected. On the civil side, the recently established Office of Civil Operations exercises direct control over

197 U.S. civilians in the field who have revolutionary development responsibilities. On the military side, the staff divisions within the military assistance command that is responsible for the activity has been expanded into a directorate headed by a general officer. A similar organizational structure is also a part of each senior corps adviser's staff. 

There is little doubt that, but for our efforts and sacrifices, South Vietnam would have collapsed militarily and politically to Communist control, and Laos, Cambodia, and Thailand would be threatened with a similar fate. Although the length of this conflict is not yet predictable, the course upon which we have embarked successfully to bring it to an end is a necessary and a sound one. We face a complex situation which will demand constant review of our tactics, adequacy of our forces and effectiveness of our operations against the enemy. 

In my opinion, the most important requirement for success is a demonstrated determination to stick to our guns. 

Our goal for 1967 is to increase the prospects for an early end to the conflict in South Vietnam which is satisfactory to the United States, to the Republic of Vietnam, and to those nations which are providing free world military assistance forces.

In conclusion-prospects for achieving our objectives are excellent. 

We have firm and determined allies in that part of the world who do not flinch in their fight for freedom and who provide us operational and support bases. We have a combined free world force, made possible and developed to a great extent, through the military assistance program. These allied forces, backed by U.S. strength, are maintaining a strong bulwark against Communist subversion and expansion-internally and externally. The tremendous resources we are now committing to Vietnam make it evident that it is in our best interest to continue the relatively modest military assistance programs for the defense and internal security of the area. It is this type of effort on our part that can help prevent "future Vietnams." I urge your continued support of the military assistance program. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Admiral.

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM O. HALL, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRA- TOR FOR ADMINISTRATION, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. HALL. I have a prepared statement and with your permission 

I would like to read it.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to appear before the committee today to discuss with you the President's requests for the contingency fund, American sponsored schools and hospitals abroad, AID's administrative expenses, and some proposed amendments affecting our personnel system. 

Contingency fund. The contingency fund is maintained to meet urgent assistance needs that are either unforeseen or cannot be accurately defined in advance. These include situations of major security interest to the United States. They also include natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.

We use the contingency fund as sparingly as circumstances permit. 

With the exception of fiscal year 1966, when the situation in Vietnam, the Dominican Republic, and elsewhere necessitated a request for supplemental contingency funds, there has been in the past few years a marked decline in the use of the contingency fund. 223

1967 Fiscal year: 

1961 

Worldwide contingency fund  1 Gross obligations $272, 638 1962 1963 1964 1965 1966 1967 (estimated) 1968 (estimated) 302, 499 149, 197 107, 387 57, 155 120, 028 51, 020 60,000 1 Represents obligations against fiscal year 1961 funds only since there was no authority in this year to reobligate recoveries. 

An authorization ceiling of $100 million is requested for each of the next 2 years. The total proposed program in fiscal year 1968 is $60 million, the lowest availability ever proposed for the contingency fund. The appropriation request for fiscal year 1968 is $31 million, which is also the smallest amount of new funds ever sought for the contingency fund.

In addition to new appropriations, $4 million is expected to be available from recoveries, and $25 million represents funds which at this time we expect to carry over from the current fiscal year. The expected carryover results from a Presidential directive to executive branch departments and agencies to save certain fiscal year 1967 funds and carry them into the next year. Twenty-five million dollars was the figure assigned to AID programs, and we have tentatively allocated this saving to the contingency fund. 

Availabilities for the fiscal year 1967 contingency fund have therefore been reduced from $76 million to $51 million. Because we now foresee rather strong pressures on use of the contingency fund in the closing months of the current year, I am not certain that we can continue to assign the entire $25 million savings to the contingency fund, although this will continue to be our objective. 

As of April 10, all $51 million had been programed, of which $32 million has been approved for funding. A complete breakdown is shown in annex A (see p. 230). The large portions include: $18.3 million for Indonesia, to permit us to take advantage of new opportunities in this large and important nation. The President made a determination last September to renew aid to Indonesia, where a new government is now rolling up its sleeves and looking to the future. The former participant training program and the supplying of educational materials is being resumed; surveys to determine the possibilities for other technical assistance projects are being initiated; and the financing of commodity imports has been authorized to assist in achieving economic recovery and stabilization. $10.6 million for Panama, to finance urban slum programs for 

Panama City and Colon, where dangerous riots occurred last summer. We think a social and political climate of stability is in the interests of the entire Western Hemisphere in the important days ahead.

225 American schools and hospitals abroad.-Sections 214 (a) and (b) of the Foreign Assistance Act authorize assistance to certain schools and hospitals abroad which are founded or sponsored by U.S. citizens. 

The United States has provided assistance under this program since 1959. 

AID's assistance helps these institutions to contribute to economic and social development, both in the countries in which they are located and in the entire region surrounding them. They do, as the Foreign 

Assistance Act states, serve "as study and demonstration centers for ideas and practices of the United States." 

One of the most important keys to development is the availability of a highly educated indigenous body of people who are able to provide political and cultural, as well as economic, leadership. The institutions assisted by the United States provide training grounds for such people. 

In areas of professional scarcity, graduates of these institutions are the doctors, nurses, teachers, businessmen, and even political leaders of their countries. A measure of the success of the program is indicated by the fact that the graduates of one of these schools-the American University of Beirut-include seven premiers, a dozen ambassadors and ministers, and as many cabinet members. 

While this is recognized by both AID and by the governments of the host countries to be a most important program, U.S. support for these institutions must be limited. Our goal must be only to provide a firm basis on which they can continue to contribute and grow from private sources.

They must ultimately be independent of U.S. aid. That is why 

AID seeks new appropriations to assist only six schools and hospitals under this program in fiscal year 1968 compared with 10 last year. The six are the American University of Beirut, The American Farm School in Greece, Robert College in Istanbul, the American University in Cairo, Escuela Agricola Panamericana in Honduras, and Project HOPE. 

The President has requested funds for a $14,029,000 program in fiscal year 1968, $3,029,000 more than in fiscal year 1967. This increase is attributable to: 

An increase of $200,000 for Robert College;

A $1.9 million increase in the operating subsidy for the American University of Beirut (AUB);

An additional $3.4 million capital improvement grant to the 

AUB for the third phase of its medical school construction; and 

An offsetting saving of $2,340,000 resulting from the fact that no assistance is requested for fiscal year 1968 to several institutions receiving asistance in fiscal year 1967.

We will continue to work closely with the six proposed recipient institutions to help them develop plans to achieve self-supporting status. 

A breakdown of the program for fiscal year 1966 and fiscal year 1967-and of the proposed fiscal year 1968 program-is set forth in annex B (see p. 231).

1967 

Administrative expenses. Funds authorized and appropriated for administrative expenses meet the costs of directing and supervising the AID program in Washington and overseas. This includes establishing program policies and standards, planning, supervising, and reviewing the actual implementation of these policies, evaluating programs and projects, and providing such key management services as accounting, inspection, auditing, personnel administration, management analysis, and administrative support. 

The President has requested new funds for fiscal year 1968 of $59.3 million. These funds, together with an estimated carryover of $750,000, will support a total program of $60.1 million, about $2 million more than this year.

Several factors necessitate this increase. Nearly half is accounted for by increased costs over which AID has no control-in-grade pay increases to Federal employees and overseas wage and price increases caused by inflation abroad.

Another 25 percent of the rise will permit resumption of some training programs for outstanding and promising locals employed by our overseas posts as well as some contracts for auditing and computer programing. These were drastically reduced in the current. fiscal year because of cuts in AID's administrative expense request last year.

We feel that these are necessary and worthwhile programs and should be resumed.

The remainder is for urgent staffing increases. The bulk of these represent new overseas positions to strengthen the Agency's audit capability. Both the General Accounting Office and congressional Operations Committees have urged AID to give additional attention to this area. The rest covers several small staff increases in Washington. 

Specifically, some new people are needed for the expanded war on hunger, for data compilation on small business programs, and to respond to the President's directive to refine an integrated planning, programing, and budgeting system in the Agency. 

It may be helpful to reconcile the program and authorization figures. While the fiscal year 1968 proposed program will be $2 million more than the fiscal year 1967 program, the authorization request of $59.3 million is $3.5 million more than the fiscal year 1967 authorization. Two factors explain this difference of about $1.5 million. 

Most of the difference is due to the $1.1 million required to meet our portion of the Federal pay raise authorized last year under the separate pay legislation. It was not included in the fiscal year 1967 

AID authorization request, but it is reflected in the fiscal year 1968 request. We met it by transfers from our other appropriation categories as authorized by general legislation. The balance of $400,000 is due to a smaller carryover of funds into fiscal year 1968 than into fiscal year 1967.

I should mention one final point on AID's administrative expenses. 

In fiscal year 1966 and fiscal year 1967, the Congress granted AID authority to transfer supporting assistance funds to the administrative expenses account in order to meet expanded expenses of the Vietnam program over and above the level originally contemplated for

227 fiscal year 1966. We are now requesting that the ceiling be raised from $5 to $11 million, primarily to reflect full year funding of partial year costs. Mr. Poats has covered this in some detail in his testimony, but I would be happy to answer any further questions you may have concerning the proposed transfer authority. This is an item which we would not expect to continue, of course, once the Vietnam program was over.

Personnel amendments.-Seven amendments affecting our person nel operations are requested this year. They are:

Authority to assign additional newly hired Foreign Service personnel initially to positions here in Washington for in-service, on-the-job experience prior to sending them abroad; 

An increase in the authorization to provide assistance to local schools abroad where AID and other U.S. Government dependents are educated; 

Authority to make AID's Foreign Service employees eligible to participate in the Foreign Service retirement system;

Authority to increase the number of positions above grade 15 at headquarters in Washington;

Liberalization of the present authority providing for transfer and detail of our employees to international organizations; 

Authority to provide for transfer of employees to foreign governments on the same basis as now authorized for transfer to international organizations; and 

Authority to procure health and accident insurance for local employees of the U.S. Government abroad when they are sent to the United States or other developed countries for training or temporary duty.

Some years ago, the committee authorized us to experiment with this on-the-job training and experience for middle- and upper-level officers receiving initial appointments in the Foreign Service. We were authorized to assign first 20 and later 40 officers to duties in Washington at any one time for up to 2 years before they went overseas. 

This period offered the officers a chance to learn about the Agency and to see how the specialty with which they were concerned was handled at headquarters.

Also, it gave the Agency a chance to size up the new officer, to arrange special training for him where required, and to evaluate his performance before we sent him abroad. Our experience with this authority has been good. While we have lost some officers during the period through resignation or health difficulties, most of the people who have completed the program have done well, both in Washington and in the field. We believe they have been more effective in their work as a result of this experience than have their colleagues who went directly overseas after a brief orientation. 

Accordingly, we are requesting an increase from 40 to 100 officers authorized at any one time for initial appointment to serve in Washington for not to exceed 2 years.

We will make every effort to minimize any adverse impact this provision may have on our domestic and Foreign Service employees

1967 

and we will carefully consider the views of any employee that may be affected.

We have discussed this matter with our employee union over a period of several months. While they have traditionally opposed such an authority, they recognize that it does give the Agency additional flexibility in securing and preparing employees for difficult overseas assignments. They are willing to accept the augmented authority, coupled with the assurances which have been given concerning its utilization. We have an understanding with the union which spells out these assurances in detail.

Our second amendment relates to the educational facilities pro- Ivided for the children of AID staff overseas. Some of these educational facilities are, at present, inferior to those which would be available to them in the United States.

We are asking for an increase of $1 million—from $1.5 million annually to $2.5 million-a year in our authority to assist schools overseas which the children of U.S. Government officials attend. 

Libraries, laboratory facilities, and better classroom facilities and teachers are needed, and our grants would be intended to provide those. 

The third proposal would enable AID's Foreign Service Reserve and Staff personnel to participate in the Foreign Service retirement system of the Department of State. That system fits more adequately the conditions of service in the developing countries than does the regular civil service retirement system. 

Under this provision, AID's Foreign Service employees, after 10 years of service in the Foreign Service, would be eligible for the same retirement benefits that the State Department's clerical staff receives under the Foreign Service retirement system.

Foreign assignments, under difficult conditions, take their toll of health and vitality, making the normal time for retirement earlier than is typical for the domestic civil service. Of course, a transition period will be provided so that those at or near the mandatory retirement age will not be unduly injured and exceptions will still be possible. The amendment provides for possible extensions of up to 5 years of added service beyond retirement age.

I should add it is our intention to make generous use of this discretion, to extend the normal mandatory age to retain the services of employees who are important to our program, so that the transition to the new system would be eased to minimize any adverse effect on the employees of a lower mandatory retirement age in the Foreign Service retirement system. This amendment would reduce mandatory age of retirement from 65 to 60.

The present retirement expectation of some employees who have had less than 15 years of service, might be 70 or 75. We have found, generally speaking, that officers beyond the age of 65 do have some difficulties overseas and are more prone to health and medical problems.

229 S We would want to bring down the age of mandatory retirement gradually. This would be done over a 5-year period, but there would still be provision for exceptions.

We have discussed this, again, with the employees' union and they are prepared to accept and support this legislation under consideration.

Our fourth request is for an increase in the number of headquarters positions at levels above grade 15. The 13 new upper level positions requested are needed for the expanded Vietnam program, the staffing for the new War on Hunger Office and our additional efforts for private enterprise.

The next two proposals would authorize the transfer of U.S. Government personnel to serve in positions in foreign governments and would extend from 3 to 5 years the period of service that may be authorized for transfers of U.S. Government personnel to international organizations. Both provisions would permit the payment to the employee of the difference between what the position in the foreign government or international organization pays and what the employee would be entitled to if he remained in his Government position. 

Employees transferred to foreign governments for duty with those governments would be assured the same rights and benefits as now apply to employees transferred to international organizations, including the right to continue Federal benefits during the period of transfer and the right to reemployment. These transfers are beneficial to the 

United States as well as to the developing countries and international agencies. If we are to move toward more use of international agencies in these programs, which is our intention and, I believe, is the will of Congress, we must encourage Americans to take assignments with these organizations. 

Lastly, we want to be able to pay for medical and accident insurance protection for foreign nationals employed by the U.S. Government who are brought to the United States or other developed countries for training. We pay these people in the less developed countries according to prevailing wage scales, and they are covered by their own social insurance plans. These wage scales are substantially lower than in this country or the European countries. 

When they come to developed countries, the cost of medical care is out of line with their salaries and their ability to pay. As they are in the United States at our initiative and for the Government's benefit, we have a responsibility to provide care for them should they become ill or have a serious accident. 

Not to do this may cause serious personal or family hardship to a local employee who may fall ill or be injured. It would be our intention to take out this insurance with a private insurance company as is our present practice with participants.

This concludes my statement. I will attempt to respond to any questions the committee may have. (Annexes A and B referred to are as follows:)

You remember we came up and had to ask for a supplemental authorization as well as a supplemental appropriation for those requirements.

Mr. BURLESON. I suppose an example of that is in the proposed language in the supplemental appropriation. In your statement you refer to the carryover of administrative funds of $750,000. The language in the supplemental is "Administrative Expenses," AID, $1,194,000 to be derived by transfer from appropriations for economic assistance, fiscal year 1967.

Why do you want to transfer the funds from the economic assistance program to administrative expenses, if you have this carryover? 

Mr. HALL. There are two types of transfers to our administrative expenses appropriation. One is the generally authorized transfer for pay increases. The other is a specific transfer to cover the administrative costs of the Vietnam program. 

When the Vietnam program was expanded very substantially 2 years ago, in lieu of providing us with an additional amount under our administrative expense authorization, which the Congress wanted to retain a fairly close control on, provision was made for a transfer from other appropriations to the administrative expense account for Vietnam, so that when the Vietnam emergency was over, that transfer could then be cut off.

Also, I think the feeling was it gave the Congress an opportunity to have some idea of the level of administrative expenses in Vietnam. 

That was not taken out of the contingency fund. That was a separate action by the Congress at the time we came up requesting funds for Vietnam.

We did ask for an expansion of the contingency fund on the program side for Vietnam, but we also requested this transfer authority. 

We started out with a small amount, and then we got a larger amount the following year, and now we are requesting $11 million, which will put these additional expenses on a full year basis.

233 We would expect that figure to come down when and if the situation in Vietnam improves and we are able to reduce our programs there.

Mr. BURLESON. I am sure Mrs. Bolton is going to ask quite a few questions about the foreign schools, institutions of higher learning that we subsidize, but just this short question. Funds provided in the contingency fund that you mentioned here for the six universities and colleges, that is not a ceiling, I take it, a limitation, because in other sections of the aid bill there is provision for loans and grants and so forth. Why this mixture, or put it another way, this is not the- Mr. HALL. There are three types of assistance that we give to educational institutions. One is the assistance to dependent schools where Americans abroad have organized a cooperative school at the post to educate their own children, and where the curriculum is basically American. It is usually a lower school and a high school. It is run normally by a local board with participation of some of the wives or mothers who do teaching. There are a few paid American teachers. We have given grants to those. 

Mr. BURLESON. That is principally what this is? 

Mr. HALL. That is the first of the three types of assistance I referred to. It is the smallest item. It describes the purpose for which we are asking $2.5 million as an annual fund. That goes to schools across the world.

The second group are the schools that have been in existence for many, many years, established by American philanthropists, missionaries, and others primarily to educate children that come from foreign countries, in other words, children of the host country where the school is located-children of the Middle East at the American University in Beirut, children coming from Turkey and surrounding countries at Robert College. These schools have been in existence a long time. They were in existence before aid ever started. 

We have a special provision in the bill which permits us to assist these schools. The primary purpose is to educate the children in the developing countries and to bring them along. 

The third kind of assistance we give to educational institutions, however, is part of our regular technical assistance on development loan program and is not a part of the request for funds under section 214. 

This assistance consists of loans primarily, but occasionally we make grants for teachers or materials to institutions that are controlled by the host country. They may be religious institutions, as in Latin 

America, or they may be state universities or state colleges, primarily at the college level. We have authority to give them both grants and loans, but we provide mostly loans. 

The loans are guaranteed by the host government and are subject to repayment. In Africa we have helped establish some new universities where there were no universities at the time the colonial rulers of Africa movd out. We have helped in a number of cases to establish secondary schools in Africa, through the provision of teachers, through some grants for educational materials, and through continuing loans in a few cases-

 AID TO SCHOOLS IN UGANDA, KENYA, AND TANZANIA 

U.S. assistance to schools in East Africa (Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania) is not related in any way to that provided the specific institutions designated under section 214 of the Foreign Assistance Act (grants to American schools and hospitals abroad). Rather this aid comes under the broader category of economic assistance financed from that portion of the technical assistance and development loan appropriations allocated for development programs in the Africa region. Significant assistance to secondary and technical education has been provided on a bilateral basis to Kenya and Tanzania as well as Uganda, such as for the Eger ton Agricultural College in Kenya, and the Dar-Es-Salaam Technical College and Morogoro Agricultural College in Tanzania. However, assistance to higher education has been primarily directed toward strengthening the University of East Africa with member schools in all three countries, through projects financed under the East Africa Regional program. The University of East Africa, formed in 1963, is made up of three constituent colleges-Makerere University College 

(Uganda), University College, Nairobi (Kenya), and University College, Dar- 

Es-Salaam (Tanzania). AID assistance to the university is primarily directed towards upgrading and expanding instruction in the fields of education, veterinary sciences, and agriculture as well as selected support to the central University designed to develop its capability as a regional institution. In addition to these continuing grant financed activities noted above, since fiscal year 1963 AID also has provided over $3.8 million in development loans to improve and expand physical facilities at the three colleges, with a further development loan planned to expand facilities at Makerere University College.

NUMBER OF PEOPLE AFFECTED AND COST OF CHANGING TO FOREIGN SERVICE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 

AID now has a total of approximately 5,000 FSR and FSS employees. It is estimated that early in 1968, the assumed effective date of this amendment, approximately 1,000 of these employees will be eligible to participate in the Foreign Service Retirement System, i.e., they will have 10 or more years of continuous foreign service and will have unlimited appointments. It is also estimated that in subsequent years the "ultimate" number of AID employees who will be active participants in the Foreign Service Retirement System at any one time will be 1,300. This latter estimate takes into account turnover among employees who will be eligible on the effective date of the amendment and increments to the number of such employees of those who will become eligible in future years. 

Retirement costs are usually stated in terms of normal cost plus interest on the unfunded liability. Normal cost is defined as the level percentage of an employee's salary that must be deposited at interest during each year of his service to finance the benefits which he and his survivors are expected to receive. 

The normal retirement costs for affected AID personnel would be greater by $3,000,000 per year in the Foreign Service Retirement System than in the Civil Service Retirement System. The higher Foreign Service normal cost is attributable, among other things to: 

1. Lower resignation rate of the Foreign Service-55 out of 100 new entrants at age 25 reach retirement while under Civil Service only 7 out of 100 reach retirement. The Government contribution on behalf of those who resign without entitlement to an annuity remains in the system and redound to the benefit of those who do retire on an annuity. 

2. Lack of agency contributions to the Foreign Service retirement fund for periods of prior service under the Civil Service Retirement System. 

Under this proposal, each AID employee transferred to the Foreign Service Retirement System will have completed 10 years under the Civil Service Retirement System. The employees' contributions but not the matching agency contributions for this service would be transferred from the Civil Service to the Foreign Service retirement fund. The normal cost of the Foreign Service Retirement System must be high enough to make up for this loss. 

3. Earlier retirement-the average Foreign Service retirement age of 58 compares to 61 under the Civil Service system. One of the reasons for the proposal is to permit and encourage employees serving under arduous circumstances to retire earlier. 

4. Slightly higher benefit formula-after a 30-year career a Foreign Service annuity would equal 60% of high-five average salary vs. 56% for the Civil 

Service a difference of 34%.

The actual difference in cost to the Government of the transfer of these employees to the Foreign Service Retirement System will be somewhat less than the $3,000,000 difference in normal cost referred to above. This difference is based, in part, on the fact that the percentage of employees in the Civil Service System who reach retirement age is considerably lower than in the Foreign Service Retirement System. If these AID employees were to remain in the Civil 

Service Retirement System, the percentage of these employees who would reach retirement age and earn an annuity would be much the same as for present employees in the Foreign Service system. This is why the true cost to the 

Government would be something less than the $3,000,000 stated above. 

In addition to the increase in the annual normal cost, the transfer of these AID employees to the Foreign Service Retirement System would increase the current $250,000,000 unfunded liability of that system by approximately $75,000,- 000. There would be a corresponding reduction in the unfunded liability of the 

Civil Service retirement fund because the obligation to pay retirement benefits to this group would shift from the Civil Service to the Foreign Service system. 

The amount of the decrease in the overall unfunded liability of $44 billion in the Civil Service retirement fund is difficult to calculate because of the different actuarial techniques employed in the two systems. Because of the factors noted

1967 

above it would be something less than the $75,000,000 increase in the unfunded liability of the Foreign Service retirement fund. The increased cost to the 

Government of this proposal would include interest on the difference between these two amounts.

Mr. GROSS. If it is desirable to provide retirement at age 60, why do you want permission to extend this for a period of 5 years? 

Mr. HALL. This is because some of our officers came into the Agency at a fairly advanced, later age, in their fifties. They have been looking forward to working for the Government until they are 65 or 70. 

Some are capable of doing this, they are young enough physically to do it. We would like to have authority over the next few years to make adjustments to fit those officers' personal situations and the Government's interests. We feel it would be unduly harsh and our employees' union felt it would be unduly harsh to pose as of a certain date a much earlier retirement in cases where people have been expecting to work until they were 65 or 68 and where they were capable of doing so. 

We would like to introduce this gradually in order to make this reform in a way which does not adversely affect the individuals involved. There are not a large number involved. I believe there are only 25 people or so to be affected by this more gradual procedure.

 DETAILED BREAKDOWN ON WHERE AND WHY NEW SUPERGRADES ARE NEEDED

DESCRIPTIONS OF SUPERGRADE POSITIONS VIETNAM BUREAU 

Deputy Assistant Administrator (AD-18)

Reviews proposals for providing advisory assistance to the Government of Vietnam on matters of development and economic policies.

Responsible for policy formulation for private lending activities, operational responsibility for Investment Surveys, Specific and Extended Risk Guaranties, and AID dollar and local currency loans to private borrowers. Directs the activities of the Private Investment Center.

Director, Finance Division (AD-17) 

He is directly responsible for all aspects of the extended risk guaranty and loan programs: analysis, negotiation and administration. He will be a member of the loan policy committee within the Center.

Director, Insurance Division (AD-17) 

He is responsible for the negotiation of insurance and guaranty contracts and loan agreements with individual investors, and will be a member of the Private 

Investment Center's loan policy committee. 

Mr. GROSS. I will tell you it doesn't make any difference what agency of Government you talk to about supergrades, that answer seems to be the same-they must type that out and send it around-for every justification for supergrades. I don't mean to be disrespectful, Mr. Hall, but that is the answer we get from every one of them, something almost verbatim. How much will they cost, the additional supergrades?

Mr. HALL. Our estimated difference of cost over and above-the difference between grade 15 and the supergrade level—would be $60,000 a year.

Mr. GROSS. On page 11 of your statement you speak of medical and accident insurance. You are asking this for foreign nationals in the 

United States. How many individuals would be covered by this new program?

Mr. HALL. This is a provision which would cover-I should make the point that it is a general provision which would be available to any U.S. agency with local employees abroad that it is educating in the United States. Our anticipation is that there would be 75 AID employees brought to the United States for training. That is primarily at the present time in auditing and accounting work. 

Mr. GROSS. These are foreign nationals?

Mr. HALL. Yes. They are people working in our mission abroad who have been working for us a number of years. We want to upgrade their skills, make them more effective, give better support to our own American nationals. That is 75-would you like me to finish the State Department would be 60, a total of 60. Commerce would like to bring 80 officers in, foreign nationals to work on commercial work that Commerce conducts overseas. The USIA would like to bring in 90. The military would like to bring in 75. The total cost of this for all agencies we estimate at $2,950. The cost of AID would be $500 a year, the State Department $550, USIA $1,000, and the other agencies, primarily the military and Commerce, would be $900.

247 Mr. GROSS. There is nothing in the bill to place a limit on number, is there?

Mr. HALL. No, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. It could be 150 or it could be a thousand. 

Mr. HALL. We could not bring in that number because these people have to be spared during the period of training from their regular work in our missions abroad. There is a definite physical limitation on how many we could bring in. 

Mr. GROSS. Would the foreign nationals pay anything toward this cost?

Mr. HALL. They would cover only the continuation of their own social security. This is primarily because we have had one or two people who have come and become involved in automobile accidents. 

We have had difficulty that way. We have had to take up collections at the post where they came from. 

I am concerned if we continue to do this we could be very embarrassed. Most of these local employees have small savings. They are operating on low salaries. They don't have the same ability to pick up a major personal disaster as the American employee. It is a safeguard to protect the Government and to protect also the employees. 

Mr. GROSS. Again we are branching out into another new program that is going to cost some money. I don't know how much. I am not completely satisfied with your answer to the amount, because it is apparently unlimited. When we go overseas we pay for our insurance. Nobody is picking up the check for Americans in training or in foreign schools of any kind; is that not true? 

Mr. HALL. That is correct.

The difference is, Mr. Gross, we come from a situation in which your salaries generally in this country are considerably higher than the salaries that prevail in those other countries. 

Mr. GROSS. We come from a nation that has the greatest debt, more debt than all the rest of the world combined. 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. Yes, sir.

I hope you are aware of that and really aware of it. Section 625 (d) (2) of the law limits the number of Foreign Service personnel who may be initially assigned to duty in the United States to a total of 40 at any time.

This bill proposes to raise this to 100, because the limitation of 40 applies to those selected for service in Vietnam? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir; it does. It covers everybody. If an officer is going to Vietnam and comes in here and is to be given on-the-job training, he has to be included in the 40. That is frankly one of the reasons we want this increased expanded authority, because it is important to us to bring some of the people in, the people who will be going to Vietnam in the future, and let them have experience here. 

We have a problem on auditors. The Moss committee was critical because our auditors in Vietnam were inexperienced since we brought them in out of private accounting firms and with brief training they had to go to Vietnam.

Mr. FRASER. 

Mr. Hall, I want to ask some questions about the training that is provided to employees of the Agency. 

Is this a matter that comes recently directly under your administration? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir.

Mr. FRASER. Can you characterize in a general way the kind of training programs that are now offered, or required of employees? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir. Our training programs with few exceptions are primarily related to specific technical jobs and technical requirements and to the orientation of people in the region to which they are going to go. We do have two or three special programs which I perhaps should mention. We have been using the War College and the 

Senior Seminary Foreign Service Institute and universities around the country to give advance training, 1 year's advance training to some of our officers in economics, a few in community developmentwork of this kind.

In addition to that, there is a joint program-two joint programsone is of a general character between all the foreign affairs agencies that are operating the Foreign Service Institute, which is basically a short course to try to familiarize officers with the problems of insurgency that may develop in the countries in which they are present, to give them some background on interagency cooperation in this field. 

This is a course in which we are trying to put all our senior people. 

We are just starting, have just started two programs for people going to Vietnam-one at the University of Hawaii which will take a small group of people, give them some background and experience in living in village conditions, will give them some general background on Vietnam and on conditions that they are likely to find there and will give them an immersion course in Vietnamese.

We have a related program which will take another group of people going to Vietnam which is a joint program between ourselves, the State Department, the CIA, USIA, and with some Defense people in it which will be calculated to do the same thing, give people basically a heavy course in Vietnamese, but also indoctrination in Vietnamese political problems, Vietnamese geography, economic problems, and the programs of the agencies involved. 

Mr. FRASER. Where is that last course?

249 Mr. HALL. The Foreign Service Institute. It will be starting in the next 10 days.

Mr. FRASER. That is in addition to the Hawaiian school. 

Mr. HALL. That is right. 

Mr. FRASER. It will not be a substitute?

Mr. HALL. No. We are going to continue the Hawaii school. We had difficulty when it first started with the first two groups. We had considerable difficulty as you might anticipate, but we have just had a survey made by a team that went out, a man from Brookings and a man from our own staff. They came back with a statement that the course is going well and we should continue. As we go along over the next year or 2 years, we are going to have similar requirements probably in Thailand and in Laos for people with this kind of background and training. We may decide to shift the Hawaii program to that kind of training. This is some time off if we do it. We will do it only after we are certain that the course of the Foreign Service Institute gives adequate preparation for Vietnam and across the board. 

Mr. FRASER. What you are saying is that we have no such training now provided for people serving in Thailand?

Mr. HALL. The only training we now give people going to Thailand and Laos is an orientation course when they first come in, an orientation on the Agency and then matter on the geography, politics, and economics of Laos and Thailand.

In some cases, we give language training. But it isn't the same character as the course we are running on Vietnam. 

Mr. FRASER. I assume that in Vietnam we are learning things about rural development and rural reconstruction that might have some application in Thailand.

How does the Agency provide for this cross fertilization of experience and ideas?

Mr. HALL. We have done it in the past historically by moving people from some of the people that served in Vietnam have been moved to Laos and to Thailand. That is one way we do it. 

Secondly, we have encouraged visits between the three countries by our people for observation. We have tried to collect written experience to the extent that it has been available and make it available to the people- 

Mr. FRASER. Written experience? 

Mr. HALL, Yes.

Mr. FRASER. Who is in charge of this written experience, Mr. Hall? 

Mr. HALL. In the past it has been primarily the desk officers who have worked on the countries. We do now have as far as Vietnam is concerned an effort-we are making an effort in an organized way to capture the experience of people through the Hawaii training program and we will be doing the same thing through the Foreign Service Institute; interviewing people returning and trying to get documentary material from them.

Mr. FRASER. You say the Hawaiian training institute now is providing the place in which experience is recorded? 

Mr. HALL. To the extent that we are doing it in an organized way. 

We have begun to do that. It is not satisfactory. We will be doing more of that at the Foreign Service Institute.

Is that a grant to meet an urgent assistance need which was unforeseen?

253 Mr. HALL. This arises in this way-that it has been the custom over the years for the United States to make some gesture toward newly independent African countries in terms of a grant for some kind of project.

We did not anticipate Lesotho would become independent this year. 

We have given them $100,000 to be used for radio transmitting equipment, to improve their internal communications. This has been the practice of some years' standing. Therefore, this grant is perfectly in accord with that practice. It was something we had not anticipated. 

We had no way of knowing what was going to happen in that particular situation.

Mr. BUCHANAN. Thank you. 

On the grants to American schools and hospitals abroad, you mentioned among those, who had initiated and sponsored such schools and hospitals, missionaries.

I wondered are we, therefore, now assisting schools that are owned and operated by religious bodies?

Mr. HALL. Not under this particular appropriation. Most of these institutions were established originally under missionary auspices; a missionary became interested in the education of the children of the country, he came back to the United States and got funds from private individuals to finance the school, get it started, so on. 

In some cases, a religious organization has given money to a school, but, as far as I know, none of these schools has a religious connection as such. Some of them receive substantial amounts of money from people of a certain religious faith because of previous interest. These are not religiously supported schools. There are many other schools around the world that are supported by religious orders-religious institutions.

In education of our Foreign Service dependents abroad, in some cases, we do make small grants to religiously supported schools. For example, if there is an Anglican order that is running an English school and there are a few American children there, we may give them a grant to buy American books; an atlas to give some American flavor to the schoolwork.

There is that kind of assistance occasionally to religious institutions.
