 ACTUARIAL AND OTHER INFORMATION COMPARING FOREIGN SERVICE AND CIVIL SERVICE RETIREMENT SYSTEMS PART I ACTUARIAL DATA ON FOREIGN SERVICE AND CIVIL SERVICE RETIREMENT SYSTEMS 

In response to Mr. Monagan's question, Mr. Hall indicated that an actuarial study had been made, and said he would supply information concerning it for the record. He was referring to the study and report made by the Cabinet Committee on Federal Staff Retirement Systems. A summary of this report is contained in House Document 402, dated March 7, 1966. The complete report is now being printed under the auspices of the Senate Post Office and Civil Service Committee and should be available in about two weeks. 

One of the most important of the Cabinet Committee's recommendations is the one to place the Civil Service and Foreign Service retirement funds on a sound financial basis. In forming its recommendations on this subject, the Committee had the benefit of advice from the senior actuaries in the Government. 

Draft legislation to implement these recommendations is now clear in the Executive Branch. We expect that it will be submitted to the Congress for consideration in the near future.

The proposal to transfer certain AID personnel from the Civil Service to the Foreign Service Retirement System is consistent with the recommendations contained in the Cabinet Committee report, and would implement its recommenda tion C.1., page 45 of House Document 402. 

Mr. Hall also indicated he would supply actuarial figures for the record. These are the actuarial cost figures supplied in the insert for page 243 about the cost of the retirement proposal.

Mr. MONAGAN. To the brief extent that we touched on these retirement systems during the consideration of the legislation to reorganize the State Department personnel, it seemed to me that we were rushing headlong into a very critical financial and fiscal situation because of lack of foresight with reference to where we were heading and especially lack of coordination of contributions and benefits and lack of coordination between programs, and that an overall examination of the retirement systems would be a very valuable thing. 

Do you have any opinion on that score? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir. There has been an overall evaluation of the retirement system. As you know, both systems are not self-supporting, in the sense that the congressional appropriations for some years were omitted for the Foreign Service system. No contribution was made by the Government.

On the civil service system side, increased benefits were voted in some years without increasing the Government's contribution. So that both systems, one might say, are insolvent in the sense that they have very large deficiencies. The Foreign Service system is more expensive actuarially, primarily because the retirement age under the Foreign

255 Service system is about 3 years earlier than under the civil service system.

Secondly, the regular Foreign Service tends to have a lower attrition rate than the civil service. You don't have people coming in and having a contribution made for them and then leaving with the Government's contribution staying in the fund.

The Foreign Service system does have a greater requirement for Government contribution. As far as the basic difference, there are several things involved as far as our people are concerned with the 10year provision. There would be some prior service requirement. I will put in a statement. 

 ACTUARIAL AND OTHER INFORMATION COMPARING FOREIGN SERVICE AND CIVIL SERVICE RETIREMENT SYSTEMS PART II MAJOR DIFFERENCES BETWEEN FOREIGN SERVICE AND CIVIL SERVICE RETIRMENT SYSTEMS 

The differences have tended to narrow over the years, but the foreign service system still retains features which compensate for certain disadvantages to the employee inherent in overseas service. Principal among these are the earlier voluntary and mandatory retirement features of the foreign service plan, a slightly more favorable formula for annuity computation, and somewhat larger survivor benefits; as illustrated below. 

A. Minimum age for voluntary retirement so 

1. Civil Service: 

a. Age 62 with 5 years service. b. Age 60 with 20 years service. c. Age 55 with 30 years service. 

2. Foreign Service: a. Age 50 with 20 years service. 

B. Mandatory (age) retirement dit-20 

1. Civil Service: Generally at or after age 70 with at least 15 years' service. 

2. Foreign Service: Generally at age 60. 

C. Computation of annuity 

1. Civil Service: 

a. General formula: 

12% of "high-5" average salary, 1st 5 years. 

14% of "high-5" average salary, 2nd 5 years. 

2% of "high-5" average salary, over 10 years. b. Maximum basic annuity: 80% of "high-5" average salary. c. Minimum Disability annuity: Not less than smaller of (1) 40% of "high-5" average salary, or (2) amount obtained under general formula after increasing actual service by time between separation date and date employee will attain age 60. 

2. Foreign Service: 

a. General formula: 2% of "high-5" average salary multiplied by years of service. b. Maximum basic annuity: 70% of "high-5" average salary. c. Minimum Disability annuity: Actual service, if less, extended to 

20 years but added service may not exceed difference between age of retirement and mandatory retirement age for class of position. 

D. Survivorship benefits: 

1. Civil Service: To widow or dependent widower of employee-55% of employees' annuity computed on “high-5" average salary plus amount for children. 

2. Foreign Service: To widow or dependent widower of employee-50% of

1967 

employees' annuity computed under minimum disability annuity formula or $2,400 for a widow if this is greater, plus amount for children.

Now on another point. There is an indication of an authorization of $175,000 for fiscal 1966 for the Polish Children's Hospital. There is nothing for 1967 or 1968. 

Is there any reason to have this item in here?

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir. The $175,000 is an item that is in there to survey the possibility of expansion of this hospital possibly as a teaching facility and, in other words, training and perhaps general instruction in pediatrics.

We are now discussing with the people who manage the hospital the way in which this feasibility survey which is to be financed by the $175,000 will be conducted. 

Depending on the outcome of that negotiation and the results of the survey, the Polish Children's Hospital may wish to propose for fiscal 1969 or perhaps some later date an additional grant of Polish currencies, or possibly dollars, for an expansion of the hospital. 

At this point, until we get this feasibility study-we don't have any basis- Mr. MONAGAN. There is no request for an authorization- 

Mr. HALL. Not pending now. There may be for fiscal 1969. There may be some proposal.

Mr. MONAGAN. The program to assist schools overseas which the children of Government officials attend, that is separate from the military program, is it not? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir.

Mr. MONAGAN. And also really separate from these universities that we have traditionally assisted? 

How many of these schools are there that are involved?

Mr. HALL. I think we are involved in about 45 schools. There is a relationship with the military in this sense that where there is a Department of Defense school, we don't assist another American dependents' school, and, if there is an American dependents' school that we are assisting, the military do not provide for a school there. They admit State and AID people and we admit Defense people. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Could you furnish a list of these schools for the record?

Mr. HALL. I will be glad to do that and show what the other sources of funds are. There are some from the State Department cultural appropriations and some from the State Department administration.

261 Mr. BURLESON. Do any other members want to be heard other than 

Mr. Gross? 

Mr. BURLESON. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS.  A question that I should have asked earlier: How much are you now expending, or are you now expending any money from the contingency fund for airlift or any other means of support for Zambia because of the disgraceful boycott this country has placed on Rhodesia?

Mr. HALL. We aren't spending any money at the present time. That airlift, I think, is no longer operative as far as I know.

Mr. GROSS. Would you check that out and also insert in the record the amount of money which you have expended up to this point? 

Mr. HALL. I will. 

Mr. GROSS. Out of previous contingency funds? 

Mr. HALL. There were expenditures last year, yes sir. 

 AMOUNT OF MONEY EXPENDED ON ZAMBIAN AIRLIFT 

One million dollars of contingency funds were provided for airlift operations in fiscal year 1966 and an additional $155,000 was used for road improvement to help eliminate the need for continued airlift. No funds have been approved for this purpose in fiscal year 1967, and none are contemplated. 

Mr. GROSS. How much is being spent out of this contingency fund for budgetary support in various countries, Mr. Hall? 

Mr. HALL. There is one item for Panama of $2.6 million. There is- 

Mr. GROSS. Is that a loan or 

Mr. HALL. That is a loan.

I am sorry. There is also a loan to Indonesia in the amount of $10 million for commodity imports which is, in effect, budgetary support. 

There is a grant of $600,000 for budgetary support to Panama, in addition to the $2.6 million of loans that I mentioned. We anticipate a $2 million grant to Jordan for budgetary support which is in the process of negotiation. 

Mr. GROSS. Would you please submit for the record the loans that have been made in the past year out of the contingency fund and those that you propose for the future that you anticipate making; have in mind? 

(The information follows:) Fiscal Year 1966 LIST OF CONTINGENCY FUND LOANS 

Ceylon: Program loan, $7,500,000. 

Ecuador: Program loan, $10,000,000.

Indonesia: Commodity financing, $17,000,000.

1967 

Mr. HALL. If they are proposed for the future, if we know about them now, for the next year, they would be in our regular budget request. That dosen't mean there may not be some, but we don't know what they would be at the moment. They would develop after the budget has gone through the Congress. We wouldn't use the contingency fund for anticipated requirements.

Mr. GROSS. What is the interest rate on the Indonesian loan, for instance? 

 INTEREST RATE ON CONTINGENCY FUND LOAN TO INDONESIA 

The interest rate on the fiscal year 1967 contingency fund loan to Indonesia is 3 percent.

Mr. HALL. I think-my recollection is-that it has a 7-year grace period and the interest I think is 3 percent. I would have to check to be sure. 

Mr. GROSS. Is this Government borrowing money at 3 percent? 

Mr. HALL. No, sir. That is a standard concessional term, I believe. 

I would like to check that answer. 

Mr. GROSS. A "standard concessional" term? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, on the development loan. 

Mr. GROSS. You used the word, "concession," is that right? 

Mr. HALL. Yes, sir. All our loans are on what we call concessional terms, as distinguished from loans or hard commercial terms. 

Mr. GROSS. I just wanted to get the word- 

Mr. HALL. I used that word, yes, sir.

Mr. GROSS. We have money to loan to- 

Mr. HALL. Soft terms, yes, sir. That is right.

Mr. GROSS. But we can't borrow in this country at that rate. 

Mr. HALL. No, sir. These interest rates do not apply in this country, that is correct. 

Mr. GROSS. Just one final question. 

Why do we need a contingency fund?

Why don't you come here in this AID bill with line items on money that you want to spend?

If you need a contingency fund for emergencies when Congress is not in session why not set up $5 million or $10 million to be drawn on if necessary? You have no hesitancy in coming in for emergency or supplemental funds for this contingency operation when Congress is in session. 

Why have a contingency fund at all?

Mr. HALL. Mr. Gross, it is to meet situations which may arise almost overnight and which we have to deal with and, to be effective, we have to be able to act immediately. 

Mr. GROSS. The gentleman from Texas, Mr. Burleson, the acting chairman of the committee, raised a question immediately after your presentation to the committee, as to the nature of the emergency in the housing situation in Panama. 

You still haven't provided a very good answer to that one.

Mr. HALL. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. GROSS. I say there is no need for a contingency fund in this bill, that the AID Agency ought to come in with line items and let

263 us pass on them on the basis of merit or demerit of the projects that you want money for and not out of a contingency fund where you can take the money and use it for military assistance or for any cockeyed purpose you want anywhere in the world.

Mr. HALL. Mr. Gross, these are carefully considered acts. They aren't taken lightly. They are carefully considered by Mr. Gaud; by the Secretary; by the President. I think we do need some flexibility. We can't possibly anticipate contingencies and emergencies that are going to arise around the world. No one has a crystal ball that good.

Mr. GROSS. About the only time you need to become serious about that is when Congress is not in session. Congress hasn't turned you down yet, as far as I know, but they ought to have done so. They haven't turned you down yet when you came in for a supplemental or emergency appropriation.

Mr. HALL. Mr. Gross, frequently we have had to act on the basis of a situation in which we have had very, very brief notice-a few daysand the action has had to be taken very promptly. 

We have tried to keep the members of this committee and the Senate committee fully informed of these developments.

Mr. GROSS. After the fact. 

Mr. HALL. If the committee would wish, we can always arrange to come up and see you beforehand.

The committee, in the past, has not wished to get into that much detail, I don't believe. 

Mr. BURLESON. Mr. Hall, thank you and your associates very much.

I express the regret of the chairman that he was unable to be here this morning for this very able presentation. 

Mr. HALL. Thank you.

Mr. BURLESON. The meeting is adjourned. 

(Whereupon, at 12:05 p.m., the committee adjourned.)

FOREIGN ASSISTANT ACT OF 1967 MONDAY, APRIL 17, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

Office  

The committee meets this morning in executive session to continue the hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to further amend the Foreign Assist ance Act of 1961. 

This is the second appearance of Secretary McNamara and General Wheeler before the committee on this bill. When they were here last week the committee had to rise early and the Secretary had another engagement, so that we asked the Secretary to come back. In response to a parliamentary inquiry by Congressman Rosenthal, the committee decided to start the questioning where we left off last week. Mr. Farbstein would have been next on the majority side. He is not present, so I will call first on Mr. Murphy. 

Mr. MURPHY.  

Mr. Secretary, when Admiral Sharp was before the committee I asked him about the new base southeast of Bangkok and whether it was being used for bombing purposes by B-52's. Do the B-52's now use that base?

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. They will use it increasingly in the months ahead as certain facilities not now in place become operational. 

Mr. MURPHY. When in Thailand I noticed that Khorat would be the logistics base for Thailand. It is your intention to make this new complex southeast of Bangkok your major logistic base?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It will be one of the major logistical bases. 

In particular it will be the major point of receipt of many of the stores that move by ship-particularly petroleum, for example-and other items that can be off-loaded there and either used at that point or moved inland without having to go through Bangkok itself. 

Mr. MURPHY. Up the river?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. 

Mr. MURPHY. The traffic is very heavy on the river at the present time? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, but we can avoid the blockages that occur because of having to move supplies through the city. 265

FOREIGN ASSISTANT ACT OF 1967 MONDAY, APRIL 17, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

Office  

The committee meets this morning in executive session to continue the hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to further amend the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961.

This is the second appearance of Secretary McNamara and General Wheeler before the committee on this bill. When they were here last week the committee had to rise early and the Secretary had another engagement, so that we asked the Secretary to come back. In response to a parliamentary inquiry by Congressman Rosenthal, the committee decided to start the questioning where we left off last week. Mr. Farbstein would have been next on the majority side. He is not present, so I will call first on Mr. Murphy. 

Mr. MURPHY.  

Mr. Secretary, when Admiral Sharp was before the committee I asked him about the new base southeast of Bangkok and whether it was being used for bombing purposes by B-52's. Do the B-52's now use that base?

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. They will use it increasingly in the months ahead as certain facilities not now in place become operational. 

Mr. MURPHY. When in Thailand I noticed that Khorat would be the logistics base for Thailand. It is your intention to make this new complex southeast of Bangkok your major logistic base?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It will be one of the major logistical bases. 

In particular it will be the major point of receipt of many of the stores that move by ship-particularly petroleum, for example-and other items that can be off-loaded there and either used at that point or moved inland without having to go through Bangkok itself. 

Mr. MURPHY. Up the river?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. 

Mr. MURPHY. The traffic is very heavy on the river at the present time? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, but we can avoid the blockages that occur because of having to move supplies through the city. 265

1967 

Mr. MURPHY. Are they building a railroad connection to the northeast?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I believe there is a road connection. Is there a railway?

STATEMENT OF GEN. EARLE G. WHEELER, U.S. ARMY, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF 

General WHEELER. There is a railroad part of the way [security deletion]. There is a road connection right now and the road is being improved over a certain section so we can have a complete bypass around the metropolitan area of Bangkok.

Mr. MURPHY. In the latter part of 1965, I understood that the Thai 

Government created a special federal security force to combat the infiltration of Communists into northeast areas, and along the Malaysian border. Are we granting aid for the maintenance of this particular force?

Secretary MCNAMARA. We grant aid to the military forces; but we do not, through the military assistance program, grant it to what I would call the police function, although the force that you are talking about combines both police and military support. So to the degree that they use military personnel, we do assist. 

Mr. MURPHY. Have you any information in reference to the success of this particular operation?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I would like General Wheeler to comment on the total insurgency problem there. It is not great at the moment. 

There is no question but that the North Vietnamese would take advantage of any opportunity for developing an insurgency program. 

[Security deletion.] 

General WHEELER. As you probably know, Mr. Murphy, there are three areas where they have insurgency problems. One is to the south. 

Mr. MURPHY. I know the areas. 

General WHEELER. The northeast is the most troublesome. In recent months there has been a stepup of subversive activity in the area. The 

Thai force that you mention has gone into the field now about three times in fairly substantial numbers and they have had modest success. 

I believe the most important fact is that since the end of 1965, the Thais have become increasingly aware of the problem and are trying to do something about it. I do believe that they are being what I would call "moderately successful" and they will do better as their organization and their intelligence improve. 

Mr. MURPHY. When I was in the eastern portion, that is in the area of infiltration [security deletion]. 

General WHEELER. [Security deletion] the federal police function of setting up an organization throughout the countryside which can feed information back to a central point so that something can be done by both the police and the military to counter the Communist infiltration. The provincial police have not been adequate in numbers, training, or equipment to take care of an insurgency. The Federal police, backed up by the military, have a greater capability to deal with this kind of problem. 

Mr. MURPHY. Thank you, sir.

267 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Thank you. 

Mr. FULTON. We are glad to have you here. I would like to speak shortly of the management of the Vietnam war. 

The President is the management head of the Vietnam war. The 

President is the Commander in Chief, and the President is also the head of the civilian pacification program in Vietnam as well, isn't that correct? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, although the details of the civilian pacification program, of course, are handled by agencies that operate within the policy he has established. 

Mr. FULTON. But the President meets all the time with administration leaders not only setting up the management structure, but likewise having conferences on how management is working out, doesn't he?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Mr. Komer in the White House follows the details of the civilian pacification program for him.

Mr. FULTON. My next question then moves to selection of Vietnam air targets. Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. We continually resurvey that particular decision because the basis for deciding not to attack the airfields to date has been that we felt we would lose more men by attacking them than by not attacking them. It is true that the Migs have knocked down 10 

U.S. aircraft in air combat, but the U.S. aircraft in the same combat have knocked down, I believe, 43 Migs, plus some additional possible/ probable losses.

The ratio is very much in our favor; and there is no question-I don't think anyone would deny this-that we would lose a significant number of men were we to attack the airfields and then continue to attack them. It should be understood that we would have to attack them more than once in order to keep them out of operation. 

It is a very simple issue in principle: Which way do you lose more men? Up to the present time, we thought we would lose more by attacking them directly. Beyond that, such an attack runs the risk of widening the war; and it is our desire to avoid that if we possibly can. 

This decision is being reviewed periodically. It is not a decision that will continue to apply tomorrow if the conditions change tomorrow.

Secretary MCNAMARA. Mr. MONAGAN. Mr. Secretary, during your statement the other day you spoke about the removal of some forces from NATO. My notes say 39,000 personnel, but that may not be an accurate description. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. 39,000 U.S.- 

Mr. MONAGAN. 39,000Secretary MCNAMARA. 39,000 U.S. personnel, including dependents, have been moved out of Europe as a part of the move out of France. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Here is a very serious question that I would like to hear you talk about. If a military and political threat still exists on the Continent, and if some of the reasons why NATO was formed still hold true, and if, as Mr. Sulzberger said in the New York Times only the other day, no Russian troops have been removed from East Germany or from Hungary or from Poland, in substance, how can we justify the removal of several divisions of our own troops from NATO when this personal presence of our troops there is such a significant factor in defense?

Secretary MCNAMARA. First, I don't believe we could justify the removal of several divisions of troops from NATO. I personally believe, and I think the Joint Chiefs would fully agree, that it would be unwise at the present time to change the military balance between East and West.

I believe that the removal of 39,000 U.S. personnel from France and their transfer back to the United States did not change the military balance, with one or two minor exceptions which I will comment on in a moment. These 39,000 people did not include personnel of major combat units. The 39,000 break down into 18,000 military and 21,000 dependents. The 18,000 military were almost entirely support personnel. 

Three reconnaissance squadrons were moved back to this country, but two were put on a rotational basis so they will rotate periodically to bases in Europe. The 18,000 military personnel included in the total of 39,000 were primarily logistical troops: I submit to you that the movement of the logistical forces, and the transfer of the lines of communication from France into the Low Countries, did not significantly change the strength of NATO forces. 

The NATO strategy is based on a forward defense. It does not contemplate withdrawing from forward areas and moving to the rear for defense in depth. It is true that, to some degree, the movement of the lines of communication from the rear forward makes them somewhat more vulnerable, but not significantly. There is an offset, however, in that the transportation system running through the Lowlands is better suited to our needs than that running through France. 

I don't believe this movement either included significant combat. units or significantly affected the military balance between East and West. 

General Wheeler, would you add to that?

General WHEELER. I would agree generally with what the Secretary said. What we have, in effect, is an entirely different military situation. Prior to the requirement by President de Gaulle that we

1967 

move our NATO installations and units out of France, we had a supply system based in depth in order to utilize the French territory properly for military logistic purposes. 

We also had stationed in France substantial air units in order to insure the same kind of depth in the disposition of our air units. This is most desirable. When we lost the use of French territory, we had to change our concept of logistical support and of air support. What has actually happened is that a certain quantity of the supplies have been moved forward into Germany, into logistic installations which we had there or which we have since activated; other supplies were moved into the United Kingdom; and, as the Secretary mentioned, a certain number of aircraft have been moved either to the United 

Kingdom or to the United States.

The net result is that the air organization on the ground having changed, these people could be withdrawn without detriment to the support of our forces over there. We are faced with a different problem. 

The solution, therefore, is different.

Can you tell us what ratio of strategic missiles you do consider necessary as a margin for safety?

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, because we don't actually calculate our strategic nuclear requirements in terms of ratios. We calculate them on a very simple principle-that we must have a strategic nuclear force large enough fully to absorb a Soviet surprise attack and survive with sufficient power to destroy the Soviet Union. 

Mr. FINDLEY. I believe you have used a 4-to-1 ratio.

Secretary MCNAMARA. We believe that only by having a power that great can we be assured of deterring a Soviet nuclear strike or a large conventional attack. What ratio will provide that deterrent capability is entirely a function of the type of force they have, the yield of their weapons, the survivability of their forces, for example, whether the weapon sites are hardened or not hardened and the composition of their delivery forces-for example, missiles versus airplanes.

Secretary MCNAMARA. We have no intention whatsoever of reducing our strength below that requirement.

CONTINUED U.S. PRESENCE IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Question. Have we assured South Vietnam of the permanence of our presence and the continuation of military aid beyond the cessation of hostilities? 

Answer. The U.S. position on this matter was enunciated by President Johnson in his Johns Hopkins address of April 7, 1965. He said: "Our objective is the independence of South Vietnam and its freedom from attack. We want nothing for ourselves-only that the people of South Vietnam be allowed to guide their own country in their own way." 

Article 29 of the Manila Communique signed by the President last October 25 

is also pertinent: "29. In particular they (the seven participating nations) declared that allied forces are in the Republic of Vietnam because that country is the object of aggression and its Government requested support in the resistence of its people to aggression. They shall be withdrawn, after close consultation, as the other side withdraws its forces to the north, ceases infiltration, and the level of violence thus subsides. Those forces will be withdrawn as soon as possible and not later than six months after the above conditions have been fulfilled." 

There are no agreements between the United States and the Republic of Vietnam concerning post-hostilities military assistance. 

STATUS OF SEATO 

Question. I am concerned about the extent to which this is a U.S. war. Are we making efforts to remodel, replace or broaden SEATO? 

Answer. There are no efforts being made to remodel or replace SEATO. SEATO is a going concern which continues to play an important role in the area in both combatting and deterring threats to peace and in contributing to progress in the area. There are no efforts underway at this time to broaden the membership of 

SEATO; however, the treaty does permit other nations to accede to the treaty.

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, sir; that doesn't affect my recommendation for the transfer. However, the recommendation for transfer is somewhat related in one sense. The military assistance budget is a relatively small amount of funds. If you begin to finance combat consumption out of that pool, facing all of the uncertainties of predicting combat requirements, then when those unforeseen requirements develop as they did, for example, in Vietnam in 1965, they must be absorbed by this very small pool to the detriment of other elements of the program. In contrast, if these programs are being financed out of the larger Defense budget, the relatively small increments required to meet changes in the combat situation can be taken care of by the inherent flexibility offered by the much larger reserves of the Defense budget. That is really the reason we recommend transfers relating to combat operations.

1967 

in racist philosophy. I am frequently pilloried by these demonstrations as a racist. I was last week. I don't like to be called a warmonger. I don't think I am. I am acting for the Nation. I carry around in my pocket, so I won't forget, a statement setting forth the ideals that I think we should support. It is a paragraph of Judge Learned Hand's, and I would like to read it to you. This is what he had to say on the specific subject:

I believe that that community is already in process of dissolution where each man begins to eye his neighbor as a possible enemy, where nonconformity with the accepted creed, political as well as religious, is a mark of disaffection; where denunciation, without specification or backing, takes the place of evidence; where orthodoxy chokes freedom of dissent; where faith in the eventual supremacy of reason has become so timid that we dare not enter our convictions in the open lists to win or lose. Such fears as these are a solvent which can eat out the cement that binds the stones together; they may in the end subject us to a despotism as evil as any that we dread; and they can be allayed only in so far as we refuse to proceed on suspicion, and trust one another until we have tangible ground for misgiving. The mutual confidence on which all else depends can be maintained only by an open mind and a brave reliance upon free discussion. 

I am as annoyed as you are by the demonstrations-more so perhaps because I am a target of them—but I would not recommend that we act, nor do I think we have the power to act to stop them.

Perhaps we are in the position of a doctor who has to rely on the forces of nature, or the forces within each society for the real progress to come about. Our efforts in many respects seem marginal. 

I just came back from a trip to Africa which reimpressed upon me that there are liberation wars in Africa which are hot ones. Several of them are in Ethiopia. These are liberation wars at the southern end of the continent. These are not the only places we see them. There are some in Latin America and some more in the Far East, the Philippines, and so on. I have the distinct impression that one of the byproducts of our Vietnam involvement is going to be an increased hesitancy on the part of the United States to get involved in anything again that looks like a Vietnam. I sensed that from the way you approach the 

Latin American problem, and in my talks with our Ambassadors in other parts of the world. There is a very clear reluctance to begin on a process that will lead us again into this kind of a situation. 

What this implies for future American policy is that if we want to have a hand in shaping what happens in the world we are going to have to rely increasingly on nonmilitary means of influencing what happens. 

This means that we have to work on the political side, the social side, to a degree far greater than we have ever done in the past. 

Because we are in Vietnam, because we have an investment there, we ought to learn everything we can from that experience; we ought to learn as much as we can about how the forces in the society can be mobilized, how social organization can lead to a sense of national identity.

Yet I find in our Government a lack of clear responsibility for this, and no clear idea to face up to what this means. This means we are losing an enormous amount of value from our Vietnam involvement. We should be learning more about these societies and how these things work out. This, in my judgment, is going to be increasingly important in future international policy decisions. This is why I was concerned. 

I take pacification as a starting point because everyone talks about it. 

I am deeply concerned that the United States is not accepting the implications that flow from our major deficits in this sector as part of our involvement in Vietnam.

I don't necessarily want you to comment on this, but I feel very strongly about this. This is why I am trying to get at this lack of resolution, the lack to focus on the problem here in Washington.

STATEMENT OF HON. HERBERT SALZMAN 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, thank you for this opportunity to appear before you to discuss the foreign aid legislation as it relates to participation in development by private American businesses and non-profit organizations, and our proposed programs in these areas for the coming fiscal year. 

Encouragaing private participation-both local and foreign-in development is a major goal of our programs. This objective is reflected in: (1) our direct assistance programs; (2) our determination to contribute to A.I.D.'s goals 299

1967 

through efforts by American private businesses, non-profit organizations, State and local governments. 

A.I.D. has in recent months:

Established an Office of Private Resources to seek greater, across-theboard, participation in development by private groups. Within this Office, a Private Investment Center is being set up as a focal point for our efforts to encourage private U.S. investment in the less developed countries. 

Launched new programs to promote U.S. investment in Africa and Latin 

America. 

Started a High Protein Food Studies program as part of the War on 

Hunger. 

Developed a pilot program to test the applicability of the "systems approach" to development problems. 

Made greater use of A.I.D. extended risk guaranties to facilitate private financing of important private projects, including two major fertilizer plants in India and Brazil. 

Formed an International Private Investment Advisory Council to improve our liaison with the U.S. business community. 

IMPROVING THE CONDITIONS FOR PRIVATE PARTICIPATION 

Certain conditions must be present in the developing countires if private investment is to flow and private institutions are to be effective. These conditions include: fiscal and monetary policies that encourage rather than inhibit private enterprise; public services and utilities adequate to support an expansion of private economic activity; pluralistic private institutions, such as cooperatives, labor and business groups, to stimulate and channel individual initiative; skilled workers and responsibile management; access to medium- and long-term credit. 

These are conditions we are apt to take for granted here at home but that exist all too rarely in less developed countries. 

A.I.D.'s direct assistance programs help to improve these conditions. 

Program loans, such as the $100 million loan to Brazil in March and the more recent $132 million loan to India, finance imports of U.S.-produced fertilizer, machine tools, chemicals and other essential commodities for use by thousands of individual businessmen and farmers. These loans are conditioned on basic reforms in import and licensing procedures that help to "free up" an economy. 

The local currencies generated by these loans are allocated for priority uses including relending to private borrowers. 

Project loans, such as a $9.5 million loan to Bolivia for road construction and a $8.9 million loan to a Brazilian utility for power plant and transmission facilities, finance the U.S. skills and equipment which help build the basic infrastructure required for increased production. 

Loans to intermediate credit institutions, such as a $5 million loan to the Nicaraguan Investment Corporation, open up sources of medium- and long-term credit to individual farmers and businessmen.

Technical assistance is used in many different ways to strengthen the private sector, for example, to help set up a modern business school in Peru, to help draft an improved investment code in Afghanistan, to help modernize tax structures in Latin America. 

In his testimony before you on April 5, Mr. Gaud stressed the key role these programs play in stimulating the private sectors in aid-receiving countries. 

You will be hearing more about them from our regional Assistant Administra tors. These programs-and the Development Loan and Technical Assistance authorizations which make them possible-are an essential complement to private U.S. groups participating more actively in the development business. 

ENCOURAGING PRIVATE PARTICIPATION 

Public resources-human and financial-are not and never will be sufficient to meet the needs of developing countries. We and the developing countries must rely to the greatest possible extent on the vast reservoir of private resources. 

Private groups in this country contribute to and benefit from our regular assistance programs. In fiscal year 1966, American businesses in all 50 States. supplied over $1.1 billion worth of chemicals, machinery, vehicles and other A.I.D.financed commodities. (See chart.)

Private U.S. groups-profit and non-profit-are also suppliers of technical skills. U.S. cooperatives are an example. A.I.D. now has world-wide agreements with eight cooperative organizations: 

Cooperative League of the U.S.A. 

Credit Union National Association. 

National Rural Electric Cooperatives Association. 

Farmers Union International Assistance Corporation. 

Foundation for Cooperative Housing.

International Cooperative Development Association. 

International Cooperative Training Center. 

National League of Insured Savings & Loan Associations. 

This gives us access to the major national, regional and local cooperatives in the United States who supply over 250 advisors and consultants at work on A.I.D. coopeartive projects in 42 countries, achieving impressive results indeed. 

In 1961 there were two active savings and loan institutions in Latin America. 

Today there are 91, with a membership of close to a half million people, and with combined savings of $165 million, an increase of $65 million over last year. 

These savings have financed the construction of 56,500 homes for 395,000 people. 

Credit unions, rural electric cooperatives and agricultural cooperatives are also increasing at a rapid rate.

In addition to our technical assistance contracts with cooperatives, universities, consulting firms and other private U.S. groups, A.I.D. is providing grant support to non-profit organizations. We help some of these organizations get started and others to expand. 

A good example is the International Executive Service Corps. The IESC, as you know, provides high quality management assistance to businesses in developing countries who need this kind of help but who could not otherwise afford it. A.I.D. encouraged the IESC's creation and provides, together with 

American businesses and foundations, financial support for IESC's operations. 

The IESC is reaching retired American businessmen and mid-career executives who are willing to volunteer their services-men A.I.D. could not hope to get on a contract or a direct hire basis. The only pay these volunteers receive is for travel and living expenses. The 2,600 experienced businessmen on IESC's roster come from large corporations and from small, in many different industries. 

Since the IESC began operations in January 1965, 190 projects have been carried out in 38 countries around the world. In this calendar year alone, IESC will start some 350 projects. The results to date have been successful. Concretely this is what they do:

A retired managing director of Standard Brands helped a vegetable oil processor in Iran with market research and sales planning. 

A mid-career banker from Chase Manhattan helped a commercial bank in Thailand revise its international lending practices and improve its internal accounting system.

An IESC volunteer with 30 years experience as head of his own concrete block business helped a producer of concrete blocks in San Salvador improve his product and sales. 

We propose to continue our support of the IESC during the coming year. 

And, now that this program is fully operative, we will be taking a close look at the amount of A.I.D. support required in subsequent years. 

The IESC is but one example of the use of A.I.D. funds as a catalyst for private effort. The Partners of the Alliance program is another. 

In this case

A.I.D. helps finance private U.S. groups at the State and local level that can effectively contribute to Latin American development. Thirty of our States and the District of Columbia are now participating in Partners programs in 15 Latin American countries. A recent A.I.D. grant to the newly-formed National Association for the Partners of the Alliance will assist the Association in sponsoring, coordinating and expanding the Partners program. 

By providing U.S. agricultural commodities under the Food for Freedom program, and ocean freight payments, we also help support the technical assistance and emergency relief activities of 67 voluntary agencies, such as Church World Services, Catholic Relief Service, the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and CARE, that are registered with A.I.D.'s Advisory Committee on 

Voluntary Foreign Aid. Many of these agencies are placing more emphasis on training and development activities, in addition to their basic relief programs, and we are encouraging them to do so.

303 There are close to five hundred private organizations in the U.S. whose money and skills play an important role in less developed countries and who now provide annually on their own an estimated three quarters of a billion dollars worth of assistance to less developed countries. Consistent with Section 601(b) (2) of the Act, we want to find ways to expand the activities of these and other groups, and to coordinate their programs more closely with our own, particularly in the field.

A.I.D.'s policy is to look first to see if private effort alone can do the job, next to hiring private organizations, and last to the use of direct-hire U.S. 

Government personnel. 

A.I.D. has regrouped certain functions in the new Office of Private Resources, which I head, to carry out this policy. It is our job to provide a central contact in AI.D. for profit and non-profit organizations, to administer A.I.D.'s private investment incentive programs for U.S. business, and to develop new ways for profit and non-profit groups to help in development. 

ENCOURAGING PRIVATE INVESTMENT 

To encourage private U.S. investment in the developing countries, we offer services that enable American businessmen- To obtain information on investment conditions and opportunities in the less developed countries; 

To investigate and survey proposed projects; 

To protect their investments against certain risks that are not present in developed countries; and

To obtain loan financing for their projects. 

We are establishing, within the Office of Private Resources, a Private Investment Center to enable U.S. investors to work with one office in obtaining the help they need from A.I.D. in going forward with their projects. Our objective will be to give early and frank indications to U.S. investors of what we can do and what we can't do, and to try to find a way to get worthwhile projects moving. 

We try first to help the investor by supplying advice and information. If this is insufficient we offer our insurance and guaranty programs. If this still isn't enough, we can make dollar or local currency loans. Our goal is to get worthwhile projects going with the minimum use of appropriated funds. 

I would like to briefly tell you about our private investment incentive programs-what they are, how they work, what they cost, what they accomplish and the changes we propose in this year's legislation. 

Information Services 

We have a central inquiry office for U.S. business firms and potential investors, that advises them on A.I.D. programs and puts them directly in touch with the person who can help them. We handle an average of 600 inquiries per month, up from 400 per month a year ago. The Center also coordinates the publication and distribution of Aids to Business and similar literature about A.I.D. programs of interest to businessmen.

Through our Catalog of Investment Information and Opportunities we make available to potential investors reports on economic conditions and feasibility studies which have been prepared by A.I.D., by other national and international organizations and by private firms. The Catalog now contains over 1600 studies. 

The Catalog also contains information on specific joint venture opportunities that have been reported through the Commercial Attaches in our Embassies overseas. A ready reference Index to the Catalog is distributed widely. Last year we sold 3600 copies of the studies and 1200 abstracts.

These con- We also make available Industry Profiles to potential investors. tain basic information on the establishment of small or medium-sized plants in specific industries, for example, fish oil and fish meal, agricultural implements and caming. In addition, we are asking for authority to reimburse more than 50 percent (the existing statutory ceiling) of the cost of investment surveys where this is necessary to move investor interest into areas that are important to the national interest, such as the War on Hunger. 

Specific Risk Guaranties 

The Specific Risk Guaranty program protects investors against certain political risks not normally present in developed countries; inconvertibility of earnings; expropriation; and war, revolution and insurrection. 

Coverage outstanding as of March 31 was $3.6 billion. We expect this year to issue a record $1 to $1 billion of specific risk insurance.

We also propose an amendment to Section 221 (b) of the Act adding a separate guaranty authority extending to such risks as the President may determine, but limited to 50 percent of any loss of equity investment. The amount of this guaranty coverage outstanding would be charged against the overall specific risk guaranty ceiling and would be limited to $125 million. 

While extended risk guaranties of equity investments are now authorized under Section 221(b)(2), we have used that authority primarily to guaranty loans rather than equity investments, and we expect to continue to do so. The proposed amendment would establish equity insurance as a separate program with its own issuing authority. Equity insurance should be a significant new inducement to private investment. 

The existing statute authorizes use of fee income to handle claims. We propose a broadening of that authority to include other administrative and operating expenses of the guaranty programs and of the related investment survey and information programs. This will help us to put these services to U.S. investors on a more businesslike basis.

Section 221 (b) (2) of the present Act authorizes us to guaranty investors in non-housing projects against loss of up to 75 percent of the investment package. 

This applies to all risks except fraud or misconduct.

Last year at this time we had to say that "Progress under this program has continued to be slow." This year I am glad to report a significant increase in the use of this authority. The four contracts authorized in 1966 equalled the number authorized during the preceding four years. Two of the four contracts cover investments in major fertilizer complexes in India and Brazil. The $40.5 million in coverage issued last year involved a total project investment of $166 million. 

In 1967 we expect to authorize an additional $100 million in coverage for 15 projects involving a total investment of some $300 million. Four of the 15 have already been authorized, and two of these were for investments in War on Hunger projects: grain marketing in Thailand and a feed and broiler operation in Korea. 

Through a new form of contract worked out with the investment community last year, we can give U.S. institutional lenders (insurance companies, pension funds, etc.) the protection they need to provide long-term U.S. financing to important private projects without the use of appropriated funds. To date, twenty U.S. financial institutions, including commercial banks and insurance companies, in 10 states, have participated in loans covered by extended risk guaranties.

We seek an increase in the ceiling on our extended risk (non-housing) authority from the present $215 million to $415 million. We also request an extension of the termination date for this program to June 30, 1971, two years beyond the two-year authorization period. This will insure investors who start planning before June 30, 1969, against the possibility that the extended risk program may lapse before then can complete their investment.

We also have authority under Sections 221(b) (2) and 244 of the Act to provide "all risk" guaranties of up to 100 percent of investments in housing projects. Under the Latin American housing program which Mr. Bronheim, Deputy Coordinator of the Alliance for Progress, will be discussing with you

Loans to American Firms 

Under the "Cooley" loan program, A.I.D. can make available U.S.-owned local currencies to American firms and their affiliates. In calendar year 1966, we authorized 41 loans in 15 countries, amounting to $42.6 million equivalent. These loans were made for such varied projects as animal feed in Sudan and Peru, integrated electronic circuits in Korea, and foodstuffs in Israel. 

Cooley funds originate from the sale of U.S. agricultural products under Title 

I of PL 480. Although PL 480 now requires a transition from local currency to dollar sales over a 5-year period, it also provides that local currency may be accepted in lieu of dollars for specified purposes, including loans to U.S. firms and their affiliates. We expect the demand for Cooley loans to continue and we will attempt to provide funds for this in negotiating new Food for Freedom sales agreements.

In some countries where Cooley funds are not available, local currencies generated by A.I.D. program loans have been set aside for relending to private borrowers, both U.S. and local. For example, we have helped to set up funds for this purpose in such countries as Brazil and Colombia. 

Dollar loans to private American and local ventures are available through A.I.D. These loans can be made where dollar financing on reasonable terms is not available from other public or private sources. In 1966 we made five dollar loans, amounting to $13.9 million, for private industrial projects. 

Finally, both dollar and local currency loans are also available through intermediate credit institutions. Since 1961 A.I.D. has made loans totaling $617 million to 72 of these institutions in 35 countries. 

In carrying out our private enterprise activities, we continue to be guided by the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Private Enterprise in Foreign Aid. A third report on the Agency's response to the Watson Committee's recommendations has just been completed and copies are being sent to each of you. We also benefit from the advice and counsel of the Private Sector Subcommitee, chaired by David Rockefeller, of the President's General Advisory Committee on Foreign Assistance Programs. In the future we will have the help of the new International Private Investment Advisory Council, the Council established in response to an amendment to last year's Act, initiated by the Committee. The IPIAC consists of the President's major U.S. business organiza tions: Committee for Economic Development, National Association of Manufacturers, National Foreign Trade Council, National Industrial Conference 

Board, U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the U.S. Council of the International 

Chamber of Commerce. We hope to have the first meeting of the Council in 

May. One of the things we want to discuss with the Council is the guidelines for the use of cost-plus incentive fee management contracts (Section 601 (b) (8)). 

RECENT DEVELOPMENTS IN OUR PRIVATE ENTERPRISE PROGRAMS 

There are several other recent developments in our private enterprise programs which I would like to mention briefly.

To increase the supply of protein foods in developing countries, we recently launched a new High Protein Food Studies Program. The first contract under this new program was signed with the Pillsbury Company of Minneapolis in 

February. With A.I.D.'s help, Pillsbury will carry out product tests and market surveys for a high protein food supplement derived from cottonseed, peanuts and soybeans. A second contract has been signed with Krausse Milling Company. We expect to sign similar contracts with other leading food companies in the near future.

Our African Bureau has two new programs underway to promote U.S. private investment in Africa. One involves A.I.D. contracts with Edge Act subsidiaries of commercial banks and leading investment banking firms to pinpoint and promote specific investment opportunities. Some 25 projects in a dozen African countries are being actively promoted at the present time; another 70 to 80 projects are being reviewed for possible promotion. The second program involves a group of major U.S. agribusiness firms in an effort to promote large-unit vertically-integrated agricultural and fisheries projects. A.I.D. is paying the cost 

77-470-67-pt. 2-

of preliminary surveys and, where warranted, detailed feasibility studies. Five study teams are already in Africa; a sixth is scheduled to go to the field before the end of this month. We are also working with private groups on a proposed 

African Investment Corporation. 

Our Latin America Bureau is helping to establish an Inter-American Investment Promotion Center which will seek to interest U.S. firms in investment opportunities identified by development banks and other institutions in Latin America.

We are starting a pilot program to test the applicability of the "systems approach" to development problems, with particular emphasis on the War on Hunger. We have discussed this program with U.S. industrial firms, who have successfully applied systems analysis and management techniques to defense and space problems, and will be exploring with them the possibility of applying these same techniques to selected foreign assistance projects. This is one way in which we are trying to involve industrial firms more heavily in our technical assistance programs.

These are the ways we in AID are working to improve the possibilities for private enterprise to function effectively in the less developed countries and how we try to encourage American businesses and non-profit organizations to take part in the development job. 

These programs are not individually glamorous but they do deal with the day-to-day realities of encouraging private initiative in less developed countries. They do something concrete about dealing with the parts of the problem we can come to grips with.

We don't have all the answers, but the clarification of our goals, the changes in our organization and the proposed changes in this year's legislation will help get the job done. It's a tough, difficult job. There are no panaceas, no easy ways. 

We welcome your suggestions and all the help you can give us in getting the job done.

Mr. SALZMAN. I would like to take a few minutes to give you a brief report on the nature of our programs and how we operate them. Our first interest is in improving conditions for private participation in development. We attempt to do this in the first instance by loans and technical assistance support to less developed countries that foster private economic activity.

AID encourages private U.S. participation by commodity procurement of AID-financed commodities. In 1966 this amounted to over $1.1 billion supplied by firms in all 50 States. AID also has some 1,400 contracts with private U.S. organizations for technical services totaling more than a half billion dollars. These go to such institutions as universities, co-ops, consultant firms, and so on. 

We also provide support for private U.S. groups such as voluntary agencies, the International Executive Service Corps, Partners of the

Alliance, and similar organizations. AID also administers a range of private investment incentive programs. To use a hypothetical example, if a company, interested in overseas development, were to approach AID, using as an example a company interested in a feed and chicken broiler operation, they would presumably first request information about the conditions in those countries that they were interested in.

We would supply this information in the first instance through our Catalog of Investment Information and Opportunities such as I hold here, as well as by meetings with our people at the Agency. 

In order to reduce this general information to specifics, we offer an investment survey program which enables the company to go to the country of its selection and make an on-the-spot investigation of the possibilities of its project being successful, which might include a

309 general economic survey, a market survey, as well as studies of the engineering and other production aspects of the contemplated investment. 

Should the survey prove satisfactory, they would then go ahead with it and there would be no further AID involvement. Should the decision, based on the investment survey, be not to proceed with the investment, AID would be prepared to reimburse that company to the extent of 50 percent of its costs upon the turning over to AID of an acceptable survey report.

In the event that the company went forward with the investment, they would probably want to insure themselves against political risks, against risks of inconvertibility, expropriation, insurrection, and the like. This program is known as the specific risk guarantee program. 

This would result in a contract between AID and the investing company insuring them against the risks I mentioned. When it comes to financing the project, we have financial assistance available in the form of an extended risk guarantee program. This is a means of guaranteeing, for example, 75 percent of a loan from a commercial bank and long-term lender. The lenders would lend the stated amount and 

AID would insure 75 percent of the total loan. 

In the event that the extended risk guarantee financing for such a loan was not for one reason or another acceptable-a particular cause for concern might be the necessity for the commercial lender or the institutional lender to guarantee and take upon itself the responsibility for the 25 percent not guaranteed by the U.S. Government--we would then consider local currency loans or dollar loans.

Obviously the proportion of each, and the circumstances under which each of these would be made available, differ with the varying projects. To give you some idea as to the use of the program, and basing the effectiveness of any program on the degree to which it is used by the respective investors, I would like to give you a few quick 

The Catalog of Investment Information is used to the extent of 6,000 requests per year.

Current AID policy is to support private participation in the investment process to the fullest. To this end the official head, the Office of Private Resources, was recently organized to give effect to the President's policy goals and the Administrator's policy goals in this area. As such, we are responsible for the administration of the programs I have outlined as well as the participation of nonprofit groups who are concerned with economic development overseas and political and social development as well. 

We look to the newly organized International Private Investment Advisory Council to work with us and guide us in our effort during the coming year. Within the Office of Private Resources we hope to organize a Private Investment Center which will provide a central reference point within the Agency for the private investors who are interested in participating in the development process. We expect to assign to each organization a particular person of high level who can render early decisions and in general assist the private institution in its dealings with the Agency.

The attitude of the Agency toward private participation I think is best expressed in the recent policy determination issued by the Administrator whereby he calls upon all AID personnel to utilize to the greatest extent possible the services and capabilities of private organizations. In the event that these efforts alone are unavailing, we will then try to use AID credit. In the last instance, will we use cash. The primary objective of this policy determination is to use the minimum number of direct-hire U.S. Government personnel and to achieve as many of our programs and as many of our goals as possible through private organizational efforts.

Recently developments in the Agency as it concerns private participation include a program designed to encourage the implementation of high-protein food supplements to the diets of various countries. We are going forward with intensive private investment promotion in Africa. This is represented by the participation of a large number of 

Edge Act subsidiaries of U.S. banks and investment bankers in seeking out investment opportunities. Also a number of agribusiness firms have been approached to undertake studies of large-unit agricultural production and processing projects in Africa. Another example is the soon forthcoming organization of the Inter-American Investment Promotion Center, designed to bring to the attention of the U.S. investment public investment opportunities in Latin America. We are also undertaking a pilot program to explore and develop the use of the "systems approach" in technical assistance and in economic development overseas. 

We have another program which we think will be of material benefit to companies who are thinking of investment overseas, wherein the U.S. 

Government expects to insure 50 percent of equity investments. This would be done on a country-by-country basis, selecting those industries which we think are of most importance in furthering AID programs and goals.

Last and by no means least, is the constant attempt to improve our present programs. This involves not only an appraisal and analysis of the investment climate in the countries themselves, as indicated by a soon to be released further response to the Watson Committee Report,

311 but it is also shown by the amendments that we request in the proposed legislation as well as the improvements that we can make as a result of administrative decisions in the implementation and operation of our programs.

These then are generally the ways in which we in AID are working to improve the possibilities for private enterprise to function effectively in the less developed countries and how we try to encourage American businesses and nonprofit organizations to take part in the development job. These programs are not individually glamorous, but they do deal with the day-to-day realities of encouraging private initiative in these countries and they do something very concrete about dealing with the parts of the problem that we can come to grips with. 

We don't have all the answers, but the clarification of our goals, the changes in our organization and the proposed changes in this year's legislation will help get the job done. It is a rough, difficult job. There are no panaceas and no easy ways. 

Speaking informally, before I came down here about 6 months ago I was in the position of a man who before he was married had six theories and no children. Now that it is 6 months later, I have six children and no theories.

Mr. SALZMAN. It doesn't take long, Mr. Congressman. This is a job that has to get done a piece at a time. We are really trying to do that piece each day which will make tomorrow come a little closer. I earnestly solicit and welcome your suggestions and any help that you can give us-me in particular-in getting this job done. I will be happy to answer any questions.

ALL STATES SHARE IN AID-FINANCED EXPORTS 

All 50 States shared in production of commodity exports under United States foreign economic aid financing during 1966. 

The AID-financed commodities include fertilizers, farm implements, industrial machinery, steel goods, pharmaceuticals, transportation equipment, and other industrial products and materials purchased by developing countries. They are used to meet current material requirements for economic development. 

Included in the procurement are materials and equipment related to the War on Hunger and participation by the United States in regional development efforts such as the Alliance for Progress in Latin America. 

The nationwide scope of production generated by the AID program is shown in an Agency summary of 1966 procurement financed under letters of credit and traced to state sources. It marked the first year in which orders were specifically recorded for all states since AID's procurement-source sampling procedure was begun in 1962. Hawaii is the newest addition to the list of AID commodity suppliers. 

The reports covered more than $600 million in production by American firms, equal to about half of the actual volume of AID-financed procurement in the United States in recent years. Because the reports include only transactions of more than $10,000, the amount recorded for each State in this sampling may be only part of its full export total under the AID program. The figures do not reflect additional AID-generated business such as respective States' portions of revenue from transportation of these goods and related port operations in many

1967 NINETY PERCENT OF AID-FINANCED COMMODITIES PURCHASED IN U.S. 

Nine of every 10 dollars spent for commodities financed by the Agency for International Development during Fiscal 1966 went to American suppliers. A preliminary report by AID also reveals that, for all categories of expenditures, nearly four of every five AID dollars remained in the United States economy. 

The high percentages of U.S. procurement were the result of stringent emphasis in the AID program to help guard the U.S. balance of payments position. 

According to the report, $1.11 billion was paid to U.S. suppliers of commodities during the year. This was 90 percent of $1.23 billion spent for all AID-financed goods. The commodities consist of the materials and equipment purchased by developing countries using AID loans and grants. 

Fiscal 1966, which ended June 30, marked the third consecutive year in which this category of U.S. export sales exceeded the billion dollar mark. 

Of the non-U.S. commodity expenditures, largely involving raw materials and semi-finished products, a total of $109.9 million was procured from primarily developing countries. Only $11.2 million worth was purchased from 19 developed countries, principally Western Europe and Japan, largely excluded as eligible procurement sources under AID financing. 

Of total AID expenditures for all goods and services, including commodity procurement, preliminary figures for the year show almost $1.7 billion spent in the 

United States-77 percent of an aggregate $2.195 billion. 

The remainder of $503 million in expenditures outside the U.S. was offset by $183 million in foreign countries' repayments (interest and principal) of previous loans by AID and predecessor agencies, leaving the "net" effect of the entire AID overseas program on the U.S. balance of payments at $320 million, or less than 15 percent of the year's total program expenditures. 

Besides regulations tying commodity procurement to American sources, the high U.S. share in the "total expenditures" accounting can be attributed to the following causes: most technical service contracts are with U.S. business firms, universities, other organizations and individuals; a high majority of shipping is directed to U.S. flag vessels, both the AID-financed industrial commodities and Food for Peace commodities distributed in developing countries by associated U.S. voluntary agencies, and similar policies to minimize dollar outlays abroad in other aspects of the program, such as AID technicians working overseas, training of foreign technicians in this country, and operational costs. 

These expenditure figures relate to the AID program only. Figures for all U.S. oversea economic aid, such as AID, Food for Peace, U.S. funds for international assistance organization, and Export-Import Bank long-term credits, also show a high composite percentage of expenditures taking place within the United States.

AGRICULTURE A GROWING FACTOR IN AID COMMODITY PROCUREMENT 

While machinery and steel mill products continued during Fiscal 1966 as the largest single groups in volume of commodity procurement under AID financing, a trend toward the materials and equipment which will support the worldwide War on Hunger by boosting agricultural development in food-short lands overseas is evidenced in the year's commodity data. 

Goods related to agricultural growth, in various commodity categories-fertilizers, various agricultural chemicals, machinerly, seeds and feeds-accounted for $173.7 million in AID-financed procurement last year. This compares with $121.9 million in Fiscal 1965 and $99.9 million in Fiscal 1964. 

Among specific industrial groups, AID-financed sales of machinery and equipment led again during Fscal 1966, with a total of $394.7 million, of which $372.7 million-94 percent-was supplied by U.S. producers. The U.S. portion marked a $63.1 million increase over Fiscal 1965 sales in this category. 

Iron and steel mill products accounted for $162.7 million of AID-financed procurement, with $133.1 million coming from U.S. mills. 

In AID-financed purchases by Latin America, Africa, and the Near East-South Asia region, U.S. commodity procurement rose to the 98-99 percent level. The 

Far East region's U.S. proportion was 70 percent, however, based largely on a 64percent level for the large AID prgoram in Vietnam 

Principal purchasers of AID-financed goods were: Vietnam, $259.1 million; 

India, $247.8 million; Pakistan, $115.1 million; Turkey, $101 million; Brazil, $99.1 million; Korea, $75 million, and Chile, $72.1 million. The U.S. share of sales was 99 percent in the cases of Indian, Pakistan, Brazil, and Chile; 97 percent for Turkey; 88 percent for Korea, and 64 percent of Vietnam purchases, as noted above.

BI-NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT FEASIBILITY STUDY 

(1) It is my understanding that a Bi-National Development Plan has been established under AID with offices in Denver, Colorado. What is the purpose of the Bi-National Development Plan? 

The purpose of the Bi-National Development Plan is to encourage the participation of democratic private and local government institutions in international development by establishing cooperative relationships between areas in the United States and areas in the developing countries. The Plan was developed by former Congressman Roy H. McVicker of Colorado. AID has agreed to finance a six months pilot study to determine the feasibility of the Plan. Mr. 

McVicker and a small staff are conducting the study, using the State of Colorado and the Central American Common Market countries as test areas. 

Financing the feasibility study is one of the actions being taken by AID to carry out the provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 calling for: (1) increased use of non-Federal resources (Section 601(b) (2)); and (2) the utilization of democratic institutions in development (Title IX). AID is also interested in determining the feasibility of the Plan because, if successful in Colorado and Central America, it might have application elsewhere. (2) Is this Bi-National Development Plan intended to recruit teachers for service in Central America?

The Bi-National Development Plan is not specifically directed to recruiting teachers for service in Central America. The purpose of the Plan is indicated in fig. (1) above. However, the proposal is based in part on Mr. McVicker's experience with a teacher exchange program involving Colorado and Guatemala, and teacher exchanges are one of a number of cooperative ventures that might be done under the Plan. (3) Is there any similarity between Colorado and Central America that would make Denver be selected on a demonstration basis? 

Colorado and Central America were selected as test areas because of: (1) the 

Director's familiarity with local groups and institutions in Colorado capable of making a significant contribution to development in Central America; (2) certain similarities in the level of industry, including the prevalence of familyowned concerns, and the geography of the two areas (recognizing that there are also significant differences); (3) Colorado's experience with a teacher exchange program involving Guatemala; and (4) the history of Spanish culture in Colorado. (4) Are there other similar projects conducted by AID in other States and, if so, where?

No, the feasibility study is not being duplicated in any other State. It is not known how many other areas the Bi-National Development Plan approach might be applied to.

327 AID has a contract with the State of California to carry out specific project activities in Chile through the Partners of the Alliance program. AID is also encouraging cooperation between individual American citizens and private citizen groups and their Latin American counterparts. At the present time, groups in 30 U.S. States and the District of Columbia are participating in 

Partners programs in 15 Latin American countries. (5) What is the total cost of this program in Colorado? 

The six month feasibility study is expected to cost approximately $65,000 including salaries, travel and overhead. (6) What is the total cost of this program throughout the United States? 

There are no additional costs other than those referred to under (5), above. (7) How many employees are there in the Colorado-Central America office in Denver?

The project staff consists of a Director, two Associate Directors, two clerical employees, five part-time Research Analysts, one part-time typist and three part-time Research Analyst volunteers. (8) Who is serving as Director, and what are his qualifications?

Roy H. McVicker is serving as Director of the project. A resume of Mr. 

McVicker's qualifications is attached as Annex-A. (9) What salary is being paid to the Director?

As a consultant to AID, Mr. McVicker receives a consultant fee of $100 per day. (10) What staff is being maintained by the Director? 

See 7, above. (11) Is his program headquartered in the plush Denver Club Building?

Office space for the project staff has been arranged by the Denver office of the General Services Administration. The staff occupies less than 1,500 square feet of office space in the Denver City Club Building, a conventional, commercial type, twenty-five story office building located in downtown Denver. The building is occupied by a large number of business firms of all sizes and types. (12) What rental is being paid? $580 per month. (13) How many clerks and secretaries are employed? 

See 7, above. (14) Have reports been prepared on the work that is being done at the 

Denver office?

Two progress reports on the Bi-National Development Feasibility Study, dated March 3 and April 3, have been prepared by the Director and submitted to the AID Administrator. The reports, including appendices, are approximately 350 and 50 pages in length, respectively. (15) Will you furnish me with a copy of all reports prepared?

Copies of the reports have been sent to Congressman Berry. (16) Will the staff members of the Bi-National Development Plan be required to travel in Central America? ཝིཝཱོ ཡཱ ། The Director and two consultants working with him left the United States on April 15 to conduct field research in the five Central American countries and Panama.
