Total estimated travel cost is $1,710 for air travel by economy-jet plus approximately $1,200 in per diem. (19) When was this plan established, and how long is it expected to continue? 

The study project was approved in January 1967 and is of approximately six months duration. (20) How many teachers have been recruited through the Denver office? 

None. See 2, above. (21) What have been the accomplishments of the Denver office?

Since the project was approved in January, the Denver office has been established and staffed; an internal audit committee and a vocational education ad-

1967 

visory group have been appointed; other programs (e.g., Partners of the Alliance, Chile-California project) have been reviewed; initial study areas have been identified (e.g., technical and vocational education, manpower planning, local government administration); and basic data has been collected, organized and initially evaluated with particular emphasis on resources in Colorado relevant to the initial study areas. (22) What is being done to publicize the program in order that they could contact more people who might be interested in involving themselves in such a program in Central America?

The project staff has had direct contacts with a number of individuals and groups in Colorado who might be qualified and willing to participate under the Plan. However, general publicity has not been sought during the feasibility study stage so as to avoid generating public enthusiasm before they are clearly defined participation opportunities. (23) Will you furnish the Committee with a general statement as to how this was established? Why it was established in Denver, Colorado, rather than in Washington?

See 1, and 3, above. The project office has been established in Denver rather than in Washington, because the U.S. research is being carried out primarily in Colorado. (24) What has been learned as a result of its establishment? What has been acccomplished, etc.

The study is intended to determine the feasibility of coupling the people and know-how of a specific area of the United States with the aspirations and needs of a developing country or region. The results of the study should be available in July 1967. At that time, AID will be in a position to assess results and to determine what further steps, if any, are indicated. 

ANNEX A Roy H. MCVICKER 

A member of the 89th Congress from the 2nd District of Colorado, Roy McVicker served on the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Inter-American Subcommittee. 

Born in a Methodist parsonage in Colorado in 1924 he received his education at Columbia College and Columbia Law School, LLB, 1950. A veteran of WW II, 

S.W. Pacific Theatre, his range of experience includes:

Professor Psychology, Colorado State College. 

Methodist Minister holding pastorates in Colorado and New York City. 

Social worker at Union Settlement in East Harlem, NYC.

Member of Colorado and New York bars and partner (on leave of absence) with the firm of McVicker, Woodford, and Myers in Colorado. 

Served as aide to President Truman in the establishment of the Admiral 

Nimitz Commission on Internal Security and Civil Rights. 

Author of Report to President Truman on British Royal Commissions. 

Member of Colorado State Senate for 8 years serving as Chairman of Committee on Education Beyond the High School and a sponsor and member of 

Governor's Local Affairs Committee to Restructure Metropolitan Government. 

While in Congress authored the Bi-National Center Plan placing teachers from school districts in America in Bi-National Centers in Latin countries. 

The plan is coordinated through the United States Information Agency, though financed and operated by a grouping of local school districts. Now studying Spanish under a tutor, his interest in Latin American affairs placed him on the Inter- 

American Subcommittee of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

McVicker also authored the plan, now under study in the State and Commerce Department to ease the balance of payments deficit by offering a 5% bonus to U.S. tourists to induce the purchase of special U.S. certificates exchangeable for American owned soft currencies abroad.

Mr. SALZMAN. We are trying to find ways of encouraging private investors to go forward with projects which we think will be healthy

1967 

projects, will be viable commercially as well as valuable to the economies of the countries themselves. In some instances the programs that we now have available are not adequate to that purpose. To reduce the risk to the potential investor, we hope that the program we have in mind will insure him against possible loss of his equity investment to the extent of 50 percent of that investment. 

We expect to use criteria generally used by private lending institutions in determining the soundness of the projects. The payment to the investor would only be occasioned by his incurring an actual loss. 

There would be no payment to him unless he himself had lost money, and then it would be on a dollar-for-dollar basis matching his loss with the amount of reimbursement by AID. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Supposing a fellow goes bankrupt and loses all his money and the creditor is supported to get that money. Do you pay the creditors for the 50-percent loss sustained?

Mr. SALZMAN. That is one of the things we are working on. This reimbursement would go to the investor himself and would not be for the benefit of creditors. Our guarantee goes to the U.S. investor, not to the foreign project.

 STATEMENT CONCERNING NEGOTIATION OF INVESTMENT GUARANTEE AGREEMENTS 

Section 620 (1) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, provides that the President shall consider terminating assistance with less developed countries which have failed to enter into agreements to institute the investment guarantee program after December 31, 1966. Since enactment in December, 1963, investment guarantee agreements have been signed with 21 countries and negotiations have been continued or initiated with many other countries. The provision has been taken into consideration in evaluating the desirability of continuing assistance in countries which have not signed such an agreement. 

Fifteen countries have not signed an agreement and are now receiving some degree of economic or military assistance. Four of those countries, Malawi, Botswana, Burundi, and The Gambia are in the final stages of negotiations. The balance or countries are as follows:

THE HIGH PROTEIN FOOD STUDIES PROGRAM-PROGRESS AND POSSIBILITIES 

A.I.D. recognizes that a major impact could be made in combatting malnutrition in the developing countries if high-protein foods were available through regular commercial channels at prices which low income groups could afford. 

Private industry, both in the less developed countries and U.S., has given this type of enterprise a low priority, seeking instead to invest their capital in more promising markets of the higher income population. 

To provide incentive to U.S. companies to explore and possibly invest in this type of enterprise, A.I.D. has developed "High Protein Food Studies Programs" under which contracts are entered into with private U.S. companies who will study markets and make market tests for commercially produced and distributed nutritious protein foods. To date, discussions have been held with over 100 companies to explain and invite their participation in the program. 

Initially up to $400,000 will be committed under six or seven contracts for a one year period. At present, three companies have their programs underway and eight additional proposals are under active discussion with the reasonable expectation that contracts will be signed. The three proposals now in effect are for a soy-based beverage in El Salvador and a soy-fortified and a protein rich food in Brazil. Proposals that are under active negotiations include wheat protein supplementation for Tunisian bread, a soy-based beverage for Brazil, and a soy-supplemented food for Thailand.

Products used or developed under these studies remain the property of the Company. The A.I.D. contribution will provide an incentive for private business to test these relatively unprofitable markets and will assist in assessing the market for the participating company. The marketing reports produced by these studies will be public documents and will be available to other companies as an assist in stimulating their interest in entering countries with their own products. 

Cottonseed represents largely untapped protein resource in many parts of the world. Because of naturally-occurring toxic factors, it requires special treatment. A.I.D.-supported research to produce cottonseed flour from cottonseed has developed a procedure that is now ready for commercial evaluation. 

A.I.D.-supported research has also made a significant gain in developing a village-scale process to manufacture full-fat soy-flour. This work will be given a full evaluation as rapidly as possible.

Food From The Sea represents another largely untapped resource. With the approval of fish protein concentrate by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, A.I.D. is no longer bound by a "hands-off" policy. Funds were recently provided by A.I.D. to the Bureau of Commercial Fisheries to increase the scale of their present facility, to undertake engineering for a larger pilot scale plant, and to start developing full-scale production facilities that are expected to be authorized for FY 1968. This will also enable the BCF to provide A.I.D. with quantities of fish protein concentrate to use in experimental programs overseas.

 RENEGOTIATION OF U.S.-OWNED LOCAL CURRENCIES- 

We have usually not found it necessary to renegotiate Public Law 480 sales agreements since there is flexibility in the use of Public Law 480 local currencies. 

If more local currencies are needed for U.S. uses, they can be had from loan repayments and from country use funds if the United States and the host government do not agree on their use within 3 years after the sale. Under the amended legislation excess currencies can be used for assistance to high priority additional development programs.

In rare instances we have also renegotiated the agreements when it was to U.S. advantage and conditions warranted. The largest such renegotiation involved Yugoslav currency which was channeled from "U.S.-use" to "country-use" to assist in the relief and reconstruction associated with the Skopje earthquake. 

Another Public Law 480 agreement, with Pakistan, was renegotiated so that we could supply the IBRD with local currencies for the Indus Basin project. 

DETAILS OF PUBLIC LAW 480 CURRENCY AGREEMENT WITH POLAND ST 

Under a series of agreements with Poland signed April 10, 1967, the Public Law 480 agreement of 1964 was changed to enable the U.S. Government to use $16.75 million in Polish currency (zlotys) to finance an English language training program, activities under the U.S. Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 in Poland and elsewhere, and travel expenses of U.S. Government officials in Poland. This total of $16.75 million in zlotys will be deducted from the amount which the Polish Government would repurchase for dollars from the U.S. 

Government-held zlotys accruing from sales of surplus agricultural commodities under the February 3, 1964, "Agreement B" Public Law 480 agreement.

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS AND LATIN AMERICAN DEBT 

Any statement by Mr. Allende about the Alliance for Progress has to be evaluated in the knowledge that Mr. Allende is the leader of the Communist- 

Socialist coalition in Chile, is an admirer of Fidel Castro, and can hardly be considered an unbiased observer. 

The fact of the matter is that both history and common sense teach us that a developing country should borrow from abroad during the early stages of its development process. By definition, a less developed country is one which has a shortage of goods of most kinds, particularly the capital goods needed to increase productive capacity. In order to grow, a country must devote a certain amount of its resources to investment rather than consumption, and, generally speaking, the larger the amount of its resources it devotes to its investment the higher will be its growth rate. Faced with a shortage of resources,

1967 

and the need to maintain a minimum level of consumption, a developing country can either accept a very low growth rate or borrow from abroad the additional resources it needs for investment. 

The latter has been the classical pattern of development all over the worldfor example, the United States borrowed very heavily from Great Britain in the 19th Century; for that matter, so did Russia borrow heavily from abroad in the early days of its economic development, i.e. prior to the revolution. There is nothing injurious, therefore, about a developing country going into debt in order to build up its productive capacity. Some of the return on the investment which has been financed by the foreign borrowing increases the goods and services available to the society. The remainder is used to pay off the foreign debt.

Thus the crucial point is how quickly the debts must be paid off. If the loans are at a fairly short term, then most of the new production made possible by the loans will have to be used to amortize them, and the borrowing country gets only little benefit. Long-term loans at moderate interest rates on the other hand permit the country to plow back most of the return on the investment into new plant and equipment and better living standards for its people while at the same time meeting its foreign debt obligations. 

That is why loans under the Alliance for Progress are are made at 40-year term, with a 10-year grace period, and low interest rates. Before the Alliance came into being, Latin America was borrowing heavily abroad at short and medium term. This resulted in extremely heavy payments for debt service in a number of the major countries of Latin America which precipitated balance of payments crises in the late 1950's and early 1960's and which required periodic reschedulings of foreign debts. It is this wasteful type of borrowing that the 

Alliance for Progress is designed to avoid. The results have been encouraging. 

While annual debt service payments increased by 130 per cent during the period of 1956-1960, in the following five years they rose by only 63 per cent, in spite of the fact that the total public debt of the area was four times larger at the end of 1965 than at the end of 1956. The maturity length of the debt contracted in 1960, the year before the Alliance for Progress started, had a weighted average of 10.7 years, but that of the debt contracted in 1964 rose to 15.4 years. 

Thus Mr. Allende's statement about the effect of the Alliance on the debt service burden of Latin America is completely contrary to the facts.

 MODERN BUSINESS SCHOOL IN PERU The Graduate School of Business Administration (ESAN) was established in 

Lima in 1964 and is the first of its kind in South America. The school trains business and industrial executives in regular academic year classes, leading to a master's degree in business administration, using the American case method technique under the guidance of Stanford University professors. The instruction includes all aspects of modern scientific management as taught in the best U.S. business schools. Enrollment totalled 174 for the first three academic years, including twelve students from six other Latin American countries. The current class (fourth) contains 82 students selected from 130 applicants with thirteen from five other countries. Fifty-five of the current students are receiving financial aid on a loan basis with funds provided by the private sector. 

Virtually all the graduates have been placed quickly due to the growing reputation of the school.

1967 

The original nine Stanford professors have been reduced to five and will gradually phase out as additional Peruvians complete doctoral programs in the United States and return to join the faculty. The 10,000 volume library is almost complete and 24 Peruvian business teaching cases have been published to replace the original U.S. materials. (The target is 50 Peruvian case studies.) 

The School also runs a shorter Executive Development Program and has trained approximately 400 students in 13-week evening extension or 4-week resident executive development courses. A special curriculum also is planned for the future for the training of professional area and regional developers.-

 SAVINGS AND LOAN INDUSTRY IN PERU-DOES IT AID LOW-INCOME PEOPLE? 

The savings and loan systems in Latin America, as in the United States, are intended to service the middle-income level of the population which can afford a reasonable level of debt service payments, made possible by long-term mortgage loans at relatively low interest rates and small downpayments. In Peru, the legislation authorizes 80% loans with a maximum interest rate of 12%, although in fact the interest ranges between 8 and 12%, and with maximum maturities of 20 years. The average sales price of homes financed through the Peruvian system is $4,000. This is a vast improvement over earlier financing. 

Since a savings and loan system by its terms means that the source of mortgage loans is the savings deposited in the association, it is, of course, essential that the mortgagor be in a position to repay his mortgage. Subsidized housing does not

351 have a place in this form of financing. Through the Inter-American Development 

Bank and the Social Progress Trust Fund, however, families who can afford minimum housing achieved by government sponsored construction and absorption by the government of certain administrative costs are being serviced. This program is being administered outside the savings and loan system by a public agency of the Government of Peru.

As the system matures and the savings base increases, it should become possible for the Peruvian savings and loan system to reach lower down in the middle income group than at present. As in this country, it will always be necessary, however, to provide other forms of assistance for the very low income groups through other measures and other financing mechanisms. For example, public rental housing, rent supplements or special assistance programs.

 CHILE/CALIFORNIA PROGRAM 

The Chile/California program is financed entirely by AID pursuant to a master contract between AID and California and various task orders governing specific project activities. Since the inception of the Chile/California program in 1963 

AID has obligated $2,380,000 for this program. Responsibility for selection of personnel for the Chile/California project rests with the State of California subject to the security approval requirement of the contract as well as the standard AID procedures for obtaining mission and country clearances applicable to all personnel assigned overseas. The contract specifies that the director of the program shall hold office at the pleasure of the Governor.

1967 

Control of funds under the program is exercised through normal AID contracting procedures. For each specific task order under the Chile/California contract a scope of work is defined and a budget estimate prepared. The State of California as the contractor then makes disbursements in accordance with the terms of the task order and from time to time submits a voucher specifying these expenditures to AID which makes reimbursement. AID by examining the contractor's vouchers determines whether or not the disbursements are allowable under the terms of the task order.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEE AGREEMENTS WITH THE UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC, ETHIOPIA, AND PAKISTAN 

On June 29, 1963, an investment guarantee agreement was signed with the United Arab Republic. The agreement allows the full range of guarantee coverage. No guarantees have been issued to U.S. investors in the United Arab Republic under the argeement as of this date, and there has been relatively little investor interest, as indicated by the fact that there are only five preliminary applications (merely an indication of interest) on file, and only two definitive applications for guarantees.

The material referred to may be found on p. 362.

353 The distinction between the range of coverage in the United Arab Republic and the range in Ethiopia (where only inconvertibility and expropriation coverages are available, is that the investiment guarantee agreement with Ethiopia does not yet allow the other coverages. The United States is now negotiating with Ethiopia to extend the agreement to allow all coverages. The coverage is also limited in Pakistan to inconvertibility and expropriation because of the limited form of the investment guarantee agreement, and there again the United States is negotiating to extend the agreement for the additional coverages. It is the policy of 

AID to try to obtain the full range of coverages in all less developed friendly countries. The principal reason that the full range of coverages is not available in all participating countries is that the guarantee agreements were negotiated prior to the availability of additional guarantees.

 ARTHUR D. LITTLE CO., INC. PROJECT IN NIGERIA 

During the past year the primary focus of the Arthur D. Little activity has shifted from investment promotion to developing the capabilities of the Nigeria Federal and Regional Ministeries of Industry in industrial planning and project appraisal. In this work the ADL staff has been associated with Nigerian counterparts in preparing the National Development Plan (1968-74), evaluating industrial investment proposals and performing surveys of existing industrial facilities with a view to improving their operations and management. Seventeen Nigerian officials have received six months intensive training at the Arthur D. Little Cambridge Office in industrial management and planning. During the past year, therefore, the Arthur D. Little Co. has not been assigned specific responsibilities for promoting foreign private investment, although it has contributed to Nigeria's capabilities to plan and implement an industrial development program including efforts to improve the climate for foreign private investment.

Even when Arthur D. Little's principal concern was investment promotion it was also engaged in developing the capabilities of the Ministries of Industry through the training program in Cambridge and on-the-job-traning of counterparts in Nigeria. The full impact of the project, therefore, could not be determined solely in terms of private investment to which Arthur D. Little personnel may have contributed directly. 

During the period 1963 through 1965, when Arthur D. Little was engaged in promotional work, over $300 million was invested in new industry in Nigeria.

Mr. FULTON. The question comes up on the rate of progress in 

South America, Latin America. For example, from 1950 to 1955 in those 5 years the average growth was 23/10 percent. From 1955 to 1960 it went down to 2 percent and under the Alliance for Progress it has only been 1510 percent. In 1966 the growth rate was 110 percent.

That seems to be a declining curve of growth rate. My comment then is what should the United States do in the private sector, if you will put a statement in the record, to change this rate of growth because it is on a diminishing cycle rather than an increasing cycle. 

One other point is this: Any country to have a viable economy needs production. So that anything the United States can do to increase production in Latin America not only helps that country but raises the level of our second best customer. Our best customer is Canada and the second best customer of the United States, for our foreign trade, consists of the Latin American nations. So we are really interested in the United States in good economic conditions in South 

America. 

One of the Latin American and South American problems is, for any U.S. businessman, the question of inflation. On inflation the recent history has been tragic in Latin America and South America. I would like you to put, with the chairman's permission, a statement in the record on the inflation and show the growth rate in these countries and also the growth rate of private industry. 

For example, since the Alliance for Progress was begun in 1961 Brazil has had a 214-percent inflation. With those problems of inflation and diminishing growth rate, I think we should have a general statement from you as to what affirmative steps should be taken by the United States to reverse this trend. 

Latin America and South America do have problems in the agriculture field. If we look at agriculture under the Alliance for Progress we find in 1966 the level of agricultural production by population was exactly the 1961 rate by population. What that means is a leveling off if not a stagnation in these agriculture production areas which I believe that private industry assisted by your good Agency can work on. My point is regardless of the Punta del Este proposals. I am talking of a much different operating level as we meet this. I would like to know what your Agency in planning could do, by a statement in the record, with the chairman's permission. 

 INFLATION AND GROWTH IN LATIN AMERICA 

The Alliance for Progress has sought to bring about balanced economic growth in Latin America, i.e. growth that betters the lot of all the people of a country and which can be maintained over a period of time. In the early years of the Alliance, the two major South American countries, Brazil and Argentina, were continuing the inflationary policies of borrowing heavily at short terms abroad to finance development at home which they had practiced in the 1950's. This foreign borrowing had permitted Brazil and Argentina to achieve high growth rates from the late 50's until 1961 and thus brought up the whole average for Latin America because the record of these two large countries weighs so heavily in the figure for the region as a whole. The slow growth of these two countries starting in 1962, as they paid the price of the "hothouse growth" of the previous period, dragged down the growth level of Latin America.

1967 

The decision of the leaders of the Latin American countries in 1961 to join with the United States in the Alliance for Progress indicates the awareness of the Latin American leaders that the growth of the kind these countries experienced in the 1950's was not satisfying the aspirations of their peoples. What was needed was a more ordered development more equitably shared. United States economic assistance has been geared to help the Latin American countries bring about that kind of development. 

Progress is being made. Those countries plagued by serious inflation are now making efforts to correct it. Although the poor performance of the Argentine economy in 1966 drew down the overall growth figure, most of the other nations have shown good growth performance in recent years. With the new commitment to the Alliance expressed in the Meeting of Presidents at Punta del Este, there is a good prospect for faster and well balanced growth in the future. 

Growth of the private sector has been approximately equal to the growth of GNP. In most countries, private sector growth in industry and commerce has been running slightly ahead of GNP and private agriculture has been a drag on development. To remedy this problem, A.I.D. lending policy now heavily favors agriculture. We also assist industry by some industry loans and seek to improve the investment climate by supporting government efforts to fight inflation. 

The key to balanced growth is a high level of both public and private sector investment combined with a stabilization policy. Examples of countries that are achieving respectable growth rates and at the same time showing success in the war against inflation are Chile and Brazil, both of which are supported by a high level of United States assistance. 

Since 1964, the Government of Brazil has been following a firm program to bring inflation under control. Its budgetary performance has been particularly good. The budget cash deficit was reduced from 46% of expenditures in 1964 to 

11% in 1966. Furthermore, while the 1964 and 1965 deficits were largely financed by printing money, the 1966 deficit was completely financed by non-inflationary means. In addition, in 1966, a tight credit policy was followed, with the result that total money supply increased less than in earlier years. Through these measures, the annual rate of inflation has been reduced from 140% in early 1964 to 41% in 1966. During the last half of 1966 the annual rate was limited to about 

25% and the government began to make further progress in 1967. 

Primarily as a result of covering budgetary deficits by borrowing from the Central Bank, Chile suffered until 1964 from persistently high rates of inflation. In both 1965 and 1966, the Chilean Government, through tax reform and administrative improvements, increased tax collections significantly and reduced deficit spending. The rate of inflation dropped to 26% in 1965 and to 17% in 1966. 

During 1967, the Government of Chile hopes to limit price increases to about 12%.

STATEMENT OF HON. LUCIUS D. BATTLE, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR NEAR EASTERN AND SOUTH ASIAN AFFAIRS Mr. Chairman and members of the committee: 

1. I am delighted to have this opportunity to lend my strong support to the proposals for the foreign assistance program for countries of the Near Eastern and South Asian area for fiscal year 1968. 

2. Our economic assistance is very important to our foreign policy in the part of the world for which I have recently assumed responsibilities as an Assistant Secretary of State. Some country programs are quite large ones, and in a number of instances our aid constitutes a major element in our overall relationship with these nations. 

3. We see our self-interest to be in their sound economic and social development, leading to stable, viable, modern societies with which the United States can enjoy the most congenial relationship. This is the aim of our policy toward the area. That, itself, is meshed with our overall goal of building a peaceful world order. 

4. A few weeks ago I returned to Washington from an assignment as Ambassador to the United Arab Republic. Upon leaving Cairo I visited several 367

1967 

countries in the Near Eastern and South Asian area, including most of those in which we are making important contributions to economic development. These visits, although brief, reaffirmed my conviction that our participation in their development is sound policy from our point of view. In spite of all that remains to be done, the picture is encouraging. I was impressed with what I learned of the growing talent and dedication of local government officials working on the various development programs. I believe that our economic and technical assistance is being used more effectively than ever before. Its use is being better coordinated both with local resources available for development and with other outside aid. This is a key point-this integration of the use of all available resources for development. Our contribution in terms of amounts is really rather marginal, but it permits us to influence the deployment of larger resources into the soundest areas of development. Local resources are, as you know, the thing that development really rides on-in India, for example, 80 percent of that tremendous effort over the last sixteen years has been paid for out of the Indian national budget. While in earlier periods we may have been sensitive to accusations about attaching strings to our aid, we are not now shy about discussing deficiencies in using our aid and insisting that the development schemes our money goes into are sound throughout. This is now understood abroad and is accepted, and suggestions for improvement in the use of assistance are being more and more welcomed. 

5. The basic reason for our foreign economic assistance program remains the same as cited by every President since 1949 when, through "Point Four," we undertook to do something about the unsatisfactory condition of humanity in the less developed but more populous parts of the globe. As Americans, with our traditions and regardless of faith, we believe that morally it is the right thing for the richest nation on this planet to assist the poorer, less-endowed nations to move up from their state of massive poverty, disease, and ignorance. Over the last two decades, other well-to-do nations have increasingly joined in the effort. We are in the century of international conscience, and more and more nations are feeling a sense of responsibility and are sharing in the effort. 

6. For the fiscal year 1968 the President has recommended an economic assistance program of $760 million for the Near Eastern and South Asian area. This will support development activities there at about the same level as during the present fiscal year. This figure was reached only after a careful reexamination of the present requirements of our foreign policy and developmental objectives, and of a careful examination also of the extent to which individual nations are making genuine efforts on their own behalf. 

7. As Assistant Administrator Williams will describe, our funds will continue to be concentrated where they can be most effective, where good foundations for growth have already been laid, and where there is real development potential. 

The major programs are in India, Pakistan, and Turkey with smaller programs in six other countries. I strongly support this request. I am convinced that it is the minimal amount needed to consolidate the gains and sustain the cadence of development. This amount will back up sound self-help efforts by the receiving countries and help to assure that other developed nations share increasingly in the effort. 

8. It is customary for each regional Assistant Secretary to take advantage of this opportunity to give the Committee a brief “Situation Report" covering his area of responsibility. 

9. The Near Eastern and South Asian area is a large one, stretching eastward from Greece to the India/Pakistan subcontinent. It is a varied region-containing 19 nations and a number of dependent and semiautonomous territories. In it are both the largest United Nations member-India, with over 500 million people, and the smallest-the Maldive Islands-with ninety thousand. It contains more than half the population of the less-developed part of the Free World. 

10. From the point of view of the East/West political divisions of the world today, it is important to note that the Near Eastern and South Asian area borders directly upon Communist territory across a good part of the globe-from Greece on the west through Turkey, Iran, and Afghanistan to Pakistan, India, and Nepal on the east. 

11. These countries, as well as the threats they face, are strikingly diversified, but a general common feature is their status as "less developed" nations. All are striving to modernize, to meet individual aspirations of their people, and, as

369 members of the world community, to play a greater role in the world scene. Yet most are held back by inadequacies in resources, in trained manpower, and, in some very important cases, in the food to live on. With few exceptions, all feel a mounting pressure of population on their resources. 

12. There is no uniform rate of progress among them, and they range from primitive mosaic societies-fractured by tribalism and held feebly together by the slenderest of political sinews-to more sophisticated countries, with highly developed constitutional systems and well on the road to agricultural sufficiency and modern industrial competence. 

13. Leaving aside the possibilities for outside aggression or subversion, the region's major peace and security problems continue to stem from long-standing disputes between India and Pakistan over Kashmir, between Israel and the Arab states, and between Greece and Turkey over Cyprus, and also now from accentuated rivalries among the Arab states themselves. These disputes divert scarce resources to armaments, and open the way to outside penetration and exploitation. Instabilities stemming from these local frictions, compounded by Communist pressures, are the main threat to the Free World interests in the area. Our development assistance, our selective military assistance, and our well-known interest in the territorial integrity of the countries in the area are all important stabilizing factors. In good measure it is because of them that direct intervention by Communist forces is not imminent. However, these local disputes do remain as important threats to peace and progress. We will continue to encourage the parties to peaceful solutions, and, where need be, to use our own influence against their resort to force. 

14. We can best view the area in terms of three sub-regions—one encompassing 

Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, and Iran; another the Arab world and Israel; and the third the South Asian subcontinent. 

15. I turn first to South Asia where development needs are most acute and where a large part of our assistance expenditures, if approved, will be made. 

SOUTH ASIA 

16. South Asia is the central core of non-Communist mainland Asia. The ability of its peoples to make economic and social progress is crucial not only to peace and stability of the area, but also to the realization of our objectives throughout all of Asia. 

17. During 1966 India and Pakistan consolidated the peace that had been established after their armed conflict of September 1965, but failed to achieve true reconciliation. The year began with the Tashkent Declaration, followed by the orderly pulling back of troops on each side. To these and other tangible signs that the two countries were seeking to reestablish their relations on a more normal basis, we responded by resuming new economic development aid to both. The months since then have seen little measurable progress toward genuine rapprochement, despite some efforts made on both sides; the estrangement continues, neither worsening nor improving, and our policy of promoting and assisting economic progress continues. I will discuss our military supply policy in a moment. 

18. Aside from, and more important than, the after effects of the September 

1965 hostilities, economic development in both India and Pakistan has been seriously impeded by the second consecutive year of serious drought. Scarce resources, importantly including limited foreign exchange, had to be diverted from development needs to pay for food imports. Additionally, large amounts of food grains have been and are being imported under concessional lending arrangements, predominantly from the United States under Public Law 480. The droughts have highlighted the need for accentuated local measures both to improve agricultural production and distribution, and to push forward with effective population planning programs as well as with the broader development effort. 

19. In India, more than 150 million people went to the polls in February for 

India's fourth general election since independence. The size of the electorate's turnout, the relatively peaceful polling, as well as the independence with which the franchise was exercised, are testimony to the strength of the democratic process in that country. While the Congress party experienced significant reverses, both in Parliament and in the state legislatures, it continues to be by far the largest political party in India. It has formed an effective new government under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and we are assured that it will continue to devote priority attention to the most pressing development needs.

1967 

20. Emphasis is on agriculture. India has announced its firm intention to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains by 1971. To meet this objective it has struck out boldly for improved production methods involving increased investment, both private and public, massive use of fertilizers, and the use of improved seeds. It is planning to cover 32 million acres with this intensified program by the end of 

1971. 

21. It has significantly relaxed the conditions for the entry of private capital in the field of fertilizer production and has committed itself to the use of scarce foreign exchange resources to import fertilizer to make up for existing deficiencies in current production. During 1966, fertilizer imports were increased 85% over 1965. 

22. We are undertaking special efforts to encourage other countries to participate in the World Bank's effort toward meeting the Indian food crisis. This will be additional to their other economic assistance. As you know, the Congress has endorsed the President's proposal that we supply up to an additional three million ton of food grains under Public Law 480, provided it is matched by other countries. 

23. In the field of overall economic policy, during the past year India took the major step of devaluing its currency by 36.5% and, with the financial support of the World Bank consortium, has liberalized its import controls to allow greatly increased imports of raw materials and spare parts needed to stimulate domestic production. 

24. Substantially increased sums are also being devoted to population control programs, and a new team of family planning administrators has been installed. 

Prime Minister Gandhi and her government insist that they are giving very high priority to family planning, and our experts believe that the government's present approach to this enormous country's massive problem of population growth is promising and will in time prove effective. 

25. Drought has also slowed the pace of Pakistan's economic development, which hitherto made model progress. During the present fiscal year Pakistan purchased almost 800,000 tons of wheat commercially, costing more than $50 million, to help meet its food deficit. This is in addition to 1.5 million tons of wheat and corn supplied under PL-480. The government is strongly developmentoriented and its increasing self-help efforts are concentrated in the priority areas of agriculture, education, and health, importantly including family planning. 

Pakistan also intends to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains by 1971. The development budget was increased 30 percent for FY 1967, important liberalization steps have been taken and private investment is being encouraged in the fertilizer and pesticide industries. 

26. These measures hold the promise of accelerated economic growth in India and Pakistan, given reasonably favorable weather conditions and continued adequate external financial support. 

27. In Ceylon, the present government, elected two years ago, has modified prior policies which, oriented toward consumption at the expense of investment, had contributed to the present balance of payments difficulties. Important remedial steps have now been taken, such as reduction of the rice subsidy and the encouragement of foreign and domestic private investment. Our assistance is provided within a multilateral framework of donors under the sponsorship of the World Bank and encourages sound economic development programs. 

28. One of the few countries of the area to maintain its independence during the colonial era, Nepal literally had to start from scratch to build a modern society some seventeen years ago. The Government in Katmandu is fully of the importance of self-help in meeting the aspirations of the Nepalese people. Its share of the development budget, 11 percent in 1963, is more than 43 percent of a vastly increased budget in 1967. Primarily emphasis of both the Nepalese effort and our aid is on rural development, for more than 90 percent of the GNP of Nepal is from agriculture. 

29. Afghanistan's Prime Minister Maiwandwal last month gave us a direct report on his government's aspirations under its new Third Five Year Plan. 

We are very pleased with the new policy directions contained in that Plan. Our aid program and the Afghan Government are placing greater emphasis on agricultural development, particularly wheat production. We also look for a greater role for private enterprise. We believe that Afghanistan is becoming more proficient in allocating its resources to development, all the more necessary now as Afghanistan proceeds with the program of political reform initiated in 1963.

371 

NEAR EAST 

30. In the Near East the problem of peace and security remains compounded by two major indigenous cross winds-the Arab/Israeli confrontation, and inter- Arab antagonisms which are becoming a greater threat to area peace. Among the Arabs the present confrontation is between the more traditional leaders in Saudi Arabia and Jordan and those in Egypt, Syria, and, to a lesser extent, Iraq who are espousing a more radical approach to internal and inter-Arab problems. 

31. During the past year both of these troublesome winds blew with increased intensity. There were serious outbreaks of violence across the Arab/Israel armistice lines, particularly along the Jordanian and Syrian borders. In November, following incidents of terrorism by Arab elements, Israel retaliated with an attack by regular forces into Jordanian territory. More recently Israel and 

Syria have clashed over questions involving the use of land in the Demilitarized Zone along the armistice line. The Security Council was requested three times last year to consider the threat to area peace. 

32. The Arab/Israel arms race intensified. To help restore equilibrium in the face of continued large-scale arms supplies to the UAR, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen by the Soviet Union, we were obliged to provide certain defensive military equipment to selected other countries in the area, including Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Jordan. 

33. Considerable concern has been centered on the Yemen situation, the current major focus of inter-Arab antagonisms. While there has been but limited fighting there, attempts during the year to settle the problem, primarily through Kuwaiti mediation between the UAR, supporting the Yemen Republican Government, and Saudi Arabia, supporting the previous royalist regime, have not succeeded. 

34. South Arabia is expected to become independent some time in 1968. The present South Arabian Federation Government faces increasing security problems as various opposition elements have resorted to harassment tactics to influence the situation. These elements do not regard the SAFG as a representative regime and boycotted the UN Special Mission which paid an abortive visit to Aden early this month. The Mission itself refused to have any dealings with the SAFG and left Aden precipitately after charging that conditions did not permit it to carry out its task. With the British definitely leaving, it is our hope that further efforts can be made which will serve to broaden the base of the post-independence government and thus increase chances for an orderly transfer of power. 

35. In Iraq the year saw considerable evidence of progress in settling the problem of the Kurdish minority, bringing with it a welcomed improvement of relations between Iraq and Iran. 

36. Egyptian efforts to attain simultaneously objectives in the areas of development, welfare, defense, and foreign affairs overtaxed the resources available to the country. The resulting very tight foreign exchange situation has been compounded by the absence of the substantial quantities of food imported from the United States under PL-480 in recent years. As the Committee undoubtedly knows, the UAR Government withdrew last month its long outstanding request for a new PL-480 agreement. The Egyptians have reacted to their difficult economic situation with a general tightening of the belt. Top priority is being give to food purchases. Budget expenditures, including those for development, have been cut back substantially. New emphasis is being placed on increasing agricultural production by obtaining as quickly as possible the benefits of the High Aswa Dam. The Egyptians are making efforts to ease the debt repayment burden through rescheduling, which several European countries have agreed to do. They see the next two to three years as difficult ones, after which the promising commercial oil discoveries made by American oil companies in the Gulf of Suez and the Western Desert should provide substantial new foreign exchange income. Our remaining aid to the UAR consists of a small technical assistance program and modest amounts of PL-480 food for an Egyptian school lunch and hospital program given through American voluntary agencies, such as CARE. We feel that continuation of this aid is fully in the United States interests. 

37. Jordan's continued vitality as an independent country continues to be an important element of peace and stability in the Near East. Its narrow resource base, sparse rainfall for agriculture, and scarcity of raw materials for industry 77-470-67-pt. 2- -8

1967 

constitute very serious economic handicaps. Additionally, political pressures in the area have forced the Government of Jordan to continue to carry a heavy burden of military expenditure. Nevertheless, it is pursuing economic and social development with gratifying results. Our supporting assistance continues to contribute an essential part to the Jordan budget and is expected to be necessary, in declining amounts, for some years to help cover ordinary budget expenditures. 

38. In Syria, a dispute over royalties on transit of Iraqi oil through the IPC pipeline led in late 1966 to forced stoppage of the flow. Last month a settlement was reached permitting resumed use of the pipeline and removing the stress on the Iraqi economy experienecd during the months of closure. 

39. We continue to urge moderation on the opposing parties in the various disputes. We follow an evenhanded approach, supporting the independence and integrity of all states in the region, fostering a dialogue with them on matters of mutual concern, and assisting as appropriate to the circumstances in their economic and social development. 

GREECE, TURKEY, IRAN, AND CYPRUS 

40. Greece, Turkey, and Iran are very different from each other, and each faces unique challenges. At the same time, all three are continuing their vigorous and fruitful efforts to strengthen their economic and social structures. Each remains our staunch ally and each plays its full part in the defense of the region against possible aggression across its northern borders. 

41. Last month we observed the Twentieth Anniversary of President Truman's appearance before the Congress to enlist its cooperation in a program of assistance to Greece essential for that country's survival. "I believe," said President 

Truman at that time, "that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.

Should we fail to aid Greece in this fateful hour, the effect will be far-reaching to the West as well as to the East." In an Anniversary 

Message on March 12, 1967, the Greek Prime Minister spoke of the gratitude of the Greek people for American aid, saying: "Thanks to that assistance, as well as our own sacrifices, we succeeded in bringing our struggle to a successful conclusion, in preserving our liberty and laying the foundations for the rehabilitation of our country." 

42. Over the years the Greek economy progressively strengthened until it reached a point in 1962 when our economic assistance was no longer necessary. 

The economic difficulties evident during part of 1965 were arrested during this past year thanks largely to courageous self-help measures by the government. 

43. While Greece continues to experience unsettled internal political conditions, we are hopeful that a degree of stability will result from elections there next month. 

44. In Turkey, outstanding economic progress is being made under a pragmatic, development-minded government. Based on present indications, a termination of outside economic assistance on concessionary terms can be foreseen in a few years--and this is something the Turks are seeking also. A solid member of both NATO and CENTO, Turkey is keeping its defenses strong but not at undue cost to economic development. It is increasing its contacts with Eastern European countries, but within the context of its close ties to the Free World and especially the United States. These close ties were solidly reaffirmed during a visit to the United States by the President of Turkey earlier this month. 

45. Although Cyprus remains an important cause of strain between Greece and Turkey, we believe that the two countries are increasingly anxious to find a settlement to the problem. Hopefully, renewed efforts will be successful. We support such efforts by these two NATO allies and have told them that we stand ready to assist in any way we can. We also continue to support the 

United Nations' effort in Cyprus, which has done much to keep the peace on the 

Island during the past three years. 

46. In Iran, the rewards of continuing programs of economic development and social reform have become more conspicuous in an atmosphere of increasing prosperity, assisted by rising oil revenues and continuing political stability. 

Our concessional economic assistance is being terminated. However, American private capital investment is increasing, and the Export-Import Bank is playing an important role in supporting Iran's economic development. Iran's current annual economic growth rate is estimated at 8-10 percent.

373 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

47. I would like now to say a few words specifically about another one of our important programs in the Near Eastern and South Asian area. This is military assistance. With it we have sought to promote general peace and stability so that countries could go forward at full pace with economic and social development. That has been the purpose of the military assistance programs. This purpose is being met, and we consider the money to have been wellspent. 

48. The amounts involved have been trending downward over the years. The major emphasis has been in those countries bordering the Communist areas and, in the current program, emphasis remains on Greece, Turkey, and Iran. In Iran, since 1964, we have been shifting from a purely grant program to a mixture of credit sales and grant. Iran's stability and independence have been significantly buttressed in recent years, and she remains a valued friend of the United States. Much smaller programs are envisaged in such countries as Jordan and 

Saudi Arabia where the money will be devoted primarily to supporting training activities and providing spare parts for equipment delivered under previous programs. We are quite enthusiastic about the training programs in U.S. service schools. They give us a chance to meet the desires of foreign governments to have selected military officers come for training here. And we have found that there has been an important additional dividend in the development of mutual understanding between foreign military officials and Americans with whom they come in contact. 

49. As the Committee knows, we suspended all military shipments to India and Pakistan in September 1965 as part of our effort to bring to an end the brief but disruptive hostilities between those countries. Since that time, we have had our military sales and assistance policies toward India and Pakistan under almost constant review. Our aim has been to help where possible with their legitimate self-defense and internal security needs, and so serve our own broader interests in the area; we have, at the same time, sought to avoid fueling an arms race between the two countries and have exerted our influence in favor of a reduction in arms spending. Accordingly, in the immediate post-Tashkent period, we modified our absolute suspension of all military deliveries to permit the sale, cash or credit, on a case-by-case basis, of a limited amount of nonlethal materiel, e.g., vehicles, communications equipment. In recent days, in an effort to give us additional tools with which to help India and Pakistan to reduce arms expenditures and move toward arms limitations, we have, after a painstaking review, and after consultation with the Congress, adopted a new military supply policy toward those countries. This policy reaffirms that there will be no grant aid of military equipment for India or Pakistan. Our military missions in both countries will be withdrawn. The new policy does allow for the cash sale of a limited amount of spare parts for previously supplied lethal equipment, permits the continuation of some credit sales for non-lethal items, and enables us to undertake training for a limited number of officers of both countries here in the United States. Each step in the implementation of this new policy will, of course, be governed by prevailing conditions of war or peace in South Asia and will be measured against our goals of facilitating a reduction in Indian and Pakistani defense spending and helping them to work out arms limitations as well. 

50. As we continue our measured military assistance to help those nations standing against Communist pressures, or to re-establish equilibrium in local power relationships, we maintain our abiding fundamental interest in social and economic development, particularly in those nations where the struggle against poverty, hunger, disease, and ignorance is most difficult. We recognize particu larly the importance of achieving a satisfactory relationship between population and food. But outside aid, including our own, can be only marginal. The main effort must continue to be by the developing nations themselves. Our role can be only to assist, to encourage, and to support them in their own self-help programs. 

At the same time, to maximize the flow of outside resources, we are working more and more closely with other developed nations outside the area who share our interest in its stability and progress. 

51. All of this is for the purpose of assisting in bringing about the kinds of stable, popularly-based societies with which we can conduct our every day relationships to our best interest and theirs. And it is on this basis, Mr. Chairman. and members of the Committee, that I strongly urge approval of the requested foreign assistance program for countries of the Near Eastern and South Asian area.

1967 STATEMENT OF HON. MAURICE J. WILLIAMS, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRATOR, Bureau FOR NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT INTRODUCTION 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am pleased to have this opportunity to present the Fiscal Year 1968 economic aid request for the Near East and South Asia, to review the objectives of the program and to justify its scale. 

For the past three years as Deputy and then Director of the AID Mission to Pakistan, I had direct experience with what we are trying to do in that part of South Asia. This experience convinces me that the AID program is achieving a significant measure of success. At the same time, I do not underestimate the obstacles and distance to our objectives. 

CONCENTRATION AND TERMINATION OF ASSISTANCE 

We continue in NESA to concentrate U.S. economic assistance in a limited number of countries. Ninety percent of the funds requested are for India, Pakistan and Turkey. The remaining ten percent support smaller programs in 

Afghanistan, Jordan, Nepal and Ceylon. A small technical assistance program is planned for the UAR.

The number of countries in NESA receiving U.S. economic assistance on special terms has declined sharply. We have completed programs in Greece, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Cyprus. Israel no longer requires the major economic assistance of earlier years. The AID Mission in Iran will have finished its work by mid 

FY 1968. Our experience, in Greece, Israel, Iran and other countries demonstrates that economic assistance, appropriately related to sound policies and economic and social reforms, creates a base for progress and self-sustaining development. 

This experience is being applied with promising results in the AID programs still underway. For example, in Turkey economic assistance and a good self-help program have accelerated the pace of development. Turkey in a few years should be able to achieve a stage of self-sustaining growth, or takeoff. In recognition of this prospect the Turkish Government has set 1973 as a target date for ending foreign aid on special terms. 

CLOSING THE FOOD GAP THE PRIORITY OBJECTIVE 

The South Asia countries, with over 600 million people and per capita income below $100 a year, are waging a grim struggle to feed and clothe their people and develop their economies. They will continue to need outside help for some time to come as they seek to achieve self-sufficiency in food, educate their people to new techniques, limit the size of families and break through the constraints hampering economic growth. After years of neglect, agriculture is now receiving the attention it deserves and closing the food gap has become the priority objective of the countries in the NESA region. These countries are removing the bureaucratic control-over prices, over deliveries, over licensing-which had made farming unprofitable and led to stagnation in the countryside. The new policies are restoring dynamism to the farms by dismantling as far as possible governmental controls in favor of free market incentives. The new policies and programs are helping to release the energies of rural peoples and are making possible sharply increasing fertilizer use, introduction of improved seed varieties which increase yields several fold, better credit programs and marketing facilities. 

We believe these concentrated efforts in agriculture can succeed in closing the food gap. 

Unfortunately the full benefits of the new policies in agriculture have not yet been realized because of two years of successive droughts in South Asia which reduced farm output, reduced demand for manufactured goods, and siphoned off scarce foreign exchange to import food. Given normal weather South Asian countries have good reason to expect a dramatic reversal of the recent trend in food output.

Both Pakistan and India are aiming to attain food self-sufficiency and a major advance in their agricultural economies in the early 1970's. The policies and priorities are right and, with our help, they appear likely to produce the desired revolution in agricultural technology and production. If, however, the objective of food self-sufficiency is to be achieved in the early 1970's both India and Pakistan will have to sustain the promising efforts already begun and concentrate their resources on development.

375 

SELF-HELP TO REDUCE DEPENDENCE ON AID 

The countries in the NESA region are developing programs in areas other than agriculture, to step up the pace of development and reduce their dependence on foreign aid. Major elements of these self-help efforts are common to many of the NESA countries. They seek to expand exports and increase their foreign exchange earnings which is the vital element for achieving independence of foreign assistance. They work at improving budget planning and tax administration in order to put to work more effectively their own resources. They press the training of entrepreneurial and technical personnel, thereby reducing the need for foreign technicians. As the supply of qualified entrepreneurial and technical manpower grows, the NESA countries tend to promote and rely increasingly on market forces to provide incentives for investment. Our AID programs are designed to assist with those self-help objectives. 

In both rural and urban areas there is a quickening of pace as development programs engage the energies of an ever broadening number of people. The people of the NESA region want to help themselves. Indeed, the drive for economic development and independence cannot be stopped for it has become a major force in the region. 

SHARING THE AID BURDEN 

Consortia are a major feature of the NESA region, and have been organized to provide assistance to India, Pakistan, and Turkey. They are an effective means of reviewing country performance, stimulating self-help efforts, assessing aid needs, coordinating approaches to aid problems, raising money and sharing the aid burden. The consortia include the World Bank, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, Canada and others. Members of the India consortium have pledged over $6 billion during the past five years; the Pakistan consortium raised about $2 billion in the same period. The U.S. share has been 

42 percent for India and 47 percent for Pakistan. The Turkey consortia, raised $1.4 billion from 1963-1966. The United States share was 44 percent and may be compared to the close to 100 percent financed by the United States in the 1950's. Recently the Aid-to-India consortium undertook the difficult task of joining the U.S. in helping to meet India's essential food needs. 

Terms of aid are also a critical factor in the effectiveness of aid. Debt service in NESA countries is growing. India's annual debt service is over $400 million for 1967, over 20 percent of foreign exchange earnings. The flow of effective aid to NESA countries will be increasingly eroded unless repayments can be held down. Otherwise levels of aid will have to increase sharply to maintain the same net flow of aid, or debt schedules will require adjustment. The United 

Kingdom and Canada among major donors have improved their aid terms significantly in the last two years and now provide development aid at zero interest rate. Other countries, as well, should join in offering terms which are suitable to development objectives.
