The $759.9 million is needed to play our part, with other Consortium members, in sustaining the pace of economic activity primarily in Turkey, India and Pakistan, and helping these countries to achieve their major self-help objectives and earlier termination of their dependence on foreign aid.

The Technical Assistance request for a 10 percent increase, from $42.2 million in FY 1967 to $47 million in FY 1968, reflects the costs of stepped-up agricultural and educational efforts in India, Pakistan, Turkey and Afghanistan. 

The sharp reduction in Supporting Assistance from $32.4 million in FY 1967 to $26.9 million in FY 1968 conforms to U.S. policy of progressively phasing out this form of grant aid.

Development loans 

The U.S. economic assistance effort in the NESA region is primarily in the form of dollar repayable loans. About 90 percent of the proposed FY 1968 program is for this type of assistance. India The level of aid we are requesting will enable us to support programs on about the same level as FY 1967. Most of the Development Loan request for India will finance imports from the United States, of essential agricultural and industrial materials and spare parts needed to help meet agricultural targets and utilize existing industrial plant capacity in the private sector. We expect that considerably more non-project development lending than we give will be provided by other members of the Indian Consortium, aside from contributions to help India meet its food needs. 

To make more effective use of the worldwide economic assistance for its development, India recently took an impressive number of difficult self-help decisions, and: 

1. Devalued the rupee by 36.5 percent in June 1966 to more appropriately reflect the value of imported goods relative to domestically produced resources and to spur exports; 

2. Reduced administrative controls over imports and investment hereby permitting the freer play of market forces; 

3. Shifted investment policies and priorities in favor of agriculture by: 

Giving agriculture first priority in the allocation of development funds;

Increasing fertilizer imports from $100 million in FY 1966 to $200 million in FY 1967 and a projected $300 million in FY 1968; 

Promoting fertilizer production through new investment incentives for private industry. Construction in starting on one new private sector plant involving the American International Oil Company (AIOC). Five other investors are well advanced in their negotiations and construction should start soon;

Introducing new higher yield seed varieties and stepping up import and production of seeds; imports of pesticides and subsidies to spray users; and 

4. Intensifying investment and administrative effort for family planning during the current Fourth Plan period. 

India's economic progress, despite these considerable efforts, has been disappointing in terms of the economic results. The war and the two droughts have adversely affected these results, but at the same time there has been a more realistic self-assessment of the weakness in Indian development. We have every reason to expect better results from India's economic programs. I believe that better economic returns are likely to be achieved with the policies and programs 

India now has underway.

Pakistan Pakistan's development program has been highly successful in recent years, keynoted by greater reliance on private initiative and market forces. Agricultural production has increased substantially, the export performance has been impressive, and the growth of GNP annually was over 5 percent during the period 1960-1965. Unfortunately, this outstanding performance was interrupted by the 

1965 conflict with India, temporary suspension of new U.S. aid obligations and the recent drought. There was a slow down of new economic activity and im-

377 position of tighter controls affecting import and investment decisions. Despite these difficulties Pakistan's economy continued to grow with an increase of GNP of 4.8 percent during FY 1966, or a 2 percent increase in per capita income. 

During the past year the Government of Pakistan has restored priority to development and it is again seeking to accelerate the pace of economic development. The aid we are requesting for Pakistan will assist this promising effort. 

Our non-project aid will help provide the imports needed to achieve agricultural and industrial objectives within a framework of liberal market policies. The 

Pakistan Government believes in the efficiency of private enterprise and is taking further steps to reduce administrative controls and increase incentives to business in widening areas of the economy. Consortium aid strongly supports that effort. We expect the remaining Consortium members to contribute very significantly in development loans to support Pakistan's planned development. 

Pakistan is carrying out highly effective reform policies and self-help efforts. 

It has: 

1. Restored high priority to development with a projected increase of 40 percent in the 1967 development budget over 1966 and 13 percent over the 

1965 (pre-conflict) level; 

2. Restored freer market incentives affecting private investment and import decisions; 

3. Maintained a highly effective export drive which has resulted in increased annual foreign exchange earnings averaging 8 percent over the last four years, and achieving better than 12 percent last year. 

4. Attacked the basic problem of agricultural development by: 

Dramatically increasing the use of fertilizer.

During the period 1960-1965 tonnage use increased threefold, and further major expansion is underway;

Actively promoting private and foreign investment in fertilizer. New private sector fertilizer plants are under consideration with participating American firms;

Rapidly shifting the distribution of fertilizer from public to private hands;

Helping farmers with private development of tubewells in the saline area of West Pakistan. Through these wells and other irrigation and soil reclamation efforts nearly 2 million acres will be added to cultivated lands; and 

Effectively encouraging local leadership and initiative in village social and economic action programs to construct small irrigation and drainage works, farm to market roads, and schools. 

5. Pakistan has also set bold targets for reducing the birth rate.

There is still much to be done, but these self-help efforts, despite war and drought, have kept the Pakistan development program moving ahead and hold the promise of significant new achievements. We expect greater efficiency in the use of existing plant capacity and a return to the pre-war GNP growth pattern of 6 percent a year.

With the programs underway there is every prospect of a major breakthrough in agricultural production, a breakthrough which could have a persuasive and accelerating effect on the tempo and pattern of development in Pakistan. With our assistance, Pakistan appears likely to attain an annual agricultural growth rate of 5 percent a year-well ahead of the rate of population increase—and to achieve relative self-sufficiency in food during 1971. Turkey

Turkey has set 1973 as the target date for ending U.S. economic assistance on special terms. Recent economic trends are encouraging and while the objective is an ambitious one, we believe it can be achieved. But Turkey will have to maintain financial stability, continue to improve the competitive character of the economy, continue to revitalize agriculture, sustain increases in exports, and slow the rapid growth in its population. Turkey's export earnings increased 

30 percent from 1963-1966, and her industrial and manufacturing output increased 30 percent in the same period.

Turkey is making impressive strides in agriculture and did not need to import food in this past year. With continuing rapid expansion in the use of fertilizer, irrigation waters and the introduction of new seed, Turkey will almost certainly become self-sufficient in food.

1967 

Turkey's current government is prepared to give more play to market forces and encourage broader participation by the private sector in development. Turkey has made clear its intention to the Consortium and the IFF that it will adhere to non-inflationary policies. 

Other NESA countries 

Development loans to India, Pakistan, and Turkey make up 97 percent of our DL aid. Most of the remaining amount will go to Jordan in support of our strategy of promoting development in order to steadily reduce, and phase out, grant budget support. We are also proposing a development loan for Ceylon as part of a multilaterally supported program. We expect other free world donors to provide additional aid to assist Ceylon. Finally, we would be prepared to consider helping Afghanistan strengthen its private sector development. 

Technical assistance

Technical Assistance helps the people of less developed countries learn the skills and develop the institutions to use more effectively their own resources, thereby progressively diminishing the need for foreign capital assistance. The result is that they are able to grow more food, improve health, and produce more essential consumer and capital goods. 

As development proceeds, with new investment in agriculture, irrigation, electric power, transport and industry, the need for Technical Assistance changes in scale and complexity. Management problems multiply, not only in government agencies struggling with new responsibilities, but also in the growing number of new private commercial and financial concerns created by the widening market economy. Technical Assistance projects, jointly developed with agencies of the NESA countries, is one of the most efficient ways to meet this need. Each project's plan of action is linked to a series of steps of learning and acting, which in the end will produce a cadre of new men experienced in handling technical and organizational problems of economic development, able to train others and to provide the base for sustaining growth in the future. 

We are requesting $47 million to finance American technicians and the training of participants for Technical Assistance Programs in India, Pakistan, Turkey, Afghanistan, Nepal, Jordan and the UAR. The funds requested also would finance the training of students from these and other Near East countries at the American University at Beirut; meetings sponsored by CENTO on technical and economic problems common to Turkey, Iran and Pakistan; and the fight against cholera, one of the most debilitating and deadly of man's enemies. 

As self-help reform programs take hold and the pace of development accelerates, there is need to reinforce the self-help process with Western know-how, particularly in the areas of agriculture, education and health. Our FY 1967 and 

1968 programs recommend a number of new or enlarged projects. These include, for example, strengthening development of new rice seed varieties in India; improving the Turkish administration and planning of its irrigation program ; introducing rational scientific techniques through Summer Training Institutes for mathematics and science teachers in East Pakistan based on the highly successful experience with this program in India; training essential technical personnel for family planning programs in India and Pakistan. 

AID Technical Assistance projects have both an immediate short term objective and longer term objectives. The American agricultural advisors in Afghanistan who are working at the demonstration centers are looking to next year's harvest but their work will affect agricultural growth prospects for a decade. 

The 240 teachers who will be working with India educators in science and math teacher training are bringing about an immediate change in curricula, but future generations of students will be the better engineers and scientists as a result. 

Statisticians in Turkey and Pakistan are working on the next census, the results of which will guide policy planners for a decade. Advice on labor disputes legislation in Turkey will influence the pattern of labor business relations and private investment potential for a generation. 

Additionally, training in the United States of participants from the NESA countries plays a vital role in strengthening cooperation with these countries and advancing peaceful development of the region. 

Supporting assistance

Only Jordan and Yemen receive grant Supporting Assistance. Supporting Assistance for NESA has been reduced from about $270 million in FY 1962 to a request for $26.9 million FY 1968.

379 Our strategy is to support Jordan's drive toward economic viability by development lending for projects which will improve its capacity to collect more tax revenues and increase export earnings, thereby eliminating the need for grant budget support. We plan to continue to reduce budget support to Jordan. The planned reduction is larger than previous annual cuts and reflects the progress Jordan has been making since 1965. 

We also maintain a Supporting Assistance program in Yemen largely to support small self-financed water systems, farm to market roads and training programs. 

In all of these programs substantial self-help performance is being achieved. 

We will continue to expect the fullest possible self-help commitment of the countries and peoples we assist so that their efforts and ours will be effective. We believe our programs promote conditions which make possible and meaningful participation by an ever-increasing number of people in economic development. 

I have tried to cover the main aspects of our proposed aid effort for FY 1968 in the Near East and South Asia—an area encompassing one-third of the world's people and a very substantial measure of our concern and aspiration for future world peace and security. I will be glad to answer any questions.

STATEMENT OF HON. MAURICE J. WILLIAMS, ASSISTANT ADMIN- ISTRATOR, BUREAU FOR NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate this opportunity to appear before the committee. I have just taken over this job, a week and a half ago, as Assistant Administrator for the Near East and South 

Asia. Prior to that, I was Deputy Director, then Director of our AID mission to Pakistan. In this capacity in working in the field for the past 31½ years, there were four questions that I kept before me: 

The first, Are we making progress in the AID business? The second, Is the country we are helping doing its utmost to help itself? 

Third, Do our Western friends share the burden of assistance? And fourth, Is there an end in sight to economic assistance?

I would like to briefly discuss these questions, Mr. Chairman, in relation to my foreign experience, which has been primarily in Pakistan. 

In the spring of 1961, when the new Kennedy administration reviewed the foreign assistance program, Pakistan was the sick man of foreign aid. The growth of the economy had not been proceeding any faster than the growth of population. Agricultural output and population were increasing annually at about 2 percent. 

The economy was relatively stagnant and this despite the fact that we had provided major efforts of economic assistance to Pakistan.

1967 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 placed emphasis on self-help. 

In other words, aid programs would be directed primarily to those countries that were prepared to make the necessary sacrifices to move their own economies forward. The act also, as you know, changed the main emphasis of aid from grants to loans. 

By 1965, 5 years later, Pakistan had achieved, with our help, a dramatic success in its economy. It had exceeded all of its planned targets. The annual growth of the GNP during 1961-65 exceeded 5 percent a year, which was well ahead of population increase. 

Agricultural production also was well ahead of population growth. 

The near stagnation of the earlier period was over in agricultural production. Investment was up. Taxes had been raised. Exports were moving ahead at 7 percent a year, compared to about half that rate of growth in the period before. There had been a complete change. 

By 1965 it was no longer possible to speak of Pakistan as the sick man of foreign aid.

How was this done? It was done, I believe, merely by a change in policies, in part, encouraged by the emphasis on self-help in foreign aid. Those policy changes included emphases on private sector development, and agriculture, and self-help efforts to raise taxes so that the financial contribution Pakistan made to development was larger than it had been before.

In a sense you might say Pakistan adopted the American model for development, and followed a policy of releasing private initiative by removing bureaucratic controls over the economy. I will give you one example. Previously all imports had been licensed. It was the Government's policy to bring imports in as cheaply as possible so that the price could be held down. This seemed a good idea, but the control of these imports through the licensing system meant distortions in allocations and the businessman or the farmer who needed the goods might or might not get them. Also it meant high prices internally. 

Production was low and capacity of existing industrial plants was utilized at something like 50 percent.

Liberalizing imports meant using the price system to allocate these resources instead of the licensing systems. Consequently the prices of imports were raised because imports are a scarce commodity in a developing country. When the market took over the allocation process businessmen could more easily get the commodities they needed, and although they paid a higher foreign exchange price, the domestic price came down as distortions were removed. Within a year the use of existing industrial capacity, instead of being at 50 percent, rose to 

90 percent.

When businessmen and farmers under a free market system are able to make decisions instead of bureaucrats, there is greater economic efficiency. This is not surprising to us in this country. An example from the agricultural sector-once import controls were relaxed and the farmer could get his hands on steel tubing, he put in tube wells. In the Punjab was $50 million of private investment in tube wells completely unplanned which meant more water and increased agricultural production. No planner in Government had foreseen this development. Without freeing up the market so that the farmers

381 could make this decision the increase in production would not have taken place.

Program loans, which are a main feature of our past and proposed program of foreign assistance in the Near East and South Asia, have played a major role in supporting private sector and free market development. If the economic policies are right, then the supply of raw materials for the farmer and for the businessman enables him to use more effectively his existing productive capacity. Program loans, within a framework of proper policy, support the private sector and lead to higher production from the existing economic plant. 

One result of getting the prices right on imports, and of increasing production, is that the economy is able to step up the level of its exports. This is exactly what Pakistan has done. Instead of exports increasing at 4 percent a year as they had previously, they increased at 7 percent a year and more recently the rate of increase in exports has been about 10 percent a year. It is the increase in exports, in earnings of foreign exchange, that is going to make these countries independent of foreign aid. This is a true index of their economic progress. Program loans make possible the increase of exports. 

In the agricultural sector, whereas previously there had been a situation of relative stagnation, of squeezing the farmer for investment in the industrial sector, establishing a free market gave proper incentives to farmers to increase production. It didn't take anything very unusual. Farmers, even those who are illiterate, will respond to the market; if the price is right, they will increase production. We know that.

The market incentive policies meant that farmers began to purchase not only steel for tube wells, but also fertilizer. Credit became important. A whole dynamic development began to take place in the agricultural sector. Instead of agriculture increasing slowly, and no more than population, it is stepped up to about 3.5 percent annual increase a year which is 1 percent more than the population increase. 

Program loans again played an important role in more fully utilizing agricultural capacity, because with new incentives and program loans farmers were able to get fertilizers, steel for tube wells, and to make the investments that increased food production. 

That is the story of Pakistan's development during the period 1961 to 1965. There was an interruption with the war with India in 1965. 

But since that time Pakistan has returned the priority emphasis to its development program and is moving forward with these same policies. 

Similar policies are being applied in India. The devaluation set a more realistic price on imports. Emphasis has been placed on agriculture. Similarly in Turkey there has been a greater emphasis on agriculture and on market incentives to get the job done. 

Our programs in the Near East and South Asia emphasize this approach to economic development. Of the economic development loans we have requested, 97 percent are for the major programs in India, Pakistan, and Turkey, where promising results are now underway in the application of free market policies releasing the initiative of private businessmen and farmers. 

Thank you. Mr. Chairman.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Williams.

Mr. Battle, my mail shows that there are quite a number of people who question whether it is a good idea for the United States to spend a lot of money making India and Pakistan economically strong as long as there is such hatred for each other. This hatred dominates their national policy. It is claimed that either one of the countries would not hesitate to turn against the United States if it was dissatisfied with the U.S. policies toward each other. 

Is Pakistan more friendly toward the United States today than it was 10 years ago?

Mr. BATTLE. Mr. Chairman, we are in the difficult position, not only with India and Pakistan but with a number of other countries in this area, of trying to get along with people who have problems with each other. There are a lot of similar cases. As far as Pakistan is concerned, we have had ups and downs in our relationships. At the moment I think we are on an upward incline.

I think in the last months relations between ourselves and the Pakistanis have improved considerably. [Security deletion] I hope that we can encourage both India and Pakistan to come to grips with some of the problems that they face [security deletion] and try to keep from turning against each other, which is really, I think, the key thing. [Security deletion.] That is the thing we must try to achieve through diplomacy, if we can.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, another matter under your juris diction: The arms race between the Arabs and Israel seems to be more intense. We are supporting Israel and Saudi Arabia and Jordan with additional arms, and the Soviets are pouring arms into the United Arab Republic and Iran and the Yemen. Is this going to get any worse than it is now? What will be the ultimate outcome of this arms race? Is it going to boil up to a real military conflict?

Mr. BATTLE. Mr. Chairman, I deplore all the arms races in my area. 

We have a number of them. Arms races are not simple things. They involve problems that frequently are highly emotional, highly charged. 

As far as the Arab-Israel arms race is concerned, I would like to make one or two comments. We must not take upon our shoulders responsibilities for [security deletion] the arms races in the world. 

Arms, unfortunately are available in the world market. They can be bought and sold. The U.S. policy on arms in the Near East has been a policy of restraint. We have tried not to become a major supplier of arms to either side in the situation. 

But as long as the Soviets pour in tremendous amounts of arms as they have done the major input of arms into the Near East has been by the Soviets and not by us-we have felt it important to supply some arms, primarily of a defensive nature, in order to restore equilibrium. I think all in all, our response has been restrained and careful. 

It is not an easy situation for us. 

We have made comparatively small sales of arms. We have continually urged restraint on both sides in the arms race. I would not venture to predict where this ends, Mr. Chairman. I hope that we and they can have enough wisdom to keep it from erupting. It is a delicate situation. It is not an easy situation. 

I think our policy must continue to be one of restraint. We must try to limit the arms that we put into that area, or indeed into any

383 arms race, to the extent we possibly can. But we cannot sit idly by and watch a complete imbalance in an arms situation growing out of Soviet arms rushing into that area.

 BULGUR WHEAT 

Bulgur is wheat that has been processed by steaming, hulling, drying and cracking. Having been processed in this way bulgur can be cooked like rice. 

Bulgur is about twice as expensive as unprocessed wheat but it is in a much more readily usable form. It is about the same price as white flour, less expensive (net to U.S.) than rice, and more nutritious than either since the wheat germ is not removed. It has an additional advantage over flour in that it does not require an oven.

In FY 1967 we are supplying bulgur under Title III programs for maternal and child-feeding programs in the following NESA countries: Jordan, Turkey, U.A.R., India and Pakistan.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Morse. 

Mr. MORSE. 

In addition to its interest in self-help, gentlemen, this committee has been concerned recently with the concept of popular participation of the development process, and to that end wrote in the act in 1966 what is now title IX, which states, "In carrying out programs authorized in this chapter, emphasis shall be placed on assuring maximum participation in the task of economic development on the part of the people of the developing countries, through the encouragement of democratic private and local governmental institutions." One of the

391 most successful programs of this type is the East Pakistan program, which preceded title IX by several years. 

I would presume that you have some intimate familiarity with that program, Mr. Williams. Would you describe it for the committee? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, thank you.

The rural works program in East Pakistan has been a program which used the proceeds of the sale of Public Law 480 commodities for rural works. The effort, however, was very much directed toward increasing the participation of local village towns, known in Pakistan as the Basic Democracies system. Each of the villages has a council; ten villages coming together from what is known as a union of councils, or a union council. Under this program the union council was authorized to seek out small development projects which would use primarily surplus or underemployed labor in this area. 

A great deal of autonomy at the local level was permitted in the selection of the projects and also in the execution of these projects, which had to meet general criteria. In other words, the Central Government's influence was minimized purposely. 

Some people feared this. They said there would be great inefficiency and you wouldn't get much development out of it. The returns have been quite outstanding in East Pakistan. The project was started first on a small scale. Then as the techniques worked out, the procedures and criteria were established, it was expanded provincewide. Some 

25,000 miles of roads have been built this way. These are all small projects. 

To some extent they are headbasket operations largely utilizing hand labor, physical labor; for culverts, small bridges, roads, irrigation and drainage works. Aside from investment in what might be called rural infrastructure, it gave life to the local councils. The people had something to work with in practical terms. They could do something about dealing with their own development problems. This, I think, is the major success of the rural works program, both in economic development terms and in terms of the development of democratic local government as defined by maximum participation and the strengthening of these local councils. 

Mr. MORSE. It would seem to me, because of the very exciting success of the East Pakistan program, that perhaps the same techniques could be applied to a greater extent throughout the NESA area. 

Do you have plans in your new job to extend the use of these techniques to other countries?

Mr. WILLIAMS. We have widely publicized the record in East Pakistan. The program was extended to West Pakistan, for example, 2 years after it began in East Pakistan. Also Nepal is an example where the same technique is being tried.

Yes, sir; wherever we can encourage this type of development, we are doing so.

 AMOUNT OF CONSORTIUM NONPROJECT PLEDGE TO TURKEY IN FISCAL YEARS 1967 AND 1968 

The consortium so far has pledged for 1967 $136 million in non-project assistance of which the U.S. share is $69 million. We expect additional non-project pledges from the other consortium members of $10-$15 million. In the fall of 1967 the consortium will review the Turkish air requirement for 1968. THURSDAY, APRIL 20, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

Office  

The committee meets this morning in executive session for a continuation of hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to further amend the Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1961. 

Our witnesses are the Honorable Joseph Palmer 2d, Assistant 

Secretary of State for African Affairs, and Mr. Herman Kleine, Acting Assistant Administrator, Bureau for Africa, Agency for

International Development. 

Mr. Secretary, I understand that both you and Mr. Kleine have prepared statements. If you wish you can summarize your statements and we will incorporate the full statements in the record after which we will direct questions to you both. (The prepared statements of Mr. Palmer and Mr. Kleine are as follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH PALMER 2D, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. Chairman, members of the Committee, I am pleased to have this opportunity to outline recent developments in Africa and to make some observations on their relationship to US interests and assistance programs. The present occasion is particularly timely because of the ferment which is taking place in the continent and the implications for US policy objectives. 

A few background observations about Africa's dimension in the world scene should be noted for perspective. Africa is more than three times the size of the US. 

A look at the map will show how this huge land mass relates to the security of other continents (and vice versa)-to Europe via the Mediterranean, to Asia via the Red Sea and Indian Ocean and to our Western Hemisphere via the

Atlantic. Africa's sea and air space can be friendly or hostile. In the comparatively hospitable climate that now exists, the US maintains transport facilities, spacetracking stations, communications, civil and military air rights, and enjoys generally favorable relations.

Africa is also a major source of minerals and other materials vital to US and other Free World economies. The Free World obtains 25 percent of its copper supplies from Africa, 72 percent of its cobalt, 77 percent of gold, 98 percent of natural diamonds, 26 percent of manganese, among other basic materials. The continent also has great reserves of petroleum, water power, iron ore, bauxite and a host of other resources. 

Linked with Africa's resource wealth is the growing US private investment now totalling $2 billion (direct investment only), which represents a seven-fold increase in the last decade and a half. The major part-in fact, about two-thirds of the total is in the newly independent states of the continent, where its rapid growth continues. US exports to Africa totalled $1.3 billion in 1966, with 60% 413

1967 

of this amount being directed again towards the newly independent nations of the continent.

Africa has over 300 million people, most of whom have gained independence only in the last decade. There are now 39 independent states where prior to 1951 there were only four. The emergence in Africa of so many states-some small in population and size and often inheriting boundaries that are neither logical nor economic has far reaching implications for African development. I will refer later to how we believe our aid program can help ameliorate some of the economic problems which result from this multiplicity of states. 

Most people in Africa live in traditional and tribal societies relatively untouched by modern life. The average per capita GNP in Africa is about $114-a poverty level. Africans aspire to improve their lot and to make the dignity of their new independence meaningful in terms of decent living standards and economic progress. This drive for progress is a major force. When progress is slow, instability is bound to result. 

Why do we aid Africa?

The 300 million Africans and their nations have an important relationship to US interests and to those of the Free World generally. I have noted the strategic position of Africa, its resources and the US investment there. Also of major significance is the relationship of African events to US foreign policy objectives, particularly as they relate to our efforts to help build a peaceful and prosperous world system in which nations can feel secure in their independence and cooperate with one another for the greater good. 

US aid provides an added measure of assurance to Africans that progress is possible in such a Free World context. Our assistance is consonant with our own historic experience and is a logical extension of our commitment to self determination by giving concrete evidence of our desire to see free nations succeed in improving the well-being of their citizens. 

President Johnson said to African representatives in May 1966, on the occasion of the anniversary of the Organization of African Unity, "We are anxious to work with you to fulfill your ambitions. Working with others, we are prepared to help you build a modern Africa."

By sharing with Africans their aspirations for progress and by helping make this possible with aid, we convert our principles into reality. As a result, common interests and mutual understanding are generated. African governments have confidence that a working relationship with us is mutually beneficial and that progress is possible in association with the Free World. But we are not "buying" support any more than they are "selling "it. What we are showing is that in an interrelated world, we have concern for African aspirations just as we hope they will understand our objectives. In my opinion, the 7 percent of our aid appropriation that goes to Africa-less than $200 million-is of fundamental importance to United States foreign policy interests on that continent. No instrument of American policy takes on greater practical meaning for these nations than our development assistance program. 

While U.S. basic interests are involved in the aid program, it would be inappropriate if I did not also mention the great American tradition of helping others in need. Throughout our history, individual Americans and private organizations have striven to help others to improve their circumstances. Our aid program is in this American tradition-our willingness to share with others a part of our affluence.

Political Developments-Instability 

Instability in Africa in the last few years has obviously had adverse effects on development. We are all familiar with its various manifestations, both present and potential: (1) Tribal and regional differences which threaten national cohesion. (2) Arbitrary boundaries inherited from colonial times are at variance with ethnic and economic considerations. (3) A tendency in some countries towards arbitrary rule and coercive measures which muffle dissent and breed discontent. (4) Non-acceptance of government by consent of the governed and of human equality in some parts of the continent. 

In the first decade of independence, the new nations of Africa are still experiencing the exciting-but sometimes painful-process of trial and error in building institutions and societies that reflect their own aspirations. Educational levels and skills are still sadly deficient-for example, literacy in some countries is

415 only 5 percent. The widespread poverty is illustrated by per capita incomes averaging about 30 cents daily. There is high mortality from disease, while dietary deficiency is endemic in many areas. 

Perhaps most important in the flux which characterizes Africa today is the imbalance between aspirations and progress. Instability is bred out of man's dissatisfaction with his situation and with his prospects. Conversely, the conviction that a better life is possible, as evidenced by some demonstrated progress, restrains man's tendency to translate despair into violent expression. In this context, US aid is especially significant because it provides, along with other assistance, the means for Africans to channel their energies toward meaningful progress. 20099 Instability in Africa must be viewed in the perspective of profound historic change and of nations seeking to lift themselves from traditional, poverty-stricken societies to modern states with adequate standards of living-a truly formidable task. Clearly, it is too much in these circumstances to expect Africa in a few years to achieve advanced forms of political democracy. On the contrary, the short term outlook is realistically one of further instability in the search for valid and enduring political institutions.

With time and experience, however, we can be optimistic that political systems will develop which will involve increasingly wide participation by all citizens and change by peaceful, legal means. I believe that Africans, as much as ourselves, look forward to the day when there will be conditions of stability and full respect for constitutional government. They too look forward to directing their energies toward development instead of fruitless adventures and strife. 

But at this stage of their history, most of the new nations are going through a period of experimentation and consolidation and are developing societies and institutions that are responsive to their aspirations societies that merge African traditions with the imperatives for modern development. They will borrow selectively from the experience of other parts of the world but will not model their societies in the image of others. They will experiment until they find an African way. 

The Coups

The problems of Nigeria in the last year or so illustrate many of the difficulties that affect much of Africa. The conflict between sectional and national interests is most serious in this country where recent eruptions of serious tribal and regional tensions are putting Nigeria's national unity and great economic potential to the test. A military coup in January 1966 overturned the civilian coalition government and brought into power a military government headed by General Ironsi from Eastern Nigeria. Resentment in the North over what was considered to be 

Ibo domination resulted in a second coup last July and in severe outbreaks of tribal violence. This, in turn, caused many deaths and a hardening of regional antagonisms. Talks among the leaders of the various regions have been held, but differences persist and the future constitutional structure of the country is far from clear. While these are problems which Nigerians must solve, we hope that the cohesion of the country will be maintained in order that it may continue to realize its great economic and political potential in Africa and in the world. 

In Congo (Kinshasa), long plagued by regional revolts and disorder and unrest in the countryside, the coup d'etat which resulted in the present government under President Mobutu has brought greater unity and order. The 1964-65 revolt has been all but liquidated. The fiat of the central government increasingly extends to the provinces, and cooperative relations have been established with most of the country's neighbors.

In Ghana, the downfall of Nkrumah was brought about by widespread popular discontent with his personal rule and with the ruinous economic policies of his regime. The new military government, which has greatly improved relations with the Free World, has also been making considerable progress_by following sound measures to return the country to a solid economic footing. It is apparent, however, from the events of the past few days, that the security of the state is not yet fully assured.

In several other countries-Dahomey, the Central African Republic, Sierra Leone, Togo, and Upper Volta, coups have occurred against a background of frustration over the lack of economic and social progress, combined with resentment against government leaders by military leaders and other elites. Yet the new governments face essentially the same problems as their predecessorsimposed by limited economic resources and development possibilities.

1967 

Communism

Communism in Africa has had to deal with Africa's determination to be independent and to resist substituting a new colonialism for the old. This general dedication to an independent and non-aligned posture has limited communist penetration and in many cases explains communist setbacks. For this and other reasons, the Red Chinese have been repulsed in Ghana, Burundi, the Central African Republic and Dahomey. The Soviet Union has also had its trials with 

African insistence on true independence and appears to have revised its tacticsif not its strategy at least to some extent. 

The poverty of Africa and frustrated aspirations for economic progress have provided openings for Communist probings, but these have been minimized by U.S. and other Free World policies and measures which provide the nations of 

Africa with a reasonable assurance for progress in freedom. As long as these nations can look forward to such progress, the forces will be diminished that seek to compromise independence through tied politico-economic arrangements with 

Communist countries. 

Southern Africa

The problems of Southern Africa are potentially dangerous to stability in this region and in other parts of Africa. They are also subject to Communist exploitation. The United States is inevitably concerned with the events affecting the region because the issues at stake relate to basic tenets of our own beliefs and to our position as a responsible member of the United Nations, i.e. self-determination, majority rule, government by consent of the governed, and equal rights for all. 

Because of differing situations, the degree and manner in which we seek to encourage progress towards these goals have naturally varied. Throughout we have sought to make our position on these principles clear at home, in Africa and the rest of the world. In so doing, we have sought, as a responsible member of the 

United Nations, to play our part in endeavoring to encourage peaceful resolution of the problems in the area which are of such demonstrated concern to the international community.

Self-Help and Private Enterprise—Preconditions for Development 

I would like to turn now from political events and discuss the economic development of the continent and how our economic assistance program relates to development. 

Foremost in our convictions concerning development is that with all the good will and economic assistance from the rest of the world a nation's progress will, in the last analysis, depend primarily on its own efforts. Thus it may be said that the mainsprings for economic progress must be generated within Africa through its own leadership, sacrifice and iniatives; these cannot, however well intentioned, be superimposed from abroad.

Therefore, emphasis on self-help is a prime focus of our assistance program. 

One outstanding example of African self-help has been the creation of the African Development Bank, where 29 nations have already subscribed $40 million of hard earned capital for the Bank which is run entirely by Africans. Another is regional cooperation for joint planning and building of projects such as multinational airlines which conserve resources by eliminating duplication and costs of expensive national airlines. Again, countries such as Tunisia and Rwanda have cooperated very closely with the IMF to realize sound policies to stabilize their currencies and economies-policies that have required belt tightening. 

African encouragement to private enterprise and investment, another important aspect of self-help, has been widespread. Africans themselves would prefer to rely more heavily on improvements in trade and private investment than on Government to Government aid which is not a panacea, although at this stage of development is essential. Indigenous and foreign private enterprise and investment are major keys to development which US programs seek to stimulate in Africa. Most African nations welcome and actively seek to bring about US and other Free World investment. As I have noted, in all of Africa, United States direct private investment has risen to $2 billion from $287 million in 1950. US investment guarantee agreements have been signed with 31 African nations and other agreements are being negotiated. Again, the Economic Commission for 

Africa convened a Conference of Industrialists and Financiers in Addis Ababa in January to explore ways to encourage foreign investment. Three prominent 

American businessmen participated in this Conference and contributed greatly to our efforts to translate our economic principles into action. We are seeking to further invest in Africa in a number of ways, including support to a US

417 private investment finance corporation which we hope will be established as a channel for US private sector loans in Africa. 

We are all aware of the fact that several states in Africa have nationalized part of their foreign investment. In large degree, this has resulted from frustration with lack of progress, the slow pace of external investment, disappointment over the volume of aid as well as low prices for exports. However, far from spurring the economy, these measures have usually had the opposite effect, by inhibiting the flow of needed private capital. 

It should be emphasized, in this connection, that while nationalization and state ownership have occurred in some African states, in most, foreign investment and enterprise are sought, encouraged and protected. Thus, in most of Africa, American businessmen have found a propitious atmosphere for mutually advantageous investment.

Development Progress in Africa 

While many difficulties prevail in the development of Africa, encouraging progress can be also reported. As an example, the Volta Dam, a major power complex, is now generating electricity and will provide Ghana and perhaps nearby countries with electric power, including power for the American privately built aluminum smelter, which has just reached the production phase. US aid, together with funds from the UK and the World Bank, have financed this Dam, a $170 million venture which has developed much good will in Ghana a fact to ponder in terms of the long term effects of assistance in our relations with a people. 

Many other AID projects, not as large as Volta, but of great importance in their own way, are also bringing development to Africa. For example, in Ethiopia an experiment station at the Ethiopian College of Agriculture has been financed by AID under a contract with Oklahoma State University and is now being run entirely by Ethiopians. The station has discovered new strains of food crops adapted to Ethiopian conditions and the College has already conferred over 300 degrees of Bachelor of Science in Agriculture. Another example is US aid to control rinderpest on a regional basis in West Africa. In one area covered by this project, 9 million cattle have been inoculated and as a result there have been no serious outbreaks of the disease. 

In other countries similar progress is evident-in Zambia, where the gross national product has risen an average of 12.5 percent in the years 1963-66, in 

Tunisia 5.3 percent, Uganda 4.1 percent, Ethiopia 3.6 percent and Kenya 5 percent. Of course these are the more optimistic examples; in many countries viability remains a real problem.

Military Assistance 

May I take a few moments to discuss the small U.S. military assistance programs in several African countries. 

First, I would like to emphasize our concern about certain areas of tension in Africa, particularly in the Maghreb and the Horn of Africa where relatively large amounts of military materiel continue to be introduced by the Soviet Union. 

Other countries in these areas have been concerned by this influx of arms and have felt compelled to increase their own defenses. The dangers of these tensions and incipient arms races are recognized, as well as the wasteful diversion of resources and energies needed for development. Solutions to the political problems that contribute to these situations are the responsibilities of the nations of Africa. 

It is a basic tenet of our policy to encourage constructive African initiatives to alleviate these tensions and to limit arms. 

In the meantime, we have provided limited assistance to certain countries to support a reasonable level of security for purely defensive purposes. While we are very much aware that military programs may divert resources from essential development, we also know that internal security and reasonable assurance against external aggression are vital to creating the conditions for economic growth. These factors are taken into careful consideration in determining our programs. Arms which are excessive to a country's legitimate needs, or its financial capacity have not and will not be provided. In this connection our programs emphasize internal security and civic action requirements.

Thus, military assistance to Africa is provided on a limited basis, the total amount requested for FY 1968 being $31.2 million. Six countries would receive grants of materiel contrasted with eight in 1967 and nine in 1966. In addition to the four countries in areas of current tension (Morocco, Tunisia, Libya and Ethiopia), we propose programs in Congo (K) and Liberia. Our program in 

Liberia is based on our long historic ties and their need for some arms. In the 

Congo the program is aimed at assisting in the development of Congolese armed

1967 

forces capable of maintaining internal security, eliminating remaining pockets of rebel activity and contributing to a unified nation which can concentrate on economic and social development. 

A New Emphasis in U.S. Aid Policy in Africa 

In the past year we have sought to strengthen our aid program to make its contribution greater to African development. Mr. Kleine will provide details of this program, but it may be appropriate for me to make a few general observations by way of background. 

In May 1966, the President directed that a reassessment of US aid policies in Africa be undertaken with the object of achieving a more effective impact of our assistance on African development. As a result, policies and programs have been reformulated. Our assessment recognized that in general the development of 

Africa's potential will be long-term, difficult and necessarily gradual. The fullest possible coordination will be required with other countries which provide much greater assistance, as well as with international organizations, and with African countries and organizations. The need for coordination has already resulted in an initiative by us and other donors to encourage the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, together with the African Development Bank, the Economic Commission for Africa and the United Nations Development Program to take a leadership role in the development of Africa's infrastructure, especially in power, transport and communications. 

The re-examination has also led to a prime emphasis on encouragement to regional cooperation. As the President has said: "Resources know no national boundaries. Rivers flow through many countries, transportation and communication networks serve different peoples, sources of electric power must be shared by neighbors. Economic advance in every part of the world has required joint enterprises to develop shared sources of wealth." 

Africans themselves are increasingly coming to recognize that their small markets, meager financial resources and artificial boundaries require a common effort to benefit from economies of scale by building factories, communications, power and other facilities on a multinational basis. They have taken at least preliminary steps to cooperate with each other in developing multinational projects which reap the efficiencies of joint planning and operations. They have combined forces to build multinational airlines and oil refineries, to conduct health drives against measles and smallpox, and to cooperate in commodity and other problems. The Economic Commission for Africa has taken a lead in economic cooperation by sponsoring Economic Communities in Eastern and West Africa. 

And as I have noted, on a continental scale, the Africal Development Bank is mobilizing financial resources for development. President Johnson has proposed sympathetic consideration of a U.S. contribution to a new special fund of the Bank. 

With the benefits of economic cooperation apparent, the current AID policy will support regional development, institutions and projects. This is also in accord with the interest of the Congress in encouraging regional cooperation in Africa, as expressed in Section 206 of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

In addition to a policy of encouraging regional and subregional economic development and institutions, we intend to give greater stress to multi-donor cooperation by encouraging and participating in projects with mixed financing that make a significant impact on African economies. 

As in the past, the major part of aid will continue to be devoted, in the context of multidonor coordination, to certain countries where prospects are good for development and where alternative sources of aid are limited. Generally, we plan to provide most US assistance where it can be most effective in development and also in some cases where exceptional situations prevail. The list of countries receiving bilateral aid is not immutable and can be altered with new conditions as need and development prospects change. 

In most countries, bilateral programs will give way to multi-national and multidonor projects as present projects are carried to completion. This does not in any sense imply any diminution in the need for US aid to Africa, but rather greater effectiveness in its application. We hope to make the transition as smoothly as possible, thereby demonstrating our continued interest and concern for helping to meet Africa's developmental needs. The continuation of the special Self- 

Help Fund will be especially important in demonstrating this interest. This 

Fund has been and should continue as a prime means of bringing small but high impact projects into being in each of these countries with a minimum of delay and "red tape" and maximum encouragement to the concept of self-help.

419 May I emphasize that the reformulation of our African aid policy will result in a substantial shift away from bilateral programs and that the pace for accomplishing the shift must be orderly. In these circumstances, quantitative restrictions on the number of countries that are to receive bilateral aid appear unnecessary and could hamper an orderly transition. The President should be free to determine, in the light of US interests, the countries in which it is necessary that funds be expended under standards laid down by the Congress. Therefore I hope that the Congress will sustain our request to delete the legislative limitations on the number of countries to which particular categories of aid may be provided. 

As a result of the new points of emphasis, we believe that US assistance will be more effective in contributing to Africa's development. We particularly hope that 

African leaders will find it possible to step-up the initiatives they have already taken to increase regional cooperation, self-help and private enterprise and that progress will be accelerated as a result of greater coordination of U.S. and other 

Free World assistance. On these pillars of regionalism, private investment, selfhelp and multilateralism, we seek to create a stronger program which will be responsive to Africa's aspirations to realize the full potential of this great continent for the benefit of its own people and of the rest of the world. 

STATEMENT OF HERMAN KLEINE, ACTING ASSISTANT ADMINISTRATOR, Bureau For AFRICA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, the proposal for fiscal year 1968 reflects, as President Johnson stated in the Foreign Aid message, "a shift in emphasis in our aid policy in Africa, to concentrate our help increasingly on regional and multinational projects." These changes do not significantly affect the total amount requested. We are recommending a program of $195 million for 

Africa in FY 1968, a figure somewhat less than our current estimate of obligations for FY 1967. The changes basically concern the methods and channels of aid administration. 

The principal elements of our changed A.I.D. policy for Africa are: (1) Multilateral coordination.-We are seeking greater agreement among donor nations and institutions and recipients concerned on the requirements, the plans, the projects, and the self-help measures and policies for development assistance. 

We have encouraged the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to take the leadership in consultative groups on particular nations such as Tunisia and Ghana, and on certain economic sectors, such as transportation and power. (2) Support for regional institutions and regional and multidonor projects.—We intend to use regional channels and methods for providing aid wherever there is a practical prospect or real mutual economic benefit to two or more cooperating African countries which can lead to better and faster development. This applies to some extent to all of Africa receiving MD assistance, but especially to the smaller countries with more meager resources. Therefore, we will shift to regional projects and assistance through regional institutions as our principal means of development assistance to these countries. About one-fifth of the FY 1968 program is intended for these activities. Moreover, in appropriate circumstances, we will also participate in multidonor financing of major capital projects. (3) Development emphasis countries.-A.I.D. will continue to devote the largest portion of its resources for Africa to certain countries, either singly or as a region, where there is a need for such assistance and where a combination of resourcesboth human and natural-and the determination to develop them justify our participating as a full and active partner in an organized multilateral effort in support of a national development plan or other major economic goal. There are currently ten countries, including three as a region, where we plan to continue substantial bilateral aid activities within such a multilateral program framework, but the list could change as countries "graduate," run into problems which impede their development promise, or qualify to be added. (4) Completion of current bilateral projects.-A.I.D. is currently funding 128 technical assistance projects in various stages of progress in countries other than the ten development emphasis ones. These and certain loan projects, which are in advanced stages of joint planning, will be carried to completion. (5) Special self-help fund.-Even after U.S. bilateral aid to many of these countries has concluded, and regional projects are operative, the need will remain for modest U.S. support for purely local, small self-help development activities. 

These are the sorts of low-cost but high return projects which this Committee stated last year was "one of the most useful and productive activities in our A.I.D. 

77-470-67-pt. 2-11

1967 

program." For this purpose, A.I.D. will continue to provide a small, limitedpurpose self-help fund in each African country, which will not go above $200,000 per country per year. 

The effects of this changed policy are: 

For FY 1968 approximately 20% of the A.I.D. program will go to regional/ multidonor activities—a figure which should rise sharply in subsequent years; about 60% will go to countries designated as the ten development emphasis countries; and about 20% to the completion of bilateral projects in other countries, a figure which should decline in subsequent years. 

For FY 1968 we are reducing the number of African countries with bilateral A.I.D. programs (exclusive of the Self-Help fund) from 34 to 29, of which those scheduled to receive loans will drop from 19 in FY 1967 to 14. By FY 1969, we estimate that the number of country programs will drop to 24, of which only the ten development emphasis countries will receive both bilateral technical assistance and development loans. After FY 1969, we expect to have bilateral technical assistance projects in 15 countries—the ten development emphasis countries and five other countries where existing projects would be in the process of being completed. The countries where new bilateral projects will not be undertaken will benefit from regional and multidonor projects. 

How did we arrive at these policy and program changes? 

The process started last May, when President Johnson called for a review of our own development policies and programs in Africa and designated Ambassador Edward M. Korry, U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia, to undertake the review. This was done during last summer. 

The main themes of the Korry Report are: 

African development will be a long-term, difficult and necessarily gradual effort, requiring the fullest possible coordination and unity of effort and purpose on the part of the United States, the other countries now providing much larger amounts of economic aid to Africa, international organizations, the African countries and their own African regional organizations. 

The coordination could best be led by an international organization; the World 

Bank is particularly well equipped to fill this role, especially in the fields of transportation, power and communications. 

The U.S. should concentrate its own bilateral development support efforts on a country basis in those African countries whose development prospects are good and where U.S. aid can be most effective. 

The U.S. should continue development assistance to other areas of Africa but primarily by assisting regional and multinational rather than strictly national development efforts and programs. 

The substantive emphasis of U.S. developmental aid should be on agriculture and rural development, education, health and population, the private sector and the infrastructure fields of transportation, power and communications. 

Specific procedural improvements are needed to achieve more effective use of both U.S. capital and technical assistance funds. 

The amount of U.S. aid to Africa need not change sharply but can and should increase gradually as the development of African institutions and the application of the Report's other recommendations provide growing opportunities for more effective use of U.S. aid.

In setting forth the A.I.D. program for Africa for FY 1968, we have taken full account of the Korry Report recommendations (outlined on pages 214-215 of the summary presentation), as well as our experience in Africa over the past few years; the Congressional limitations on the number of country programs; 

Congressional encouragement to engage in regional projects; the large role of other countries in supplying aid to Africa; and the consequent desirability of much greater coordination. I have already indicated that our plans call for continued reduction in the numbers of bilateral aid programs. We feel that the formal numerical restrictions in the Foreign Assistance Act should not be retained. 

I should now like to speak a little more about each of the principal elements of the changed A.I.D. policy for Africa, and about some of the programs we are planning for the coming fiscal year. 

Multilateral Coordination in the Development Emphasis Countries 

There are certain African countries which are in themselves large enough units for development emphasis. They have the combination of size, population and resources sufficient to give them a good prospect of economic development in a reasonable time, so that they will then be able to continue their growth without aid, and they have demonstrated their determination to develop.

421 One example is Tunisia. Notwithstanding Tunisia's difficulties in making the transition from a dependent protectorate economy_to a competitive, independent one, the loss of much preferential access to the French market, a critical balance-of-payments situation and the need for a basic reorientation of its agricultural production, the Tunisian economy averaged a 52% growth rate from 1962 to the present. Tunisia is making progress in diversifying production and increasing its foreign exchange earnings. Its self-help efforts have been commendable, particularly in adjusting capital investment to match resource availabilities, in accepting a rigorous monetary stabilization program, and in adopting an improved budgetary system. The government has taken steps to improve the private investment climate with the result that Firestone Tire, Singer Sewing Machine and various American hotel builders have entered the country. Tunisia is also taking systematic steps to reduce its rapid population growth rate.

Tunisia is one of the countries where several donors in addition to the U.S. are providing substantial assistance. The World Bank chairs a "consultative group" of these donors, takes an active role in diagnosing Tunisia's problems recommending needed actions and joining in supplying needed funds. The other donors are: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, West Germany, Italy, Kuwait, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, as well as the International Monetary Fund. 

Consultative groups exist or are planned for several other countries. The 

IMF chairs a group for Ghana. Elsewhere, in other development emphasis countries, we look forward to a greater role for the World Bank and the IMF: 

Ethiopia has asked the IBRD for help with its next development plan; and the 

IMF is already playing a larger role in Liberian stabilization efforts. 

In all of these instances, our approach is to obtain a multilateral effect by having an impartial international organization assume a leadership role in the sensitive functions of obtaining agreement on economic policies, development priorities and the aid recipient's economic performance requirements. These will set the basis for our development assistance, and encourage even greater participation by other donors. In these cases, I wish to emphasize that the World Bank's leadership and services will not mean any less control or responsibility on our part of the expenditure of U.S. funds.

Examples of what A.I.D. plans to do in several development emphasis countries follow:

An A.I.D. program loan to Tunisia for essential commodity imports will help to increase its economic growth rate while avoiding significant inflationary pressure, and to encourage both domestic and foreign private investment. As now, its disbursement will be tied to Tunisian performance on monetary and fiscal policies agreed with the IMF. A.I.D. also will help Tunisia to increase its agricultural production through improving water resources, increasing food and livestock production, and training. An FY 1968 development loan is planned to develop ground water resources and related irrigation activities. We are also planning to continue assisting in postgraduate business administration training. 

We shall also participate with other countries and institutions in helping with Tunisia's active family planning program. 

Another development emphasis country is Ghana which, despite the serious economic disruption caused by the extravagance and mismanagement of the Nkrumah administration which ended a year ago, is starting to recover. The new government, following closely the advice of the IMF and the IBRD, has adopted a wide range of progressive and prudent policies to meet Ghana's economic problems. We are supporting and encouraging this stabilization program. A program loan and a PL 480 sales program are planned this year, which with assistance from other sources, should help provide essential imports which will strengthen Ghana's productive capacity, help relieve its critical balance-of-payments deficit, and enable Ghana to lay the groundwork for renewed development progress. 

Through technical assistance, we hope to assist the Government in its programs of reform of agriculture, industry and other vital sectors. 

U.S. aid to Nigeria is intended to help realize its long-run development potential which remains great, particularly if the Nigerians are successful in resolving their current problems in a manner which maintains the cohesion of the country. The situation in Nigeria is under continual review and the program will be revised, if necessary, to meet changed conditions.

1967 Broader Aspects of Multilateral Coordination 

Country development programs are not the only setting in which multilateral coordination under international agency leadership can speed development and enhance the usefulness of our own development funds. In the major economic sectors of transportation, power and communications, with their great cost and broad continent-wide and sub-regional significance, there is the same need for coordinated use of all external aid funds and agreement among donors and with African countries and organizations_on_policies and priorities. I am happy to report that representatives of the IBRD, the African Development Bank, the UN Economic Commission for Africa, and the UN Development Program have recently met to plan the means for coordination of development efforts on an Africa-wide basis in these economic sectors. At the appropriate time, the U.S. and other bilateral donors look forward to participating in the work of this group of organizations. 

Support for Regional Institutions and Projects 

Another main element of the changed A.I.D. policy for Africa is our intention to provide aid to a number of countries principally through regional institutions and projects rather than by our previous bilateral methods. Our purpose is to encourage regional solutions to development problems, because in many areas this should yield better and faster development progress through the more efficient use of resources, and is in accord with the known intentions and desires of many Africans.

First of all, we plan to assist African regional institutions, such as the African Development Bank, the Scientific, Technical and Research Commission of the Organization for African Unity, the UN Economic Commission for Africa and its sub-regional economic communities, and other African organizations of more limited geographic or technical scope. We shall offer technical assistance to help strengthen them in their own efforts. In the case of the African Development 

Bank, President Johnson has said that we will seek appropriate means of responding to its recent request to the United States-and other non-African nationsfor participation in a special fund, which would be used by the ADB primarily for regional projects and for help to the poorer African countries. 

We also intend to finance directly certain regional capital and technical assistance projects undertaken jointly by two or more African countries for their mutual benefit. The largest single regional project is the five-year campaign to eradicate smallpox and control measles in 19 West and Central African countries, by giving over 100 million smallpox vaccinations to people all ages and 25 million measles injections to children (ages 1-6). A.I.D. will provide $11.7 million in FY 

1968, the second year of this program, to finance the services of the U.S. Public 

Health Service, train Africans and provide vaccines. The African nations, two 

African regional health organizations and the World Health Organization are also sharing in the cost and operation of this project. 

Other regional projects include A feasibility study on establishing an African population study center; 

Undergraduate and graduate scholarship programs in Africa and the United States, with a concerted effort to improve selected higher education facilities in África and thereby encourage African students to complete their studies on that continent; 

Continuing support to the Heavy Equipment Training Center in Togo, which provides for the training of operators and maintenance men from a dozen francophone states;

Livestock improvement through support for a 14-nation rinderpest control program jointly with the African Scientific, Technical and Research Commission, the EEC, and several other countries. 

Surveys for improving wheat seed in North and East Africa, livestock marketing and rice growing in West Africa, and agricultural mechanization; and Surveys of regional power, transport and telecommunications projects. 

A.I.D. will also participate with other donors and international organizations in major capital projects, whether in individual countries or groups of countries. 

One such project under consideration is the Trans-Cameroon railroad construction in which we would be cooperating with France and the European Economic Community. Another such project which is under consideration involves joint support under IBRD leadership with several European countries, the EEC, and several private banks for the construction of an iron ore railway from the interior of Gabon to the port of Libreville.

423 A.I.D. also is encouraging the creation of a U.S. private investment corporation, to be wholly owned by private U.S. financial institutions, but to be assisted initially by a "seed-capital" loan from A.I.D. This would provide loans to enterprises in Africa which present worthwhile private investment opportunities. 

Supporting Assistance 

Our estimate of $14 million in Supporting Assistance type of aid for FY 1968 is a decline from $24 million in FY 1966 and $19 million in FY 1967, and represents only 7% of the aid to Africa. The downward trend in Supporting Assistance represented by this estimate is heartening. It represents our best estimate as of now-although other emergency situations might arise during the year which would require the use of Supporting Assistance or the Contingency Fund. Most of the $14 million is planned for use in the Congo (Kinshasa), where we anticipate the need to support the IMF-led economic stabilization program for a least another year.

In the Congo, the relative stability of the Mobutu government, combined with the favorable effects of the earlier monetary reform and the recent settlement of the copper dispute, have brought about considerable improvement in agricultural and mining production. Our support is essential, however, to maintain the favorable trends in this vast, rich and strategically located country. 

Completion of Current Bilateral Projects 

The shift in emphasis of U.S. assistance to regional and multilateral activity is not something that can be done overnight. While we do not plan to undertake new country projects, either development lending or technical assistance, in the other 25 African countries, we have bilateral "unfinished business" to complete in those countries. For example, there are currently technical assistance projects financed by the U.S. and the host countries running in many of these countries, such as- Agriculture training projects in Dahomey, Niger, Togo, the Malagasy 

Republic, Malawi, Sierra Leone and Zambia;

Livestock improvement projects in Upper Volta, Mali, and Niger; 

Improved soil and water conservation training in the Somali Republic, Togo, Dahomey, and Niger;

Vocational education projects in Gabon, Malawi, Zambia, Sierra Leone, and the Somali Republic;

Public service training in Rwanda; and 

Civil police training in Rwanda, the Somali Republic, Ivory Coast, Chad, and Niger.

In all there are 128 of these technical assistance projects being funded in FY 1967 in 23 countries where new projects are not contemplated. These will be gradually brought to a successful conclusion which will accomplish the intended purposes and thus not waste past investment by the recipients and the 

We also have loan projects in advanced stages of joint planning in some of these areas, such as an important highway in Malawi to connect agricultural areas of the country with the heavily populated southern region and a safe water system for the capital of the Somali Republic. 

It would, we believe, be both economically and diplomatically unsound to break off such projects and plans where they have already gone so far. 

Finally, I should like to emphasize the importance to our new aid approach of the small Special Self-Help Fund in each country. Although it represents only 

1% of our aid to Africa this year, and 12% in FY 1968, it serves a unique purpose. 

With a ceiling of no more than $200,000 per country-and that amount will only be used in countries where other bilateral activities will be coming to an end-it will provide visible, quickly available and simply administered U.S. assistance to small-scale, locally-sponsored development activities, particularly those with tangible, popular involvement, as in village and community volunteer construction or improvement projects. Many of these also involve U.S. Peace Corps volunteers. 

The unique value of this Fund has been well proven and attested by our experience with it over the last two years in such projects as- Machinery and tools for a fishing boat building cooperative in Dahomey; 

Materials for an irrigation system built by a vegetable farmers' cooperative in Gabon;

Equipment for a university soil conservation and reforestation training camp in the Malagasy Republic; and

1967 

Construction materials to complete a library in the Somali Republic, with volunteer labor under Peace Corps direction.

Mr. Chairman, I have undertaken to describe and explain the reasons for, as well as some of the effects of, our recent A.I.D. policy changes for Africa. 

We believe they will give us better results for the funds expended, will permit us to make a more definite and incisive impact on the pace and direction of African economic development, and will thus advance both Africa's growth and U.S. foreign policy interests on that continent.
