A more prosperous Africa should help make a more stable Africa and help achieve a reduction in the tensions and frictions which may threaten world peace.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH PALMER 2D, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. PALMER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I am glad to outline the situation in Africa and make some observations about U.S. assistance programs in Africa. 

I think this is a particularly opportune time to do this because of the ferment which has been taking place in the continent and the implications therefore for our policy objectives. 

I would like to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, by way of background about Africa's dimension on the world scene. As we all know, it is more than three times the size of the United States. It is a very strategic area. Its air and sea space can be friendly or hostile. In the comparatively hospitable climate that now exists in our relationships there we maintain space-tracking stations, communications, civil and military air rights and enjoy generally favorable relations. 

Africa is also a major source of vital raw materials and minerals in the free world. The free world gets about 25 percent of its copper supplies from Africa, about 70 percent of its cobalt, 77 percent of gold, 98 percent of natural diamonds, 26 percent of manganese.

The continent also has great reserves of petroleum, waterpower, iron ore, bauxite and other resources. 

The level of U.S. investment in Africa, private investment, is rising. 

It now totals about $2 billion. This is direct investment only, which represents a sevenfold increase in the last 15 years. About two-thirds of the total is in the newly independent countries of Africa where its rapid growth continues. Our exports to Africa totaled $1.3 billion in 

1966, with 60 percent of this amount being to the newly independent countries. 

The continent has over 300 million people, most of whom have gained independence only in the last 10 years. There are now 39 independent African States, where prior to 1951 there were only four. 

The emergence in Africa of so many States, Mr. Chairman, some small in population and size and inheriting boundaries that are neither logical nor economic, has far-reaching implications for the development of the continent.

I shall say a few more words about this later on. I think we should also realize that most people in Africa live in traditional and tribal societies, relatively untouched by modern life. The average per capita 

GNP is still about $114 a year, which is a poverty level. The Africans do aspire to improve their lot and to make the dignity of their new independence meaningful in terms of decent living standards and economic progress. This drive for progress is a major force in the continent. When progress is slow, instability is bound to result.

425 The 300 million Africans and their nations have an important relationship to U.S. interests and to those of the free world. Of major significance is the relationship of African events to our foreign policy objectives, particularly as they relate to our efforts to build a peaceful and prosperous world system in which nations can feel secure in their independence and cooperate with one another for the greater good. 

Our aid provides an added measure of assurance to Africans that progress is possible in such a free world context. This is consonant with our own experience and is a logical extension of our commitment to self-determination by giving concrete evidence of our desire to see free nations succeed in improving the well-being of their citizens. 

By sharing with Africans their aspirations for progress and by helping to make this possible by aid, we convert our principles into reality. 

As a result, common interests and mutual understanding are generated. African governments have confidence that a working relationship with us is mutually beneficial and that progress is possible in association with the free world.

But we are not buying support any more than the Africans are selling it. What we are showing is that in an interrelated world we have concern for their aspirations just as we hope they will understand our objectives. In my opinion, the 7 percent of our aid appropriation that goes to Africa-less than $200 million-is of fundamental importance to U.S. policy interests on that continent. 

Instability in Africa in the last few years, Mr. Chairman, has obviously had an adverse effect on development. We are all familiar with the various manifestations of it, both present and potential. 

First of all the tribal and regional differences which threaten national cohesion. Second, arbitrary boundaries inherited from colonial times are at variance with ethnic and economic considerations. Third, a tendency in some countries toward arbitrary rule and coercive measures which muffle dissent and breed discontent, and fourth, nonacceptance of government by consent of the governed and of human equality in some parts of the continent. 

In the first decade of independence, the new nations of Africa are still experiencing the exciting-but sometimes painful-process of trial and error in building institutions and societies that reflect their own aspirations. Educational levels and skills are still sadly deficientfor example, literacy in some countries is only 5 percent. The widespread poverty is illustrated by per capita incomes averaging about 30 cents a day. There is high mortality from disease, while dietary deficiency is endemic in many areas. 

Perhaps most important in the flux which characterizes Africa today is the imbalance between aspirations and progress. Instability is bred out of man's dissatisfaction with his situation and with his prospects. Conversely, the conviction that a better life is possible, as evidenced by some demonstrated progress, restrains man's tendency to translate despair into violent expression. In this context, U.S. aid is especially significant because it provides, along with other assistance, the means for Africans to channel their energies toward meaningful progress.

Instability in Africa must be viewed in the perspective of profound historic change and of nations seeking to lift themselves from traditional, poverty-stricken societies to modern states with adequate standards of living-a truly formidable task.

1967 

Clearly, it is too much in these circumstances to expect Africa in a few years to achieve advanced forms of political democracy. On the contrary, the short-term outlook is realistically one of further instability in the search for valid and enduring political institutions. 

I am also convinced that we can be optimistic that political systems will develop in Africa that will have wide participation. I think the 

Africans look forward to the day when there will be conditions of stability and respect for constiutional government. I think that the problems of Nigeria in the last year or so illustrate many of the difficulties that affect much of Africa. The conflict between sectional and national interests is most serious in this country where recent eruptions of tribal and regional tensions are putting national unity and great economic potential to the test. 

We are all familiar with the military coup that took place in 1966, headed by General Ironsi of eastern Nigeria. Resentment in the north over what was considered to be an eastern domination resulted in a second coup last July and severe outbreaks of tribal violence. 

This in turn caused many deaths and a hardening of regional antagonisms. Talks among the leaders of the various regions have been held, but differences persist. The future constitutional structure of the country is far from clear. These are problems that the Nigerians themselves must solve. We hope that the cohesion of the country will be maintained in order that it may continue to realize its great potential in Africa and in the world.

In the Congo, which has been plagued since independence by revolts and disorder and unrest in the countryside, the coup d'etat which resulted in the present Government under President Mobutu has brought greater unity and order. The 1964-65 revolt has been all but liquidated. The fiat of the Central Government increasingly extends to the Provinces, and cooperative relations have been established with most of the country's neighbors. 

In Ghana, the downfall of Nkrumah was brought about by widespread popular discontent with his personal rule and with the ruinous economic policies of his regime. The new military government, which has greatly improved relations with the free world, has also been making considerable progress by following sound measures to return the country to a solid economic footing. It is apparent, however, from the events of the past few days, that the security of the state is not yet fully assured.

In several other countries, Dahomey, the Central African Republic, Sierra Leone, Togo, and Upper Volta, coups have occurred. Yet the new governments face essentially the same problems as their predecessors-imposed by limited economic resources and development possibilities. 

I would like to say a word on communism. Communism in Africa has had to deal with Africa's determination to be independent and to resist substituting a new colonialism for the old. This general dedication to an independent and nonalined posture has limited Communist penetration and in many cases explains Communist setbacks. For this and other reasons, the Red Chinese have been repulsed in Ghana, Burundi, the Central African Republic, and Dahomey. 

The Soviet Union has also had its trials with African insistence on true independence and appears to have revised its tactics-if not its strategy at least to some extent.

427 The poverty of Africa and frustrated aspirations for economic progress have provided openings for Communist probings, but these have been minimized by U.S. and other free world policies and measures which provide the nations of Africa with a reasonable assurance for progress in freedom. As long as these nations can look forward to such progress, the forces will be diminished that seek to compromise independence.

The problems of southern Africa are potentially dangerous also to stability in this region and in other parts of Africa. They are also subject to Communist exploitation. The United States is inevitably concerned in these problems because they affect basic elements of our own beliefs and our position as a responsible member of the U.N.; that is, self determination, majority rule, government by consent of the governed, and equal rights for all. Because of differing situations, the degree and manner in which we seek to encourage progress toward these goals have naturally varied. 

Throughout we have sought to make our position on these principles clear at home, in Africa, and the rest of the world. In so doing, we have sought to play our part in endeavoring to encourage peaceful resolution of the problems in the area which are of such demonstrated concern to the international community. 

I would like to turn now from political events and discuss the economic development of the continent and how our economic assistance program relates to development. 

Foremost in our convictions concerning development is that with all the good will and economic assistance from the rest of the world, a nation's progress will, in the last analysis, depend primarily on its own efforts. Thus, it may be said that the mainsprings for economic progress must be generated within Africa. Therefore, emphasis on self-help is a prime focus of our assistance program. One outstanding example of African self-help has been the creation of the African Development Bank, where 29 nations have already subscribed $40 million of hard-earned capital for the Bank, which is run entirely by Africans. President Johnson has proposed sympathetic consideration of a U.S. contribution to a special fund of the Bank. 

Another is regional cooperation for joint planning and building_of projects, such as multinational airlines, which conserve resources by eliminating duplication and costs of expensive national airlines. 

Again, countries such as Tunisia and Rwanda have cooperated very closely with the IMF to realize sound policies to stabilize their currencies and economies-policies that have required belt tightening. 

African encouragement to private enterprise and investment, another important aspect of self-help, has been widespread. Africans themselves would prefer to rely more heavily on improvements in trade and private investment than on government-to-government aid, which is not a panacea, although at this stage of development is essential.

Indigenous and foreign private enterprise and investment are major keys to development which U.S. programs seek to stimulate in Africa. 

U.S. investment guarantee agreements have been signed with 31 

African nations and other agreements are being negotiated. 

We are all aware of the fact that several states in Africa have nationalized part of their foreign investment. In large degree, this has

1967 

resulted from frustration with lack of progress, the slow pace of external investment, disappointment over the volume of aid as well as low prices for exports. However, far from spurring the economy, these measures have usually had the opposite effect, by inhibiting the flow of needed private capital. 

It should be emphasized, however, that while nationalization and state ownership have occurred in some African countries, in most of them foreign investment and enterprise have been encouraged and protected. Thus, in most of Africa, U.S. businessmen have found a propitious atmosphere for mutually advantageous investment. 

While many difficulties prevail in the development of Africa, encouraging progress can be also reported. As an example, the Volta 

Dam, a major power complex, is now generating electricity and will provide Ghana and perhaps nearby countries with electric power, including power for the American privately built aluminum smelter, which has just reached the production phase. 

I have summarized other examples in my statement and I think at this point I would like to pass over and say a few words on military assistance.

First, I would like to emphasize our concern about certain areas of tension in Africa, particularly in the Maghreb and the horn of Africa where relatively large amounts of military materiel continue to be introduced by the Soviet Union. Other countries in these areas have been concerned by this influx of arms and have felt compelled to increase their own defenses.

The dangers of these tensions and incipient arms races are recognized, as well as the wasteful diversion of resources and energies needed for development. Solutions to the political problems that contribute to these situations are the responsibilities of the nations of Africa. It is a basic tenet of our policy to encourage constructive 

African initiatives to alleviate these tensions and to limit arms. 

In the meantime, we have provided limited assistance to certain countries to support a reasonable level of security for purely defensive purposes. While we are very much aware that military programs may divert resources from essential development, we also know that internal security and reasonable assurance against external aggression are vital to creating the conditions for economic growth. 

These factors are taken into careful consideration in determining our programs. Arms which are excessive to a country's legitimate needs or its financial capacity have not and will not be provided. In this connection our programs emphasize internal security and civic action requirements.

Thus, military assistance to Africa is provided on a limited basis, the total amount requested for fiscal year 1968 being $31.2 million. 

Six countries would receive grants of materiel contrasted with eight in 1967 and nine in 1966. (Discussion off the record.)

Mr. PALMER. In the past year we have sought to strengthen our aid program to make its contribution greater to African development. 

Mr. Kleine will provide the details of this program, but it may be appropriate for me to make a few general observations by way of background.

In May 1966 the President directed that a reassessment of U.S. aid policies in Africa be undertaken with the object of achieving a more

429 effective impact of our assistance on African development. As a result, policies and programs have been reformulated. 

Our assessment recognized that in general the development of Africa's potential will be long term, difficult, and necessarily gradual. 

The fullest possible coordination will be required with other countries which provide much greater assistance, as well as with international organizations, and with African countries and organizations. 

The need for coordination has already resulted in an initiative by us and other donors to encourage the International Bank for Recon struction and Development, together with the African Development 

Bank, the Economic Commission for Africa, and the United Nations development program to take a leadership role in the development of Africa's infrastructure, especially in power, transport, and communications.

The reexamination has also led to a prime emphasis on encouragement to regional cooperation. As the President has said: 

Resources know no national boundaries. Rivers flow through many countries, transportation and communication networks serve different peoples, sources of electric power must be shared by neighbors. Economic advance in every part of the world has required joint enterprises to develop shared sources of wealth. 

Africans themselves are increasingly coming to recognize that their small markets, meager financial resources, and artificial boundaries require a common effort to benefit from economies of scale by building factories, communications, power, and other facilities on a multinational basis.

With the benefits of economic cooperation apparent, the current AID policy will support regional development, institutions, and projects. This is also in accord with the interest of the Congress in encouraging regional cooperation in Africa, as expressed in section 206 of the 

Foreign Assistance Act. 

In addition to a policy of encouraging regional and subregional economic development and institutions, we intend to give greater stress to multidonor cooperation by encouraging and participating in projects with mixed financing that make a significant impact on 

African economies.

As in the past, the major part of aid will continue to be devoted, in the context of multidonor coordination, to certain countries where prospects are good for development and where alternative sources of aid are limited. Generally, we plan to provide most U.S. assistance where it can be most effective in development and also in some cases where exceptional situations prevail. The list of countries receiving bilateral aid is not immutable and can be altered with new conditions as need and development prospects change. 

In most countries, bilateral programs will give way to multinational and multidonor projects as present projects are carried to completion. 

This does not in any sense imply any diminution in the need for U.S. aid to Africa, but rather greater effectiveness in its application. 

We hope to make the transition as smoothly as possible, thereby demonstrating our continued interest and concern for helping to meet Africa's development needs. The continuation of the special self-help fund will be especially important in demonstrating this interest. This fund has been and should continue as a prime means of bringing small but high-impact projects into being in each of these countries with a

1967 

minimum of delay and red tape and maximum encouragement to the concept of self-help. 

May I emphasize that the reformulation of our African aid policy will result in a substantial shift away from bilateral programs and that the pace for accomplishing the shift must be orderly. In these circumstances, quantitative restrictions on the number of countries that are to receive bilateral aid appear unnecessary and could hamper an orderly transition. The President should be free to determine, in the light of U.S. interests, the countries in which it is necessary that funds be expended under standards laid down by the Congress. 

Therefore, I hope that the Congress will sustain our request to delete the legislative limitations on the number of countries to which particular categories of aid may be provided. 

As a result of the new points of emphasis, we believe that U.S. assistance will be more effective in contributing to Africa's development. We particularly hope that African leaders will find it possible to step up the initiatives they have already taken to increase regional cooperation, self-help, and private enterprise and that progress will be accelerated as a result of greater coordination of U.S. and other free world assistance.

On these pillars of regionalism, private investment, self-help, and and multilateralism, we seek to create a stronger program which will be responsive to Africa's aspirations to realize the full potential of this great continent for the benefit of its own people and of the rest of the world.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Kleine. 

STATEMENT OF HERMAN KLEINE, ACTING ASSISTANT ADMINIS- TRATOR, BUREAU FOR AFRICA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. KLEINE. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I appreciate the opportunity of presenting AID's fiscal 1968 proposal for Africa. The proposal reflects the President's statement in his foreign aid message of February in which he said:

We anticipate a shift in emphasis in our aid policy in Africa, to concentrate our help increasingly on regional and multinational projects. 

These changes do not significantly affect the amounts of assistance that we are seeking. Indeed, the amount of assistance being sought for fiscal 1968 is $195 million, which is roughly what we anticipate will be obligated in this fiscal year. The changes are basically in methods and channels of aid administration. 

The principal elements of this policy are the following: 

One, multilateral coordination. In this we are seeking greater agreement among the donor nations and institutions and the recipients concerned on requirements, plans, priorities, and self-help measures for development assistance. We have encouraged the World Bank and IMF to take leadership in consultative groups and other arrangements on particular countries such as Tunisia and Ghana and with regard to certain economic sectors, such as transportation and power. 

Second, support for the regional institutions and regional and multidonor projects. We intend to use regional channels and methods for providing aid wherever there is a practical prospect of real mutual

431 benefit to two or more cooperating African countries. This applies to some extent to all of Africa receiving aid assistance but especially to the smaller countries with more meager resources. Therefore, we will shift to regional projects and assistance through regional institutions as our principal means of development assistance to these countries. 

About one-fifth of the fiscal year 1968 program is intended for these kinds of activities. In appropriate circumstances we plan too to participate in multidonor financing of major capital projects. 

Third, development emphasis countries. AID will continue as in the past to devote the largest portion of its resources to certain countries either singly or as a region, where there is a need for such assistance and where a combination of resources, both human and natural, and the determination to develop them themselves justify our participating as a full and active partner in an organized multilateral effort. 

There are currently 10 countries including three as a region, where we plan to continue substantially bilateral aid activities within such a multilateral program framework. But the list could change, as Mr. 

Palmer indicated, as countries "graduate," or run into problems which may impede their development promise, or qualify to be added. 

The list of 10 shown in the congressional presentation materials are composed of the following: Tunisia, Morocco, Sudan, Ethiopia, Liberia, Nigeria, Ghana, and three East African countries, Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania.

Four, the completion of current bilateral projects. AID currently is financing 128 on-going technical assistance projects in various stages of completion in countries other than the 10 development emphasis ones. These and certain loan projects which are in advanced stages of joint planning will be carried out to completion. 

The fifth, as Mr. Palmer mentioned, is the special self-help fund. 

Even after U.S. bilateral aid to many of these countries has concluded and regional projects are operative, the need will remain we feel for modest U.S. support for purely local small, self-help development activities. These are the sort of low cost but high return projects which this committee stated last year was "one of the most useful and productive activities in our AID program." For this purpose 

AID plans to continue to provide a small limited-purpose, self-help fund in each African country, which will not go above $200,000 per year.

The effect of this changed policy is that for fiscal 1968 approximately 20 percent of the AID program will go to regional and multidonor activities. This figure should increase rapidly in the following years. About 60 percent will go to countries which we have designated as development emphasis countries. About 20 percent to the completion of bilateral projects in other countries. 

This figure we anticipate will decline in subsequent years. Also for fiscal 1968 we are reducing the number of African countries with bilateral aid programs exclusive of the self-help fund. The numbers will be reduced from 34 in this fiscal year to 29, of which those scheduled to receive loans will drop from 19 scheduled in this fiscal year to 14 in fiscal 1968. By fiscal 1969 we estimate-it can be only an estimatethat the number of country programs will decline to 24 of which only the 10 development emphasis countries will receive both bilateral technical assistance and development loans. After fiscal 1969 we

1967 

expect to have bilateral technical assistance projects in 15 countries, the 10 development emphasis countries, and five other countries where existing projects will be continuing toward completion. 

The other countries where new bilateral projects will not be undertaken will of course continue to benefit from regional and multidonor projects. 

How did we arrive at these policy and program changes? The process began last May when President Johnson called for a review of our development policies and programs in Africa and designated Ambassador Korry, U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia, to undertake the review. 

This was done during last summer. 

The main themes of the Korry report are: 

African development will be a long-term, difficult and necessarily gradual effort, requiring the fullest possible coordination and unity of effort and purpose on the part of the United States, the other countries now providing much larger amounts of economic aid to Africa, international organizations, the African countries and their own Áfrican regional organizations. 

The coordination could best be led by an international organization: the World Bank is particularly well equipped to fill this role, especially in the fields of transportation, power and communications. 

The United States should concentrate its own bilateral development support efforts on a country basis in those African countries whose development prospects are good and where U.S. aid can be most effective. 

The United States should continue development assistance to other areas of Africa but primarily by assisting regional and multinational rather than strictly national development efforts and programs. 

The substantive emphasis of U.S. developmental aid should be on agriculture and rural development, education, health and population, the private sector and the infrastructure fields of transportation, power and communications.

Specific procedural improvements are needed to achieve more effective use of both U.S. capital and technical assistance funds. 

The amount of U.S. aid to Africa need not change sharply but can and should increase gradually as the development of African institutions and the application of the report's other recommendations provide growing opportunities for more effective use of U.S. aid. 

In setting forth the AID program for Africa for next year we have taken full account of the Korry report recommendations, outlined on pages 214-215 of the summary presentation, as well as our experience in Africa over the past few years; the congressional limitations on the number of country programs; congressional encouragement to engage in regional projects; the large role of other countries in supplying aid to Africa; and the consequent desirability of much greater coordination. I have already indicated that our plans call for continued reduction in the numbers of bilateral aid programs. We feel that the formal numerical restrictions in the Foreign Assistance Act should not be retained.

I should now like to speak a little more about each of the principal elements of the changed AID policy for Africa, and about some of the programs we are planning for the coming fiscal year. 

There are certain African countries which are in themselves large enough units for development emphasis. They have the combination

433 of size, population, and resources sufficient to give them a good prospect of economic development in a reasonable time, so that they will then be able to continue their growth without aid, and they have demonstrated their determination to develop. 

One example is Tunisia. Notwithstanding Tunisia's difficulties in making the transition from a dependent protectorate economy to a competitive, independent one, the loss of much preferential access to the French market, a critical balance-of-payments situation and the need for a basic reorientation of its agricultural production, the Tunisian economy averaged a 5%½ percent growth rate from 1962 to the present. It is taking the self-help steps which have encouraged the donors to contribute to its development. 

It is encouraging an attractive climate for private investment and is also taking systematic steps in reducing its population growth rate. 

Therefore Tunisia is one of the countries where several donors in addition to the United States are providing substantial assistance. 

The World Bank chairs a consultative group of these donors, takes an active role in diagnosing Tunisia's problems, recommending needed actions and joining in supplying needed funds. The other donors are: 

Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, West Germany, Italy, Kuwait, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United 

Kingdom, as well as the International Monetary Fund.

Consultative groups exist or are planned for several other countries. 

The IMF chairs a group for Ghana in an arrangement in which there is participation of a number of other donors. Elsewhere, in other development emphasis countries, we look forward to a greater role for the World Bank and the IMF. Ethiopia has asked the IBRD for help with its next development plan; and the IMF is already playing a larger role in Liberian stabilization efforts. 

In all of these instances, our approach is to obtain a multilateral effect by having an impartial international organization assume a leadership role in the sensitive functions of obtaining agreement on economic policies, development priorities and the aid recipient's economic performance requirements.

These will set the basis for our development assistance, and encourage even greater participation by other donors. In these cases, I wish to emphasize that the World Bank's leadership and services will not mean any less control or responsibility on our part of the expenditure of U.S. funds.

I will not take the time of the committee to repeat what is contained in my statement on examples of what we have in mind for several other development emphasis countries. 

I should state with regard to aid to Nigeria that its purpose is to help realize its long run development potential which remains great, particularly if the Nigerians are successful in resolving their current problems in a manner which maintains the cohesion of the country. 

The situation in Nigeria remains under continual review and the program will be revised if necessary to meet changed conditions. 

There are some broader aspects of multilateral coordination, Mr. 

Chairman, for country development programs are not the only setting in which multilateral coordination under international agency leadership can speed development and enhance the usefulness of our own development funds.

1967 

In the major economic sectors of transportation, power, and communications with their great cost and broad continent-wide and subregional significance, there is the same need for coordinated use of all external aid funds and agreement among donors and with African countries and organizations on policies and priorities. 

I am happy to report that representatives of the IBRD, the African Development Bank, the U.N. Economic Commission for Africa, and the U.Ñ. development program have recently met to plan the means for coordination of development efforts of an Africa-wide basis in these economic sectors. At the appropriate time, the United States and other bilateral donors look forward to participating in the work of this group of organizations. 

Another main element of the changed AID policy for Africa is our intention to provide aid to a number of countries principally through regional institutions and projects rather than by our previous bilateral methods. Our purpose is to encourage regional solutions to development problems, because in many areas this should yield better and faster development progress through the more efficient use of resources, and is in accord with the known intentions and desires of many Africans.

First of all, we plan to assist African regional institutions, such as the African Development Bank, the Scientific, Technical and Research 

Commission of the Organization for African Unity, the U.N. Economic 

Commission for Africa and its subregional economic communities, and other African organizations of more limited geographic or technical scope. 

We shall offer technical assistance to help strengthen them in their own efforts.

In the case of the African Development Bank, President Johnson has said that we will seek appropriate means of responding to its recent request to the United States and other non-African nationsfor participation in a special fund, which would be used by the ADB primarily for regional projects and for help to the poorer African countries.

We also intend to finance, directly, certain regional capital and technical assistance projects undertaken jointly by two or more African countries for their mutual benefit. The largest single regional project is the 5-year campaign to eradicate smallpox and control measles in 19 west and central African countries, by giving over 100 million smallpox vaccinations to people of all ages and 25 million measles injections to children of ages 1 to 6. AID will provide $11.7 million in fiscal year 1968, the second year of this program, to finance the services of the U.S. Public Health Service, train Africans and provide vaccines. The African nations, two African regional health organizations and the World Health Organization are also sharing in the cost and operation of this project. 

My statement includes other examples of regional projects that we have underway or planned, but I will spare the time of the committee and not read them at this time.

AID will also participate with other donors and international organizations in major capital projects, whether in individual countries or groups of countries. One such project under consideration is the Trans-Cameroon railroad construction in which we would be cooperating with France and the European Economic Community.

435 Another such project which is under consideration involves joint support under IBRD leadership with several European countries, the EEC, and several private banks for the construction of an iron ore railway from the interior of Gabon to the port of Libreville. 

AID also is encouraging the creation of a U.S. private investment corporation, to be wholly owned by private U.S. financial institutions, but to be assisted initially by a seed-capital loan from AID. This would provide loans to enterprises in Africa which present worthwhile private investment opportunities. 

Our estimate of $14 million in supporting assistance type of aid for fiscal year 1968 is a decline from $24 million in fiscal year 1966 and $19 million in fiscal year 1967, and represents only 7 percent of the aid to Africa. The downward trend in supporting assistance represented by this estimate is heartening. It represents our best estimate as of now-although other emergency situations might arise during the year which would require the use of supporting assistance or the contingency fund. Most of the $14 million is planned for use in the 

Congo, where we anticipate the need to support the IMF-led economic stabilization program for at least another In the Congo, the relative stability of the Mobutu government, combined with the favorable effects of the earlier monetary reform and the recent settlement of the copper dispute, have brought about considerable improvement in agricultural and mining production. 

Our support is essential, however, to maintain the favorable trends in this vast, rich, and strategically located country. 

We have already mentioned, Mr. Chairman, our intention to complete current bilateral projects. We feel that there is unfinished business of a bilateral nature in a number of African countries and we would anticipate expediting these activities to a reasonable point of conclusion. There are, as I mentioned, some 128 of these projects being funded in this fiscal year for these countries. 

We also have a few loan projects in advanced stages of joint planning in some of these areas, such as an important highway in Malawi to connect agricultural areas of the country with the heavily populated southern region and a safe water system for the capital of the Somali 

Republic. 

It would, we believe, be both economically and diplomatically unsound to break off such projects and plans where they have already gone so far.

Finally, I should like to emphasize the importance to our new aid approach of the small special self-help fund in each country. 

Although it represents only 1 percent of our aid to Africa this year, and 12 percent in fiscal year 1968, it serves a unique purpose. 

Mr. Chairman, I have undertaken to describe briefly and explain the reasons for, as well as some of the effects of, our recent AID policy changes for Africa. We believe they will give us better results for the funds expended, will permit us to make a more definite and incisive impact on the pace and direction of African economic development, and will thus advance both Africa's growth and U.S. foreign policy interest on that continent.

Mr. PALMER. Mrs. Bolton, I would like to say to you that in developing this we did try very hard, as Mr. Kleine has indicated, to take into account what we had understood the sense of Congress to be, as expressed in section 206 of the Foreign Assistance Act and the legislative history of the House report.

Third, there is a resolution jointly sponsored by the United States and Canada and Italy, which provides for consultations with representative elements of South-West Africa, looking toward an eventual creation of what is called in the resolution a nucleus of self-government, but which is gradualist in its approach to the problem and does not contemplate any setting up of an administration or full measures to enforce it at the present time.

Mr. SELDEN.  

Mr. Secretary, what is official U.S. policy at this time toward the present Government of Rhodesia?

Mr. PALMER. We do not, Mr. Congressman, recognize the present 

Government of Southern Rhodesia. We continue to regard Southern 

Rhodesia as the sovereign responsibility of the United Kingdom. We, along with most members of the United Nations, do favor the principles and programs that actually have been initiated to try to encourage the Government of Rhodesia by peaceful means to move toward majority rule within the country. We have cooperated and intend to continue to cooperate with the United Nations in the program of mandatory sanctions that was initiated last December. 

Mr. SELDEN. On what reasoning did we base the imposition of sanctions against Rhodesia?

Mr. PALMER. The considerations were that we regard this as an illegal rebellion. We regard the territory as one in which the United 

Kingdom continues to have responsibility and also a responsibility of the United Nations under article 73 of the charter with respect to non-self-governing territories. We regarded this as being a matter within the competence of the United Nations because of the fact that the United Kingdom Government, which is responsible for the territory, asked for the assistance of the United Nations in ending the rebellion there.

1967 

Mr. SELDEN. Do we consider this rebellion any more illegal than our own rebellion against Great Britain? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, we do.

Mr. SELDEN. In what way? 

Mr. PALMER. Let me address myself both to the legalities of it, and to the moral issues of it. It has been the considered view of the international community, expressed on many occasions, that the perpetuation of minority rule in Southern Rhodesia was not in accordance with the established principles of the United Nations. 

There was a finding by the Security Council at the time that mandatory sanctions were imposed that the continuation of this situation did constitute a threat to the peace. 

Many people have mentioned article 2(7) of the United Nations Charter, the so-called domestic jurisdiction clause of the charter, as being in opposition to or as precluding the type of actions that have been taken.

The fact is, that Southern Rhodesia is not a state. It has not been recognized by anybody as a state.

Second, the situation is not domestic, since it involves international responsibilities of the United Kingdom. 

Third, the Security Council action is not intervention since it took place at the request of the legitimate sovereign. 

Fourth, that clause, in any event, makes an exception for measures-enforcement measures-such as economic sanctions that are decided upon by that body. 

Mr. SELDEN. I gather from what you have said, then, that the international community has gone on record as against minority rule? 

By the "international community," do you mean the United Nations? 

Mr. PALMER. Did I mean- 

Mr. SELDEN. By "the international community" are you referring to the United Nations? 

Mr. PALMER. What I intended to say, Mr. Congressman, was that the United Nations in this instance felt that the perpetuation of minority rule in Southern Rhodesia could lead to a threat to the peace in that area. 

Mr. SELDEN. You said, "in this instance." The U.N. is opposed to minority rule. Is it only in this instance?

Mr. PALMER. There are different kinds of minority rule. I think anyone would have to say that it is very difficult to prove in a great many cases that a particular regime may fit the definition of majority rule.

I think what makes this situation unusual and unique is that this is perpetuated on a basis of race. 

Mr. SELDEN. Wouldn't you say, though, Mr. Secretary, that there are dozens of nations in the United Nations who do not have majority rule? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, sir. There are. But I don't know of many other instances where it is being perpetuated on the basis of race. 

Mr. SELDEN. Is minority rule bad only when it is on race?

Mr. PALMER. We would hope that the entire world would move toward a situation where all citizens played an effective part in the conduct of their own Mr. SELDEN. Why are we taking this position only on the basis of race, rather than in all instances where there is minority rule?

445 Mr. PALMER. Because, as I said, of the unique combination of factors that are inherent in this case, because of the fact that the U.N. does have a responsibility here that arises under Britain's responsibilities under article 73, because of the fact that Britain has brought the case to the United Nations.

I think we can't correct every situation; but there are a combination of circumstances here involving international responsibility that do give a basis for action in this case.

Mr. SELDEN. Mr. Morse. 

Mr. MORSE. Mr. Secretary, Mr. Kleine, last year upon motion of

Mr. Fraser, this committee incorporated what is now title IX, section 

281, into the act. I shall quote the language of the title: 

Section 281: 

In carrying out programs authorized in this chapter, emphasis shall be placed on assuring maximum participation in the task of economic development on the part of the people of the developing countries through the encouragement of democratic private and local governmental institutions. 

This title was not intended to require a recipient nation to adopt any particular form of government or to establish any particular political institutions. It is predicated on the thesis that if the people themselves are involved and engaged in the process of development, the process will be more effective and more lasting. I would appreciate your advice as to what has been done within your area of geographic responsibility as to the implementation of title IX. 

Mr. KLEINE. Mr. Congressman, since the enactment of this provision there has been considerable study and analysis of its implications and certainly great recognition as to its importance in the overall programing of U.S. assistance. There has been a central agency effort in which each of the regional bureaus, including the Africa Bureau, has participated. These intra-agency activities and studies are continuing and we anticipate that this next month there will be a comprehensive report submitted to the Congress on what the Agency has done and what it is contemplating.

The results of the study and consideration thus far seem to lead in certain directions, such as that there are no wholesale prescriptions that can be applied across the board, that the approach should necessarily and desirably be on a country-by-country basis. 

Also, that this is not an activity that should be carried out by imposition on the recipient Government, but in cooperation with the recipient Government; that there should be a joint recognition if at

449 all possible of the nature of the problem, identification of economic and social objectives; that there should not be special programs per se, but that this ingredient should be considered in the programing process.

Indeed, for many years when programs for individual countries have been developed, they have been developed within the overall context of the country team assessment of what are the basic problems in each country.

To be more specific, in Liberia it has been well recognized that it is important to engage the rural population more in the whole process of development. We have identified this need. We have attempted to work in the rural area in bringing more education, better administration to these people. 

A similar situation exists in Sierra Leone. It is on a case-by-case basis. 

We have not as yet reached the formula for each of these situations. 

We are planning to identify a few countries where we might make a more intensive pilot effort, an examination, bringing in experts from the outside who can bring something to this very sensitive problem, and which then could provide a more firm basis on which we can include this ingredient more intensively in our program. 

That is briefly where we now stand. 

Mr. MORSE. It is very helpful. 

What direction have you received from the Administrator as to the implementation of title IX? 

Mr. KLEINE. The Agency under the Administrator is utilizing our program coordination office to spearhead this since it is an agencywide effort. With this group each of the bureaus is associated, so we are moving step-by-step together. 

Mr. MORSE. What communication has gone from your office to the mission directors with reference to title IX? 

Mr. KLEINE. There have been worldwide circular airgrams; the process of educating, so to speak, our people in the field is already underway. We did, Mr. Congressman, have a special study that we had undertaken on Liberia itself just prior to the enactment of the legislation, and we have been using that as part of the background in programing our activities in that country.

 PORT OF MONROVIA 

The title to the installations at the Port of Monrovia passed in 1964 to the Liberian Government under an agreement in which the latter assumed the obligation to pay approximately the $19 million in construction costs. The Monrovia 

Port Management Company, composed of representatives of the Liberian Government and of the major U.S. users of the Port, retained its management responsibilities however at the request of President Tubman. This arrangement continues at present. Thus far the Port Management Company has provided the funds to pay the Liberian Government's annual installments due to the U.S. Government under the 1964 Agreement.

The present rate structure is generally that existing at the time of the transfer of title. However, the Port Management Company is actively considering an increase in the various port charges at the request of the Liberian Government. 

The increased rate structure would permit additional needed upkeep and improvements in the Port's facilities. We understand that the Port Management 

Company's proposals will be presented to President Tubman in the near future.

 STATUS OF LIBERIAN PORT OF BUCHANAN 

1 The port of Buchanan was built by the Liberian American-Swedish Minerals Company (LAMCO) as part of an iron ore mine-railroad-port complex. The 

165 mile railroad and artificial deep water harbor and port facilities were completed in 1963-1964. The total cost of the LAMCO complex was about $217.8 million of which the Export-Import Bank loaned $34.5 million for purchase of 

U.S. goods and services for portions of the mining facilities, railroad and port. 

In 1965 the Export-Import Bank made an additional loan of $23.1 million as part of a $51.4 million program for construction of an iron ore washing plant and a pelletizing plant which will increase productive capacity from 7.5 million to 10 million tons per annum.

Although designed primarily for the shipment of iron ore, the port has two additional quays for handling general cargo. LAMCO presently manages the commercial facilities at Buchanan. The LAMCO railroad is available for the carriage of commodities other than iron ore, but such traffic is presently limited. 

The Government of Liberia and LAMCO recently negotiated agreements with the Government of Guinea which provide for the use of Buchanan and for transportation on the LAMCO railroad of Guinean exports and imports. 

A.I.D. is financing a general economic survey of the area of Liberia southeast of the railroad which connects with the port of Buchanan. This study will consider future development of the area and requirements for roads and ports, particularly for the movement of timber and other commodities. The study will examine the port of Buchanan to determine what role this port and the connecting transportation system can play in the future economic activity of the area.
