We meet in executive session today for a continuation of the hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to further amend the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

Our witnesses this morning are the Honorable Joseph J. Sisco, Assistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs, and Mr. Louis Frechtling, Director, Office of International Administration, Bureau of International Organization Affairs, Department of State.

Mr. Secretary, you have a prepared statement, and you may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH J. SISCO, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS 

Mr. SISCO.  I have a rather lengthy statement which, with your permission, I would like to insert in the record. I merely want to make a few observations and give maximum opportunity to members of the committee to ask whatever questions may interest them. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, your statement will be made a part of the record. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Sisco is as follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH J. SISCO, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS 

Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee, I am pleased to testify in support of the President's request for voluntary contributions to international organizations and programs. 

The Bureau of International Organization Affairs, which I head, is responsible for U.S. contributions to international bodies in which this country is represented. 

As the Committee knows, contributions in the nature of dues are presented as part of the State Department's regular budget. Voluntary contributions authorized under the Foreign Assistance Act are also administered by my Bureau, by delegagation from the Administrator of the Agency for International Development.

The President has recommended new obligational authority just under $141 million for fiscal year 1968, approximately the same as the $140.4 million appropriated for fiscal year 1967. However, it should be noted that the 1967 availability is actually $147.7 million, which includes $7.3 million in carryover funds available to reduce the fiscal year 1967 appropriation request. In effect, then, the program for fiscal year 1968 is $6.7 million less than the present year's estimate. 

The three items showing an increase are our projected contribution to the United Nations Development Fund ($5.0 million), an increase in our special contribution 457

1967 

for Viet Nam ($1.0 million), and the inclusion, for the first time, of a contribution to UN programs for South Africans ($150 thousand). On the other side of the ledger we have six decreases totalling $12.9 million in our contributions to UNICEF, UN Technical and Operational Assistance to the Congo, Indus Basin Develop ment Fund, and the two UN peacekeeping efforts, plus the elimination of the International Secretariat for Volunteer Service from the estimates. The remaining five items are unchanged.

Of the total requested, about 85 percent is for multilateral programs of economic assistance and the remainder is for UN programs to maintain peace and security. 

Aid given through multilateral channels is a significant component of our total effort to assist the less developed nations in building their economies. The channeling of aid through international bodies is very much in the U.S. national interest for it helps share the burden with other developed nations and helps stimulate the incentive of these nations to step up their own aid efforts. It also helps in achieving a larger measure of self-help since the counterpart contributions of countries assisted by UN economic agencies are as high and in some cases higher than under bilateral programs. Our contributions are generally 40 percent of the total contributions to the international programs involved. 

We now have almost twenty years of experience behind us in the area of economic assistance. Today we have a better idea of what development aid can do and what it cannot do, what it can accomplish and what it cannot accomplish. 

We have a firmer knowledge of economic development as a process which, though complex, must be treated in a unified way. It calls for coordinated action on the part of the various bodies such as the UN itself, WHO, FAO, UNESCO, ILO and other technical agencies. Such coordination is increasingly being achieved by the 

UN Development Program. 

We are equally aware that steady economic growth is fundamental to the establishment of the stable political systems which it is in our national interest to foster in the less developed parts of the world. This, in the final analysis, is, of course, the objective which underlies the requests we are making of you today. 

The appropriations we are requesting for U.S. contributions to UN peacekeeping are, in my judgment, equally important to out national interest. These funds help support the costs of the UN Emergency Force in the Middle East and the UN Force in Cyprus. Measured in terms of the return we get in the maintenance of security and stability in those troubled areas, they are funds well spent.

The UN has undertaken some dozen peacekeeping operations in its history. 

All have served the cause of peace and have been consistent with our own foreign policy interests. As a result, we continue to regard UN peacekeeping as an important option in our overall security. Our financial contribution, which constitutes approximately 40 percent of the total cost, is, I believe, a reasonable price to pay to preserve the peace in various trouble spots. The UN Development Program (UNDP) is the major multilateral activity in the field of economic assistance to which the U.S. contributes from Foreign 

Assistance funds. Created two years ago by merger of the Expanded Program of 

Technical Assistance and the Special Fund, the UNDP now has a unified management. The UNDP receives contributions from virtually every country which is a member of the United Nations or of one of its related organizations. With these contributions the UNDP conducts over 3,400 projects in more than 120 underdeveloped countries and territories. These projects are carried out by the specialized agencies of the United Nations and by the UN itself. 

The projects include pre-investment surveys of resources, assessments of their economic potential, and measures to assure the follow-up investment required to realize that potential; centers for advanced education, technical and vocational training, and development planning studies; institutes to carry out developmentoriented research and to apply modern technology; the provision of experts to assist the developing countries in the planning and implementation of programs and projects for their economic and social growth; fellowships for specialized training and work experience abroad; and seminars for the international exchange of development knowledge and techniques. The projects range in cost from a few thousand dollars to several million each, in duration from a few months to five years, and in coverage from demonstration in a single village to a major continental region.

Some measure of the impact of the UNDP since its inception is indicated by the following data:

459 Seventy-seven preinvestment surveys and feasibility studies have been completed, 31 of which have already produced sizeable follow-up investment. Each one dollar spent on these 31 projects has yielded over $40 of investment. 

The total follow-up investment, both from public and private sources, from these 31 projects is $1.6 billion thus far. 

Over 300,000 men and women have been equipped in their own countries, and 36,000 more abroad with technical knowledge, skills and experience essential for increasing national output.

More than 19,000 international experts have served in the low income countries. 

Under the leadership of its administrator, Mr. Paul Hoffman, the program is consistently seeking to direct its limited resources into channels that will have the greatest effect on the building of stronger economies in the less developed countries. 

At its last meeting in January 1967 the Governing Council of the UNDP generally endorsed greater attention to agricultural and rural development. The UNDP is also emphasizing, where appropriate, assistance in family planning, expansion of the tourist industry and mobilization of youth for useful service. 

Taking into account the rising number of specific requests for aid in these areas and the demonstrated willingness of other countries to increase their support of the program, it is proposed that the U.S. increase its pledge for 1968 to $75 million subject, of course, to the 40% matching formula. 

In December, 1966 the UN Children's Fund (UNICEF) celebrated its 20th anniversary. During these two decades UNICEF has done much to help improve the lives of children of the world. Since 1950 when UNICEF shifted from emergency assistance to war-torn Europe and Asia to its program of long-term assistance to developing countries, UNICEF has equipped more than 33,000 health services ranging from simple village dispensaries to modern pediatric wards. These facilities have provided service to over 70 million mothers and children. Through UNICEF activities about 100 million persons around the world have been examined for yaws and 41 million have been treated. About 200 million persons have been protected against tuberculosis through the use of the BCG vaccine. 

More than 210 milk processing plants in 41 countries have been or are presently being equipped by UNICEF. Assistance has also been given to applied nutrition projects in 53 countries to stimulate greater production and use of nutritious foods.

Since the inauguration of UNICEF aid to education and vocational training in 1962, UNICEF has helped equip about 6,600 primary schools, 137 secondary schools, 295 teacher training centers and 289 vocational and prevocational training centers. About one-third of UNICEF's program expenditures are now devoted to the training of local personnel to staff vital programs for children. 

To date UNICEF stipends and fellowships have been used for training almost 165,000 persons in the developing countries for work on various programs benefiting children. An additional 55,000 persons are currently receiving training with 

UNICEF assistance.

The UNICEF Executive Board, at its May 1966 meeting, established a target of $50 million annual income by 1970. The United States supported this target and reiterated its willingness, subject to Congressional approval, to consider an increase in its contribution if other governments increase their contributions so as to maintain a 40 (U.S.)-60 ratio. Achievement of this target would mean substantially increased funds for vocational training, education and nutritional programs, as well as an expansion of maternal and child health services, including family planning, family and child welfare services, and improvements in village water supply and environmental sanitation.

It is proposed that the United States pledge $12 million for calendar year 1968, subject to the limitation that the U.S. share shall not exceed 40 percent of the total contributions of governments.

Compared with the massive AID program and the substantial humanitarian and economic assistance provided by other free-world nations and voluntary agencies, assistance to Viet Nam furnished by the United Nations system of organizations is small in volume. It is nevertheless highly significant: it not only helps to meet essential humanitarian, economic, and social needs but also establishes a United Nations presence in the war-torn country, a link to the family of nations. 

Beyond this, present UN programs help to lay a foundation for greatly expanded assistance in the rehabilitation and economic and social development of Viet Nam once peace has been achieved. For these reasons, the U.S. has recently worked with the Government of Vietnam and several agencies of the UN system to encourage the expansion of UN programs in Viet Nam.

1967 

Results have been encouraging. UN agencies have strengthened their field staffs in Viet Nam: UNICEF has appointed a new Country Representative and a UNDP new Resident Representative has been on board since December. The number of UN system experts in Viet Nam almost doubled in 1966 to 27. There has also been increase in the volume of UN system assistance to Viet Nam. Total expenditures by the UN and its related agencies rose from $729,000 in 1966 to an estimated total of approximately $1,336,000 in 1967. The UN and the specialized agencies provided $208,000 from their regular budgets in 1966, compared with an estimated $359,000 in 1967. UNDP and UNICEF provided $521,000 in 1966 from voluntary contributions, compared with an estimated $977,000 in 1967. 

The programs thus financed include promotion of health services, public health administration, maternal and child health, disease control (leprosy and tuberculosis), mental health and nutrition; social welfare training and services including rehabilitation of war-injured; assistance to orphanages; the provision of experts in such fields as statistics, public finance and administration, labor administration, economic planning, telecommunications, meteorology and civil aviation; programs in animal pathology and provision of animal vaccines; and fellowships for Vietnamese to study in these fields in Viet Nam and abroad. 

The UNDP has also undertaken, with UNESCO as the executing agent, to assist in the establishment of a National Technical Center (approximate total international contribution-$1.5 million) while the U.N. Bureau of Social Affairs is working on a plan of operations for the establishment of a training center for social welfare personnel. 

The UNDP approved this year a Fisheries Development Project including exploratory and experimental fishing in the waters of the South China Sea, to be executed by FAO at a cost of $1.3 million. The Government of Viet Nam requested that the scope of this project be enlarged to be extended from coastal to deep sea fishing to provide a firm foundation for development of a large scale modern fishing industry. The U.S. expects to provide, through a funds-in-trust arrangement with FAO, about $750,000 from fiscal year 1967 funds for the expansion of the project.

The $2 million which we are requesting for fiscal year 1968 would be used for further funds-in-trust arrangements, partly to continue our support to the fisheries project as well as for other UN activities in Viet Nam which the UN agencies alone are not able to finance from their resources. 

Other countries are also interested in the possibilities of expanding UN programs in Viet Nam through funds-in-trust arrangements. The Dutch Government has already committed $1 million to this end. It is our hope that others will follow suit and that as a result UN programs and activities will continue to be expanded.

The Indus Basin Development Fund administered by the World Bank is now in its seventh year. Major contracting was completed in January 1967 and overall construction is generally on or ahead of schedule. The massive program for providing arable land for over 50 million people in Pakistan and India was approximately 75 percent completed as at the end of 1966. 

On the basis of estimates of payments which will be due contractors working on the Indus project, the World Bank plans to call for $25.5 million in U.S. dollar grant contributions during fiscal year 1968. While the actual calls made by the World Bank have varied from initial estimates, such variations do not affect the total amount of the U.S. commitment to the Indus Basin Fund. 

The purpose of the UN program of technical and operational assistance to the Congo (Kinshasa) is to recruit international personnel with the necessary skills and language ability to meet the Congo's critical need for technical advisers and operational experts. Since 1960 the UN program has played an important role in the Congo's survival and its ability to exercise its governmental functions. 

The program provides technical and operational assistance in the fields of agriculture, aviation, public works, public administration, public finance, advisory and public health services, social affairs and community development, telecommunications, meteorology and postal services. The 1968 estimate provides for a total UN program of 287 experts compared with 443 experts in 1967. 

Since independence the Congo has been an arena of instability in Central Africa. U.S. programs are directed towards establishing the Congo as a unified, viable, independent state capable of maintaining political stability, internal security, and a reasonable rate of economic and social development. The UN program of technical and operational assistance contributes to that objective. 

It is proposed that a contribution of $3 million be made in fiscal year 1968 as compared with over $4 million in recent years.

461 The fiscal year 1968 request for the World Food Program, is $2.0 million representing the third and last installment of our second three-year pledge. Taking into account the amounts appropriated for the fiscal years 1966 and 1967, this will meet the full $6 million cash component pledged by Secretary Freeman at a session held in January, 1966. Also pledged was up to $92 million in agricultural commodities and shipping services estimated at $32.0 million to move the commodities to their destinations. The commodity pledge included a 50 percent matching provision and the cash pledge a limitation of 40 percent. Other countries have pledged sufficient cash, $29.8 million as of February 28, 1967, to draw down the full $6.0 million pledged by the United States. The second three-year period which had drawn $215.3 million in pledges from all countries, as of February 28, 1967, as compared to $93.9 million for the first three year period, has as its continuing purpose the utilization of foodstuffs on a multilateral basis to promote economic and social development. 

The operational program of the International Atomic Energy Agency is principally concerned with the orderly promotion and development of the peaceful uses of atomic energy so that the development countries may share in the broad spectrum of benefits afforded by atomic science. The program consists primarily of provision of fellowships for study abroad and of experts and equipment for training in atomic science in the developing countries themselves. The importance that the developing countries place on this program is attested by a resolution sponsored by them and approved at the Agency's 10th General Conference which calls for a review of the Agency's activities "in order to find ways and means to increase its assistance to developing countries." 

The Executive Branch proposes to pledge up to $600,000, with a limitation of 35 percent of total cash contributions, to the Agency's program for 1968. This is a reduction from the 1967 share of 37.5 percent and another step in the continuing reduction in the U.S. share which was 50 percent prior to 1965. In addition, it is proposed to make available fellowships for training in the United States, the services of U.S. experts, and small equipment grants with maximum value of $400,000. 

Thus, a total of $1 million, the same as previous years, is proposed for FY 1968. 

A contribution is proposed to the UN Institute for Training and Research, an organ of the UN designed to train international civil servants as well as diplomats of the devloping countries, and to conduct research on important problems of concern to the UN. $400,000 is requested for contribution to the 1968 regular budget of the Institute, with a limitation of 40 percent on our contribution. In addition, $100,000, without a percentage limitation, is requested to finance Adlai E. Stevenson memorial fellowships administered by the Institute. The total of $500,000 for this purpose is the same amount as provided for 1967. 

The Institute, which came into existence in March 1965 is now operating three programs previously operated by the UN Secretariat-a training program for foreign service officers from newly independent countries, group training programs in techniques and procedures of Technical Assistance, and training programs in development financing. In addition, two new programs were started: a group training program for Deputy Resident Representatives, and a seminar on major problems of UN technical assistance.

On the research side, the Institute is concentrating on programs oriented to UN needs and has given high priority to studies related to the needs of the developing countries and the implications of scientific and technological developments for UN activities, including new social science techniques. 

We are also proposing a contribution of $150,000, to the International Agency for Research on Cancer, which has been established at Lyon, France, under the auspices of the World Health Organization. In addition to the United States, seven other nations (the United Kingdom, Israel, Italy, West Germany, France, Australia and the U.S.S.R.) are supporting an international attack on cancer, at this point primarily through research on the epidemiology of the disease. Each of the members has agreed to contribute $150,000 annually for five years. II 1 The second major category of programs proposed for U.S. support in fiscal year 1968 comprise those designed to maintain peace and promote stability in the Near East.

The UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East 

(UNRWA) is a subsidiary organ of the United Nations, established by the General Assembly in 1949. It has a two-fold task: first, to provide food, health and relief services, and shelter for the refugees; second, to provide education and

1967 

training to refugee children and young adults including general education, vocational and teacher training, and university scholarships. There were, at the end of 1966, 1,330,077 refugees. Of these 859,966 were receiving rations, 250,137 were receiving education in elementary and preparatory schools, 3,585 were receiving vocational or teacher training, and 590 refugees were scholarship recipients.

The United Nations has made repeated efforts to find a way to settle the Palestine refugee problem. These efforts, however, have not succeeded largely because of the unwillingness of the two sides to agree on a solution. UN resolutions have repeatedly affirmed the principle that refugees willing to live at peace with their neighbors should be permitted to return to their homes or be compensated for their properties left behind in Israel. No means of applying this principle has yet been found. Meanwhile, the UNRWA program, by providing for the minimum needs of the refugees, has helped prevent the problem from becoming any worse and, through its education program, has provided a means for the slow but steady rehabilitation of some of the refugees. 

The problem of rectifying the ration rolls so as to assure the most equitable distribution of relief based on need continues to be a major preoccupation of the Commissioner General of UNRWA. The latter has sought ways to make meaningful progress on rectification, which he must accomplish with the cooperation of the host governments concerned, and was able to report some progress last year. 

The United States has continually urged the Commissioner General to make every effort to remove the existing abuses and plans to continue to do so in the future. 

He has given assurance to interested governments, including the United States, that their contributions will not be used to furnish assistance to refugees receiving military training under the auspices of the Palestine Liberation Organization. 

In view of the continuing natural increase of the refugee population and of the rising prices of goods and services purchased by UNRWA, the Executive Branch recommends a contribution of $13.3 million in dollars and U.S. owned foreign currencies for fiscal year 1968, which is at the same level as the fiscal year 1967 contribution. In addition, contributions in agricultural commodities amounting to $8.9 million are proposed for fiscal year 1968, the same level as in recent years.

The Commissioner General has addressed an appeal to all member countries of the UN calling or additional or new contributions to UNRWA, and several governments have expressed a willingness to increase their contributions over previous levels. The United States supports the efforts of the Commissioner 

General to raise funds from additional sources, and it is expected that the U.S. share of total government contributions will gradually decrease. 

The United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF), established during the Suez 

Crisis in 1956, has the mission of maintaining peace and stability along the Armistice Demarcation Line and International Frontier between Israel and the United Arab Republic. As a "buffer" force, it accomplishes a major United 

Nations and United States policy objective of helping to keep the peace between the U.A.R. and Israel. 

The size of the force was reduced by 622 men in 1965-1966, and as of July 

31, 1966 its strength was 3.959. In September 1966 the Secretary General annour.ced his intention to further reduce it to 3,400 provided conditions in the area remained relatively quiet. This reduction was effected by the end of the year. 

In his September report on UNEF the Secretary General stated that "at its present strength (3,959) the force is operating without an effective reserve, and, of course, would have to continue to do so under a further reduction (3,400). 

There is, perhaps, an element of risk in this, but only in the event of some unanticipated emergency. Any significant lowering of this basic figure (3,400), however, would make it impossible for the force to carry on as a peace force with its present functions and responsibilities. It would become, in effect, an elaborate observation operation. This is pointed out because it needs to be made very clear that any action which would result in a reduction of the Force below the basic figure indicated would have the unavoidable result, for all practical purposes, of changing the nature of the operation in a fundamental way." 

The UN General Assembly financed the 1967 costs of UNEF by apportioning $740,000 among the economically less developed members and $13,260,000 among the economically developed members. The apportionments were made to each group in the proportions determined by their regular budget percentage. An additional 25% apportionment was added to each developed member's share to cover reserve requirements in case of a shortfall. The total apportioned for 1967 was $17,315,000. The United States apportionment for calendar year 1967 (U.S.

463 fiscal year 1968) under the General Assembly resolution is $6.3 million, which is about $450,000 less than the previous year. 

Funds available for voluntary contributions are being used this year to meet the United States share of the costs of the UN Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP). 

No estimate for this purpose is shown for the fiscal year 1968 since the UN Security Council mandate continues the force only through June 26, 1967. 

UNFICYP is supported on a voluntary basis by cash contributions from various governments including the Government of Cyprus and by troop contingents provided by governments. The estimated cost of maintaining the force for calendar year 1966 was $19,705,000 of which the United States pledged $8 million. The 

United States pledge was made possible through the reprogramming of funds available under Chapter 3 of the Foreign Assistance Act. The cost estimate for the first half of the calendar year 1967 is $9,675,000 of which the United States pledged $4 million (41.3%) from funds reprogrammed under Chapter 3. If the 

Security Council continues the mandate of the UNFICYP as is likely, we would hope to be able to fund further United States pledges in the fiscal year 1967 and 1968 through reprogramming available funds or from the A.I.D. contingency fund.

III 

Lastly, a voluntary contribution of up to $150,000 to UN programs for South 

Africans is proposed.

In 1964 the UN Security Council authorized the Secretary-General to establish an educational and training program for South Africans who had fled from their country. A pilot program was established in 1965 which was financed by contributions of $247,000 from several countries, including $75,000 from the United States. Under this program, scholarships were granted to 45 South Africans, most of whom are studying in the United Kingdom. The program needs additional funds if it is to meet the needs of young South Africans. 

The UN General Assembly in 1965 established a Trust Fund for South Africa which would provide legal assistance to persons charged under discriminatory and repressive legislation in South Africa, relief for dependents of persons persecuted by the Government of South Africa for acts arising from opposition to the policies of apartheid, education of prisoners, their children and other dependents, and relief for refugees from South Africa. Eleven nations have already pledged about $200,000 to the Trust Fund. It is proposed that the U.S. pledge a contribution to the Fund.

Mr. Sisco. Mr. Chairman, over the last 6 or 8 months there have been perhaps a dozen principal developments at the U.N. which I would like to cite very briefly for the information of the committee. 

Going back to the last session of the General Assembly, that Assembly reelected U Thant as the Secretary General, and thereby averted what otherwise could have been a very significant constitutional crisis. We think this is an important development not because the 

United States necessarily agrees with U Thant in all particulars, but largely because of the fact that we feel that the Secretary General conceives of this organization very much in the same terms as we do; namely, an action organization whose functions are to help keep the peace and to help promote economic and social development in a number of countries around the world. 

During the past year also we have continued our efforts-unsuccessfully, I might say-to try to involve the United Nations in the Vietnam problem. I think it can be said that the U.N. has been no more successful than any of the other numerous bilateral meetings in which we have sought to settle this very difficult problem. 

We have, however, over the past year begun to expand the role of the United Nations specialized agencies in Vietnam in the field of social welfare and health and education, very modestly as a complement to our own bilateral program designed to help in the rehabilitation of South Vietnam.

1967 

A third principal development has been the conclusion of the outer space treaty which was negotiated by Ambassador Goldberg with 27 other members of the U.N. Outer Space Committee. This treaty prohibits all activities on celestial bodies, including the moon, for military purposes. We consider this to be one of the major achievements during this past year at the U.N. 

I might also note that at the past General Assembly the question of Red China's admission once again arose, and the vote in support of our position was greater than at any time in the last 5 years. I think the answer is very simple to find, namely, that Red China's own actions are going a long way to cause members to look with great reserve on its possible admission. In effect, Red China is excluding itself from this organization. 

In the Middle East we have several continuing United Nations operations. You have the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization, the Palestine Refugee Agency, and the United Nations Emergency Force, all of which are helping to contribute to stability in that area. Moreover, there is a second on-going peacekeeping operation, the United Nations Force in Cyprus, which is helping to keep a lid on that situation.

Another significant action was taken last December when the Security Council voted to apply mandatory economic sanctions against Southern Rhodesia. This was unprecedented in the history of the organization. These sanctions are being applied today by the 

United Kingdom, the United States, and the majority of the members of the United Nations.

On the economic side I would just say a word regarding the major program in the field of economic development and technical assistance; namely, the U.N. development program itself. 

The program has improved in management. It has demonstrated over the past years a capability to engender self-help efforts on the part of recipients, partly because a number of the lesser developed countries tend to identify themselves with these programs rather directly, and partly because of the fact that the United Nations has considerable prestige in a number of these less developed countries. 

Paul Hoffman, who as you know is the prominent American in charge of this program, has done an exceedingly good job in managing it. Recently he has released data to show what the program is doing. 

He said that by the end of 1966 77 preinvestment surveys and feasibility studies have been completed, 31 of which have already produced sizable followup investment. He says that each dollar spent on these 

31 projects has produced over $40 of investment, a total of more than $1.6 billion thus far since the inauguration of this program. 

Mr. Chairman, I ought to say a few words on peacekeeping and the financial situation at the U.N. The financial situation remains unresolved. The Soviet bloc remains in arrears. You may have read in the press recently that Ambassador Fedorenko of the Soviet Union made a statement indicating that the Soviet Union intended to make a voluntary contribution in the near future with a view to helping alleviate the financial difficulties of the organization. We have heard this kind of statement time and time again. Personally, I will believe it when I see it.

465 I have some serious doubts that the Soviet Union is going to make such a contribution or if it does that it will be much more than a symbolic one. The constitutional differences between ourselves and the 

Soviet Union continue. They still want to reduce the United Nations to a debating society. We in turn want the United Nations to continue to be an organization that can help to maintain the peace. Because of this continuing constitutional difference, I am not at all optimistic, regardless of Ambassador Fedorenko's speeches, that the Russians are very serious about helping alleviate the financial difficulties of the organization.

This concludes my brief remarks, Mr. Chairman. I will be very glad to respond to queries from the members of the committee. 

Mr. Secretary, on page 5 of your statement you say "77 preinvestment surveys and feasibility studies have been completed, 31 of which have already produced sizable followup investment. Each dollar spent on these 31 projects has yielded over $40 of investment. The total followup investment, both from public and private sources, from these 31 projects is $1.6 billion thus far." 

Where does this money come from? Commercial investors, or from governments?

Mr. Sisco. Mr. Chairman, it is a combination of sources-some from governments, some from private investors, and some from international lending institutions. Some of it is American and some of it of course is from the other members of the United Nations. This is a program incidentally where practically every member of the United Nations makes some kind of voluntary contribution. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, on page 8 of your statement you make reference to expansion of the United Nations operations in Vietnam. It appears that several organizations connected with the United Nations are conducting operations there. We all would like to have the United Nations take over the whole operation in Vietnam if it could. What sort of programs, what is the U.N. running in Vietnam?

Mr. Sisco. The principal one that I would cite is one that is about to get in operation. In January 1966 the United Nations development program approved a fisheries development project, including exploratory and experimental fishing in the waters of the South China Sea. 

This project is to be executed by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the U.N. at a cost of a little over a million dollars. The Government of Vietnam requested that the scope of this project be enlarged and extended from coastal to deep sea fishing. 

We expect to provide through a funds-in-trust arrangement with the FAO about $750,000 this fiscal year for this expansion. There are also some other programs that are just getting off the ground, Mr. Chairman. The World Health Organization has some people there and some teams who are trying to help out with some of the sanitation problems.

UNICEF has a few people in Vietnam who are trying to help out with the education of children. I mentioned that we have the FAO. 

The staffs of U.N. agencies are being enlarged in Vietnam slowly but it is a very modest operation. 

For example, the U.N. agencies now have about 27 people. So it is really a drop in the bucket as compared to what we are doing on the

1967 

bilateral side. Our hope is that the more the U.N. can do, the more these other countries will help to share the burden. In the fisheries project I mentioned, the Dutch have committed themselves to a million dollars. The more we can bring in the U.N., the more we can bring in indirectly other countries in this situation. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, I remember back in 1950 there was strong support in the U.N. for the Special United Nations Fund for Economic Development, the so-called SUNFED, to which we were opposed on the ground that it was a device that we could expect to put up most of the money but to be outvoted on decisions as to spending the money. How does the United Nations development. program differ from SUNFED?

Mr. Sisco. SUNFED primarily was intended to be a capital investment fund. We felt that with the World Bank and IDA available, there was no need to create a SUNFED. The Special Fund Sector of the UNDP, of course, gets into preinvestment surveys and provides technical experts, whereas SUNFED was focused almost exclusively on capital investment.

As long as we continue to maintain this position of reserve, Mr. 

Chairman, this SUNFED, of course, will never be created as an actual fund. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, I see that you are recommending in the new authority $141 million for fiscal 1968, which you say is approximately the same as appropriated for fiscal year 1967. However, on the first paragraph of your statement you say that you had actually $147 million which includes $7,500,000 carryover in funds available from 1967. 

Mr. Secretary, do you expect that with the recommendation you make this year that you will have any carryover in fiscal year 1968? 

Mr. Sisco. To the best of our judgment, we are going to be running very close to the margin, and I would doubt there is going to be any carryover. It is very tight at the moment, as we see it. 

Chairman MORGAN. I see you have some tentative estimates for fiscal 1969. Are any of these programs for which you seek obligational authority in 1968 which will be terminating in 1969? Could we look forward to terminating or reducing some of these programs after 1968? 

Mr. Sisco. I would point to the following, Mr. Chairman. With respect to the assistance program for the Congo, we definitely have a policy of phasing this thing out. This year, for example, we are proposing a million dollars less than last year. Our projection for 

1969 is another million less. There is a reduction there. 

On the whole the same line items which are proposed for 1968 are contemplated for 1969, with the exception of one new item which I ought to mention. At the moment there is a discussion going on in the World Meteorological Organization regarding the establishment of the so-called World Weather Watch. If everything goes as we expect it to go, Mr. Chairman, this program should begin to become operational. We will need money in fiscal year 1969. So we would anticipate there would be a new line item for the World Weather Watch and some authority requested for that. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, last year this committee saw fit to write into the bill an authorization for an extra million dollars for UNICEF.

467 Upon examination of the presentation books, it appears that 114 countries pledged contributions in calendar 1966 compared to 117 in calender 1965. We hoped that the extra contribution we gave 

UNICEF last year in the amount of $1 million would arouse additional interest on the part of some of the contributing countries, but it looks as though the contributions are going down. 

Is there any reason you can give us for that? 

Mr. Sisco. Happily, Mr. Chairman, what you thought might happen last year has happened. Since the issuance of this presentation book, we have received from UNICEF its final statement of the governmental pledges for the year and, frankly, we are pleased to note that the number of governments contributing for 1966 is 120 rather than the 114 mentioned in the presentation book. 

So modest as it is, it does represent an increase of three contributing countries to the program above what it was the year before. It has stimulated additional interest.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, did the Soviets and Communist bloc countries make their UNICEF contributions?

Mr. Sisco. The Soviet Union and the Soviet bloc—this is a voluntary program, you understand, Mr. Chairman-do make voluntary contributions to UNICEF. I would say they are modest by comparison with ours. For example, the Soviet Union has been contributing on the average of $675,000 per year to this program. That is true in 1965, 1966, and 1967.

Then, you have modest contributions from the Ukraine and from a number of the other eastern Europeans. I would be very glad to put the precise figures in the record if you would like, Mr. Chairman.

(The material referred to follows:) STATEMENT ON UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM IN CUBA 

UNDP financial resources are comprised of over 90 different currencies, which, under arrangements determined by the donor, may be partly or fully convertible or unconvertible. Voluntary cash contributions by governments provide the bulk of UNDP funds, and they constitute a form of national resources. Use

473 of the currency of a particular country in support of a UNDP activity constitutes the use by UNDP of the national resources of the donor, to assist the recipient. 

Assistance supplied to governments by UNDP generally takes form of expert personnel, equipment and supplies, and training facilities outside the recipient country. 

In the case of UNDP projects of assistance to Cuba, neither the US nor the Cuban government could be expected to allow US nationals to serve on a UNDP project in Cuba, or to allow Cuban nationals to undertake training in the United States. Export control of the United States would not permit shipment to Cuba of project equipment and supplies from the United States. In these circumstances, it is appropriate that the UNDP administration should take steps to ensure that US resources would not be used for support of a UNDP project in Cuba. 

Accordingly, the Special Fund announced in February 1963 the arrangements under which Special Fund assistance to the central agricultural experiment station in Cuba would be given. Included in that announcement was the statement that not a single American dollar would be used; no part of the US contribution would be devoted to finance the project; other currencies available in 

Special Funds resources would be used exclusively. Accounting arrangements were established to ensure that this undertaking was fully implemented. 

The policy applied to the agricultural experiment station was extended in 1966 to cover the second Special Fund project in Cuba, covering assistance to the faculty of technology at the University of Havana, which was approved by the Governing Council in Janaury of that year. Same policy will be applied to such projects as may be approved for Cuba under the technical assistance component of UNDP.

Mr. Sisco. The assistance I was talking about, Mr. Gross, is for

Mr. SISCO. Yes, sir.

STATEMENT OF LOUIS FRECHTLING, DIRECTOR, OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL ADMINISTRATION, BUREAU OF INTERNA- TIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS, DEPARTMENT OF STATE Mr. FRECHTLING. Mr. Chairman and Mr. Fascell, the increase in the unexpended balances comes about essentially as the result of several changes that have been made in the practice of transmitting

475 funds to the international organizations. Our practice through, say, the late fifties was to transmit U.S. dollar checks after the organizations had provided certified copies of receipts from other governments. 

In view of the balance-of-payments problem which became acute in recent years, we first turned to another mechanism, which is the use of the so-called Treasury bond. That Treasury bond was passed to the organization in place of dollars and was at the disposal of the organization to cash when it actually needed the funds. 

This tended to defer the effect on our balance of payments until the funds were actually needed by the organization. 

However, under Treasury and Budget Bureau accounting procedures, as soon as we purchased that bond, that amount became an expenditure for the purposes of tables like this. Treasury then shifted to a letter-of-credit procedure, which procedure is also used by AID in most of its operations. Instead of giving an organization such as the 

UNDP a dollar check or Treasury bond, we now give them a letter of credit.

Expenditures are recorded, only as the organization draws down on the letter of credit. Thus, it defers both the balance of payments effects and the budgetary expenditures.

Mr. FASCELL. The increase in the pipeline is a bookkeeping increase caused by deferral of expenditures through the use of letter of credit; and credits against the fund are made only as drawn by the expending agency? 

Mr. FRECHTLING. That is essentially correct. 

Mr. FASCELL. Is that done on a monthly basis? 

Is that the normal accounting practice? 

Mr. FRECHTLING. The drawdown on the letter of credit- 

Mr. FASCELL. Daily, weekly, or monthly?

When is the settlement of the account for accounting purposes? 

Mr. FRECHTLING. For accounting purposes, expenditures are recorded as the letter of credit is drawn down. 

Mr. FASCELL. Is there no interim credit?

Mr. FRECHTLING. The organizations are asked, as I indicated before, to draw on letters of credit only when they actually need the funds for expenditure. Insofar as they have irrevocable letters of credit, they can make their plans and commitments to suppliers or to contractors- 

Mr. FASCELL. The letter of credit is not a credit against the pipeline until it is fully expended; is that correct? 

What you are saying is whether it takes a week or 6 months to draw down the irrevocable letter of credit, it is only to the point where the full letter is used that it is credited against the pipeline figure and this accounts for the buildup in the pipeline?

Mr. FRECHTLING. Expenditures are recorded for U.S. accounting purposes when drawdowns are made on letters of credit. These drawdowns may be for the full amount of the letter of credit or for part of it. In many cases substantial time elapses between the issuance of a letter of credit and the final drawdown-sometimes as much as 

15 months.

Mr. FASCELL. The presentation book refers to two recent pledges that the Government made to the world food program. The first pledge involved $92 million in commodities, $32 million in shipping costs, and $6 million for administrative expenses for 1966-68. That was subject to a 50 percent matching formula.

1967 

It would appear from the tables here that the response from other countries hasn't been too good. The pledging drive netted only onehalf of the announced goal of $275 million and yet we made another pledge. 

Is this a double matching or is this a separate one? 

Where are we?

Mr. Sisco. I think Mr. Frechtling, who works on this problem in detail, would like to also address himself to that, Mr. Fascell. 

Mr. FRECHTLING. Mr. Fascell, the presentation book on page 91 tends to suggest, as your question indicates, a situation which is not actually true.

May I say that in our participation in these various international organizations one of our objectives is to maximize the contributions of other wealthy countries to these international programs. Our matching formula is one of the devices we use to do this. We put up a dollar, they put up a dollar and a half.

In the world food program, we made an initial pledge as stated on page 91; it was in three parts. It had to do with commodities which we offered on a 50 percent matching formula, and shipping services, and then $6 million in cash for administration costs on a 40 percent matching formula.

As the pledges came in after 6 months it was obvious that a lot of other countries weren't in the position we were of having substantial export surpluses of agricultural commodities. 

So they tended to pledge more cash relatively and fewer commodities and, therefore, there was no incentive for new cash pledges. They had already matched our $6 million in cash; much more than matched it. They had pledged $26 million and we had pledged $6 million on the 

40 percent basis, so they had pledged $17 million more in cash than was needed to match our cash pledge. There was no particular incentive at that stage for other prospective donors to make additional cash contributions.

Some of the countries, we were told, were thinking of getting cash appropriations and then buying commodities in a third country to contribute to the world food program and thereby maximize the total contribution, because they would draw down more commodities from us.

The revision of our pledge work in July, 1966 only applies to new pledges and still requires a dollar of cash from other countries which we will then match with a dollar's worth of commodities. 

This may be a complex answer. I think the simple answer is that other donors have cash and don't have commodities, whereas our initial pledge was largely in commodities. We are saying, in effect, that we will with respect to pledges made after July 31, 1966, match a dollar of cash from other countries with a dollar's worth of commodities.

Mr. FASCELL. We are saying that as of when, and for how long, and for how much? 

Mr. FRECHTLING. Beginning with July 31, 1966, through the second 

3-year period which the world food program is now in, which ends in 1968. 

In any case, it is subject to the limitation of $92 million as the maximum amount of agricultural commodities, and it is still subject to the 50-50 matching formula.

477 Mr. FASCELL. Subject to a $92 million value on and subject to—— 

Mr. FRECHTLING. Fifty percent matching formula. 

May I restate it?

As indicated on page 91 of the presentation book, our initial pledge was $92 million in agricultural commodities, subject to a 50 percent matching formula. 

Mr. FASCELL. Stop right there for a minute.

That means that you would have a total of $184 million of commodities in dollar value?

Mr. FRECHTLING. Right, if other countries also contributed $92 million in commodities. 

Mr. FASCELL. That is commodities; not dollars? 

Mr. FRECHTLING. Yes.

Mr. FASCELL. OK. 

Mr. FRECHTLING. We also said we would contribute $6 million in cash for administrative and operational costs for the program, subject to a 40 percent matching formula. It is the cash, incidentally, that we are asking for, of course, in this particular presentation. 

When the pledges came in, other donors had made more cash available, relative to our pledge, than they had commodities.

ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS BY MR. FASCELL 

GENERAL Question: The total Chapter 3 pipeline will be in excess of $190 million as of 

June 30 of this year. Can you give us a breakdown of that pipeline?

Answer: The level of the unexpended balances in the appropriation for voluntary contributions to international organizations and programs is related primarily to two factors:

1967 

1. Use of the letter of credit. The United States now makes payments to international organizations in the form of letters of credit when it is apparent that the organization does not need the U.S. contribution to make early expenditures. This procedure was initiated in 1965. Transfer of the letter of credit to the organization assures it of payment for the United States and thereby enables the organization to make firm plans for assistance projects. The organization draws on the letter of credit only as it needs cash for expenditure. For 

U.S. accounting purposes, expenditures are recorded only when drawdowns are made on the letter of credit.

As of March 31, 1967, there was $97.5 million outstanding in the form of unredeemed letters of credit and shown in U.S. accounting records as unliquidated obligations. Under earlier arrangements, this amount would have been recorded as expended. 

2. Lag between fiscal periods of the United States and of the international organizations. Appropriations sought by the Executive Branch in the Chapter 3 request relate generally to the fiscal periods (calendar years) of the organizations beginning six months after the end of the U.S. fiscal year (July 1 to June 30). 

Thus the funds requested by the Executive Branch for FY 1967 in most cases relate to the organizations' activities for CY 1967. 

In those cases where the United States does not use the letter of credit procedure, cash payments are made on a schedule which is related to the organizations' cash needs. Those requirements tend to peak late in the calendar year. As of 

March 31, 1967, only about $26.5 million had been expended against obligations of $137.5 million incurred from FY 1967 funds.

Question: Is there any coordination between the new UN Development Program and the UN Program of Technical Assistance funded out of the regular 

UN budget?

Answer: Activities of the UN Development Program and the UN Regular 

Technical Assistance Program are coordinated in several ways: first, the UNDP 

Governing Council, of which we are a member, reviews the UN Regular Technical Assistance Program and approves the level of its program and expenditures; second, the UNDP Resident Representatives consult with the recipient governments regarding projects under the UN Development Program and the UN Regular Technical Assistance Program. These representatives also supervise and coordinate the execution of projects under both programs. Third, the Commissioner for Technical Co-operation at United Nations Headquarters coordinates both the UN Regular Technical Assistance Program and the projects for which the UN serves as the executing agent for the UN Development Program.

INDUS BASIN DEVELOPMENT FUND 

Question: A $25.5 million grant is being proposed for Indus in fiscal 1968. 

What is the balance of the U.S. commitment with respect to grant aid for this project and when will this commitment be discharged? 

Answer: The U.S. has pledged $295.5 million in grants for the Indus Fund and about $100 million will remain to be paid after fiscal 1968. This commitment will be paid in installments, according to calls for funds made by the World Bank, over the remainder of the Indus Basin program. 

Question: The bill would authorize a $51.2 million loan in addition to the grant contribution. When is that loan to be disbursed? 

Answer: Disbursement of the loan is expected to begin in fiscal year 1969. 

Question: Last year's presentation indicated that the final installment of our local currency commitment was to be made during fiscal 1967. The amount involved was approximately $1 million. Has that commitment been discharged? 

Answer: The final installment, amounting to $938,000, was paid in October 1966. 

U.N. TECHNICAL AND OPERATIONAL ASSISTANCE TO THE CONGO 

Question: The presentation book indicates that the special project arrangement for the Congo was terminated this year, and that the total UN program for that country was reduced substantially. This does not seem to be reflected in the size of our contribution. The U.S. contribution in fiscal 1967-$4.5 million-is only 10 percent smaller than our $5 million contribution in fiscal 1966. How do you account for this?

Answer: Prior to FY 1967 the US contribution was divided into two parts. 

One part was used for the special project arrangement and the other part was used for the UN Fund. In FY 1966 we contributed $4 million to the special project arrangement and $0.7 million to the UN Fund. In FY 1967 the two parts were combined and the special project arrangement was discontinued. However, the specific projects that the UN was financing were not discontinued. We are planning to contribute $4.5 million to the combined program (the UN Fund) in FY 

1967. A substantial reduction in the UN program will be made in the FY 1968 program. This is the reason that our request for FY 1968 is $3 million as compared with $4.5 million in FY 1967.

Question: What percentage of the UN Fund for the Congo is represented by the U.S. contribution in fiscal 1967?

Answer: We estimate that the U.S. contribution will be about 67 percent of the UN Fund in 1967 but will drop to about 48 percent in 1968. 

SPECIAL PROGRAM FOR VIETNAM 

Question: $2 million is being proposed for this program for fiscal 1968. How is that money going to be used?

Answer: This $2 million would be used for further funds-in-trust arrangements, to continue our support of the Fisheries Project and for other programs which the UN agencies are unable to finance on their own. Such programs are in the fields of public health administration, disease control, social welfare training and public finance and administration.

UNITED NATIONS RELIEF AND WORKS AGENCY (UNRWA) 

Question: No reduction is being proposed in the U.S. cash contribution to this program for fiscal year 1968. Why? We have cut this program 5 percent in 1965, and again 5 percent in 1966. Further, the Committee has indicated its belief that further reductions should be forthcoming on a regular basis. Do you think there is any chance of this program being phased out eventually if we continue our contributions at the present level?

Answer: We do not expect to continue our contribution at present levels indefinitely. But a further cut this year, in the wake of our cuts of the past two

481 years amounting to $2.5 million, would not be good policy. Our cuts of the past two years contributed to an already weak UNRWA budgetary condition and a further cut this year would only aggravate that condition. We continue to feel that our share of UNRWA costs, which for the past two years has been at the 65% level, should be reduced gradually toward a level corresponding more closely to the level of our other voluntary contributions to UN programs. But, we do not believe that reductions should be made at a fixed yearly rate, without regard to the humanitarian and political considerations which may be involved in any given year.

Question: Has any progress been made in rectifying the relief rolls? Has the number of refugees on those rolls decreased? 

Answer: There has been some progress. UNRWA states that the ration rolls in Lebanon are reasonably satisfactory. In the Gaza Strip there has been some rectification with the cooperation of the host government. In Syria and Jordan very little progress has been made. Some years ago UNRWA placed a ceiling on the ration rolls because of a limitation of funds. Consequently, there is a large backlog of children (296,000) who are eligible for rations who are not receiving them. When an ineligible person is removed from the rolls he is replaced by an eligible child. So, even though rectification goes on, there is very little decrease in the net number on the rolls. At the end of December 1966, 859,966 refugees were receiving rations; this compares with 873,123 at the end of December 1965a decrease of 13,157.

Question: How long is the UN going to keep up the fiction of a "reserve fund" when what they are really talking about are shares allocated to, but not paid by, other countries?

Answer: The reserve fund is required in order to provide a minimum amount for this operation. The reserve fund may have to be continued as long as the members of the UN deem it necessary to retain the UNEF. The current UNEF resolution and reserve fund procedure provide the best apparent way to apportion the financial responsibility for this operation among the greatest number of member countries. The resolution provides that countries contributing to the reserve fund may be reimbursed on a pro-rated basis when the General Assembly determines that the additional amounts are no longer needed.

1967 INTERNATIONAL SECRETARIAT FOR VOLUNTEER SERVICE 

Question: Is the U.S. withdrawing its financial support from the International 

Secretariat for Volunteer Service (a) because others are not contributing enough or (b) because a Swiss national was elected Secretary General and the organization may be moving out of the U.S.? 

Answer: The U.S. has been supporting ISVS activities in two ways: (1) through a cash contribution sought under Chapter III of the Foreign Assistance Act; and (2) through the detail of personnel on a non-reimbursable basis to work on the staff of ISVS. Since FY 1964, detailed personnel have largely come from the 

Peace Corps. For FY 1968, the U.S. proposes to limit its support to the detail of personnel. It is not currently considering a cash contribution. 

In the past three years, the United States has attempted to encourage broader participation in ISVS. It became apparent that, with a preponderance of U.S. personnel and early relatively large financial support, steps would have to be taken to reduce the U.S. involvement in ISVS without appearing to be withdrawing support of its work. 

Since FY 1966 the U.S. has reduced the number of detailed personnel to achieve a more equitable balance on the professional staff of ISVS. In addition, the U.S. has contributed modest funds on a 28 percent matching basis to encourage more countries to contribute. Currently, ISVS is supported financially by eleven countries. At or before the World Assembly in New Delhi, four additional countries expressed their intention to join the Council by contributing to the ISVS budget. 

Contributions from other countries have been steadily increasing. 

The U.S. has also actively supported the election of a non-American to the post of Secretary General, held by an American since 1963. In March 1967, Dr. 

Michael von Schenck, a Swiss citizen, was elected Secretary General effective April 4, 1967. The U.S. supported his election. Whether the headquarters will move to Europe or remain in Washington has not, as yet, been determined by the Council. It is not a factor in determining U.S. support for ISVS in 1968. 

Question: What is the relationship between ISVS and the Peace Corps? 

Answer: The International Secretariat for Volunteer Service (ISVS) is an international organization composed of 46 member countries. Of the 46, eleven contribute personnel or funds, ten of whom constitute the Council, the key policy-making group. The United States Government is a member of the Assembly and Council.

As a result of a delegation of authority from the Secretary of State to the Director of the Peace Corps, the Peace Corps acts as a liaison between the U.S. 

Government and ISVS to insure proper cooperation, and to avoid duplication of effort. The Peace Corps, also under its authority, has detailed personnel to the staff of ISVS as have four other countries. For FY 1968 the Peace Corps plans to continue with the detail of up to three staff members. 

Question: Has the Peace Corps in fact taken over the job of encouraging and aiding other countries to establish their own Peace Corps? 

Answer: No. Since 1963, when Congress amended the Peace Corps Act by adding Title III, the Peace Corps has had authority to provide bilateral technical assistance to encourage other countries to set up voluntary programs. Other nations also provide bilateral technical assistance. 

Although ISVS does provide limited technical assistance on a multilateral basis, the Articles governing ISVS make it clear the requests for technical assistance first must be referred to the Council to insure that bilateral aid is not being provided or is not forthcoming. If neither is the case and multilateral aid appears to be the most effective, or most feasible, ISVS proceeds. This process ensures coordination of effort and use of limited ISVS resources for activities that otherwise would not be supported. 

Question: The International Secretariat was originally recommended to this 

Committee on the grounds that an international organization would be more effective than a U.S. national outfit like the Peace Corps in stimulating the growth

483 of volunteer services in certain sensitive geographical areas. What has happened to change that situation and is this a question of Parkinson's law operating on our own Peace Corps?

Answer: The situation has not changed. The ISVS is considered an effective organization. It receives from many, and distributes to all its members, data relevent to voluntary programs. In more sensitive countries, such as Kenya, ISVS is able to render technical assistance more effectively than any bilateral program. The Peace Corps' efforts in encouraging such programs have not been subject to Parkinson's law. The Peace Corps' budget for its Title III activities for FY 1968 is below that of FY 1967. Expenditures for 1967 will be below those for FY 1966. Currently the staff of the Division of National Voluntary Service 

Programs, the division which administers Title III, has four fewer people than when it was established in 1963.

1,979, 000 1,876, 000 Question: Could you also furnish a breakdown of the $400,000 which is used for fellowships and related undertakings? Is any portion of that money used to pay U.S. Government personnel for attending technical meetings? And what steps have been taken pursuant to our Committee's report last year to make certain that there is no duplication between exchanges financed under this authorization and those authorized by the Fulbright-Hays Act and other statutes?

Answer: The $400,000 item includes: $120,000, administered by the Atomic 

Energy Commission, for the provision of experts and small equipment grants; and $280,000, administered by the National Academy of Sciences, for fellowships for study in the United States. 

Of the above $120,000, approximately $32,000 is used to provide United States experts at panels and study groups of the Agency dealing with specific technical problems. Normally, about 24 experts are made available to the Agency each year, one-third of whom are Government personnel. 

The fellowship program is administered by the National Academy of Sciences under a detailed contract. As of January 1, 1967, under this program, there were 

49 fellows from 23 countries actively engaged in study at 23 universities, 7 national laboratories, and 4 other institutions. Their areas of study were: health physics (10), radioisotope applications (9), reactor materials (1), reactor engineering (16), power reactors (2), nuclear physics (7), nuclear and radiochemistry (3), and atomic energy, law, economics, literature, and special library training (1). 

To the best of our knowledge, there has been no duplication between the IAEA fellowship program as administered by AID under a contract with the National Academy of Sciences and the fellowship program under the Fulbright-Hays Act. 

The IAEA fellowships provide on an average a one-year program of training in the United States, with full financial support, for nuclear scientists at the graduate doctoral and postdoctoral level. Fellowship awards are only granted to individuals from less developed countries. Fulbright fellowships are granted under a different concept, i.e., broader country coverage, broader fields of study, limited financial support and primarily at the undergraduate level.

 THE FINDLEY AMENDMENT AND THE WORLD FOOD PROGRAM 

The "Findley amendment" is contained in the Agricultural Appropriation Act for FY 1967 (P.L. 89-566) and provides: "That no funds appropriated by this Act shall be used to formulate or administer programs for the sale of agri cultural commodities pursuant to Titles I or IV of Public Law 480, 83rd Congress, as amended, to any nation which sells or furnishes or which permits ships or aircraft under its registry to transport to North Vietnam any equipment, materials or commodities, so long as North Vietnam is governed by a Communist regime." 

Congressman Findley was the author of a similar amendment which appears in section 103 of the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, as amended (P.L. 480). That section states that: "The President shall *** (d) 

make sales agreements only with those countries which he determines to be friendly to the United States * * *. As used in this Act, 'friendly country' shall not include *** (3) for the purpose only of sales of agricultural commodities under Title I of this Act, any nation which sells or furnishes or permits ships or aircraft under its registry to transport to or from Cuba or North Vietnam (excluding United States installations in Cuba) any equipment, materials, or commodities so long as they are governed by a Communist regime: Provided, That with respect to furnishing, selling, or selling and transporting to Cuba medical supplies, nonstrategic raw materials for agriculture, and nonstrategic agricultural or food commodities, sales agreements may be entered into if the President finds with respect to each such country, and so informs the Senate and the House of Representatives of the reasons therefor, that the making of each such agreement would

1967 

be in the national interest of the United States and all such findings and reasons therefor shall be published in the Federal Register * * *”

The commodities donated by the United States through the World Food Program are provided under the authority of Title II of P.L. 480. Thus, such commodities are not affected by the provisions cited above, which apply only to Titles 

I and IV, and Title I, respectively, of P.L. 480.

 ASSISTANCE BY THE UNITED NATIONS AGENCIES TO VIETNAM AND SOVIET UNION CONTRIBUTIONS 

Contributions from the U.S.S. R. represent a very small fraction (approximately 

3 percent) of the funds expended by UN agencies for assistance to the Republic of Vietnam.

As indicated in Mr. Sisco's opening statement, expenditures by UN agencies in Vietnam in 1966 are estimated at $729,000. 

The UN Development Program (UNDP) expended $277,000 for technical experts. The U.S.S.R.'s voluntary contribution to the UNDP is made in rubles which may be used in most part only for costs of Soviet experts, commodities purchased in the Soviet Union, and fellowships tenable in the Soviet Union. 

The U.S.S.R. would not provide such assistance to Vietnam through the UNDP and the Government of Vietnam would not accept it. 

The UN Children's Fund (UNICEF) expended $244,000 in Vietnam for commodity support of health and education projects. The U.S.S. R.'s voluntary contribution to UNICEF is made in non-convertible rubles, most of which are currently used for purchase in the U.S.S. R. of chemical raw materials for the manufacture of DDT outside the U.S.S. R. UNICEF is not currently supporting any malaria eradication activities in Vietnam. 

The UN provided $34,000 in technical assistance to Vietnam, financed by the assessed budget of the UN proper. The U.S.S. R.'s contribution to this part of the UN budget is made in rubles which are not being accepted by the UN. 

WHO, IAEA, and UNESCO expended $174,000 in technical activities financed by their assessed budgets. As the U.S.S. R.'s share of these budgets is about 14 percent, its share of the expenditures of the three specialized agencies is about $24,000.

Mr. HAMILTON. I noticed a rather sharp decrease in the number of technical experts going to the Congo. It is on page 11 of your statement. In 1968 the U.N. program calls for 287 compared with 443 in 

1967. What is the significance of that sharp decrease?

Mr. Sisco. May I go back briefly to the early history of this program. During the heyday of the Congo operation between 1960 and 

1964 we had a considerably greater number of experts who helped in operations of this fledgling state in practically every facet of government.

In fact, the U.N. experts for all practical purposes were in the various ministries helping to advise and provide the technical expertise needed. The situation now, regardless of the Congo's recent difficulties, which are really reflective of its being a developing country, is, first, they are better able to stand on their own feet; second, they have more people of their own now who are better trained; and third, the Belgians on a bilateral basis are taking up the slack very considerably. out

So that you will find that we are phasing out our support of this particular program. We have moved down from $4 million to $3 million this year, and hope to cut down a million subsequently. We think we can phase out this U.N. program over the next several years because the Congolese with the help of the Belgians can do it on their own.

Is that your judgment too?

Mr. SISCO. That is correct; it has never come to a vote. I think the closest that one can come to this kind of a guess would be this: that if you compare the number of countries in the U.N., 122, the number that recognize Red China on the one hand, and the number that recognize the Republic of China on Taiwan, or the number of countries that recognize neither, I think you will find a rather interesting split.

There are a number more that recognize the Republic of China than Red China. I would say that there is an overlapping majority. 

My judgment would be today that the required two-thirds majority would not be there. But there is substantial sentiment among the U.N. membership for a two-China solution. 

Mr. HAMILTON. But you don't see that coming to a head or a vote in the immediate future?

Mr. Sisco. I do not for the reason that I cited very briefly earlier. 

Both China's oppose a two-China soulution. As you know, we have made major efforts to keep Red China out of the organization. We find as a result of the behavior of Red China over these last years that the votes rolled in. That is why this was won by such a substantial majority at the last Assembly. It is Red China's policy of self-exclusion which is also a major contributing factor.

1967 

Mr. HAMILTON. May I ask you to go into more detail in this problem of the weighted vote. What kind of criteria are we considering if we can ever get this committee underway?

Mr. Sisco. I think in general there are two ways in which voting in the U.N. General Assembly can be weighted a little more in the direction of the major contributors. First, you could come up, technically speaking, with a weighted voting formula. But problems arise in selecting a basis for the formula. If population were used, I think you would find that the U.S. relative weight would not be particularly advantageous to us. 

Secondly, since the constitutional amendment of the charter is subject to veto, you are not about to get a pure and simple weighted formula. We are looking really to two kinds of informal means. First, take the peacekeeping area. We made a concerete proposal to the effect that a committee ought to be established on which the major contributors would be the predominant influence, and that this committee would have the job of determining the finances of a peacekeeping operation. On the basis of the U.S. proposal, the Assembly would not be able to act without the prior recommendation of this particular committee.

We have pressed this proposal, but we haven't really been able to get sufficient support in the General Assembly to get it adopted. 

Secondly, in the so-called UNCTAD, which is the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development-this is a U.N. organization that is working in the trade and development field-we set up what was called a conciliation procedure. It is essentially a cooling-off procedure.

What was agreed to was this: Whenever there was a fundamental difference between the major contributors and the recipients, it made no sense whatever to adopt symbolic resolutions that the major contributors are going to disregard. After all if you are going to get any significant decisions on trade and development, the 15 countries that I talked about earlier which represent the real economic power of the world, must agree. You can put all these symbolic resolutions on the book and nothing will happen. 

In other words, we said it takes two to tango. So we pressed and succeeded in getting adopted a conciliation procedure whereby if there is a fundamental difference, this cooling-off procedure takes place. 

No formal proposal can be voted unless a number of conciliation procedures designed to achieve a consensus are first exhausted. We haven't tested this procedure to see if it will work, but at least the underdeveloped countries are inhibited for a certain period of time from steamrolling resolutions over the objections of the major contributors.

Mr. HAMILTON. Thank you.
