Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gross, I think the only reduction that has been made has been forced by this committee in an amendment reducing our contribution 5 percent a year. There seems to be no initiative from the agency to reduce its budget. 

Mr. GROSS. I think that is right, Mr. Chairman, but I don't find anything laudable about that. Laudable, yes, that the committee would force some reduction, but far from laudable on the part of those who are directly responsible for a solution of this program. 

What can you report on the effectiveness of the educational and training programs conducted with these funds? I am not asking now about how many persons are being trained, but how many have been trained, moved out, and found jobs as a result of this undertaking? 

Mr. Sisco. The UNRWA has a very substantial vocational educational program in every one of these countries, Jordan, Lebanon, and in the Gaza Strip. What they are doing is training these people in two ways, one, to move them on to higher education, and secondly, I think the most successful part of the educational program, and I have seen these firsthand myself in the last year, are these vocational schools where refugees are being trained and are going out to get jobs.

Mr. Gross, the reason why the number of refugees isn't less today than it was 5 or 10 or 15 years ago is not because a number of these people aren't being trained and finding jobs. The reason is that you have a population explosion among the refugees, so that the reductions made in the number of adults on the ration rolls are more than being compensated for by newborn children of the refugee parents. 

Mr. GROSS. It is a problem that has been with us much too long, Mr. Sisco.

Mr. Sisco. It has, but UNRWA is helping to maintain stability in an area which could become a tinderbox. 

Mr. GROSS. It ought to be solved by the principal parties. It ought to be solved by the Arabs and Israelis. Are the Israelis permitting any substantial migration into Israel? 

Mr. SISCO. There has been no agreement on this question of refugees. For this reason there hasn't been much movement. Most of the movement has come from where these refugee camps are located now; namely, in Lebanon, Jordan, Syria and the Gaza Strip. I doubt the refugees are seriously interested in going back to Israel, but those that are moving out of these camps are really trying to find a livelihood in the respective Arab host countries. 

For example, there are camps in Jordan. The moment one of these fellows is trained and he is out of a camp, he goes on to try to find a job either in Jordan or another Arab country.

Mr. GROSS. Tell me, Mr. Sisco, how is the boycott of Rhodesia succeeding, or is it succeeding?

Mr. Sisco. This is very difficult to judge, Mr. Gross. The prime leverage in this situation is really by the United Kingdom whose exports and imports far outstrip our own. U.S. trade in items affected by United Nations mandatory sanctions involved about $866 million of our 1965 imports from Rhodesia and $2.7 million of our 1965 

exports to Rhodesia. 

We don't have a lot of economic leverage in this situation. How is it going? We are told that, particularly in view of the tobacco embargo, farmers are feeling the pinch. On the other hand, even though there are difficulties, there is no sign that the application of the sanctions has, in fact, moved the Rhodesians any closer to an agreement with the British. I would just add one other thing, Mr. Gross: 

We see this as a problem whose primary responsibility is Great Britain's. It brought the problem to the U.N. and asked for assistance. 

Our national interest in the Rhodesian situation san be stated simply: 

We are interested in stability in the southern part of Africa, and we want here, and are trying to take actions which will promote a peaceful solution and contribute to stability in the area. 

Whether it will or not, it is pretty hard to hazard a guess at the moment.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Sisco, will you bring us up to date on the

International Atomic Energy Agency? It has been with us for quite a while now. There seems to have been some change in their original functions since the Agency started. Just what does this Agency do in regard to the peaceful use of atomic energy?

Mr. Sisco. Largely it is three kinds. One, training of personnel; two, fellowships; and, three, regional centers. This organization has been a relatively stable one in terms of both its programs and budgets. 

I think, Mr. Chairman, that if we get a nonproliferation treaty, and if in fact the International Atomic Energy Agency is given the responsibility to inspect and provide safeguards, then the operational program of this organization is going to increase very substantially. 

For example, right now if I recall the figure, the IAEA has about 15 inspectors involved in their present safeguard system. Our representative to IAEA, Dr. Henry Smythe, told me yesterday that there are something like 20 or 25 countries that have reactors for peaceful purposes which are being inspected by the IAEA. IAEA is doing this with about 15 inspectors. If we ever get to an agreement on the nonproliferation treaty, our AEC has figured out that the staff is going to have to increase, at least initially, to 75. The operational budget would go up in such circumstances.

We are not asking for additional money for this purpose at this time because we don't really know whether we will achieve such an agreement.

Chairman MORGAN. Our contribution is about a million dollars.

Mr. Sisco. In recent years it has been $1.3 million.

501 Mr. Sisco. IAEA has two budgets, the first is the regular budget which is supported by assessments on members. The total assessment for 1966, Mr. Chairman, is $8.4 million. The second budget is for the operational program and is supported by voluntary contributions, that budget in 1966 totaled, $1.3 million.

Mr. PALMER. Mr. Chairman, the Indus program is a 10-year program which began in fiscal year 1961, and should be completed about fiscal year 1971. 

Chairman MORGAN. Is the program operating on schedule? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, sir, it is. In fact, it is somewhat ahead of schedule.

Chairman MORGAN. That largest dam-I have forgotten the name of it has it been completed?

Mr. PALMER. The dam is the Mangla Dam and it is expected to be completed this summer. The dam was closed a month or two ago and they have started filling the reservoir. The generators will be put in shortly and they will finish it this summer. 

Chairman MORGAN. This program was sold to the Congress in 

1961, on the basis that it would take care of approximately 50 or 60 million people as a result of the reclamation of land. Has the program progressed far enough for some of the land to be now under cultivation? 

Mr. PALMER. The Indus program was devised to shift water from 

Pakistan to India and from the western rivers in the Indus Basin to the eastern half of the basin in order to replace water allocated to India under the Indus Water Treaty. At the same time there are major agricultural programs going forward. Progress has been quite notable over the last 5 or 6 years.

Chairman MORGAN. Have any of the countries that have entered into the original agreement reneged on any of their obligations? 

Mr. PALMER. No, sir. 

Chairman MORGAN. They have committed all they said they would so far? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, sir.

Chairman MORGAN. We have been contributing to this program for approximately 6 years. The book mentions Australia, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, and Pakistan. Are there any other countries making a contribution?

Mr. PALMER. Did you mention Germany? 

Chairman MORGAN. Germany, yes. Canada, Germany. 

Mr. PALMER. India also has made a contribution, not to the Indus fund proper, but under the separate treaty with Pakistan, and the Indian contribution then becomes part of the total support for the program. 

Chairman MORGAN. What do they contribute? Labor or what?

Mr. PALMER. They contribute in pounds sterling and have made their payments on schedule. 

Chairman MORGAN. They have made their payments on schedule? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, sir.

1967 

Chairman MORGAN. There has been some change in the estimated cost since it started in 1961. I believe it is going to cost a lot more money than we thought in 1961, is that correct? 

Mr. PALMER. In 1964 the members of the Indus program agreed to enlarge the fund by an amount totaling $315 million in foreign exchange costs. It was clearly agreed and understood at that time that this was the final obligation of all the member countries toward the Indus Basin program. There would be no further responsibility or obligation to provide additional funds. 

Chairman MORGAN. What will be the U.S. total contribution per centagewise?

Mr. PALMER. The U.S. contribution is 44 percent of the foreign exchange costs and slightly more than 44 percent of the local currency costs. It averages to 44 percent of total costs. 

Chairman MORGAN. What would be Western Germany's contribu tion, percentagewise? 

Mr. PALMER. Germany's percentage contribution is 5.4 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. How about Australia? 

Mr. PALMER. 2.8 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. Canada? 

Mr. PALMER. 4 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. New Zealand? 

Mr. PALMER. 0.4 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. United Kingdom? 

Mr. PALMER. 10.3 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. Pakistan? 

Mr. PALMER. 0.2 percent.

Chairman MORGAN. India? 

Mr. PALMER. 18.3 percent. These percentages apply to the dollar costs. The Pakistan Government is responsible for financing all of the rupee costs other than those provided by the United States. 

Thus her share of rupee costs is estimated at about the equivalent of $290 million.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS. Is this a hydroelectric project in addition to irrigation? 

Mr. PALMER. Yes, sir. The Indus Basin program provides for diversion of water for irrigation and for production of power. 

Mr. GROSS. Mr. Chairman, may I ask who is providing turbines for the powerplant, for the hydroplant?

MI. PALMER. I would have to supply that for the record. The major contractors have been U.S. firms and we have obtained contracts for 54 percent of the foreign exchange costs compared to 44 percent of our share of financial contributions. 

 DONOR OF TURBINES FOR INDUS BASIN PROJECT 

The contract for the hydraulic turbines at Mangla Dam was awarded to the 

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Co. of Japan. 

Mr. GROSS. Thank you.

Chairman MORGAN. Any further questions? 

If not, thank you, Mr. Sisco.

STATEMENT OF GEN. THEODORE J. CONWAY, U.S. ARMY, U.S. 

COMMANDER IN CHIEF, MIDDLE EAST, AFRICA SOUTH OF THE SAHARA, AND SOUTHERN ASIA, AND COMMANDER IN CHIEF, U.S. STRIKE COMMAND General CONWAY.  

10001 Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is an honor for me to be here and to present the proposed fiscal year 1968 military assistance programs for selected countries in my area of responsibility. 

This area is outlined in the map Sahara Desert, and South Asiasat has been provided. You will note it embraces of the (less Turkey), Africa south military used when referring to this area is "MEAFSA" which was derived by combining the first letters of the names of the principal regions in the area. 

I am accompanied this morning by members of my staff: Ambassador J. O. Bell, my foreign affairs adviser, and Lt. Col. L. M. Kellam. 

Also here are Vice Adm. L. C. Heinz and Mr. Peter Knaur from the 

Office of the Secretary of Defense. 

505

1967 

My distinguished predecessor, Gen. Paul D. Adams, appeared before you a number of times. When he retired in October last year, I became CINCSTRIKE and USCINCMEAFSA. 

As Commander in Chief of MEAFSA, I am charged by the Joint 

I am required to conduct planning to meet likely contingencies or emergencies which might arise. Second, I maintain relationships, and provide liaison, with the armed forces of foreign countries in which we are represented. 

Finally, I am responsible for the supervision of all military assistance programs in this area.

Chiefs of Staff with three basic functions. First, ergencies which 

Earlier this month, Secretary McNamara and Vice Adm. Heinz appeared before this committee to present testimonies in support of the entire military assistance program for fiscal year 1968. As you recall, the sum requested for the program was $596 million. Today, I would like to focus your attention on one comparatively small portion of the overall program that for the MEAFSA area. For this area, a total of $53.9 million, or less than 10 percent of the overall program, is being requested for 17 countries that have been selected to continue to receive military assistance-11 of which will receive training in the 

United States only.

During the current fiscal year, the military assistance program dollar cost for the MEAFSA area has amounted to approximately $68.1 million. The program for fiscal year 1968 is approximately 20 percent ($14.2 million) less than the current program. in Referring to the map which was handed out, the countries colored gray and black are those presently scheduled for grant aid military assistance. The five countries which will receive both materiel and training are: Iran, Jordan, Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of the 

Congo and Liberia. Except for Jordan, we maintain a military assistance advisory group or mission in each of these countries. Jordan's program is administered by the U.S. defense attaché, who is responsible to me for military assistance matters. 1657 

Of the $53.9 million planned for the MEAFSA area, 95.8 percent is in support of these five countries. 

The largest scheduled grant aid recipient is Iran. Because of its location, this country is of strategic importance and should also be capable of defending against aggression and maintaining internal 

The proposed program for Iran will continue to fulfill our commitments by providing both materiel and training. 

Our second largest recipient of aid is Ethiopia. The program is designed primarily to enhance stability and security within the country. 

The military assistance program for Ethiopia provides materiel and training to improve the Ethiopian armed forces' internal security capability at the minimum level required. Follow-on support is provided to insure the proper maintenance and use of previously furnished materiel. 

For the past year and a half, we have conducted a substantial incountry training program. As stated by General Adams last year, the training began in October 1965, with the principal emphasis aimed at the company and battalion level. Only limited advisory assistance was provided for the staffs at higher headquarters. 

The additional training, which we completed in December 1966, had good results. Most significant are the improved professional capa-

507 bilities and increased enthusiasm shown by Ethiopian Army personnel at every level. 

To insure that, these first-year achievements are continued, we have planned a small follow-on effort in-country for the next 2 years. 

Costs of the follow-on program are reflected in the total training planned for Ethiopia.looks all

Our next country is the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The principal U.S. objective is, in conjunction with other countries, to assist the Congolese to maintain internal stability. Our aim is to enable the Congolese Armed Forces, together with civil police and other national security forces, to maintain internal security and to contribute to the development of the country. 

Most of the U.S. assistance to the Congolese Army and gendarmerie is to provide materiel. This assistance will improve internal security by providing support to those units which could be employed in operations directed against insurgent forces.

Next, in order of military assistance, is Jordan. Jordan requires a military capability in order to defend itself. The military assistance program to Jordan began in 1957 and has been maintained through fiscal year 1967. The purpose has been to provide a program to equip the Jordan Arab Army. However, in November 1966, an Israeli attack took place at the village of Samu, west of the River Jordan near the 

Dead Sea, which resulted in additional U.S. military assistance. In

December 1966, the U.S. Government and Jordan agreed on a shipment of arms and materiel. This increase raised the fiscal year 1967 program somewhat. The materiel requested was delivered on time. 

Since the inception of MAP to Jordan, the United States has provided military items, services, and training assistance. For fiscal year 

1968, we plan to provide continued assistance. 

In the last country receiving materiel assistance in this program, Liberia, our objective is to improve the ability of the host government's military forces to maintain order and to carry out civic action programs useful to the country's economic development. A third of the fiscal year 1968 program for Liberia is scheduled for training. Half of the program will provide materiel. The remaining funds will support the maintenance of previously provided materiel. 

The remaining 12 countries will receive military assistance only in the form of training. Saudi Arabia is programed for in-country training as well as training in the United States. Part of this grant aid military assistance will support the training of selected students in the United States. The remainder will support mission operations, including in-country training. 

I would now like to discuss the situation in India and Pakistan, even though there are no military assistance funds programed for either country. Neither of these two countries received grant aid military assistance in fiscal year 1967; nor is either country scheduled for grant materiel aid in fiscal year 1968. As a result of their war in 

1965, President Johnson suspended all military assistance, including foreign military sales, to India and Pakistan. Deliveries of grant aid were stopped at all points along the supply line, and we have since determined to terminate materiel grant aid to these countries. 

We have reduced the strengths of the supply mission in India and the MAAG in Pakistan through normal attrition. In line with our

1967 

new sales policies recently announced for these two countries, the final personnel adjustments are now under study. 

The remaining countries programed for grant aid military assistance in fiscal year 1968 are programed only for training in the United 

States. 

This training will be conducted in U.S. military schools or through orientation tours. Each of these programs will be administered by the accredited U.S. defense attaché during fiscal year 1968. 

The funds expended in these training programs are relatively small. 

While in the United States, foreign trainees meet and get to know many U.S. military contemporaries. Additionally, they are exposed to 

American communities and our way of life. The attitudes reflected by most foreign personnel trained in our U.S. military education system are gratifying. We try to insure that only the more promising military students are selected for this training. Many of these trainees later become military and political leaders in their home countries. 

In addition to technical and service school training, we arrange for a number of senior foreign defense officials-both military and civilian-to participate in orientation tours in the United States. 

There tours of U.S. military installations point toward a specific area of interest to the visitors, local points of interest, social contact with U.S. officers and civilian officials, and military briefings. These tours provide an excellent opportunity for the future leaders of foreign nations to gain firsthand knowledge of the American Military 

Establishment and the American people. 

There are 11 of these "training in the United States only countries." 

They are: Afghanistan, Ceylon, Ghana, Guinea, Iraq, Lebanon, Nepal, Nigeria, Senegal, Sudan, and Syria.

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee: The military assistance programs proposed for countries in the MEAFSA area have been designed to make the most effective utilization of grant aid in serving the national interest of the United States. The $53.9 million requested for fiscal year 1968 will provide minimum support to achieve U.S. objectives in my area of responsibility.

This concludes my prepared remarks. I will now entertain your questions.

 NUCLEAR NONPROLIFERATION TREATY DRAFT 

As presently constituted, the draft nuclear nonproliferation treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union would not obligate nuclear powers such as the United States or the Soviet Union to defend nonnuclear powers such as Egypt and India against nuclear attack. We have recognized and the nonnuclear states have made it clear that these nations must be provided some assurance against the threat of nuclear attack. The subject is under discussion among many nations. The State Department and ACDA will consult with the Congress as discussions evolve.

Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

Our witness this morning is Gen. Robert W. Porter, U.S. Army, Commander in Chief, U.S. Southern Command.

STATEMENT BY GEN. ROBERT W. PORTER, Jr., U.S. ARMY, COM- MANDER IN CHIEF, U.S. SOUTHERN COMMAND 

General PORTER. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a privilege to appear again before this committee and report on what the military assistance program is accomplishing in Latin America. I concluded my report to you a year go with the following statement:

A continuation of current favorable developments in Latin America and an effective fight against unfavorable developments will depend in large part on our pursuing present policies to support and advise the Latin American armed forces under the military assistance program. Besed on the experience gained from years of service and over 200,000 miles of travel in Latin America, I believe that this statement is valid today. Certainly it is in consonance with the President's 

February 9, 1967, message to the Congress on foreign aid in which he said:

The threat to our security posed by internal subversion and insurgency cannot be countered by withdrawal, isolation, or indifference.

It is too early to report to you the impact on U.S. objectives in 

Latin America of changes made in the military assistance program by the 89th Congress. However, I must state that Latin America is involved in a critical struggle to channel explosive, dynamic political and economic forces into areas where they can be of constructive value. The widely disparate problems which face our Latin American friends, and their continuing efforts to contain these turbulent forces, are not well understood.

The Alliance for Progress, keystone of U.S. policy in Latin America, encompasses within its charter the ideals and aspirations of the American Republics for the satisfaction of their social and economic needs. 

Unquestionably, the Alliance's program is a bold, imaginative under- 535

1967 

taking. However, no program of social and economic development will flourish in a climate of political turmoil and internal instability. Thus, if we are to foster the dynamic evolution of the forces which encourage social and economic development, we must assist in the establishment of that degree of internal security and political stability necessary to provide the Alliance for Progress with an environment in which to germinate. 

The strategic importance of Latin America to the United States stems from the area's geographical location, economic potentials and its continued friendly political orientation. 

Militarily, Latin America protects our southern flank. It includes within its bounds vital U.S. air and naval bases and important communications, missile and satellite tracking stations. The absence of a serious, direct threat to the United States from the south, except for the Cuban situation, has allowed the United States to devote its primary emphasis and the bulk of its resources to the more immediately threatened areas of Europe and Asia. There is no certainty that this situation will always prevail. Whether Latin America remains a source of strength for the United States or a fertile avenue of infiltration and approach by potential enemies, will largely depend on the wisdom and consistency of our policy during the next 10 years. 

The Central American isthmus is of particular strategic significance. 

It dominates the sea, land, aerial and other lines of communications between North and South America, and permits access by relatively defensible routes to the raw materials of South America. At the other end of the continent, the southern tip of South America (including the 

Straits of Magellan, Tierra del Fuego, and the Drake Passage) will assume greater strategic importance in the future. Because of Panama 

Canal limitations, increasing numbers of large tankers and warships are required to use the natural water passageways of this area. Last year, 400 oceangoing vessels transited the Straits of Magellan, and the number is increasing each year.

Next to Canada and Western Europe, more U.S. private capital is invested in Latin America than in any other area of the world. In addition, we have a long-term commitment in the Alliance for Progress to assist the Latin American people in their difficult struggle toward economic and social betterment. U.S. access to the region's key raw materials will continue to be important, despite technological advances in the development of synthetic substitutes. 

Latin America's political orientation is of the highest concern to us. Its pro-Western orientation has been evident year after year in the United Nations and other international organizations. 

Latin America's social, economic, and political problems make it a prime target for communism. The problem is magnified by very rapid population growth. This projected demographic explosion will impose rapidly growing demands on governments and underdeveloped economies, and will make Latin America even more ripe for internal disorders and Communist exploitation. 

To carry out this exploitation, Communist insurgent forces, often labeled as bandits, terrorists, guerrillas or revolutionary forces, must gain the support or at least acquiescence of the people in the area of operations by the most expedient means. These means include direct appeals for support of their cause, blackmail, terrorism, assassination and full-scale insurgency. Unless counter action is taken

537 promptly, the movement gains momentum and can eventually threaten the existence of the duly-constituted government. 

Efforts to stimulate, coordinate and unify the Communist movement in Latin America are still underway. Two major conferences have been held in Havana-one in 1964 and one in 1966. A third one-the Latin American Peoples' Solidarity Conference is scheduled to be held in Havana in late July 1967. A permanent apparatusthe Latin American Solidarity Organization (LASO)-was established as a by-product of the 1966 Havana Tri-Continental Conference. LASO's operational base is in Havana; and its objective is to encourage, support, and coordinate Communist subversion in the hemisphere. LASO is actively pursuing the goals for which it was created. 

Radio Havana, as well as Radio Moscow and Peiping, is continuously beaming subversive propaganda to Latin America. 

Cuba has already trained several thousand terrorists and guerrillas who are prepared to initiate and support disorders, riots, and insurgency whenever the situation is ripe. 

The guerrilla problem appeared to be waning in Venezuela last summer, but additional support and encouragement from Cuba produced a new series of dramatic terrorist and guerrilla actions. The continuing acts of violence have been met by firm government countermeasures. In an unprecedented act, President Leoni moved troops into the previously sacrosanct Caracas' Central University. You will recall that these troops uncovered a vast guerrilla operations center, an arsenal of weapons and a subversive propaganda mill. More recently, there has been an upsurge in guerrilla activities and an increasing capability of the Venezuelan Communists to open a third guerrilla front in the East.

Active insurgency operations continue in Colombia, despite determined government efforts to eliminate the threat. During the past few weeks, Communist guerrillas, who are operating in an area larger than South Vietnam, renewed their attacks and killed over 35 security force personnel in five widespread incidents. The government responded by declaring a state of siege in certain Departments, rounding up known subversives and launching a major counterinsurgency operation. These new Communist initiatives, and the required government countermeasures, divert additional resources from essential social and economic programs. 

You will recall that in April of last year, the interim government of Guatemala had succeeded in establishing sufficient law and order so that elections could be held. President Mendez was inaugurated, and his government has made considerable progress in controlling the terrorists and guerrillas. The Guatemalan armed forces launched major operations against two distinct Communist guerrilla movements-driving them into inaccessible jungle-covered mountains. 

The fighting continues with Castro-Communist support of the guerrillas. While contained for the present, the Communist insurgency situation in Guatemala is potentially dangerous. 

Communists have recently opened new guerrilla front in Bolivia. 

On March 23, a Bolivian army patrol was ambushed by a guerrilla band of unknown size. Seven of the patrol were killed. The remainder, including six wounded, were captured and subsequently released. 

Again on April 10, an encounter between army forces and guerrillas

1967 

in the same general area demonstrated that the guerrillas are well armed and well trained. This insurgency is potentially dangerous. 

Moreover, serious disorders, riots, and insurgency could develop rapidly in other countries. 

The Chinese and Cuban Communists have announced that they will continue to press for immediate campaigns of terrorism and guerrilla warfare. Other Communists will continue their more subtle, long-range plans to extend Communist power and influence throughout the area.

Castro's longstanding desire to assume leadership of the Communist "revolution" in Latin America, and his often stated belief that all Communists should rally to the support of Hanoi and the Vietcong, will result in continued and increasing Communist activity. One of 

Castro's objectives will be to assist the Vietcong by diverting U.S. attention and resources to other critical areas. The Communists know that events in Vietnam will have a direct bearing on the success or failure of their campaign in Latin America.

The inability of governments to attain a sufficient rate of economic development to meet social pressures, together with high population growth and the continuing migration to the cities, will continue to generate more serious problems. The urban areas will become even more the centers of power, and their masses will become more susceptible to demagogic agitation and Communist exploitation. The 

Communist movement can be expected to become more aggressive, concentrating more attention on labor, students, and the urban slums. 

When added to the already-serious situation, this increasing urben threat will create a serious internal security problem for the governments of Latin America.

The military has frequently proven to be the most cohesive force available to assure public order and support of resolute governments attempting to maintain internal security. Latin American armed forces, acting in conjunction with the police and other security forces, have helped to control disorders and riots, contained or eliminated terrorists and guerrillas, and discouraged those elements which are tempted to resort to violence to overthrow the government. The Communists and Communist-supported elements will exploit the paths of least resistance. It follows, therefore, that in most countries, any weakening of the armed forces to the extent that they could not cope successfully with insurgencv, riots, or other threats to law and order would encourage militant Communists to undertake campaigns of violence as the most expedient means of attaining their goals. 

Of course, some of the Latin American military have not always played a democratic, stabilizing role. Nevertheless, during the past year, the effectiveness of the military's internal security measures and their support of constitutional government have contributed to what can only be called a landmark in the history of Latin America. In an area where elections normally have been marked by great political agitation and violence-and where changes in government have more often than not resulted from the overthrow of the existing regimes, we have witnessed 10 elections and only one coup. 

It is significant that, in the past year, three military governments gave way to democratic rule, and that the leaders of all the countries where political changes occurred are friendly toward the United States and endorse the goals of the Alliance for Progress.

539 U.S. strategy for Latin America recognizes the importance of the 

Latin American armed forces and the valu ble contribution they can make in support of the political, social, and economic goals of the 

Alliance for Progress.

A basic goal of U.S. military strategy is to assure that Latin American governments possess the capability to maintain internal security. 

Our military assistance program supports this strategy. 

Through military assistance, we have encouraged and supported the development of small, mobile rapid-reaction forces; tactical air support; and maritime defense forces-equipped in most cases with selected, fairly modern items of U.S. equipment needed to cope successfully with the insurgent threat. Forces such as these are, today, actively engaged in counterinsurgency operations in Colombia, Guatemala, and Venezuela.

To improve the effectiveness of military forces for national and international operations, we have fostered interservice and regional cooperation, assisted in the establishment of integrated command and control centers with common operating procedures, and supported the conduct of joint/combined exercises. These efforts contribute to the successful Inter-American Peace Force operation in the Dominican Republic and the equally successful counterguerrilla campaign in Peru.

In close coordination with USAID, we have continued the emphasis on civic action as a means of helping to sustain progress toward social and economic betterment and improving the image of the armed forces in the eyes of the people. Civic action forces also contribute to internal security by representing the authority of the government in remote areas and by gaining support of the people in rural areas, thereby denying safe haven to insurgent groups. Latin American armed forces have been contributing to the national development of their countries for many years. These contributions have varied in degree of sophistication from repair of rustic schools and well drilling to highway construction and air transportation. The important thing to remember about military civic action is that it is doing essential things which otherwise would not be done at all.

Although limited by the lack of an effective military agency within the Organization of American States for the development of joint/ combined military plans, progress has been made in the area of regional organizations and activities in consonance with the intent of section 511(b) of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

The Central American Defense Council (CONDECA) is continuing to show real promise as a regional organization.

We have encouraged and supported regional conferences and seminars to consider ways and means of improving intelligence, communications, legal, medical, and logistics systems. 

In the key area of logistics, more effective logistics systems and an appreciation of resource management are beginning to emerge. Top military officials are making more realistic appraisals of the need for technically qualified manpower, natural resource development and in-country production of essential military items. At the same time, we are devoting more effort to the orientation and training of young officers in the fields of maintenance, supply and management. 

Although the Military Assistance Program is only 3.9 percent of the total United States effort in Latin America, we have used the

1967 

program and our close rapport with the Latin American military to discourage the acquisition of overly-sophisticated, non-essential equipment. With few exceptions, military equipment has been acquired from United States sources.

I believe that the Military Assistance Program's contributions to the attainment of United States objectives in Latin America more than justify the investment.

Unfortunately, there is a misconception in the minds of some Americans relative to the term "internal security" and to the objectives that are being pursued through United States military assistance. 

To some, the provision of United States military assistance constitutes an unwarranted meddling in the internal affairs of the American Republics; a contribution to the so-called "arms race" in Latin 

America; an encouragement of unnecessary, expensive or sophisticated equipment; and an indorsement of military dictatorships. 

Exaggerated press reports concerning Latin American military activities, including recent and prospective purchases of so-called sophisticated military equipment, tend to confirm these misconceptions.

The facts are that we are in Latin America at the express invitations of governments who value our advice and assistance. They appreciate our presence and consider that our efforts are in their best interests as they continue the struggle for political stability and social and economic viability.

The so-called "arms race" has been grossly exaggerated. Assistant 

Secretary Gordon properly termed it "an arms crawl." There is no evidence that any Latin American country is involving itself in a genuine arms race with its neighbors for either offensive or defensive purposes. In most cases, they are simply trying to replace obsolete, antiquated equipment which is uneconomical to maintain and sometimes unsafe to operate. Contrary to popular assertions, most countries now buying modern equipment for their armed forces are doing so, for the most part, within normal budgetary levels. 

Defense budgets in Latin America generally constitute a small portion of the national resources available. The combined defense budgets of 16 countries amount to less than 13% of the combined national budgets of these countries. Moreover, approximately 90% of these defense budgets is devoted to administrative support, force maintenance and non-military projects. In addition to military activities, the Latin American armed forces utilize their limited resources for a host of functions normally accomplished by civilian agencies in other countries.

Many of the critics of military assistance to Latin America would be surprised to learn that overall United States grant aid is running about 5% of the total military outlays of the Latin American countries. 

Nonetheless, it constitutes a very significant portion of the amount allocated to force modernization, ranging from 50% to over 90% of total force improvement expenditures in a number of cases. 

Reference to the Latin American military still conjures up images of pompus, bemedaled men-"Caudillos" with little interest in or understanding of their peoples' problems and aspirations. Mr. David 

Rockefeller has stated that: "This false concept does a disservice to many members of the armed forces in Latin America. The current generation of military

541 leaders includes men of considerable sophistication in economic and social matters, and a sincere desire to improve the lot of the poor and quicken the pace of economic growth."

I share his view. I have found most contemporary military leaders to be professionally qualified and sincerely concerned about the need for relative political stability and social and economic progress. I also see more and more young career officers from middle-class families, who have been exposed to university educations, taking on their responsibilities with a greater awareness of the socio-economic needs of their countries.

While the facts seem clear to most of us on the ground in Latin America who deal with the problem on a day-to-day basis, the misconception has prevailed. This misconception, together with the concern over more immediate problems in Asia and Europe and the competition for funds to support other essential programs, has resulted in the imposition of severe limitations on the Military Assistance Program for Latin America.

The total for grant aid and sales (except training) and for the value of ships transferred under ship loan legislation cannot exceed $85 million.

The fiscal year 1967 and fiscal year 1968 grant programs have been reduced. The final amount of the reduction will depend on the volume of sales consummated in each fiscal year. 

As I have said, it is too early to provide a detailed assessment of the impact of these limitations.

The fiscal year 1968 grant program, under consideration by the Congress, now totals $45.5 million. It includes $13 million for training and $32.5 million for materiel and related services. This leaves $52.5 million under the $85 million ceiling for cash or credit sales and for the value of ships transferred under ship loan legislation. The $13 million for training includes training in the United States, in the Canal Zone where all instruction is in Spanish, and in-country through the use of mobile training teams. The $32.5 million for materiel and related services includes $4.1 million in supply operations for delivery of materiel in prior year programs. This leaves $28.4 million for the materiel programs. These programs include communication equipment for command and control; aircraft, patrol boats and vehicles for mobility; weapons; and maintenance support. 

We do not think that the United States should fully equip the armed forces of Latin America. What we are doing at best is helping those countries establish realistic force and equipment requirements to meet the threat to their security. Within budgetary limitations of the military assistance program, we try to provide grant equipment and training to establish a small foundation upon which each country can build a modest force tailored to its own security needs. 

Under the new limitations, we are endeavoring to provide essential support to the countries with the greatest need. Other equipment must be provided from their own resources. We, of course, will make every effort to insure that U.S. sales meet the same criteria that we have established for grant aid.

Our road ahead is full of obstacles. For the foreseeable future, Latin 

America will continue to be plagued by its political, social and economic problems which will create an environment of discontent and violence. In my opinion, the main Communist campaign in Latin

1967 

America is still ahead of us; and we can expect an intensification of 

Communist subversion and insurgency efforts. 

To meet this challenge, we should continue to assist the armed forces of Latin America in all appropriate ways. 

We are prepared to utilize the resources of the U.S. Southern 

Command to continue to assist in the development of effective armed forces and to maintain close rapport with the Latin America military. 

We will continue to foster regional and subregional military cooperation and to support projects for strengthening the Inter-American security system.

We shall endeavor to take greater initiative to blunt Communist efforts in the area of propaganda and psychological warfare. 

And, we should continue to point out the key importance of Latin America and the constructive role that the Latin American military are playing in their societies to achieve Alliance for Progress goals.

General Porter, during the time that General O'Meara was in command in Panama a survey team from this committee visited the schools run by the United States in Panama to train Latin American military personnel. They brought back very favorable reports. Would you describe briefly the schools that we are now operating in training military personnel from Latin American countries, and why it is so desirable to operate schools in Panama for this purpose?

General PORTER. We have schools in which the instruction is in 

Spanish, and which use the same type unsophisticated equipment as that in the countries' armed forces. These schools-I will talk first about the Army school, which is called the School of the Americas. It has graduated about 20,000 students in its life. The school runs courses which deal with everything from the training of radio and communications technicians to a command and staff course. These courses are given to personnel of most Latin American armed forces. 

In these courses we concentrate on the problem of insurgency. We also take up the matters of training, programing, and budgeting. By association, many of the concepts and philosophies that we have in our country as far as government is concerned, and the apolitical role that our people in the military play in government rubs off on them. 

We also talk to them on civic action and the various aspects of nation. building to which the military in these countries can contribute. 

There are now beginning to be a number of graduates of these schools in key staff positions in the military forces of the various countries. This has been happening over the past 2 or 3 years, and I must say that, as a result, considerable progress has been made in liberalization of their policies and their thinking. Improvement has been made in training their young draftees, and preparing them to go back into civil life to play a useful role in the community. 

In the Air Force school we are doing about the same thing, but we are teaching principally technical courses for mechanics, radio operators, and enlisted personnel who service the aircraft that are utilized in Latin America.

The Navy has a small-craft training school of very modest size in the Canal Zone.

It is my judgment that actually, dollar for dollar, we are getting more for our money out of these schools than anything else we are doing down there. [Security deletion.]

 CHINESE COMMUNIST ROLE AND INFLUENCE IN LATIN AMERICAN INSURGENCY 

Latin America is viewed by the Chinese Communists as an area where they can expand their influence, especially among the Communist parties. They see in the area a parallel with China before they came to power and consider their methods and experience particularly applicable to Latin American Communist revolutionary efforts. They have worked hard to establish a presence and gain a position of ideological leadership through a variety of methods-cultural, propaganda, commercial, and political. Along with these activities, the Chinese have encouraged violent revolution and provided some funds and training to selected subversive groups. [Security deletion.] 

[Security deletion.] However, Peiping's call for revolution strikes a sympathetic chord among younger, more fanatical Communists, many of whom are breaking away from old-line Soviet-oriented parties and forming dissident movements dedicated to violence. The great difficulty now facing the Chinese is that these dissident elements look to Cuba rather than China. The problem of distance-Peiping's only diplomatic mission in the hemisphere is in Havana-bas been magnified by the struggle for world leadership of the Communist movement. 

The use of Cuba has been greatly restricted as a base for Chinese subversive operations, and the recent coolness in Sino-Cuban relations has tended to isolate pro-Chinese dissident groups.
