(The prepared statement of Mr. Gordon follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. LINCOLN GORDON, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTER-AMERICAN AFFAIRS, AND U.S. COORDINATOR, ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a pleasure to come before you today to speak in support of the proposed Fiscal Year 1968 A.I.D. program for Latin America under the Alliance for Progress. 

This program is designed to support the far-reaching decisions subscribed to by the Presidents of the OAS member countries at the Summit Meeting in Uru. guay two weeks ago. Before outlining the program itself, I should like to comment briefly on the character and significance of those Inter-American Pres. idential agreements.

The Summit Meeting 

This meeting was carefully prepared over a period of seven months. It concentrated by common consent on specific measures to speed economic and social development. The meeting's lack of dramatic surprises should not detract from the truly historic significance of the decisions taken by the Presidents. 

Here for the first time was a meeting of the highest political leaders of this Hemisphere focused on action to promote greater unity within Latin America and more effective inter-American cooperation to accelerate economic and social progress and to improve the conditions for Latin America's international trade. 

The Presidents were not responding to an immediate political or military crisis. 

Their discussions dealt with economic and social policy matters. But they were all aware that their decisions in these fields, and the subsequent actions to carry out these decisions, would shape the political as well as the economic destiny of the Western Hemisphere, and its position in world affairs, for many years to come. The critical decisions, notwithstanding the long process of technical preparations, would not have been made without bringing together the Chiefs of State for a definitive expression of political will at the highest level. 77-470-67-pt. 3-5 563

1967 

The essence of the Summit agreements was a vigorous reaffirmation and consolidation of the basic principles of the Alliance for Progress-Latin American national self-help for accelerated development, institutional modernization and reform, and external support organized through multilateral instruments of inter-American cooperation-but now with a strong new thrust toward Latin American economic and physical integration. 

The idea of a Latin American Common Market was converted from a vague, formless, and timeless aspiration into a specific commitment with a timetable, a definition of concrete steps for its achievement, and a procedure for putting these steps into effect.

In singling out agricultural modernization and educational improvement, along with health, for especially intensive action, the Presidents were building deliberately on the experience of the first five and one-half years of the Alliance. 

This experience had demonstrated that in these key sectors of social investment, the progress achieved, although substantial, was insufficient to meet the pressing needs of their peoples, and that higher rates of overall economic growth are directly dependent on more rapid headway in these sectors. 

Also, at Punta del Este for the first time the critical role of science and technology was given full recognition, and agreement reached on a far-reaching regional program to bring Latin America into active participation in modern developments in these fields.

The discussions of trade policy were helpful in illuminating the complementarity of aid and trade in achieving developmental goals. While our final understandings on trade policy fell short of Latin American hopes in some respects, they did open up important policy directions for the improvement of Latin America's trading position in the world without unfavorable effect on our own balance of payments and without damaging the interests of other less developed regions of the world.

The Presidents also emphasized the importance of avoiding the diversion of scarce resources into the competitive acquisition of unnecessary armaments. 

Two other major themes ran throughout the Summit preparations and discussions. One was the need to raise the targets of overall economic growth through a balanced development of industry and agriculture, not only to raise living standards but also to provide productive employment opportunities for the rapidly growing labor force. The second was the need to secure broader popular participation in the developmental process through genuinely democratic institutions such as cooperatives, trade unions, small and medium business enterprises, and local community development activities. 

In all these decisions, and in the bilateral and multilateral discussions leading up to them, there was evident a remarkable maturing of Latin American attitudes over the past few years. The Latin American leadership of today clearly recognizes its own primary responsibility for national and collective action to speed development and it displays a growing self-confidence in its capacity to carry forward these actions.

SELF-HELP PERFORMANCE 

Even as we launched the Alliance six years ago, we understood that economic development was of necessity a slow and painstaking process, which required vigilance and patience hard to come by in these urgent times. It is for this reason-because Latin America starts from an economic base so low in comparison to our own-that we cannot expect miraculous overnight transformation. 

Nevertheless, the available indicators of economic progress for the short period during which the Alliance has been in operation suggest that we have already had some visible success. 

Growth Trends

The Charter of Punta del Este enunciated a minimum goal of 2½ percent per capita GNP of growth. In 1964 and 1965, the Hemisphere surpassed that target. 

In 1966 the overall growth rate reached only about 1.1 percnt. We have every reason to believe, however, that this disappointing experience of 1966 will not be repeated, because we can trace the short fall to bad weather and a consequent drop of agricultural production in Brazil, and to a short-lived recession in Argentina. The rest of Latin America, taken together, exceeded the 22 percent per capita target.

Given the long-term nature of the development process, annual figures are less important than a broader perspective. In the past three years of the Alliance, average per capita growth has been over 2 percent. This compares very favorably

565 with an average growth of only 0.9 percent in the first three years of the Alliance. 

The trend is clearly in the right direction. 

Population and Growth 

Aside from untoward events such as droughts and recessions, the most significant element affecting per capita growth continues to be the high population growth rate which averages around three percent a year throughout Latin America. It is instructive to realize that if the U.S. population were growing at this rate, our per capita GNP growth of 4.3 percent during 1966 would have been reduced to 2.4 percent. 

Gross Investment

The Meeting of the Chiefs of State yielded vivid confirmation of changing attitudes, as I have earlier noted. The evidence from actual performance is no less dramatic. During the past six years the gross investment of the Latin countries approximated $91 billion, of which $79 billion-about 87 percentcame from within Latin America itself. During that period, United States public programs committed $6.5 billion in assistance of all kinds to these countries; other international agencies committed about $2.3 billion. The OECD (DAC) countries provided $1.1 billion. Private investment totaled $2.1 billion, bringing the total level of external commitments to Latin America to $12.0 billion for the six year period. This level represents 13 percent of gross investment during that period.

It is easy to forget that the Latin countries are carrying by far the greater share of the burden of their own development. It could not be otherwise, as the Latin 

American Presidents were clearly aware at the recent Meeting of the Chiefs of State. And they have pledged themselves to even greater internal efforts for development in the years ahead. 

Control of Inflation 

We are particularly impressed, looking back over recent history, with the determination Latin countries are exhibiting in their fight against inflation. 

Inflation has been a traditionally serious problem in many South American countries, including Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Uruguay and Bolivia. 

In all these countries, comprehensive stabilization programs have been undertaken and are achieving significant results. Brazil has cut its inflation from an annual rate of eighty percent in 1964 to about forty percent in 1966, and in recent months has brought the rate down still further. Chile is within sight of bringing inflation under control, having reduced the rate from forty percent in 1964, to seventeen percent last year, with still less expected this year. 

This record of resource mobilization and struggle against inflation shows political courage, and a new spirit of responsibility in the direction of broad economic policies in Latin America. This spirit and courage augur well for the continuing and expanded process of inter-American cooperation under the Alliance for Progress to which the program before you today is addressed. 

Political Development and Title IX 

Parallel with this evolution of general economic policies, there has been a growing concern with the broadening of direct popular participation in the process of national development. This is in line with Title IX of the Foreign 

Assistance Act added by the 89th Congress last September. It provides that: "Emphasis shall be placed on insuring maximum participation in the task of economic development on the part of the people of the developing countries, through the encouragement of democratic private and local governmental institutions." 

The traditional centralistic nature of many Latin American governments creates obstacles to dramatic progress, but there is real evidence of changing attitudes. For example, Colombia is planning a significant decentralization of responsibility for educational financing to the local community level. Peru recently completed its second municipal elections since the enactment of the new municipal election law in the fall of 1963. This law provided for elections at the local municipal level for the first time in forty-five years. Parallel with these developments, Peru has mounted a nation-wide community development program designed to broaden the base of local participation in the planning and execution of local development projects. Brazil has established a national water fund to finance locally planned and implemented water and sewer systems. Panama is carrying out a national program of assistance to those communities which are willing to invest their labor in the construction of local schools.

1967 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE SUMMIT DECISIONS 

The necessary actions to carry out the specific decisions taken at the Summit Meeting fall into various categories. With respect to the formation of a Common 

Market, the responsibility is almost wholly Latin American, and the next steps will be taken in the appropriate forums of the Latin American Free Trade Association and the Central American Common Market. As projected in President 

Johnson's message of March 13 to the Congress, we have expressed our wholehearted support for the movement toward a Latin American Common Market, and at the appropriate time recommendations will be made to the Congress for United States participation in financial arrangements to assist the Latin counries in the various types of adjustment required in the difficult period of transition to full economic integration.

Added support for multinational projects of infrastructure will be undertaken in the first instance through the Inter-American Development Bank. The Annual 

Meeting of the IDB's Board of Governors is taking place in Washington these very days, and recommendations for replenishment of its Fund for Special Operations, with special attention to the needs for multinational projects, will be submitted in the very near future to the Banking and Currency Committees of both Houses.

To help its Alliance partners work toward the new growth goals set by the meeting, and to give special emphasis to agriculture, education, health and science, A.I.D. proposes a total F.Y. 1968 program of $723.6 million in Alliance loans, technical assistance, and supporting assistance. This program includes the additional $100 million for expanded programs in these key fields as recommended by President Johnson in his message of March 13 and reaffirmed at Punta del Este. We are requesting that $10 million of this $100 million add-on be added to the Grant Technical Assistance Program to help finance some of the new multilateral programs in education and science for which the President proposed our support, particularly the Inter-American Science Foundation and the Multi- National Institutes of Science of Technology. The remaining $90 million of the proposed $100 million add-on will be used for development loans. 

Fiscal Year 1968 Program 

To finance the proposed program of $723.6 million, we are requesting New 

Obligational Authority (NOA) of $673.5 million-$643.0 million in Alliance loans and technical assistance, and $30.5 million in supporting assistance. The $643 million requested for Alliance loans and technical assistance fits well within the $750 million authorization which the Congress approved for the Alliance for Fiscal Years 1968 and 1969. However, we are asking that the provision of the 

Authorization which limits the amount which may be used for grants be raised from the present level of $100 million to $110 million for fiscal year 1968 and $115 for fiscal year 1969. This will be necessary to permit the initiation of the new multilateral programs in education and science mentioned above. 

Alliance Development Loans 

Within the FY 1968 loan program of $578.1 million [security deletion]. 

As I emphasized in my presentation last year, the program loan has proved to be an extremely useful device to complement large, well-conceived development programs requiring a high degree of self-help on the part of the host country. The policies and reforms undertaken by the countries, to which this kind of support is addressed, cover the entire range of development problems from tax reform and control of inflation, to reforms in government administration, economic planning, education and agricultural development. 

For example, in Chile A.I.D. program loans have enabled the Government to maintain a much-needed expansion of investment while, at the same time, reducing inflation from thirty-nine percent in 1964 to seventeen percent at the end of 1966. Tax revenues have increased by twenty-five percent per year in real terms during President Frei's two years in office. 

Sector Loans 

This year (Fiscal Year 1967) we have begun to use a new lending technique called the sector loan, which borrows heavily on the concept used by the Federal Government to finance state programs in health and education. In contrast to program loans, which are peculiarly suitable to realize "economy-wide" fiscal and monetary reforms, the sector loan concentrates on a single priority sector of the economy such as agriculture or education. To qualify for this type of loan, the host country must establish a sector program which includes any necessary

567 reforms in policies affecting the sector, and must increase its investment in the sector. This new lending technique will permit A.I.D. to support and encourage intensive efforts in these lagging and critical sectors. [Security deletion.] 

Project Loans 

Project loans for such purposes as private development banks, public industrial credit, urban development, community and cooperative development, road construction and maintenance, especially in rural areas, rural electrification, fertilizer imports, private industrial undertakings, and continued support for the Central American Bank for Economic Integration account for the remain ing [security deletion] amount of the proposed Fiscal Year 1968 Alliance Loan Program. 

Supporting Assistance 

This year sees the termination of two supporting assistance programs in Trinidad and Tobago and Bolivia. [Security deletion.] In addition, a small $1.5 million supporting assistance program will be continued in Haiti, to fund an on-going malaria eradication program. Except in this latter case, all of this year's supporting assistance programs for Latin America are loan programs. 

Alliance Technical Assistance 

A technical assistance program totaling $115 million is planned for Fiscal Year 1968. The major part of these funds will be used for programs in education, agriculture, health and science. A.I.D. relies heavily on the contract expertise of U.S. universities, business firms and non-profit organizations to provide assistance in specialized fields for building viable development institutions in 

Latin America. As of September 1966, over 360 A.I.D. contracts, totaling over $90 million, were operating in Latin America. Of this number, 57 were contracts with American universities totaling $39 million. 

The Partners of the Alliance program provides a wide spectrum of private sector expertise that is being utilized to achieve overall Alliance objectives. At present there are private sector groups from thirty states which are working with counterpart groups in fifteen Latin American countries in the fields of commercial investment activities, transportation problems, education needs, and development of civic organizations. 

The U.S. Department of Agriculture and A.I.D. are working jointly in fifteen countries throughout the hemisphere helping the ministries to reorganize administration, revamp price policies, and develop the institutions necessary for training, demonstration and research related to increased production and improved land use.

Approximately twenty million dollars of technical assistance is proposed for education. American universities are building counterpart centers of learning in at least twelve countries.

The American Institute for Free Labor Development (AIFLD) is helping to develop democratic trade union movements in 20 countries of the region. In addition to worker education seminars and training, AIFLD is also sponsoring a variety of social projects, such as workers' banks, low-cost housing, and community action activities. Technical assistance programs in these activities in 

Fiscal Year 1968 will total over $5 million. 

The Internal Revenue Service is assisting some eighteen countries in improving tax administration and collection. As a result of the program, which in Fiscal 

Year 1968 will total approximately $2.1 million, 13 countries have instituted programs to identify delinquent taxpayers, and for the first time tax evaders are being prosecuted.

Through the assistance of the Department of Labor, country-by country analyses of manpower requirements are being made which provide a base for developing appropriate training and education programs in Latin America. In addition to the above programs, over ten other U.S. government agencies are assisting in the Alliance effort.

THE NEW INITIATIVES 

Over the past two years, the A.I.D. program in Latin America has placed increasingly heavy emphasis on programs in the three sectors-agriculture, education and health. In Fiscal Year 1966, thirty percent and in Fiscal Year 1967 forty percent of our total program was invested in these three sectors, and in Fiscal Year 1968 we propose to allocate $465 million or sixty-four percent of our program to these sectors.

1967 Agriculture 

For Fiscal Year 1968 thirty-five percent or $299.6 million of the total A.I.D. program for Latin America is programmed for use in the development of Latin American agriculture. The reasons for this great emphasis on agriculture are: first, to enable the rapidly growing population of Latin America to reach adequate dietary levels; second, to allow agriculture, which is the largest single sector of economic activity in the Latin American region, to grow more rapidly; third, to develop Latin American resources to the point where Latin America can make a substantial contribution towards meeting the growing world food deficit; and fourth, to expand national markets and provide more customers for manufactured goods. 

Even though half of Latin America's 220 million population is engaged in agriculture, Latin America imports $600 million worth of agriculture commodities each year. The best informed estimates are that two-thirds of this present import level can and should be grown within the Latin American countries. In addition, Latin America's exports of agricultural products-particularly foodstuffs can also be increased greatly. 

Present agricultural production in Latin America is below adequate dietary levels, but above starvation levels. Food production is increasing at approximately the same rate as population is increasing; thus on a per capita basis, the position of Latin American agriculture is almost stagnant. 

In order to close the gap between the present low production levels and present needs, both to enable Latin America to increase the nutrition level and to contribute to the alleviation of the world food shortage, the Latin American farmer must be given the incentive to produce, as well as the infrastructure of storage, marketing and transportation facilities. Agrarian reform programs must be accelerated. Programs must be designed to reduce the spread between farm prices and consumer costs; to reduce the cost of agricultural inputs; to increase the use of modern technology; to increase the availability of farm credit, and to alter government policies that act as a disincentive to investment in the agricultural sector (for example, import duties, export taxes, arbitrary tax controls, unfavorable exchange rates, etc.).

A recent study published by the Inter-American Development Bank estimates that the agricultural sector of Latin America should grow by approximately five percent per year. In order to maintain a five percent growth rate, approximately 

1.5 billion dollars must be added to the approximately 2.0 billion invested in 

Latin American agriculture each year-a seventy-five percent increase. Most of this amount will have to come from within the Latin American countries themselves, but a significant portion will have to come from the external assistance provided by AID and the IDB, and the IBRD. 

Coffee diversification It is important to note the existence of a potentially serious problem in Latin American agriculture which is a cause for grave concern. Enough coffee is presently held in surplus stocks to meet world import requirements for a year and a half. At present prices production is too attractive. Brazil is the only country which has committed sizeable resources to cutting back production. Unless other countries take comparable measures, Brazil cannot be expected to continue its bold and praiseworthy program. The smaller countries, however, lack the financial resources needed to diversify their agriculture. 

The alternatives to diversification are so ominous that the United States feels it must help launch a serious diversification program. Unless production is cut back to match export quotas under the International Coffee Agreement, the Agreement will eventually collapse. If the Agreement were to fail, it is estimated that receipts from coffee would drop immediately [security deletion]. 

It might take five years for the market to turn around and prices to strengthen. 

On the upswing, they would probably exceed any reasonable long-term level. 

Such boom and bust fluctuations are ruinous to the producing countries and also damaging to consumers.

In Fiscal Year 1968, A.I.D. proposes to lend approximately $15 million to the coffee diversification fund proposed to be established and financed primarily by the producing members of the International Coffee Agreement. This loan is the support proposed by the President in his speech at Punta del Este to stimulate and encourage a world attack on the chronic oversupply of coffee with all its disastrous consequences for the earning capabilities of the less developed coffee producers.

569 Education The expansion and reform of educational systems is a necessary prerequisite for adequate rates of economic growth in every developing country. Nearly all 

Latin American countries have made progress during the last five years in expanding educational opportunities. Since 1961 primary school enrollments have increased by twenty-three percent, secondary school enrollment by fifty percent and university enrollment by thirty-nine percent. Most countries have increased their university budgets by 150 to 200 percent. 

While these achievements are significant, they have not been nearly enough to begin to keep up with Latin America's rapidly expanding population, and to close the gap created by Latin America's overwhelming educational deficit. 

Fifty percent of Latin American school age youth are still not enrolled in primary school. Primary school dropout rates are around seventy-five percent. Secondary school dropout rates often reach eighty percent, and the number of adult illiterates has reached fifty million. Quality gains in Latin American education have not matched quantitative expansion. Limited resources have been devoted principally to the construction of classrooms and the raising of teachers salaries. 

Budget allocations for books, teacher training, laboratory equipment, audio visual aids and curriculum modernization have been grossly inadequate. 

Latin America's current annual investment in education is about $2.5 billion. 

Total external assistance (including $41 million from AID) in the current year is about $90 million or less than four percent of the total investment. For maximum effect, A.I.D. assistance must be channeled into undertakings of highmultiplier value which stress modernization and reform rather merely "bricks and mortar."

From the inception of the Alliance for Progress through June 30, 1966, education and planning offices have been established in eleven countries with U.S. assistance, either through A.I.D. or the Social Progress Trust Fund of the Inter- 

American Development Bank; 24,500 classrooms were built; 26,000 new teachers were trained; and over 100,000 teachers were given refresher courses. 

A.I.D. assistance to Latin American universities is helping to transform them into institutions capable of producing the trained scientists, agronomists, engineers and businessmen which these rapidly modernizing societies need. A.I.D. has over fifty-two contracts (which have a total value of over $34.6 million) with 

U.S. universities to provide technical assistance to Latin American universities. 

In Peru and Brazil, technicians from U.S. universities have helped to establish outstanding land-grant-type colleges. Faculty members have received up-to-date training in the U.S. and have returned to their universities to organize new courses of instruction. In Colombia, Brazil and Peru Schools of Business Administration have been reorganized and up-graded with the help of U.S. universities, and students are now being taught by the casebook method. At the three major 

Ecuadorian universities science and engineering laboratories have been established to provide for student experimentation. In almost all of the universities assisted by A.I.D. the numbers of students enrolled and the numbers of graduates have greatly increased. Library resources have been improved and the number of full time faculty has increased. 

The IDB contribution to university development in Latin America has also been considerable. They have provided loans amounting to $66 million for the construction and equipment of university buildings, libraries and laboratories, as well as technical assistance.

In order to continue and expand these programs, A.I.D. proposes that $130 million be utilized in Fiscal Year 1968 to augment the attack on Latin America's educational deficit. The fiscal 1968 program gives high priority to expansion of national programs to provide secondary, vocational and higher education. Also included are programs to initiate a multilateral program to assist the countries in education planning, research and curricula modernization, as well as a multinational training center in educational television and a pilot educational television demonstration project in Central America. This program also provides for increased support to scholarship and fellowship programs to cope with the immediate critical shortage of professional manpower in fields of high priority to economic and social development. The successful program of textbook translation and distribution will be expanded in Fiscal Year 1968. 

Science and Technology

At the recent Summit meeting, the Presidents gave heavy emphasis to the role of science and technology in the development process. They agreed to expand national science programs to promote the training of scientists and technicians,

1967 

and to foster conditions favoring the full utilization of scientific and technical talent in the solution of development problems. The Presidents also agreed to establish a Regional Science Program. One main element of this program calls for the establishment of multinational Institutes of Science and Technology to serve as Latin American centers of excellence in graduate and post-graduate level research and training in the sciences closely related to development problems. 

In addition, the President proposed that an Inter-American Science Foundation be established to assist national programs by providing grants for research and equipment, award fellowships, and give leadership to science teaching at all levels throughout the hemisphere.

The Presidents directed that the Inter-American Cultural Council shall call a meeting of high-ranking, qualified persons, experienced in science, technology and university education within 120 days of the conclusion of the Summit Meeting. This group will make recommendations on the administration, financing, and location of the Multi-National Institutes of Science and Technology. In addition, we will suggest that this group make recommendations on the organization, responsibilities, and financing of an Inter-American Science Foundation. 

REVIEW OF MAJOR POLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS 

Before concluding this presentation, I should like to summarize the main political developments in Latin America during the past year. 

In this period, two new countries reached independent status: Guyana in May, 1966 and Barbados in November, 1966. Both countries have joined the United 

Nations. Trinidad and Tobago, which became independent earlier, has now joined the OAS as its 22nd member. Jamaica and Barbados have under review the possibility of joining the OAS. [Security Deletion]. 

Representative government has been strengthened and the crisis atmosphere of the early years of the Alliance has substantially passed. There were nine elections in Latin America last year. 

Some of them took place in countries where governments had been particularly unstable, yet all election results have been respected. 

The peaceful election and inauguration of President Balaguer in Dominican Republic were encouraging signs, that the democratic stability prerequisite to development can be maintained on that island. 

The actions of the administration of Carlos Lleras Restrepo since his accession to the presidency of Colombia promise well for the future development of that country. [Security deletion]. 

During 1966 and early 1967 four Central American countries held elections— 

Costa Rica, Guatemala, Nicaragua and El Salvador. Costa Rican voters demon strated the effectiveness of their democratic system by transferring the office of president to the opposition party in the elections of March, 1966. The new government failed to win a majority in the legislative assembly, however, [security deletion]. In Guatemala, a military regime handed over the reins of government on July 1, 1966, to the popularly elected candidate of an opposition party. After a difficult initial period marked by violence from extremists of both the Right and the Left, the Mendez Montenegro administration has checked guerilla insurgency, and is now moving ahead with an ambitious program of development and social reforms within the framework of the Alliance for Progress. In Nicaragua, the February, 1967, presidential elections were held on schedule, although marred by violence prior to election day. 

The President-elect, Anastasio Somoza, is to take office in May. In El Salvador, the voters, faced with a choice among political ideologies covering the spectrum from Right to Left, selected a moderate candidate in free elections held in March, 1967. 

The inauguration of President Costa e Silva of Brazil is a major step in the return of that country to full constitutional procedures. The extra-constitutional powers asserted by the previous regime have lapsed. The National Renovation 

Alliance party, which supported Castello Bronco and Costa e Silva, won a twothirds majority in freely contested Congressional elections last November. The new administration is maintaining the main elements of the economic reform program initiated by the previous government. It is making a determined effort to give greater attention to the immediate economic hardships of the people, by establishing better relations with labor and students, and by supporting the vigorous development of the private sector. [Security deletion]. 

Despite two rather well publicized domestic political setbacks, President Frei continues his effective leadership of Chile [security deletion].

571 The government's program of "revolution in liberty" continues to make advances in reducing inflation, mobilizing revenues for developments, massive improvement in the quality and scope of educational opportunities. Chile is facing the problem of all democracies with great social deficits of trying to keep expenditures in line with resources. Recognizing that revenues from copper sales were higher than in previous years, and determined that this windfall should not result in a general demand to loosen discipline in the fight against inflation, Chile decided not to request a program loan from the United States this year. 

With the recent decline in copper prices, there may be a need to review this decision.

In November 1966, Uruguayan voters elected to adopt a new constitution sponsored by majority elements of the two major parties and chose as president, Oscar D. Gestido. The new constitution does away with the former collegiate system of having nine presidents and should allow much more effective leadership by the executive. In the 10 years since his retirement from the Air Force, General Gestido has served in a number of senior government administrative positions. He [security deletion] has indicated his intention of carrying out a stabilization and development program to put the country back on its feet. 

In Ecuador, the military junta which had ruled the country since July of 1963, relinquished power early last year to a civilian provisional president. Since that time an elected Constituent Assembly has been seated and as its first item of business elected Otto Arosemena Gomez as Interim Constitutional President. 

Direct Presidential elections have been scheduled for June, 1968. [Security deletion.]

In summary, all but one of the unconstitutional changes of government which have occurred since the Alliance for Progress was born have been succeeded by governments selected through constitutional procedures. The Argentine regime is now concentrating on economic reconstruction, and it has indicated its ultimate intention to reestablish a constitutional and democratic political order. The frequency of unscheduled changes of government or military coups in the hemisphere has declined, as civilian regimes have given their people positive leadership in programs of economic and social development. It is one of the more significant achievements of the Alliance for Progress that governmentswhether civilian or military-which come to power must now prove to the people that they are acting on their behalf. [Security deletion.] 

The progress of such regimes as Paraguay in liberalizing the political system is further confirmation of this encouraging trend, President Alfredo Stroessner's announced program of building the political institutions of his country was carried a step further in February 1967 by the legal recognition of the opposition Liberal Party. Two other opposition parties had been recognized in 1962 and 1964. The entry of these parties into the nation's political life together with increasing freedom of the press, represents a major achievement in Paraguay. 

In May 1967, Paraguay will hold elections for a National Assembly which will prepare a new constitution. The Alliance for Progress, by fomenting the creation of more effective and more numerous institutions devoted to development also promotes a more middle class mentality and middle-level manpower dedicated to promoting economic and social growth and development. 

Despite these encouraging signs, it must still be recognized that the political development of some countries of Latin America has a long way to go. Given the major continuing problems of economic and social development, this fact is not surprising. Nevertheless, the experience of the first six years of the Alliance suggests that evolution toward stable democratic political institutions must be encouraged by specific programs directed toward this end. Also, this evolution will be faster when it is accompanied by rapid rates of economic growth. 

Parallel with this evolution of general economic policies, there has been a growing concern with the broadening of direct popular participation in the process of national development. This is in line with Title IX of the Foreign Assistance 

Act, added by the 89th Congress last September, as has already been mentioned. 

Military Assistance Program 

The Military Assistance portion of our program in Latin America in FY 1968 was discussed in detail with you yesterday by General Porter. 

During the past year, Communist-supported subversion has continued as a potential threat to the political stability of many Latin American countries. In such cases, Governments have found it necessary to divert energy and resources from constructive nation-building in order to protect their people from guerrillas

1967 

and terrorist bands. While these bands are meeting with little military success, even in the three countries where the threats to stability have been most persistent-Colombia, Guatemala and Venezuela, this is no cause for relaxing vigilance. Indeed, very recent guerrilla outbreaks in Bolivia underline the necessity for such vigilance.

Communist intentions to support increased Latin American (as well as African and Asian) insurgency were reaffirmed at the so-called Tri-Continental Conference at Habana in January, 1966, which created the Habana-based Tri- Continental Organization (AALAPSO) to carry out their objections of assisting what the Communists call "Wars of National Liberation." A closely allied 

Latin American Solidarity Organization (LASO) was also created for the same purpose. LASO's first full "solidarity" conference has been scheduled for late 

July in Habana. Only a few weeks ago, in March of this year, Castro again called on his Latin American followers to launch new campaigns of violence. 

Despite the fact that there is considerable disagreement inside the international Communist movement (e.g., among the Cubans, Soviets, Chinese, and Latin 

American Communist and other extremist Marxist groups) the prospect is for new outbreaks of Communist-sponsored violence in Latin America in the coming year, posing further challenges to selected governments and Alliance for Progress goals.

In recognition of this, the United States Foreign Assistance program for FY 1968 includes $85 million of military assistance in grants and credits and $13 million for training expenses to help Latin American governments preserve internal stability against Communist-backed disruption. Through the AID Public 

Safety program, assistance is also planned to improve the capabilities of Latin American police forces as the first line of defense against subversion and violence. 

The maintenance of internal security is a necessary condition of economic and social progress and the growth of political democracy. It would be short-sighted to fail to maintain vigilance on this front or to curtail further our modest support for this indispensable form of insurance. I urge the Committee to give its full support to these program proposals. 

A.I.D. and the U.S. Balance of Payments 

In closing, I would like to say a few words about the relationship of our A.I.D. program to our own balance of payments. It has been suggested from time to time that U.S. foreign aid disbursements have a negative impact on the U.S. balance of payments.

In the case of Latin America this concern is not borne out by an examination of the data for recent years since aid-tying procedures have become more effective. Latin America has not been using U.S. assistance and other earnings in the 

United States to finance net purchases or to service debt in other industrialized countries. Rather, the data suggest that for three of the last four years, Latin 

America has earned apparent surpluses with Europe and Japan; moreover, in 

1965 and 1966, Latin America (including the IDB) has been in deficit with the United States (on a liquidity definition of the U.S. balance). In spite of a substantial increase in its total foreign exchange reserves in recent years, Latin America's holdings of gold have declined by $435 million since 1961. Since the beginning (1961) of the Alliance for Progress, the U.S. share of the Latin American market declined initially, but has subsequently been maintained. This is the case even when the calculation excludes imports financed by U.S. aid. (There is an increase, of course, still greater when such imports are included.) 

Similar trends are apparent in those countries in which U.S. assistance is high. 

Improved techniques for utilizing A.I.D. dollars which were put into effect by the largest aid recipients during the last two years are helping to increase the U.S. market share in those countries. This record shows that U.S. economic assistance to Latin America has not created difficulties for the U.S. balance of payments, and there is no evidence that a reduction in such assistance would in any way improve our balance of payments. 

With this as background, I would like to call your attention to the President's remarks at the Summit Meeting on a proposal, which is very attractive in Latin America, that the U.S. permit Latin suppliers to bid for procurement orders, financed by A.I.D. funds. Referring to this proposal, the President said: "I have been informed of the great importance which you attach to the use of Alliance for Progress funds to finance procurement in other Alliance for Progress countries as well as in the United States. I know that you are all aware of the United States balance of payments problems and we deeply appreciate your cooperation in helping us meet them.

573 "The cooperative nature of our Alliance is very important to me. I want you to know that we shall undertake consultations on this matter. We shall try to establish whether we can agree that aid funds for capital projects and related technical assistance can be used in Alliance for Progress countries in ways which will protect the U.S. balance of payments." 

I have been consulting with the subcommittee on Latin American affairs of both the House and Senate and various other Members of Congress on a concrete proposal to meet long felt Latin American aspirations without endangering our own balance of payments. 

[Security deletion.] CONCLUSION 

The Hemispheric Meeting of Chiefs of State has given a new impetus to the Alliance for Progress. Latin America is prepared to raise its growth targets, increase its self-help, and move rapidly toward the creation of a Common Market. 

It is in our interest to increase our cooperation with Latin America to help them achieve these goals which are vital to the peace and security of the Hemisphere. Mr. Chairman, I urge the Committee and the Congress to support these requests for funds in Fiscal Year 1968 which in the opinion of the President, which I fully share, are the minimum to fulfill U.S. responsibilities as an Alliance partner.
