 U.S. INFORMATION AGENCY PROGRAM IN LATIN AMERICA 

Over the years the U.S. Information Agency has developed effective techniques to get America's message across to audiences where it will do the most good. 

These techniques involve use of the mass media, exhibits, seminars, binational center activities, and educational and cultural exchanges. Particular attention is given to the selection of people for field posts who can speak the language of the country and who are fully knowledgeable in Agency techniques and policies. 

Today USIA has people at 42 major posts in every Latin American country except Cuba and including Guyana, French West Indies, Jamaica and Trinidad. 

The Agency also provides personnel assistance to 113 binational centers in 19 countries. There are a total of 307 American employees, and 790 local employees in Latin America.

OVERALL POLICY LINES 

The U.S. Information Agency is committed to furthering the objectives of the 

Alliance for Progress by all means at its command. It seeks to promote greater awareness of what the Alliance is attempting to bring about in this hemisphere and endeavors, through the printed and spoken word, to stimulate Latin Americans to participate fully in this great cooperative venture. 

The emphasis in this effort is placed on output to increase understanding of the meaning of the Alliance by (1) showing through example the benefits it is achieving for the individual; (2) stressing the responsibility of the Latin 

Americans to help themselves; and (3) explaining the advantages of working through democratic systems.

601 USIA is increasing its emphasis on building the image of the U.S. as a strong, trustworthy leader toward a peaceful and secure future. This is being done by (1) stressing the progressive character of our society, and its diversity, embodying elements of the program of the Great Society; (2) countering stereotype criticisms of the United States, especially among Latin American university students; (3) deepening appreciation for U.S. cultural values; and (4) emphasizing U.S. support for international organizations, particularly the Organization of 

American States, as the best means of achieving world peace and social and economic progress, within a framework of law, order and social justice. 

The Agency exposes the true nature of Communism, as contrasted with its promises, by (1) unmasking its failures to satisfy the legitimate aspirations of its people; (2) alerting Latin America to active Communist subversion and 

Communist-aided insurgency; and (3) exploiting the Cuba story as an example of Communist methods in this hemisphere. 

USIA operations vary from country to country, with Public Affairs Officer at each post responsible for choosing the best way to tell America's story. 

In each case, the Public Affairs Officer gears his programs to the objectives set out for him by the Ambassador. USIA field operations are fully integrated into the country team concept, and all its operations at the country level are a part of the total United States Government effort in that particular country. 

AUDIENCES 

Even though Agency efforts vary from country to country, it is possible to generalize about the major audiences that all posts are trying to reach. Perhaps the most significant of these, in terms of the present as well as the future, is the student audience.

The Latin American university student is similar in many ways to students everywhere. He is impressionable, eager for experiences that will help mould his future, impatient with the past. He is also living in a very special intellectual and political climate. For the Latin Amercan university s a hotbed of political ferment, sheltered by the concept of university autonomy which prevents normal police, governmental or community intervention in university affairs. 

This fact has allowed the Latin American university to become privileged ground for the Communists. They have taken advantage of it to gain control of student movements, influence the appointment of leftist instructors, and introduce Communist literature and ideas. 

In view of the above, the Agency has an uphill fight to get its message to university students. In addition to use of various media products, USIA is attempting to reach them through seminars, travel grants to the United States, informal discussions, books and activities at binational centers. The binational center is one of the principal points of contact with students, and for this reason the Agency is devoting a great deal of effort to strengthening this program. 

Labor continues to be another priority audience. The Agency has special programs designed to influence the labor audience along democratic lines. Increased personal contact and further experience with Latin American labor, coupled with more and better media products from Washington, have extended the reach of USIA posts in activities directed toward labor. 

The Agency has produced cartoon books, motion pictures, radio programs, and other materials on labor themes, and USIA posts hold seminars and discussion groups with important leaders of the labor movement. They show films in union halls, and establish labor libraries in locations where they will be heavily patronized by trade union members. They edit magazines read by labor leaders. 

Agency officers in the field are also in daily contact with the communicators in each country, that is the people who run newspapers, radio stations, and the like, through which the U.S. message can be carried throughout the country. 

To implement these general policy guidelines aimed at varied audience groups, USIA employs a wide range of programs in the various media. RADIO Voice of America (VOA) short-wave services to Latin America now program 12½ hours daily in regular airshow time, of which nine are in Spanish and the balance in Portuguese to Brazil. An additional hour in service feeds is transmitted daily for rebroadcast on individual radio stations and networks. 

Far more significant in terms of local audiences, however, are the USIA programs carried by standard band stations all over Latin America. Upwards

1967 

of 1,500 Latin American radio stations are now broadcasting USIA programs to their local audiences, to the tune of more than 11,000 hours per week. This includes direct relay of VOA shortwave broadcasts, VOA feature materials provided to them on tape, and local radio production of field posts. 

Included in this material are programs directed especially to Cuba. These go out over regular shortwave frequencies, and also over one medium-wave transmitter located in the Florida Keys. The programs are aimed at keeping the people of Cuba informed about our foreign policy positions and world happenings in general.

USIA programs about Cuba also are heard in the rest of the hemisphere. They tell of the harsh experiences sustained by the people of Cuba under Communist tyranny and point to the economic and political weaknesses of the Castro regime. 

PRESS AND PUBLICATIONS 

The daily wireless file to Latin America via radio teletype, averaging 50,000 words per week in the Spanish language, goes to all major posts. It consists of important texts, foreign policy pronouncements of top people in government, interviews, features, and news stories of significance to U.S. foreign policy. A separate file in English goes to Rio for translating into Portuguese. 

USIA officers in the field make many uses of this output. Much of it is adapted for placement in foreign newspapers. It also provides background material for officers in their daily contact with foreign news media and government officials. 

The press office in Washington also sends, by mail, an average of 15,000 words of feature material and 2,000 photos weekly to field posts. This consists of special packets, illustrated press features, picture stories, and items of special interest and significance to student and labor audiences relating to the Alliance for Progress and anti-Communism. 

The Agency produces many types of publications, including cartoon books which have been printed and distributed in excess of 60 million copies during the past several years. The cartoon book format is particularly effective in reaching mass audiences in areas where effective literacy is generally low. 

In its use of the printed word, the Agency concentrates most heavily on positive themes related to accomplishments under the Alliance for Progress, and the democratic process. 

MOTION PICTURES 

USIA produces an average of 20 documentary films a year on global themes. 

Besides this, there is considerable film production directed specifically to one or another country or area of the world. 

For Latin America, USIA has a regular monthly filmed news digest titled Horizons which is placed primarily in commercial theaters. This reel deals with economic, social, political progress in Latin America and developments within the United States which have special interest or adaptability to Latin America. 

The Agency also produces specialized films of a documentary nature. Among these, for example, are the self-help series, such as the School at Rincon Santo, which tells how an impoverished Colombian rural community banded together to build a schoolhouse. As in the case of pamphlets, USIA has found the animated cartoon to be an effective way of carrying USIA message through films. 

All films serviced from Washington to Latin America are dubbed into Spanish (or Portuguese, as appropriate) for immediate local use. In addition to use in commercial circuits, field posts make extensive use of them through selective showings to student and labor audiences, mobile unit trips into working-class residential areas of the large cities and to campesino gatherings in the countryside, and screenings by the Ambassador to top leaders of the country. Thus 

USIA films reach key audiences all over the area. 

TELEVISION 

This medium has continued to grow tremendously. No longer is it restricted to the upper middle class. Today television antennas appear in vast numbers in the poorer areas of the great cities. TV is increasingly becoming a medium which can and does reach vast urban audiences in almost all Latin American countries. 

USIA programming on television attempts to keep pace with this growth. For the past several years USIA has produced a weekly TV show for the area which was shown regularly on 114 Latin American TV stations. USIA is now revamping this show to give it even greater viewer appeal and impact.

603 One of the recent USIA television efforts is a 26-episode dramatized series which promotes self-help by depicting how the people of a typical urban middle to lower class residential neighborhood band together to improve health, education, and other faciilties. A second dramatic series deals with the efforts of a crusading 

Latin journalist to expose Communist efforts in his country. 

Other recent television productions dealt with the Communist-sponsored Tri- Continental Conference in Havana, the fifth anniversary of the Alliance for Progress, and the visit of Astronauts Gordon and Armstrong to Latin America. 

The Agency has also adapted two television specials on Viet Nam, which were produced by Latin Americans, to give its output on this difficult issue a Latin perspective. BOOKS In the 1966 fiscal year, 431 titles and reprints in 4,403,868 copies were published in Spanish and Portuguese under the Latin American Book Program of the Agency, which functions under contract, with Latin American commercial publishers and distributors. Since 1963, the first year in which there was a sharp upturn in USIA supported publishing activities in Latin America, about 1,200 titles and reprints in more than 12 million copies have come out in Spanish and Portuguese. 

Twenty-nine titles in 145,000 copies in English were also published under this program during the 1966 fiscal year. These titles are in the Ladder Series, i.e., books in simplified English designed primarily for students of English. The 

Ladder Series were introduced into Latin America for the first time in FY 1965. 

Through its translation program, the Agency has made available to key Latin American groups at relatively low prices a broad selection of important American books in history, the social sciences, international relations, natural science and technology, literature and the arts. University and secondary school teachers and students, professionals and intellectuals, political and military leaders, businessmen, and labor leaders have been prime target groups. The quality of the books translated has been demonstrated by the fact that many Latin American universities have adopted program books as texts or collateral reading. 

As the program has gathered momentum and as Latin American publishers have gained more confidence in the program from the point of view of their own profits, they have become more willing to sign contracts calling for reduced subsidies. Thus, the Agency is reducing its support gradually but still maintaining much the same scope and magnitude of the program. 

The Agency is giving increased attention to the distribution and promotion of program books and its Regional Book Officers are traveling constantly in the area in order to ensure that USIA books are reaching the book buying public in Latin America. USIA efforts along these lines have contributed to an overall improvement in the book distribution network in the area. 

CULTURAL OPERATIONS 

The Agency conducts many and diverse cultural activities, such as exhibits, concerts, lectures, and seminars, to convey to the foreign audience a broad spectrum of historical and contemporary cultural development in the United States. 

USIA cultural affairs officers have field responsibility for the cultural and educational exchange programs of the Department of State. Great care is exercised to ensure that educational exchange grants to visit the United States are awarded to the best qualified candidates, whose selection will further U.S. foreign policy objectives. USIA is responsible also for arrangements and publicity for American performing artists and groups visiting Latin America under the cultural presentations program. In many Latin American countries, Agency libraries and reading rooms offer unusually fine facilities to students, government officials, journalists and intellectuals. Two outstanding examples in the area are the Benjamin Frank lin Library in Mexico City and the Abraham Lincoln Library in Buenos Aires. 

The varied collections of books, periodicals, and reference materials offer a comprehensive view of past and present U.S. life and culture. 

In recent years, binational centers have become important and prestigious cultural institutions in the 111 Latin American communities where they now flourish. They have developed far beyond the original concept of English-teaching institutes. While still essentially cultural by nature, binational centers are now more actively engaged in promoting such objectives as the Alliance for Progress and democratic development.

1967 

Binational centers afford particularly effective contact with university students, who come to learn English, utilize library facilities, participate in social activities, or attend the seminars and forums. Twenty-two student affairs officers assigned to large centers located in university cities are actively engaged in developing dialogues with Latin American students, participating in student activities, and assisting in educational exchange programs. 

RESEARCH 

A vital aspect of the total Agency effort in Latin America involves the selective use of research to assure that media products are on target and that the message they carry is right for the intended audience. 

USIA makes regular studies of some of its programs to get audience reactions. 

Of equal utility are are the various studies Agency researchers have made into the attitudes of the principal audience groups in Latin America. It is important, for example, to know in general what these groups think about various issues. 

An example of the value and application of research is the recent study of the misconceptions about the United States and U.S. policies held by Latin 

American students. Utilizing this study, the Agency is developing carefully tailored pamphlets, feature articles, speeches, films and related materials for field officers to use in their student activities. In this way, USIA hopes in time to overcome these misconceptions, or at least make its case abundantly understood by students in all of Latin America. 

After a period of time has elapsed in the presentation of the U.S. message, Agency researchers again study Latin American attitudes to ascertain the effectiveness of the presentation in influencing public opinion. This final refinement of the research science increasingly enables the Agency to determine the value and efficiency of its various informational programs.

 TAX DELINQUENCY LAWS IN LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES, COLLECTION FIGURES, AND GROUPS AFFECTED 

The citation Mrs. Kelly is referring to on p. 18 of Mr. Gordon's testimony reads as follows: IRS is assisting some 18 countries in improving tax administration and collections. Thirteen countries have instituted programs to identify delinquent taxpayers and for the first time tax evaders are being prosecuted. 

The thirteen countries are: Argentina Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Equador, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay.

IRS indicates that the percentage of collections of delinquent accounts and returns to total receipts are not yet available for all countries. The tax teams in the countries indicated are working to develop data of this kind as a by-product of tax statistics management. However, because the installation of such a system requires a high level of sophistication, it is anticipated that the process will be a long, hard one. 

While total statistical data is not available at this time, representative items from country reports are listed below: 

Brazil: "After inflationary adjustment, receipts for the year (1966) average out at 29.3% above receipts for last year; not included is 900 million cruzeiros which did not come into the Treasury due to tax investment concession given on income taxes. 50% over last year (1965)".

In a special taxpayer compliance measurement program conducted in four cities of Brazil for returns filed or due in 1965, the percentage of non-filers averaged about 47%. In auditing the first 613 of these cases the total additional tax assessed amounted to over $200,000.

 AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, LATIN AMERICA HOUSING GUARANTY 

PROGRAM 

The Latin America Housing Guaranty Program consists of three phases. The first of these includes all relevant Congressional authorizations through the FAA of 1964 totalling $250,000,000 designed to create "pilot demonstration" projects similar to FHA insured projects in the United States. 

Phase two comprises the $150,000,000 authorized in the FAA of 1965 for the purpose of "institution building," which includes the following four programs: 

1. Credit Institutions 2. Housing Projects for Lower Income Families 3. Institutions Important to the Alliance 4. Local Participation 

Phase three is the renewed pilot demonstration program authorized by the 1966 FAA, which increased the guaranty authority by $50,000,000.

Mr. GROSS. Why should we give anything to these areas? 

Mr. GORDON. They are of great interest to us. They are of strategic interest. In fact, the tendency has been, since they have become independent especially, for their trading patterns to shift in the direction of the United States as well. 

Mr. GROSS. Is there any area of the world, any country in the world, any territory in the world, that we are not interested in if they want some money from us?

Mr. GORDON. We don't supply money to all of the countries in Latin 

America. I would say there is no part of the Western Hemisphere in which we don't have a very considerable strategic and economic interest.

Mr. GROSS. How much do the Latin American countries pay in debt service charges; that is, amortization of interest? 

Mr. GORDON. During calendar year 1966 the total paid in amortization, including Brazil, was $1,034 million and in interest, including Brazil, $284 million, making a grand total of $1,665 million, including Brazil. 

Mr. GROSS. Are any of them delinquent?

Mr. GORDON. Not significantly. I believe there was one very small delinquency, but I would like to submit that for the record if I might. 

Mr. GROSS. I wish you would along with the loans that have been converted to grants, if any. 

Mr. GORDON. Certainly.

Mr. Selden.

Mr. SELDEN.  

Mr. Secretary, yesterday General Porter indicated in his testimony that while antiguerrilla activity in Guatemala had been stepped up considerably and the situation there had improved the situation had deteriorated to some extent in Venezuela, Colombia, and Bolivia. Is that statement confirmed by your information?

Mr. GORDON. Yes. It depends on which time period you are taking. 

In Venezuela it is a lot better than it was 3 or 4 years ago. But the guerrillas are being more active than they were 6 or 8 months ago. 

Mr. SELDEN. Is it worse than it was 6 months ago? 

Mr. GORDON. Yes; and in Colombia also.

Mr. SELDEN. We have been appropriating funds each year for a number of years, and I think correctly so, for antisubversive training and equipment in the different countries of Latin America on a bilateral basis. How do you account for the fact that in Guatemala, for example, antisubversive activities are having some effect, but in Colombia and Venezuela and Bolivia the situation is deteriorating? 

Mr. GORDON. I don't think it has anything to do with the training or equipment. I think it has to do with the targets of opportunity which the guerrillas have selected. To some extent there are differ-

615 ences of policy among the different Communist groups within these countries. In the case of Guatemala basically the improvement can be accounted for by the fact that the army in cooperation with the police forces is undertaking a more effective effort [security deletion]. 

In the case of Colombia and Venezuela the police have been working strenuously for years. There is no reduction in their efforts to try to cope with this thing. What there has been in the last few months has been an increase in the actual terrorist activity [security deletion]. 

Given the conditions of terrain, a small group like that can do a great deal of damage. It really requires an organized force which is many times its size in order to cope with it effectively. 

Mr. SELDEN. You indicate there are just a few hundred guerrillas. 

How do you account for the Government of Guatemala being able to effectively counter the efforts of a few hundred guerrillas in equally bad terrain and the armies and the Governments of Venezuela and 

Colombia being unable to do so?

Mr. GORDON. I don't think I would put it that way, Mr. Selden. 

The Guatemalan situation has improved, but the Guatemalan situation relatively was much worse before [security deletion]. 

Mr. SELDEN. Your testimony and General Porter's testimony in this connection are contrary. He feels the situation has greatly improved in Guatemala and many of the guerrillas have been either captured or killed.

Mr. GORDON. I agree with this. 

Mr. SELDEN. But this is not the case in Colombia and Venezuela. 

Are these differences due to the differences of attitude of the Governments in power? Is the Government of Guatemala making a greater effort to counter these guerrilla activities than the Governments of 

Venezuela and Colombia?

Mr. GORDON. I don't think so. I think the basic point is that the 

Guatemalan situation was very bad a year ago [security deletion]. It has greatly improved because the Government through the army and police and also through various civic activities has taken effective measures. In Guatemala there are a number of parts of the countryside where recently they have organized demonstrations of local townspeople, the farmers and so on, in support of the Government, to show that they want law and order and want to be able to develop in peace and they don't want this kind of guerrilla activity [security deletion]. 

Mr. SELDEN. [Security deletion.] Mr. GORDON. [Security deleton.] In the case of Colombia and 

Venezuela, they have been working at this for years and working hard. 

The situation in those countries is not nearly so bad as the Guatemalan situation was a year ago. That is what I mean by saying that Guatemala had a great deal more room for improvement and the Government's actions, in fact, have improved. 

Mr. SELDEN. I gathered from the testimony yesterday, and I could tell from Mrs. Kelly's questions that she did also, that antiguerrilla efforts in Guatemala are much greater and more effective today than in Columbia and Venezuela. That was from the testimony we received yesterday, and I was interested in getting your comments on it. 

I would like to ask several questions on another problem. How much has been authorized and appropriated by our Government to the so called Social Progress Trust Fund? 

Mr. GORDON. The Social Progress Trust Fund is now practically ex pired.

That was set up, as you recall, in 1961 pursuant to the Act of

1967 

Bogotá. Our original contribution to it was $394 million. The following year there was one supplementary contribution of $131 million.

Mr. GORDON. No, sir; I believe that was 1963.

In 1964 it was decided to put an end to the Social Progress Trust Fund but to enlarge the Fund for Special Operations of the Bank and to let its funds be used for the kind of purposes that the Social Progress Trust Fund had been used for. We increased our contribution to that to a rate of $250 million a year and are now proposing starting this year to raise it to $300 million. 

Mr. SELDEN. I am interested at this point only in the Social Progress Trust Fund, and, as I understand your testimony, we have authorized and appropriated $525 million. 

Mr. GORDON. That is right.

Mr. BRONHEIM. $501 million has already been committed. It is a matter of dispensing down against those projects.

3 or 4 years to complete.

Mr. SELDEN. Is the Inter-American Development Bank-

Mr. SELDEN. Does any agency of our Government, any independent agency, have a right to audit the expenditure of these funds?

Mr. SELDEN. Would a U.S. agency, such as the General Accounting 

Office, have a right to go in and audit these funds?

Mr. BRONHEIM. I would have to check the trust agreement. I think it would be unlikely.

AUDIT OF INTER-AMERICAN DEVELOPMENT BANK FUNDS Section 5.02 of the Social Progress Trust Fund Agreement states that the 

"Bank shall exercise the same care in the discharge of its functions under the agreement as it exercises with respect to the administration and management of its own affairs." The Charter of the Bank, in discussing the administration of the Bank's own funds, calls for the publication of an "annual report containing an audited statement of the Bank's accounts." To comply with this requirement the Inter-American Development Bank has retained an independent firm of auditors. The firm, Price Waterhouse, has an outstanding reputation, and we have complete confidence in their ability to audit thoroughly and accurately all the Bank's operations, including those as SPTF administrator. 

In addition Section 5.04 of the Trust Fund Agreement provides, "The Bank shall include in its annual and quarterly reports a separate section containing appropriate information with respect to the receipts and disbursements of, and balances in, the Fund. In addition, within sixty days after the close of each annual accounting period the Administrator shall issue a detailed report containing appropriate information with respect to operations of the Fund, the progress of the projects for which disbursements were made and other matters relating to the Fund, including a factual presentation of the measures being taken in the borrowing countries to accomplish the objectives stated in Section 1 of the Act of Bogota. Observations which the United States may desire to make to the Administrator upon any such annual report shall be presented as promptly as possible and ordinarily within the annual accounting period in which the report is received." AID is in close informal contact with the Bank staff on problems involved in administering SPTF loans. The U.S. has not made any formal observations to the Bank regarding any item in the Bank's reports. Through the office of the US Executive Director of the IDB, AID and the Treasury have been able to obtain any information they have needed and they fully expect this cooperation to continue. It is through their representatives to international financial institutions that the interests of member countries are protected. It would be most inappropriate for an international financial institution to turn over its records for an additional audit by an agency of the government of any single member. Such a precedent, if established, might lead to a request for similar privileges by other member or donor governments, which in turn would create severe managerial and administrative problems for the Bank. 

Since the IDB is an international financial agency, the SPTF agreement does not contain a provision which would permit auditing of its books and records by the U.S. Government. Existing legislation does not permit this government to audit the Bank's books and records. Since the Bank already provides for an independent audit of its operations by a firm of reputable public accounts, additional audits would not appear necessary. This practice is also followed by the World 

Bank and its associated agencies.

9, 000, 000 21, 619, 000 Mr. MORSE. I realize this is not in your area of responsibility, but in the military assistance program presentation book which was made available to the committee, in support of the Latin American position of the program, there is a statement supporting civic action. Let me recite to you from page 88 of that book: 

Civic action promotes both United States and host country objectives by enhancing internal security and stability through strengthening the economic and social welfare of the nation and by increasing local support of the government by the people. 

We have a civic action program in Argentina. The only inference 

I can draw from that is that the purpose of the civic action program is to increase local support of that Government on the part of the people of Argentina. 

Mr. GORDON. I am not responsible for the sentence, but I don't think it was intended to refer to a case like Argentina. 

Mr. MORSE. We are providing civic action program to the Government of Argentina, are we not?

Mr. GORDON. The civic action program, of course, goes back before the change of regime in Argentina. This is in the northern and very underdeveloped and rather poor part of the country. I am sure the reference in the sentence, and I agree with it as a general matter, pertains to cases like the Amazon region of Brazil and to a number of Central American cases, where the armed forces are the only connection that isolated people have with the nation as a whole. 

Mr. MORSE. I was curious 

Mr. GORDON. I am told that the Argentine case amounted to only $100,000 worth in 1967.

Mr. MORSE. With reference to the immigration picture in Latin 

America are there organized attempts being made through the Alliance to motivate trained people from Latin American countries to remain

1967 

in their countries to implement the developmental process, to avoid the "brain drain," so to speak?

Mr. GORDON. This is a matter which I have a very special interest in. 

A great deal of emphasis was placed on the development of science and technology in the Presidential agreement at Punta del Este. This was an element very much in the minds of all the people who worked on the proposals. A comprehensive study on the subject was made this year. 

I will be glad to supply it to the committee if you don't already have a copy. It is a very interesting study, particularly in regard to various types of specially trained people who have been trained in the United States. It discusses what proportions of them have stayed, and so on. (The following study relating to the "brain drain" problem in relation to Latin America was submitted to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and may be found in the files of the committee:) 

Pan American Health Organization. Migration of Health Personnel, Scientists and Engineers from Latin America. Prepared for the PAHO Advisory Committee on Medical Research by the PAHO Subcommittee on Migration. Washington, D.C., September, 1966.

Mr. GORDON. A rather large number of people in the medical and nursing professions have stayed, but a surprisingly low number have stayed in the case of engineering. In pure sciences the proportion who have stayed varies from country to country. Sometimes it is affected by political conditions in the particular country concerned. It is clear that in that kind of skill, which is the main reason for the "brain drain" to the extent it exists, it is not so much differential in salaries as it is the lack of opportunity in the countries concerned for people to really use the skills they acquire. One of the purposes of the promotion of an intensive scientific and technological development in Latin America is not only for its effect on the actual development there but also its effect in providing opportunities and in keeping qualified Latin Americansand there are some very good ones at home working on their own problems. 

Mr. MORSE. Are there any programs that Latin American nations are undertaking to prevent the "brain drain"?

Mr. GORDON. What they can do is the positive thing. Their improvements of their own universities and their development of natural science and technology programs is important. About half a dozen countries have made progress in these directions already. One thing that all the Latin Presidents agreed on at Punta del Este was that they should institute programs of this sort on a national basis as well as cooperating with one another and us. There is a lot being done. Government fellowships of course, do have special provisions for trying to see that the beneficiaries, the recipients of them, do go back home. This is also done by the Rockefeller Foundation and by some of the other private institutions in this field. 

Mr. MORSE. What is the picture as to the flight of capital at the present time in Latin America?

Mr. GORDON. There are no good statistics on this. Our impression from indirect evidence is that it has improved a good deal. It has improved basically for two reasons: One is that there have been vigorous efforts on the anti-inflation front in some of the countries that have

621 most suffered from inflation. Those are summarized in my initial statement.

Second, because in some of the countries when flight of capital was encouraged by guerrilla activity or political instability, there has been progress in getting these things under control. We know of no case at the present time where there is evidence of a massive capital flight. We know of several cases where there has been a substantial reflow of capital that had gone out in the past.

With reference to the coffee diversification proposal, my understanding is that at least two major coffee producing countries in Latin America have failed to restrict coffee production in line with the proposals of the International Coffee Agreement. 1967 

to comment on this, the attempts to create any meaningful control is torn down by infractions.

The Brazilians have done the best. They are the largest producer. The Colombians have got some real difficulties in that most of their coffee is grown in very hilly areas where it is hard to find alternative crops to grow. 

Technically, it is hard to do a diversification job. Nonetheless, they are beginning to approach it seriously. They at least have been retaining their surplus coffee. They have not been violating their quotas as some of the smaller countries have done. 

The whole notion of the diversification fund- Mr. MONAGAN. Wasn't there a violation in a form of barter that they were carrying on with some of the European countries? 

Mr. GORDON. There have been up until this year a number of techniques, rather clever techniques, for evading the quota agreements. 

There was so-called tourist coffee, coffee that turned up in places like Aruba, which doesn't produce any coffee at all, and was reexported from there to the various markets. 

The import registration technique, which is now applied by us and by other consuming countries, has tended to bottle up these evasive devices. 

On the production side, the whole notion of the diversification fund was that no country would get anything out of it, unless it had a clearcut plan for getting its coffee production under control. 

Mr. MONAGAN. I would say it should go beyond a plan. We could have a plan without compliance or enforcement. I think you are saying that you agree with my point.

Mr. GORDON. I do. 

Mr. MONAGAN. With reference to Chile, we know, as you say, that after they boosted the price of copper up to almost a dollar, it is now back to 45 cents or maybe below that. Mr. GORDON. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. MONAGAN. At the present time, as I read the figures, there is a $63.5 million total of project, sector, and technical assistance, and then the Public Law 480 dollar sales. Is this last a "wash" figure? In other words, we show appropriations of $20 million, but then do we collect $20 million in dollars for food sales? 

Mr. GORDON. AID as such doesn't get into the financing.

Mr. MONAGAN. I understand that. I am calculating the total commitment to the country.

Mr. GORDON. In counting total aid to the country, in addition to the AID figures that you have before you, we, of course, add whatever they may get in Public Law 480. Dollar credit sales have now become the primary Public Law 480 vehicle. We have pretty much stopped the sales for local currencies. Most of the Public Law 480 assistance to all of Latin America now is in long-term loans. 

Mr. MONAGAN. This would be dollar sales. It could be easily taken out of the program since we get back in dollars what we set up on the other side of the ledger?

623 Mr. GORDON. Yes, when we calculate a country's needs, of course, if they are getting any Public Law 480 assistance, we count that as one of the credits against their total needs. I will be glad to furnish a further explanation for the record. 

 RELATION OF PUBLIC LAW 480 DOLLAR SALES PROGRAM TO TOTAL ASSISTANCE 

The P.L. 480 dollar sales program can be considered a "wash figure," only in the same sense as the appropriations for Alliance Loans. 

A P.L. 480 dollar sales program to Chile would be similar to any other dollar loan, i.e., long-term dollar credit. The terms of repayment are negotiated like project development loans. In this case, the financing is used to purchase food rather than other imports. P.L. 480 food sales in Chile generate local currencies which, in turn, are used to finance economic and social projects and otherwise accelerate economic activities that should increase the GNP of Chile-enabling them to repay the U.S. over the following 19 years.

Consequently, the repayments for food sales that accrue to the U.S. cannot be juxtaposed with the rest of the program in any one year, since they are not received by the U.S. in the same year (the only payment received the same year as the sales agreement is the down payment required under the new legislationup to 25 percent).

Mr. MONAGAN. Just briefly, the program loans are for stabilization, you say. How does that operate specifically?

Mr. GORDON. Not just for stabilization. They are really support for an overall development program. In case of inflation, stabilization policies become important parts of the undertakings of the country and our program loans play an important role in supporting these policies. But there are also other objectives of the program loan such as increasing the proportion of the government revenues that go into investment instead of new current expenditures, increasing the proportions devoted to agriculture and education as priority matters, improving their administrative arrangements for the handling of public investments. They are tailored to each country. Typically, the authorities of each country will set forth in a letter to the chairman of CIAP or in one case to the World Bank, which has been a leader in this thing, the qualitative contents of the development program plus a series of qualitative undertakings. Our program loan assistance has tended to be related to that. Each quarter there is a careful review of what has actually happened, and the release of the next slice of the program loan assistance depends in fact on the performance of the country in relation to those undertakings. They are stabilization, they are developmental, and they are administrative. Each one is developed in accordance with the particular situation of the country. It is not just stabilization.

Mr. GORDON. If I could add one word, Mr. Chairman, they have usually been paralleled by International Monetary Fund agreements. 

Mr. FULTON. I would like to ask you to put in the record some statements to explain certain of your comments. You have given the critical decisions in general that would not have been made but for the chiefs of state meeting at Punta del Este. Would you put those specific points in the record so that we can see these points by number, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?

Mr. GORDON. Certainly.

1967 CRITICAL DECISIONS THAT WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN MADE WERE IT NOT FOR THE SUMMIT MEETING IN PUNTA DEL ESTE 

1. The decision that, building on the experience of the first six years of the 

Alliance, the sights of the Alliance should be raised to higher growth rate goals and more rapid social advances, and that all members of the Alliance should undertake increased efforts to this end. 

2. The specific Latin American decision to create progressively, beginning in 

1970, the Latin American Common Market, to be substantially in operation not later than 1985. The associated decisions on specific steps to achieve this end, including especially the placing in effect within the Latin American Free Trade Area, starting in 1970, of a system of programmed elimination of duties and non-tariff trade restrictions and of a system of external tariff harmonization in order to establish progressively a common external tariff; and the provision for a joint committee of the Latin American Free Trade Area and Central American Common Market Executive Secretariats to coordinate implementation of the integration decisions. 

3. The decision by all Alliance countries to seek additional resources for the 

Inter-American Bank specifically for multinational transportation, power, telecommunications and river development projects which will bring Latin American countries closer together and facilitate integration, and to place increased emphasis on the development of such projects. 

4. The decision by all Alliance countries to seek more resources for, and devote increased efforts to, agriculture and education, coupled with the agreement on specific actions to be taken to achieve improved country agriculture and educational programs. 

5. The decision to establish an Inter-American Science Program, to include the strengthening of training and research in science and technology at all levels and the greater use of scientific methods. 

6. The decision by the Latin American countries to eliminate unnecessary military expenditures.

Mr. FULTON. On page 3 of your statement you state the critical role of science and technology was given full recognition and agreement reached on a far-reaching regional program to bring Latin America into active participation and modern developments in these fields. 

You have said on another page what the Agency is doing within Latin America, and what Latin America is doing in this particular instance. 

I am interested in the correlation with our U.S. programs, and what type of liason there will be with these various agencies. 

 CORRELATION OF LATIN AMERICAN AND U.S. SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PROGRAMS 

One of the primary objectives of the proposed Inter-American Science Foundation is that it will serve as a coordinating body for multinational efforts in improving science and technology in Latin America. The premise is that this group would review proposals from the U.S. or Latin American scientific communities to work jointly on development problems, assess the merits of these proposals, and be a focal point for either directly supporting these efforts or channeling external resources for their operation. 

One of the functions of the Foundation is to serve as a scientific and technical information clearing house. Hence, a major task of this entity would be to keep current with scientific programs under way in the hemisphere and passing on the results of research pertinent to developmental needs. 

It is also assumed that there would be strong U.S. representation on the Board of Directors of the Foundation. The U.S. representative would undoubtedly perform necessary liaison with the Office of Science and Technology to ensure a correlation of U.S. research and programs in developmental technology and those operations undertaken in Latin America of direct interest to the Foundation. 

Mr. FULTON. The next point is on page 4; you say that the United 

States opened up important policy directions for the improvement of Latin America's trading position in the world, and "without unfavorable effects on our own U.S. balance of payments," and, second, without damaging the interests of other less developed regions of the world.

625 1 Would you please supply some detail on the second part of that statement as follows: "without damaging the interests of other less developed regions of the world." How could that be, and how did the 

Agency avoid this result? What means and methods were taken by the heads of countries at Punta del Este? 

 THE EFFECT OF IMPROVEMENT OF LATIN AMERICA'S TRADING POSITION ON OTHER LESS DEVELOPED REGIONS OF THE WORLD 

We are making every effort to keep our commercial policy attuned to the needs of all developing countries. 

We are participating in commodity arangements and study groups in an attempt to deal effectively with the short-run and the long-run difficulties of particular commodities important to the trade of developing countries, regardless of region. 

In the Kennedy Round negotiations, we are working intensively to encourage all the developed countries to make maximum tariff reductions on industrial and agricultural products of particular interest to developing countries and to reduce or eliminate non-tariff barriers so as to make progress towards meeting the aspirations of the less developed countries to achieve a larger role in world trade.

Looking beyond the completion of the Kennedy Round negotiations, we have been examining the kind of trade initiatives we should propose, convinced that our future trade policy must pay special attention to the needs of all developing countries.

As President Johnson stated at the April Summit Meeting of the American Chiefs of State at Punta del Este, "We have been exploring with other major industralized countries what practical steps can be taken to increase the export earnings of all developing countries. We recognize that comparable tariff treatment may not always permit developing countries to advance as rapidly as desired. Temporary tariff advantages for all developing countries by all industralized countries would be one way to deal with this. "We think this idea is worth pursuing. We will be discussing it further with members of our Congress, with business and labor leaders, and we will seek the cooperation of other Governments in the world trading community to see whether a broad consensus can be reached along these lines." 

We recognize that existing bilateral preferences cannot realistically be eliminated overnight unless present beneficiaries are convinced that they will receive equivalent advantages either by the institution of a system of generalized preferences or in some other way. 

This question of compensation is one that requires further analysis. We need more information about the value of existing discriminatory preferences. There are some features of bilateral preferential arrangements which appear to have an adverse effect on the process of economic development. For example, such arrangements often are reciprocal, providing for preferential entry of developed country products into the markets of the less developed country. This restricts the feedom of the less developed country to acquire resources from the most efficient suppliers, and thus wastes scarce foreign exchange. Discriminatory or bilateral arrangements, because of the structure of the preferences, may also encourage the less developed countries to continue to rely too heavily on exports of primary commodities.

1967 GNP GROWTH IN LATIN AMERICA: THE ALLIANCE PERIOD 

The chart below shows the latest AID estimates for average growth rates in total and per capita GNP during the Alliance for Progress period. It illustrates the effect on regional growth trends when one or two large countries fare less well than others in the region. This effect is particularly plain in 1966, when the combination of a recession in Argentina and a fall in agricultural production due primarily to bad weather and the coffee reduction program in Brazil held the regional growth to an estimated 1.1% per capita. 

Excluding these two countries, the region saw about a 2.7% per capita growth in 1966 and, despite some fluctuations from year to year, has achieved a 2.5% average over the Alliance period as a whole. 

The graph also illustrates how growth in total GNP is reduced on a per capita basis by rapid population growth. Half the countries of the region and the regional total excluding Argentina and Brazil show an average rate of growth in total GNP for 1961 through 1966 higher than that of the U.S. (5.4%) for the same period. Yet the average per capita growth rates in Latin America are almost all below the U.S. average of 4% for 1961-66. This is simply to say that the Alliance for Progress has set high targets, given the realities existing in Latin America. As these targets are met in much of the region, higher ones are being set for the future. Nicaragua..

 SUMMARY OF GOVERNMENT FINANCES IN LATIN AMERICA 

The following three tables provide the key figures on Latin American central government finances during the Alliance for Progress period. The trends clearly show the growing determination of the governments of most of the countries of the region to mobilize increased resources for development and to allocate more of those resources to the prime fields of agriculture and education. The first table is a standardized summary of revenue and expenditure patterns similar to that shown for the five major aid recipients in the Summary Presentation book. The second shows revenues collections as a percentage of Gross National 

Product. The third presents the first results of improved direct AID reporting of expenditures on key government activities. 

The first table shows the income of the governments from domestic revenues, their total spending, their investment expenditures, and their overall deficit before borrowing or foreign assistance. Tax revenues have been broken out separately to clarify the relation of tax and non-tax recipients to the total. Perhaps the most significant trend shown here is the ability of most of the countries, even those that have been struggling with inflation, to increase the share of total expenditures devoted to capital outlay while reducing the deficit in pro- 77-470-67-pt. 3- -9

1967 

portion to total expenditures. Most striking is the case of Brazil, which recently has been able to increase federal capital outlay from less than 30% of expenditures to over 40% while reducing the deficit from over 40% to approximately 10%. In Chile, likewise, government investment has risen from around 30% to over 35% of total expenditure, while the deficit has been cut from a 20% level to less than 10%. Colombia, despite legislative problems requiring last-minute measures to increase revenues, has managed to maintain capital outlays at a level over 35% of expenditures and reduce the deficit from a high of 20% of expenditures in 1962 to an estimated six or seven percent in 1966. Even the Dominican 

Republic, which had only negligible capital outlay in 1965, regained the level of earlier years in 1966 while more than halving the amount of expenditures financed by borrowing and foreign aid. 

The second table highlights the growth of domestic revenues in terms of the total economy. It shows that in most countries, revenues have not only kept pace with economic growth but have actually gained markedly, demonstrating improved flexibility of the tax structure in recent years, especially since 1963. 

While total revenue measured as a percentage of the GNP for the region is as high in 1961 as in 1966, it is heavily influenced by the marked fall in Argentina. 

Exclusive of the effect of Argentina, the total shows an upward trend from about 13.3% of GNP in 1961 to an estimated 14.2% in 1966, paced in particular by Brazil and Chile.

The final table indicates that the increasing mobilization of resources has led to increased central government expenditures on education and agriculture, sectors that are generally considered vital to development efforts. The figures relate to total expenditures, both current and capital, since the distinction between most operating expenditures and "investment" in these fields is somewhat tenuous. Teachers' and extension agents' salaries, for example, are by definition current, operating expenses, but in terms of development efforts they are clearly an "investment" in future growth. For reasons that are detailed in the notes to that table, the available information tends to understate the total public effort in education and agriculture, particularly in countries such as Brazil and Mexico, where local government contributions to these fields are substantial. །'༑ 1 ;དཱ་༢

GENERAL NOTE 

This table represents a first attempt to classify Latin American Central Government expenditures by function. Although uniformity of concept and definition was sought, Central Government expenditure patterns do not provide full intercountry compara bility. This is due to the fact that some governmental systems are more decentralized than others, giving more or less authority to state and local units and to autonomous agencies and enterprises. Availability of information from the latter is much more restricted than for central governments. 

In education, some central governments, such as Chile, have complete responsibility for public education, while in others, such as Brazil, state and local governments provide much of the direction and financing. In some cases, shared taxes or grants may go unearmarked to regional or local units and so cannot be allocated to specific functional expenditures of the Central Government. In agriculture, large portions of the overall development programs are often carried out by agricultural credit banks, or agrarian reform agencies, or area development authorities, that may be largely financed outside the Central Government budget, whether through their own revenues, or through domestic or foreign borrowing. Also, some countries may classify such items as irrigation and farm-to-market roads in agricultural expenditure while others do not. Defense, while almost exclusively a Central Government function, may appear higher as a percentage of total expenditures in federal or relatively decentralized countries because the Central Government total does not include activities carried on by other levels of government. 

Because of these data limitations, the levels of Central Government expenditure cannot be a dependable indicator of the absolute or relative size of total expenditure in these functional fields. However, the trends in the percentages devoted to agriculture and education do provide an indication of the trend of total development efforts because in most cases, increased Central Government expenditure acts to promote increased efforts throughout the country.

 INTER-AMERICAN SCIENCE FOUNDATION AND MULTI-NATIONAL INSTITUTES OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY I. MULTI-NATIONAL INSTITUTES OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY 

An Inter-American group of distinguished leaders in the fields of science, technology, and higher education would be appointed by the Inter-American Cultural Council to develop detailed recommendations on two or three multi-national institutes for graduate level training and research in science and technology. The 

United States will suggest that the same group develop the details for the Inter- 

American Foundation for Science and Technology.

The establishment and operation of the institutes, which would be located in Latin America, would probably be governed by the following principles: 

1. The institutes should be designed to offer training and research at the graduate level not now adequately provided by national programs. Emphasis should be placed on training leading to advanced degrees in science and technology and on research contributing directly or indirectly to Latin America's development. 

2. Each institute should be in close proximity to an established and successful 

Latin American educational institution, but entirely autonomous with respect to program and administration. 

3. The financing, administration, teaching and research staff, and student bodies of the institutes should be multi-national in character. 

4. Each institute should be governed by a multi-national board. 

5. Each institute might receive technical assistance through consortia of the 

United States universities and colleges. 

As now envisioned, again subject to the determinations of the aforementioned group, each institute would be governed by a multi-national board which might be composed of distinguished men of science and technology from those Latin American countries participating in the particular institute, the IDB, United States, the Minister of Education of the host country, and the rector of the local, nearby university. The Board would select the director of the multi-national institute, set policy and program direction, adopt basic rules and regulations, approve the the budget, and oversee the selection of faculty and staff, as well as serving as a channel for support from public and private, national and multi-national entities.

The faculties would meet professional standards acceptable to the World's Scientific Community and would be composed of qualified personnel of all nationalities with particular emphasis on the recruitment of Latin Americans and North Americans. Special effort would be made to persuade Latin Americans now engaged in scientific and technological endeavors in the United States and Europe to join the faculties. To facilitate this effort, a survey of Latin American scientific and technological talent, resident in the United States, should be made. 

The broad program of the institutes should be suggested by the OAS study group. However, the main emphasis of each institute will be on training, leading to advanced degrees in particular aspects of science and technology including

637 1 research related to Latin America's development problems. The institutes would also conduct special short courses, workshops, seminars and lecture programs. 

One of their purposes would be the upgrading of undergraduate teaching in science and technology through special courses for the professors in participating 

The financial arrangements for the institutes would reflect the multi-national character of the undertaking.

II. INTER-AMERICAN FOUNDATION FOR SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY 

An Inter-American group would be appointed by the Inter-American Cultural Council to develop detailed recomendations on the Foundation's organization, funding, and operation.

With respect to functions, the proposed Foundation would perform the following, subject of course, to the final recommendations of the aforementioned group: 

1. Strengthen institutions, and groups of institutions, which have demonstrated quality and viability, or which have adequate plans for becoming centers of strength, either in special problem areas (e.g., agriculture) or in special scientific fields (e.g., physics). 

2. Make grants to individuals or groups of individuals to support meritorious research efforts. 

3. Identify the major technological problems that hamper development by evaluating the work that is actually carried out by the various scientific organizations in the region. 

4. Analyze existing technical teaching systems, bearing local conditions in mind, and formulate recommendations on how to improve the systems of teaching in Latin America. Provide support for summer science institutes for high school teachers. 

5. Study measures needed to enable national and international resources to be channeled to the technological development of the region. 

6. Provide an up-to-date assessment of institutional strengths and weaknesses to be made available upon request to organizations considering technical assistance grants or loans. 

7. Compile inventories, in the fields of applied sciences and technologies, of qualified personnel and training and applied research establishments in the region. 

8. Collect and distribute technological information and organize a Documentation Service specializing in the field of activities of the Center; encourage other countries of the region to organize information services and to exchange information and experiences. Strengthen and assist in the development of adequate scientific and technical libraries. 

9. Seek coordination of efforts of technological research institutes in the region to include the exchange of research workers and professors among the 

Latin countries. 

10. Organize regional courses for graduates in the various fields of technology and the applied sciences and administer a program of fellowships.

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS PARTNERS OF THE ALLIANCE 

The Charter of Punta del Este declares the Alliance for Progress to be an alliance of the peoples and governments of the American republics. Although 

U.S. participation in the Alliance is necessarily oriented toward institution building government-to-government programs at the broad economic and social development level, the essential participation of the people of the Americas in an effort designed to afford them the opportunity to contribute directly to their own development has not been overlooked.

To develop and coordinate this active private sector participation within the spirit of the Charter, the Partners of the Alliance office was established in AID under the direction of a Special Assistant to the U.S. Coordinator. This office coordinates the joint development and implementation by counterpart U.S. and 

Latin American committees of (a) small socially oriented self-help impact projects in Latin American rural villages and urban slum areas; (b) educational, other cultural and technical exchanges and (c) investment and commercial relationships. Evidence of self-help is a requisite in evaluating project assistance requirements and eligibility for participation in partnership sponsored programs. 

The Partners of the Alliance has evolved into a flexible program involving the community and private sector leaders of 31 U.S. states and a like number of areas in 15 Latin American countries. All 31 areas have had direct contact with

639 their Latin American counterparts either through Latin American field trips for U.S. committees or U.S. visits by representatives of the Latin American Partners. 

Actively participating in the program are not only leading citizens as individuals but also such groups as: Business and Professional Women, League of Women 

Voters, Jaycees, Chambers of Commerce, World Trade Committees, Teachers Associations, Lions, Rotary, Altrusta, University and High School Students, Hospital Associations, General Federation of Womens Clubs, Trade Unions, Manufacturers Associations, School Systems, Legislative Groups, etc. 

A four-man AID Partners staff acts as a catalyst to bring together the known need and the available resource. Their functions include: a) Providing program background material and information as requested by local groups in the U.S. and Latin America; b) Participating in local group meetings throughout the U.S., upon request, to discuss the program as the basis for establishing a Partners organization and marshalling local resources for direct participation: c) Coordinating an alliance with a counterpart organization in Latin America through the country USAID with the participation of Embassy Staff, Peace Corps and interested public and private organizations. 

A key factor in the development of the program is the emphasis placed on the two-way aspect of a "partnership." The Partners of the Alliance is not a charity program nor is it one in which one area patronizingly "adopts" another area. 

The U.S. Partner can learn as well as teach and receive as well as assist. 

On January 7, 1967 AID issued a $131,500 grant to help establish the National Association of the Partners of the Alliance. Incorporated on a non-profit basis, NAPA is the logical next step toward moving the Partners program into the private sector on a self-sustaining basis. NAPA will seek private foundation and corporate funds to help maintain the program. NAPA will assume some of the functions of the AID staff and will maintain a field operations' staff to help speed up project presentation and implementation.

Mr. FRASER. 

I would like to find out something about the country of Argentina. 

I have been asking a series of questions of witnesses to determine why we are giving them grant military aid when they don't qualify for economic aid, and when there seems to be a pretty repressive regime. 

Mr. GORDON. The amounts are small. This is pursuant to an understanding that was developed several years ago. There was no military assistance for Argentina in the early years in the program. Back in 

1962 and 1963 we began discussing with the Argentine authorities [security deletion] a limited program to them based partly on some important military considerations. The Navy, for example, was growing obsolete and they had requested some destroyers under the ship loan program. A couple of those were approved by specific legislation 

2 years ago.

The Argentine Navy is potentially important in the guarding of the Straits of Magellan in the event of difficulties in that part of the world, and, of course, for surveillance along the coastline. They also offered to participate and did participate briefly in the Cuban quarantine in the time of the crisis in 1962. They came very close to participating in the Inter-American peace defense in the Dominican Republic, but for political reasons they refrained.

We have felt it would be undesirable to have a brusk termination of that program. [Security deletion] and most of what we are doing now

 RECENT DEVELOPMENTS IN ARGENTINA 

During the first nine months of its administration the Argentine Government devoted most of its energy to the solution of economic problems, holding that economic revitalization, including stabilization and curtailment of inflation, along with increase domestic and foreign investment, is the means to achieve political as well as economic stability. The Government leaders believe that the old Argentine political ssytem, characterized by strong personalism and severely fragmented political parties that assumed power by small pluralities of the vote, made a sham of democracy and lacked the ability to carry out programs for the benefit of the nation as a whole. They believe the country needs a period free from traditional political activities and agitation in order to rebuild economic confidence and create an atmosphere conducive to a return to effective constitutional democracy. When it assumed power, the Ongania Government stated that it intended to remain until it had created such an atmosphere. [Security deletion.] When a Government institutes a program that involves elements or economic austerity, it is inevitable that it will encounter resistence and opposition by the sectors who feel their interests are being adversely affected, even in the short run. This is the situation with respect to the Ongania 

Government's relationships with Argentina's organized labor movement. [Security deletion.] The first resistence to his program arose from his efforts [security deletion] to alter [security deletion] work rules in the ports, which were said to be the most expensive and inefficient in the world. Although the majority of the

643 labor movement did not support the portworkers in their attempts to strike, they did increasingly resist the government when it attempted to reduce the deficit of $1 million a day suffered by the State-owned railroads by changing work rules, consolidating facilities, and reducing featherbedding. Complaining that the Government's economic policies were making labor bear the brunt of the austerity program, the labor leaders called for a 24-hour general strike in early March and a 48-hour strike at the end of March. The Government warned that it would dismiss or suspend any state workers who joined the strike and would take measures against any unions involved. This warning, without the use of violence, reduced the effectiveness of the first strike, which was only partially successful, and caused labor to call off the second planned walkout. 

The few unions that did participate in force lost their legal status, and the railroad union, which was most active in these events, was intervened by the government—that is, its leaders were replaced by Government-appointed officials. 

[Security deletion.] 

With respect to general political activity. as noted above the Government wants a period of political moratorium, and hence has suspended all political parties and their activities. However, individual freedoms and freedom of the press have in general been respected. In this regard, the Ongania Government has been characterized by many observers of the Argentine scene as a "most liberal" military regime.

The problem of credit cooperatives, which the Government undertook to regulate soon after it took power, raised a hue and cry, as many of them were controlled by persons of the Jewish faith, and anti-Semitic motives were alleged. 

However, the regulations imposed were designed to reduce inflationary credit practices made possible by the fact that the credit institutions did not come under the general banking laws. There has been no evidence of anti-Semitic motives on the part of the Government. The credit cooperatives have continued to operate under the new regulations. Other types of cooperatives have not been bothered by the Government. 

Shortly after the coup. local elected officials were replaced by Governmentappointed officials, apparently as part of the plan to reduce political activity. 

However, the Government has indicated that it believes that local government is the area in which efforts to restore democratic methods should begin when political activity is reinitiated. Community development projects in the rural areas and in cities and towns remote from the capital are growing. 

[Security deletion.]
