STATEMENT OF GEN. LYMAN L. LEMNITZER, SUPREME ALLIED COMMANDER, EUROPE, AND COMMANDER IN CHIEF, U.S. EURO- PEAN COMMAND General LEMNITZER.  

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee: It is again a real pleasure for me to appear before this committee in support of the U.S. military assistance program. This is my 18th consecutive appearance before the Congress on the question of military assistance. I take great pride in having had the opportunity to participate for so many years in the development and implementation of the program which, in my view, has contributed so much to the security of the free world. 

It was my privilege as the first Director of Military Assistance to share in the original planning of the military assistance program, and in the initiation of its operations. Since then, from a number of different vantage points, and covering a period of almost continuous association with the program since 1949, I have had the opportunity to supervise and observe its later contributions to the security of the United States and our allies-both in the Far East and, for the past four-anda-half years, in Europe, as Supreme Allied Commander, Europe and Commander in Chief of the U.S. European Command. Among the many accomplishments of the program was the rebuilding of military strength in Europe in the early days of NATO, when the United States was the principal source of military equipment which was so badly needed in the European area. 645

1967 

While the military assistance program was designed to follow immediately behind the Marshall plan, and to provide rebuilding of mili tary strength in Europe, its scope has not, by any means, been limited to Europe. It was the military assistance program that was responsible for building military strength in the Republic of Korea, Southeast Asia, and many other parts of the world. Thus, it can truly be said that this program has been global in character. 

I continue to be a strong supporter of the military assistance program. It has demonstrated that it is vital to our national interests and security. It is an integral part of the U.S. defense effort. With regard to Europe in particular, it has helped to create deterrent forces among our allies-deterrent forces that have played a key part in maintaining peace and security, and in preventing any Communist military "adventures" in that part of the world. 

The military assistance program planned for fiscal year 1968 in the U.S. European Command is influenced by two major facts. The first of these is the Soviet and Warsaw Pact military capabilities. The second is the continuing shift from grant assistance to military sales in those countries which have attained the economic capability of meeting their own defense requirements.

The military assistance planned in the area of the U.S. European 

Command reflects the concept of collective and mutual security which is the basis of unified actions by nations of the free world. The basis for the level and type of our military effort in NATO Europe is the military threat presented by the Soviet Union and other Warsaw Pact nations. This threat includes impressive forces of all types-land, sea, and air; nuclear and nonnuclear.

Apart from maintaining and increasing its own great military strength, the Soviet Union has been providing the forces of the other Warsaw Pact nations with increasing amounts of modernized military equipment. This equipment has greatly improved their military capabilities.

Three Soviet fleets, based in the Black, the Baltic and the Barents Seas, constitute the naval threat to NATO. 

Air support for an attack against Western Europe could be drawn from Soviet air units based in the Warsaw Pact countries and in the western part of the Soviet Union. 

Soviet military assistance has permitted Algeria to improve its military capabilities beyond the level required for internal securityindeed, to a level which is causing concern for peace and stability on the southern littoral of the Mediterranean. 

This, briefly, is the Communist threat which faces my NATO command, Allied Command Europe, along its 3,600 mile frontier, which extends from the northern tip of Norway to the eastern frontier of Turkey. The defense effort within this area causes the requirements of the European Command military assistance program to vary over a wide range from major grant aid programs in Greece and Turkey on the critical southeast flank of NATO to major sales programs in the United Kingdom and the Federal Republic of Germany. 

I would first like to discuss with you our major grant aid programs in Greece and Turkey. Next, I will discuss the programs in Spain, Portugal and Libya. Then, I will review the programs proposed for 

Morocco and Tunisia. Finally, I will discuss the phased-out portions

647 of our programs in economically developed European countries and review the roles of our military assistance advisory groups in countries no longer receiving grant assistance.

With regard to Greece and Turkey, military assistance was initiated under the Truman doctrine, before the original mutual defense assistance program was approved by the Congress. 

The proposed programs for Greece and Turkey will provide some force modernization; however, the emphasis of the program is on the maintenance of current forces. Key items here are: fighter aircraft, utility aircraft, tanks, landing craft, vehicles and equipment to increase combat mobility, fire power and communications. United States military assistance support is necessary in order that the armed forces of Greece and Turkey will be capable of performing their assigned NATO missions. 

In fiscal year 1968, military assistance to Spain and Portugal in Western Europe and Libya in north Africa involves special considerations. The proposed program for Portugal provides training and selected maintenance support. The program for Spain consists primarily of components and equipment for navy construction, support of air defense and training. Military assistance for Libya is designed to contribute to the development and improvement of the Libyan armed forces in their internal security role. 

Two other countries on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa are in the area of the European Command and have grant aid programs. These are Morocco and Tunisia. Both programs are designed to insure the limited defensive capabilities of these countries and, in this way, contribute to the stability of the area. 

Since my last appearance before this committee, we have terminated aid in two other countries of Europe-Denmark and Norway. All that now remains is to complete deliveries of materiel from prior year commitments. 

A most important phase of past military assistance in the United States European Command consisted of the multinational undertaking-NATO infrastructure and the operating costs of International Military Headquarters and Agencies. These programs have been proposed for transfer to the Department of Defense budget in fiscal year 1968. Infrastructure is absolutely vital to the defense of Allied Command Europe, and has contributed enormously to the strong military posture which NATO has today. We and the other NATO countries are contributing to our common defense by sharing costs in the construction of essential military facilities. This is a common effort which is enabling us to integrate and strengthen our defenses in Europe. I cannot overemphasize the importance of its benefits both to the United 

States and to NATO.

I would like to touch briefly on France and NATO. The geographical position of France provided the land area needed for the deployment of NATO forces and installations in greater depth in Central Europe. The loss of this depth increases to some degree the vulnerability of our forces and installations and requires a reorientation of some of our support concepts. In the reorientation, every effort is being made to adjust to NATO military structure so that we can continue to provide the necessary deterrent and defense in NATO Europe without France.

1967 

The two headquarters which I command as Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Commander-in-Chief, United States European Command-SHAPE and USEUCOM-have moved from France and have been operational in Belgium and Germany since last month. 

These two moves differed in a number of ways. 

The transfer of SHAPE to Belgium involved the construction of a new headquarters, together with support facilities in a rural location some 30 difficult miles from Brussels. With the continued cooperation of the Belgian Government and people, this new facility will enable SHAPE to continue to operate effectively. However, much remains to be done. We hope that by the end of the summer, the critical family housing problem will be resolved and that school, hospital and other support facilities will be constructed and in full operation. 

The move of the U.S. European Command to Patch Barracks in 

Vaihingen near Stuttgart, Germany was completed in mid-March.

This headquarters was able to move into a headquarters complex which was vacated by the consolidation of the 7th U.S. Army Headquarters and the Headquarters of U.S. Army Europe, USEUCOM March 1415, 1967.

The overall relocation project also involved the movement of vast tonnages of supplies and equipment located along the line of communications through France to the U.S. 7th Army in Germany. I can now report that this move was successfully carried out. The only personnel now remaining in France are those required to complete the transfer or sale of material and those remaining to provide adequate support to the dependents of U.S. military personnel. 

Before I conclude, I would like to make two additional points. 

The first concerns the importance of military assistance training. 

Aircraft, ships and tanks are essential to an adequate military force. 

However, a trained man is still the most important factor in the establishment of a modern military force. It is he who must use and maintain the equipment, and he must not be overlooked. Unless these highly trained personnel are available, weapons are useless. 

I believe that the most enduring value of the military assistance dollar is achieved through the training of allied personnel, training which is conducted in the United States, in the European Command and in the host countries. The United States, with its relatively great size and resources compared to our allies, has developed training organization, methods and facilities far beyond the capabilities of our allies. By providing allied military personnel the opportunity of benefitting from this training establishment, we significantly increase their operational readiness and hence the effectiveness of our common defense efforts. We also provide them a high standard of training methods to emulate in their own forces. Furthermore, we promote standardization of tactics and techniques which pays big dividends in allied operations. Finally, by bringing allied personnel of many nations into association with each other and with our American personnel, we develop friendships, understanding and rapport which are of incalcuable value. The selection process utilized by the various nations to pick officers to attend our senior service colleges generally results in the choice of those high type individuals who are destined ultimately to fill positions of great responsibility and influence in their own countries.

649 I am convinced that MAP training contributes greatly to the strength of our collective defense effort and to long-term mutual understanding between the United States and the other countries. 

The final point I desire to make concerns the importance I attach to our military assistance advisory groups, or MAAG's. The personnel in our MAAG's work jointly with their counterparts in the host countries on a daily basis. The value of these person-to-person relationships in furthering our objectives of peace and security should not be underestimated.

The chief of the MAAG is a member of the U.S. Ambassador's country team, and is thereby in a position to insure thorough coordination of U.S. MAP policy objectives with overall U.S. national objectives in the country.

The initial purpose of MAAG's was, of course, to administer grant aid military assistance programs in the host countries. In some countries, this remains their purpose. However, grant aid programs have been phased out in those European nations which have achieved economic recovery. Large quantities of grant aid equipment remain in the active inventories of these latter countries, and there remains also a statutory requirement to maintain surveillance over this equipment for proper utilization and upkeep. The MAAG's are the agencies best suited and capable of performing this function effectively. This active supervision permits early identification of equipment which may become excess to the host country's need, and subsequently can be redistributed to meet grant aid requirements in other countries. 

The military assistance program now includes aspects which have been added since the initial establishment of MAAG's. Among these are activities in connection with multilateral production programs, cooperative research and development programs, cooperative logistics arrangements, and military assistance sales. All of these require increased involvement on the part of the MAAG's. 

The professional understanding, trust and confidence between MAAG personnel and their counterparts in host countries are important assets which are being applied to these additional activities. 

These are established assets which assist us in furthering U.S. objectives. 

Close supervision of the MAAG strengths is maintained through a European Command effort called the resources management program. 

This program provides periodic review of personnel strengths vis-avis MAAG missions to insure that the minimum level, consistent with essential operations, is maintained.

A continuing in-country U.S. military presence is of incalcuable advantage to the United States. It is my view that continued U.S. leadership in Europe is necessary for maintaining peace in an important area of the world which is vital to U.S. security interests. So long as the MAAG's continue to make a useful contribution to this objective, I consider that it would be highly imprudent to reduce their capability substantially. 

In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I remain convinced, as I have been in my previous 17 consecutive appearances before the Congress on this question, that the U.S. military assistance program continues to serve the security our our country well, and that it continues to support the foreign policy and general welfare of the United States and to carry

1967 

out the intent of the Congress to promote the peace. The European area provides an example of an effectiveness of the application of selfhelp programs and mutual application of the principles of collective under consideration will continue to enhance the military posture of our allies and, in turn, promote our mutual security. This, I believe, provides the surest way to the development and maintenance of the collective strength necessary to deter aggression in Europe. Accordingly, I recommend and urge your support of this program. 

Mr. Chairman, this completes my prepared statement.

My mission as a NATO commander, to defend Allied Command Europe or NATO Europe as far forward as possible, which has been given to me by the political and top military authorities of NATO, is unchanged. I have the same mission. The military capability of the forces confronting my command with which my forces would be engaged in an emergency have not only not been diminished or reduced, they are improving in their capability from year to year.

FRIDAY, APRIL 28, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS,

Our witness this morning is the Honorable Joseph Palmer 2d, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs.

Mr. Secretary, when you were here last week it was requested by some of the members who didn't get a chance to ask questions that we have you come back. Would you in about 5 minutes give us a recent report on some of the current activities in Ghana and Nigeria? 

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH PALMER 2D, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. PALMER. I would be very happy to, Mr. Chairman. 

As you are aware, the situation in Ghana, since the downfall of Nkrumah, has been characterized by a military regime which has taken over the reins of government. Its first effort was to try to remove the people and to change the forces that characterized the Nkrumah regime and to concentrate its effort on the internal development of Ghana.

I should say the removal of the Nkrumah government in this coup was welcomed by the bulk of the Ghanaian people and the National Liberation Council had quite wide popular support when it assumed power. It is being advised through a series of committees that have been set up, manned by senior civil servants and including private civilians. The council has announced that it intends in due course to move to civilian rule.

One of the greatest efforts has been to try to revamp the economy which was in terrible condition when they took over. Ghana was very much overcommitted, particularly in terms of its short- and mediumterm obligations.

A program was initiated in consultation with the International Monetary Fund and in connection with the principal countries who had been supplying assistance to Ghana to try to achieve a rescheduling of the Ghana debt problem. This exercise has now been completed and the way is now opening for Ghana to be able to lay plans and to 669

1967 

talk to other donor countries about the possibility of putting new impetus into its development plan. 

As we all know, only a few days ago on the 17th of April there was a brief effort by elements of the Ghana army to overthrow the regime of the National Liberation Council. According to our information, the rebel group was small; it consisted of about 130 men and about half a dozen or so middle grade and junior officers. It does not appear to have been well planned. They were relying on support, and with the factor of surprise they did gain some key facilities, including the radio station. The rest of the troops remained loyal, however, and the rebels surrendered without a struggle. 

The authority of the National Liberation Council has now been reestablished. We don't yet know the entire story of the attempted coup and there is continued widespread speculation about it, but I think it is generally felt that Nkrumah did not have a hand in this particular episode. [Security deletion.] 

Nevertheless, I don't mean to minimize at all the importance of this. 

It is a disturbing development in a country that had seemed to be making considerable progress on the road back. However, the present government is back in the saddle again.

Nigeria, of course, has been beset by continuing instability ever since the first coup at the beginning of last year. The causes for this 

I think are known to all of us. It is a country of about 50 million people. It is composed of over 250 different tribal elements. Although a considerable amount of progress had been made before the independence period and in the postindependence period toward welding all these diverse elements into a nation, it has been quite apparent from the beginning that many of the basic stresses and strains that characterize the society were cause for concern. 

These regional suspicions and differences have intensified under the impact of recent events. General Ironsi, who took over the reins of government at the time that the civilian government was ousted in 

January 1966 was an Ibo from eastern Nigeria. Northern Nigeria subsequently believed that the Federal Government was being dominated by the east.

Of course the resentment that flowed from the assassination of Prime Minister Balewa also rankled in the north. The result of this was a further coup-I should also have said that there was great unrest within the army in July of last year that resulted in the death of General Ironsi and brought to power Colonel Gowan and a new group of army officers. This was followed very quickly, because of regional tensions, by large-scale massacre of Ibos in northern Nigeria beginning in September.

Since that time there has been a general tendency on the part of the east, in resentment of these developments, to try to seek greater and greater autonomy within its own region. A series of financial steps have been taken, economic steps, and constitutional steps, to try to assure that the east has a very high degree of autonomy within the present structure. This has led to at least one round of negotiations that was undertaken in Ghana at the initiative of General Ankrah, who reflected the common concern that if these trends continued, that the Federation of Nigeria might dissolve or at least that the eastern region might withdraw from it.

671 A series of decisions in principle were taken which moved the overall structure of Nigeria toward very much of a confederation in which power was devolved to the Supreme Military Council with any one of the regions having a veto power over the acts of the Central Government. Eastern Nigeria, while it has not directly rejected this arrangement, nevertheless has said it must have greater fiscal autonomy, so it in turn has taken a number of steps to take over a great many of the responsibilities that previously had been exercised by the Federal Government, particularly insofar as the collection of revenues is concerned.

I would like to say if I may off the record— 

Chairman MORGAN. Off the record. 

(Discussion off the record.)

Mr. PALMER. I would like to simply add that the Federal Government has announced a program of trying to bring the various parts of the country back together again, including a resumption of the constitutional conference and steps that would bring civilians into active positions in the Government by December of this year; into the Federal Executive Council, including the possibility of creation of new states throughout the country, which the Federal Government feels might bring about a greater balance and remove some of the fears of the domination of one area, of one region, by another region. 

The great question is whether or not they will all be able to get together to discuss these matters further. The Government of Ghana is continuing to try to be helpful in this matter and it is possible that there will be a further meeting of all the parties concerned some time in the near future.

Insofar as the capital assistance program is concerned, we have taken a wait and see attitude on new capital loans. We have been proceeding in terms of preliminary work, surveys, engineering work, but have not undertaken new capital assistance loans for construction during this interim period.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, if I could ask one question in what appears to be a departure of our policy as to assistance in Africa. In the past State and AID have defended our aid to small countries in Africa, to countries like Gambia, in that the United States should show a direct interest primarily for political reasons.

Now as I understand it AID is moving away from the concept of bilateral aid to Africa to multilateral aid. I am wondering what has happened in the past few years in Africa that makes it no longer necessary for us to provide direct aid. 

Mr. PALMER. I think there are several things, Mr. Congressman. 

I think the Africans themselves have come increasingly to realize that they can get an added dimension to development through cooperative means, that many of their economies are so small and their opportunities for development so limited that they can get a greater reward if they can cooperate with one another on a regional basis. I would like to make it very clear that when we talk about regionalism, Mr. 

Congressman, we are not talking about necessarily funneling money through formalized regional structures. 

We have a very pragmatic approach. A road that might benefit more than one country, for example, would under our criteria qualify as a regional project or similarly an institution training automobile mechanics from several countries, and so forth. If they can do this on a regional basis, training nationals of other countries can be a more efficient organization and can accomplish more than if it is confined to one country.

We are talking pragmatically, as I say, on this question. Not all of our aid would go through multinational channels. Another possible formula, of course, is a multidonor project. Whatever the projects are, they will continue to be directed toward the problems of these countries and will continue for the overwhelming part to be identified with the United States.

We think that through means such as this we can make a bigger contribution, a better contribution to the development of many of these countries. I would add one more thing, and that is there is a provision in our presentation for the continuation of a self-help fund which would be available in all countries. Of course other forms of assistance such as Public Law 480 and Peace Corps and Export-Import Bank assistance will continue to be available on a bilateral basis. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

The Soviet Union has continued to develop its political relations with Africa.

Volta, to exchange ambassadors with the USSR. [Security deletion.] 

The Soviet Union's major involvement in Africa is with Algeria. [Security deletion.] The USSR sent high-ranking military and civilian delegations to the 

November 1 anniversary celebrations in 1966. It announced shortly before this that it would sell Algeria 200,000 tons of wheat. [Security deletion.] Economic cooperation continues. 

The Soviets have also paid special attention to Morocco, despite support of Algeria. King Hassan II made a state visit to the USSR in October [security deletion]. Other agreements were reached on cultural, technical specialist, and radio and television exchanges. 

[Security deletion.]

1967 

Soviet economic relations with other African states are growing. Sierra Leone began to receive equipment for its first Soviet project-rice irrigation. Senegal agreed to purchase 10 Soviet fishing vessels, the first major step under a 1965 agreement for the development of a tuna processing complex. Mauritania signed its first trade agreement with the Soviet Union; it will exchange agricultural products for Soviet manufactures. Soviet experts arrived in Cameroon to plan the agricultural and veterinary school the Soviets are to build. In Ethiopia, the 

Soviet-built oil refinery at Assab has begun operating. Five doctors have arrived in Chad under the first Soviet aid project in that country. The Soviets agreed in March to accept sugar from Congo-Brazzaville in exchange for Soviet machinery and equipment, even though Cuba now supplies all of the sugar the Soviet 

Union needs. 

[Security deletion.] CHINESE COMMUNIST ACTIVITY 

Events in China so far, have had little visible effect on Chinese projects or deliveries. The Chinese have, in fact, continued to offer additional aid. A Guinean delegation signed a new economic cooperation agreement in Peking November 16, 1966. When the Mauritanian Foreign Minister visited Peking in February, 1967, he signed agreements for cultural, technical, and commercial and economic cooperation. The Chinese offered a credit of $4 million to cover technical assistance and equipment for approved development projects. An agreement with 

Somalia providing for aid in the fields of agriculture, irrigation and industry was signed in Mogadiscio in October 1966. No specific projects or amounts of money have been mentioned.

(The information requested follows:) UNITED NATIONS ECONOMIC COMMISSION FOR AFRICA (ECA) MEMBERS 

All independent African countries (South Africa excepted until conditions be come propitious for participation) are full members. Non-independent African territories and their metropoles participate as associate members. 

FUNCTIONS 

The ECA is a UN regional body created by the Economic and Social Council in 1958 as one of four Regional Commissions. It is dedicated to the promotion and planning of African economic and social development through cooperative and regional action by African States. In 1965 and 1966, the ECA sponsored meetings on economic cooperation in each of the four African subregions-East, Central, North, and West. The establishment of the Economic Community of 

Eastern Africa was a result of one of these meetings held in Lusaka in 1965. 

The Articles of Association for the Economic Community of Western Africa, which resulted from another ECA meeting, are about to be signed. 

Two of the major accomplishments of the ECA have been the establishment of the African Development Institute at Dakar and sponsoring the formation of the African Development Bank (now completely autonomous) at Abidjan. In addition, the Commission has established statistical training centers at Addis 

Ababa, Yaounde, Dar-es-Salaam, and Achimota (Ghana).

The ECA has an expert staff and carries on extensive research an planning activities primarily from the Addis Ababa headquarters. 

ORGANIZATION 

There is a Secretariat at Addis Ababa headed by a Secretary General (currently Mr. Robert K. A. Gardiner of Ghana).

The ECA has subregional offices, each with a resident director, at Kinshasa, Lusaka, Niamey and Tangier.

The ECA has held eight annual plenary sessions, the last one in Lagos in February 1967. 

U.S. ROLE 

The United States gives active support and encouragement to the various programs carried on by the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA). Although the 

United States is not a member of ECA, we maintain a full-time liaison officer for work with the secretariat in Addis Ababa, attend the more important ECA meetings, and provide some technical experts at its request. 

UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM IN AFRICA THE UNDP 

The United Nations Development Program (UNDP) is the major UN technical assistance donor. The UNDP is essentially a financing and management organization; its programs are executed by the UN and the Specialized Agencies (FAO, WHO, etc). The United States has pledged to contribute up to $70 million to the 

UNDP in 1967, on a 40% matching basis. 

The UNDP assistance is of two types; technical assistance, and pre-investment surveys. The technical assistance component (formerly EPTA) administers standards technical assistance programs, through the provision of experts, training grants and project-related equipment, in all sectors of the economy. 

EPTA projects are normally of a 1-2 year duration. The pre-investment component (Special Fund) carries out resource surveys, and assists in the establishment and operation of training and research institutes. Special Fund projects are normally 3-5 years in duration.

ASSISTANCE TO AFRICA 

Africa currently receives the largest share of UNDP assistance, or 37% of the entire UNDP program. The African share includes $210 million in cumulative long-range Special Fund commitments since 1960, as well as $10 million in new technical assistance for FY 1967-68. 

Cooperation between AID and the UN in Africa (and elsewhere for that matter) in the technical assistance field takes place both at the program formulation and execution stages. 

United States and UNDP field staff are under instruction to maintain continuing consultation and exchange of information through mechanisms appropriate .to the individual recipient country. Coordination is carried on in the following ways: 

1. Technical and policy review of UNDP project proposals. 

2. Regular review by AID/W evaluation teams of arrangements for coordination between the U.S. and the UN. 

3. Informal policy and technical consultation between: 

(a) U.S. Government and UNDP Headquarters staff. 

(b) UN Resident Representatives and U.S. Government staff. (c) USAID Directors and staff and UNDP Headquarters staff (e.g., Resident Representatives visit AID for briefing, while AID Mission Directors do the reverse). (d) Formal USG statements to UNDP Governing Council. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Buchanan. 

Mr. BUCHANAN.  

Mr. Secretary, if I can correctly interpret this book before me of proposed programs, in the case of Ghana the cumulative assistance which Ghana had received from Communist bloc countries through 1965 was $231 million, in international agencies it was $63.4 million, from other free world nations it was $33.6 million, and from us was, after you take out the repayment and interest, $171.7 million, of which $22 million was in terms of grants. Since Nkrumah's shortcomings had been well known for some time and his policies and nature of his government before his ouster, and since we state, and rightly so, that the basic U.S. objective is to help Ghana evolve democratic policies and institutions and assume a stronger role in international affairs, which does now seem much more likely than under Mr. Nkrumah's leadership, do you feel that his ouster might have come sooner had the United States been less generous, and I wonder if in this policy of the past state of our generosity it did not help support a regime which was very much the wrong kind from the point of view of our purposes in 

Ghana and Africa?

Mr. KLEINE. It would be interesting to comment on the figures themselves, Mr. Buchanan. If you look at the trend line you will find that the major input into Ghana from the United States occurred in fiscal years 1961 and 1962. That was the Volta complex-hydroelectric and aluminum smelter for which a total of $82 million was obligated out of economic assistance funds and $65 million additional under Eximbank authority. When it became quite clear that Nkrumah's economic policies were and how they were going to affect his economy, plus the political problems that arose, our program was drastically reduced. And during the years after 1962 we maintained just a minimum of activity, all in the technical assistance field, and primarily in the agricultural area working with the farmers and institutions on at grassroots level to help the farmers improve their operations. We maintained this very low minimal level right up until the passing from the political scene of Nkrumah in 1966. It is only since that passing that we have again taken a renewed interest and have been, as Mr. Palmer

1967 

indicated, very pleased with the actions, the self-help actions that have been taken by the new leadership.

While we don't anticipate being an overwhelming presence as a donor, we do hope and expect to be an active participant with others under the leadership of the IMF and World Bank in furthering economic development in Ghana. 

Mr. PALMER. I would only like to add to that, Mr. Congressman, if 

I may, that we feel that having maintained this minimal program in the latter years of Nkrumah and particularly in projects that were closely related to people, that we feel this was a significant factor in letting the people of Ghana know we had not forgotten them, and from everything that we have heard in the post-Nkrumah period was very deeply appreciated. It was directed more toward the people. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Thank you, both, for this clarification. I don't believe the information before me showed this trend, and I appreciate the expansion. However, I think, of course you must keep in mind, as

Mr. PALMER. We do.

Mr. BUCHANAN. This would be very important, it would seem to me, in Africa as well as elsewhere.

Mr. KLEINE. There was a period just before Nkrumah fell that his government came to us with a whopping request for Public Law 480 assistance. It was not given.

Mr. BUCHANAN. That is good. 

Let me ask a question about Nigeria. As is stated concerning our program in Nigeria, the principal impediment to sustained progress is the adverse effect that internal dissents and external dislocations have had on Nigeria, and there are other obstacles, including the ethnic, resource and educational dissimilarities among regions, which complicate unification and economic development. Is it not true that the probable result will be that the eastern region will break away, and if and when this takes place, if it breaks away from the federation, what do you think will happen to the other regions? Will they too form independent states, or will the federation be maintained? 

Mr. PALMER. I do not think it is absolutely a foregone conclusion as yet, Mr. Congressman, that the country will break up altogether. 

This is a case in which there is a conflict between reason and emotion, and there are still voices of reason and a recognition of the value of the common market and the importance of common services. It is quite possible that it might move toward a very, very loose confederation or some kind of a common market arrangement. I think it is very difficult to say what we would do under particular circumstances until we actually know what the form of any association may be.

MONDAY, MAY 1, 1967 

HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

The committee met at 10:10 a.m., in room 2172, Rayburn House 

Office Building, Hon. Clement J. Zablocki presiding. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The committee will come to order.

We will resume the hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to amend further the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, and for other purposes.

We are privileged to have as our first witness today Mr. J. Orrin 

Shipe, managing director, CUNA International, Inc.

Mr. Shipe, you have a prepared statement and you may proceed, sir. 

STATEMENT OF J. ORRIN SHIPE, MANAGING DIRECTOR, CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC. 

Mr. SHIPE. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, first I would like to introduce my colleague, Mr. Donald Melvin, who is director of our legal affairs here in the Washington office. 

CUNA International, Inc., is a federation of credit union leagues organized in the various States of the United States, the various Provinces of Canada, and some 70 other countries throughout the world. There are approximately 45,000 credit unions throughout the world. Of this number, some 22,600 are in the United States, and they have a total membership of approximately 18 million members. 

CUNA International, Inc., is a contractor with the Agency for 

International Development. We furnish technical assistance for the establishment of credit unions in 12 countries in Latin America and in three countries in Africa.

As a contractor, we feel obligated to report to the Congress on the progress that is being made in establishing credit unions. At the same time, we seek your support and assistance in obtaining an amendment to the act which we believe will help us to do a better job with minimal cost to the United States.

During the calendar year 1966, the number of credit unions in 

Latin America increased from 1,912 to 2,216; the number of credit union members increased from 463,516 to 589,591; members' savings increased from $32 million to $41.4 million; loans outstanding increased from $29 million to $37.2 million. Cumulative loans since 

July 1962, the date we began operations under an AID contract, reached $111.7 million as of the end of 1966. 

There are approximately 266 members per credit union and the average saving per member is approximately $70. We estimate that 693

1967 

the credit unions have saved members approximately $5 million in interest during 1966. This assumes, of course, that the member would have been able to borrow elsewhere. 

Recently, we have begun a regional credit union development program in East Africa-specifically, Tanzania, Kenya, and Uganda. 

As of September 30, 1966, these countries had a total of 188 credit unions with 21,600 members and $480,000 in member savings. Loans to members exceed $400,000 to date. 

While these statistics are impressive, they do not begin to tell the true story of what credit unions are actually doing in these countries. 

That story is much more instructive and interesting. Therefore, we have included an appendix containing all the statistics on a countryby-country basis. 

The real significance of the development of a credit union movement in these countries is that it is (1) substantially and unequivocally a self-help program that marshals the individual financial resources in the form of savings of low-income people and puts them to use for home and family, agriculture production, low cost homes, medical and educational expenses, and as capital for small business enterprises; (2) that it furnishes an uncomplicated democratically structured institution which the members can operate themselves; and (3) that it provides a basic organizational framework which can be expanded to develop many other programs and services. 

It has long been recognized that a developing country must expand its productive capacity in order to develop the volume of goods and services to a level that will begin to satisfy the needs of its people. 

Capital formation and credit are essential to such expansion. 

For these reasons, the AID program is replete with means of encouraging the flow of outside capital into the underdeveloped countries: development loans, investment guarantees, et cetera. Yet, the credit union movement is one of the few AID-funded programs that is devoted primarily to gathering the financial resources of low-income people and putting them to multiple productive uses. 

To those administering the AID program, the means may not be as sophisticated or as glamorous as a commercial paper or stock market, but it is effective. Moreover, it is being accomplished by people with such low incomes that they do not have access to international financial markets where savings often leave the country in what has come to be known as flight capital.

This marshaling of savings and the consequent availability of credit is of such extreme importance that AID helped to establish a Cooperative Development Bank in Ecuador and has granted it a loan of $1.2 million. Credit unions purchased 80 percent of the voting stock in the bank and have borrowed from it. 

The credit union in turn loaned the money to its members who put it to use to increase their earnings. The increase in earnings resulted in an increase in savings, thereby making more credit available. 

This use of outside loans to generate inside savings is an extremely important concept which needs to be expanded and given widespread application.

In addition to being an ideal mechanism for the marshaling of savings, the credit union is an uncomplicated, democratically structured institution which the members operate themselves. The members elect their own board of directors, supervisory committee, and credit committee on the basis of one vote per member.

695 In many communities the credit union is the only forum where free discussion takes place in accordance with simplified parliamentary procedure. Moreover, in most countries the credit unions have grouped together in federations. 

These federations will eventually become self-sustaining by means of dues revenues. They conduct education and training activities and furnish services similar to trade associations in this country. Some of these federations are now establishing regional confederations. A more explicit example of conformity to title IX would be difficult to find. 

One of the most surprising realizations gained from our involvement in the AID program is that the credit union provides the basic structure through which people can mobilize their savings and thereby obtain the capital they need to develop other self-help institutional programs.

This flexibility has been demonstrated most effectively in a cooperative experiment to provide low cost self-help housing in Panama and in the establishment of a directed agricultural production credit system in Ecuador.

The self-help housing project was a cooperative venture which included other AID contractors. The credit union was chosen as the nucleus for the project because the local families had established good savings records and it constituted an effective precooperative structure. 

The members of the credit union had gained group experience and organization, families had learned to save regularly and had accumulated enough to make small downpayments on their homes. In addition, the credit union facilities were ideal for the receipt of loan payments and for assisting in the daily conduct of the housing program. In order to participate in this self-help housing experiment, each credit union family had to contribute both labor and a supply of local free materials such as cane for the house wall, poles for the house framework, and sand. It is estimated that the total contribution of the individual family represented 27 percent of the house cost. 

The total value of the house upon completion was approximately $365. 

Since the individual had contributed $65 of his own in labor and materials, this left a $300 amount to be financed. Of this, the member was required to make a downpayment of $30 and the loan principal of $270 was to be repaid over a period of approximately 8 years at a rate of interest of 42 percent. This amounted to a monthly payment of approximately $4, easily within the reach of those buying the houses.

While this was a simple demonstration project financed with a $3,000 grant from the Agency for International Development, it proved that really low-cost housing can be made available simply and effectively through the cooperation of the credit union members. 

As the recent issue of World Business has stated so well in a different context, "unless these small but important ways of improving living conditions are recognized, the task of building new housing units that meet minimum standards becomes almost insuperable.' 

The establishment of a directed agricultural production credit system has also demonstrated extreme flexibility in the agricultural area. 

In essence, this program adopted some of the principles of the production credit associations in the United States and combined them with the credit union principles.

In this instance a local credit union in Ecuador hired a bus and arranged for a group of small farmers to take a trip to visit the near-

1967 

est experimental farm. After seeing what could be accomplished, the farmers returned to their community and sought loans from the credit union for purposes such as hog production, chicken raising, and various other farming enterprises. The farmers thus combined capital and technical "know-how." One young girl acquired a flock of 500 sex link chickens. The members of a local club borrowed from the credit union to build a bread oven and instead of having bread delivered once a week from the nearest city, they baked their own bread. A farmer earned $30 a month raising and selling hogs. The credit union eventually increased its savings and adopted a policy of planning its loan portfolios so that 80 percent of the loans are made for production purposes and the other 20 percent for consumer or emergency purposes.

In both of these examples, the credit union was used as the basic vehicle for helping to solve two of the developing country's most pressing problems, housing and agricultural production. When these programs become more widespread in rural areas, they may help to stem the migration of people from rural to urban areas. In the long run, the discouragement of migration will cost less than solving the problems resulting from increased urbanization. 

This report may indicate to you that we don't have any problems. 

We do have problems and we need you help to solve one of them. 

You will recall that last year at the request of Congressman Fulton we prepared an amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act which would have provided an investment guarantee for loans made by investors to credit unions in Latin America. We again make that request and we have attached a suggested amendment which has been drafted to accomplish this purpose.

We think it is essential that this guarantee be provided for loans made to credit unions. Earlier in our statement, we indicated that the establishment of a Cooperative Development Bank in Ecuador and its consequent use of outside loans to generate inside savings proved to be extremely successful. This success has indicated to us that we must expand this mechanism. We think that the appropriate means to expand this mechanism is to encourage participation by other investors, including credit unions, in the United States. We believe that by making additional funds available to credit unions in developing countries, this method will be beneficial in that it will have the advantage of opening up a more personal relationship between members of credit unions in this country and the members of credit unions in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. At the same time, we would like to make it clear that we would seek loans from investors other than credit unions. We believe that their assistance and interest would also be beneficial to the overall solution of the problems with which we are confronted. 

In the language which we have prepared, you will note that we have asked for a guarantee of 100 percent. Initially, we think that this is essential since this is a relatively new concept. Moreover, the laws governing credit union operations in this country are rather restrictive and generally do not allow a credit union to invest in obligations that are not guaranteed by some agency of the Government. Also, this is somewhat different from the 100-percent guarantees which are now available for investors in savings and loan associations in Latin America where, generally speaking, there is a completed house which can serve as security for some loans.

697 1 We are not asking for very much. We have restricted the authorization for such investment guarantees to approximately $1 million and limited its application to Latin America. This has been done for two reasons. First, we believe that it will take time to interest 

U.S. investors in the program, and, secondly, we believe that $1 million will be relatively insignificant insofar as the U.S. balance of payments is concerned. In this latter regard, we note that the administration recently informed the Congress that the United States has a surplus balance-of-payments position with the Latin American countries.

We cannot overemphasize our earnestness concerning this matter. 

We need to try this concept and we urge the committee to give us its support in this matter. 

Our plans for future development of the credit union movement in Latin America are moving forward. We are in the process of establishing a bonding program for credit unions in Latin America which will enable credit unions to obtain adequate protection at minimum cost. In addition, we have recently published a ""Technical Operational 

Manual for Credit Unions" which is being widely distributed throughout Latin America. At the same time, studies are being made concerning the applicability of a data processing centralized bookkeeping system and a correspondence educational course is being set up. 

These steps are being taken in addition to the many seminars and other educational activities which we are constantly conducting throughout the area.

In closing we would like to state that we obtain a considerable amount of satisfaction from the job that we are doing, and we would like to thank the members of the committee for ourselves and on behalf of the credit union members in Latin America and Africa for the support that you have given to us. Your interest and generosity, on behalf of the American people has brought hope into the lives of many people.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Shipe.

Has the amendment that you are proposing to section 104 of H.R. 

7099, to authorize the issuance of 100 percent guarantees for credit unions in Latin America, been discussed with the investment guarantee people of AID? 

STATEMENT OF DONALD J. MELVIN, DIRECTOR OF LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENTAL AFFAIRS, CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC. 

Mr. MELVIN. Casual discussions took place. Last year the same amendment was offered and AID was supposed to have issued a report to the committee concerning its advisability. As far as we were able to determine, the report was inconclusive. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. What was their attitude as to its acceptability? 

Mr. MELVIN. In this review they supported it, but the problem was with the balance of payments. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you. I have no further questions. 

Mr. FULTON. Are you referring to the amendment that I had suggested to them or one of your own?

I didn't find the country of Argentina being listed. They are not a member of CUNA?

Mr. SHIPE. No, they are not a member of CUNA. There is an unusual activity in Argentina. Although we have had a number of visitations there we have yet to find a group that we can work with like we have in Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru, and Venezuela, and other countries. We tried to find a basis that has a certain very essential requisite before we get a program launched. Further, AID has not been inclined, because of the Government's situation, and the local situation itself, to generate a contract. 

Mr. FRASER. Could you spell out a little more fully what you mean when you say you cannot find any group to work with there? 

Mr. SHIPE. The credit union activity in Argentina really has some unorthodox characteristics. Because of this and because of the governmental situation, which has been quite unstable so far as credit union possibilities are concerned, and because some of the elements within this unorthodox operation have great differences of opinion among themselves, we haven't been able to find a basis to work with any cohesive group.

Mr. FRASER. I was curious to know what the unorthodox arrangements are.

Mr. SHIPE. They vary. Some of the types of operation are not what we would call a credit union by the yardstick that we utilize; that is, a group having a common bond of interest as an employment association or residence, and following very basic cooperative principles of one member, one vote, pooling the savings, making the savings available to themselves, and sharing what profit, as such, would result.

Mr. FRASER. There is a law as to that. 

Mr. SHIPE. The law is ambiguous. The government a year ago took possession, in effect, of the organizations which are there. 

Mr. FRASER. I recall the report that they took over the credit unions. What has happened since?

Mr. SHIPE. We are not too familiar with what has happened since. 

Our communication has not been as adequate as we would like. We had quite a discussion with two of the elements from the Argentine at a conference we held in Jamaica last October. At this conference we asked the various cooperative credit union groups throughout the world to come together. Argentine did send two groups but they were battling among themselves. It was difficult to communicate or to find a basis for a modus operandi. 

Mr. FRASER. Do you know why the Argentine Government took over the credit unions there?

Mr. SHIPE. It is not too clear. There are some who say it was because they were exceeding their proper role, and there are others who say they were not obeying some of the basic laws of the country. 

Mr. FRASER. I notice you are only in three countries in Africa. 

How is it you are in only three countries in Africa?

Mr. SHIPE. We are anxious to be in more countries than three. We have been working with the countries in Africa in two approaches. 

CUNA International not only is developing credit unions in the underdeveloped countries through AID contracts but through a portion of its own budget. If the AID contract does not jell because one of the local country governments is not interested, or is not desirous, or the AID administration is not ready to allocate funds or program there because of other fiscal reasons, we are there before the

701 AID program and are there during the AID program in this other budget of CUNA's funds. This is limited because we have to spread it over quite a bit of the world. We have to find the parts of the world, the countries where there are certain favorable elements: one, that there is enough people who are interested and who are capable and desirous of helping develop a program; two, that there is reasonable governmental support in that we have legislation so that the government will enact a law so that they will follow certain legal standards. 

So if these factors are there, and we have manpower and budget available, then we try to generate the program. Essentially, it has been the convincing of countries in Africa and the AID administration that more contracts should be launched for the development of African credit union programs. It looks more favorable than it has in the past.

Mr. FRASER. Finally, I would like to ask about the proposal for the Inter-American Cooperative Bank. My impression is that this hasn't gotten very far. I may not be up to date on it. Do you have any knowledge of it? What is your opinion about this with respect to the work in the credit union field? 

Mr. SHIPE. I am more knowledgeable how it applies to specific credit union activity and development. We feel it has promise and possibility for accelerated credit union assistance. We cite specifically the outstanding development in Ecuador. This same program is now being launched in Peru. We expect a similar approach in Bolivia and we expect good results to come from it. 

We would have to confess that we don't feel that the Inter-American Cooperative Bank has moved as rapidly as we think it should or could. We see indications this will be improved in the future. 

Mr. FRASER. There has been a slowdown in AID, itself?

Mr. SHIPE. I wouldn't go so far as to say "in AID itself." Everyone involved hasn't been giving it as much shoulder to the wheel as we in the International Mr. FRASER. If this would become a vehicle for channeling loan money it could also become a source of educational assistance? 

Mr. SHIPE. Yes.

Mr. FRASER. This could be run by the Latin Americans, themselves, which would be a very desirable arrangement.

Mr. TAFT. Mr. Shipe, may I compliment you for a very fine statement, and also say that I think the credit union movement deserves a great deal of credit for their efforts in this connection and the progress they have been able to make. 

I was interested in two or three things in your statement. I notice that your approach to the East African situation is a regional approach in the three East Africa countries. Has the breaking down of the 

East African currency union had an effect upon your operations there? 

Mr. SHIPE. Not as yet. We haven't felt any problem because we are so basic in the service that we provide through credit unions to the people that we really don't get into that sophisticated financial stream of activity.

1967 

Mr. TAFT. I see that your exhibits while they cover Latin America don't cover the operations in East Africa. What has the experience been in a general way as to the number of credit unions that have been formed, the deposits and loans and other operations?

Mr. SHIPE. On page 2 we have statistics regarding the total credit unions, 188 credit unions in the three African countries, 21,000 members, and 480,000 member savings and loans to date. We consider this good progress from the standpoint of the job, the hill to climb there, the illiteracy, the lack of any basic background or skills in working together. It is rather amazing, Congressman Taft, how far back we have to start with these people as compared to this country, the illiteracy, the lack of any know-how in democratic procedures, or handling their own finances, plus a great deal of plain distrust which has to be overcome insofar as their being convinced they can do this themselves, and that their money will be there and somebody won't run away with it.

We are pleased so far with the progress and the people we have working there on the program report good progress. We expect it to accelerate much more rapidly after the first 2 or 3 miles are covered which has been the accomplishment to date. 

Mr. TAFT. How do the activities break down between the three 

African countries?

Mr. SHIPE. Tanzania was our first spot, and these other spots have come since.

I might add, too, Congressman Taft from Ohio, that the Ohio Credit Union League has made a contribution of several thousand dollars to assist the pioneering development in Lagos. 

Mr. TAFT. You have spoken in Latin America particularly of the successes that you had. My colleague, Mr. Fraser, got into the Argentinian situation which I don't know whether you would rate it as a success or failure or a zero factor; what other failures have you had?

How many credit unions that have been set up in Latin America have gone out of business in the last 3 or 4 years?

Mr. SHIPE. I couldn't give you at this moment an exact figure. 

However, I could say this, that the number of credit unions which have not gotten off the ground, so to speak, are no greater than here. 

In fact, I think the number is less. It has not been a matter of concern from the standpoint of our analysis of where we have come and where we are going. We just recently had a session in Panama called by 

CUNA International of the representatives of the countries; there were 15 countries there.

We discussed the progress and future operations, and this was not more than of normal concern. We have the usual problems of giving adequate field assistance and adequate training, but we are happy to report that the people are approaching it with good zeal and good application. 

Mr. TAFT. What mechanics do you have for inspection of the various credit union operations, governmental or otherwise?

Mr. SHIPE. Let me recite how we do it in Ecuador; this is a good example, and Bolivia is similar.

The credit unions operate their own credit union league; it provides an inspection service and it gets a monthly report from each of the credit unions. If they find a problem developing, where there might be delinquent loans or inadquate bookkeeping, then field assistance

703 from the federation, plus assistance which has come from the Peace Corps is made available. Ecuador has employed over the last several years about 40 to 50 Peace Corps volunteers in the training of these people in the operation of their credit union, their bookkeeping and education, and it has been outstandingly successful. 

Mr. TAFT. Going back for a moment to the East African area, what percentage of employees of the credit unions are of African extraction and what percentage if any are of Asiatic extraction?

Mr. SHIPE. The people that we put over there as technicians and as trainers are from the United States. They work with the local people, natives, in training them to become adequately backgrounded and skilled so they carry on the work and we will pull our people out as fast as the native people themselves can pick up and carry on. 

Mr. TAFT. By "natives," you mean African extraction as compared to Asiatic extraction? 

Mr. SHIPE. Yes.

Mr. TAFT. I ask those questions because East Africa is somewhat dominated by the Indian interests. 

Mr. SHIPE. Our workings so far have been with the native African people, themselves. These are the people who are primarily in their government and in their various organizations who are interested in getting the credit union program underway and we have that as our area of operation.

Mr. TAFT. With regard, Mr. Shipe, to the amendment that is proposed and attached to your testimony, is the 100-percent figure in your opinion a sacrosanct figure, or could something less than 100 percent requiring some risk capital to be involved be feasible? 

Mr. SHIPE. It is not a figure that we feel would be necessarily sacrosanct, but we feel it would be helpful in getting the program moving without an overextension of effort to convince people that they ought to experiment. We feel this would help to get the wheel moving and turning. If it were less it would probably take more effort to convince people it should be done. We are engaged in a program of trying to develop credit union relationships-such as a credit union in Ohio having a relationship with Peru or Bolivia. We have already had a group of credit union people organize a tour which went to Colombia and visited the credit union people there, even brought them some adding machines and established contacts so there would be this communication back and forth. 

We feel this interlending between credit unions here and in Latin America is a good program and it should be encouraged, and it takes some convincing, some education, some persuading, and we feel that 100 percent guarantee in the amount we ask for is a nominal amount. 

We feel the 100 percent would be helpful to launch the program more quickly and more successfully and without a lot of great effort which is demanded in other necessary areas. 

Mr. TAFT. Do you think you would have as direct interest and attention as there would be if you had a 10-percent risk factor which the sponsor would himself be carrying?

Mr. SHIPE. I think the pluses of the 100 percent offset the factor that you mentioned, which has merit. Not everyone is in favor of oversea credit union development activity. Not all of the people are as missionary minded as the majority, and we do have some who say we still have an awful lot to do right back here in Mansfield, Ohio; why go into Illinois or into Panama or to Argentina.

STATEMENT OF EDWIN CHRISTIANSON, VICE PRESIDENT, NATIONAL FARMERS UNION Mr. CHRISTIANSON, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the National Farmers Union is a grassroots organization interested in bread-and-butter issues. But our members concern themselves with other matters besides farm prices and farm income. 

This is because our members know that what they are able to take in and what they are required to pay out depends on many things other than the weather, hard work, and good luck. 

Our members are family farmers, and they are keenly concerned about which way our agriculture is going. They feel strongly that family farms are necessary in a vital, healthy rural society which rests on the idea of democracy and private enterprise. 

So, it is understandable why our members are not only concerned about farm production and farm prices, but about schools and education, health and medicine, recreation and ways for developing a fuller life. We believe that this not only can be achieved, but is being slowly reached by using all of the resources of our pluralistic society, in which the individual and the government make their contributions. 

The Farmers Union is concerned not only with the well-being of its members, but of all farmers. We are aware that we need the support and good will of many other groups and organizations when we face a common problem, and that the self-help of individual initiative must be complemented by cooperative effort and supported by sound legislation.

The members of the Farmers Union are also aware that their own well-being requires them and all the farmers in our country-to look beyond provincial borders and even beyond our national horizons, because in the world today there is only one agricultural problem: how to produce more.

While in the United States we may debate about marketable surpluses, throughout the world the challenge to men and nations is how to meet the specter of hunger and even starvation by increasing yields in lands where the wooden hoe and the bent back are still the symbol of agriculture. So, as producers of food which now goes abroad, the American farmers feel that they should have a part in deciding how it can be used best.

This is one reason why the National Farmers Union has consistently supported the foreign aid programs of the U.S. Government, had the personal concern of its members in how our food commodities were distributed and used, and now strongly supports the overall program of the Agency for International Development, but especially its emphasis on expanding agricultural production abroad. 

We await with considerable interest for signs of the effective utilization of resources in the newly created Office of the War on Hunger in AID, ostensibly created to activate the President's all-out commitment to transforming traditional agriculture into a productive system. We believe in this area that the establishment of cooperatives will contribute both to increasing production and improving income of producers. 

We are aware that for many people the measurement of our foreign aid success is still thought of in terms of huge loans and grants made for the purpose of financing AID capital projects such as roads, bridges, 77-470-67-pt. 4- -2

1967 

fertilizer factories, irrigation systems and the like. These huge and dramatic projects, costing many millions of dollars, are being carried on by private American construction and engineering firms in more than 50 countries. They are demonstrations of the engineering skills of this country. We should be proud of them and the contribution they make to the economies of the developing countries. 

Without detracting from their contribution, the National Farmers Union, at the same time, must be reflecting the views of many sympathetic Americans, when we express the wish that more of AID's efforts could have gone into the building of democratic institutions, and in the use of U.S. resources in so doing. 

Vice President Humphrey called for such action when as a U.S. 

Senator he had included in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 a section that provides that "it is declared to be the policy of the United States *** to encourage the development and use of cooperatives, credit unions, and savings and loan associations ***" as part of our foreign aid program. 

At that time, the Vice President said that "In the cooperative idea, we are exporting one of the finest products of a democratic society. 

And the cooperative program is not one of dollars, but of people.' 

This call for intensifying the participation of people in self-help projects has been sounded again by Representative Fraser, of Minnesota, who was joined by both Republicans and Democrats, in his emphasis on the use of democratic institutions abroad. I refer to title 

IX, section 281 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966, which states: 

In carrying out programs authorized in this chapter, emphasis shall be placed on assuring maximum participation in the task of economic development on the part of the people of the developing countries, through the encouragement of democratic private and local governmental institutions. 

And in order that there be no misunderstanding, the House of Representatives stated quite clearly that new attention must be given in the administration of U.S. development assistance programs to the goal of attaining a larger measure of popular participation in development.

The House of Representatives statement then goes on to declare that:

This goal can best be achieved through the fostering of cooperatives, labor unions, trade and related associations, community action groups, and other organizations which provide the training ground for leadership and democratic processes; through making possible increased participation of such groups and of individuals in the planning, execution, and evaluation of development undertakings, through broader and more effective utilization of the experience and resources of existing private and voluntary organizations; and, generally, through the building of democratic private and public institutions on all levels-local, State, and National.

That certainly is clearly stated. But the House went one step further to warn those engaged in carrying out the programs of U.S. development assistance that- *** it has become increasingly clear that failure to engage all of the available human resources in the task of development not only acts as a brake on economic growth but also does little to cure the basic causes of social and political instability which pose a constant threat to the gains being achieved on economic fronts. 

This is the kind of assistance that our members can understand and want to have a hand in. This is person-to-person involvement, seeking to embrace as large a part of the total population as possible in pro-

707 grams that call up new skills and develop new resources. This is the kind of development in which U.S. cooperatives and other private and nongovernment enterprises can actively assist. 

It is to be noted, however, that last year out of the more than 1,300 technical service contracts with a total value of approximately $439 million, the cooperative portion with contractors amounted to less than $6 million, and the total of all assistance for all kinds of cooperative development was only $9.5 million. 

We feel this figure should be considerably increased. Actually we say a figure should be increased and we justify this by saying that even with this rather limited kind of assistance for cooperative development, over a 5-year period, AID has in one way or another been involved with more than 40,000 cooperatives with 16 million members in 54 countries.

In the area of food and agricultural development, which certainly is of deep personal interest to many of our members, the National Farmers Union is encouraged that the AID program gives highest priority on the war on hunger which the President announced last year. We believe that the proposed $668 million which AID is prepared to invest to support the efforts of the developing countries to feed themselvcs is a wise increase over the $504 million earmarked for fiscal year 1967, provided it is providently expended and there is some relation between crash programs to step up production and the creation of storage, transportation, processing, and marketing institutions-in which cooperatives should play a dominant part-so that the producers have reasonable hope of being materially rewarded for the increases they are able to raise. 

One of the few really bold, pioneering international efforts by our Government in foreign aid has been our food for peace program. It is our hope that new, creative, and fertile concepts will be injected in the food aid program as it is involved in the war on hunger, and that in the process AID is constantly reminded of the American producers' role in this area. Here, too, is an opportunity to tap the vast resources of U.S. cooperatives, farm organizations, and private agricultural enterprises-mainly technical know-how and skills in the broad agribusiness community-to provide the developing countries with the best and most knowledgeable kind of functional assistance. 

We note that the International Cooperative Development Service now is a part of the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise, and that this may be an opportunity to utilize the special resources of cooperative enterprises and those of commercial enterprises to achieve maximum benefits in many of the developing countries. Just as there is a cordial and profitable relationship between these different kinds of private enterprise in the United States, it should be encouraged abroad to strengthen the free enterprise economies of these emerging nations. 

The National Farmers Union has approached the world's agricultural problems on a multilateral basis, working closely with agricultural organizations of the other countries of the world through the International Federation of Agricultural Producers. Our members believe that this is the most effective way of providing technical assistance, grants, and loans to developing countries. We are pleased and encouraged every time we are aware that the steps of AID and our 

Government are in that direction.

1967 

The members of the Farmers Union have for several years now been hosts to small farmers from South America, and French-speaking Africans who hold important agricultural and cooperative posts in their countries. These farm and cooperative people are brought to the 

United States by AID, but they come to the farm homes as guests of the people. Here they truly learn what U.S. farm life is like, what the functions of democracy are, and the operations of community institutions, ranging from cooperatives and credit associations to the local school, church, and business enterprises. 

Through our affiliated cooperatives, and from out of our own Farmers Union ranks, we have sent a number of co-op specialists abroad to Uganda and Kenya and Liberia in Africa, and to Thailand and Nepal and the Philippines in the Far East, to work with the people in gaining an education, in improving business and accounting methods, in teaching them to do better for themselves. 

Other organizations are engaged in similar work. We are only beginning to scratch the surface. We believe that there is great need to step up the kind of assistance and to reach more people faster. We also believe that cooperative-type assistance is essential if this goal is to be achieved.

As we said last year, "We believe that no nation can continue to be rich and secure simply by isolating itself from the poverty and hunger of the surrounding nations and that our Nation's agriculture cannot hope to prosper and achieve more for the producers so long as most of the world's farmers can hardly feed themselves. "We feel strongly that only when there is a world-planned food program can there be a sound foundation for developing a world peace. "That is why we give strong support to the efforts of the Agency for International Development to help people in the new and developing nations throughout the world to help themselves." 

This we still believe.

We want to express our thanks to the chairman and to the members of the committee for the opportunity we have of presenting the statement here this morning.

STATEMENT OF REUBEN L. JOHNSON, DIRECTOR OF LEGISLATIVE SERVICES, NATIONAL FARMERS UNION

Mr. FRASER. I know there has been a lot of discussion in the country and around the world about the growing gap between productivity and consumption of food. I may be mistaken in my impressions, but it would seem to me that if the problem is as urgent as it seems to be, we would be doing far more than we are doing today to respond to that need. 

Have I been oversold on the problem, or undersold on our response? 

Mr. CHRISTIANSON. We agree that much more should be done and we feel much more could be done. Mr. FRASER. For example, if I understand the problem correctly, and I am sure everyone concerned with rural development is still searching for the answers, there are multiple efforts that are required.

They are going around doing things but these are not tied in with a

total attack on the problems. They are isolated contracts that are being carried on.
