My sense is that we are only touching the problem which is of tremendous dimensions. 

Mr. JOHNSON. I agree wholly with what you say, Congressman.

We certainly have merely just scratched the surface in our own help. 

I would like to go one step further and I know you share concern about this as well, that first we should try to coordinate our own program better, and then the second step and equally as important in my opinion, is attempting to try to get other countries to join us in the aid effort.

The monumental scope of this problem of hunger in the world and the realization that by 1980 we will be unable to produce the food needed to feed the population of the world-by the most optimistic predictions 1985-certainly would indicate that we need to deal with this problem through a multilateral approach. 

Our leadership in this direction has been encouraging. I hope we will be able to approach the problem of hunger on this basis. 

I was looking recently at a bulletin put out by FAO. This bulletin in brief not only describes the problem of population increase and the food shortage, but talks about the Indicative World Plan for Agricultural Development-a plan which has been in effect since about 1965. 

We have worked closely with the FAO and our Government to attempt to try to bring some indicativeness into this problem, to define it and try to interest leaders of the world in trying to do something about it. I understand that a further phase of it will be revealed at the second World Food Congress to be held in Europe in the summer of 1968.

I am sure our Government will be there and will be an important part of this effort. 

Mr. FRASER. I was struck by the fact that within the last year I believe there was a call for the recruitment of Peace Corps personnel to serve in India to work as newly educated agricultural technicians, to help in India to move the agricultutal efforts along. The fact that this comes now rather than 2 years ago or 4 years ago, the fact that they are relying on the Peace Corps as a source, suggests that the Government has great difficulty in securing this kind of trained personnel. 

To my knowledge today there is still no adequate training program for people who are going to serve in this capacity, working in the rural areas. That is the impression I have. There is no total integration of this, no Joint Chiefs of Staff, who are marshaling our assets and defining the resources we need to create and having the responsibility for seeing that these things happen. 

I find there is a great gap between our dialog and our response.

STATEMENT OF SAMUEL GREENE, FOUNDER AND DIRECTOR OF THE FUNDACION DEL CENTAVO (PENNY FOUNDATION) IN GUATEMALA 

Mr. GREENE. I will read my statement, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. FRASER. Mr. Chairman, Mr. Greene, I have to leave because

I have to go down and watch AID sign a contract on some agricultural

713 research. I want to say I have read your statement and I agree thoroughly with what you have to say and commend you for what you are doing, and the insights you are bringing to the committee. 

I think it is an excellent statement. 

Mr. GREENE. Thank you. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Greene, if you will proceed. 

Mr. GREENE. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am honored to have been invited to appear before this committee to make a statement about my activities in Guatemala as pertinent to U.S. efforts to help underdeveloped countries. I hope this statement merits your time.

When I withdrew from business activities in the States in 1960 and retired to my home at Lake Atitlan in Guatemala, I knew I had to find some useful activity there. For a year I traveled up and down the country, often on horseback, to remote villages, and came back always with reinforced convictions that the great efforts of the United States must be concentrated on helping the rural people. 

I found in most cases poverty and desperate conditions. To most 

Americans it is incomprehensible that most people do not have water, sewerage, health facilities, and are undernourished. I found that these people had dignity, were honest and honorable, but were without hope.

It seemed to me our job was to give them hope; and this meant the creation of some mechanism which would show the people how they could, through their own efforts, improve their lives. 

I came to the conclusion that these people could do all the necessary labor themselves, absorbing some of their underemployment, and using what I call the biggest bank in the world, the two hands of the poor man. But I also concluded that they could and would pay for the necessary material if the cost was within the range of their capacity. 

If I go into a village and say, "We will give you pipe for water for $1,000," they look at me in amazement. A thousand dollars is an incomprehensible figure to them. If I say, "We will give you pipe for water for 1 or 2 cents a day per family, and will give you material for a latrine for 2 cents a week per family, or give you an electric plant for 3 cents a day per bulb," they understand, and immediately form a committee to work with me.

I started with several convictions. I would not go and seek out projects. The villagers have to come to me. We would give them what they wanted as long as it was a reasonable request-and I find they are always reasonable. If they want an electric plant and I think they should have water they get the electric plant. They have made their consensus and who am I to change it?

I launched the Fundacion del Centavo in 1963-since then a legal Guatemalan organization, and spent a year raising the funds to get it going. I believe there is not enough U.S. or foreign money to do the work that has to be done; therefore, I made up my mind that the 

Guatemalan private sector was the one to provide the initial capital for a revolving fund, and they did.

Since 1963 we have financed 31 projects in 31 communities which have benefited about 25,000 people. The projects include the intro-

1967 

duction of potable water, electric plants, production co-ops, consumer co-ops, recolonization, schools, clinics, latrines, and the financing of fertilizers and insecticides. We have helped young men with tools after they graduated from their training schools. Currently there is a backlog of 50 projects, and more requests are coming in every day. 

The Foundation is also setting up what I believe is the soundest of all agrarian reform procedures, under a "buy, work, and pay" plan. 

It insures to the peasants immediate legal ownership of land, in contrast to a projected and uncertain ownership in a distant future. 

This is a realistic agrarian reform, not a political one, and has a greater chance of social and economic success. 

The terms of our loans are the following: Project loans range from $100 to $11,000-the $11,000 was for the recolonization project-the minimum time for repayment is 3 years, and the interest charge is 8 percent a year on the unpaid balance and a one-time charge of 6 percent for administrative expenses. This adds about one-third of 

1 penny per family to the daily cost of repayment. (The 8-percent interest charge is commented on later.) Our accounting records show that our capital is intact and all expenses are covered. 

There are many valuable and surprising byproducts of this work. 

Barbara Ward states that a major problem of underdeveloped countries is overspending and undersaving. When the people pay for our projects they are actually saving, as I will explain. All economists agree that we must increase consumption among the rural people for the economy to develop and must also make taxpayers of them. Our projects make consumers of the rual people by their buying material from the city businessman. If we go into a village which has an average income of $120 per annum per family, and we take about $12 per annum from that family for pipe, we have made a new taxpayer of the family, and they are paying for what is customarily the responsibility of a federal government. 

There is another startling byproduct of this self-help method. The village improvements do not cost the families 1 cent. No matter what ideology you believe in, no matter what economic system you are living in, there is one thing which is built into all of them: the poor man pays qualitatively and quantitatively the most for everything he buys. 

How does the work of the Foundation relieve this situation? 

Let me illustrate. The people have discovered that if they get drinking water through our help at 3 cents per day per family, the whole family saves more than that through much lower medicine costs, because they are no longer drinking parasitic water. 

An electric plant at 3 cents a day per bulb, half for amortization, half for service, leaves them with money in their pockets, because they had spent more than that for candles and kerosene. As a family repays a dollar a month for a loan to establish a consumer cooperative, they discover that the co-op's volume buying enables it to sell at lower prices, thus saving them more than $1 a month. 

Our idea that rural people want improvements, are willing to do all the labor and to pay for material, has been tried and proven correct. 

This idea should now be extended. I have just come from the Dominican Republic, sent there by the Pan American Development Foundation, affiliated with the OAS, to help them start the penny idea there in their new Dominican Foundation. The conditions there are the same as in Guatemala. I am certain we have made a good start now in the Dominican Republic.

715 I respectfully urge the Congress to find ways of directing loan capital for this type of help, involving only the private sector in the different countries, where it must match new funds with its own contributions. I have told the Guatemalan private sector I would not bring in a dollar of loan money until they matched it with 50 cents. 

The Pan American Development Foundation is one organization already established in the United States to handle such loans and activities in Latin America. I should like to add that although we have used only private money up to now the Inter-American Development Bank, for all its multimillion-dollar projects, has found time to study our activities, and has just given us a grant to institutionalize the Fundacion del Centavo. 

These funds will be used to train a Guatemalan successor to myself, and to provide the administrative basis for an expanded lending program. All the directors of the Foundation are Guatemalans, as are also all the officers. Most of them are graduates of American universities. Now, the day-to-day management belongs in the hands of a Guatemalan. Perhaps, then, I can be used to start this type of foundation in other countries.

I believe foreign aid moneys should be allocated to revolving funds, whereby the same moneys can be used over and over again rather than in one-shot expenditures. The former method is cheaper and conducive to local cooperation. I believe only in the use of money, and not the spending of it, for foreign aid. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Greene, for your excellent statement. It is my understanding that you are here at the suggestion of 

Mr. Taft. I will defer to Mr. Taft.

Mr. GREENE. I am.

Mr. GREENE. Yes, I have retired to Guatemala, Mr. Taft. 

Mr. TAFT. How long have you lived down there?

United States?

Mr. GREENE. Right. 

Mr. TAFT. Could you describe for us some of the other activities you have been engaged in, in Guatemala?

Mr. GREENE. We have started two other programs. One is in the field of health. I believe that practically all of our foreign aid is wasted unless we can establish a healthy base among the people of the country. It is tragic the small amount of money that is being

1967 

spent for health in Central America. It is very low in Guatemala; despite the present, biggest budget they have ever had for health, they are spending less than a penny a day per capita. All Central 

America is the same. Panama, which is somewhat richer, is up to 

2 cents.

I have asked many Guatemalan doctors why they don't go out into the rural areas. They have a very honest answer: "We are afraid we can't make a living there." I therefore started a program in which the Centavo Foundation plays a part-a five-point program to enable doctors to start a practice in the rural areas. Up to now there has been only one doctor to about every 200,000 people. 

I said to the doctors, "Go out and select your location. We will advance to you $200 a month for 2 years to help you get established. 

We will help you with equipment. But you must enter into a contract to pay this money back to us." 

After the doctors will have been out there for 2 years we will give them a scholarship for 1 year's further study in the United States. 

When the doctors know how many villages they can cover from the base they have established, we will connect their villages with their car and office, and with the largest hospital in Guatemala City, by means of radio phones, equipment for which the people will pay us back 3 cents a week per family.

The doctors are our representatives in their respective areas for projects for the Foundation. They establish a reciprocal feeling of good faith between themselves and the people in the rural areas. Thus the people begin to realize how much the doctors are trying to help them.

We are also using the doctors in a birth-delay program, and the doctors are studying the latest devices for birth control, and they will work with the people in a birth control program. 

The third program we have just started is one which will help reduce usury. The rural people never have any money, and when they die they must be buried in 24 hours. There is an immediate need for money for a plot, a coffin, candles, and even for drinks. So they get into the hands of the usurers, at 10 percent a month, and they never get out. We have just arranged with the largest insurance company in Guatemala-and it has been started also in the Dominican Republic-for a group life insurance policy for males-a $100 life insurance policy at 3 cents a week. That will be a very successful program. It is another form of bringing about savings. 

Mr. TAFT. Mr. Greene, thank you very much. The organization that you described originally, the insurance company, is a profit or nonprofit corporation?

Mr. GREENE. It is a profit organization. The largest insurance company in Guatemala.

Mr. HAMILTON. I want to compliment you on your statement and what you have done in Guatemala. I think it is a remarkable record.

Mr. GREENE. The AID mission in Guatemala is composed of very devoted, hard-working men, who give it their time, energy, and health to do the work. But I think that, like all AID missions, they come with conditioned thinking and preconceived notions, as if the United States is a macrocosm of what had to be done and that the undeveloped countries are the microcosm. They believe, usually, that that which works in the affluent, industrialized United States needs only to be reduced in scale for emerging lands. This concept just doesn't work. A shift in the basic idea is needed-less work from on top down and much more from below up. 

What I am saying does not apply only to Guatemala and the AID mission there. I think it applies to all our AID work.

I have been advocating and writing for the last 5 years that we must take what I call the big leap forward. That is, with television. 

I have prepared a program to put a television set in every village. 

We are not going anywhere until we work in that direction. If they double the budget, they would have 2% cents a day for education. 

All of Latin America suffers under a similar handicap. For 1965, the last figures I saw, the per capita expenditure on education by the Latin American governments was $7.95 per annum, which is a little over two cents a day. Under such conditions everything we do there for education is, in my judgment, an exercise in futility.

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM P. BUNDY, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS 

It is always a pleasure as well as a privilege to testify before this distinguished Committee. This is my fourth appearance in my present capacity, on behalf of the President's Foreign Assistance Program. 

My task today is to set forth the basic policy framework of our programs in East Asia, and then to discuss the policy factors that have entered into the programs country-by-country. 

Over the past months, we in the Department of State have worked closely with AID and the Department of Defense on the FY '68 presentation, which your Committee now has before it. [Security deletion.] 

Before going into the specific programs, I should like to state in a brief form the highlights of our policies in East Asia and the Pacific, for which these assistance programs are the indispensable tool. 

A. THE POLICY FRAMEWORK 

Like all our policies worldwide, our policies in East Asia and the Pacific, and the assistance programs that support them, are based squarely on the national interests of the United States.

The central propositions are twofold. First, that the extension of hostile control over other nations or wide areas of Asia, specifically by Communist China, North Korea, and North Viet-Nam, would in a very short time create a situation that would menace all the countries of the area and present a direct and major threat to the most concrete national interests of this country. Second, and directly related to the first proposition, is the belief that an East Asia and Pacific region comprised of free and independent states working effectively for the welfare of 77-470-67-pt. 4- -3 721

1967 

their peoples is in the long run both essential to preventing the extension of hostile power and, more broadly, to our worldwide interest in peace and progress. 

These two propositions have been the cornerstones of our policy in East Asia and the Pacific at least since 1950, and indeed in their essential elements since the end of World War II. They have been consistently carried out under four 

Presidents and under both parties. 

Most recently, our objectives have been eloquently set forth in the Goals of Freedom stated in the Manila Conference of October 1966, in which the United States joined with six other East Asian and Pacific nations in declaring “our unity, our resolve, and our purpose in seeking together" four goals of freedom. These are "1. To be free from aggression. "2. To conquer hunger, illiteracy, and disease. "3. To build a region of security, order, and progress. "4. To seek reconciliation and peace throughout Asia and the Pacific." 

The Manila Conference was the occasion for affirming these goals, which we deeply believe to be shared not only by the six nations that joined in that Declaration but by all the free nations of the area. 

At the same time, the fact that these goals could be declared at Manila, and considered realistic as never before, reflected the tremendous constructive changes now taking place in East Asia and the Pacific. It is not too much to say that we may well stand at a turning point in the evolution of Asia toward the kind of free and independent states that the nations of Asia seek, each in its own way, and that we, in our national interests, wish to support. 

Viet-Nam is, of course, at the forefront of our thinking, and is by far the largest single item in the program before you. Unless we can achieve a just and honorable peace in Viet-Nam, the security and the confidence of other nations of Asia are bound to be gravely affected. Viet-Nam must be able to work out its own future without external interference.

But, at the same time, our effort in Viet-Nam has already had a significant effect in Asia. The nations of Asia had begun to make major progress even before we took our major force and action decisions in Viet-Nam. Since those decisions, that progress has been accelerated in individual nations, and there has been an historic beginning in true regional cooperation. These developments mean that in the area as a whole there is now a much greater hope than at any time in the past that East Asia can become the kind of region its people want and that we support. 

Behind these great and emerging changes lies an atmosphere of growing confidence. This atmosphere rests on the demonstrated achievements of the nations of East Asia. But it draws great strength also from the demonstration that we and others have provided in Viet-Nam that we will assist, as necessary and where we are wanted, to provide security for these nations. And it depends deeply also on the belief that essential economic assistance will continue to be provided by the United States and increasingly by those other developed nations in a position to assist.

In discussing the specific programs we are putting before you, I shall go into more detail on some of the developments of the past two years, as well as the underlying progress that has continued for a longer period. Let me only mention the major change in Indonesia and the emergence of new regional institutions, notably the Asian Development Bank, the Asian Pacific Council of ten nations, the ASA grouping of Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines in Southeast Asia, and the host of constructive international cooperative efforts centered on education, transportation, development of the Mekong Valley, and other projects of a regional nature. 

In essence, East Asia is on the move, as never before in its history. Our role is that of a partner in the great changes that are underway. In that role, we are already joined by nations of the region itself Japan, Australia, and New Zealand-and there have come into being multilateral frameworks for assistance to Thailand, Malaysia, and-in the past year-for the critical situation in 

Indonesia. 

As the discussion below shows, our role differs greatly from one country to another. We cannot and should not act where we are not wanted or where there are not adequate local government programs to support. More and more, we shall act in concert with others, and the burden of assistance will thus be more widely and fairly shared. 

But act we must. The programs before this Committee are a very small fraction of the financial burden-not to mention the lives-that our essential secu-

723 rity efforts in Viet-Nam are costing us. We have made every effort to keep these programs to the lowest figures that will get on with the job. We beli ve that the authorization and appropriation of these programs is essential to our national interests. Viet-Nam 

B. SPECIFIC PROGRAMS 

For Viet-Nam, the programs before you cover [security deletion] million for economic types of assistance. Military assistance to South Viet-Nam is included, as last year, in the basic Department of Defense budget. 

The programs before you are a vital part of our war effort in Viet-Nam, and should be viewed in that light. They are directed basically to providing a flow of commodities adequate to meet the needs of the people and to control inflationary pressures that might otherwise as they threatened to do last year-bring our whole effort to a halt and cause serious adverse political repercussions. The second basic purpose is to improve the life of the Vietnamese people particularly in rural areas. This is a desirable purpose in its own right. It is also essential for maintaining and strengthening the confidence of the people in their government and in the effectiveness of non-Communist procedures.

I shall not go into further detail on these purposes [security deletion] which Mr. Poats will more fully discuss. Let me, however, mention some of the political elements and pacification elements of the situation that, in conjunction with the marked military progress, cause us to believe that over-all trends in Viet-Nam are now clearly moving in a favorable direction. 

First, the current village and hamlet elections. There now have been four rounds of these,¹ and the results have been most encouraging. Well over 2 million voters have gone to the polls-participation of about 80 percent. This process will continue in the weeks ahead. By mid-June some 13,000 local officials will have been elected in over 1,000 villages and 4,500 hamlets throughout the secure areas of the country. In the face of skepticism that free elections could be held in a country in the midst of a vicious war, this will be the second major election successfully organized and carried through by the government in less than a year. 

We believe this election is a critical step forward in restoring local government Second, relations of the Constituent Assembly and the Directorate. Under the 

Constitution, the Assembly will have responsibility for the preparation of electoral, political party and press laws and for supervision of the presidential elections. At one time there were those on the Directorate who felt the Assembly was exceeding its mandate. Chief of State Thieu and Prime Minister Ky deserve credit for persuading their colleagues to accept these controversial transition provisions of the Constitution-a reflection of their concern increasingly to involve civilian political elements in South Viet-Nam's Government.

Third, deterioration in the Viet Cong's morale. Since last fall, and especially in recent weeks, there has been a steep rise in the number of defectors from the Viet Cong. The national government has just issued a proclamation offering those misled or coerced by the Viet Cong the opportunity to rejoin Vietnamese society with full rights of citizenship and protection under the Constitution. This program of national reconciliation could be one of major military and political significance. 

Fourth, the accelerating momentum of revolutionary development. During the past year the organizational ground work has been laid for a more effective program of pacification and rural development. On February 1 the program had 

35,000 workers grouped into some 500 teams-seven times the number available a year ago. By the end of 1967 the GVN hopes to increase these numbers to 

50,000. While changing men's minds and the society in which a people lives cannot be accomplished overnight we now anticipate steady and lasting progress. 

In summary, in all areas of the Vietnamese conflict there is forward movement. 

In this, our aid program plays a vital role-by maintaining economic stability, supporting revolutionary development, providing war and refugee relief, and creating the conditions for economic progress. Laos For Laos, the program for FY'68 calls for a total of [security deletion] million in economic assistance. 

Military assistance to Laos, for FY'68, is not included in the over-all Military 

Assistance Program, but rather in the Department of Defense budget. [Security deletion.] 

Though overshadowed in public media by the struggle in Viet-Nam, this conflict in Laos continues steadily at many points throughout the eastern portion ! As of Apr. 23 inclusive.

1967 

of the country from north to south. Defense against Communist Pathet Lao attacks, supported by the North Vietnamese, exacts considerable human and economic cost. But looking beyond today's sacrifices, the past year has been a good one from the standpoint of both Lao national interest and our own. 

The Mekong valley remains free. The Government's forces have made gains in the see-saw, guerrilla-type_fighting. Notably, they have regained the fertile 

Nam Bac valley northeast of Luang Prabang, which had been under Communist control for several years. Control of this valley, lying on the traditional invasion route from Dien Bien Phu, substantially enhances security of the royal capital. 

New methods have also been found-increasingly effective for detecting, slowing and harassing the infiltration of men and supplies over the trail network through Laos from North to South Viet-Nam-although interdiction of these routes remains beyond Lao capabilities.

As Pathet Lao morale and capabilities have been reduced-by successful operations of the government forces, by persistent air attacks against supply routes, and by declining local support for the Communist guerrilla movement- North Vietnamese forces have taken an increasing role in Communist combat operations.

Despite persistent Communist pressures, the forms of the 1962 settlement have been preserved. Elections for a new National Assembly were held early this year in conditions of freedom throughout government-held areas. Souvanna Phouma has since been working out a limited cabinet reorganization to reflect the new balance of forces within a generally improved environment between conservative and neutralist elements. His able Minister of Finance, Sisouk na Champassak, has improved fiscal administration and reduced the government deficit about as much as we consider feasible if the government is to retain the confidence and support of a people at war. The departure of the colorful General Kong Le was a byproduct of efforts among the Lao to work toward a useful degree of reintegration between neutralist and other government forces. 

One of the distinctive ingredients of our assistance program is the village cluster concept of community development, stressing self-help principles. Some 350,000 people, or 15 percent of the population of essentially rural Laos, are now affectedand motivated to greater efforts on their own behalf. This program is undertaken in support of the efforts of the Lao authorities to build confidence in, and support for the government. We are also optimistic that efforts to increase agricultural production will, barring repetition of the disastrous flood of 1966, bring Laos to self-sufficiency in rice within a few years. Such gains, though necessarily limited, are reassuring because progress continues even in the midst of war. 

Another component of our assistance effort is the multilateral Foreign Exchange Operations Fund (FEOF), to which several other countries are contributing. The 

Fund has been successful in stabilizing the Lao currency. It requires our continuing support. 

An important element of our policy is retention of the multilateral support for Laos symbolized by the 1962 Geneva Accords [security deletion] and to reduce the burden on the United States of the foreign assistance without which the nation could not live. While substantial economic aid is being provided from numerous sources, we continue to seek to increase both the number of donors and their share of total requirements. Souvanna has been skillful in retaining international political support, not only from France and British Commonwealth members but also, at least passively, the Soviet Union. [Security deletion.] Thailand For Thailand, we are projecting economic assistance of [security deletion] million.

As in the case of Laos and Vietnam, we are proposing that military assistance to 

Thailand be handled in the Defense Department budget. [Security deletion]. 

While the Thai forces are not engaged in conventional combat [security deletion] they confront a significant and potentially serious security situation, particularly in the northeast area of the country, that arises directly from external intervention and support by North Vietnam and Communist China. 

In Thailand we see a good example of collective security at work in Southeast Asia.

As a member of SEATO, Thailand has faithfully carried out its obligations to come to the defense of a beleaguered neighbor.

Last May, Thailand announced its decision to commit air and naval units to Viet-Nam, in January its decision also to contribute ground forces. The Thai 

Armed Forces now are readying a combat team of some 2,500 men.

725 A most important contribution also is Thailand's policy to grant United States Air Force units access to its air bases. [Security deletion.] The sorties they fly against North Viet-Nam [security deletion] are an important part of our military effort. Thailand recently lifted virtually all restrictions on publicity about the operations of our aircraft in Viet-Nam.

In early March, Thailand agreed to permit the use of U Tapao Air Base for 

B-52 operations. [Security deletion.] Operations began in mid-April. 

Having shown its willingness to meet the obligations of collective security, Thailand has clearly earned the right to its benefits. And it has come under increasing Communist pressure during the past year as Peking and Hanoi strive to create a so-called "War of National Liberation." However, Thailand has needed and wanted only technical, materiel and training assistance. It is determined to defeat the Communist insurgents itself-without the participation of our forces. For several months, beginning last spring, we provided helicopter lift to Thai police and armed forces. This effort was necessary to allow time for training of Thai pilots in helicopter operations. [Security deletion.] United 

States-manned helicopters were withdrawn on January 31, as scheduled. 

The Thai Government has mounted a vigorous dry season offensive against the guerrillas, while carrying forward programs aimed at improving living conditions and cementing the loyalties of the population. The government's response has prevented the insurgents, now estimated at below 1,500 men, from establishing firm control over their mountain redoubts and surrounding villages, on which they must depend for food supply and other support. However, despite these successes, controlling the insurgency clearly will be a long and costly struggle. 

Our continued assistance will be required in the form of training, equipment, and technical aid.

Meanwhile, Thailand's remarkable economic performance continues. Growth in GNP in 1966 exceeded 8 percent. Exports, amounting to some $700 million, reached a new high. Despite floods which wiped out crops in areas along the 

Mekong, agricultural output increased by 4.5 percent. The new five-year Development Plan envisages further improvement of agricultural productivity, encouragement of diversified light industries, and accelerated investment in infrastructure projects. 

Thailand also provides strong leadership in the field of regional cooperation. 

Bangkok is a center of international activities-seat of the ECAFE Secretariat and most ECAFE committees, SEATO, the regional UNESCO and FAO representatives, the Mekong Committee, and the temporary headquarters of 

SEAMES, the Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Secretariat. The Asian 

Pacific Council's Standing Committee now meets regularly in Bangkok under 

Thai chairmanship.

Thai resources will be strained increasingly in coming years by the double requirement of an accelerating development and security effort. There will be a substantial rise in import requirements. To the extent they cannot be covered by Thai foreign exchange earnings these requirements will have to be met by greater foreign borrowing and a drawdown of Thailand's carefully accumulated reserves, which are an important factor in attracting vitally needed foreign capital.

U.S. assistance, therefore, remains essential. Economic aid will remain focused, for the present, on counter-insurgency and accelerated rural development in the North and Northeast Provinces. Military assistance will be aimed at further strengthening Thai capabilities to cope with the insurgency and deal with limited conventional military threats to the Mekong valley. 

Finally, let me call attention to the multilateral basis that already exists for development assistance to Thailand. [Security deletion.] From FY '63 to FY '68 

Thailand has received or will receive assistance from other countries and international agencies totalling $191 million [security deletion]. This amount very greatly exceeds that part of the United States economic assistance program for the same period directed to development as distinguished from programs directed at internal security and related rural development. Under World Bank auspices, a consultative group of thirteen countries was formed in 1965 for aid to Thailand. 

It is now expected that other donors will provide about two-thirds of the aid requirements for Thailand's second Five-Year Plan running from CY '67 to

CY '71. 

In short, Thailand should be looked at in two ways. First, as a country that confronts a significant internal security threat from Hanoi and Peking, and needs our economic and military assistance to that end. But, second, as a nation that has shown what sound policies, national cohesion, and effective effort can do.

1967 

With a low per capita GNP of only about $125, Thailand will continue to need external help. But the Thai have shown that they fully deserve such help and can use it effectively, and we believe that they will receive the bulk of their development needs from other nations and sources. There could be no better example of the constructive trends of which the nations of the area are capable if their security can be assured.

Korea For Korea, we are proposing [security deletion] million in economic assistance and [security deletion] million in military assistance. [Security deletion.] 

Korea has continued to make remarkable progress-political and economic. 

A new sense of self-confidence and self-assurance is sweeping the country. 

Korea's growing stature in international relations was dramatized by its initiative in convening the highly successful Asian and Pacific Conference (ASPAC) in Seoul last June. Another important step during the past year was the commitment of additional Korean troops in Viet-Nam, bringing the total number of ROK troops there to 46,000 men. Korea is working effectively with the Consultative 

Group established under World Bank auspices to coordinate and focus the interest of other industrial nations on the opportunities and requirements of Korea's second five-year development plan. Korea has overcome its attitude of dependence on the United States and is moving toward self-support. 

Meanwhile, Korea's own political institutions are becoming stronger. The regime has successfully made the transition from military to civilian rule. It has weathered internal political storms. [Security deletion]. Political activity is now focused on the Presidential election on May 3 and the National Assembly elections on June 8.

Progress on the economic front has been a major element in Korea's growing self-confidence. Korea's GNP last year rose by 12 percent (real terms). Exports increased almost 40 percent to about $250 million. Gold and foreign exchange holdings now stand at $256 million. Impressed by their own progress Koreans now are looking forward to the time when they will be free of reliance on U.S. concessional aid. 

While these achievements are considerable, they must be kept in perspective Korea still faces major problems. Population is growing at about 2.5 percent a year-though the government is making efforts to gain acceptance for family planning. Average per capita income, about $110, remains low even compared to many other developing countries in East Asia. The rising rate of investment required to sustain the momentum of economic growth, together with the burden of a large standing army, necessitates even greater efforts to raise the rate of domestic savings. 

U.S. economic and military aid remains vital to Korea's economic progress. 

Together with help from other countries, assistance on the scale proposed involves a careful balancing of all these requirements-to ensure continued combat readiness of the 600,000 man armed forces while maintaining the momentum of Korea's remarkable political self-assertion and economic development. 

In summary, Korea too has demonstrated in recent years what a vigorous Asian nation can do under conditions of security. Korean progress is above all a reflection of sound government policies and the quality of the Korean people. 

But I think it fair to say that it reflects also the wisdom and soundness of the assistance policies that we have pursued in Korea over many years. 

All of us can remember when questions were raised about our past assistance programs on the grounds that Korea was foundering and would never be able to take charge of its own affairs. Such doubts must by now have been conclusively resolved. For the Korea that is proudly fighting alongside us in Viet-Nam, taking a lead in regional cooperation in Asia, and advancing the progress of its people at rates close to those of Japan a decade ago is a Korea that has shown itself worthy of our continued support. 

The example of Korea has, indeed, had a marked effect on the rest of Asia. 

Representatives of other Asian nations have been quietly visiting Korea in the last two years to see how it was done. And I might add that private business in the United States, in Japan and in the nations of Europe is now taking a vastly increased interest in Korea. Last month, former Under Secretary George Ball visited Korea with a delegation representing twenty-seven American business firms; when these representatives saw what Korea was doing [security deletion] of them instituted surveys to explore the possibility of investment in Korea. 

This trend shows great promise for the future, and Japan's increasing economic help under the Japan/Korea Normalization Agreement of late 1965 is also playing

727 a major part. But, I repeat, our help continues to be needed to provide the essential public investment for a nation that still stands at a low stage of economic development.

Republic of China 

For the Republic of China, we are projecting [security deletion] million in military assistance. Economic assistance for the Republic of China, as the Committee knows was terminated in 1965, as a result of strong economic progress that made possible Chinese reliance on international institutions and private investment.

The situation of the Republic of China remains favorable. During the past year the Republic has made progress in strengthening its international position and in further developing Taiwan's economy. Several factors have contributed to a new and strong sense of confidence. 

First, the events on the China Mainland. The GRC considers these events dramatic confirmation of the growing ineffectiveness of Communist rule for solving the Mainland's problems. We have no evidence, however, that the GRC is preparing for moves to intervene. In his New Year's message, President Chiang explicitly stated that in recovery of the Mainland political means must take precedence over military action.

Second, related to these events, the dramatic improvement in the GRC's favor of the General Assembly vote on the China representation issue. 

Third, its forceful participation in regional cooperation. The Republic of China is a charter member of the Asian Development Bank. It has made useful proposals for cooperative developmental projects under the auspices of ASPAC. 

It is examining with the Republic of Korea the possibilities of closer cooperation in the field of trade and industrial development. 

Fourth, its contribution to the struggle in Viet-Nam. The GRC is providing under contract to AID, useful and effective assistance to South Viet-Nam, principally in the field of agriculture but also in health, electric power, and education. 

Fifth, the GRC's growing role in economic assistance to other developing countries. Since 1961, under its "Vanguard" Program, the GRC has been sending trained farmers from Taiwan to teach modern agricultural methods in friendly less-developed countries. There are now some 560 agricultural technicians working under this program in twenty-three countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America. 

This program not only provides effective economic assistance, it also has been important in impeding Chinese Communist attempts to gain a foothold in Africa [security deletion]. 

In connection with this "Vanguard" Program by the Chinese, let me explain to the Committee the support which we are giving. Over the past three years, the 

Chinese have brought this program gradually to an annual expenditure of approximately $5 million. Foreign exchange needs for this program were met by Chinese resources, while the budget was supplied from the local currency fund established to handle the proceeds of past AID programs. 

A year ago, it became clear that the program could and should be greatly expanded, to a level three or four times the $3 million level that then prevailed. 

The Republic of China asked us to consider a PL-480 program of commodities needed in Taiwan, with part of the proceeds to be made available in support of "Vanguard." After careful negotiation, the Administration has approved and laid before the appropriate committees of the Congress an agreement to provide a total of $18.75 million in PL-480 commodities, under Title I, in each of the next two years. One-half will be used to support "Vanguard"; the other half of the proceeds will go to local US uses such as base costs, Viet-Nam housing, etc.—all of these being needs that we would otherwise have had to meet through a direct dollar outflow. This agreement is now being negotiated with the Chinese Government.

In essence, we are financing aid programs in the agricultural field in Africa and elsewhere with the help of the Chinese at a lower cost and with an input of their resources that maximizes the total benefit. 

In the economic field, development efforts now increasingly emphasize industrialization. Exports last year rose by 14 percent to some $560 million. 

A notable development is the growing interest in the Republic in the strengthening of higher education. The number of college and university students has more than doubled since 1963. Universities have just accepted their first doctoral candidates in the sciences. The Chinese Government has begun a program to reduce the "brain drain" by creating graduate centers which would partly replace advanced education abroad. These and other measures augur for rapid growth of Taiwan's

1967 

educated groups in the years ahead, adding a powerful stimulus to the country's intellectual and cultural life. 

Although the growth of Taiwan's economy continues along the projections which led us to close out the AID mission in 1965, the Republic, with a per capita GNP of only about $230, remains unable to bear its large defense burden alone. 

Defense expenditures continue at about 10 percent of GNP and more than half the consolidated national and provincial budgets. Substantial military assistance remains necessary if the GRC is to maintain its defensive capability without sacrificing continued economic and social growth. 

A major part of our military assistance program for FY 1968 will be devoted to strengthening Taiwan's air defense. [Security deletion.] A cut in this program would have serious implications for the mission envisaged for the GRC's forces in our joint planning for the defense of Taiwan and the Penghus. 

Indonesia 

I turn next to Indonesia, where we are proposing [security deletion] million in economic assistance and [security deletion] million in military assistance limited to non-combat civic action purposes. 

We all know that two years ago Indonesia, under Sukarno, was sharply hostile to the United States, engaged in a sterile but dangerous confrontation with Malaysia and Singapore, and headed domestically for dominant Communist influence and for what might have amounted in effect to Chinese Communist control. In that period, we had reduced our assistance programs virtually to nil. 

The change since that time has been dramatic. After defeating the abortive 

Communist coup of October 1, 1965, the Army and associated civilian non- Communist political figures-under the leadership of General Suharto and Adam Malik principally-moved in March 1966 to strip Sukarno of a large share of his power. Last month, Sukarno's power was totally withdrawn, and it seems clear that Suharto is now in effective control. 

This has been a tremendously important change to Southeast Asia as a whole. 

A hostile and eventually Communist Indonesia could over time have undermined all that we were doing to defend Viet-Nam and to preserve the security of the rest of Southeast Asia. The present Indonesia-nationalist, prepared to live at peace with its neighbors, and directing its attention to its long-neglected economic problems-not only is a highly significant development in terms of Indonesia's own history, aspirations, and the welfare of its people-it also opens the way to a Southeast Asian community of nations living at peace and making human betterment its central objective. 

[Security deletion.] 

About a year ago, as we foreshadowed at the time to this Committee and others, it became clear that there was a need for emergency assistance. Accordingly, we bagan to provide urgently needed PL 480 commodities, notably cotton and rice. Most recently, we drew on the AID contingency fund for loans related to spare parts for industry. The cumulative total of our efforts to date, including commitments made so far in CY '67, is [security deletion] million, most of it 

PL 480.

Last summer, Indonesia began to plan its future seriously, and we and the other major creditor nations joined together to consider what we should do about Indonesia's debt burden, which it clearly was unable to handle either as to principal or interest. Meetings were held in Tokyo in July and September, and a final agreement was reached Paris in December, under which Indonesia has been totally relieved of servicing its public debts for this year, with the possibility of extension, and generous but realistic future grace periods and payment terms have been laid out. The Soviet Union, which holds about 40 percent of the Indonesian debt, did not participate in the group, but negotiated bilaterally a similar rescheduling agreement on very liberal terms. It seems clear that the USSR is conforming its own debt arrangements to those extended by other creditors including ourselves.

In effect, this debt arrangement made it possible for Indonesia to devote its resources to putting its chaotic economy in order. But it was clear all along that more would be needed, and the creditor group met in Amsterdam in February to consider a common framework of action by way of economic assistance. 

Indonesia's immediate need, during 1967, is to meet a foreign exchange gap estimated by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank at about $200 million. The principal method for meeting this gap is the supply of commodities urgently needed to keep the Indonesian economy afloat.

At Amsterdam, the United States stated that we would be prepared to provide long-term credits to meet up to one-third of the 1967 gap. We gave this under-

729 taking on two conditions that Indonesia would be successful in mobilizing the remaining two-thirds from other donors, and that Indonesia would continue the generally sound economic policies it was following to meet run-away inflation, to allocate its resources soundly in a desperate situation, and to encourgae private foreign investment that could over the years translate Indonesia's vast potential into solid growth. 

The program before you reflects the requirements to fully meet our Amsterdam undertaking. The Amsterdam group will meet again in June, and prospects now appear favorable that other nations will come forward with the remaining twothirds of the need. Moreover, Suharto is continuing the promising economic policies he had begun. [Security deletion] Suharto and his Cabinet have taken courageous steps to commence the task of economic rehabilitation and political reconstruction. They have turned to the IMF and IBRD for advice, and with their help have inaugurated an economic program designed to stabilize the economy and restore market forces as the principal allocative mechanism of the nation's economic life. To encourage foreign investment it has passed a new investment law and returned to foreign owners factories and plantations taken over by the previous regime. 

The regime thus is endeavoring to build a new national consensus centered upon economic recovery and resumption of economic growth. 

[Security deletion.] 

So we must look at our policy toward Indonesia one step at a time. We are entirely clear, as are the other participating nations as well as Indonesia's former enemies in Malaysia and Singapore, that essential assistance must be provided if Indonesia is to become a stable and useful nation in Southeast Asia. We are also quite clear that the problem must be approached on a multilateral basis, [security deletion]. And, finally, we are entirely clear that Indonesia must pursue the soundest possible policies. 

The economic future of Indonesia could be bright. The resources are there. 

But to get to the point where its resources can be properly developed we shall have to go through the present year and perhaps a longer period of what might be called sustaining assistance. To get Indonesia over the hump may require greater efforts, for a short period at least, by ourselves and other nations. 

But the stakes are high. With its population of 107 million people, Indonesia is by far the largest country in Southeast Asia. It is vitally in our national interest to maintain and strengthen the dramatic favorable changes that have taken place in the last two years. [Security deletion.]

The election of Ferdinand Marcos as President in November 1965 brought to power the most skilled, vigorous and attractive leader the Philippines has produced in some time. During his first year in office he has succeeded in arresting in some areas the politico-economic deterioration in the Philippines of the last few years. [Security deletion.]

[Security deletion] the Marcos Administration has taken important steps to improve the Philippines' economic management, such as a [security deletion] campaign to combat smuggling, and a variety of measures to improve monetary fiscal policies.

1967 

deletion]. The growth of the economy, which was impressive in the 1950's, has slowed down considerably in recent years and is just keeping ahead of population increase one of the highest in East Asia.

Lack of roads has become a serious impediment to adequate security in the countryside, to moving crops to market, and to the basic communications needs of the rural areas. At the same time, these battalions have already been able to show great progress in road building. To meet their equipment needs, President Johnson undertook last fall to support five battalions and to consider the support of an additional five. The Philippines have gone ahead to develop these battalions and are employing them effectively even with current limited equipment [security deletion.] 

In essence, our economic assistance program is aimed with new vigor at the critical problem of rural development, without which there will be a growing security danger in the Philippines. Our military assistance program is directed at internal security but plays a part also in the vital work of development. 

Lastly, let me call attention to one other promising feature in the Philippine situation. A year ago, the Philippines had failed to carry out their side of certain undertakings with the World Bank, and their relationswith the Bank were strained. 

Last summer, they put their house in order. Since then, the Bank has come forward with an additional $37 million in new loans. Negotiations are continuing for additional Bank projects, and the Philippines have fully accepted our advice that they develop their relationship with the Bank to the maximum, not only for future Bank loans but because the Bank could serve as the focal point for assistance from other countries. In short, the Philippines and we have been taking at least the first steps toward a broader framework of assistance from the Bank and other countires.

C. COUNTRIES NOT INCLUDED IN THE PROGRAM 

Malaysia and Singapore

As Annex C shows, both Malaysia and Singapore stand well above most of the nations of Asia in per capita GNP. Both have followed sound and progressive economic policies for many years. 

In the case of Malaysia [security deletion]. 

In support of her current five-year plan, which is being assisted by a group of nations that met in London last May, we have given an order-of-magnitude statement of intent to provide approximately $50 million in various types of support over the life of the plan. We envisage that the great bulk of this assistance will be through loans by the Export-Import Bank, and discussions have begun in this direction. The Malaysian situation bears watching closely, for the fact is that lower prices for tin and above all the drastic reduction in world rubber prices have created a much less favorable outlook for Malaysia than would have appeared to be the case even two years ago. The dangers to the Malaysian economy from declining export prices are heightened by the economy's heavy dependencealmost 40 percent on the export sector. Thus, despite her relatively advanced economic situation, Malaysia confronts the difficult problem of advancing the welfare of her people, and a continuing political problem of keeping harmonious relationships between the Malay and Chinese communities within her borders. 

In particular, the agricultural sector will need a great deal of attention in the years ahead to increase food production for the rapidly growing population, extend areas of irrigation, diversify agricultural crops and lessen dependence on a few exports with precarious market prospects. In addition, Sarawak and Sabah remain troublesome and potentially difficult, and represent an economic burden on the Federation.

For all these reasons, we shall have to keep the picture in Malaysia under close and continuing review.

In Singapore, we have no program of assistance. Our only recent action has been to authorize the commercial sale of rifles. Singapore is a relatively advanced and sophisticated, though small, nation. Her principal need is for markets for what she can produce and handle as a center of entrepôt trade for the area. 

Yet, again, we must continue to watch the situation in Singapore. Past birth rates were extremely high there, although they have been lately much reduced. 

Capital requirements are large for development of the economy's productive capacity as well as infra-structure, housing and other needs of a complicated urban society. In the rapidly growing labor force, there is currently significant unemployment. [Security deletion] we must continue to watch the situation in 

Singapore, particularly from the standpoint of our trade policies and the encouragement of regional cooperation, in which Singapore could play a useful and effective role.

Japan, Australia, New Zealand Japan, Australia, and New Zealand are not included in the program before you. All of these belong in the category of developed nations, although we are entitled to note that Japan's extraordinary progress owes much to the major economic assistance that we provided until the mid-Fifties. 

Japan in particular can and must play a major role in the development of East Asia. On the security side, Japan can and should do more for its own defense, but

1967 

the prohibitions of her Constitution as well as broader policy considerations preclude her taking a major regional role in this field of endeavor in the near future. It therefore is on the economic side that Japan can above all fulfill her proper role. And in the past two years, Japan has moved a long way toward doing so. Specifically, Japan's aid capital flows, on a net basis, to developing countries have risen from $304 million in CY 1964 to an estimated [security deletion] in CY 1966 (DAC definition) or from .48 per cent of national income to an estimated 

77 per cent despite a per capita GNP which, at less than $1,000, remains considerably below that of most developed countries. The official portion of this capital flow has increased even more dramatically, from $116 million in CY '64 to about $280 million in CY '66. For CY '67, projections indicate a further sharp increase of net capital flows, public and private, to developing countries [security deletion].

On a broad basis, Japan has committed herself publicly to a goal of providing 1 per cent of her GNP for foreign aid, with major emphasis on Asia. The 1967-68 budget brings Japan much closer to this goal. 

More specifically, Japan in late 1965 committed herself to providing Korea a total of $500 million in grants and soft public loans over a period of years, with another $300 million of private credits. Last May, Japan gave the largest single statement of intent to support the Malaysian five-year program. And in the context of the Amsterdam grouping of nations assisting Indonesia, Japan has now decided to make a $60 million contribution in 1967, roughly equal to our own. 

In the field of regional cooperation, Japan has been a consistent leader. Japan convened the first Ministerial Conference on Southeast Asian Economic Development in Tokyo in the spring of 1966. It followed this with the convening of the 

Asian Agricultural Conference last winter and with a highly promising proposal for an Asian Agricultural Development Fund under the auspices of the Asian Development Bank. The Bank itself is headed by a distinguished Japanese, Mr. 

Takeshi Watanabe. 

In addition, Japan has been a major contributor of non-military assistance to South Viet-Nam. It has recently announced its intent to increase substantially its 1967 contribution. [Security deletion] is doing a great deal, and, with the reelection of Prime Minister Sato and the attitudes of his government, the way seems clear for Japan to do even more.

The same is true for Australia and New Zealand, two of our staunchest allies. 

They are both contributors to the allied military effort in Viet-Nam. Both have long records of limited economic assistance to Asian countries under the Colombo Plan and directly in areas of responsibility. New Zealand, which is currently undergoing a balance of payments problem, is averaging aid of about $10 million. 

Australian economic aid, which has been doubling in the last five years, now is close to $150 million, with about one-half going to the territories of Papua and New Guinea. We are hopeful for a further significant increase in the year ahead. 

CONCLUSION 

As one looks at the history of our economic and military assistance programs in East Asia and the Pacific, certain highlights are evident. 

First, the success stories in Japan, the Republic of China, and-in recent years-Thailand and Korea. These cases show what can be done and they show also that the burden of economic assistance can in many cases be gradually reduced or eliminated, and what continuing burdens remain can be shared more equitably with other nations and agencies. 

Second, the war-related situations in Viet-Nam, Laos, and the security needs of 

Thailand must continue to be met in full.

Third, there remain difficult situations, notably the Philippines and Indonesia, in which we must weigh our policies carefully but in which judicious and carefully prepared assistance can be of enormous importance in bringing about lasting stability.

In the aggregate, the economic and military assistance programs before you are significantly lower than, say, five years ago or during the Fifties if one leaves out the amounts directly related to the conflict in Viet-Nam. The purpose of our efforts throughout the area is in large part to avoid another Viet-Nam. The trends in the direction of stability are now on the whole extremely encouraging. This is a time when our continued support of the programs before you could play a vital part in a new Asia.

STATEMENT OF HON. RUTHERFORD M. POATS, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRATOR FOR FAR EAST, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the privilege of reporting to the Foreign Affairs 

Committee on our economic aid activities in East Asia and to present the programs we recommend for Fiscal Year 1968. 

The members of this Committee are very familiar with the evolution of U.S. policy in East Asia. Successive U.S. Administrations, with bipartisan support of the Congress, have engaged the military, political and economic resources of the U.S. to help vulnerable and poor countries in East Asia maintain their independence and progress toward building viable societies. 

We are not undertaking this economic assistance effort in East Asia singlehanded. Japan has become a major donor. Other Western countries, the World

1967 

Bank and United Nations organizations help, as we show in detail in the printed presentation books on pages 283, and 288 and 292. Still, the U.S. economic aid programs constitute, through their size, motivation and contents, vital outside assistance to the achievement of dynamic economic stability, economic and social development and security of several East Asian countries. These aid programs can best be described as falling into four major categories: 

First, programs to support large scale, active military and counter-insurgency efforts, such as in Vietnam and to a lesser degree, in Laos. 

Second, programs aimed at heading off the full-scale emergence of a threatening 

Communist insurgency, as in Thailand.

Third, programs designed to achieve long-range-economic and social development, hand in hand with stabilization measures. These are the programs we have in Korea, the Philippines and Indonesia. 

Fourth, projects and programs to encourage and assist-along with other contributors Asian efforts toward regional economic integration and development. 

The four categories I have outlined are not mutually exclusive. In a single country, such as in Laos, we find elements of all four. But these descriptive cate gories highlight the main thrust of the country programs I will describe. Before 

I do so, I would like to put in perspective the overall size and the functional emphasis of our East Asian plans. 

Seen in the perspective of the last two years, our FY 1968 program in East 

Asia is as follows:
