The bulk of our authorization request, $550 million, is for Vietnam, as in FY 1967. I presented the Vietnam program to the Committee on 4 April and will not repeat that presentation today. The Vietnam program is submitted as a separate line item in the budget request for FY 1968. 

For the remainder of East Asia, we propose an AID program in FY 1968 of $260 million. This sum would appear to be level with our FY 1967 plans of $263 million but there are important differences. 

First: The opportunities and the requirements for effective regional cooperation are growing. The Executive Branch is, therefore, considering the introduction of separate legislation to support special regional funds to be administered by the Asian Development Bank.

Second: Within the $260 million requested by AID for East Asia (other than 

Vietnam) there are shifts in emphasis from the current fiscal year. Although 

Korea's needs are declining, the requirements to participate in the multilateral economic stabilization program of Indonesia, the Philippine agricultural develop ment effort and Thailand's rural development and security programs will offset savings.

The emphasis in all our programs is on rural development. Our motivation is simple. If the East Asian nations are to achieve viable independence, they must urgently accelerate economic and social progress among their rural people and create a community of interest betweeen villager and government. That means better health services for the rural population. It means more opportunities for education, more literacy in the hinterland. It means family planning, so the hard-won progress in food production is not nullified by too-rapid population growth.

And all this can only be achieved if there is peace and safety in the countryside. 

Hand in hand with this effort to give the rural people a better break, go their and our efforts to wage the War on Hunger. Mr. Gaud in his testimony has out-

735 lined the world-wide situation. The plain grim facts are that given present trends, the average man, woman and child in the less-developed countries will have less to eat each year. This is true for several countries of East Asia. Food aid can stave off famine for only a relatively few more years. The people in East Asia as in all the less developed countries need urgently to get access to and to apply the wonders of modern technology to their rice paddies, pig, corn, vegetable and other farm production. Their farmers must learn a lot, and the countries as a whole must invest much more in irrigation, farm to market roads, better seeds, more acreage. All this they need to do now, but they can't do it without technical and financial assistance from the developed countries. 

There is yet a third dimension to rural development. That is the encouragement of democratic private and local governmental institutions to foster greater participation by the people themselves in the challenge of development. We in AID recognize that economic development is not an end in itself, that it is only a part of social and political progress. We are trying to make our people more cognizant of this composite goal. But we cannot give any assurance that we know how we can best use economic and other U.S. resources to give maximum impetus to this highly intricate process. We, therefore, expect to learn from the hearings now underway in Congressman Zablocki's Sub-Committee, exploring ways to do this job better.

SOUTHEAST ASIA REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

The regional programs reflect a remarkable and hopeful new departure for Southeast Asia. As the Committee knows, there is little traditional basis for political and economic cooperation among most of the countries of Southeast Asia. Their pre-independence ties were almost exclusively with their colonial metropoles, and there are strong traditional rivalries. 

A few years ago, when AID witnesses testified before this Committee, there was no mention of Asian regional cooperation as a major or even a secondary theme of our aid effort. But since then, the pace of regional cooperation has quickened sharply. A milestone was the President's Baltimore address in April 

1965, when he encouraged Asian leaders to launch new or intensified efforts for regional economic development and pledged his support. Eugene Black is representing the President in international discussions advancing this concept. 

New regional institutions and programs are rapidly being established or planned. 

Best known is the Asian Development Bank (ADB) with over 60% of its capital contributed by Asian countries. Another landmark is the Southeast Asia Ministers of Education Council. Others include the Southeast Asian Agricultural Develop ment Conference, initiated by Japan in December 1966, and looking toward an ADB special fund for agriculture; a prospective similar group on transportation development proposed by Malaysia; the reactivation of the Association of Southeast Asia (Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia) and the creation of the Asian and Pacific Council last June in Seoul by nine member nations. The Mekong Committee and other functions of the UN Commission for Asia and the Far East are continuing and expanding their programs. From these many gatherings of able 

Asian leaders, concrete plans are emerging for regional projects. 

If current discussions involving the ADB and regional and donor countries result in early establishment of special funds within the ADB, the ADB would be the principal institution through which regional programs would be financed. 

Grants to educational programs, however, will probably be through joint action of technical assistance donors outside the ADB mechanism. In agriculture, our largest contribution of AID funds would be for surveys in the Mekong Valley. 

The most extensive of these covers the Pa Mong area in Thailand and Laos, being undertaken now by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation. It is a multi-year survey for which we request in FY 1968 $3.5 million. We are also asking for authority to support an Asian Regional Vegetable and Marketing Research Center, to be located in Taiwan. The major U.S. contribution to Southeast 

Asian regional agricultural development would be possible U.S. participation in special funds to be administered by the Asian Development Bank. 

In the field of education, we are planning to support projects developed by the Southeast Asia Ministers of Education Council and its permanent secretariat 

(SEAMES). Outstanding among these is the Asian Institute of Technology at Bangkok, formerly the SEATO Graduate School of Engineering. U.S. members of its Board of Trustees are: Henry Heald, former President of the Ford Foundation; John Hrones, Provost of the Case Institute of Technology and James Linen, President of Time Magazine. We propose to contribute 50% of the operating cost over the next 7 years. Total U.S. contribution for the expanded institute over the

1967 

next 5-7 years would be approximately $18 million. In FY 68, we recommend $5.3 million to support various SEAMES projects, with about one-third for the Asian 

Institute of Technology. Others are: The Regional Institute for Agriculture and Math Education at Los Banos, Philippines, a Center for Tropical Medicine in 

Bangkok, a Science Center at Penang, Malaysia, an English Language Center at

Singapore and an Instructional Materials Workshop in Saigon. 

In the field of regional health efforts, we plan to continue assistance to the important SEATO Cholera Research Center in East Pakistan. 

These projects are more than just desirable activities which will bring some physical results in the form of more food, better health and more educated people. 

These visible results, while needed, are not the whole story. Effective regional projects and institutions can build a sense of mutual commitment among the countries of Southeast Asia and strengthen the stake of many aid-giving nations in the peace and progress of Southeast Asia as a whole. Out of this can come a new era, after the war in Vietnam, which offers a prospect of both accelerated development and a stronger political basis for peace in this area. KOREA Mr. Gaud described to the Committee a few weeks ago Korea's accelerating drive toward self-support. In many respects-tax collection gains, savings, gains in investment rates, family planning-Korea recently has been a model development case. Tax collections for instance, went from $160 million in 1963 to $416 million in 1966, a two-and-a-half fold increase in four years. Over the same time span industrial production shot up 43 per cent. And the agricultural production index, the hardest of all to get moving, shows consistent strides; against 100 at the 1957-59 base, it was 107 in 1963 but 153 in 1966. Domestic savings kept pace; $215 million in 1966 versus just under $100 million in 1963. However, with all these impressive percentage gains, Korea still has a long way to go. Its per capita income is below $120. It still has a large trade deficit and needs outside capital for investments. The country has large defense outlays to shoulder, with nearly 

600,000 troops in Korea and 46,000 fighting on our side in Vietnam. We cannot yet say that Korea is a success story but we believe it is getting there. As the 

Korean Minister for Commerce and Industry said in New York last month, with justified pride: "Look at Korea today." The country is pulsing with activity. 

This kind of performance deserves and gets our help. In FY 1968 we propose continuation of the same basic program that helped Korea achieve real growth rates of more than 8% in 1964 and 1965, and nearly 12% in 1966. 

The keystone of our program in Korea is the encouragement of economic policies which provide the right environment for economic growth, in particular in the private sector. These policies are advanced through the provision of economic advisers and training. They are also aided by making our commodity assistance, both Supporting Assistance and Program Loan, contingent on specific fiscal and financial self-help measures by Korea, such as targets for money supply, credit, domestic revenues, which are jointly agreed on between the Korean Government and ourselves. To assist the Koreans in developing good investment policies, we are providing advisers in banking and credit, at both the national policy making level and particular lending institutions. Advice is also being provided in domestic revenue collection.

We will contribute to industrial development with development loans in such areas as power, transportation and refineries. We are also considering additional loans to Korean financial institutions for relending to private industry. To provide a broader technological and scientific basis for industrial growth, we are helping establish the Korean Institute of Science and Technology, which will do applied research and make studies for Korean industry. AID is continuing its advice on export promotion. Korea's exports doubled from $126 million in 1964 to $270 million in 1966, an eight fold increase since 1960.

Agriculture is not neglected. We are continuing support of a program which has increased grain production on an average of 6.3% a year since 1960. An important part of this program is P.L. 480 assistance. We are also providing advisers in national education policy development, and support for expansion of Korea's already established family planning program. 

We are not alone as aid givers in Korea. A Consultative Group for Korea was organized in December 1966 under World Bank leadership. Members are Australia, Belgium, Canada, China (Taiwan), France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the U.S. Japan is providing grants and soft loans of $50 million per year. Korea is now drawing on a $15 million German aid commitment.

737 

PHILIPPINES 

For some years now, we have carried out limited training and institution building programs only in the Philippines, to prepare for the day when a purposefully directed national will for economic and social development would emerge. We believe this is now becoming a reality with President Marcos' government. It may be none too soon, because the Philippines is again confronted with insecurity, social unrest and a still minor threat of Communist-leaning insurgents. The Joint Communique of Presidents Johnson and Marcos, issued here last September, re-emphasized our close political-economic ties and assured the Philippines of U.S. interest in assisting its rural development. 

We are planning an expansion of our program contingent upon Philippine self-help measures and effective use of all available foreign assistance. Most of the development capital the Philippines need will come from private lenders and international institutions. 

The Government is seeking means to raise domestic revenues, to alleviate a critical shortage of pesos for government development programs, primarily in rural infrastructure. It is conducting a major campaign to increase customs revenue and has pending several bills to increase taxes. It has taken new initiatives in public debt management by successfully floating a series of short-term treasury notes. In addition, the Development Bank of the Philippines, a Government corporation, successfully floated a 100 million peso ($25 million) bond issue to finance a large scale program of industrial refinancing and development. 

Our program gives priority to rural development and rice production. It is concentrated in eleven provinces, including the areas of social unrest. About two thirds of our planned development loans would support these efforts. Other loans would be for health purposes and for intermediate private lending institutions for industry and agro-business. We also envisage substantial P.L. 480 dollar credit sales, which will assist the Philippines Government meet the pressure on its peso resources. 

Our major technical assistance effort will be directed towards rural improvement and emphasize better agriculture techniques. Eradication of malaria will remain the focus of our health activities. We propose increases in our aid to tax administration, financial management and law enforcement, and are budgeting $1.5 million for these purposes.

INDONESIA 

The new Indonesian Government is at work clearing away the economic rubble left by mismanagement. Expenditures on useless prestige projects have been halted, the costly confrontation with Malaysia ended, revenue collections raised and the deficit of state-owned companies reduced. Market forces and private enterprise are gradually taking the determining role in shaping Indonesia's trade and investments. The International Monetary Fund has endorsed the 

Indonesian stabilization planning.

Last December, Japan, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Britain and the United States agreed on generous interim debt relief for Indonesia. 

About $300 million of payments due these countries through 1967 are postponed until 1971. The U.S. share in this postponement is $50 million. A new meeting this fall will consider debts falling due next year.

New aid to support the economic revival effort is being arranged in a similar international consultation group, also joined by Canada, Australia, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. These banks, however, are not able to help finance the current import requirements of Indonesia. The group accepted the IMF aid requirements estimate of about $200 million in import arrivals during this calendar year. We offered to meet one third of this requirement, largely through sales of P.L. 480 cotton, and other agricultural commodities and in part through AID loans, provided first, the other donors match our contribution two for one and second, the Indonesians continue to receive IMF endorsement of their stabilization efforts. 

Our FY 1968 program provides, apart from P.L. 480, substantial commodity assistance through AID program loans. These will meet Indonesian import requirements for such essentials as industrial spare parts and materials and transportation equipment. Technical Assistance requirements are estimated at $3 million. Maximum Indonesian involvement in the planning process and multinational participation are the paramount considerations in formulating projects. 

We will focus on education and training. Education materials, technical advice, training and commodities will be provided in support of the recommendations of the current Development Book Planning Survey. Participant training will be given 

77-470-67-pt. 44

1967 

to a substantial number of Indonesians to help supply managerial, professional and technical skills needed if Indonesia's stabilization efforts are to succeed. 

BURMA 

I reported to the Committee last year that prevailing conditions in Burma did not in our view warrant substantial new economic aid commitments. This is still the situation. We need only monitoring and technical supervision for the AID projects started in earlier years to insure their businesslike completion. For this purpose, we are programming $200,000 in Technical Assistance Funds. LAOS Large-scale U.S. aid is essential to the survival and strengthening of Laos as a neutral buffer between the ricelands of Southeast Asia and Communist China and 

North Vietnam.

Sporadic warfare with the Pathet Lao Communists and continuous invasion by the North Vietnamese forces the Lao Government to maintain a military establishment out of all proportion to the country's size and resources. Poor and lacking a significant tax base, Laos must nonetheless radically enlarge government services such as education and agricultural extension if the country is to progress toward economic independence. In the circumstances the Lao people and government have been meeting these challenges well. The areas and population under Government control have been growing, indicating greater military effectiveness. At the same time, the budget deficit is being steadily reduced. In 1966, the price rise in 

Vientiane was only 7%, just slightly higher than in neighboring Thailand. This progress would not have been possible without the stabilization aid of the United States and other foreign donors (U.K., Japan, France, Australia), mainly through the Foreign Exchange Operations Fund. Continued help of this kind in the frame work of the IMF-sponsored stabilization program is essential to prevent runaway inflation which could only lead to political and military collapse. 

Direct aid is also needed to help the Lao deal with their security-related problems, for example, to feed and clothe 250,000 refugees, many of whom hope to return to their montainous homes now under Communist control. As some are resettled in permanent or temporary locations, the ebb and flow of warfare creates new refugees, some of whom have fled many times before Communist incursions. 

Airlift operations to reach isolated refugee groups are a substantial cost element in the AID program. 

We are working closely, and successfully, with the Lao authorities to reduce the cost of economic stabilization and security programs by such measures as limiting inflationary demands on the economy, speeding settlement of refugees on land which can support them or offering other gainful employment, hastening the construction of roads to reduce the cost of air transportation. 

The Lao Government, with our help, is using what resources can be spared from stabilization and security programs to lay the foundation for future development. AID developmental project assistance is concentrated in the simpler, most direct forms of economic and social betterment, such as expanding primary and some secondary education, promoting improved rice seed varieties and low-cost water control. Encouraging progress toward self-sufficiency in rice was set back last fall by a Mekong flood of unprecedented dimensions. 

AID technicians work directly with the authorities in thirteen village cluster areas to expand the Lao Government's ability to help its rural population improve its own lot; we are seeking improvement of communications, credit and marketing mechanisms to create incentives for production in areas previously isolated from the rest of the economy. A new, but promising activity is encouragement of small industry based on local markets and local materials. 

Clearly the future of Laos depends very heavily on what happens in neighboring areas, and particularly on the willingness of the Communist powers to let this small country develop in peace. Within the limits of the present situation, the 

Lao authorities are making increasingly good use of the assistance available to them, and are making perceptible gains. THAILAND The principal purpose of our aid to Thailand is to help the Thai Government contain the Communist-led subversive movement before it becomes a major threat to Thai security. Peking and Hanoi are following the familiar pattern of supplying outside support, including cadre training, to small dissident elements

739 inside the country. The Thai Government is responding wisely by dealing vigorously with the social, economic and security conditions which produce weaknesses or disaffection which the Communists can exploit. This approach calls for acselerating the development of responsive, effective local government and other popularly-based institutions for the benefit of the rural population, particularly in the Northeast where Communist activities are most significant. We are helping this effort because we have a vital interest in the security of our ally Thailand. 

The Thai economy is progressing well under able financial leadership. The annual GNP growth rate has averaged about 7% for the past five years. Domestic savings have gone from 17% of GNP in 1957-1959 to an estimated 23% in 1966, a commendably high ratio. Agriculture expanded at a 5% rate in the last 5 years, another excellent performance. Increasing re ceipts from invisibles, and foreign capital inflows more than cover the trade deficit, which was $161 million in 1966. 

Gold and foreign exchange reserves have grown to over $900 million, but foreign debt service claims on these reserves also are substantial. 

The Thai are financing with their own resources a rapidly increasing proportion of their development and counter-insurgency programs. However, it must be remembered that this capacity is limited by a small economy with a per capita GNP of only $125 and only about $60 in the Northeast. The Thai Government pays from its budget all the local currency costs of joint Thai-AID projects. 

U.S. aid is essentially technical assistance with a large commodity component in police and engineering and construction equipment. The joint projects concentrated in the Northeast are of two types: 

1. Expansion and up-grading of the Thai civil police forces to increase their coverage of the countryside and their ability to deal with small scale insurgency and maintain law and order. 

2. Increasing the ability of the Thai Government, especially the agencies of local administration, to provide services needed by the rural people. Most of our money buys construction equipment to build roads, dig wells, small ponds and other rural self-help projects, and demonstration commodities to promote improved agricultural practices and small agriculturally based industries. Aid is also provided for health services, education and rural electrification. The University of Kentucky has recently signed an AID contract to advise a new Thai institute conducting applied agricultural research in the Northeast. 

Perhaps the most significant element of our whole effort is the assistance we are giving to the Thai program of strengthening institutions of rural government, particularly the provincial governors and their staffs, township councils and village land committees. We have recently described these efforts in some detail to the 

Far East Subcommittee.

In addition, we continue to supply technical aid to help the Thai overcome bottlenecks in the development of their economy. Aid to private enterprise, such as inventment guarantees and investment surveys are making an important contribution in encouraging American investment in fields contributing to rural betterment, such as fertilizer production and growing and processing agricultural products for export.

More than half of past economic assistance to Thailand has come from other donors, with the World Bank in the lead. A Consultative Group was formed in 

1965 under World Bank auspices. Members are Japan, the UK, Canada, New 

Zealand, the EEC countries, Austria, Denmark, Switzerland and ourselves. 

Other donors will probably provide over two-thirds of the aid requirements under 

Thailand's Second Five-Year Plan. 

Thailand's position in Southeast Asia, its partnership with us in promoting regional economic development and security, its constructive performance in dealing with rural development problems and the threat of Communist insurgency make a strong case for continued AID assistance. 

SUMMARY 

We believe the programs proposed are essential to support U.S. interests in 

East Asia, and that they are, in the words of the President, the minimum contribution to mutual security and international development which we can safely make in this area.

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed, Mr. Secretary.

STATEMENT OF HON. RUTHERFORD M. POATS, ASSISTANT AD- MINISTRATOR FOR FAR EAST, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. POATS. Mr. Chairman, I appeared before the committee on 

April 4 and gave a presentation on our program in Vietnam. I have not repeated that presentation in my statement submitted to the committee today, but of course will be prepared to answer questions on Vietnam. My statement today deals with the other East Asian countries.

You will note on the bottom of page 1 and the top of page 2 an attempt to describe the diversity of the economic assistance programs in East Asia. At the bottom of page 2 a summary table is given on the proposed programs as compared with the 2 preceding years. 

Distributed to the members at your chairs is a more detailed breakout of the appropriation bases for the total submission. The main characteristic of the trends in our program; that is, the concentration on rural development, is reflected in several pages of the statement, pages 3 and 4.

741 I also devoted more than the normal attention this year to the very encouraging trend toward regional cooperation to which we are responding with a number of efforts designed to stimulate and encourage the creation of institutions for economic cooperation and development. These will, of course, have, if they are successful, a significant political contribution to make the stability [security deletion] as well as the development of Southeast Asia. 

Finally I should like to note that in addition to this unclassified statement there are several points which the committee will be interested in with respect to unusual types of funding arrangements. 

One of them is an arrangement with the Defense Department in Vietnam under which the U.S. military services are undertaking several activities which are of a civil character, but which are deemed by the Defense Department to be essential to military operations. 

These are outlined in the presentation book which you have before you and I will be prepared to specify those if the committee is interested. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. POATS. Mr. Chairman, I think the final point I would like to make is that we are feeling our way in Indonesia toward the establishment of an international consultative group which would provide the coordination of donor countries' civil efforts and international advice to the Indonesian Government in its very difficult stabilization problem. This will lead, we believe, to a development program conducted with the same sort of multilateral support. 

We have been able in this case to restrict the U.S. contribution to the multilateral stabilization fund to one-third of the total contribution. We also are in this case offering the so-called DAC terms as the terms of the U.S. loans to Indonesia and so far several other countries have met those terms. So we are, at the moment—and I believe this will be true throughout-providing our aid on the same terms as the other major contributors. 

I believe that concludes the points that are not reflected in my statement.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Poats.

Mr. Secretary, it has been said for years that the Korean war brought about the economic recovery of Japan. The U.S. expenditures related to our military operations in Korea benefited Japan to such a degree that economic aid was no longer needed by Japan. 

Will you tell the committee to what extent our U.S. expenditures relating to military operations in Vietnam have benefited the countries in Asia and what countries are benefited most from these expenditures?

743 Mr. BUNDY. Mr. Chairman, I haven't the figures on that before me. I will make a few general comments and if you wish I will submit a more detailed statement for the record on that because I think it is a matter that is of proper concern to this committee. (A classified memorandum was subsequently supplied in response to Chairman Morgan.) 

Mr. BUNDY. The fact is that our procurement overseas, which of course we are doing only where there are clear major factors of advantage in terms of availability or a shortness of time required, factors of that sort, are a significant element. I think particularly in that connection of Korea where I think, and I will check this for the record, we are spending $50 to $60 million a year in offshore procurement. This has been a real extra boost to the Korean economy. 

All over the area the outflow that arises also from our R. & R. program in Vietnam is a tonic. It is so in Singapore. It is so to a lesser degree in the Philippines [security deletion]. 

Korea is the one that most comes to mind in proportionate terms. 

Japan also I think is getting a considerable share of these orders because of its capacity. There is no doubt this offshore procurement incident to Vietnam is an additional factor. I would say that it is just that, that it is an additional booster. 

I myself would feel without having gone back and researched the Japanese case in detail, that what we spent in Japan incident to the Korean war was an additional factor there only, and not the major factor by any means. I think Japan has shown over the years that it would have prospered in due time in any event. I think it hastened that and speeded it up.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, on pages 44 and 45 of your statement you discuss some of the economic programs that Japan has financed. [Security deletion.] 

Can we expect more from Japan in economic aid to Southeast Asia if their economic conditions continue to improve? 

Mr. BUNDY. I think we can, Mr. Chairman, without any doubt.

I think they are aiming at this 1-percent figure. The 1-percent figure in round numbers would be $900 million-plus. 

I think a nation such as Japan, although its per capita GNP is only at the $900 level-so it is not at the same level as the European countries Japan is only spending a little over 1 percent of its GNP on defense which is much less than the percentage we or the European countries are spending.

It is reasonable to look to the Japanese to get right up to the 1 percent. The Japanese GNP keeps going and it will mean than an aid effort equivalent to 1 percent of GNP itself will also rise. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, do we take into consideration in planning our economic aid programs, the economic advantages of nations in the area which derive benefits from military assistance spending? 

Mr. BUNDY. From the offshore procurement? We do indeed, Mr.

Chairman. Take the case of Korea, the total picture in Korea for example is permitting a very sharp downward trend in supporting assistance. This is a budgetary item. But the magnitude of this budget support reflects the overall economic health of Korea. To the extent that offshore procurement by us contributed to Korea's ongoing economic strength, it is taken into account.

1967 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, should we assume that if the military aid expenditures for East Asia decrease the economic condition of South Korea would suffer a setback? 

Mr. BUNDY. It might to a small degree, Mr. Chairman. But my overall feeling is that if they can keep up with anything like the growth rate they have had in the last 3 years which was 9 percent in 1964 and 1965, and 12 percent in 1966, if they can keep that up, I think the effect would be very small and recouped by Korea's growth process. 

There might be some.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, could you furnish to the committee the total estimated dollar expenditures in Thailand during the next fiscal year of U.S. Defense Department funds? 

Mr. BUNDY. Yes, sir; I can. I can give you an order of magnitude which I will have to check for the record. Our total military expenditure construction program was quite major last year but it is now tapering off. We have Sattahip mostly completed which is the big base for B-52's. The total of our expenditures which we have assessed as to whether it would lead to inflation was about 2 percent of GNP in Thailand. That is not an order of mangitude that posed any serious threat to inflation in the country. It is several hundred million dollars. 

That is the total cost of the installations. A very high proportion of that is not dollar outflow in the sense that the equipment and the materials, and so on, are purchased in this country in most cases. Mrs. Bolton.

Mr. BUNDY. The Chinese population is substantial in Thailand. I would have to check this, it is around 2 or 3 million.

745 1 has been much accelerated in the past 10 years. We thought this was a serious problem 10 years ago, but would not regard it in that light today.

Mrs. BOLTON. What are the main exports from Thailand, and where do they go?

Mr. BUNDY. The main exports, rice is a major export, that goes all over the area. They have done a real job of increasing their rice exports and have been picking up a lot of the markets that for instance the Burmese used to have. Burmese rice exports are way down from above 

2 million to a half million tons this year. They go all over the area. 

They go to, I think I will have to check-to Japan. Among other things as you probably know they have given a $20 million credit for rice sales to Vietnam. We buy rice there for our own program in Vietnam on a limited scale, I think. 

Mr. POATS. The Vietnamese Government does. 

Mr. BUNDY. It is the Vietnamese Government purchase, not our own.

Mrs. BOLTON. Indonesia, what are the prospects for a general election there?

Mr. BUNDY. [Security deletion.] 

Mrs. BOLTON. What has happened out there to justify our aid?

Mr. BUNDY. Above all, Mrs. Bolton, a complete change in the whole outlook of the Government. This Government is a nationalist government but it is prepared to live at peace with its neighbors. 

One of the very first things it set about doing was to wind up the socalled confrontation with Malaysia and Singapore, preliminary agreement in Bangkok last May or June, and a final agreement in Djakarta in August, which is now being fully carried out. 

Then at least two other things have to be said, that as of October 1, 1965, Indonesia was headed for Communist control without any question. This has been prevented I think in a bloodier way than any of us would have liked, but understandably in view of the way the Communists have behaved. 

The third thing is that they are attacking their economic problem seriously. I think it is very much in our national interest to assist them to do that to ward off chaos and get them started so they can stand on their own feet. 

Mrs. BOLTON. How are they doing with their debts to Russia?

Mr. BUNDY. That is covered in some detail in my statement, but in short form the debt to Russia, which is about 40 percent of the total of the $2 billion-plus external debts, is covered by bilateral agreement. Since the original agreement between the Indonesians and the Russians in October the rest of the creditor countries have made the Paris agreement, which may be very slightly more generous in the short run and to which we now believe at any moment the Russians will have to accommodate. There is no question of the Russians getting more favorable treatment. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What would the outlook be for any Indonesian armed forces in Vietnam?

Mr. BUNDY. [Security deletion] the attitude seems pretty clear that they want to preserve a neutral position in respect to the Vietnam conflict. However, I can assure you on the basis of personal experience in a visit there about 6 weeks ago that one doesn't encounter criticism of what we are doing in Vietnam there.

Mrs. BOLTON. One does not? 

Mr. BUNDY. One does not.

Mr. BUNDY. Mrs. Bolton, it is certainly not a sure thing. [Security deletion.] It makes sense to give [security deletion] assistance to spread the new miracle rice. It makes sense to support them on irrigation. If they can succeed with land reform this would be a fundamental and favorable change. It makes sense to support Marcos' road program, which involves these engineer construction battalions which are valid military units but are really building roads [security deletion]. I think it is important to back Marcos in trying to do it. 

Mrs. BOLTON. How much of the money we give gets to the place where it should?

Mr. BUNDY. I think we have pretty good controls on that. I would like to ask Mr. Poats to comment on the technique aspects. I think we do have pretty good control on that. 

Mr. POATS. Our aid, Mrs. Bolton, in the current year and in the past year has been entirely in technical assistance to Government entities in which we provide goods and services with our own people involved in the projects at close range. So they see the use of the equipment. Second, the United States has made Public Law 480 sales and grants, primarily a sales program which produces a dollar debt to the United States over a long period and an immediate peso income to the Government which it can use in the short term to fund agricultural development and related activities. That has been the nature of the program. 

This year we are considering a loan application for feasibility studies to undertake proper examination of proposed projects and put them in a position to apply to various lending agencies, particularly the World Bank and other hard lenders on projects. And, second, a loan of about $4%½ million to resume the development, which had been interrupted, of their irrigation systems in the areas of greatest rice production.

For next year we propose an expansion in the technical assistance program in several areas one is police advisory training. This problem of law and order is one of the basic problems. Second, in the area of tax administration where they need some help, and, third, in the area of, and this is the big dollar increase in the program, in further loans directly related to Marcos' 11-province rice production drive. 

We expect those loans to be largely for agricultural sector imports, particularly agricultural equipment; perhaps a small loan for potable water projects, well-drilling equipment and so on. 

These are all concentrated on that aspect of the Marcos' administration campaign which is moving, in which there is some dynamic

747 leadership and drive and a real political commitment. [Security deletion.] We are not giving general budget support or general financial assistance. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Do you have any control of the money, watching what they do with it?

Mr. POATS. Yes, each of these projects is covered by a detailed project agreement and covenants- 

Mrs. BOLTON. Do they work?

Mr. POATS. We don't go forward with the next stage of the projectwith the commitment of funds-until the covenants have been met, the conditions precedent met. The area in which you are more likely to have diversion of aid in any country is in general balance-of-payments support. We are not engaging in that kind of program in the 

Philippines at this time. We will not go forward with a number of these projects unless there is a specific commitment of local currency funds on their part to undertake it. It is true that sometimes the commitment of this sort is made and then it is not delivered upon. You have a suspension of the project. That happened in the Philippines several years ago in a highway project. At that point we stopped further disbursements on the program and got it straightened out.

749 The election is tomorrow. We don't have a long wait for a verification or a determination of that prediction. That is the going prediction in 

Seoul. There is very little difference in the prediction of the majority, anywhere from a half million to a million and a half is on people's tongues out there. I think that is a safe bet. The significance of these incidents, we have watched those closely, and I had a discussion last week with the Vice Foreign Minister of Korea who was here, I found he was quite clear that he believed these were simply efforts by the North Koreans to stir things up during election time. He pointed to the fact that there had been a similar spate of incidents during the November 1963 election, Park won, of course, and there was another spate last fall during the time of the Manila Conference and during the time of the President's visit to Korea. I think these are muscleflexing exercises by the North. We do not see any indication that they portend a serious military effort. We have to keep the basic defense establishment in Korea.

You don't spell out what the money is going to provide. Mr. Poats briefly stated it here but perhaps I haven't read enough of the written material you have given us. Could you explain what the increased assistance is going to be aimed at which hadn't been hit before?

Mr. BUNDY. The breakdown which is found on page 140 of the basic presentation book- Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. We don't have much access to these books, either.

Mr. BUNDY. The principal item in which there is really great change in the program before us is in the [security deletion] agricultural area. This is at the root of things in the Philippines. Anybody who goes there will see the contrast between garish Manila and barrios which haven't made any headway at all for years.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. BUNDY. That is where the real increase is taking place. There is a small increase in technical assistance. [Security deletion] of that goes to the agricultural sector for all manner of purposes directly related to remedying the biggest basic broad defect in the Philippines which is the disparity between the cities and the countryside. This is where your trouble can come from. 

It is why people are discontented. It is a good part of the reason why the Huks are having even limited success at the present time. This is the core of the problem. Better agricultural techniques, irrigation, rural credit, which among other things includes freeing Philippine money which is the basis of it for land reform on a limited scale in central Luzon where they are tackling this problem.

753 Lastly, development loans [security deletion] in the area of industrial development. This is really a desperate need there for them to have their own industrial enterprises to soak up the kind of people swarming to the cities. I think [security deletion] in the rural sector and [security deletion] in the industrial sectors is the right balance in the Philippines at the present time.

The point I am making is that these are serious programs directed to the very root problems of this country. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. In the military aid program [security deletion].

Mr. BUNDY. In the program before you, the specific items on the 

MAP side [security deletion]. 

The state of the record is that President Johnson told President Marcos he would consider it. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. [Security deletion.] Is there anything that the United States can do to encourage that process? 

Mr. BUNDY. We have certainly made it very clear that we think this is a high-priority need, and we have explored with them whether they have available the funds to do that which is necessary. On the whole I believe they do. Mr. Poats?

Mr. POATS. A good part of the Public Law 480 proceeds are going into aspects of the rural development program which touch on land reform. For example, part of the proceeds are going into the financing of rural credit institutions which are essential to carry out a land reform which sticks. The expansion of the Philippine agricultural extension service has been focused in the 11-province corn-rice program and in those areas where the land reform districts have been established. They are acting on land reform but they are moving rather slowly on that aspect of it concerning the Government purchase and resale of land. They are moving on other aspects fairly vigorously. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. One quick question on Indonesia, if I have time, Mr. Chairman.

I notice, Mr. Bundy, you describe the assistance that is planned for Indonesia this year as basically sustaining assistance, that we haven't yet a picture of the long-range needs of the country. I assume there is going to be substantially more needed from other countries if Indonesia is to get back on its feet. Is this simply tiding it over until the review of the situation has been completed? 

Mr. BUNDY. It is tiding it over, Congressman, and there will be more needed I think somewhat more in the next 2 or 3 years to do that job alone. What we are looking for as they get hold of their affairs is an influx of private investment, the revival of things like the rubber situation, even though world rubber prices are low, unfortunately, at the present time, and a general taking hold with considerable emphasis on the private sector. Obviously the opportunities are there. Your hardheaded bankers like Mr. Black will tell you that Indonesia will bloom like a rose under proper management. That can't be expected to take place for another 2 or 3 years. 

Mr. POATS. So far as the developmental requirement of the country is concerned, we need a lot more facts before we can develop a program. 

The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, a number of private foundations, are interested in doing studies which would provide the basis for a sensible program. For this year and next year the overriding requirement is to get hold of the inflation, check it, to 

77-470-67-pt. 4- -5

1967 

establish a stabilization program including domestic banking and monetary and fiscal policies, and to establish a base from which an orderly development could begin. Consequently, the Indonesian 

Government has choked off expenditures for development in the process of attempting to get hold of its budget, and to achieve monetary stabilization. They are being advised in this by the International 

Monetary Fund. We hope in the course of this year a good part of the very ambitious expectations they have advanced to the members of the international group will be fulfilled so that they can start thinking seriously about development in the following years. The likelihood, I believe, is that the additional funds required for development can come largely from the Asian Development Bank if special funds of the bank are established.

COMMUNIST AID TO BURMA 

The principal communist aid program to Burma is an $84 million loan from Communist China granted in 1961, which the Burmese appear to be drawing on fairly slowly. The Burmese also have economic cooperation agreements with several Eastern European countries which involve extension of relatively modest amounts of credit to Burma. The Soviet Union has remaining only a small program devoted principally to the completion of a dam project begun in 1962. 

Mr. MURPHY. In reference to a question by Mr. Adair, you spoke of an editorial appearing in the New York Times last Sunday. 

Mr. BUNDY. It was a news story on the front page by Drew Middleton. 

Mr. MURPHY. I didn't quite understand your answer. If I understood correctly, there are about 12 million oversea Chinese and about

755 10 million are located in Southeast Asia. Originally they were very pro-Western, then, with the developments in China that they started going into a neutral position and in the last few years they were becoming very pro-Communist China. 

I can't quite understand just exactly what Mr. Middleton said in reference to the oversea Chinese attitude with the present setup in China. In the past the oversea Chinese have been sending a great deal of money back because there are about 10 million dependents in two provinces where the Red Chinese have been receiving part of their hard money. Aside from Thailand there has been an assimilation of oversea Chinese. In Indonesia they made a choice with reference to citizenship between China and Indonesia. I would like to know what brought about this change in attitude by these oversea Chinese? 

Mr. BUNDY. This is a matter of degree. I think it has taken a sharp turn in the direction that Mr. Middleton describes in the last year and a half since the cultural revolution, Mr. Murphy. Essentially you did have quite a set in the direction of a very strong sense of attachment to Communist China in the middle fifties. The failure of the Great Leap, I think, took some of the bloom off the rose as to the way the oversea Chinese looked at the mainland. The pull remains strong. What has happened, I think, as a result of the cultural revolution, is that they have now begun to feel, as Middleton puts it, that communism is absolutely definitely not the wave of the future. 

Related with that, interrelated, is the other aspect of the oversea Chinese in Southeast Asia, which is their degree of assimilation in the countries in which they live. I mentioned Thailand where that has succeeded. In other places it has been uneven. It hasn't been bad in 

Vietnam. It is a constant situation in Malaysia where you have an even balance. [Security deletion.] In Indonesia you had in the last couple of weeks a recurrence of popular attacks on the Chinese and they are in a constantly edgy situation. The fact that there was Chinese Communist support for the PKI in Indonesia put all the Chinese, and particularly those with a connection to the Communist apparatus, in a difficult situation and led to their being a significant proportion of those killed in Indonesia, though not nearly as big as some reports made out. 

It is uneven. I would say in general the overall trend line you have is twofold: disillusionment with the mainland. The remittances are really a family matter, they are not a matter of Royalty, they have tended to drop somewhat, not sharply because it is more important to them to support their relatives in the troubled situation that now prevails on the mainland. There is a growing disillusionment with the mainland; and there is a related but somewhat separate growing assimilation on the whole to their local countries. 

I think both of these are useful and healthy trends.

Mr. Bundy, how many South Vietnamese men are now under arms?

Mr. BUNDY. In round numbers [security deletion]. That includes the regular forces, the regional forces, the popular forces, and the police, which may be considered as essentially- Mr. FOUNTAIN. How many are engaged in actual combat with the 

North Vietnamese and the Vietcong?

Mr. BUNDY. At one time or another every one of those would be likely to be in a combat situation. Your police, for example, although dispersed over the villages, are subject to attack. The casualty rates in the regional forces and popular forces during most periods have run very comparable to the army forces. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. How many are engaged in implementation of the pacification program?

Mr. BUNDY. There again it would be hard to arrive at an overall number. In most pacification situations the regional and public forces and police have a direct role. A high proportion of those forces could be said to be engaged in pacification purposes. Their essential mission is to hold onto a particular portion of the country. 

The significant change in this area, Mr. Fountain, in the past 

6 months, really is whereas about 20 percent of the combat battalions of the regular army were engaged in wholly clear and hold operations last October, it is going up [security deletion] very rapidly. They have gotten [security deletion] now and they have been doing a limited amount of retraining of those battalions so there is a greater commitment of of regular army to that. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. What is South Vietnam's total capability? 

Mr. BUNDY. It is pretty close to the line now on the manpower basis in our judgment, sir. We have had increases in the armed forces in the last 2 years, significant ones. [Security deletion.] We have been biting in hard on manpower requirements in a lot of other areas across the board [security deletion].

1967 

Mr. POATS. There are net additions coming along in the revolutionary development cadre, an additional [security deletion]. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. How effective is their system of taking men in the armed forces? Are there large numbers that escape the draft for one or a number of reasons because of any defect in the system? 

Mr. BUNDY. I think the system has failings, Mr. Fountain. They have desertion problems. They don't seem to get the students in 

Saigon to anywhere near the degree that they should. There may be a degree, I think it is very small, of a fellow finding his way into a position that isn't wholly valid.

In the draft system that they have it is the draftees who are only 15 percent of the total force who are the major source of desertions. 

The desertion figures are still higher than we would like, but they are very much less than they were a year ago. 

In the first 3 months of this year your monthly desertion figures are running in the 6,000 to 7,000 range, whereas they ran in the 13,000 to 14,000 range for many, many months in the first 6 months of last year. The problem is still a significant one, but it is not as bad as it was. I mention it in connection with the question about the draft because a high proportion of those are draftees who desert, pick up again, go back through the milk. It is almost a swinging door operation as it sounds to me as I have heard it described. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Did you say only about 15 percent are drafted?

Mr. BUNDY. Fifteen percent of the total force is drafted. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Eighty-five percent are volunteers? 

Mr. BUNDY. Yes.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Whalley. 

Mr. Bundy, we have heard about differences between Russia and 

Red China for many months. About 3 weeks ago it was announced 

Red China and Russia had gotten together on aid to North Vietnam. 

Yesterday in the May Day parade in Moscow, Russian leaders denounced Red China, and the Red China representatives_walked out. Was this just window dressing, or what is the true story? 

Mr. BUNDY. I will not give you assurance, but a reasonably confident answer on that, sir. That is to the broad effect that the differences between them remain as deep as they have been right along. [Security deletion.] There had been undoubtedly some kind of friction from time to time in the transit of Soviet and Eastern European goods across Communist China.

However, we watched very closely and as far as we could tell there was never a real stoppage or slowdown-as I put it in a figure of speech, the hose wasn't being squeezed, but it was being jiggled. This led to recriminations between the two and so on. Undoubtedly they were partly taking a stick to beat each other.

These recriminations began to ease off and we had third country reports, which appeared creditable, that there had been some kind of understanding that goods would move freely. This may well have involved, as other reports suggested, the North Vietnamese taking title in effect at the Chinese border so they became North Vietnamese goods and this eased the problem.

We watched closely when we got these reports whether it meant there was a political drawing together in any significant degree. The great bulk of the reports, plus our reading of these denunciations between the two, is that it does not have any significant meaning as to a drawing together, that they are as far apart as before. 

Mr. WHALLEY. On page 43, Mr. Bundy, you say Japan in particular can and must play a major role in development of East Asia. "On the security side, Japan can and should do more for its own defense, but the prohibitions of her Constitution" prevents this. 

Isn't it possible to persuade Japan to change its Constitution and join forces with us since it would apparently be the loser if Red 

China would take over?

Mr. BUNDY. There is no question that the Japanese themselves would see their security interests in that light. The question is not only the Constitution, but really the whole set of psychological factors [security deletion] and frankly a feeling that they have done pretty well without getting into the military business. 

I don't think anybody who has tried to judge this [security deletion] think there is a prayer they would change their Constitution. 

That alone, I think, cuts it off as a present possibility. I can't look ahead 5 or 10 years and say what might happen. I would say one further thing as a matter of whether it be wise for us to push them hard. I think we should push them to carry the burden of their own defense to a greater degree [security deletion]. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Can I ask one more question?

Red China?

Mr. BUNDY. No; they are very careful about anything that can be used in a war, and particularly careful about technology associated with missiles or nuclear development. It is entirely nonstrategic, that I would vouch for. I don't have the commodity breakdown, but I will supply that for the record.

Mr. FARBSTEIN.  eeeeee 72 216 55 13 (1) 194 (1) 194 Mr. Bundy, is it your opinion that we have placed as much emphasis as we should upon the pacification of South Vietnam, and are we doing all we possibly could insofar as the distribution of land, assistance to the farmers and the general well-being of the people? 

Mr. BUNDY. We have certainly placed great emphasis on it, Congressman. I don't think at any time we could ever say we have ever done as much as we should, and we have to do more. Just to take one area where you do have the problem of how you go about it, and that is land reform. In fact, in the past 6 months Thieu and Ky have made significant but still limited gestures of distributing land titles and these are valid and useful acts. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. BUNDY. They have it very much in the forefront of their thinking. We have gone back and forth over it. I think it is something they will continue to make slow progress on. We are pushing them in that direction.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Doesn't the Government itself own and control certain acreage of land that they have done nothing with? Why haven't they distributed that land? 

Mr. BUNDY. I am not an expert on that. I can only give you a partial answer, and that is my fault. This acreage is a small percentage of the total land area and they haven't distributed it all- 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Why? This is the point I am trying to find out.

Mr. BUNDY. I don't know offhand the answer to Mr. Poats can comment.

Mr. POATS. The Government has under several acts acquired land- 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. A little louder.

Mr. POATS (continuing). Distributed about 600,000 acres. They have 1 million acres that have not been resold to farmers. Much of this land is in VC controlled areas which they cannot get access to. 

Practically all of this land is occupied by farmers and they are farming it as squatters. In some cases this land is being rented by local governments to tenants at reasonable rates and in some cases at excessive rates.

765 The Government is moving into areas where they can have access with a very limited staff. This is one of the great problems, inadequate staffs, to take parcels of land which they own and sell them. They have been inhibited in this in many cases by local officials stating that to drive the present squatters off this land and to instead require them to pay for it would not serve the short-term pacification interest of the Government. 

There is also, I am sure, some local advantage to a local official in renting land to people and collecting funds in that way for local government operations. [Security deletion.] 

The present program of the Government includes a more vigorous administration of the existing law with respect to maintaining a ceiling on rentals to be paid by tenants. That is being executed with considerable help from the revolutionary development cadre, one of whom in each group is trained to watch for violations of existing law. 

As Mr. Bundy said, they are issuing firm titles to those who have already acquired the land with tentative titles. We are working in 

An Giang Province 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. You take up my time with a lot of details which are insignificant really. It would seem to me that if we pushed this distribution of land in the most feasible way, and some of our money be spent for it, we would be saved a lot of grief. If South Vietnam was pacified and and the way of life of the peasant were made easier the soil would not be fertile for the Vietcong and revolution. 

It would seem therefore that this should be our main purpose in the south and done as quickly as possible. Let me inquire how many 

Vietcong are in the forces opposing the United States, South Vietnam and so on, the armies? How many Vietcong are part of those forces?

Mr. BUNDY. In round numbers the total Vietcong and North 

Vietnamese strength is about 285,000, Mr. Farbstein, of which between 

40,000 and 50,000 are North Vietnamese regulars; and another x thousand, 20,000 to 30,000 possibly, are people who came down from the north, southerners who had gone north. About these 20,000 to 30,000, this is the total number of relocated southerners that we believe returned south; their numbers, of course, have probably been reduced by battle losses and disease. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. You would say there are about how many? 

Mr. BUNDY. 285,000 is the total.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. We have about a million in the field our side has about a million?

Mr. BUNDY. Somewhat more. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. A little bit more? 

Mr. BUNDY. Yes.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I don't think there is any possibility, and it has generally been admitted, that the opposition can win at this stage. If that is so, with a holding operation in the north, with speedy pacification of the south, this agonizing situation might be straightened out. 

I can't at this point ask you to be clairvoyant; and I can't expect you will make a determination of a problem that has been so difficult to solve by all the good minds, not alone in this country, but in the world, however, I want to get your reaction; with a holding operation in the north, inasmuch as Hanoi can't win; if we could rush the pacification of the south by land distribution, by whatever means possible, reestablishment of a true democratic government, don't you think

1967 

we could see a way out sooner than the way it appears today-bogged down in South Vietnam?

Mr. BUNDY. Mr. Farbstein, I have no doubt whatsoever that progress on pacification and progress in getting a democratic and a widely supported government are absolutely fundamental to success and, if achieved, particularly the latter, could make a tremendous difference in the rate of progress. I think the political front is critical at all times and doubly critical this year and over the next 4 or 5 months. 

Pacification is a slow job. In round numbers it got going to some extent in 1965 and-these are the type of figures that I would hate to be held to—we moved from 51 percent of the population under effective control to 57. The targets for this year are another 7 or 8 percent.

That looks slow in percentage terms to get to whatever a really good figure would be-80 percent, let's say--where you would have the thing on the way to solution. I think, as you say, we have got to bend every effort on that front. This is what we have been trying to do right along really, but with increased emphasis for at least 15 months now. The Honolulu Conference was the benchmark in February last year. They themselves have been doing it. 

You have to have effective government performance. It wasn't really for a long time up to the level of effectiveness such that it could get on with this job. It has been in the last 20 months. I agree with your emphasis on this. I think that the political front, if it goes well, will make the pacification job easier. 

I think our military success will help the pacification job. The pacification job is the slowest, and it should go well with the other two problems. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. One question about the third front. What is your definition of a democratic government, a truly democratic government in South Vietnam? Who is to propose that democratic government? 

Is there anything in their constitution that restricts the composition of the democratic government; and who may vote in the democratic election?

Mr. BUNDY. The answer to the third question is "No." It is on honest participation with as many voters as possible. It won't be all the voters in this election because you have security situations. I don't want to suggest to you that there won't be a degree of irregularity in this election. I think that can be expected in any country that has not had working experience with democracy. 

We ourselves had a high degree of irregularity 50 years ago and I have heard of recent instances. I think we have to be realistic in judging this.

The objective is clear. I think they see it in the same way, a large participation in the government, a minimum of irregularity and a government that is accepted as the honest choice of the voters.

Mr. POATS. The new government has deliberately gone about a concentrated program of rice production which is crucial to the Philippines, and an important contribution to their war on hunger. It is that program that we are proposing to support.

I think the threat should not be considered as an insurgency threat, but decay, which will stimulate unrest among the peasants of which the Huks would take advantage.

Mr. POATS. One of the AID program increases from $250,000 this year to $1 million next year in the support of the police work. 

Mr. BUNDY. We have to do both. It is the basic condition of the country that concerns us. 

Mr. TAFT. What is the situation developing in Indonesia insofar as the inflation problem is concerned?

Mr. BUNDY. The arithmetic of that is a little outlandish. January to June 1966, prices went up fourfold, I think. In June 1966 to December they doubled. It will be considered a major victory if they can be

1967 

kept to only doubling in the current year. All economic discussions of inflation are on a new plane in Indonesia, so to speak. 

Mr. Poats can talk about what he thinks of the chances of leveling off. 

Mr. POATS. In the first quarter of this calendar year the Indonesian budget was balanced [security deletion]. The declines in rice prices were substantial. There were declines in some other basic products. 

The International Monetary Fund is working very closely with them to keep this lid on. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. TAFT. What do we plan to do about it?

Mr. POATS. We think it will be held down. It has already reached the point where the rupiah has been stabilized in a floating exchange rate of around 90 to the dollar, whereas it was escalating geometrically last year.

The key to whether it will be successful, I think, will be the effectiveness of the bank credit and the tax measures. We don't know yet how effective they are going to be. We have said to them-all the donors have said to them-that without an IMF endorsement that their efforts have been reasonably successful, that they are sticking to the stabilization program, we cannot contribute.

One is that you could talk to the President or you could talk to some of the Ministers. In repeated conferences you could nudge them. 

That would be one way. Another way would be to try to sponsor a conference of Southeast Asian nations, maybe under U.N. auspices, or have some other country initiate it, in which you might take up the subject of what is the importance of decentralized governmental powers vis-a-vis development. What has the experience been? People could be invited from the Philippines who are in a position of power,

773 political power. Who would initiate that kind of conference, who would sit down in the State Department and AID and think about this? 

We don't want to be too pushy as Americans, but to find an indirect route to do this. 

Who would do this in AID or State and be in a position to implement it?

Mr. BUNDY. Frankly, we would look to Mr. Poats primarily on this area. It is something we give some thought to. By way of example there is now a conference on urban growth in Asia, in Honolulu. This is being attended by a lot of American experts on urban problems, including some of our quite senior officials. 

Mr. POATS. It was organized jointly by the Governor of Hawaii, the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and the AID 

Administrator.

Mr. BUNDY. I think your suggestion has a lot of merit to it. You have got to keep the U.S. role palatable, low posture; that is right. 

That is Reischauer's phrase. [Security deletion.] The more you make it Asian, the better. Frankly, almost any government in Asia has this centralization problem. It is a problem in Thailand, a problem everywhere.

Mr. FRASER. The problem bugs me. I have been interested in this general subject. The way our Government is organized here in Washington doesn't lend itself to this kind of total approach. The guy working on the Philippine desk in AID is not going to think in terms of an Asian conference, or he may not see within his grasp the opportunities for our exchange program, to get a USIA lecturer over there in the Philippines that might talk about some of these problems. 

I don't get the sense that there is this kind of a total comprehension and responsibility centered in one place so that one can try to use all these indirect routes which I think are terribly important. I think the most effective contribution we can make is in the area of ideas and people who know how to go into these societies and are not too visible, and who are acceptable and work well. It isn't a question of money. 

I can't find anywhere in the way we approach these problems anything except a separation of responsibilities so you don't get at it. This follows an impression from last week that this Philippine problem is of enormous concern. Really, if the Philippines were to go down the drain by some person organizing politically and introducing a highly coercive regime, Communist or otherwise, it would be a blow to the United States. It would represent a real failure on the part of the United States. 

What I am not asking for are extra programs thrown in the Philippines of the kind that would create a reaction. I am thinking of some kind of centralized planning and stopping the buck at one person and say to him "You figure out all the ways that are required to work with these problems." You might bring in some of the German foundations that are working throughout the world, working at education, and so on. There are a lot of resources, a lot of countries around the world; they can come in and reduce our visibility. But who sits with this total perspective, and the competency to make things happen? 

Mr. BUNDY. We have become more and more regional in our approach and thinking very rapidly in the last 2 or 3 years. Take this meeting of education ministers where we are undertaking to support projects with the authorization of Congress. This is something we did a great deal to stimulate. I have seen an awful lot happen in this area,

1967 

because somebody in AID is looking at the problems that have a common contact among these countries. They, themselves are. You get this agricultural conference that the Japanese have stimulated, conferences on Southeast Asia. A lot of this will come out. Transportation is an area where they are starting to work together. I see no reason in principle at least why the same principles that have perked up these schemes, and that includes some Americans in the AID organization, couldn't go to work on problems of centralized government.

Mr. FRASER. Take the cooperatives. They have sagged. We might want to get the Swedish in. Who can do that?

Mr. BUNDY. We can do that. 

Mr. FRASER. It is the problem of who sits there day after day with the responsibility for this. 

Mr. BUNDY. I think myself that is a very doubtful starter. It is so broken down in the Philippines. 

Mr. POATS. With respect of who would do that in other countries, the AID mission in the various countries maintains contact with the governments on matters other than AID projects. It is in contact with other aid contributors. It maintains a record of what the others are doing. We have a consultative group on technical assistance that considers these problems. Its focus is largely on developmental matters. The focus of the international institutions is on economic development, rather neutral on political matters. "Let's not get into controversy about the internal management of the countries," is their general approach. I think it is a weakness. I don't think we have really considered it at all. I agree. 

The question you raise in relation to Southeast Asia regional development is whether there could be common ground for considering common internal political organizations questions. We, very frankly, shy away from it a bit. We are looking for things that are acceptable to the largest number of diverse countries, to try to attract people of countries of different political institutions and ideology into a common cause, and to introduce into that questions of political organization I suspect would cause many to shy away. 

Maybe we are being too cautious.

Mr. FRASER. I don't know what the techniques are. The problem is in the beginning to center some of the responsibility on a person and give him the resources with which he can try to figure out what is needed. The truth of the matter is that no matter what you have to talk about with the other country, you can find some way to do it that is soft and indirect and not in a setting where you get a reaction against it.

I think the Philippines are so important I would establish something very high level and begin to really pull together all the resources, the United Nations agencies, our friends around the world who are involved in a variety of activities which are suitable for trying to stimulate ideas- Mr. POATS. The point of assembly of these ideas and different expertise is Mr. Bundy's interagency group. 

Mr. FRASER. I don't believe in committees if you will forgive me.

Mr. POATS. It is not a committee, it is more an action board that deals with different problems, and he has considerable directive authority. This would be the present forum available for that sort of thing, and the country desk officers would bring these things up.

775 In addition, the regional program organization in Washington_in the Far East Bureau of AID includes participation by people in other agencies, including Mr. Bundy's bureau. We are making some changes in that organization now to get more direct participation and fulltime participation of people from the political side of the house. I do know that doesn't fully answer the question. I think it is a weakness in the present approach.

Mr. FRASER. I know you can't reorganize the Government to meet every unique situation. I would think the Philippines are of such importance that one ought to think very seriously about trying to establish a little group or something that really thinks hard about these things and begins to sort out the different ways in which we could move. I am more and more concerned about that we not have high visibility.

Mr. BUNDY. Let us work on that. It is a good idea.

The committee meets this morning in open session for a continuation of the hearings on H.R. 7099, a bill to further amend the Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1961. 

Our first witness this morning is John C. Lynn, legislative director, American Farm Bureau Federation. Mr. Lynn is accompanied by 

Mr. Herbert E. Harris II, legislative counsel, AFBF. 

Mr. Lynn, we welcome you back to the Committee on Foreign

I examined your statement last night and, as usual, I found it to be informative and stimulating. For many years I have noted that the
