STATEMENT OF JOHN C. LYNN, LEGISLATIVE DIRECTOR, AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

Mr. LYNN. In light of the fact that we distributed the statement ahead of time, we will highlight the statement and file the text for the record. 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Lynn is as follows:) STATEMENT OF JOHN C. LYNN, LEGISLATIVE DIRECTOR, AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

We appreciate the opportunity to present the views of the American Farm Bureau Federation with respect to authorizations for the fiscal 1968 foreign aid program. 

Farm Bureau is the largest general farm organization with a voluntary paid membership of 1,703,908 member families in over 2,770 County Farm Bureaus in 49 states and Puerto Rico. These families are much concerned, as are many other groups of citizens, with respect to federal budget deficits, the national debt, our balance of payments, and foreign policy decisions because all of these problems have a direct bearing on their well being and prosperity. Through a program of policy development at county, state, and national levels, they have given thoughtful consideration to these problems and the official voting delegates of the member 

State Farm Bureaus in convention in December, 1966 concluded in part as follows: 

"The United States should demonstrate to the world that a dynamic, private, competitive enterprise system is a major factor in contributing to a more abundant life for all people. "This requires- "World investment. 777

1967 

"Movement of goods and services among nations. "Abandonment of policies which restrict the production and distribution of goods and services. "The United States is an example of the progress possible in a free society. 

Our assistance to less developed nations should be based on carefully prepared, long range plans on which there is mutual agreement and which give proper consideration to the ability of these nations to utilize this aid. "An effective program of U.S. assistance should incorporate- "(1) Technical assistance at a level consistent with each nation's current development. "(2) Loans on the basis of sound commercial standards when there is reasonable expectation of repayment. "(3) Military assistance where this is determined to be essential to nations demonstrating a strong will to maintain freedom and independence. "(4) Food aid purchased from the market and based on the recipient nation's needs-not on surplus disposal." 

We believe that the Congress should continue to guide the operation of this program through its annual review. However, we could support authorizations in this area for more than one year's duration if they are based upon sound longterm plans for individual nations. 

We have attached to this statement a detailed breakdown indicating our recommendations for appropriations for the Foreign Assistance Program for fiscal 1968. 

The new spending authority requested (NOA) in the Budget Message totals about $3 billion ($2.5 billion for economic aid and $.5 billion for military assistance). This amount compares with $2.870 billion appropriated by the Congress for fiscal 1967. We recommended $1.670 billion new spending authority for fiscal 

1968. This, coupled with the transfer of $1.772 billion from the Food for Peace 

Program, will make available a total of $3.442 billion for fiscal 1968. 

It is evident that AID continues to have difficulty in developing sound programs based on the needs and desires of the recipient countries and the foreign policy objectives of the United States. It appears that there still are excess funds in the pipeline and that a further tightening of requirements and expenditures can be made.

Experience clearly demonstrates that we cannot buy friends and cooperation with money and that we cannot remake people or governments in our own image. 

We should continue to try to help those who need and want our help, making available only such amounts as they can use efficiently and effectively. 

We should give assistance only on the basis of soundly conceived plans that show good possibilities of achievement.

We should insist that private enterprise, both domestic and foreign, be encouraged in countries that are seeking aid for economic development. 

We should continue to insist that our economically strong allies assume responsibility for aid to the areas where they have a major trading and political interest.

We believe that the money should be fitted to plans based on sound, well thought-out development programs, rather than the plans to the money. 

Military assistance

We have repeatedly questioned whether military assistance should be a part of foreign aid or be a part of the Defense Department Appropriation. We believe this money should be a part of the Defense budget and have recommended this to the Appropriations Committee members. 

We think this is sound and were pleased to note that the fiscal 1968 budget has transferred nearly $200 million foreign aid-military assistance programing to the Defense Department budget. This is a step in the right direction, but more than $500 million of military assistance still remains in the foreign aid budget requests. Development loans The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, authorized for an 8-year period through fiscal 1969, and $8.8 billion program of development loans to be administered by AID. A total of $618 million was appropriated in 1966, $500 million in 1967 and the 1968 request is for $774 million. Despite the reduced appropriations in recent years, the unobligated balance at the beginning of fiscal 1968 is estimated at $350 million. This is in addition to obligated, unspent balances of $1.3 billion. It is apparent, with the size of unobligated carryover, that demands do not justify the increased appropriation request.

779 It is interesting to note that the United States has six major direct foreign aid loan programs in operation, with loans outstanding totaling about $13.6 billion (based on the latest information available to us). 

In addition, there are available funds of the Eximbank, totaling $9.0 billion and the dollar pledges of the United States as capital to the International Monetary Fund, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the 

International Development Association, the International Finance Corporation, the Inter-American Development Bank, and the Asian Development Bank, which add to a total of about $16.5 billion. Therefore, in all of these institutions there is more than $25.0 billion of U.S. public funds available for foreign assistance loans. The interest earned and repayments from loans by all of these institutions are available for reloaning. Also there is about $600 million of Public Law 480 foreign currencies becoming available annually for loans to recipient countries, and $300 million for grants. 

Alliance for Progress

The Administration's request is for a 5-year authorization for the Alliance for Progress amounting to $850 million per year through fiscal 1971, with the proviso that $100 million each year shall also be available in the form of economic grants. It is proposed that the appropriation for fiscal 1968 be $443 million for loans. 

Economic grants

The economic grant program includes funds for technical cooperation and economic development, American schools and hospitals abroad, supporting assistance, contingency fund, international organizations, and administrative expenses.

The spending authority requested for these categories totals $1,313 million, or $89 million more than was appropriated for fiscal 1967. 

The request includes $140 million to be contributed by the United States to international organizations for various and sundry purposes. It should be noted that planned expenditures in fiscal 1968 total $140 million. We believe that $90 million of new spending authority will be ample for fiscal 1968. 

We are concerned that the U.S. contribution to most of these programs is out of proportion to the control we have over them and that they are not very effective. 

We should resist the attempts of a large number of small countries which contribute a small proportion of the funds, to extend and enlarge these programs over the objections of those contributing the major share. 

For administrative expenses the request is for $59.3 million for fiscal 1968, compared with $55.8 million in fiscal 1967. We note that this figure rises each year, although the program level has declined. We believe that under the President's stated policy-helping only those who are willing to help themselves-the program level will be decreased and that, therefore, the administrative costs can be decreased. We recommend a total of $55 million for fiscal 1968. 

Marketing food for freedom

We favor the use of food to assist less developed nations seeking to move toward goals of economic growth, prosperity, and peace. We recommend a program to offer such assistance in a manner that will provide for constructive changes in existing programs.

For many years the United States has been supplying substantial quantities of food to less developed nations under programs such as Public Law 480. 

It has become apparent that changes in approach to food aid could greatly enhance the value of these programs. Farm Bureau recognized the need for such changes and recommended last year a "Marketing Food for Freedom" program.

This program could be adequately financed from funds now being appropriated for price supports, direct payments to agricultural producers, and Public Law 480. 

It should- (1) Be designed to work in harmony with the free market system domestically and to foster expansion of world trade on a commercial basis. (2) Be designed to reduce the costs of government farm programs by providing markets instead of subsidy payments and other price support activities for affected commodities-and not just to add another program. (3) Provide that quantities of commodities to be shipped under the program shall be established and announced far enough in advance to enable farmers to make needed adjustments in production and marketing plans. (4) Provide that once an agreement is reached on the commodities a given nation is to receive, that nation shall be authorized to select the class, grade,

1967 

and quality of product; determine the markets through which purchases are to be made; and to make its own transportation arrangements. (5) Provide that the United States shall not relinquish authority or decision-making responsibility to an international agency or a quasi-governmental corporation.

Such a program would be based on a free agriculture geared to a market system. 

This would provide the economic climate in which American farmers would be encouraged to meet the challenge of a hungry world. There is a clear and present danger that this purpose will be subverted by some in the so-called agri-business community who apparently are prepared to accommodate big government advocates bent on manipulating food supplies and prices without regard to its potential adverse effect on farmers and farm income. 

The Committee will recall that President Johnson's message on "Food for Freedom" last year contained recommendations in general agreement with the five points previously referred to. Among the changes to the program recommended by the President were the following:

Make self-help an integral part of our food aid program. 

Eliminate the "surplus" requirement for food aid. 

Provide for better coordination of food aid with other economic assistance. 

Unfortunately the extension of Public Law 480, passed by Congress last year, did not achieve the objective of eliminating the "surplus" requirement for food aid. Food aid is still largely controlled by a determination of "availability" made by the Secretary of Agriculture. It is apparent that such a determination is largely geared to the government's domestic farm policy objectives rather than food aid requirements.

Dairy products are a good example of programing on a surplus disposal basis instead of a food aid basis. The following table illustrates the point: 

Noncommercial and food aid exports 1964. 1965. 1966. [Million pounds]

Year 

1 Fat solids basis (nonfat dry milk excluded).

Milk equivalent 1 Nonfat dry milk 6, 504 1,278 1,422 863 400 There can be no logical or legitimate explanation for this type of programing other than the obvious fact that the food aid program has been used in one instance to dispose of government stocks and in the second instance to restrict dairy export marketings. The present situation in the U.S. dairy industry is not unrelated to such policies. 

If food aid, economic assistance, and technical assistance are to be coordinated, it seems apparent that they must be administered by the same government agency. U.S. assistance should be offered to less-developed countries as a unified program containing those elements that will best fit each country's developmental needs. 

In this manner, a less-developed country-which has designed its own selfhelp program for development-can confer with the United States on a “package program" of assistance. We believe that country-by-country programs-mutually agreed to by the recipient country and the United States-should be submitted to Congress so that foreign aid money can be appropriated in an intelligent and constructive manner. 

We recommend that (1) Congress appropriate funds for food aid in the same manner that it appropriates funds for other foreign assistance, and (2) the commodities to be shipped under food-aid agreements be purchased through regular market channels.

There would be no need to use the Commodity Credit Corporation to finance such a program; there would be no reason to charge the department of agriculture for the cost of such a program. This would be a food-aid program based on what the people of recipient countries need and could use effectively. It would not be surplus disposal. It would be designed to meet humanitarian and foreign policy objectives of the United States.

781 We recommend that the authorization and appropriation for the "Food for Peace" program be transferred from the Department of Agriculture to AID. 

On March 15, 1967, the President signed an Executive Order placing overall direction of the program in a War on Hunger Policy Committee, which is chaired by the Secretary of State. The Budget should reflect this change in Executive 

Branch responsibility. 

Conclusions 

You may note that we have recommended some sharp cuts in authorizations for fiscal 1968. With the transfer of the appropriation for Food for Peace program (formerly Public Law 480), totaling $1,772 million, and our proposed authorizations for economic assistance for AID, totaling $1,670 million, there would be available to AID for foreign economic assistance the total of $3,442 million for fiscal 1968.

We sincerely believe that food aid can be made to play a more important role in our economic assistance programs to the developing nations. This will be very necessary if the President's proposals are carried out properly. We believe that our aid programs are spread over too many countries. If the program of assistance is limited only to those where the leaders and the people are sincere in their efforts to increase their food supply and really undertake a sound development program, the overall cost to the U.S. will be lowered to the levels we recommend. In such cases we believe great progress can be achieved. 

Again we say let's fit the money to sound workable plans, not the plans to the money.

Mr. LYNN. It is always a pleasure to appear before this committee because we have a deep interest in the problems you are dealing with

1967 

here. It is encouraging too to see some progress being made in getting our ideas in the legislation. 

We have made specific recommendations for your consideration. 

In your bill, Mr. Morgan, H.R. 7099, on which the hearings are being held we see a lot of evidence of policies being included that we have been recommending over the years. It is very difficult for a civilian organization such as ours to know all the facts in connection with a very complicated program such as foreign aid, but we have had more people travel abroad in the last 18 months—that is, officials of the Farm Bureau-than I think than at any time before. We have paid very close attention to the reports that these people have given us, and I think in our policies reflect the thoughts of these "farmer experts". 

We suggest than an effective program for U.S. assistance should incorporate technical assistance at a level consistent with each nation's current development. 

I was impressed with two of these reports we received after our State Farm Bureau people visited certain countries. One of these gentlemen reported that he went 125 miles into the interior and found a very ingenious American who had in some way finagled a water pump. Since the water was only about 12 feet from the surface, this fellow had irrigated 10 acres of land very successfully. This man wondered with all the expenditures that we make, why this might not be a good project. This was in India. This gentlemen was from 

Illinois. He described this irrigated part of this area as looking like a farm in Bloomington.

I cite this only as an example. Another report that we got from another State Farm Bureau leader said how badly these people needed dairy products and how easy it would be to reconstitute butter fat and dried milk to produce the supply of milk products to improve the diets of the people. 

I mention these two only as examples. I think the self-help criteria that are outlited in your bill, beginning on page 6-and I will not read them the five points, or six points that are made there state clearly the recommendations that we are making with regard to self-help programs. 

We comment on page 2 that we are perfectly prepared to support legislation that makes longer authorizations than from year to year, because we firmly believe that we will get better results by fitting the money to the plans, rather than the plans to the money. We have repeated this for a couple or 3 years. We still believe it is a sound approach.

We have to wait, of course, until the appropriation is made, but oftentimes there is a tendency for the U.S. agency administering this program to get together some plans and utilize the money. What we mean by fitting the money to the plans, we ought to decide our long range objectives in certain countries. I heard a statement yesterday that we are checking into, that about two-thirds of the world's hungry people are in Communist territory, one third are outside, and of that one third, about two thirds are in India. This gets this problem down to where I can understand it. We are checking out these figures. 

If we are to make real progress, we ought to decide what our objective is in India, for example. Then each year have the admin-

783 istration come before this committee and let you judge how well they have done in executing what you set out to do under the plan. 

Then let's all work to get the money to carry out what together you think has been accomplished and what should be accomplished the next year.

We have made specific recommendations, with regard to authorizations Mr. Chairman, and I have attached to this statement. We will not detail these. These by and large are based on trying to keep the level of new spending authority for this program at about the same level as for fiscal 1967. 

One point that you need to keep in mind when you are considering our total recommended figure for this program is that we recommend that the food-for-freedom or food-for-peace program be transferred to the AID program. 

On page 2 we indicate what this will add, if you take these two together, then you would have available some $3,442 million for fiscal 1968 which would be considerably more real money than was appropriated last year.

As I said, we will not detail the specific recommendations unless you have questions. We would like to go now, and I would like to call on Mr. Harris to discuss the marketing food-for-freedom program briefly. We believe this is the best contribution we can make to the work of the committee.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Harris. 

STATEMENT OF HERBERT E. HARRIS II, LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL, AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

Mr. HARRIS. 

I know that this committee, and especially the chairman, Mrs. 

Bolton, and Mr. Adair, are familiar with the Farm Bureau's connection with the Public Law 480 program. We worked hard 12 or 13 years ago in the development of the Public Law 480 program. Many on this committee are the ones who supplied the original initiative to get the job done. pro- It had become pretty obvious in the last 4 or 5 years that this gram needed redirection if we were going to achieve the objectives that food aid should achieve. We believe there should be a growing independence of underdeveloped nations rather than a growing dependence, a planned program in the food aid and we should dispel the notion of surplus dumping, surplus disposal of products that happen to be in store in the United States. 

We had recommended strongly as the years went by and the consideration of the extension of Public Law 480 came up, a new program which we called Marketing Food for Freedom. It contained many of the elements of self-help that you now have in the foreign aid bill that you are considering, but the principal notion that we tried to get adopted in the legislation was the idea that the food aid should be geared to what countries needed and could effectively use, not what we happen to have in storage, or what we want to get rid of. 

There was a tremendous amount of talk about this idea last year, a tremendous amount of dialog and debate about it. The legislation finally becomes law but we still have basically the same type of program; that is, we will program those products for export which the

1967 

Secretary of Agriculture determines to be available. This is no farther removed from the concept of surplus disposal than we started with. 

The notion of a marketing food for freedom program is that you determine how food aid can gear into your total foreign aid package. 

You determine how much can effectively be used by the countries that need it and who meet the standards set up in section 208. Then you program for the commodity. Then allow that total demand to be felt in the market, then American farmers can produce the products to meet the demand. 

There is no need to produce the products and surplus ahead of time and store it and then hope that it will be programed. You can program it and then go to the market and buy it. Let the market feel the effect of this total demand. 

The President last year in his message recognized this fact I believe very clearly in his food for freedom message. I would like to quote you just a paragraph of what he said at that time. Among the changes to the program recommended by the President were the following: 

One, make self-help an integral part of our food aid program. Two, eliminate the surplus requirement for food aid. Three, provide for better coordination of food aid with other economic assistance. 

As I say, we do not think the surplus requirement has been eliminated from the program and we think this is a basic step that has to be taken. Let me buttress this point, if I may, by the figures we have shown on page 7 of our statement. These are the figures that show the programing, noncommercial and food aid exports of dairy products in the last 3 years. You will notice that the milk equivalent which we have determined on a fat solids basis-this is on the top of page 7-in 1964 we programed 6,504 million pounds of milk equivalent. In 1965 we programed 1,422 million pounds of milk equivalent. In 1966, my latest figures indicate we programed zero pounds of milk equivalent.

Mrs. BOLTON. Why? 

Mr. HARRIS. I think that there can be no logical or legitimate answer to that question, Mrs. Bolton, except that the programing has been based on domestic farm policy objectives rather than on food aid requirements. We have had a concerted effort beginning over a year ago to depress the price of dairy products. There was an effort to restrict exports of dairy products, there was an effort to increase the import of dairy products. There is an effort to cut down consumption of dairy products by the defense establishment. In the past 3 months we have suffered the consequences of those policies. We have had the unfortunate occurrence, unfortunate from the farmers' standpoint, unfortunate from the international relations standpoint, of dumping milk in fields when there were hungry people around the world. This is why we want to emphasize today that food aid and especially the nutrients that are contained in products like dairy products, should be programed on the basis of need and go into the market on an advance basis and allow the market to indicate to the producer, yes, these products are needed, and they are going to be programed on a continuing basis. 

This is why we recommend specifically that Congress appropriate funds for food aid in the same manner that it appropriates funds for other foreign assistance. The commodities to be shipped under food

785 aid agreements should be purchased through regular market channels, and that the total foreign aid program, including food aid, be in one bill, and thereby take steps toward having a coordinated program of foreign aid, not having two or three or four different compartments. 

In this way we would not require the back door financing of CCC. 

You would not gear it to the surplus disposal program, but what it is intended to do. 

The executive branch has recognized the need to do this in a way, although they have difficulty sometimes making up their minds depending on what forum they are arguing in and who happens to win that day, but you all noted, I am sure, the announcement on March 15 where the President established a War on Hunger Interagency Subcommittee. It is significant to note here that the Chairman of that Committee is the Secretary of State, not the Secretary of Agriculture, and that it is recognized that the coordination of the war on hunger is a foreign policy objective and not a domestic farm policy objective. 

It seems to me that the legislative process and the budget should reflect that basic executive department decision.

Mr. MORSE. 

Mr. Lynn and Mr. Harris, I would like to find out how this program that you advocate would operate. Would you describe what you contemplate in some greater detail than is set forth in your prepared statement as to the food-for-peace program? 

Mr. HARRIS. It is not a great deal different from what we are doing right now. It is different from what a lot of people understood that we were doing now, though. Under a current food aid program, Public 

Law 480 as it operates a purchase authorization is usually issued by the Department of Agriculture to the importing country, their agent, and that piece of paper, that purchase authorization can be taken to the market and bought by many exporters and used to buy from many exporters, wheat or some other commodity. When that exporter makes shipment he files his paper and gets payment directly from the 

CCC for the purchase made. 

Mr. MORSE. You are talking about the Public Law 480 program?

Mr. HARRIS. The way it operates. There is to a large extent a confusion that does exist as to how Public Law 480 has actually operated in the past.

Mr. MORSE. At what price level would these transactions be conducted?

Mr. HARRIS. At that point as soon as you have an authorization to buy x amount of wheat you are into the market making a purchase exactly like any other commercial purchase. At a point the exporter may not know whether it is a Public Law 480 sale or a straight commercial sale because it is handled exactly the same. 

Mr. MORSE. And it doesn't make any difference? 

Mr. HARRIS. No, sir. What we are saying is that you should not have to make a determination-let's take an example. If you want to rig the price of one wheat all you have to do is specify on the purchase authorization the type of wheat that is other than the type that you want to rig. Our Soft Red Spring wheat folks have been unhappy for a number of years because the purchase authorizations have come out in a way that cut them out from competing from this type of shipment. That decision wasn't made on a food aid basis, it was made on a domestic policy basis. 

What we are saying is, let the importing country determine what they need under the general guidance of our total foreign aid requirements. Then let them go into the market and get what they want from the market on the basis of purchase authorizations from AID rather than the Department of Agriculture. 

Mr. LYNN. Just to supplement this, one reason that the dairy products were not continued in the program was the fact that the Commodity Credit stocks did get down. We were very happy that this happened. We worked hard to change the food for peace program to cut out the word "surplus" because we were hoping that the Secretary of Agriculture would continue to program dairy products at about the same 5-billion-pound rate that he had done in 1964. 

Mr. MORSE. How much leadtime would it take to program this proposal?

Mr. LYNN. It depends a lot on the commodity. It takes longer to build up a cow herd, of course, than it does to raise a crop of wheat. I

1967 

think farmers if they had real confidence again that these things were going to work so as to have good prices, rather than depress their prices by manipulating the domestic program, I think you would be surprised how well they would respond. 

Mr. HARRIS. I doubt the lead time on one end would take any longer than the leadtime on the other end. The effect of programing of food aid to underdeveloped countries needs lead time. You cannot just lay dried skim milk down on the dock and expect it to be used effectively in a food aid program in that country. You need lead time in that kind of program. Just as you need lead time for our production to reflect this demand that is coming. I think they mutually balance. 

Mr. MORSE. Do you know offhand what the amount of the Public

Mr. HARRIS. It has been fairly constant. We will program at about $1.7 billion a year.

Mr. HARRIS. I don't believe we advocate any specific level but advocate reflecting the programing that seems to be adequate. STATEMENT OF H. HAINES TURNER, BLOOMINGTON, IND., FOR THE FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL LEGISLATION 

Mr. TURNER. Mr. Chairman, as you have said, I am H. Haines 

Turner. I am from Bloomington, Ind. At the present time I am on leave of absence from my regular work which is with Indiana University, working as a volunteer for a year and a half for the American 

Friends Service Committee. 

I have been in South Vietnam for 8 months to help to set up a project for the American Friends Service Committee. At the present time I am working in their headquarters in Philadelphia on a program to help the refugees in a very small way, to help them we hope in South Vietnam. 

I am seeking specialists in making and fitting artificial limbs, physiotherapists, nurses, occupational therapists who are willing to go and work as volunteers in South Vietnam to help the civilians who have been injured there. If any of you can give me any good leads for these specialists, who are very scarce and very hard to find, I would apprciate it.

I thank you very much for the opportunity to say a few words to you this morning. As you know, I am here as a representative of the 

Friends Committee on National Legislation.

If you are willing to depart a little from the prepared statement, I would like to summarize some of these points rather briefly and say a little bit more about my own experience and observations in South Vietnam. 

I would like to say first that our Friends Committee believes that the requests of the administration for development aid and technical assistance should be larger. We do not feel that they are adequate. 

There is a growing gap between the less developed and the more developed nations. We Friends would advocate that the United States take the lead and contribute not just 1 percent of our national income to help these less developed countries, but that we would recommend that we contribute 2 percent of the national income. 

Our second point would be that more effort should be given to strengthening regional and United Nations programs. Our committee endorses the President's appeal for more regional development. At the same time, we note with regret that the United States is refusing

1967 

to help to build a $33 million dam in the Cambodian section of the Mekong, President Johnson, as you know, in his speech 2 or 3 years ago, praised the development of the Mekong River and said it could help to offset the destructive war in Vietnam. The United States did in effect pledge we would help with it and we should. 

The third point I would like to make briefly is that contributions for family planning should be increased. I am sure other witnesses will be telling you the same thing. 

Fourth, military aid should be realistically examined. Nearly every year newspapers report some incidents of the misuse of U.S. military aid. One year it was in the Pakistan-Indian war. This year it is the coup by which military officers suspended the democratic procedures in Greece.

But to turn to my own experiences in South Vietnam. I was sent there in May of last year and came back in January this year. I was sent to South Vietnam by the American Friends Service Committee to set up a small program under which American volunteers might work as assistants to Vietnamese social service agencies. This is a very small program. We have only six volunteers in South Vietnam at the present time. We intend to have a total of 10 volunteers by next September. However, we believe that this program is probably different from almost any other program undertaken in Vietnam by Americans. First, of course, our volunteers must learn the Vietnamese language. Secondly, each young man or young woman whom we send works for a private agency run by the Vietnamese people, a private social service agency, and he works as a helper to the Vietnamese. Third, he or she lives among the Vietnamese people. These volunteers do not go as advisers. They do not bring any sum of money or any material aids to offer to the Vietnamese. They go only to offer their own services. We believe this creates a different relationship between our American volunteers and the Vietnamese people with whom they associate. Thus it is possible that we have a better opportunity to become acquainted with those people and to know how these people feel and think. 

I must admit that the observations that I have been able to draw from our experience are contradictory. During my service in South 

Vietnam I could see the people would benefit from more aid if the war were to be ended. There is a tremendous shortage of doctors, nurses, hospitals. There are not enough schools for all the children and in most of the schools the children only get 2 or 3 hours of school a day. 

They have to go in short shifts. Thus I see many needs for economic assistance to the people of South Vietnam. I am sure they feel these needs. Nevertheless, it is my observation the Vietnamese people even in the cities and towns that are under the jurisdiction of the Saigon government do not want the American aid program. In fact, I am afraid they are beginning to resent the U.S. aid program. This I suppose goes back to the fact that the Vietnamese, like many of the rest of us, are proud people. They want independence. The members of this committee know their history. The Vietnamese fought for many centuries to secure independence from China. Then they fought to overthrow the French. I believe that we Americans and our Government have been sincere in thinking that we were trying to bring freedom to the people of South Vietnam. But in the past 2 years some tremendous changes have been taking place in South Vietnam and

795 in the attitude of the urban people who formerly supported the United States. It is primarily in the cities, in Saigon, in particular, that I spent my time.

In December I talked with a Vietnamese editor of a daily newspaper in Saigon. He said in effect:

What we want is freedom and self-respect for South Vietnam, but we have instead humiliation. The French who had less money and fewer staff to send to 

Vietnam had their governors in the main cities of our country, but they had the administration done through Vietnamese subordinates in the province capitals. 

You Americans have advisers in almost every town, American advisers on military affairs, on health affairs, on economic matters, and education affairs. 

Of course even though our U.S. representatives call themselves advisers, the Vietnamese know that they are more expert in their fields and better trained than they themselves are. They know they have the access to the purse strings. So in place after place, and time after time, the Vietnamese officials find that the American advisers are actually running their country for them. The South Vietnamese even in the cities who have said, "yes, we must have the help of the American Army to save us from Communist domination," are now saying "we are becoming a colony of the United States." 

I talked also with a well educated Vietnamese man who has been active in social service work in Saigon for more than 10 years, cooperating with American social workers. He told me that prejudice against Americans is growing steadily. "Think, for example," he said, "our Government has assigned three battalions of the South Vietnamese Army to guard the city of Saigon. Then the American Army assigned three battalions of Americans to guard the city of Saigon. So the 

Vietnamese soldiers ask: 'What are we here for? The Americans do not respect us.' 222 Perhaps the contradiction which I am presenting to you in the attitudes of these Vietnamese people in the cities of South Vietnam may be related to the contradiction of what we are trying to do there. 

We are trying to win a war, through the use of artillery and bombs and at the same time we are trying to provide economic aid. Maybe these are actually contradictory. 

To conclude my remarks, I have talked about South Vietnam, but similar economic and social conditions exist in other parts of the world, where people are also hungry, living on a very low standard of living and wanting something better. And yet the people in those nations are also proud. They do not want to be dependent on some larger nation. In South Vietnam the United States has tended to concentrate on unilateral economic aid. I would like to suggest that the United 

States should give more of its aid in other nations as well as in South Vietnam through multilateral, agencies such as the United Nations agencies.

I have seen something of the work of the United Nations agencies in South Vietnam. Those programs are accepted by the Vietnamese people because they do not represent a threat to them in any way. 

The people who direct those programs are not representing any one nation. They are representing many different nations. They are impartial. We must keep the United Nations impartial. We must avoid the tendency to use the United Nations where it benefits us as in South Vietnam while discouraging the use of United Nations funds in other countries such as Cuba where it is helping somebody with whom we happen to disagree.

1967 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Turner.

Mr. Turner, we will put your entire statement in the record and permit you to make whatever corrections you want to make of your additional remarks.

I am H. Hanes Turner, of Bloomington, Indiana. I here represent the Friends

Committee on National Legislation, a Quaker agency. While the FCNL does not attempt to speak for all Friends, it does include Friends appointed by 20 of the 26 Yearly Meetings and 10 Friends organizations. FCNL, the last grew out of my personal experience in South Vietnam. 

1. The Administration's requests for development aid and technical assistance are not adequate. There is a growing gap between the developed and the underdeveloped world. Yet our aid program is slightly less than 7/10th of 1% our national income. 

This program is largely loans, repayable in dollars and tied to U.S. procurement. 

World Bank President George Woods has offered an indictment of aid providers which must be applicable to some extent to the United States and I quote: "Most providers of aid. have used overseas assistance as a subsidy for their own industries . . as a way of exporting goods and services at higher than world prices. It is estimated that the donor countries put a value on their annual aid about $1 billion a year higher than the same goods and services would bring in competitive world markets. Most of the financing of development-about three-quarters of it comes from the developing countries themselves, and it is right and proper for them to be carrying the main responsiblity. . . But the industrial countries are not doing enough to enable the less developed nations to earn their own way. The effective tariffs on imports from developing countries are commonly from 20 to 40 percent-a high margin in any case, but extremely so since this protection is being afforded to mature economies from economies which in many cases are still in their infant years. Six years ago, the official net flow of financial resources from the industrialized countries reached a level of about $6 billion a year. Today, after five years of unprecedented prosperity in the donor countries, the figure is about the same. Of the $200 billion by which the production of the industrialized countries has grown in that interval, none has been put at the disposal of the developing countries through programs of assistance.

We Friends feel that the United States should take the lead in calling for a more imaginative program. The UN has recommended that the developed nations contribute 1% of their gross national product to the development process. We recommend a 2% contribution so that some of the gap can be closed as quickly as possible. 

2. More effort should be given to strengthening regional and UN programs. Our 

Committee endorses the President's appeal for more regional development and we strongly favor the proposed requirement that not less than 85% of all development loan funds be spent through UN or other multilateral or regional agencies. 

Yet we have noted with the deepest regret that the United States is refusing to help build a $33 million dam in the Cambodian section of the Mekong. We would hope that the Foreign Affairs Committee would urge the Administration to reconsider this action. UN Secretary General U Thant has labeled the Mekong Basin development "one of the most important and *** significant activities ever undertaken by the United Nations" which, if it "succeeds, *** will stand as a monument, *** for all other regions to emulate." President Johnson has lauded the project ever since 1965 as a work of peace, which could help offset the destructive war in Vietnam by providing "food and water and power on a scale to dwarf even our own TVA." 

3. More effort should be centered on reinforcing the integrity and impartiality of the UN. In his recent appearance before this Committee, Assistant Secretary of State, Joseph J. Sisco pointed out that the United States has been working with the Government of South Vietnam "to encourage the expansion of UN programs in Vietnam." I can personally attest to the material effectiveness and

797 importance of some of these programs such as health care and educational assistance. The Vietnamese people accept these, because they are not the programs of any one country and they do not represent the danger of domination by a foreign power. But there is a contradiction here the UN is acceptable in Vietnam because it is an impartial body, but the fact that UN agencies are engaged in South Vietnam may undermine this reputation for impartiality with other nations who fear that the United States is trying to "use" the UN in a hot war. 

This is particularly true since the United States is opposing FAO and UNESCO projects in Cuba which are very similar to the projects this nation has urged in South Vietnam; and has vigorously protested any aid to North Vietnam. We are concerned over the possibility that anything that feeds the charge that the United States is "using" the UN might adversely affect the UN's ability to mediate the war. Therefore we would hope that something could be done to reinforce the 

UN's credentials for impartiality. Might not one possibility be for this Committee to urge the Administration to acquiesce in UN aid to Communist areas such as Cuba or North Vietnam or North Korea, or East Germany, as the need and the desire may arise? ​4. Contributions for Family Planning should be increased. We understand the 

Aid Agency expects to allocate $20 million for population control activities in fiscal 1968; this seems far too little and we would urge this Committee to incorporate the basic components of the Fulbright bill, S. 1264, into the pending legislation. 

S. 1264 would authorize the expenditure of $50 million a year for each of the next three fiscal years for birth control programs carried on by foreign governments, the UN and private agencies. 

5. Military aid should be realistically examined. Nearly every year, newspapers report some instance of the misuse of U.S. military aid; one year it was the 

Pakistani-Indian war, this year it is the coup by which military officers suspended democratic procedures in Greece. Only 10 days before this last coup, the Secretary of Defense told this Committee that Greece "has been heavily dependent upon military assistance for its equipment needs since World War II." 

6. But to turn to my central point. I spent eight months in South Vietnam, from May 10, 1966 until January 14, 1967. I was sent to South Vietnam by the

American Friends Service Committee to set up a small program under which American_volunteers might work as assistants to Vietnamese social service agencies. This is a very small program. We have only six volunteers in South 

Vietnam at the present time, and intend to have a total of ten by next September. 

However, we believe that this program is probably different from almost any other program undertaken in Vietnam by Americans. First, of course, our volunteers must learn the Vietnamese language. Secondly, each young man or young women works for a private agency run by the Vietnamese people and he works as a helper to the Vietnamese. Third, he or she lives among the Vietnamese people.

These volunteers do not go as "advisors;" they do not bring any sum of money or any material aids to offer the Vietnamese; they go only to offer their own services. 

We believe that this creates a different relationship between our American volunteers and the Vietnamese with whom they associate. Thus, it is possible that we have a better opportunity to become acquainted, to know how these 

Vietnamese feel and think.

During my service in South Vietnam, I could see that the people would benefit from more aid-if the war could be ended. There is a tremendous shortage of doctors, nurses and hospitals. There are not enough schools for all of the children, and in most schools the children only get two or three hours of school a day. 

They have hardly any social workers in Saigon-to say nothing of the services of of social welfare needed by the people. Housing is very crowded, and there is hardly anything in the way of parks or playgrounds or recreation space for the children. There is no safe water unless one boils it. Traffic conditions in Saigon are terrible and even a greater burden on the poor Vietnamese who must get to work than they are upon the Americans who suffer through them. 

Thus, I see many needs for economic assistance to the people of South Vietnam Nevertheless, it is my observation that the Vietnamese people—even in the cities and towns under the supervision of the Saigon government-do not want the American aid program. In fact, I am afraid that they are beginning to resent the U.S. aid program. 

The Vietnamese are a proud people and they want independence. The members of this Committee know their history. For 1,000 years they were ruled by the 

Chinese, against their will. Then they succeeded in about the year 1000 A.D. in achieving their independence from China. About 100 years ago, Vietnam was captured by the French with the aid of modern weapons. Then, for many years, Vietnamese nationalists tried to overthrow the French. Finally, they succeeded;

1967 

they thought they would again rule their own country. This has not happened although I believe that we Americans and our government were sincere in thinking that we were trying to bring freedom to the people of South Vietnam. Yet the 

Vietnamese have continued to suffer the ravages of war. 

In the past two years, tremendous changes have taken place in the cities of South Vietnam, and the suffering and the dying are increasing in the countryside. 

I don't know the countryside as well as the cities, but the attitude of the people in the cities has changed. They see continually more and more American soldiers entering their country, and more American advisors. They feel the fabric of their society is being destroyed by the war. 

In December, I talked with the Vietnamese editor of a daily newspaper in Saigon. He said in effect: What we want is freedom and self respect for South 

Vietnam, but we have, instead, humiliation. The French, who had less money and fewer staff to send to Vietnam, had their governors in the main cities of our country, but they had the administration done through Vietnamese subordinates in the province capitals. You Americans have advisors in almost every town, American advisors on military affairs, on health affairs, on economic matters, on education affairs. And, of course, even though our representatives in Vietnam call themselves "advisors," the Vietnamese know that they are more expert in their fields and better trained, and they know that they have access to the purse strings; so in place after place, and time after time, the Vietnamese officials find that the American advisors are actually running their country for them. 

The Vietnamese, even of the cities, who have said "Yes, we must have the help of the American Army to save us from Communist domination," are now saying "We are becoming a colony of the United States.' 

I talked also with a well educated Vietnamese man who has been active in social service work in Saigon for more than ten years, cooperating with American social workers. He told me that the prejudice against Americans is growing steadily. 

Think, for example, he said: Our government has assigned three battalions of the South Vietnamese Army to guard the City of Saigon. Then the American 

Army assigned three battalions of Americans to guard the City of Saigon. So the 

Vietnamese soldiers ask: "What are we here for? The Americans do not respect us." 

It is instances such as these which have led me to question the validity of Assistant Administrator Poats' assertion that U.S. military and civil efforts in 

Vietnam are "interdependent." I would call them opposites. The Aid agency cannot help bring about social reform and economic development in a situation where the U.S. military are making as many refugees as are resettling; causing more and more people to congregate in already overcrowded cities; and contributing more and more civilian casualties to the already overtaxed hospitals. By trying to carry out such an impossible assignment in an impossibly short period of time, the Aid agency is incurring the resentment of the Vietnamese people-not necessarily the officials but the people and are contributing to the Vietnamese belief that Americans have taken over their country. 

CONCLUSION 

Future Vietnams might be avoided if the world would concentrate on defeating the basic enemies of hunger, ignorance, and despair. Such a goal can only be attained if the United States greatly expands its economic aid program and increasingly channels aid funds through multilateral agencies which are more committed to the brotherhood of man and the fundamental dignity of each individual than to particular political forms.

799 present time the Vietcong and the North Vietnamese forces would move in. The people who have been relying on us, and I think many of the liberal forces, the university student groups to whom I talked, I don't know what would happen to those people. I think we might see-

STATEMENT OF DR. N. R. DANIELIAN, PRESIDENT, INTERNA- TIONAL ECONOMIC POLICY ASSOCIATION

STATEMENT OF N. R. DANIELIAN, PRESIDENT, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC POLICY ASSOCIATION INTRODUCTION 

The International Economic Policy Association represents a group of American international business corporations vitally concerned with the success of our foreign economic programs, in the interest of free world security and prosperity. 

I think it would be preferable at the outset to outline briefly the recommendations of the Association, which are elaborated at length in this statement. 

RECOMMENDATIONS The Association recommends- 

1. That Congress adopt an amendment to specify the steps necessary to create an attractive climate for private investment, as one of the important self-help criteria. 

2. That Congress make clear that those provisions of Sections 202 and 252 which require that 50 per centum of the funds provided for Development Loans and the Alliance for Progress be used to encourage development through private enterprise must be used directly and exclusively for such purposes. 

3. That Congress delete the proposed amendment of Section 638 which would allow the continuation of investment guaranties in a country where assistance has been withdrawn under Section 620(e) because of an uncompensated expropriation. 

4. That Congress authorize the extension of guaranties and insurance for private investment to $9 billion proposed in Section 221(b).

1967 

5. That Congress authorize the use of funds provided for in Section 222(b) to assure adequate staffing of our embassies with industrial experts at the Ministerial level to accelerate private development programs in those countries where investment guaranties are stimulating large new investments. 

6. That Congress eliminate Section 205 and Section 251(h) which permit the channeling of bilateral aid funds to multilateral financial institutions with serious adverse effects on the U.S. balance of payments and bypassing of long established Congressional policies under the Foreign Assistance Act. 

7. That, while accepting the concept of providing aid under multilateral auspices such as consortia, the Congress amend Section 210(a) to delete the provision that aid funds provided under this Act should be "administered" by multilateral lending institutions or international organizations. The word "administered" should be changed to "coordinated with.' 29 8. That the U.S. aid program be reoriented from the existing line-of-credit basis to provide real resources-U.S. goods and technical services-for specific projects. "Program" loans should be given only in emergency situations and not on a regular basis, and they should be taken out of the category of "Development Loans" and placed in the President's contingency fund, which should be increased accordingly. 

9. That Congress impose a statutory limit of 25 years on all Development 

Loans, including Alliance for Progress Loans, as redefined above, and should instead authorize a more realistic grant assistance for countries which are not in a financial position to accept such loan assistance, on condition that other free world aid-giving countries adopt comparable provisions. 

10. That Congress limit its authorizations for U.S. bilateral economic assistance to one year in order to have an annual review of what progress is being made.

IMPORTANCE OF U.S. FOREIGN AID 

The bilateral foreign aid activities of the United States constitute a major part of foreign economic policy. The latest available statistics of the OECD indicate that the United States, from 1963 through 1965, contributed $11.1 billion or 59 percent of total bilateral assistance disbursed ($18.9 billion) for economic development by the industrialized countries of the DAC (see Table 1). 

After deducting amortization and interest receipts from each country's gross contribution, the total net transfer is reduced to $15.7 billion, of which the U.S. share is $9.6 billion, or 61 percent.

Nor is this the whole story. The bulk of U.S. economic aid is in the form of 40: year loans at 22 percent interest, while most other donor countries provide aid at close to commercial terms. For example, between 1962 and 1965, the average maturity on U.S. loan commitments was 31 years, while for France it was 16 years, West Germany 17 years, Italy 8 years, Japan 14 years, and so on. Only 

Canada has substantially liberalized its lending terms and Canada's bilateral aid, although substantial in relation to her GNP, only amounts to about $100 million a year. Interest rates on U.S. commitments averaged 2.6 percent between 

1962 and 1965, while those of France averaged 3.8 percent, West Germany 4.2 percent, Italy 5.2 percent and Japan 5.0 percent (see Table 2). Without wishing to belabor the point, it is clear that the United States provides not only the bulk of the aid from the industrialized free world countries (about 60 percent) but also on the softest terms.

SPECIFIC SELF-HELP CRITERIA 

The Association has long advocated the necessity of self-help on the part of the less developed countries. We were most pleased with the succinct statement in the President's message on foreign aid where he stated “. nations develop primarily through their own efforts. Our programs can only be supplements, not substitutes. This is the overriding principle." We were also pleased to see this followed by specific provision of self-help criteria in Section 208 of the proposed legislation. However, the role which private foreign investment alone can play in bringing capital, know-how and training to the developing nations, which is so well recognized in Section 601, is so important that special attention should be given to the extent to which aid-receiving countries are taking the necessary steps to attract it. We would, therefore, recommend that Section 208 be amended along the following lines.

Delete the proposed Section 208(b) and replace it with the following language: "(b) the extent to which the government of the country is creating a favorable climate for private enterprise and investment, both domestic and foreign, as a necessary element in economic development by— "I. providing for maximum private ownership and initiative in ne as well as existing industry, including manufacturing, financing, distribution, and merchandising; "ii. assuring nondiscriminatory treatment between national and nonnational, and between public and private, enterprises and products; "iii. providing for unrestricted remittance of amortization of investment, interest and dividend payments; "iv. providing adequate protection for industrial property rights; "v. enacting tax laws with rates of taxation designed to promote optimum utilization of private investment capital, both foreign and domestic.'

807 Countries which have adopted such measures have demonstrated how effective they can be in increasing the inflow of foreign private investment. When Brazil took such steps just a few years ago the results were immediate. Other countries have achieved similar results. 

FIFTY PERCENT OF FUNDS FOR PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

Authorizations in Sections 202 and 252 provide that "not less than 50 per centum of the funds appropriated. shall be available for loans made to encourage economic development through private enterprise.' This applies to 

Development Loan funds and Alliance for Progress funds. Despite this provision only $425 million of the $2.9 billion provided to Latin America since 1961 has been used directly for such purposes through the funding of intermediate credit institutions and cooperatives for relending to the private sector. The Administration's contention is that almost any expenditure on roads, power, education or health meets this criterion. The purpose of this provision was to assure that at least half of the loan funds appropriated should be devoted to those private enterprise activities which provide production and jobs. Clearly, the program has not been administered in such a fashion as to achieve this desired result. Therefore, we propose that provision be made that 50 per centum of the funds provided for Development Loans and the Alliance for Progress must be used directly for development through private enterprise. This might best be accomplished by requiring that such funds be used for the development and funding of credit institutions for relending to the private sector and for the creation of institutions such as Development Finance Corporations on a national as well as a regional basis, which would seek out and promote private, productive enterprise. Such funds should be available not only for capital development, but also for the working capital needs of private business. 

TERMINATION OF GUARANTY PROGRAM WHEN ASSISTANCE SUSPENDED 

Section 620(e), the Hickenlooper Amendment, provides that the President shall suspend assistance to the government of any country where, after January 1, 1962, a country or any of its subdivisions has expropriated property owned by any U.S. citizen, repudiated or nullified existing contracts or agreements with any 

U.S. citizen, or taken steps which have the effect of expropriation without making full and adequate reparation within six months. In the present act it is proposed that Section 638 shall be amended to provide that no provision of the act shall be so construed as to prohibit the issuance of investment guaranties. This amendment would mean that, where there has been expropriation of the property of a U.S. citizen without full and prompt compensation and assistance is cut off, the 

United States would still be prepared to guaranty further investments in the country in question. This is patently inconsistent. It is recommended that the proposed amendment to Section 638 be deleted.

ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON SELF-HELP 

The National Advisory Committee on Self-help, proposed in Section 209, could serve a very useful function. Since this committee is to render an annual report which will be submitted to the Congress, it would be desirable that the Congress should have some say in the selection of its members. It is, therefore, recommended that Section 209(a) be amended as follows: 

"Sec. 208. National Advisory Committee on Self-Help.-(a) There is hereby established a National Advisory Committee on Self-Help, consisting of 24 members, of which 14 shall be appointed by the President, 5 by the Senate Foreign 

Relations Committee and 5 by the Foreign Affairs Committee of the House of 

Representatives. In making the appointments particular emphasis shall be placed on the selection of recognized authorities in professional or technical fields related to economic, social and political development of less developed countries and on members of the general public who are leaders in the economic, social and political life of the United States. The President shall designate one member of the Committee to serve as Chairman."

INVESTMENT GUARANTY PROGRAM 

I would like to comment on the investment guaranty program. You will recall that in 1963 we recommended reduction of the cost of combined specific risk guaranties to one percent. Our Association is very pleased that AID has recently

1967 

reduced the premium for combined specific risk guaranty coverage from 1½ percent to 11% percent. This should encourage more U.S. investment in less developed countries at a smaller initial cost. We still hope that the cost may be further reduced to one percent.

The success of this program can be seen from the use which has been made of it by investors just in the field of specific risk guaranties. At the end of December 

1963, there were 778 contracts in an amount of just under $1.5 billion; in 1964 there were 1,271 contracts in an amount of just over $2.2 billion; in 1965 there were 1,919 contracts in an amount exceeding $3.1 billion; and in 1966 there were 

2,491 contracts in an amount exceeding $3.9 billion. Such a growth in the use of this guaranty program certainly suggests that it is a useful means of promoting increased private investment and helping the developing countries in their economic advancement.

The guaranty program has proved to be a very successful instrument for increasing the flow of private capital to the less developed countries. After much thought and discussion within our policy committees, we concluded that the specific risk investment guaranty program would be much improved if civil disturbances and riots were covered under AID's guaranty program. In many less developed countries it is not possible to obtain from commercial insurance companies coverage against these two specific risks, or if it is available the rates are exorbitant. In countries where general political unrest is prevalent, very often foreign businesses become the focal point of riots or civil disturbances which do not amount to insurrection or revolution. In such cases it is our understanding that the war, revolution and insurrection specific risk insurance of AID has not been applicable in the past. We feel that extending the coverage of this specific risk guaranty to riots and civil disturbances would help to diminish the fears and reluctance of U.S. business to invest in such areas. We, therefore, support the inclusion of "civil strife" in Section 221(b)(1)(c).

We are pleased to note that the President has recommended that the authorized face value of investment guaranties be increased to $9 billion. In 1963 we had recommended $5 billion. The Congress then approved a limit of $2.5 billion, raising it to $5 billion in 1965. We are glad to see this new initiative on the part of the Administration, and support it. 

We hope that the necessary administrative actions will be taken to provide the increased personnel that such an expanding program will require. I am sure the revenues from the fees would justify such an expansion. 

EMBASSY STAFFING TO PROMOTE PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

One phase of the administrative problem is to provide top level industrial experts at the Ministerial level in our embassies abroad in those countries where this investment guaranty program is bringing large, new investments to spur the private development programs. The funds provided in Section 222(b) should be available to meet the cost of such staffing. Certainly, this function of harnessing private investment in economic development is at least equally as important as government-to-government aid. 

MULTILATERALIZATION OF AID 

In his message on foreign aid the President stated his belief that one of the six guiding principles on which our foreign assistance program should be based was 'Multilateralism-every advanced nation has a duty to contribute its share of the cost." In his discussion he noted that in considering the share which advanced nations bear of this burden it is not enough to count just economic and food aid. 

He went on to say, "Our defense expenditures far exceed those of all other free nations combined and serve their common interest. This burden must be counted in the balance." With these sentiments our Association is completely in accord. We support every effort to secure a more equitable sharing of this burden.

CHANNELING OF BILATERAL AID FUNDS THROUGH MULTILATERAL INSTITUTIONS 

Our Association has consistently opposed the diversion of U.S. bilateral aid funds through multilateral financial institutions. This position of our group is not based on any general opposition to multilateral institutions. We recognize that these international organizations have many advantages.

809 It is our belief that the Foreign Assistance Act should deal with the bilateral aid program and that authorizations and appropriations for international agencies should come up for consideration on their own merits. Where aid funds provided by this Act are used in conjunction with international agencies, either directly or through consortia, the conditions applicable thereto should conform with this Act.

We believe these are desirable conditions. We have, therefore, opposed, and continue to oppose, Section 205 of the Foreign Assistance Act which gives the President discretionary authority to transfer up to 10 percent of the funds ap propriated for Development Loans to the International Development Association, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the International 

Finance Corporation, or the Asian Development Bank, and Section 251(h) 

which authorizes the transfer of up to 15 percent of Alliance for Progress funds to the same institutions except for the Asian Development Bank, to be used by them under their individual_criteria and administrative rules and regulations rather than those governing U.S. bilateral aid programs. 

Congress approved an authorization of $200 million for the Asian Development Bank for fiscal years 1966-1970. Congress has regularly considered proposals for contributions to other multilateral lending institutions. If more funds are needed for the Asian Development Bank, the International Development Association, the World Bank or any other multilateral financial institution, then authorizations and appropriations for them should be requested and considered on their merits. We should keep our bilateral and multilateral programs separate. 

MULTILATERAL PROGRAMS 

The idea of multilateral programs as a means of securing a more equitable sharing of the burden of aid, as proposed in the President's message, has much to recommend it. If such an approach gave hope of that result we would support it. 

We have some suggestions about the provisions proposed in Section 210(a). 

That Section suggests that this multilateral approach would have the advantage of securing "participation of other donors." It does not speak of securing a more equitable sharing of the burden by others. This is becoming critical as debt burden on some less developed countries rises. If it were not for the role played by our long-term, low-interest loans, our sales of agricultural products for local currencies, and the long-term, no-interest loans of the International Development Association (financed to the tune of 40 percent by the United States), some of these countries would not be able to meet their current debt commitments. This condition is aggravated by the fact that much of the so-called "aid" advanced by other countries is on hard commercial terms. If there is to be real burden sharing, the terms and conditions should be comparable. This has not been the case in the past. Much of our own aid on soft terms has had the effect of increasing recipient countries' resources so that they can repay other creditor countries, with adverse effects on our balance of payments. 

The importance of this consideration can be seen from a comparison of the assistance granted to the Indian Government between 1960 and 1964 and the reapyments to each donor country (see Tables 3 and 4). Hard currency repayments to the United States amounted to only $78 million since 1960, as compared to economic and food aid in the amount of $1,934 million, which means net aid of $1,856 million. In contrast, repayments to other country donors amounted to $309 million, and disbursements to $1,302 million, or net aid of $993 million. 

Thus, the net transfer of resources from the United States was approximately twice that of all other countries combined. In the case of the World Bank, hard currency repayments amounted to $71 million and new disbursements to $192 million, or a net of $121 million. This, of course, is supplemented by net new commitments by IDA of $190 million with no repayments contemplated before the year 2000.¹

The consortium idea would be a good one if we used it as a forum to secure an equitable sharing of the aid burden in terms and conditions as well as in mere quantity. Where other donors lend at 5-6 percent for 10-15 years, while the

United States lends at 40 years with 2½ percent interest charged after the first 10 years, this is hardly burden sharing. If the concept of multilateral programs is to have real meaning, we will have to achieve equity in terms and conditions as well as amounts of aid.

This will be achieved only where the United States bargains hard with its other aidgiving associates and not where it makes concessions whether the others are willing to do so or not. The recent situation in India hardly suggests that we have reached the point where we are willing to demand enough of our associates. On April 6, 1967 it was reported from Paris, where the ten-nation Aid India Consortium was meeting, that one way of helping India to meet its requirements for aid was to postpone its debt payments for this year which amounted to $450 million. Of the ten countries involved, the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, along with the World Bank, agreed to postpone India's obligations for this year. There was no word as to what concessions other creditors had made. This is hardly a good example of equitable burden sharing.

Section 210(a) suggests that multilateral programs would result in "greater encouragement of self-help performance." This is, at best, dubious. The multilateral lending institutions have paid attention to planning of programs and feasibility of projects. Where their own hard currency resources were at stake, they have paid due attention to prospects for repayment. But it is not clear that there is a sufficient appreciation of the role which private investment can play in the development process. Unless our representatives in such institutions or our

1967 

representatives in the various multilateral programs take a strong stand for this so important aspect of self-help, it may well be disregarded. 

Finally, Section 210(a) provides: 

"Accordingly, it is the sense of the Congress that wherever practicable development assistance should be administered by multilateral lending institutions or other international organizations, including such mechanisms as consortia and consultative groups consisting of representatives of the less developed country and of donor nations for the purpose of planning levels and terms of aid, coordinating and administering multi-donor projects and generally coordinating assistance programs to the recipient country." (Emphasis supplied.)

Such language suggests the possibility that U.S. bilateral aid funds would again be turned over to multilateral lending institutions for use outside the conditions set forth in this Act. It is therefore recommended that the language of 

Section 210(a) should be amended by striking "should be administered by" and "and administering" and inserting in the first instance "should be coordinated with"; by deleting "generally coordinating assistance programs to the recipient country," and adding "provided that funds authorized and appropriated under this Act shall be administered according to its provisions.' 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE AND THE U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

The U.S. balance of payments deficits continue to be a serious and vexing problem. Thanks to the cooperation of private business and banking, under the voluntary restraint programs, the total U.S. deficit for 1966 was held to $1.4 billion compared with $1.3 billion in 1965 and $2.8 billion in 1964. However, even with the effectiveness of these restraint programs, the relatively small deficit was the result of unusually favorable, short-term and reversible factors. 

Without these factors the deficit would have been in the $3-4 billion range. The goal of the Administration is to eliminate the deficit, and the necessary increase in dollar expenditures in Vietnam makes this difficult to achieve. In addition to the increased outlays for military expenditures and economic aid to Vietnam, the inflationary pressures and general prosperity of the present U.S. economy caused imports in 1966 to rise by 19 percent, while exports rose only 11 percent. The total 

1966 trade surplus was $3.8 billion compared with $4.8 billion in 1965, and $6.7 billion in 1964. If aid-financed exports are excluded, then our commercial trade surplus in 1966 was negligible-only $0.5 billion. If imports continue to rise at a much faster pace than exports, the favorable U.S. trade surplus will diminish further, making it increasingly difficult to finance large government expenditures abroad. 

Despite the "tying" of U.S. bilateral aid and military offset sales, the deficits on the government account in the U.S. balance of payments have averaged about $3.4 billion a year over the 1960-1965 period, and preliminary estimates indicate that the government balance of payments deficit in 1966 was $3.9 billion (see 

Table 6). These figures exclude the proceeds from the sale of medium-term Ù.S. 

Government securities to foreign governments and debt prepayments of foreign governments, since these items are really techniques of financing the hardcore deficits resulting from U.S. Government activities abroad.
