It should be noted that considered together, all private transactions in the U.S. international accounts, including exports and imports, tourism, transportation services, bank loans, direct investments and the earnings thereon, have been in balance for a long time, and in most years have resulted in a slight surplus. 

These surpluses, however, have not been large enough since 1949 (except for 1957) to overcome the deficits in the government account. 

Total recorded balance of payments relationships by major areas of the world indicate that the United States has been in approximate balance or surplus in most recent years with Europe, including all of the expenditures for imports, bank loans, portfolio investments, direct investments, shipping, tourism, and other services.

However, the United States has been in deficit in its recorded transactions with Asia including Japan, Africa, South America, and international institutions. 

The countries of Western Europe have been earning surpluses not in their trade and financial dealings directly with the United States, but from their trade and investment income in Asia, South America, and Africa. These are the areas where the United States is experiencing balance of payments deficts. These are also the places where the United States is spending the largest amounts for military presence and foreign aid.

The total government account outflows, which averaged about $8 billion a year, include military expenditures, foreign aid, Food for Peace shipments, relief and other government expenditures abroad. These sizable expenditures, which were only partially offset by the value of "tied" exports under foreign aid, P. L. 480, and the sale of military hardware, increased to $9.5 billion in 1966 as a result of 

Vietnam. The Government's foreign accounts have, therefore, fallen consistently short of being in balance and threaten to get worse.

The total U.S. foreign aid spending request for fiscal year 1968 is $5.6 billion, excluding military assistance to Vietnam, Thailand and Laos, and a probable further contribution to IDA of an unspecified amount (see Table 7). We are convinced that "tying" bilateral aid to U.S. procurement has not eradicated the substantial adverse balance of payments effect of aid disbursements. 

The "substitution" of credit sales for cash sales resulting from "program" loans to Latin America, the Near East, and South Asian areas is an acute problem. 

Program loan commitments in FY 1966 amounted to $1.6 billion, as compared to only $0.4 billion for capital projects. A "program" or balance of payments loan permits the recipient country to use aid funds to purchase U.S. commodities in an approved classification of goods. In the absence of foreign aid, many of these products, however, would have been bought with dollars the country already owned. "Tied" assistance thus enables the aid-receiving country to use the aid funds to pay for ordinary commercial procurement from the United States and to transfer its earned dollars for purchases in other countries. This is what is meant by the substitution effect of "tied" economic assistance.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE AND U.S. TRADE 

An examination of net nonmilitary assistance and the U.S. trade balance with selected countries, which have received between 50 and 60 percent of total U.S. aid for the years 1958-1965,2 shows clearly that total net U.S. economic assistance exceeded our trade surpluses with these selected countries by an amount fluctuating between $1.3 and $1.7 billion a year (see Table 8).

ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1967 

In 1958, U.S. net economic assistance to these 25 countries amounted to $1.8 billion and the U.S. trade surplus with them was only $251 million, leaving a difference of about $1.5 billion. It is important to note that in 1965, when U.S. economic assistance was substantially "tied" to U.S. procurement, the difference between the U.S. trade surplus ($0.9 billion) and U.S. economic assistance ($2.5 billion) with these 25 countries, remained at about the same level-$1.6 billion. Thus, it is clear that, though "tied" aid has resulted in increased U.S. exports and a larger U.S. trade surplus with these countries, there remains a substantial difference between U.S. economic assistance and the U.S. trade surplus. This is fairly conclusive evidence that "tied" aid does not end the adverse effects of foreign aid upon the U.S. balance of payments. 

In Latin America the case is quite clear. Total Latin American imports from all sources were up $548 million on an average during the years 1961-1965, compared with the 1956-1960 period (see Table 9). Between these two periods, however, total Latin American imports from the United States were down by an average of $8 million. This occurred in spite of the fact that total U.S. bilateral aid disbursements almost doubled from an average of $367 million during 19561960 to an average of $655 million during 1961-1966, and were on an increasingly "tied" basis; in spite of additional dollar disbursements of $587 million by the 

Inter-American Development Bank; and in spite of increased Latin American export earnings in the United States by an average of $267 million per year over the average for the 1956-1960 period.

Factual analysis of aid and trade for the three "program" loan countries in Latin America-Brazil, Chile and Colombia-indicates a substantial amount of substitution. 

In the case of Brazil, the U.S. share of total imports averaged 31.4 percent between 1955 and 1960, before tied aid; after tying, it has averaged 32.2 percent. 

The estimated export gain from tying aid between 1961 and 1965 has been only $60 million (see Table 10), while the balance of payments cost of aid has been $720 million over this period. 

In the case of Chile, the U.S. market share before tying averaged 48.8 percent; after tying it dropped to an average of 37.8 percent in spite of the large increases in disbursements under the Alliance for Progress. There has been an actual export loss in spite of tying aid of $322 million from 1961 to 1965, and a total adverse balance of payments cost of $630 million (see Table 11). 

A similar situation exists in Colombia (see Table 12), where our market share has dropped in spite of increased aid on a tied basis. Here again there has been an export loss of $107 million in spite of tied aid and a total balance of payments cost of $259 million. 

It is our understanding that various Departments in the U.S. Government are making assiduous efforts to insure additionality for U.S. exports under our aid programs. We hope that these efforts will bear fruit. It seems to us, however, that the best way of assuring "additionality" would be to emphasize the transfer of real resources for specific projects which would not exist in the absence of such aid. 77-470-67-pt. 4- -9

U.S. AID MUST BE IN REAL RESOURCES FOR PROJECTS 

In the light of these facts, the Association's position is that the U.S. aid program must be reoriented to a basis of providing real resources-U.S. goods and technical services for specific incremental projects. "Program" assistance should be phased out as quickly and as completely as possible. Local costs of approved projects must be financed by the recipient governments from local revenues, not dollars. 

In those instances where excess local currencies are available from P.L. 480, Title I sales, they should be utilized for payment of local costs of projects. In this way, the problem of substitution could be substantially eliminated. 

In order to achieve this transition, we recommend the following amendments to the authorizing sections for Development Loans and Alliance for Progress 

Loans: 

A. Subsection (a) of Section 201 is amended to read as follows: 

"Section 201 General Authority-(a) The President shall establish a fund to be known as the 'Development Assistance Fund' to be used by the President to furnish assistance pursuant to the authority contained in this Title." 

Subsection (b) of Section 201 should be amended by striking out the first sentence and substituting the following language: "(b) The President is authorized to make available, on credit, by purchase in the United States, any commodities, raw materials and capital equipment produced, grown or extracted in the United States and/or technical assistance from the United States for specific projects to promote the economic development of less developed countries and areas with emphasis upon assisting projects contained in a coherent, balanced, long-range economic development program. 

Credits extended under the authority of this Title are to be payable as to principal and interest in United States dollars on such terms and conditions as the President may determine; provided that, in no case shall the length of such dollar credits exceed 25 years, or be utilized to pay for the local labor costs connected with such projects." 

B. Subsection (a) of Section 251 is amended by striking out the last sentence and substituting the following language: "The President is authorized to make available, on credit, by purchase in the United States, any commodities, raw materials and capital equipment produced, grown or extracted in the United States and/or technical assistance from the United States for specific projects to promote the economic development of countries and areas in Latin America with emphasis upon assisting projects contained in a coherent, balanced, long-range economic development program. 

Credits extended under the authority of this Title, whether payable as to principal and interest in United States dollars or in local currencies of the recipient country, are to be upon such terms and conditions as the President may determine; provided that, in no case shall the length of such credits exceed 25 years or be utilized for local labor costs connected with such projects." 

We must begin to tailor our aid programs to the existing U.S. balance of payments position. This does not necessarily mean that we must decrease the total amount of U.S. aid but it does mean that aid must take a form that does not have an adverse impact upon the U.S. balance of payments. We have made these suggestions before. The State Department has not seen fit to accept them, and the balance of payments deficits have continued unabated. As things stand, we are financing a good part of our aid by borrowing abroad and selling gold. There is a limit to our ability to help shore up other countries' balance of payments at the expense of our own, lest an international financial crisis overtake us. This is why I persist in opposing program loans, and recommend that we devise new administrative techniques to emphasize real resources transfers. 

TERMS FOR EXTENDING DEVELOPMENT LOANS AND ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS LOANS The present authority in Sections 201 and 253 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1967 permits the President to make loans "payable as to principal and interest in United States dollars" on such terms and conditions as he may determine. 

The only restriction imposed is that on interest rates set forth in Section 201(d). 

In actual practice, the AID Agency and its predecessor agencies have extended loans on terms generally between 30 and 40 years' duration, with up to 10 years of grace period. The charge is usually one percent during the grace period and 

22 percent thereafter, as required by Section 201(d). 

The Association feels that Congress should impose a statutory limit of 25 years on all Development Loans, including Alliance for Progress Loans. The Associa tion's position is based upon the reality that political leaders of less developed

1967 

countries, faced with a present crisis, may not be too sensitive or aware of the difficulties of repayment of loans over a 30or 40-year period. We believe that a 

25-year term would create a greater sense of responsibility in the recipient government towards the economic utilization of dollar aid funds. There may be countries which are in such poor financial condition that they could not reasonably accept loans on such terms. In such cases it would be preferable to be straightforward and make grants. We recommend that a portion of the funds appropriated should be available for grants to meet such cases but only on the condition that other aid-giving countries provide funds in the same way. 

The United States is practically the only country that gives loans of more than 30 years' duration (ref. Table 2). The vast majority of other OECD countries' bilateral aid is in the form of loans anywhere from 7 to 20 years. The French, who are not reluctant to acclaim their magnanimity in giving over one percent of their gross national product as aid, grant most of this aid to former colonies as supplier credits and "technical assistance." Very little is on soft terms, without a "quid pro quo." 

It is clear that most other countries make capital available for shorter periods and on much harder terms than the United States. This dispels the frequent assertion that some European countries contribute a larger percentage of their gross national product to foreign aid than the United States. The comparison is not valid. Their contribution is still mainly in the form of commercial investment rather than foreign aid as we understand the term. 

There is no quick way of remedying this situation. The U.S. Government has made continuing and diligent efforts to get the other OECD countries to extend more aid at lower interest rates and at longer terms than 5, 10, or 15 years. 

Only Canada has responded generously to the effort. Both France and Germany have hardened their terms. Our Association urges the Government to continue working through the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) of the OECD and by direct diplomatic representation to seek to coordinate and share with the other OECD countries the burden of economic aid to developing countries. If the United States works in the proposed multilateral programs on this basis, it should make clear how our 40-year low interest loans have disguised the debt burden problem and allowed other countries to continue to make hard loans or investments. Here we can begin to share the burden. Better we raise the debt burden issue directly in this fashion by hardening the terms of our loans, even if we have to work out a rescheduling of debt with all other lenders on equitable terms, than go on providing the funds which make possibly the repayment of the investments of other developed countries with little net benefit to the aidreceiving country.

We feel that the whole problem of aid to the developing countries could be more equitably, efficiently and effectively handled if specific requirements of less developed countries, in terms of capital goods for specific projects and related technical services and general technical assistance, were presented to the OECD. 

These requests could then be allocated among the developed member countries of the OECD on the basis of capacity to produce and willingness to finance. Hopefully, aid would be extended by the participating OECD countries on comparable terms. If we cannot yet do this through the OECD for assistance generally, we might make a beginning through the multilateral programs proposed in this bill. 

On our part, we would change the wording of the authorizing sections of the Foreign Assistance Act, as recommended above, to furnish only real goods and services for specific projects, instead of money. This should help persuade other countries that there is no future in their expectation that continuing balance of payments loans on soft terms by the United States will continue to favor the repayment of their hard loans, and they may come around to our view. 

TWO-YEAR AUTHORIZATION FOR THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

All the Titles and Sections of the proposed bill are for two years covering fiscal years 1968-1969. If Congress approves the bill in its prsesent form, there will be no need for the managers of the program to appear next year before the House 

Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations Committees to justify the author ization. The appropriation requests could be submitted directly to the House and 

Senate Appropriations Committees. These Committees, as a matter of Congressional rule and tradition, do not ordinarily review policy issues. Thus, the public would be foreclosed from its only forum in Congress to express its views and observations on the administration of foreion aid. 

The argument, so often raised, that this is the only way to achieve long-range planning, is overemphasized. The United States has been extending foreign

823 assistance around the world since 1945-$79 billion in economic assistance and $34 billion in military assistance over the 1946-1965 period (see Table 13). Is it a reasonable conclusion that the United States will suddenly, unilaterally, and capriciously terminate assistance? We think not. The historical facts refute the contention that long-range planning cannot be done on an annual authorization and appropriation basis. Each of the major recipients of assistance has a development plan and these have been funded each year. The nine wise men and CIAP proceed to their review and appraisal of Latin American plans regularly and reasonable means are found to fund those which can be justified. There has been much comment in Congress about the difficulties and continual controversy attendant on the annual review of foreign aid. Responsibility and often irksome work are the price of power, and having been elected and entrusted with the power of making laws and spending the public's money, Congress should not shirk the responsibility of frequent review of programs. We therefore recommend that the principle of annual authorizations and review should be continued.

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed, sir.

Mr. DANIELIAN. It is always a pleasure, Mr. Chairman, to appear before this committee which has the responsibility to review the administration's conduct of foreign policy. 

I have with me here Mr. William Moran, vice president and executive director of our organization. Mr. Moran has extensive experience in the foreign aid field having had responsible positions in Europe and Africa. He has just recently returned from a trip to South America. 

And Mr. Best, senior economist, whose specialty is in the balance-ofpayments field. He has worked in this area in the Treasury Department. I want to acknowledge my obligation to them in the preparation of the statement.

I submit herewith a detailed factual presentation of our views on the Foreign Assistance Act for the record and trust the members of

1967 

this committee will find it useful in their deliberations. In the interest of brevity I will present here a summary of the major recommendations contained in that statement. 

Year after year we take great pains in making a thorough analysis of the provisions and administration of the various foreign assistance programs presented to Congress. It is only human sometimes to wonder whether this extensive effort has been worth undertaking. 

Such a review establishes the fact beyond doubt that both the Congress and the Executive have been both cooperative and responsive. For this we thank you.

Just last year we strongly recommended to the House and Senate Committees on Agriculture the inclusion of specific self-help criteria in the food-for-peace legislation. For a while administration spokesmen were dubious about being specific and opposed this proposal. Nevertheless, the Congress did include the specific criteria. Before the year was out the administration was citing these very provisions and putting them to good use. We are delighted to see this acceptance of the concept of self-help.

We have strongly supported section 620(e), the Hickenlooper amendment, even though the administration has at times worried about the possible adverse reaction of sensitive AID-receiving countries. 

Despite those reservations, that section has served us well. Except for countries under Communist dominations, there has been little action to expropriate or even threat to expropriate American private investment since it became a part of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

This is progress. 

In 1963 we proposed the inclusion in the act of section 620(1) providing for termination of aid to countries which did not enter into an agreement to institute the investment guaranty program. This was resisted by the administration but it too became law. Again, the fears of the administration were not realized; rather a number of countries entered into agreement and found that the guaranty program was instrumental in bringing about substantial new private investment to their own advantage. We have, from the beginning, been in favor of a strong program of guaranties of private investments. In earlier years. this program was given little importance or attention. Now, however, it has proved its efficiency and is getting the recognition and strong support it deserves-witness the fact that the administration itself is recommending an increase in the limit of coverage to $9 billion, which we support.

Since 1963 we have called attention to the fact that merely tying aid; that is, requiring procurement in the United States, was not adequate to prevent adverse effects on our balance of payments because of the substitution of aid procurement for commercial transactions which would have occurred in any event. We have pressed for the concept of "additionality," which is to say that aid should give rise to new procurement in the United States in addition to that which could otherwise be expected, thus avoiding adverse effects on our balance of payments. We are glad to note that the Treasury Department accepts this idea and is pushing for it. So far, it seems to have gotten a better reception in the Inter-American Development Bank than in AID, but we are moving in the right direction. 

In 1959 the then Senate majority leader, Mr. Johnson, proposed an amendment to the Mutual Security Act which would provide the

825 President with a special education and training fund. He advocated also an inter-American educational foundation. I strongly supported this idea in my testimony before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee since our association has consistently recommended greater attention to education in our AID programs. The proposal was adopted as section 412 of the Mutual Security Act of 1959 but was repealed by section 204 (k) of the 1960 act at the request of the State Department. What a pity that was. We have come full circle with the recent summit agreement at Punta del Este where provision was made for the very sort of activity proposed in 1959. We shall, of course, strongly support proposals for increased emphasis on education. 

These few examples, and there are many more, reassure me that a useful function is served in making and presenting objective studies of this program, even though at times it does not appear to be the most popular thing to do. It is this belief which causes me to appear before you each year with the hope that further progress may be made.

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT THROUGH PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

In 1963, by specific votes on the floor of the House, amendments were adopted to sections 202 and 252 to provide that "Not less than 50 per centum of the funds appropriated... shall be available for loans made to encourage economic development through private enterprise." We have waited 4 years for this provision to be effectively administered. I am sorry to have to report that this provision of law is being honored only in the breach. The Department of State contends that aid expenditures on almost anything-roads, power, education and health, public works-meet this requirement since they provide the underpinning for private enterprise. As a result of this rather farfetched interpretation, of the $2.9 billion provided to Latin America since 1961, only $425 million, or less than 15 percent, has been used to fund intermediate credit institutions and cooperatives so that they could relend to the private sector. Looking at the worldwide program, Mr. Salzman, Assistant Administrator for AID, testified before this committee on April 18 that AID has made loans of $617 million for intermediate credit institutions since 1961, compared with total AID loans to the world of $6.3 billion during fiscal years 1962 through 

1966. He also mentioned that dollar loans to private American and local ventures are available through AID and five such loans for private industrial projects were made in 1966 in the total amount of $13.9 million. None of these activities adds up to anything like the statutory requirement that 50 percent of the funds provided for development assistance and the Alliance for Progress should be employed through private enterprise.

I want to make it clear that we are not here referring to supporting assistance to countries such as Vietnam. 

It is my recollection that at the time of the conference between the House and the Senate, spokesmen for the administration tried to change the working to read "to private enterprise," but members of this committee stood firm on the words "through private enterprise." For those who were so sensitive to the semantic nuances of that one word "through" instead of "to" not to understand the significance of the difference, and to disregard it in administration, shows less regard for congressional intent than we, as citizens, like to see.

1967 

The purpose of the provisions cited was to assure that at least half of the loan funds appropriated should be devoted to those private enterprise activities which provide production and jobs. Clearly, the program has not been administered in such a fashion as to achieve this desired result. Therefore, we hope that the committee will give appropriate expression to its determination that the law must be observed and that 50 percent of the funds provided for development loans and the Alliance for Progress must be used directly for development through private enterprise.

In mentioning private enterprise I want to make certain that it is meant to mean local enterprises as well as foreign enterprise. 

This might best be accomplished by requiring that such funds be used for the development and funding of credit institutions for relending to the private sector and for the creation of institutions such as development finance corporations on a national as well as a regional basis, which would seek out and promote private, productive enterprise. Such funds should be available not only for capital development, but also for the working capital needs of private business. We are pleased to note that AID Administrator Gaud has instructed under date of February 10 his field personnel to give priority to private contractors in the execution of programs. Let us also allocate the statutory limit of funds in the private sector. 

We hope to encourage local private firms, as well as foreign. And we believe we will get more economic development per dollar of investment of U.S. taxpayers' money, with greater speed, and with better chance of repayment, than than government-to-government transactions. 

SELF-HELP CRITERIA 

The President's insistence on self-help as a condition for receiving U.S. assistance is welcome, and we support it, as are the self-help criteria in section 208. Foreign aid can be effective only if the receiving countries help themselves. However, despite the recognition given the importance of private foreign investment in section 601, these criteria do not adequately indicate the steps aid recipients should take in promoting private initiative, domestic, and foreign. We realize that the U.S. Congress cannot legislate domestic policies for other countries. On the other hand, since so much of public funds is being appropriated for economic development, the Congress, as representatives of the public, is entitled to express its views as to how this can be achieved and the taxpayers' money used productively. Congressional expressions have great influence: They are read by other governments; they ought to be read by administrators of the programs both here and abroad. They set guidelines of policy which, over a period of time, when administered with subtlety and discretion, may even be accepted by reasonable leaders of other countries. Sometimes, as in the case of India, we may have to insist on their acceptance lest the situation deteriorate into economic chaos. 

For these reasons we recommend that section 208(b) should be amended to call specifically on these governments to create a favorable climate for private enterprise and investment through- (1) Providing for maximum private ownership and initiative in new as well as existing industry, including manufacturing, financing, distribution, and merchandising;

827 (2) Assuring nondiscriminatory treatment between national and nonnational, and between public and private, enterprises and products; (3) Providing for unrestricted remittance of amortization of at investment, interest, and dividend payments; (4) Providing adequate protection for industrial property rights; and (5) Enacting tax laws with rates of taxation designed to promote optimum utilization of private investment capital, both foreign and domestic.

Such an amendment was accepted by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee last year, but was eliminated in conference. In view of the very great use the President has been able to make with a similar set of provisions in the food-for-freedom legislation, we beseech this committee to give him as useful guidelines these parallel provisions in the Foreign Assistance Act. 

CONTINUING GUARANTEE PROGRAM AFTER TERMINATION OF ASSISTANCE 

The Hickenlooper amendment, section 620(e), provides for the termination of assistance when a country expropriates the property of, or nullifies a contract with, a U.S. citizen, and fails to make restitution of full value within a specified period. 

The present bill proposes to amend section 638 so as to provide that when assistance is terminated this will not apply to the investment guarantee program. It is inappropriate that the United States should continue to issue guarantees of investments in a country when assistance has been terminated under section 620(e) for expropriation. It is, therefore, recommended that the proposed amendment to section 

638 should be deleted.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEE PROGRAM 

The investment guarantee program, which we have long supported, has proven to be quite useful. Amounts guaranteed under the program have risen from $1.5 billion at the end of December 1963 to $3.9 billion at the end of December 1966.

The new act proposes to include protection for losses arising from "civil strife," which is in line with our previous recommendations. 

It proposes to include provision for guarantees of 50 percent of equity investments under the specific risk guarantee program. It also proposes an increase in the authorization for guarantees from $7 billion to $9 billion. We support all of these proposals. We also note that AID last year reduced the premium for combined specific risk guarantee coverage from 1½ percent to 1% percent. We shall continue to advocate this. There is already nearly $40 million in accumulated premiums and the annual fees are estimated at $10 million in calendar 1967.

STAFFING TO PROMOTE PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

There is an urgent need for top level industrial experts at the ministerial level in our embassies abroad where we seek to promote economic development. They are needed to seek out prospects for private investments and help bring them to fruition under the private

1967 

enterprise provisions of sections 202 and 252 and through an even wider use of the investment guarantee program. The funds provided in section 222(b) should be available to meet the cost of such staffing. 

Certainly, this function of harnessing private investment to economic development is at least as important as government-to-government programs.

CHANNELING OF BILATERAL AID FUNDS THROUGH MULTILATERAL INSTITUTIONS 

We believe the Foreign Assistance Act should deal with the bilateral aid program and that authorizations for international agencies should be considered on their own merits. This position of our group is not based on any general opposition to multilateral institutions. We recognize that these international organizations have many advantages. However, where aid funds provided by this act are used in conjunction with international agencies, either directly or through consortia, the conditions applicable thereto should conform with the provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

We believe these are desirable conditions. We have, therefore, opposed, and continue to oppose, section 205 and section 251(h) of the Foreign Assistance Act, which give the President discretionary authority to transfer up to 10 percent of the funds appropriated for development loans and 15 percent of the funds appropriated for the 

Alliance for Progress to the International Development Association or other international lending institutions, to be used by them under their individual criteria and administrative rules and regulations rather than those governing U.S. bilateral aid programs. 

We should keep our bilateral and multilateral programs separate. 

If sections 205 and 251 (h) are continued, then they should specify that funds so allocated shall be subject to the provisions of the 

Foreign Assistance Act. 

MULTILATERAL PROGRAMS 

The idea of multilateral programs as a means of securing a more equitable sharing of the burden of aid, as proposed in the President's message, has much to recommend it. If such an approach gave hope of that result we would support it. We have some doubt that it will. 

Quantities of aid given by others are not comparable with U.S. aid because most other countries exact commercial rates of interest and lend for shorter periods. After years of effort, the burden of aid on easy terms still falls upon the United States. 

We have distinct reservations about the provisions proposed in section 210(a). This states it to be the sense of Congress "That wherever practicable development assistance should be administered by multilateral lending institutions or other international organizations. . 

Such language suggests the possibility that U.S. bilateral aid funds would again be turned over to multilateral lending institutions for use outside the constraints set forth in this act. It is therefore recommended that the language of section 210(a) should be amended by striking "should be adminstered by" and "and administering" and inserting in the first instance "should be coordinated with"; and by

829 deleting "generally coordinating assistance programs to the recipient country" and adding "provided that funds authorized and appropriated under this Act shall be adminstered according to its provisions." 

AID ON A REAL RESOURCE, NOT LINE-OF-CREDIT, BASIS 

The U.S. balance-of-payments deficits continue to be a serious and vexing problem. Despite the "tying" of U.S. bilateral aid and military offset sales, the deficits on the Government account in the U.S. balance of payments have averaged about $3.4 billion a year over the 1960-1965 period, and preliminary estimates indicate that the Government account balance-of-payments deficit in 1966 was $3.9 billion. 

The countries of Western Europe have been earning surpluses not in their trade and financial dealings directly with the United States, but from their trade and investment income in Asia, South America, and Africa. These are the areas where the United States is experiencing balance-of-payments deficits. These are also the places where the 

United States is spending the largest amounts for military presence and foreign aid.

The "substitution" of credit sales for cash sales resulting from "program" loans to Latin America, the Near East, and South Asian areas is an acute problem. A "program" or balance of payments loan permits the recipient country to use AID funds to purchase U.S. commodities in an approved classification of goods. In the absence of foreign aid many of these products would have been bought with dollars the country already owned. "Tied" assistance thus enables the aid-receiving country to use the AID funds for its customary commercial procurement from the United States and to transfer its earned dollars for purchases in other countries. This is what is meant by the substitution effect of "tied" economic assistance.

In the light of these facts, the association's position is that the U.S. aid program must be reoriented to a basis of providing real resources-U.S. goods and technical services-for specific incremental projects. "Program" assistance should be phased out as quickly and as completely as possible. Local costs of approved projects must be financed by the recipient governments from local sources, not dollars. 

In this way, the problem of substitution and the adverse effect of the foreign aid program on our balance of payments could be substantially eliminated. 

Sections 201 and 251 of the act should be amended in such a fashion as to require the provision of AID only in this way. 

TERMS FOR DEVELOPMENT LOANS AND ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS LOANS 

The present authority in sections 201 and 251 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1967 permits the President to make loans "payable as to principal and interest in United States dollars" on such terms and conditions as he may determine. The only restriction imposed is that on interest rates set forth in section 201(d). In actual practice the AID agency and its predecessors have extended loans on terms generally between 30 and 40 years' duration, with up to 10 years of grace period. The charge is usually 1 percent during the grace period and 2½ percent thereafter, as required by section 201 (d).

1967 

The association feels that Congress should impose a statutory limit of 25 years on all development loans, including Alliance for Progress loans. The association's position is based upon the reality that political leaders of less developed countries, faced with a present crisis, may not be too sensitive or aware of the difficulties of repayment of loans over a 30or 40-year period. We believe that a 25-year term would create a greater sense of responsibility in the recipient government toward the economic utilization of dollar aid funds. There may be countries which are in such poor financial condition that they could not reasonably accept loans on such terms. In such cases it would be preferable to be straightforward and make grants, and we would so recommend.

Most other countries make capital available for shorter periods and on much harder terms than the United States. There is no quick way of remedying this situation. The United States has made diligent efforts in the OECD to get other countries to extend more aid on easier terms. Only Canada has responded to this effort. We should also try to make clear that our long-term, low-interest loans, are used in large part to repay harder credits given by other countries, reducing the net amounts of new funds available to the receiving countries. 

When a soft loan makes it possible to repay a hard loan, whether from the World Bank or some foreign country, the recipient country does not have resources equal to the sum total of the hard loan and the soft loan. On the contrary, the real resources left in the country are the soft loans minus the hard loans, and minus the interest and commission paid on the hard loans. 

It is better that we should raise the debt burden issue directly in this fashion, by tightening up our terms, and then forming a rescheduling of debt with all other lenders on equitable terms, rather than go on providing the funds which make possible the repayment of the investments of other countries with little net benefit to the aidreceiving countries, and adverse effects on the U.S. balance of payments. A rescheduling of hard loans by other countries would indeed be an aid contribution. 

2-YEAR AUTHORIZATION FOR THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

All the titles and sections of the proposed bill are for 2 years covering fiscal years 1968-69. If Congress approves the bill in its present form there will be no need for the managers of the program to appear next year before the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations Committees to justify the authorization. Thus the public would be foreclosed from its only forum in Congress to express its views and observations on the administration of foreign aid. 

The long history of regular annual appropriations of large amounts for foreign assistance and the way in which so many countries have proceeded with long-range plans in anticipation of such help renders specious the argument that multiyear authorizations are necessary for planning. Burdensome as the annual review may be for the Congress, it is in the best interest of the United States and the foreign assistance program. We, therefore, recommend that the authorization be limited to the 1 year, fiscal 1968.

I know as few others how diligently the members of this committee work on problems which enhance the welfare and security of our

Our witness this morning is the Honorable Dean Rusk, Secretary of State. With Mr. Rusk is the Honorable William S. Gaud, Administrator, Agency for International Development, and Mr. Daniel

sir.

Mr. Secretary, you have a prepared statement and you may proceed, STATEMENT OF HON. DEAN RUSK, SECRETARY OF STATE 

Secretary RUSK. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and distinguished members of this committee. I do very much appreciate the opportunity of appearing before you in support of the President's economic and military assistance programs. 

Twenty years ago President Truman transmitted to the Congress a recommendation for funds to help reconstruct war-torn Europe. The 

Marshall plan was launched. President Truman called it "an investment toward the peace and security of the world and toward the realization of hope and confidence in a better way of life for the future ***" This creative act of statesmanship accomplished everything that President Truman had hoped. Within a comparatively few years free Europe became economically strong and politically stable. 

The focus of our foreign assistance programs has long since shifted from Europe to the less developed countries, but our purposes are basically the same. Our programs today, as they were 20 years ago, are "an investment toward the peace and security of the world * * *"

The job that we are trying to do today is much more complex than it was during the Marshall plan. The task today is the building of viable societies in the less developed countries, not merely the rebuilding of temporarily shattered and advanced economies, as in Europe. 

The dominant facts of life in the developing countries are impatience, unrest and, above all, rapid change. Men see widening alternatives and expansive futures. Disillusionment must not follow. Frustrated so- 835

1967 

cieties lack stability; they are prey to subversion and aggression; they themselves are sometimes hostile and aggressive. We must help to encourage the dynamic elements of the new societies to address themselves to constructive tasks of economic, social, and political progress. 

In most developing countries, the obstacles to steady progress are formidable. In varying degrees, these countries lack the technology and managerial experience which are the basic tools of the economically advanced nations. They lack the foreign exchange needed to invest in their futures. And often they lack the sound policies, institutions and laws needed to modernize rapidly. 

It is important that we and the other economically advanced countries share with the less developed countries our technological knowledge and our experience in organizing complex economic and social enterprises. It is important that we and others provide some financial assistance. 

The United States has and has had a strong commitment to foreign aid and the job that we, other developed nations, and the less developed nations have to do together. Last year the Congress expressed this commitment by authorizing development loans and the Alliance for Progress through fiscal year 1969. This year the President has requested similar authorizations for all other Foreign Assistance Act programs. I urge this committee and the Congress to authorize all economic and military assistance programs through fiscal year 1969. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Secretary McNamara has appeared before the committee to discuss with you the proposed military assistance program; and other witnesses, including the Assistant Secretaries of State responsible for the geographic regions concerned, have discussed with you how these programs support the foreign policy and the defense interests of the 

United States.

I should like at this time to state my conviction that this programfor which the President is requesting $596 million in new appropriations for fiscal year 1968-is the minimum necessary to support the foreign policy of our country. 

It will be used primarily for these purposes: 

To strengthen the ability of friendly nations adjacent to the Soviet Union or Communist China to meet external military threats; 

To help developing nations protect themselves against internal violence and thereby provide the stability that is essential to development; and 

To provide essential military help to four or five countries so that their development programs will not be paralyzed by military requirements. 

The military assistance program is a necessary complement to the economic assistance program; and it is a small insurance policy against the growth of situations around the world which might require far greater commitments of our resources, perhaps even including our military manpower.

I fully support the proposed transfer of military assistance programs for Laos, Thailand, NATO infrastructure and international

837 5 military headquarters from the military assistance accounts to the regular Defense Department budget. By mutual agreement with Secretary McNamara, the Department of State will continue, as in the past, to coordinate these programs with our overall political and economic interests in each area.

I strongly urge approval of the military assistance program for fiscal year 1968.

ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE 

Over the past years both the Congress and the Executive have learned a good deal about the development process and the role the United States can and should play in it. The legislation and program before this committee reflect that experience. 

The less developed countries hold in their own hands the keys to their own future. It is their efforts-not ours or those of other donor countries that will open the doors to better lives for their peoples. 

That is why we insist on self-help. This is not just because it is important that the taxpayer's dollar yield a dollar's worth of return, but for the deep humanitarian reason that without self-help the job cannot be done. I have said to this committee on a number of occasions that this central point ought to be obvious because external help runs in the neighborhood of up to 2 percent, in some cases more, of the gross national product of the receiving country. Although the 2 percent can be important, what happens to the 98 percent will determine whether the needs of the peoples of the receiving country will be met. 

As Mr. Gaud mentioned when he appeared before this committee on 

April 5, the legislation before you emphasizes the importance of selfhelp in a number of ways, including authorization for a National 

Advisory Committee on Self-Help. 

There have been remarkable adjustments in the AID program to reflect our balance-of-payments problems. In fiscal year 1959 only 40 percent of AID funds were spent for U.S. goods and services. In fiscal year 1968 it is estimated that 87 percent of AID expenditures will be for American goods and services and that the net adverse impact of the program on the U.S. balance of payments will be about $107 million. 

The United States must continue to watch carefully its balance of payments. That is why the AID program today transfers U.S. skills and commodities-not U.S. dollars-to the less developed countries. 

Governmental actions are important, but without private sector support the job cannot be done. That is why the AID program works both with and through American private enterprise and other private organizations in helping to build strong private sectors in the developing countries.

We cannot do everything everywhere. The job is too big. That is why we concentrate our programs in a few key countries and on a few key problems-agriculture, education, and health. 

The United States is not the only advanced country which recognizes its stake in development. Other developed nations now have strong aid programs. It is to our advantage to coordinate our program with theirs and to encourage them to enlarge their programs. That is why we prefer to provide most of our development loans in a multilateral framework.

Cooperation among the less developed countries themselves can lead to faster progress. Many of them face the same challenges; and

1967 

1 by pooling resources and energies they will be better able to meet these challenges. That is why the United States actively encourages and supports regional efforts. The movement toward regionalism reflects the growing recognition among both advanced and developing countries of the necessity for economic and political interdependence. 

We are hopeful that the momentum of regional cooperation will be quickened in the next few years. 

One can anticipate, I think, some favorable and perhaps even some dramatic developments in Latin America and in the Far East in this direction.

These are the main principles of the proposed AID program and legislation. Mr. Gaud and others have discussed them in detail with you.

The President originally requested a total of $2.53 billion in new appropriations to carry out the proposed AID program for fiscal year 1968. In addition, as I have previously discussed with the committee, he plans to request an additional $100 million for the Alliance for Progress in connection with the recent summit conference. This would bring the total request for fiscal year 1968 to $2.63 billion. The $100 million, however, is included in the President's budget, and therefore the size of the Federal budget would not be increased by this request. 

This is a prudent request and takes into account the burdens resulting from the struggle in Vietnam. A strict and simple standard was applied to the AID budget: What is the minimum amount needed to serve our short-term security interests and to maintain the forward momentum in less developed countries that is essential to our long range security? The AID budget request reflects this approach. And it is worth noting that the fiscal year 1968 Foreign Assistance Act request, along with other foreign assistance requests such as Peace Corps, Public Law 480, and contributions to the International Development Association, total less than 0.7 percent of our GNP. By contrast, to think of another day, in 1949 economic assistance funds totaled nearly 3 percent of our gross national product. 

We know that time is short, and we must use it to our best advantage. If we have inadequate aid programs, if progress in most developing countries is not visible and continuous, we shall be living in a less stable and more threatening world. But time can be our ally, if we use our opportunities wisely to help build economic and social strength and political stability in the developing areas of the world. While setbacks in the developing countries have occurred, and will occur, there is ground for encouragement. 

In Latin America the Alliance for Progress, now 6 years old, is in some ways a touchstone of our efforts in the less developed areas of the world.

We know the perils to our own security of economic or political instability and social injustice in Latin America. While the Castro regime in Cuba has made a mockery of the aspirations of the Cuban people, it continues to be a reminder of the urgency of our common tasks in Latin America. Castro-supported subversion and insurgency have been quashed in a number of countries. But recent outbreaks in 

Venezuela and Bolivia indicate a continuing potential for disorder and violence, which warns against apathy. In the Dominican Republic we are working now to help repair a legacy of injustice and inaction and potential outside threat.

839 There is increasing evidence that the Alliance is taking hold and that most Latin American nations are making healthy strides toward stability and future self-sufficiency. In all but a few, governments are now working to meet the needs of all the people. Much has been done to improve tax structures and tax administration, to fight inflation, and to strengthen institutions required for more productive private enterprise. A start has been made to expand education and health facilities, and a number of countries have instituted far-ranging agricultural and land reforms. Of course, much remains to be done. 

The recent meeting of Presidents in Uruguay expressed an understanding of the tasks ahead. The summit conference not only reaffirmed the basic tenets of the Alliance for Progress, but placed new emphasis on accelerated progress in the vital areas of agriculture, health, education, and science. It also made a historic decision to undertake the economic integration of the countries of Latin 

America. 

Long before the summit, President Johnson said, "We are ready to work in close cooperation toward an integrated Latin America. To my fellow Presidents I pledge: Move boldly along this path and the

United States will be at your side." At long last, a concrete commitment to a continental common market has been set in motion. A timetable and technical procedures for moving ahead have been agreed upon. This is a very important milestone. 

I am confident that discussions at the summit will lead to a greatly increased number of regional development projects in Latin America. 

With the cooperation of the Inter-American Development Bank, we will support some of these promising initiatives. The future of Latin 

America depends to a considerable degree on the growth of effective multinational projects-transportation and communication links, educational and training centers, joint industrial ventures, and frontier and river basin development projects. 

I am glad to take the opportunity of thanking this committee and the House of Representatives for the nonpartisan support of the President through the resolution adopted by the House prior to the summit conference. I assure you that it was much appreciated and was helpful in our deliberations at Punta del Este. 

Because of the interest of this committee and the enactment last year of title IX of the Foreign Assistance Act, our attention is more clearly focused on the creation and growth of local institutions, both private and public, to promote democratic participation in economic, Social, and political development. There already have been some notable achievements. In the last 2 years, for example, in Central America alone, more than 479 credit unions were organized, with 76,000 members. The recent local municipal elections in Peru were the first held in the last 40 years. As the committee knows, and as the Presidents of the hemisphere clearly recognized at Punta del Este, people with a personal stake in a nation's progress will work toward responsible and effective government. Those nations will move quickest who rely on expanding sources of local initiative. 

A number of Latin American countries are particularly well placed to influence favorably the future course of the Alliance. Brazil, for example, is so large that its performance strongly influences events in the rest of the hemisphere. Some countries such as Mexico and Vene-

1967 

zuela, are now in a position to lend a hand to their neighbors in speeding their development. The Central American countries are setting the pace in economic integration.

Our largest program in Latin America is for Brazil. Its land mass is larger than the continental United States, and its people comprise onehalf of all South Americans. A healthy Brazil is essential to a prospering Alliance. In the last 3 years, the drive to stabilize Brazil's economy and curb the inflation which had distorted national life for many years has achieved a measure of success. The annual rate of inflation has dropped from a peak of 140 percent in early 1964 to the current level of about 25 to 30 percent. Our large fiscal year 1968 aid program will help a new government to sustain improvement in agriculture, housing, and health, while stemming continuous inflationary pressures. 

The countries of the Near East and South Asia are more distant, but hardly less important than those in Latin America to the establishment of a reliable and durable peace. For this reason, I regard economic assistance to these countries as a vital necessity. 

We are pleased that the three major aid recipients there-India, Pakistan, and Turkey-have increasingly turned their great talents to the domestic challenges of modernization. These three countries will get about 90 percent of fiscal year 1968 development assistance planned for this region.

Excepting only Vietnam, the India program is our largest economic aid program, although we provide less than half of India's external aid. Members of the consortium for India have pledged over $6 billion for the third 5-year plan and the first year of the fourth plan-our share has been 42 percent. The efforts of the India consortium reflect not only India's great needs, but the supreme importance which all free nations attach to Indian strength and independence.

Indian development efforts are sharply focused on the food and population problem. Over 40 percent of the proposed AID funds will be used to help India improve food output. The Indian Government plans to double its outlays for agriculture over the next 5 years and to quadruple spending for family planning programs. Fertilizer purchases increased over 85 percent over the last year. Crash programs in farmland development have been initiated, and the supply of improved seeds and pesticides has been increased. I think it is imperative that we continue to give India the backing it requires in its days of difficulty.

We hope that India and Pakistan can find a way to achieve genuine cooperation in the subcontinent. Such cooperation would constitute a formidable bulwark of free world strength. Pakistan is on its way to realizing its potentials. Its economic performance has been very good. 

Our planned program for Pakistan is also one of our largest, although again our assistance is more than matched by others. 

The strategic importance of Turkey has been obvious for generations, poised as it is on the flanks of East Europe, Russia, and the Near East. Our large but declining level of economic assistance there is designed to facilitate the Turkish Government's goal of self-sustaining growth by 1973. Turkey's performance has been impressive. 

For example, in 1966 its GNP increased by over 8 percent, agricultural production went up 11 percent, and its foreign exchange earnings increased by over 15 percent.

841 Our sympathies run deep for African aspirations for more decent and plentiful lives. We fully realize the importance of Africa in our contemporary world. Its land mass is more than three times our own, and it holds 300 million people. It is rich in natural resources important to the international community. Its geographical location is pivotal. 

There continues to be political instability in Africa. Some 35 countries are experiencing the growing pains of new independence. In these formative years our help can be important in determining the type of societies that will develop in Africa and the role they will play in world affairs.

While we regard African developments with close attention, other advanced nations mainly, Great Britain and France-with long historical relations with Africa, have provided the most assistance, along with international institutions. AID's African program averages less than $200 million a year. Other U.S. programs, such as food for freedom and Peace Corps, bring our total share to about 25 percent of annual free world assistance to Africa. 

We have sought to make our aid in Africa more effective and efficient. In the last year, we have reexamined our approach to helping 

African nations and have recast our AID policies and programs in Africa along lines which will emphasize regional projects and multilateral participation, and will reduce the number of African countries with bilateral AID programs. I understand that State Department and AID witnesses have appeared before you and testified extensively on the details of this approach. In brief, AID has regular bilateral development assistance programs in 34 countries in Africa in the current fiscal year.

Under the new policy, AID will continue bilateral programs-coordinated in most cases with other donors-in 10 African countries: 

Nigeria, Tunisia, Morocco, Sudan, Ghana, Ethiopia, Liberia, and the three countries of east Africa: Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. In other

African countries, as existing activities are completed over the next few years, AID expects to shift most assistance to regional and multilateral projects and reduce the number of bilateral programs substantially. An indispensable part of this policy will be our continued use of a modest self-help fund in each country for short-term, high-impact projects. 

The reduction of programs must be gradual to avoid the waste involved in stopping technical assistance projects that are only partially completed or in not going ahead with development loans that have reached an advanced stage of joint planning. We need flexibility to carry out this policy and achieve our foreign policy objectives. For these and other important reasons I do not think it is wise to impose arbitrary ceilings on the number of countries eligible for aid. For example, if one wishes to render assistance to some 500 million people in India one can deal with one government. If one wishes to render assistance to 500 million people in all of Latin America and Africa combined one must take into account the fact that there are 55 or 60 governments in those two areas. 

This new aid policy should prove effective in serving both our interests and the development needs of the Africans. If adjustments in the policy prove necessary, we will make them. The Africans them-

1967 

selves recognize the need for multinational efforts to overcome the limitations of natural resources and boundaries. Nowhere is the idea of regional cooperation more relevant for achieving the commonly shared goal of a better future. We are encouraged by the progress initiated by the Africans in instituting the African Development Bank, which was conceived and organized and is capitalized entirely by Africans. We and other donors plan to provide help to a new special fund of the Bank. Regional development schemes should receive in fiscal year 1968 twice the funds that they received in fiscal year 1966. These include projects for agricultural production, disease control, regional training, and education.

In East Asia, Vietnam and her Southeast Asian neighbors are a most crucial battleground in the struggle for a durable world order. In 

Vietnam, it is necessary for us to meet our commitments because our commitments are the principal support for the structure of peace. We have sought repeatedly to bring the other side to the conference table, thus far without success. We must persist in all our efforts. As I have said before, our economic assistance programs, while smaller in scale, are as important as our military efforts in the achievement of our objectives. For fiscal year 1968 we plan to use $550 million. These funds will serve four vital purposes.

First, in a most literal sense, they will support the drive to build a viable nation, piece by piece, area by area, in which all the South Vietnamese may identify themselves with national purposes and national programs to achieve security and order. Our aid helps with the task of reconstruction and development for the future and helps to sustain the morale of the South Vietnamese today. 

Second, another sizable portion of our funds will help maintain economic stability in the midst of the war. The commodity import program which we finance has dampened dangerous inflationary pressures.

Third, we conduct programs to relieve wartime suffering and dislocation. AID personnel and our military forces work in close partnership to cope directly with the human and material destruction of war. 

Fourth, we are building for the future, with a growing program of long-term development in electrical power, transportation, agriculture, medicine, and other fields.

Like the war itself, the conditions under which we conduct our economic assistance are most difficult. In 1965, rapidly increasing military expenditures threatened the South Vietnamese economy with crippling inflation which might well have undercut the whole military effort. Rather than risk this threat, we decided to expand quickly and sizably the AID commodity import program. We made this necessary decision knowing full well that for a while there would be some theft and diversion, and we would suffer enormous problems stemming from logistics limitations. 

AID simply did not have a large enough staff, at the time; there were not enough end-use inspectors or auditors, and it would take time to get them out to Vietnam; port facilities, storage and transportation facilities, and so on were at that time inadequate to the expansion of the import program. We knew all that at the time, and went ahead anyway, because, as I said, the only alternative was to risk the real threat of ruinous inflation. Thefts and diversions of goods, corruption,

843 and other serious dislocations are inevitable in some measure under wartime conditions.

But we have made important progress over the last year and particularly the last 6 months in overcoming these difficulties. We have placed some U.S. military in operational control of handling commodities in transit between port and warehouse; the AID mission has doubled its audit staff; it has instituted an automated accounting system; sent a U.S. Bureau of Customs team to assist the Vietnam 

Customs Office; and much more. We are keeping a close watch on all aspects of the aid program, and we are encouraged by the rapidly growing effectiveness of the necessary controls.

I believe that we are already witnessing the dividends of our stand in Vietnam. A few years ago, it was assumed by many in Southeast 

Asia and the western Pacific that mainland China was the wave of the future. Now, throughout all the free nations of east Asia we sense economic progress. They are also working together more and more effectively. 

Nowhere is the momentum of regional cooperation more evident than in East Asia and the western Pacific. The Asian Development 

Bank is now established and in business. Development of the Mekong 

Valley is proceeding despite the war. Throughout East Asia a variety of regional associations are taking root, all founded on a common interest to foster development in a climate of peace. Cooperative arrangments in education, agriculture, transportation, and communications are coming into existence rapidly. 

In Thailand and Laos, it is necessary to conduct substantial economic aid programs to thwart increased Communist subversion and insurgency. Other nations are helping. We expect that requirements for more conventional types of development assistance to Thailand over the next several years will be met by a combination of governments and international institutions. 

Korea is now growing at an annual rate of 8 percent and will likely repeat the gratifying economic and social successes already achieved in Taiwan. Both nations show what can be accomplished in a relatively few years. Dean Jacoby in his newly published study on Taiwan development has concluded that, while vigorous self-help efforts were the key to success, it would nonetheless have taken Taiwan as much as 40 years to achieve self-supporting growth, not 15, without substantial American assistance.

Indonesia is now at the start of this journey, and the new government is committed to addressing the energies of the Indonesian people to the problems of internal construction. We are prepared to support sound stabilization and development programs along with other governments and international agencies.

Mr. Chairman, this is my seventh formal appearance before your committee to seek your authorization of foreign aid.

There is involved here a fundamental issue in our relations with the rest of the world, particularly with the struggling underdeveloped world. The economic growth and power of the United States are almost beyond comprehension. Our gross national product equals that of all of NATO and Japan combined; it is twice that of the Soviet 

Union, with the gap continuing to widen; it is 10 times that of Mainland China with its 700 million people; it is 10 times that of all of

1967 

Latin America. This year's defense budget of the United States equals the total gross national product of Latin America. If we are to be negligent about the needs of the rest of the world, we shall soon be in a position of a voracious nation calling upon the rest of the world to feed our own economy in order to widen the gap between us and all the rest. We cannot accept so stark a contrast between the future we would ask for ourselves and the future to which others can aspire. If we are not to become isolated by the choice of others, we must make it clear that we are prepared to engage in their problems, help to share their burdens and be ourselves a good citizen nation in the community of nations. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, for your attention. 

Mr. Secretary, before we ask questions, I want to tell the committee that it has always been customary for the Secretary to be our first witness to begin the hearings on foreign aid. This year he was delayed because of his busy schedule and has not been available until the latter part of the hearings.

If there are any questions you want to ask in executive session he will come back next week, or as soon as his schedule permits. 

Mr. Secretary, most of the presentation which has been submitted to the committee during the last several weeks has emphasized economic development and the long-range objectives of the U.S. foreign policy. Most of the members of the committee have been inclined to think of foreign aid as a tool to be used in the implementation of U.S. foreign policy rather than to relate it entirely to long-range economic development. 

Mr. Secretary, do you regard economic aid and military aid as important tools for use in dealing with immediate problems which confront the United States in various parts of the world? 

Secretary RUSK. I think, sir, that varies somewhat with the individual situation. Broadly speaking, I think it is fair to say, and I don't think this is just floating in the clouds, that the United States has a major national interest in the independence and safety of, say, the members of the United Nations.

Where you find a country that is secure from outside attack, willing to cooperate across its national frontiers with us and its own neighbors, and getting on with its internal job, there is a situation which broadly speaking is in the interest of the United States. It fits into that pattern of the world community that was written into the United Nations Charter at the end of the last war. So this is why we support the World 

Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the United Nations, and why we have some rather broad AID programs in different parts of the world.

In particular situations it is an instrument of foreign policy and must be considered on that basis. For example, our economic assistance in Vietnam at the present time is a major part of a very specific situation. 

We find that aid relationships sometimes are complicated by actions taken by the recipient country. We have tried to make it clear that the United States is not just an old cow that gives more milk the more it is kicked in the flanks. If anybody doesn't want reasonable relations with the United States, then he will have to adjust to the consequences.

There is an end to our patience.

I think, Mr. Chairman, the leverage of foreign aid is primarily aimed at the internal policies, the development efforts made by the countries themselves. There are situations where the failure of self-help has caused us greatly to cut back, perhaps even to eliminate, any bilateral aid programs of our own. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, would you say that foreign aid is directed toward solving or avoiding problems that might become acute 5 or 10 years from now?

Secretary RUSK. I think, sir, that if we look forward to a situation where the developing countries look to the future with hopelessness, that we would have an increasingly dangerous situation in the world. 

Our aid programs and the programs of other advanced countries have to take that very much into account. 

You see, Mr. Chairman, mass communications have spread the word of what can be done among the developing countries. They no longer accept misery and disease as a part of the state of nature or something imposed upon them by providence, because they see and hear that these problems are being licked in other parts of the world. They want some of that, and they want it fast. There is bound to be considerable political restlessness if there is not some visible movement toward economic and social development. I would think the implication of your question would be that it is very much true that we are building for the longer range here when we help countries get onto a steady course of progress. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, you mentioned the limit of the number of countries to which various types of foreign aid would be provided. Does this handicap you in dealing with situations as they may arise?

Secretary RUSK. I suppose this is a professional bias on the part of anyone sitting in this particular chair, but legislative inhibitions, legislative restrictions, which run usually on an annual cycle, make it very difficult for us to move promptly and adjust quickly to changes in different situations. We do need flexibility. 

I understand the concerns of the Congress which have caused them from time to time to impose certain inflexibilities into our legislation. 

In the matter of the number of countries, we would be glad to see countries group themselves and make use of their own regional institutions in working out their own aid. If we are denied the flexibility legislatively to do certain things that have to be done in our own interest by an artificial limitation on the number of countries, I think that is a disadvantage to us.

I would hope that the Congress this year would give thought to that, not because there is a great argument over policy, but because there is an operational problem if we have legislative inhibitions against the flexibility we need.

Chairman MORGAN. The limitations on the number of countries originated in the other body, not on this side of the Capitol.

It just seems to me it is a complicating additional step. 

Secretary RUSK. Mr. Adair, let me just comment on two factors, sort of working in both directions on that. In exercising my responsibility for coordinating military assistance under the existing legislation to Thailand and to Laos, I have to take very heavily into account the actual military situation in those countries. So that my coordination has to reach over and assume or take into account the very heavy military responsibility of those carrying the battle. 

Similarly, looking at it the other way around, in the case of, say, Vietnam, when decisions are made with respect to force levels by the Vietnamese and the order of magnitude of weapons and other equipment made available to the Vietnamese, I take part in those discussions myself. So that we do coordinate and we do work together on that part of the program that you have already approved as going into the military budget.

These things mesh together, and it is very hard to see how in such a situation as obtains in those three countries we could do otherwise than expect the Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense to work closely together with the advice of the Joint Chiefs and under the general direction of the President.

Mr. ADAIR. That argument certainly has a great deal of validity with respect to that geographic area, but how about the NATŎ infrastructure and the international military headquarters?

Secretary RUSK. This is a matter about which we are very much concerned at the present time, Mr. Adair. It has been one of the leading countries of Africa. It has shown promise in its ability to move its economy forward. We would hope this would not be set back by these regional differences that exist there at the present time. 

To answer your question directly: yes, general developments there affecting the ability to use external resources would be one of the major considerations in what we do for the future.

Secretary RUSK. We are discussing in NATO rotating up to 35,000. 

The central item in the rotation would have to do with having one division on a rotational basis. The central idea would be that two brigades of that division would be in this country and one brigade would at all times be in Europe at the division headquarters. These brigades would succeed each other at intervals of 6 months. 

All of the dependents of all three brigades would be back in this country. Once a year the division would be concentrated in NATO, in 

Europe, for division exercises. The two brigades in this country would be on a readiness basis at all times to be returned promptly to the 

NATO area, if needed.

When we first made our troop commitment to NATO back in 1951 and 1952, Secretary Marshall, who was then Secretary of Defense, spoke in terms of approximately six divisions. In fact, we went forward at that time on the basis of 52% divisions. Over the years we have added one-third of a division so we have six divisions there. 

What we have in mind is that we would keep five and a third divisions in NATO as part of the very powerful 7th Army, in a force that has been greatly strengthened not only by increase in weapons but with massive increment in nuclear capability and by a much higher degree of mobility.

At the same time we would test the capabilities of the dual basing concept with respect to the rotation of this limited number of ground forces and the rotation of long-range, high-speed aircraft.

Secretary RUSK. Mrs. KELLY. Would you say

Secretary RUSK. I think the important point about the action taken by France is that by withdrawing from the integrated forces of
