855 that Castro was not an acceptable answer in this hemisphere. The problem in the Dominican Republic in regard to hemisphere policy was to give the Dominican people a chance to choose their own government in between these two extremes, both of which had been repudiated by the hemisphere.

Those elections were held. I think there has been a special circumstance there. I would not think the Dominican story meant that we anticipated intervening all over the place because there has been tyranny or inaction.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Whalley. 

Mr. Secretary, few people in the world have so many difficult problems as yourself. I don't see how you can continue to work so hard and be so optimistic about the outcome when there seems to be so many roadblocks. Has the United Nations acted in the problems of Vietnam, the Middle East, and Latin America?

Secretary RUSK. As far as Vietnam is concerned, the answer is "No" at the present time, unless one includes the personal efforts, the private efforts, of the Secretary General. We have taken the Vietnam question to the United Nations on several occasions, most recently and most formally in January 1966, when we asked for full discussion, and there is now pending before the Security Council a resolution in which the Security Council would ask the two sides to come together and move this matter to a negotiated and peaceful settlement. 

The problem in the United Nations is that both Hanoi and Peking have made it very clear they will have nothing to do with the United Nations, that this is not a United Nations responsibility. 

That has had two effects. One is that it has helped to confirm the 

Soviet view that they will not support United Nations activity in Vietnam, and everyone would expect that the Soviet Union would veto any resolution before the Security Council. This combination of resistance on the part of the Communist countries has caused a good many of the other members to believe that, under those circumstances, it is not good for the United Nations to try to intrude into a situation if by doing so it might get in the way of the use of other machinery. 

Let me just illustrate this for a moment. When we were in the Security Council on the last occasion, the Soviet representative said in effect, "this is not the business of the U.N. This is the business of the 

Geneva machinery." Whereupon Ambassador Goldberg said "All right, we will not quarrel with you. Let's use the Geneva machinery right now." That proved to be impossible. And the answer on Vietnam is that we believe that it is a responsibility of the U.N. and we would like to see the United Nations take it seriously and do what it can in this situation, but for reasons I have indicated the United Nations has been reluctant.

As far as Latin America is concerned, there are some specialized agencies of the U.N. that are active in Latin America. Some of those are combined with hemisphere organizations such as the Pan American Sanitary Bureau, which is also the World Health Organization branch in Latin America. But as far as political matters are concerned, the hemisphere has a strong tradition of wanting to deal with its own

1967 

political questions within the framework of the OAS and the institutions of the hemisphere. 

You may recall that in 1945, at the United Nations Charter drafting conference, it was the Latin Americans who pressed very hard for the regional organizations clause of the present United Nations Charter. 

So, in the absence of an unforeseen and major development of the sort that is not now apparent, I think we can expect that the Latin Americans themselves would prefer to handle their problems within the hemisphere, not excluding the jurisdiction of the U.N. but taking care of them in the hemisphere if possible. And the United Nations thus far has been reasonably content to have that happen. 

In the Near East the U.N. is somewhat more active, but at the pres ent time without decisive results on a number of points. The U.N. has been active in Cyprus where it has organized the U.N. Force on 

Cyprus. They have recently had a commission going into Aden, trying to work some things out there. There have been some difficulties about that commission, as you know. They have the standing commitment in their United Nations Emergency Force in the Near East, the watching force that arose in connection with the Israel-Arab conflict. The 

United Nations is reasonably active in the political questions of the Near East. They do have from time to time, as you know, before the 

Security Council the various clashes which have occurred along the frontiers between Israel and Syria or Jordan. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Everyone seems to know that most of the difficulties in Latin America stem from Cuba. Can't we do something more about 

Cuba and get to the root of the trouble? 

Secretary RUSK. In July 1964 the foreign ministers of the hemisphere imposed upon Cuba all of the peaceful sanctions that are available under the Rio Pact. They did warn Cuba at that time that a continuation of Cuban armed interference in other countries would raise the prospect of the use of armed force to resist that kind of interference. 

Also at that time, Mr. Whalley, the hemisphere asked our friends in other countries to accept the same measures with respect to Cuba that the hemisphere had placed against Cuba, in effect meaning a suspension of diplomatic relations and a suspension of trade relationships, with the exception of food and medicine. Other countries have not responded in this way.

I can tell you that it is not just we who are disappointed that others have not shown more solidarity with the hemisphere in this matter: the Latin Americans themselves are becoming increasingly concerned about this because it is apparent that Castro has not fully heeded these warnings that he had in July 1964 and that there are some activities going on in three or perhaps four countries, small-scale perhaps, but nevertheless there, which show that Castro has not abandoned his desire to interfere illegally in the affairs of other countries in the hemisphere.

In continuing that program he apparently has had some differences with the Soviet Union. He seems to be somewhere between the attitudes of the Soviet Union and Peking on this matter. My guess is that this matter will be discussed before too long in the OAS on the basis of later information that has been developed.

I would have to see the full reports, Mr. Gross, and try to run them down to be able to respond directly to the question you had. (The following was subsequently furnished by Secretary Rusk for inclusion in the record:)

RENEWED ACTIVITY ON THE PART OF THE COMMUNISTS IN LATIN AMERICA 

There is to be held in Havana next July a meeting of the Latin American Solidarity Organization (LASO). This is an outgrowth of the so-called Tri-Continental Conference held in Havana in January 1966. The latter created an organization based in Havana, the Afro-Asian-Latin American Peoples Solidarity Organization (AALAPSO), and the Latin American and Caribbean delegations created a closely associated Latin American Solidarity Organization (LASO), both dedicated to supporting "national liberation movements" in the overthrow of present governments. To date the AALAPSO and LASO have primarily represented new labels on an old Cuban bottle. The inspiration for their activities clearly comes from Cuba which, long before the Tri-Continental Conference, was openly supporting subversive activities throughout the Hemisphere. 

The U.S. and other nations of the Hemisphere showed an immediate recognition of the potentialities for mischief of the AALAPSO and the LASO. Both the 

Tri-Continental Conference and the permanent organizations, as well as the official or semi-official participation of certain countries, were forcefully denounced by the Council of the Organization of American States and by the Latin American group in the United Nations. 

[Security deletion.] 

A further limitation on the effectiveness of AALAPSO is an amendment to Section 620 (i) of the Foreign Assistance Act, included in Public Law 89-583. 

This puts all present and prospective United States foreign aid recipients on notice that nations will become ineligible for assistance by engaging in or pre-

1967 

paring military aggresion, or being represented officially at any international conference to plan insurrection or subversive activity. 

Among recommendations which received the general endorsement of the OAS Council to counter the challenge of AALAPSO were: (1) measures to strengthen individual and collective antisubversive capability; (2) diplomatic steps to discourage future official and semi-official participation in the permanent organizations and future conferences; and (3) a new effort to persuade friendly nonmember countries to restrict trade with Cuba. There has already been significant follow-up action on these recommendations.

United States policy with respect to the Cuban subversive threat in Latin America has been based on both short and long range programs. In the immediate sense, through a variety of measures we have assisted the internal security forces of Latin American governments to strengthen their capability to overcome subversive threats. In a longer range sense, the Alliance for Progress is intended to reduce those conditions which present a fertile ground for revolutionary agitation.

Thus, while we take seriously the threat of Cuban-inspired subversion in Latin America, it is not unmanageable. We are alert to the danger, as are our partners in the Organization of American States, and the latter, with our help, have shown an increased ability to cope with the problem. 

RENEWED SOVIET ACTIVITY IN CUBA 

With respect to recent reports that there is taking place in Cuba significant build-up of arms and military forces from the Soviet Union, the United States intelligence community, which maintains a constant watchfulness on this subject and has many sources of information including the results of aerial surveillance, does not find any evidence to bear out such reports.

ROLE OF HO CHI MINH 

The important consideration here is that Ho Chi Minh entertains pretensions to the establishment of a greater Vietnam than is encompassed by the present borders of that divided nation. Laotian Premier Souvanna Phouma has only recently condemned North Vietnamese aggression in Laos. It is known that 

North Vietnam has conducted training for insurgency and terrorism in Thailand at least since 1962. These involvements suggest that North Vietnamese ambitions under Ho's leadership are anything but conducive to stability in 

Southeast Asia.

POLITICAL DEVELOPMENT IN VIETNAM 

General Ky has himself recognized, in public statements, that his government does not enjoy the mandate accorded a government which has been freely elected. 

Barely six months after his government assumed office, on January 15, 1966, Prime Minister Ky announced the intentions of his government to return to a constitutional system and to establish elected and representative institutions. 

Throughout 1966 the government took a number of significant steps to lead the country in this direction and to involve, increasingly, civilian participation in the ruling process. On June 7, 1966 the 10-man military Directorate was enlarged to include 10 civilians representing various political and religious groupings. 

On July 5 a Peoples Army Council consisting of 59 civilians and 20 military officers was created for the purpose of advising the Prime Minister on political, economic, and social problems with which the government was dealing. In accordance with his January 15 statement and with a decree issued by Chief of State Nguyen Van Thieu on April 14, elections for a constituent assembly were conducted on September 11. 

Observed by more than 500 foreign press members and a large resident diplomatic corps, these elections were considered to be the fairest and freest national elections ever conducted in Viet-Nam. Some 81% of the registered electorate, or approximately 56% of those old enough to vote, cast ballots in the face of Viet Cong threats and extensive Viet Cong efforts to prevent the electorate from exercising their franchise. For six months the 117 Deputies in the Assembly engaged in free and open debate in preparing a draft constitution. Despite some dissatisfaction among some of the military with regard to certain provisions of the constitution, the Directorate accepted the draft constitution without change and the constitution was promulgated on April 1, 1967. Already some seven candidates have announced their intention to run for President, under the new Constitution, in the elections which are scheduled for early September of this year. Among the announced candidates are such respected nationalist figures as 

Phan Khac Suu-Chairman of the Constituent Assembly and former Chief of State, former Prime Minister Tran Van Huong, and Revolutionary Dai Viet leader Ha Thuc Ky. Elections for the bicameral national legislature are also scheduled for this Fall.

In addition to the efforts of the present government to develop representative institutions at the central government level, the government is conducting local elections throughout the country. Elections for village councils, who under a recent decree will enjoy extensive self-governing powers, were conducted during the period of April 2-30 in 984 villages. Hamlet elections are scheduled for the period May 14-June 11 in some 4600 hamlets for hamlet chiefs and deputy hamlet chiefs. Additional elections at the village and hamlet levels through the rest of 1967 will mean that by the end of this year approximately three-fifths of the rural population, outside of the six autonomous cities, will have elected their own local government.

When the above sequence of events is reviewed, it is clear that the charge of Prime Minister Ky being a "ruthless dictator" cannot be substantiated, nor has all internal opposition been oppressed. From the floor of the Constituent 

Assembly, in the local press, and in many quarters in Vietnam criticism of the government can be heard and read. Prime Minister Ky has never indicated that his only political hero is Adolf Hitler. The statement to which this charge is related was made some eight months before Ky was designated Prime Minister and he has frequently since then indicated that he has a number of political heroes, that he deplores the tactics and methods employed by Hitler in supressing opposition, and that his only reference to Hitler's ability was in the context of

1967 

the need in Viet-Nam for leadership and a sense of discipline in order to face communist aggression. For example, on July 15, 1965 Ky stated: "The idea is far from me of praising Hitler or adopting his view especially when here in Viet-Nam, nobody can forget the inhuman methods he used during the second World War, which the Communists are using right now in our land.”

865 14 As far the the U.N. Charter is concerned, the U.N. Charter clearly, under article 51, anticipated there would be situations in which the United Nations itself could not deal with the situation, and it reserved the right of individual and collective self-defense. So this is collective self-defense being exercised by South Vietnam and its friends in that part of the world and ourselves. 

As far the the SEATO treaty is concerned, article 4, paragraph 1, of the SEATO treaty says that in the event of aggression by means of armed attack against a member of SEATO or a protocol state of SEATO and South Vietnam is a protocol state of SEATO each member will act to meet the common danger. There is an armed attack, there is aggression by means of armed attack going on against South Vietnam. We have had to face soberly and seriously and responsibly the question of what steps we shall take to meet the common danger. 

Everybody knows what our answer is. Others have come to different kinds of answers. But five members of SEATO have troops there helping to carry this battle. This is the kind of situation which was anticipated when SEATO was formed, when the treaty was underwritten by a very large vote in our Senate. The hope was-and it is always our hope that the very formation of a defense treaty would be a sufficient warning to the other side that "you better leave these countries alone or there will be trouble." The hope was that it would deter. That hope did not come out in fact in this particular situation.

 POSSIBLE INCREASE OF U.S. FORCES IN VIETNAM AND ESCALATION OF WAR 

In recent days there has been a spate of speculative stories about impending increases in the strength of US forces in Viet-Nam suggesting that the total may soon rise to 600,000.

All decisions about the nature and level of our military effort in Viet-Nam are based on a careful consideration of the views of the government's military and civilian experts. In making these decisions the President and his close advisers have been guided both by the demands imposed upon us by the need to meet increased aggression and by the need for restraint in the application of force to avoid an unwanted wider war. The situation is constantly being reviewed. If the enemy increases his effort, we must see what sort of response is called for on our side. Additional forces may or may not be the answer. Obviously it would be unwise to speculate on these matters in advance of any decision to increase our forces in Viet-Nam. As the Secretary said in his appearance before the Committee, the President does not now have recommendations along this line in front of him for consideration.

As for the general question of "escalation", the United States has taken no steps to widen the war. Our military effort is designed to put pressure on the enemy-both in South Viet-Nam and in North Viet-Nam-to convince him that his aggression cannot succeed. That pressure will be maintained, and where necessary increased, so long as the enemy chooses to continue and even to step up his aggression. As has been widely reported, the North Vietnamese, following up their massive resupply effort during the Tet truce, have concentrated three, and possibly four divisions, in and near the Demilitarized Zone. These troops are supporting what appears to be a major enemy effort against the two northernmost provinces of South Viet-Nam. Elsewhere in South Viet-Nam there seems to be

871 no slackening of the efforts of the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces to strength their general military position and to press ahead with their campaign of terror which most recently has been focused on candidates for the village council elections and Revolutionary Development workers. The military measures we have taken in response to the enemy's latest moves are directed solely at his ability to wage war against South Viet-Nam and against our forces in the area.

On April 7, 1965, President Johnson called upon "... the countries of Southeast

Asia to associate themselves in a greatly expanded cooperative effort for development". Illustrations of expanded regional cooperation in East Asia that have occurred since 1965 are as follows: 66 

1. The establishment of the Asian Development Bank. 

2. Japan's initiative to convene the Southeast Asia Development Conference that was held in Tokyo, April 1966 and a second Southeast Asia Development 

Conference that was held in Manila last April. 

3. Last December's Southeast Asia Agricultural Conference. 

4. Initiation of regular consultations among central bankers and planners in

ASIAN DEVELOPMENT BANK 

The Asian Development Bank was formally opened December 17, 1965 at Manila. Composed of 19 regional countries and 12 non-regional countries, subscription pledges now total $965 million. Regional countries have pledged $615 million and non-regional $350 million which includes a U.S, subscription of $200 million. Japan's subscription equals that of the U.S. Membership of 

Switzerland with a subscription of $5 million has been authorized but has not yet become effective.

Ten percent of the Asian Development Bank's regular capital can be used for "soft window" operations. All other lending from its ordinary capital resources must be at conventional terms similar to those of the IBRD. 

In recognition of the need for concessional capital for development in many of the countries of Southeast Asia, the President in his State of the Union Address on January 10, stated that he would seek a special $200 million authorization from the Congress for East Asian regional program. The most likely uses of the $200 million U.S. contribution to the Special Funds of the ADB would be for agriculture development, the Mekong Development Program, and regional transportation activities.

1967 REGIONAL EDUCATION 

In November 1965, the Thai Minister of Education called a meeting of Ministers of Education from six Southeast Asian countries: Thailand, Laos, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam were represented. They reviewed their problems and priorities in the field of education and each presented his views as to possible areas of regional cooperation. It was the unanimous view of these Ministers that a number of activities of interest to them could be developed or improved by coordination or joint effort of one kind or another. One of the most attractive ideas was that of agreeing to identify certain existing institutions for up-grading into centers of excellence to serve more than one country.

To carry out the professional and administrative responsibilities included in such an undertaking, the Ministers established an ad hoc Secretariat called 

SEAMES-Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Secretariat. 

The Ministers of Education held a Second Conference in Manila in November 1966. Indonesia joined the group at this meeting. At this second meeting the 

Ministers formalized their heretofore ad hoc arrangements by agreeing to establish a Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Council, for which they approved a draft charter; and authorized the creation of a permanent Secretariat. They also agreed to support the following ten regional proposals: 

1. The Asian Institute of Technology (Thailand)-as the successor to the existing SEATO Graduate School of Engineering. 

2. A Southeast Asian Regional Center for Tropical Medicine-to coordinate reasearch activities of five national centers.

3. A Regional Institute for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture 

(Philippines) — -as a new program to be added to the Los Banos complex.

4. A Southeast Asian Institute of Higher Education-an institute being established with Ford Foundation support by UNESCO and the International 

Association of Universities. 

5. A Regional Center for Education in Science and Mathematics (Malaysia) 

to train specialists from the member countries in the use of new techniques and materials for teaching science and mathematics. 

6. A Regional English Language Center (Singapore)-to train specialists in English teaching from member countries. 

7. A Task Force to study the problem of book needs and recommend areas for joint action. 

8. A Regional Institute of Educational Radio and Television-to exchange information and assist with development of skills in educational programming in these media. 

9. Instructional Materials Workshop (Vietnam). 

10. A Second Southeast Asian Regional Manpower Assessment and Educa tional Planning Seminar (Thailand).

MEKONG PROGRAM 

The lower Mekong River is one of the great natural resources of Southeast Asia. Its exploitation for hydroelectric power and irrigation is a feature of any long range development plan for this region, including Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Exploitation of its tributaries in Thailand already has begun. 

To assist with the development of Lower Mekong River Basin, the UN Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East (ESCAFE), in 1957, established the Mekong Committee which is comprised of the four Mekong riparian countries (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam).

The Mekong Committee has used its first decade to focus its energies and limited resources on an extensive program of data collection and comprehensive planning. There was no alternative. Ten years ago practically nothing was known about the river's characteristics-about its flow, its discharge, its navigability, about its development potential. Data had to be collected, an overall Basin plan had to be developed and economic and social studies had to be gotten underway. 

Now that considerable data has been collected the Mekong Committee is beginning to concentrate on the implementation of development projects. Last year, two tributary dams were completed in Northeast Thailand which produce the only electric power ever to flow from the Mekong. The Nam Ngum tributary dam at Laos received international financing last year from eight countries. 

The World Bank is administering the project. The U.S. contributed half of the

873 $25 million needed. An interesting feature of that project is the agreement between Thailand and Laos to exchange electricity-an essential feature of larger projects to come. The Mekong Committee and the UN are now attempting to rease funds for a priority tributary project in Cambodia. To provide an orderly framework for future financing of Mekong development programs, the Mekong Committee has under consideration a proposal for establishing a Mekong 

Development Fund to be administered by the Asian Development Bank. 

SOUTHEAST ASIA DEVELOPMENT CONFERENCES 

April 26-28, 1966 the second annual Ministerial Conference on Southeast

Asian Development was held in Manila. The first was held a year ago in Tokyo. 

There have, of course, long been other Asian meetings on development problems, such as those held under the auspices of ECAFE and the Colombo Plan. What is unique and especially attractive about these two Ministerial Conferences and other new regional groups is their specific focus on organizing and getting underway particular cooperative regional action programs. These new organizations build upon and could bring to practical fruition the broad aims and general plans nurtured in Asia under international sponsorship for the more than ten years. 

One of the most significant actions of the Conference in Manila (April 26-28) was the decision to ask the Asian Bank to proceed with completion of a proposal for establishment of an Agriculture Fund to be used primarily in Southeast Asia to meet the desperately urgent need for increased food production. The 

President of the Asian Bank reported to the Conference that the Bank's Directors had considered and approved, in principle, the Bank's administering such a Fund. 

The idea for the Fund arose at the first Southeast Asia Conference in Tokyo and was developed by a conference of Asian agricultural experts and officials last 

A second important action was suggested by the Government of Malaysiapreparation of a regional plan for transportation and communications development in Southeast Asia. These two fields are obvious means of regional integration which also would accelerate economic development of the countries involved. Over the coming months there will be Malaysian-sponsored meetings of experts and officials, in which U.S. technicians will participate, aimed at producing a proposal for coordinated development in these major fields. Malaysia and the other countries involved undoubtedly will look to the Asian Bank as a source of financial assistance for some of the resulting proposals.

 CLARIFICATION OF POPULATION POLICY 

A joint exposition of U.S. foreign aid policy relating to problems of population growth was issued December 20, 1966, by the Secretary of State, the AID Administrator, the Acting Director of the Peace Corps, and the Director of the U.S. Information Agency. This policy statement emphasized that high priority will be given by these agencies to helping the efforts of less-developed countries for checking excessive population growth and for increasing food production. 

Through the Agency for International Development, initial assistance for family planning programs and related preliminary activities has thus far been provided to 25 countries, including a number in Latin America. Though much of this help is of limited scope, significant action-assistance is currently being provided for broad-scale field programs in Turkey, Pakistan, India, Korea, Honduras, and Jamaica. The program in Taiwan is also benefiting from Chinese-held funds originally generated by AID assistance. 

Interest in family planning action is increasing in the less-developed countries. The generally growing realization of the impact of population growth upon food supplies and national development, as well as AID's assistance in the family planning field, reflect a worldwide increase in concern with the harmful effects of rapid population growth upon social and economic progress. It is certain, for one thing, that the essential efforts to increase food production would eventually prove inadequate if current trends in population continue. 

U.S. assistance for population programs in the less-developed countries is extended as part of the overall objective of the U.S. in assisting the development of less-advanced countries. In assisting these programs, our objective is to contribute, as a responsible member of the community of nations, to the betterment of human welfare and the strengthening of free nations and institutions.

875 AID assistance in the population programs field is guided by the following principles: 

1. Help is given in response to specific requests of the recipient countries. It is to supplement each country's own efforts. 

2. Programs eligible for assistance are those in which individual participation is wholly voluntary and in which each individual is free to choose methods of family planning which are in keeping with his or her beliefs, culture, and personal wishes. 

3. AID does not advocate any specific population policy for another country, or any particular method of family planning. Its aim is to provide needed assistance upon request so that people everywhere may have the freedom to control their reproduction, health, and welfare if they so desire. 

AID assistance may now include funding for the purchase of contraceptive supplies and devices needed in carrying out country programs and/or financial assistance for indigenous manufacture of such supplies and devices. 

The help of multilateral agencies, other nations, and voluntary and educational institutions is encouraged. The population problem is of worldwide scope, calling for the broadest possible participation in the tasks of assistance and program action. AID assistance for country and regional projects will be channeled to those projects for which satisfactory help cannot be provided through other sources under appropriate circumstances. 

In extending assistance for family planning programs and their development, the Agency for International Development emphasizes the necessity for selfhelp action in the population field. AID's help for family planning programs, including its assistance for preliminary studies of population problems, is extended with a view to developing and aiding self-help upon these problems. 

AID extends assistance to countries that request help in population programs, where individual participation and choice of methods are wholly voluntary. Family planning is a subject of much delicacy. It is important that AID's assistance be kept completely free of any coercive elements. Despite the unquestioned need for self-help by the developing countries in increasing their food production and in taking other measures essential for their economic and social development, AID does not believe it appropriate to make the adoption of family planning programs a beginning pre-condition for assistance in the population field, or a pre-condition for rendering other types of assistance. The need for voluntary action cannot be disregarded or minimized. 

It is true, nevertheless, that family planning is a matter of high priority urgency. AID has stated the clear policy of providing and helping provide essential aid to those countries which have voluntary population programs that allow for individual freedom of choice. This setting of voluntary action, together with positive aid and encouragement by AID, offers the prospect of continually broadening achievement for family planning in many countries and widely varying cultures.

 IUD'S IN INDIA 

The Government of India has been expanding and strengthening its family planning program since early 1965. Though the program is beset by many difficul ties, both technical and administrative, its leaders report continuing advances in program development and implementation. 

To strengthen the Central Government's organization and leadership for family planning, the former Ministry of Health was designated in 1966 as the Ministry of Health and Family Planning, with a Secretary of Family Planning and a 

Commissioner of Family Planning. In this new structure, such needed attention is being given to expanding State Government participation. 

As of March 1, 1967, the Commissioner of Family Planning reported that 1,543,377 Indian women had accepted IUCDs (intra-uterine contraceptive devices) since July 1965, of which 744,130 were in the 1966-67 year; also that 

2,138,133 sterilizations had been performed since 1956, of which 639,000 were in 1966-67. 

On March 1, 1967, the national program had 1,563 family planning centers in urban areas and 4,275 major centers in rural areas. In addition, there were 10,313 sub-centers doing family planning work in rural areas, plus 8,690 other medical centers in rural areas which were distributing contraceptives without separate family planning staffs.

Although there has been significant progress in the program, in a short time as above, the family planning program of India is still proceeding on too small a scale, at a too-leisurely pace, and through too-limited techniques and action in relation to the huge tasks ahead. With India's population increasing over 1 million per month, it is evident that present efforts are only a fraction of those required for achieving the stated goal in birth rate reduction. The program's almost exclusive emphasis upon IUCDs in 1965 and early 1966 handicapped the use of additional means of contraception, such as contraceptive pills and condoms. Experience has shown that some women have difficulties with the 

IUCDS; also that a significant percentage of the devices are removed or lost within the first year after insertion. Inadequate numbers of women doctors also impede the adoption of IUCDs. 

This experience is leading the program to give greater attention to supplementary contraceptive means; including the condom, sterilizations, and the pill. 

Limited experimentation in use of the pill is now under way. The Government of India is also contemplating considerable expansion in distribution of condoms, including subsidized distribution through commercial channels. The condom distribution now planned will be based upon increasing indigenous production of condoms, plus importation of large supplies pending the availability of adequate production facilities.

STATEMENT OF DWIGHT D. TOWNSEND, VICE PRESIDENT AND DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC AFFAIRS FOR THE COOPERATIVE LEAGUE OF THE AITED STATES OF AMERICA 

Mr. TOWNSEND. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, speaking for the 

Cooperative League of the U.S.A., we are grateful for the chance your committee is giving us, as you have done in other years, to report on our stewardship in discharging responsibilities we have assumed in the cooperative development phase of our country's foreign aid program. We also plan to use this opportunity to suggest to you ways in which the cooperative effort t can be made more usefulmore effective-in achieving this program's long-range goals. 

It is good to be able to report that the membership of cooperatives are steadfast in their support of what our country is attempting to do in the underdeveloped world. This support ranges from formal resolutions to such personal actions as giving of money to support our own assistance program-called Worldwide Co-op Partners and through opening their homes and extending hospitality to cooperators who come here from other nations. 201 77-470-67-pt. 4- -13 881

1967 

They show it, too, through the willingness of scores of American cooperative leaders to accept arduous assignments, taking them where amenities are few in order to serve as advisers and consultants on cooperative projects. This they do at personal sacrifice and much inconvenience which few of them bother to mention when they get home.

As all but the new committee members already know, our league is a federation of customer-owned businesses in such fields as farm marketing and supply, housing, rural electrics, insurance, credit unions, groceries, and group health plans, operating at the State, regional, and national levels, with a membership of more than 18 million families. It is easy for people in cooperatives who have pulled together in these various ways for their economic salvation to identify with something like America's foreign aid program which has the same motivation and the same goals.

We took new heart, Mr. Chairman, from one aspect of last year's foreign aid bill approved by this committee, because in it you incorporated title IX, directing those who administer foreign aid to use to the greatest possible extent the largely untapped resources of knowhow, interest, and specific technique present in the private enterprise sector of the U.S. economy. Nowhere is this more applicable than with the leadership of our country's cooperative movement. 

Long before the way was opened for us to cooperate with the Agency for International Development, the Peace Corps, and the food for peace programs, the Cooperative League, with what were admittedly meager resources, opened an office in India where American cooperatives could help the people of that great subcontinent to derive some of the benefits available through introduction of the cooperative techniques in a place where the need is so overwhelmingly great. 

The man who operates that office, Dr. Allie Felder, is the Cooperative 

League's "man in India," working alongside Indian leaders to help make the term "cooperative" meaningful at all levels of Indian society. 

The league, by sending Dr. Felder to India, anticipated the direction foreign aid is taking in the mid 1960's. He had been there 5 years before the Congress approved the Humphrey amendment in 1961 which called for a concerted program to accomplish through foreign aid what he went out to New Delhi to do. He had been there a full 

10 years when Congress took another landmark step last year, adding through title IX a more careful spelling out of that, toward which the original Humphrey amendment was pointing.

Dr. Felder anticipated what the Congress had in mind when it passed the Humphrey amendment directing the Agency for International Development to make use of the talents and manpower of the cooperative organizations in this country to build counterpart organizations in the developing countries.. 

Again, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry Dr. Felder is ill this morning and will not be able to be here, because I am quite sure he would be able to fill in a number of important answers that the committee might have.

Another example to which we direct the attention of the committee involves the Cooperative League's housing affiliate, the Foundation for Cooperative Housing, and the credit union international organization. FCH, working with the Housing Agency of Panama (IVU) and the credit union people, has a program which makes it possible for a

FOREIGN 'ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1967 

883 -farmer to get a shell house for $350. No palaces, they are nevertheless substantially better shelter than the thatched roofs and mud floors of the structures they replace. 

This co-op inspired effort consists of a house designed for expansion eventually to one as large as the family needs. It starts with a slab, some sturdy pillars, and a strong metal roof. These houses are built in groups of 10 or more at one time. Credit unions are the local organizational focus, the community institution around which the housing is built. Members save their first $35 for a downpayment in the credit union. When the housing is completed they pay $5 a month to the credit union to discharge the original loan. 1 Once the basic home is completed a team of Peace Corps volunteers then works with the specialists of the Foundation for Cooperative Housing and the local credit union to teach the farmers how to split and tie the bamboo-a native material in abundant supply-used in the walls. A CINVARAM machine such as CARE distributes throughout Latin America is secured so that the farmer can make his own building blocks for the rest of the exterior and to build a wall around the property if he chooses.

The Peace Corps volunteers, in ways reminiscent of U.S. home extension workers, help the campesino family to master practices leading to greater livability.

When the first downpayments are in for 10 houses, there is enough money to build house No. 11. A few months later, the monthly payments bring in enough to build house No. 12 and so on. The people in the field estimate that somewhere between 35 and 50 houses will be built with the initial revolving fund of $3,500 from AID which is set aside for the original 10-house project. monThe work of the Foundation for Cooperative Housing isn't limited to housing for the campesino. There are self-help housing projects in 

David, Panama, and a slum clearance and relocation project in downtown Panama City where people in slum areas are brought to a new housing site just outside Panama City.

I am going to move over, if I may, to another part of my testimony which I think you will find of interest. These are testimony of accomplishments, and they repeat the success story that each have related. It is the middle of page 5. 

I would like to suggest the FCH experience is just one part of the overall experience of the cooperative movement of the United States as it reaches out to help people in other countries to achieve greater participation in their own economic life. 

As further example, the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, another member of the Cooperative League of the USA, is scoring some dramatic successes with its rural electric cooperatives in less developed countries. 

New industries are springing up on cooperative electric lines in 

Nicaragua and Ecuador. Construction is moving forward in Brazil,

Costa Rica, and Colombia; and work leading to construction is progressing in many other Latin American countries. 

In East Asia three cooperatives are teaching democracy while bringing light and power to rural areas in South Vietnam; two are now being planned in the Philippines. NRECA specialists have planned six economically feasible cooperatives in India, and three of them will be started immediately. Cooperative rural electrification

1967 

can greatly increase food production, and NRECA's team of specialists planned projects around the use of power for irrigation pumping. The three initial pilot projects will provide 112,500 kilowatts for irrigation use; this will produce 56,250 tons of food annually, according to data given the team by India's State Electricity Board. This is a small beginning but we feel it is a step in the right direction. 

Electrification through cooperative organizations also brings the special benefit that comes from people working together and with their government to achieve the common objectives of personal and community development. 1: 

I would like to skip a paragraph to the middle of page 6 and suggest, sir, that some of the farmers who are working on this program are the same farmers who strung the lines and wired the homes in this country 30 years ago and are showing others how to perform these same chores in Latin America today. i lange ondinsd On the top of page 7, I would like to refer to the credit union movement. 21 In the field of credit the credit union movement under the guidance of the Credit Union National Association's international program is writing a glowing chapter in this story, with hundreds of new credit unions coming into being, especially in Latin America. 

The membership in all types of cooperatives are giving in larger amounts each year to the Cooperative League's own fund for helping the young cooperative movement in dozens of countries to get on a firm footing. As I mentioned before, we call this fund Worldwide 

Co-op Partners and the relatively limited amount raised in this way is used for projects with special potential that is outside the reach of the AID program. This fund gives everyone connected with cooperatives a sense of involvement in our foreign assistance work, as their thoughts and interest follow their dollars to where they are finally spent. Our members recognize, along with millions of fellow Americans, that this program must move from stage to stage as conditions change on the world scene. Twenty years ago it focused on a war-ravaged 

Europe with its economic back broken. All that is changed now, though the prospect for improvement at least on the surface was grim indeed, and the pessimists were out in full cry then as now, saying we are licked before we start. Mr. Chairman, people who believe in cooperatives as an economic tool simply refuse to buy that. We have seen how the magic of selfhelp when seasoned with people-to-people humanness and technical know-how can make a difference. The beginnings are often small, but when they truly address themselves to people's needs they fuse into a trend that can involve whole peoples and routs the most formidable problems. 

I would like to skip over, if I may, now, Mr. Chairman, to the middle of page 8 to suggest is there progress on which to base this optimism that we talk about. We think there is. 

In the league's annual report to the Agency for International Development for 1966 the story of this progress was reported in such concrete terms as "the organization of 98 new primary cooperativesmembership 21,630"; "10,500 persons trained in cooperative techniques"; "per capita income of craftsmen involved in cooperative artisan project increased, in Colombia 37 percent, Ecuador 62 percent, and in Peru over 1,000 percent."botiboann þým

885 The Ecuadorean coffee cooperatives captured 9 percent of the national export quota and raised producers' income $2 a bag. Membership in the Organization of Cooperatives of the Americas (OCA) rose from 56 to 90 active members. The league also reported to AID that in the period since the last report experience has opened the eyes of cooperators as never before to the role they can play in solving the two most oppressive challenges: greater food production and capital development. As regards the last named, a specialist in capital development furnished by our organization has been advising the Korean Ministry of Finance with special reference to the role credit unions and insurance can play.

With your permission, Mr. Chairman, the statement will conclude with some general observations on what we are attempting and how you can help us to do it better. We believe very strongly that ours is a way of getting more of the foreign aid energy past the governmental bureaucracies and capital cities and out to the farm and village level, where the people and the problems are. It is a way of coming to close grips with the reality of any given situation. The local cooperative is a small staging ground to show what democracy is all about by encouraging the people who are members to practice it. There is room in cooperative development for all to help: the natural community leaders, eager young Peace Corpsmen, the teachers, everybody who sees a need and wants to do something about it. 

Comparatively small amounts of money are involved for essentially we are exporting a technique that lets men of good will work together along sound economic lines to lick their own problems. It has been tested on every continent and under the most adverse as well as favorable conditions. There is no longer a serious question that it works. It enables people to mobilize and use their own resources, including some they didn't know they had. When you call, as you did in the foreign aid legislation of 1966 in title IX, for the maximum use of this country's private resources you are giving official sanction to what we are talking about.

To make title IX really work we urge the committee to write into the bill a directive that in each AID mission there be at least one officer who knows cooperation and cooperatives. Some missions have such people but many do not, and when there is no one so qualified, it leads to indifference and misunderstanding as we try to carry out our part of the bargain. For the beacon which marks success for cooperative effort is when the local leadership, the homegrown leadership, begins to direct the credit union or the local co-op. This is not always fully appreciated by administrators more accustomed to handing the keys of a new building to a government minister or cutting the ribbon that opens a new road. People's institutions grow to success in less spectacular ways but they are meant to last longer and in the long run will make a greater difference. 

In this testimony we have telescoped the story of cooperatives in foreign aid far too ruthlessly in the interest of time and space. Cutting it to a realistic length is not easy because it is a story we rejoice in telling and wish more could hear about. 

We hope it moves this committee and the 90th Congress to (1) emphasize to all who administer aid overseas that you mean what you say in title IX and want to see the greatest possible use of private resources of this country including the dedicated brainpower of those

who direct this Nation's cooperatives; and (2) that you will keep support for this program at a level realistic in terms of our gross national product and what we spend for other things. 

Mr. Chairman, many of our accomplishments on behalf of the citizens of developing countries are measured in terms of things to use like housing, credit, electric lines, et cetera. But one intangible that we overlook is the degree of self-reliance, self,-respect, and a high regard for democratic processes so essential in the makeup of a developing nation. It is most difficult to put a dollar mark on the value of this kind of endeavor, or to imagine the dimension of world turmoil if we do not.

STATEMENT OF DR. DAVID A. WAAS FOR THE GENERAL BROTHER- HOOD BOARD OF THE BRETHREN (CHAIRMAN, DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY AND POLITICAL SCIENCE, MANCHESTER COLLEGE, NORTH MANCHESTER, INDIANA) 

Dr. WAAS. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am 

David A. Waas, chairman of the Department of History and Political 

Science, Manchester College, North Manchester, Ind., speaking in behalf of the General Brotherhood Board of the Church of the Brethren. The Church of the Brethren is one of the three historic peace churches. It has a long and deep commitment to seeking ways in which world peace, and the stability in which peace can grow, can be achieved. We feel that in this moment in history world stability and long-range peace are in jeopardy from forces far more global than the immediate threat posed by the Communist philosophy Despite the character of our deep involvement in Southeast Asia, the essential question before us in the late 1960's is not whether military power can contain the spread of communism, but whether human concern and economic power can create conditions which will make communism unnecessary. Christian compassion and humanitarian sensitivity, as well as economic and political self-interest, push us to a consideration of how the spread of a dehumanizing philosophy such as communism can be halted. We are pushed to such considerations because, if present global trends are not modified no amount of military power, even wielded by such a nation as the United States, will be able to stem the tide of radical, violent economic and social upheaval in dozens of nations. As the gap between the rich, developed nations including the Soviet Union-and the poor, underdeveloped nations widens, the alternatives facing nations become more stark and the imperatives for action become more demanding. In his encyclical letter, Populorum Progressio (On the Development of 

Peoples) His Holiness, Pope Paul VI, makes a "solemn appeal" to "men of good will" to take steps toward the development of man's full potential. He pointed out that we live in a "such world" and that a "cry of anguish" can be heard from hungry, hopeless, desperate men the world over, a cry which must be answered if civilization is to endure. Pope Paul stated further that "the superfluous wealth of the rich countries should be placed at the service of poor nations ***.

If today's flourishing civilizations remain selfishly wrapped up in themselves, they could easily place their highest values in jeopardy, sacrificing their will to be great to the desire to possess more." 

The staggering problems faced by the underdeveloped nations and the gap between them and the rich nations accelerates with the years. 

Gentlemen, in fewer years than those since the inauguration of Franklin Roosevelt, the populations of almost all of Africa, Asia and Latin America will double. Japan is the only significant exception in the entire area. (World Population Data Sheet-1966, Population 

Reference Bureau, Washington, D.C., December 1966.) During every hour of every day the earth's population rises by almost 7,000, and even more important, the bulk of those being born will live out their lives in societies which are unable to provide them with even the most basic essentials for life. The most rapid rates of growth are in those

1967 

areas which can least afford it. With population rising material and physical need is rapidly increasing. Poverty, hunger, ignorance and ill health can be found in every nation, but in many these four horsemen dominate the social order. And yet these are ills which can be cured. It is true, thousands of Americans are working selflessly around the clock, around the globe to combat these ills. They are sponsored by churches, private agencies, foundations and our Government. But while their services are valiant and thrilling to relate, they are, in the light of the need, pathetically small. 

In view of the stated problems, and out of wide experience in working with government assistance programs, in maintaining its own mission, relief, and service agencies, and in relating to the work of other service groups, we of the Church of the Brethern feel a strong commitment to the principle of expanded economic assistance. We feel that long-range planning, both for the uplift of peoples and for the peace and stability of the world, must include expanded economic aid from the United States. Our support of an expansion in economic aid stems from Christian concern for fellow men and the belief that social and economic instability are festers which cannot be controlled by military prowess. 

Yet when these sores break open men around the globe are immediately affected. Future Vietnams lie only slightly beneath the surface, in 

Oceania, in Africa, in Asia, and perhaps Latin America, and what is to be one to blunt or prevent them?

It is our position that even massive military aid can be only a short-term deterrent, and may be quite shortsighted. Once given, a 

Sherman tank can fire this direction as easily as another. Military assistance also speaks to a very small proportion of the people of an underdeveloped nation and history demonstrates for us that they are not only small in number but temporary in tenure. Only a sophisticated people, who have less need for internal army operations are able to see the army in any light other than a force of oppression. 

Only in rare instances can the military establishment in an underdeveloped area be considered to be constructive. But we recognize that national policy demands that the American Government seek immediate international stability and that military assistance may be an effective tool to serve that temporary end. 

But what of tomorrow? American churchmen and Congressmen alike have the responsibility to look beyond the quest for an immediate international calm. While the original motives may differ, the ultimate challenge to them is the same. The humanitarian and the statesman must ask what are we doing to assure peace for future generations? 

It seems clear that without unprecedented effort and investment of human resources and funds, poverty, hunger, ignorance and ill health will be ever increasingly dominant themes in world society. These ills create frustration and explosive, hostile people, and no amount of military power or wishful thinking will make them less so. 

While it is not within the power of the United States to significantly change the rising rate of population growth, it is within the power of the United States to significantly effect the ability of people around the world to feed themselves, to house themselves, and to educate themselves. Here American power can be a dramatic force for good. 

Here American will, wealth, and technical "know-how" can dramatically alter the course of human events in our own time and in the time of our children. Experimental agricultural stations, hydro-

electric units, farm to market roads, school houses, hospitals, and wells speak not only to the ills of society but to the frustrations of the people. In contrast to military assistance they speak constructively to countless people in each area involved. Few average citizens in emerging nations show pride in tanks and warplanes, regardless of who has provided them. But many Americans have been led by such a citizen to a simple irrigation project or bridge or library where, with eyes algow, he tells of what we, American and African, have done. 

And American and African alike are renewed, given hope and a sense of the future. Something has been built which has endless potential for good, and in the last analysis, will create more stability than any type of military strength.

Economic assistance has the ability to not only serve the present, but to create the atmosphere and conditions for self-generating strength and growth. It can be argued that the U.S. Government is not a service agency, but it is responsible to work for a world in which justice, order and peace are uppermost, in which nations-America among themcan flourish and cooperate. Economic assistance, generously given, can work deliberately and steadily to this end. I say "generously" because it is difficult to say how much positive relationship was established by the fabled dimes given by John D. Rockefeller to those who asked for help. In the face of great and staggering need on one hand and considerable wealth on the other, niggardly assistance might even have a negative effect. 

In light of these considerations we urge (1) That continuing efforts be made to distinguish between military and economic assistance, and that they be dealt with as distinct and separate factors. I would commend the committee and the Congress on the work that has been done in this light in past bills. (2) That economic assistance be expanded. Churches and private agencies need to double and redouble their efforts, but 1 percent of gross national product would be a reasonable guide. for the U.S. Government in planning its assistance. Such a guideline would allow for an expanding program as needs continue to rise. (3) That there be a greater grant commitment to education. 

Significant economic development and political and social progress are dependent upon the development of human resources. 

Private agencies equipped to deal with educational problems should be assisted extensively more than at present. (4) That more extensive use be made of multilateral agencies such as the United Nations in administering aid funds. (5) That increased effort be made toward population control through family planning. Control of population is essential to enable emerging peoples to deal more effectively with problems of economic and educational development. 

In summary let me return to the words of Pope Paul who warns that "this common task will not succeed without concerted, constant, and courageous efforts. But let everyone be convinced of this: The very life of poor nations, civil peace in developing countries, and world peace itself are at stake." It is a gigantic undertaking, the assisting of underdeveloped peoples of the world, but to use Theodore Roosevelt's words:

1967 

Either we will fail greatly or succeed greatly, but we cannot avoid the endeavor from which either great failure or great success must come. Even if we would, we cannot play a small part. If we should try, all that would follow would be that we should play a large part ignobly or shamefully. (James D. Richardson, ed., A 

Compilation of the Messages and Papers of the Presidents-1789 to 1902, Washington, 1904. Vol. X, p. 511.)

STATEMENT OF DR. VICTORIA SCHUCK FOR THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITY WOMEN, PROFESSOR OF POLIT- ICAL SCIENCE, MOUNT HOLYOKE COLLEGE, SOUTH HADLEY, MASS. 

Dr. SCHUCK. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am 

Dr. Victoria Schuck, professor of political science, Mount Holyoke

College, South Hadley, Mass. I am the legislative chairman of the 

American Association of University Women-an organization with a membership of 173,911, organized into 1,607 branches in the 50 States, Guam, and the District of Columbia.

The AAUW is pleased to submit this statement in support of the foreign assistance bill of 1967. In so doing, this association emphasizes, as in previous statements, that aid to the less developed countries must not be viewed as a charitable enterprise or an emergency measure but rather should be regarded as a continuing responsibility consistent with the objectives of U.S. foreign policy. 

In light of our past level of expenditures in aid to less developed countries through U.S. assistance programs, we further emphasize the need to build upon these investments by the passage of this legislation without decrease in the funds allocated to aid programs. AAUW has supported and continues to support the encouraging of multilateral programs and a self-help philosophy. But in our opinion, there

903 is some danger in the proposals before this committee of weakening our own on-going technical assistance and development programs by overemphasizing the merits of such international development assistance programs at this time. 

We also strongly support programs which encourage the development of private enterprise activities in the developing countries. 

Greater participation of U.S. private institutions and businesses in activities in these countries will also be of benefit-both to the developing economies and to U.S. business interests and should be encouraged. 

Consistent with the principle of multiyear authorization, we urge the passage of a 2-year authorization bill in which the appropriation is increased to a level more consistent with the urgency of the needs of the less developed countries of the world. 

We cannot stress too greatly the importance of the expansion of programs to broaden educational opportunities at all age levels, and at all educational levels from basic education through professional training in the developing countries. 

A population whose health needs are ignored does not flourish either socially or economically. We urge continuing emphasis upon the training of health professions personnel; the provision of health services; and population planning assistance when requested. 

AAUW encourages the directing of assistance funds to areas of primary importance such as agricultural development programs and the allocation of aid resources to programs judged to be of highest priority within the particular national context and at the same time are consistent with overall U.S. foreign policy objectives. 

I should like to add a few words about my personal experiences concerning our foreign aid programs in Southeast Asia where I spent 3 months under a grant last summer studying government personnel and budgeting especially in Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. I had opportunities to consult with more than 200 officials, civil servants, newspapermen, and businessmen and other nationals of these countries. My research gave me a chance to work with our AID staffs, and observe the operation of our AID programs, and to note the significance of these programs to American foreign policy. 

We do not have AID programs in Malaysia or Singapore. From my many discussions with Cabinet members in these countries, we should seriously consider inaugurating such assistance.

In Vietnam and Thailand, I found dedicated hardworking American staffs sensitive to the needs of these countries and often functioning under extreme hardships. Especially in Vietnam, there were shortages, of personnel, particularly in the province and district offices. Although staff buildup has been rapid and energetic, current levels-particularly in the provinces-are not yet sufficient to meet our expanded objectives in these areas. 

In developing countries where the national administration or bureaucracy and I use the word in the best sense to differentiate this branch from others in government-must carry the load of modernization and innovation, tremendous assistance can be given by the public administration specialists from the United States through the 

AID program. 

To mention just one other area, agriculture, we are rendering significant service both in Vietnam and Thailand. In Vietnam, our agricultural specialists in the midst of war conditions are introducing

1967 

methods of production which are contributing and will continue to contribute to greater food production. Specific programs which will improve the supply of food include the poultry and pig production and the crop rotation system. In one of the villages, a farmer out of gratitude offered to give us a duck-to bring this discussion down to personal and human terms. 

In Thailand, if Thai and American policy is to succeed in the northeast Provinces (I spent some time in Udorn and Khonkean) where the Communist threat is a very real one, the AID agriculture policy will bear a major responsibility. It was a matter of great pride to observe our programs and to receive the Thai reaction to them. I spent a day at an agribusiness meeting at which Thai and American officials met with the Thai equivalent of our extension agents and had a chance to see the strides being made in the introduction of new production and marketing methods. 

When one is in the field, as it were, and aware of local needs and conditions, one is repeatedly impressed with the wisdom of decentralizing decisionmaking to our field offices in programs and methods to execute them. We have made mistakes (what country does not?) but we have learned, and I believe that we have experienced personnel who are capable of making decisions in the best interests of our policy and the respective country. 

Grave difficulties often arise from the timing of the enactment of this legislation. Frequently there are but 7 months of the fiscal year following the date of appropriations in which programs can be firmly planned and carried out. To insure continuity and to make possible the long-range planning necessary for effective development, a multiauthorization of at least 2 years to me would seem imperative. 

May I add remarks about our food program in India? I had the opportunity to talk with Mrs. Gandhi about the grave economic problems confronting that country as well as to meet with American AID personnel. There is no question in my mind that, inasmuch as 

Indian officials are aware of the shortcomings of their past efforts in self-help and are attempting to correct these, we need to extend our food program to assist that country in every way possible. 

For these reasons-the disparities between the economy of the United States and the political and social development of these nations and the realization of a constructive American foreign policy- I think the foreign aid program should not merely be continued but expanded.

It is apparently a competent government which is doing everything it can to fight the Communist elements. 

It is competent not only in this respect but in carrying out a rural development program. While I think from the overall standpoint of 

American policy, we consider Malaysia within the British sphere of influence, there would be ways in which we could assist them as in rural development. 

Mr. ADAIR. Thank you.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS. 

Dr. Schuck, I don't suppose you are acquainted with the Weidler report on Vietnam? Have you ever seen it?

Dr. SCHUCK. No, sir, I am not acquainted with it. 

Mr. GROSS. It is quite critical in some areas of the use of funds under the present administration, and since you haven't seen it, I will not go any further with that.

Can I assume that the study grant you had was a study grant provided by the American Association of University Women?

Dr. SCHUCK. No, sir; this was a study grant which came from the four colleges of the Connecticut Valley as a consequence of a Ford Foundation grant for Asian and African studies. 

Mr. GROSS. You, I believe, would be, in advocating a 2-year program, foreclosing this committee to an annual review of the program, would you?

Dr. SCHUCK. No, sir; I think this could be worked out through the investigatory function of this committee. Of course it could be worked out in terms of the appropriation. 

Mr GROSS. You don't anticipate that if we put this on a 2-year or multiyear basis, this committee would give it much more than a once-over-lightly treatment as a matter of annual review. You surely don't believe that.

Dr. SCHUCK. I am sure, knowing the members of this committee, they would give full attention to it.

907 1 Mr. GROSS. We would if we had the opportunity. The chances are we wouldn't have the opportunity to do it. I thoroughly disagree, especially in the light of the way this program has fallen flat on its face in so many areas of the world. The gentleman from Indiana mentioned Malaysia. He might have mentioned Cambodia where we sunk a good many million dollars and apparently it is down the drain. 

You didn't get into Cambodia, did you, on your trip last summer? 

Dr. SCHUCK. No, sir; I made no study of Cambodia. I think if

I may comment on this, our attention is directed toward the need for the multiauthorization, because the people in the field are unable to plan adequately. Even though the programs may be proposed originally from the field to the national office and eventually to the Congress, there is no way to pin these down until the authorization and appropriations have been made. Therefore the Agency is unable, it seems to me, to take advantage of the opportunity of long-range planning. I should not think for a moment that this committee would abdicate its review.

Mr. GROSS. Having been in Vietnam, I wonder how you can say you could have very much advance planning. How do you know from one day to the next what the situation will be in Vietnam? After hearing all the witnesses that have come before this committee, I don't know what the future holds for Vietnam and I don't think most of the witnesses have the slightest conception what the situation will be in a month from now or 2 months or 6 months, in Vietnam. 

I don't see how with that as a focal point for the moment, how you can plan far in the future in Vietnam. 

Dr. SCHUCK. My remarks here are based on two levels of planning: one on long-range, and the other, you suggest, on short-term planning. 

Obviously we have to be able to adjust to changing situations. My testimony is designed to reorganize these two aspects of planning. 

Mr. GROSS. Dr. Schuck, some of us on this committee, some of us in Congress thought there was planning for the future in the United Nations and SEATO and various other organizations around the world, planning for the future, effective planning for the future. 

Yet we find when we get in a situation such as we are in in Vietnam that we have very few friends around the world; those upon whom we have lavished so much deliver so little. Having lavished billions upon billions around the world, we then get into a situation such as we are in today, and we find it is American blood that is being spilled. 

Almost no one else seems to be interested. 

This movement from the start was supposed to be dedicated to the purpose of heading off Communist aggression, the Communist conspiracy and takeover of people, yet those who live on the threshold of the Communists, are doing all too little these days. I don't know how people who advocate this giveaway program can explain this situation. I would like to hear an explanation from some of those who so ardently support the continuation of the spending of billions of dollars that we don't have in this country. 

You were present when I mentioned a moment ago the anticipated deficit of $18 to $20 billion next year. I am sure you are well aware that we have $336 billion of debt in this country, more debt than the

rest of the world combined. Yet people come here advocating the expenditure of money we don't have around the world. 

You suggest in your statement, Dr. Schuck, an expansion of this program, not maintain it at this level, but increase it. I don't know by how much. Are you speaking now in that statement for the American Association of University Women or is this a personal statement? 

Dr. SCHUCK. I will stand on the statement in the first two pages as far as the Association of University Women is concerned. May I give my personal reaction Mr. GROSS. The first group of witnesses this morning represents the Citizens

STATEMENT OF BRIG. GEN. BONNER FELLERS, U.S. ARMY (RE- TIRED), NATIONAL CHAIRMAN, CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COM-
