General FELLERS. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, my name is Bonner Fellers. I am grateful for the opportunity again to appear before this distinguished committee. I have served 30 years in the Regular Army. For 2 years, 1940-42, I was with the British the U.S. observer of combat in the Libyan Desert campaigns. De as During the years 1943-46 I participated in the war in the Pacific. 

There my principal assignments were Chief of Joint Planning under General MacArthur, his military secretary, and Chief of Psychological Warfare against the Japanese forces and homeland. Õ! a 

PROPOSED MILITARY ASSISTANCE, FISCAL 1968 

OTEZ For the Near East and South Asia $234 million has been requested mostly for Greece, Turkey and Iran. [From the President's Foreign Aid message to the 

Congress, on February 9, 1967.] 911

1967 

In past years U.S. military assistance of $1.9 billion has been granted to Greece and $2.7 billion to Turkey. Since Greece and Turkey are traditional enemies and momentarily at sword's point over Cyprus, the need for additional military assistance is not apparent. The present military revolt against constitutional government in Greece doubtless was effected with military equipment provided by the U.S. military assistance program. 

A huge segment of Iran floats on oil. In 1965 crude oil production was reported to be 93%½ million metric tons. Since World War II, Iran has been given $761 million in U.S. military assistance. If she needs more she herself can afford to buy it. 

For East Asia, I recommend $282 million, almost entirely for Korea and Taiwan. [Also from the President's message of February 9, 1967.] 

Korea has received $2.4 billion in U.S. military assistance. Her fighting forces in Vietnam are being supported from the U.S. defense budget. Korea's economy is expanding rapidly. Taiwan has received $2.6 billion in U.S. military assistance. 

Far East regional military assistance in prior years totals $2.7 billion. South Vietnam and the United States have not invited Nationalist China's forces to participate in the war. Taiwan's economy is flourishing. Before the President's request is granted, the need should be established as imperative. 

For Latin America, I recommend $45 million largely for internal security and training. [Also from the President's message of February 9, 1967.] 

In the past, Latin America has been given $1 billion U.S. military assistance. The Latin American continent receives incidental hemisphere protection from the U.S. Air Force and Navy. This billion dollars in U.S. military assistance, in several instances, has provided forces for the military to overthrow constitutional governments. 

The Cuban Communist infiltration can best be stopped at its source and someday the United States will have no choice other than to liberate Cuba.

For Africa, I recommend $31 million, heavily concentrated in countries where we have major interests and where there are problems of internal security. [Also from the President's message of February 9, 1967.] 

Africa has received $209 million in military assistance. These countries, nearly all of which have not yet started to emerge, need no more military assistance to enable them to kill one another. 

EUROPE 

The pullout of U.S. installations from France has been costly. The 

U.S. decision to pull back 35,000 troops from West Germany is correct. When U.S. troops were initially sent to Europe it was understood they would be returned to the United States as soon as Europeans could recover from the war and provide their own garrisons. 

Some time after General Eisenhower's arrival in Europe to set up NATO, he announced at a press conference that in 2 years his U.S. forces, replaced by Europeans, could be sent back to the United States. 

However, Europe moved into a strong economy which it was reluctant to disrupt by raising armies; consequently, U.S. troops have remained. 

Today, Europe with a population of 400 million and with a strong

913 economy can well afford to provide such ground forces as she deems necessary. Only our token forces in Berlin need remain. 

The free countries of Europe and the United States cannot afford to match the size of the Red army. The Kremlin is obliged to keep a large peacetime standing army; the enslaved, restless population is forced to endure its own military occupation. 

If the Kremlin has aggressive intent it can be deterred, not by land armies in Europe, but rather by superior strategic striking weapons from the sky. Unfortunately the United States lags in developing such a striking force.

CONTAINMENT FORCES 

In recent years Secretary McNamara has stressed military assistance to countries contiguous to the border of the Eurasian Communist bloc. These countries include, Greece, Turkey, Pakistan, India, Southeast Asia, the off-shore island chain of the Philippines, Taiwan, Japan, and lastly South Korea. In these areas the U.S. has doled out some $15 billion in military assistance.

However, if the Red forces decided to invade areas south of their borders, except in the present war zone, resistance would be slight. 

Red forces would enjoy the element of surprise, concentration of power, and air support. More U.S. military assistance to these contiguous countries, South Vietnam excepted, would be a waste of valuable means.

WHY MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

The CFAC receives frequent queries as to why the Congress continues to approve military assistance. Perhaps, the principal reason is the fear that in this turbulent world we cannot stand alone. A second reason is the hope that military assistance will somehow, at material saving, enable the free world to contain communism. A third reason is the economic aid program would have rough going in the Congress were it not tied to military assistance. 

It must be a frustrating disillusionment for one-worlders to realize that the United States is being compelled to stand alone. Allies for whom we joined in two world wars now give aid and comfort to our enemy. The military assistance program is making it crystal clear allies cannot be bought. State and Defense Departments officials testify military assistance is essential to our survival. Consequently, economic aid, tied to military assistance, wins congressional support which it might not enjoy as a separate proposal.

President Eisenhower spoke of military assistance in glowing terms. 

On March 3, 1959, he advised the Congress our friends among the free world make available to us for the use of our forces 250 strategic bases, 5 million ground forces, 30,000 aircraft, 2,500 combat vessels.

These available strength figures led the President to conclude: 

Dollar for dollar our expenditures for the mutual security program, after we have once achieved a reasonable military posture for ourselves, will buy more security than far greater additional expenditures for our own forces. [President 

Dwight D. Eisenhower, to the Congress, 3/13/'59.]

The continuous unjustifiable optimism of most foreign aiders toward our $36 billion military assistance program is incompatible with the facts. Except for South Korean forces and those of South Vietnam—

1967 

both victims of aggression-only token military assistance has been as- extended to us in our two most recent Asian wars. Token mustralia, sistance in Vietnam by Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Australia, and New Zealand is being given because, if the Reds win in Vietnam, these countries may soon be next. And they will need the only help in sight-faithful Uncle Sam! quoso quilia nwo ali gumbos of Den mumi gvizzeroms and ailing sdi bergoy 97

I am quoting from the President again on the foreign aid program in his message to Congress:04 TZUK ZIZIZ05 

The programs I propose represent the we can

ZTZOD contribution to mutual security and international development which wafely make. 

There are some who say that even this request should be foregone in view of the needs at home and the costs of the struggle in Vietnam. 

Nothing could be more short-sighted and self-defeating. This country-the wealthiest in human history-can well afford to devote less than seven-tenths of one percent of its national income to reduce the chances of future Vietnams. 

THE ENORMITY OF FOREIGN AID 

Foreign aid advocates are inclined to hide the true cost of their program. In the preceding quotation the President makes the aid burden as light as a feather by comparing it to seven-tenths of 1 percent of our national income which in 1966 was $610 billion. 

But this $610 billion is a statistic, not a fund from which foreign aid could be drawn. Foreign aid must be drawn from taxes and borrowed or printed dollars. Foreign aid costs can meaningfully be compared only to actual Federal receipts or Federal deficits or debts. For fiscal 

1967 the administration estimated its administrative receipts at $126.7 billion and its estimated deficit at $9.7 billion. On May 3, 1967, the U.S. gross public debt was $327.3 billion. Foreign aid from 1946 to include fiscal 1967 totals some $132.6 billion. 

By simple arithmetic, therefore, for fiscal 1967, foreign aid is the equivalent of 7.1 percent of Federal receipts and 93 percent of the 

Federal deficit. Total foreign aid expenditures (fiscal 1946-67) are the equivalent of 40 percent of the total gross public debt. 

THE WAY OUT 

The President's assurance is empty that foreign aid spending will "reduce the chances of future Vietnams." Contrariwise, Secretary of

State Rusk has given foreign aid as one of five reasons for our intervention in Vietnam.

Foreign aid entangles the U.S. in the military, economic, political, and psychological affairs of recipient countries. This every recipient resents. Two measures are n necessary to "reduce the chances of future 

Vietnams." As quickly as is feasible terminate foreign aid. Lift restrictions on U.S. air and sea power and win the war in Vietnam quickly and decisively.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General Fellers. 

Mr. Lory, you may proceed, sir. 11

STATEMENT OF MILTON M. LORY, SIOUX CITY, IOWA, REPRESENT- ING THE CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMITTEE 

Mr. LORY. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, thank you for the privilege of appearing before you to make a statement on foreign aid in Latin America. 

Sunday evening, April 2, Mrs. Lory and I disembarked from a Pan

American plane that had brought us from Caracas to Miami. We had just completed a 13,000-mile tour that had taken us into every country of South America. 

Since I speak Spanish rather fluently, we did not take a conducted tour. Our tickets were "open." We arranged our own travel plans, making our way by whatever means were available, car, boat, railway, bus, and many flights on 14 different airlines. Only two flights were by jet because most airport runways were too short. This gave us an opportunity to talk, visit, and make acquaintances and observe in a manner not afforded by the usual manner of tourist travel. 

One does not have to be an economist to see what, in a great part, our foreign aid has done to the welfare of South America. Almost everywhere economic instability and monetary turmoil were evident. 

I am not familiar with all of the South American giveaway programs, nor do I know the grand total of them all-but if the last 6 years of Alliance for Progress handouts of $9.9 billion is concernedthat alone would be $50 for every man, woman, and child on that continent. Even this amount has aided economic disruption. I would like to see an audit of the money we have put out in South America. 

Inflation is rampant everywhere and much of it for no apparent good reason. These countries have not contributed substantially to any world war efforts or to those of Korea or Vietnam, neither have they lavished their wealth on any foreign aid programs of their own. 

You just don't see children, newsboys, bootblacks, with handfuls of paper money to know that something is fiscally wrong with their country. The depreciation of currencies is appalling and the fright of its continued imminence devastating. I am surprised, that American bank note is not doing better on the New York Stock Exchange. Coins are now nonexistent in many areas. 

The cruzeiro is the unit of exchange in Brazil. I hold here a 500 cruzeiro note. In 1950, only 17 short years ago, this piece of paper would have been worth $30. It is now worth about 19 cents. I do not have to tell you what this has done to the people, particularly the poor of Brazil. The rice and beans they buy goes up in price faster than their income. Truly the rich are getting richer and the poor poorer. 

The fabulous homes, apartment houses, skyscraper, and other evidence of luxury and lavish living attest to the many inequities greatly induced by our foreign aid. I only cite here Brazil as it is the most glaring example of inflation.c

What is disturbing and highly inconvenient is that in some places. after purchasing a country's money at a bank, and being promised that you can redeem it when you leave, the bank will not give you back U.S. dollars when you go to exchange it-a downright dishonest move. 

No matter what we may think of our greatly weakened U.S. dollarit is still the best currency in the world and is universally sought. I 1

1967 

have continually noted this and have marvelled at the strength of our dollar in the 90 countries of the world I have visited. Yet I am concerned about its future value, knowing how foreign aid has harmed it. 

In Santiago, Chile, the elevator operator at our hotel would stop his lift between floors and offer to sell me, Chilean escudos for U.S. dollars at a substantial discount. 

A financial upheaval took place in Argentina while we were in Buenos Aires. (And I might interject here that there appears more tranquillity there than in many other places in South America. It is more like the United States.)

Banks were all closed. It was a bank holiday such as we had in 1933. 

The Argentine peso was to be devalued. It was the big topic of conversation everywhere. Everyone wanted dollars. What would the government peg the peso in relation to the U.S. dollar? 300, 325, 350 pesos to the dollar? Rumors were rampant. Speculation was widespread. The peso which in 1950 was worth 11 cents was worth about one-third of a cent. 

9 vd bebrol

In one morning in Buenos Aires, successively, I bought 290, 295, and 

300 pesos per dollar. At our hotel when dollars were presented for pesos the desk clerk would smilingly say, "hot money, these dollars go into the refrigerator." 

At 9 o'clock the night before we left Buenos Aires for Montevideo the Government preempted all radio and TV time and announced that the Argentine peso would be pegged at 350 to the U.S. dollar. Had we come to Buenos Aires a week later we would have profited by this devaluation as we could buy more for the dollar.

It was bantered around Buenos Aires that the same night the new price was announced US$2 million came out of hiding. In São Paulo, Brazil, I was informed that over US$6 million came out of hiding after Brazil's recent 22 percent devaluation.

In only one city where we wished to make purchases with U.S. dollars were we turned down and that was in Caracas, Venezuela. 

This was certainly not because the worth of the dollar was not known. 

We were refused merely to show a dislike for us. 

While on the subject of inflation in South America, and Brazil in particular, I should mention that which is most responsible for the economic woes of that land. It is the building of Brasília, the new capital, located about 600 miles inland from Rio de Janeiro. 

Started in 1960, the millions, yes, hundreds of millions that have been spent in creating this municipal fantasia beggars description. 

I only wish I could take you on my motion picture tour of that cityplanning and architectural wonder of the age-made possible only through our foreign aid. Probably you have seen it on your TV's. 

It was a noble idea, to get the people "off the beaches" and endeavor to instill in them some of the pioneering instinct that built the U.S. 

West, but it just hasn't worked. Those brought to this 39-square-mile federal district to do the construction work, and others induced to come here, are not going out on the surrounding fertile land to develop it, start farms, and raise the much needed food. Instead they congregate in villages outside the federal district and live as they did before leaving the big coastal cities. We took a native bus to some of these places. One village about 15 miles from Brasília we learned now

917 has a population of over a quarter of a million. In spite of foreign aid Brasília is breaking Brazil.

These people seem to not want to better their lot. They just want to herd together and have more children. Much could be said about the frightening population explosion in South America but time will not permit.

The numbers of persons seen around the plush hotels who are engaged in some phases of our giveaway programs is distressing and inclined to raise one's hackles. They don't live like most tourists and businessmen. They have better quarters and eat better food. Many seem downright unfriendly. They, probably are afraid of being questioned about their activities or their consciences are bothering them. 

We met individuals in isolated areas who became disgusted with the Peace Corps and quit. Some of their comments were most interesting.

One of the most glaring examples of waste was noted in Georgetown, the capital of Guyana,, formerly British Guiana. A block from our hotel was situated a fine Carnegie library exceedingly ample for the needs of the community. Two or three blocks up this street, the main thoroughfare of Georgetown, is a nice new John F. Kennedy Library.

The U.S. consulate or Embassy is nearby across the street. It is a good structure in keeping with the dignity usually accorded our diplomatic service. Directly across from our Embassy is a most expansive building housing AID. Why it is there and for what purposes the people couldn't do for themselves I could not ascertain. 

The dislike for U.S. citizens in South America is noticeable. It is increasing as I noted from a previous visit some years ago. Some of the incidents are subtle and some not so subtle. Most tourists we met told us the same and related incidents they had experienced. It is not hard to find the familiar "Yanqui go home" signs on walls, particularly around universities. I didn't know the word "Yankee" could be spelled so many ways. Yankee, Yanky, Yanki, Yanqui, Yankie, Yanquee, and just plain Yank. An added appendage to the "Yanqui go home" is "Viva le Guerrillas," meaning of course the Castroites or Communists. 

When talking to a sincere South American about world affairs I found much confusion over our role in Vietnam. It was difficult to say we were resisting communism when he brought up Cuba and asked why we do not destroy Castro. That was continually thrown at us. 

There are continual skirmishes between regular army troops and the guerrillas in the countries of northern South America. În one battle near where we were, according to the papers, 19 regular troops were killed and of course many more guerrillas or Communists. An 

AP dispatch only a few days ago told of a skirmish in Bolivia. Undoubtedly there is much more of this going on than we know. 

In conclusion, I feel that the continuance of foreign aid in South America is doing those people an injustice and is most damaging to the United States. It is putting the bellows to the fires of inflation and hatred. These people will never be satisfied. They will continue to want more and more and it is inconceivable that they be given preferential treatment for exports to the United States, as they are asking. 

We are financing competition with U.S. firms. Any relaxation of the way Alliance for Progress funds should be spent in the United States

1967 

is not good. The old adage, "He who pays the fiddler calls the tune," certainly should apply here.

It is reported that billions of dollars of the wealthy in South America are in Swiss and other banks and in foreign investments. Is it reasonable that we should pour money into an area that its citizens do not consider a good risk?

If the people of the United States were adequately given the facts of our foreign aid and a referendum could be had, it would be voted down. 

Again I thank you for this opportunity to present my views on this subject. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Lory.

STATEMENT OF DR. ELGIN GROSECLOSE, ECONOMIC CONSULTANT, REPRESENTING THE CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMITTEE Dr. GROSECLOSE. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, thank you for the privilege of again presenting our views on the foreign aid program. While the administration request under programs authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act is for slightly over $3.1 billion and administration spokesmen make much of its being the smallest foreign aid request in years, your committee is, of course, not misled.

Your committee realizes, as the distinguished chairman of the House Subcommittee on Appropriations, Congressman Otto A. Passman, has pointed out, this authorization deals with less than a third of the total foreign aid spending, which in turn does not include the military expenditures in Vietnam nor the economic aid expenditures in that area, now carried under the Department of Defense or other budgets. 

This requested authorization of $3.1 billion does not deal with the enormous sums being provided abroad through the food-for-peace program, the Peace Corps, Export-Import Bank lending, and the lending of various international agencies which are financed by the American people either through official appropriations or through borrowing in the U.S. money markets against the guarantee of the U.S. 

Treasury-such as the multimillion-dollar bond issue of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development recently sold in 

New York.

COMMERCIAL NATURE OF FOREIGN AID 

During the colloquy following our appearance before this committee last year, one of the distinguished members explained the rationale behind foreign aid as follows:

We are an export country. We produce more than we can consume or use. 

Our assisting countries to develop economically provides markets for U.S. products. 

Here, of course, is the naked truth regarding foreign aid, and why it receives so much support in the Congress. We are a surplus country and this surplus, it seems, must be drawn off as a cow must be milked to relieve its stress, or as a beehive must be robbed of its honey, or as in medieval times the affluent were periodically subjected to a bloodletting in the interest of their health.

919 Whether the theory is sound or not, it at least reveals the hypocrisy of the claim that foreign aid is the discharge of a great moral obligation to the rest of the world. Foreign aid, under this theory, is a necessity because the people of the United States, it would seem, are already too well circumstanced, too well provided, according to the John Kenneth Galbraith theory, with finned automobiles, washing machines, hair dryers, clothing, amusements, and the like; therefore, we must find some way of taking it away from them and redistributing it to the people of the other countries overseas. 

It is too bad the clergy who regularly come before the Congress to urge foreign aid-and I note the announcement last December that seven major denominations had set up a special Washington office to lobby for an $18 to $20 billion increase in foreign aid-it is too bad, I say, that these well-meaning clergy could not understand the Congress so well and save themselves this expenditure of time and money which could be better spent in foreign missions because Congress apparently will do its duty regardless of the petitions of the pious. 

This is a gospel and theory of foreign aid that should also be explained not only to the clergy but to their brothers of the administration who are preaching the poverty of America, and asking for billions to use on poverty in Harlem, Appalachia, and Watts, and other areas of our great country. 

This theory of our affluence should also be of interest to the housing industry now in the severest depression in years despite U.S. Census reports for 1960, that over 18 percent of all the housing units in this country were substandard, meaning dilapidated or lacking one or more plumbing facilities, and that over 27 million housing units, or over 46 percent, were 30 years old or older.

Some relief from burdensome taxes levied to milk off our surplus for foreign distribution would no doubt be welcomed by this ailing industry..

To Let us examine for a moment this theory that foreign aid is a necessary giveaway to absorb the U.S. surplus of industrial production. 

According to the March issue of the Survey of Current Business, the official source for balance-of-payments data, in 1966 the United States exported merchandise to the total value of $29.2 billion and imported merchandise to the value of $25.5 billion, leaving a net export balance of around $3.7 billion. 

However, U.S. grants, including military grants and capital outflows in 1966, totaled $4.6 billion, or $1 billion more than our export balance was able to sustain, or to put it another way the export surplus of $3.7 billion is completely illusory if the stimulus of Government-financed exports is excluded. o Actually, according to the official statistics, only $2.9 billion of the $4.6 billion Government grants abroad was used to finance exports of merchandise; a figure which blows into a cocked hat, incidentally, a claim of the administration that 90 percent of foreign aid goes to finance exports. If we include services along with merchandise we obtain a total of $3.9 billion, which is still far short of the 90 percent boasted by the administration.

Moreover, as was brought out in testimony by Dr. N. R. Danielian last year before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, there is little evidence that foreign aid does stimulate U.S. exports. obThus, in 1958, in the case of 25 countries receiving aid to the total of $1.7 billion, the U.S. trade surplus with these countries as only $251 million, leaving a difference of about $1.5 billion, which was used to buy goods and services elsewhere (generally Europe) or to obtain goods here which they were able to pay for with their own exports. 

In 1964 when U.S. assistance was substantially "tied" to U.S. procurement, the difference between the U.S. trade surplus ($1.1 billion) and U.S. economic assistance ($2.5 billion) remained at about the same level; that is, $1.4 billion.

Thus, although "tied" aid resulted in increased U.S. exports and a larger U.S. trade surplus with these countries, it did not improve the net difference between U.S. economic assistance and U.S. trade surque surplus. In other words, there is no evidence that "tied" aid ended the adverse effects of foreign aid on the U.S. balance of payments.

1967 

In the case of Latin America, U.S. exports did not increase but actually were less in 1964 than they were in 1957 despite an increase of U.S. net aid to those countries from $320 million to $489 million.

THE DILEMMA-TRADE OR A SOUND DOLLAR? 

We are now faced with another aspect of this theory of giving away our substance in order to promote the U.S. economy, particularly the export economy. It is well understood that some two-thirds of the world's trade travels on the American dollar; that is to say, merchandise and services are priced in dollars regardless of the market in which they are sold-even Russian commodities for sale in other countries than the United States are priced in dollars, Contracts are made in dollars. A large portion of the European capital market today is done in Eurodollars. It is not too much to say that the dollar is the universal currency to an extent that not even sterling in its halcyon days ever was. Beyond this we may say that the health of international trade and commerce depends upon sound dollar and an available dollar. 

However, the dollar today is everywhere in question. In our anxiety supply the rest of the world with the means by which to buy our exports, by giving them foreign aid dollars to spend in our markets, we have so corrupted the standard of value that it is everywhere in question.

European bankers frankly are alarmed and while no rescue operations have been undertaken of the magnitude that were started in 1961 in regard to British sterling, the fact is that next to Great Britain the United States had been the largest borrower from the International Monetary Fund, with borrowings of $1.64 billion at the end of February. 42 In addition, the Treasury, through the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, has had to arrange standby credits with various foreign central banks totaling $412 billion as of the end of February. This means of relief was started in 1962. For some time, also, Treasury authorities have been promoting a so-called central reserve unit or "paper gold" substitute for the dollar. nigh paper The realities are that the stability of the dollar cannot be maintained as long as the reserves by which it is supported are continually wasted away, and no official effort worthy of the name has been made to reduce the drain which is causing this waste. J oli poillid 7.12 

Since foreign aid began our gold reserves have been reduced by nearly a half from around $25 billion to around $13 billion currently, while foreign dollar claims have risen to more than $31 billion. 

Since 1961 various administrations have been telling us that the balance of payments will soon be redressed, but each year passes and while the actual amount of the deficit fluctuates it continues to remain serious in terms of gold loss and increase of liabilities to foreigners. 

The deficit in 1966 was $1.4 billion against $1.3 billion in 1965.

Such improvement as has been achieved has been largely in the private sector, such as reduction in private investments abroad which

923 create a return flow of income. Meantime expenditures for foreign aid and military operations in Vietnam continue to climb. The plain fact is that the deficit of international payments will not be corrected until the wasteful foreign aid program is eliminated. 

Inasmuch as there is no constitutional warrant for a policy of taxing U.S. citizens for the benefit of peoples of other sovereignties, we urge this committee to announce its opposition to the whole theory of foreign aid, except for disaster relief and deny authorization for the expenditures and programs included in the Foreign Assistance 

Act. The

How oft englob It is important to note that the economic exchange process is not complete with the first step of exchanging goods for money, but only after the second step of exchanging the money for another economic good.on with

If one individual or group of individuals exchanges goods or services for money, and retains or hoards part of this money-failing to exchange it for other goods and services, then an imbalance results. 

It means that others have production for which there is no market. 

Conversely, if by any means an individual or a nation obtains money without having supplied some goods or services for it, then there are also predictable In this basicnsequences from this type of imbalance. 

In this basic equation of economic exchange we see the fundamentals of trade between nations. Basically, a nation exchanges goods and services for goods and services; and normally, money is used to expedite the exchange. If the export and import of goods and services does not balance, then money will flow into or out of the country and there are economic consequences from this, for both those that lose money and those that gain. We shall see that the transfer of money directly, as gifts, introduces some complications but does not alter the fundamentals of the exchange process. ya Note that in the case of our foreign aid we take some of the money, which is merely a tool that we use for bringing about exchange of goods and services, and give it to foreigners. This moves the dollars out of our economy and into the economy of other nations. Now if the recipients of aid dollars promptly spent those dollars in the United States for goods and services, then we would merely have used our dollars as a tool for distributing some of our goods and services to other peoples.

We shall see shortly that this is not what has happened. The outflow of foreign aid dollars has left us with too few dollars to match our production, and foreigners with money in excess of their production of goods and services. 

The consequence of this is unemployment and a slower rate of industrial growth in the United States; and, by contrast, inflationary pressures and overstimulated growth in recipient countries. In this way we are said to export inflation.

THE BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS THREATS { 

The "balance of payments" is the term which is used to indicate the balance or lack of balance between the total flow of goods and services between one nation and all others. The balance of payments, of course, shows the sum of the net of foreign trade; the net of exchange of services (shipping, insurance, tourism, et cetera); the net on capital flow; and the net on gifts and loansoddalone p 

It is important to note that in the international marketplace there is no difference between dollars obtained from trade and dollars obtained from tourists and capital flow or from gifts. It is the total balance of payments that indicates our economic balance with the rest of the world. Our negative balance of payments merely means that more our dollars are leaving this country than are returning. 

I need not remind this committee of the size of our foreign grants and aid; how that it has actually increased in recent years instead of tapering off, and in total has now exceeded $123 billion. 

If all the foreign aid and loan dollars were spent in this country, there might still be serious problems, but they would not directly influence our balance of payments. This is a hypothetical question, however, because these dollars have not all been coming back to buy the products of our labor. The fact that foreign aid has added, and continues to add, to our negative balance of payments is reason enough for drastic cuts in the AID program. etto y 

The seriousness of the problem becomes evident when we take note of our international balance sheet. Chart 1 shows the balance of payments for the postwar years. Since 1949 there has been a persistent negative balance, except for the year 1957 when the Suez crisis forced Europe to buy oil from the dollar area. In recent years, this problem has become so severe that the Treasury has employed various schemes to postpone and forestall a crisis. These transactions make the official balance-of-payments deficit look smaller than it really is. 06 In chart 1 the solid line shows the balance of payments as usually quoted; the dashed line shows the negative balance on current account. 

The difference is the amount of prepayment of debt by the Germans and French, prepayment by the for purchase of military equipment, and the U.S. borrowing of foreign currencies. Germans

The improvement was the result of an improvement of our fundamental position. Also, crop shortages in 

Europe and the U.S.S.R. greatly improved agricultural exports in recent years, particularly 1965.

Since the private sector has a favorable balance, it must be the public sector-Government actions that cause the negative balance. 

There are several important components of the Government dollar flowout. One is the large number of Government people stationed and working overseas. Another is the more than three-fourths of a billion dollars sent overseas yearly as pensions. Third is the overseas expenditure for Vietnam. Fourth is the continuing large outflow of dollars in the form of aid grants and loans. 

When we examine the continuing outflow of dollars, we find that the basic cause rests in two facts: One is our massive foreign aid gifts which transfers dollars overseas; the other is the lack of competitiveness, on the average, of U.S. producers when they meet foreign competitors in world markets.

However sound the program of rehabilitation for Europe and Japan was at the end of the war, that job has long since been done. We can no longer afford the dollar drain even if the results from our present aid were good, which they are not. Y GTAAN

1967 

In the past year, spokesmen for foreign aid, sensitive to the impact of these dollar exports on our balance-of-payments problem, have claimed that 80 percent or more of foreign aid dollars are now being spent in the United States. Careful reading of official reports show that the emphasis is focused on aid expended for commodities. 

In 1966, $1.111 billion of the $1.232 billion for commodities were spent in the United States-90 percent. But, the amount of foreign aid spent on commodities is only a small part of the total. For example, in fiscal 1966 only $1.232 billion were spent on commodities out of a total of foreign grants and loans of $6.751 billion. 

Other expenditures include offshore purchases, foreign labor, and more than 3,300 personnel who are stationed overseas to administer aid. Even the $2.944 billion which the Department of Commerce reports as "Exports of goods and services financed by Government grants and loans" is less than half of the total of $6.751 billion (including military), and, therefore, a large portion of the aid dollars continue to contribute to our balance-of-payments problem. 

Figure 5 shows the history of commodities purchased with aid and the amount that was spent in the United States. In the early postwar years, most of it was spent here because we had capacity while the Europeans and Japanese were rebuilding theirs. As foreign capacity developed, more and more of the aid dollars were spent for foreign products because of lower price. In the last couple of years, we have tied aid to U.S. purchases and have reversed the trend.

It appears that in 1966 the total nonmilitary program of authorized aid was $8.1 billion, or $2.5 billion more than shown by the AID report. When all of the subsidiary requests are counted, the administration has requested more than $10 billion for the coming year. 

By focusing attention only on the foreign assistance requests and the agricultural commodities items under Public Law 480, the administration has diverted attention from the size of the total program, which has now grown to be larger than it was in the very first year of operation. It is no wonder that we continue to have a balance-ofpayments problem.

The outflow of dollars through these special programs is no less real because they are not labeled "foreign aid." The difference between the size of the total figure and the balance-of-payments deficit indicates that more of our exports are supported by our own dollars than can be shown directly. 

STOPGAP PALLIATIVES 

Because of the persistence and amount of the dollar outflow, in the past 3 years the Executive has taken many stopgap defensive actions to minimize the loss of gold.

Some of these actions are restrictions: The amount of goods which a tourist can bring back duty free, special taxation on foreign earnings and on foreign investments, renewed emphasis on "Buy American” policy, and direct and indirect export subsidies.

OF 1967 

We have urged foreigners, particularly the Germans and French, to prepay installments on long-term debt. And finally, our Treasury has been borrowing foreign currencies in an effort to minimize the gold loss. 

These stopgap actions have bought time, but we have not used the time to solve the fundamental problems which we still have to face. 

The consequences of continuing on the collision course which we have been pursuing will be disastrous. About 70 percent of the $31.4 billion of short-term claims against our gold are now being used by foreigners to support their monetary systems as though these dollar claims were, in fact, gold. Moreover, the other 30 percent can be used similarly, if private holders of dollars deliver them to their central banks. 

After all, we have promised to redeem all their dollars in gold whenever requested to do so. As a result of this, both we and the foreigners are extending credit against the same gold supply. When the day of reckoning comes, there will not be enough to go around. 

This is precisely the situation that led up to the banking problem in 1929 and brought the free world currency relations down together. 

The recent action by Congress to remove the 25-percent gold requirement against Federal Reserve bank deposits was necessary because we were reaching an impasse. Our dwindling gold reserve could no longer meet both the legal requirements for our own banking system and gold requests by foreigners for some of their dollar claims. 

This is another stopgap action which can buy us some time, but which does not solve the basic problem. If we continue on our present course, it will be only a matter of months before Congress will have to be asked to remove the gold clause altogether. At the end of 

1966, our free gold (the excess over and above the 25-percent cover for Federal Reserve notes) was only $3.3 billion. 

The sound, the basic, the ultimate action which we shall have to take to solve the balance-of-payments problem is to (1) cut foreign aid drastically, and (2) become competitive again in world markets.

The fact that we are, on the average, noncompetitive is clearly evident to any careful student, as indicated in numerous ways: 

1. Only after 5 years of massive injection of credit and easy money have we reduced unemployment in this country. By contrast, the economies of Europe and Japan were expanding so fast that they had to initiate restrictive monetary policies to slow down their "overheated" economies. In the 1950's and early 1960's, the industrial growth rates in Europe have been twice that of ours, and in Japan, three times. Even in international markets the customer seeks out the best buy. 

2. The character of our trade has changed. As recently as 1950 we imported primarily raw materials, tropical products, and products of low labor content, while we exported primarily finished manufactured goods of high labor content. By 1960 this had changed. We now export more agricultural products, raw materials, scrap iron, and products of low labor content, and import mostly finished products of high labor content cameras, typewriters, radios, TV's, watches, automobiles, scientific instruments, fabrics and clothing, and so forth. bobial a od 

3. Even our trade balance indicates our lack of competitiveness. 

The Department of Commerce data on trade shows a favorable bal- 

---

1967 

ance, with exports exceeding imports by $4 to $5 billion. Included in the export data, however, are products which we buy with our own dollars and ship overseas. This, of course, includes that part of the foreign aid dollar which is spent in the United States. When we subtract out the shipments to military establishments, the agricultural products under Public Law 480, and agricultural products which are subsidized, we find that the export surplus vanishes. 

Chart 7 shows U.S. imports and our exports adjusted to remove those which are bought with our dollars or subsidized. 

This portion of our exports has some significance for our balance of payments, but it does not indicate competitiveness. 

Moreover, the Commerce Department estimates that $2 to $3 billion of the remaining exports are shipped from American companies to overseas subsidiaries. In many cases, of course, these are not competitive shipments either.

Moreover, we count our imports on a foreign free-on-board value, whereas other countries count their foreign trade on a cost, insurance, and freight included value. Since our imports arrive on foreign bottoms, we actually pay out dollars for the landed cost. Were we to count our imports on a cost, insurance, and freight basis, we would have to add 15 to 17 percent to the value of our imports. 

Chart 8 shows the imports adjusted upward by 15 percent to adjust to a landed cost basis. It is clear, then, that even our trade balance adjusted to a competitive basis is unfavorable.

CHART 8 blod va birgumb and h No. 4, the final evidence of noncompetitiveness is, of course, the continuing negative balance of payments. If we were fully competitive in the world markets, the dollars which foreigners obtain by whatever means would be spent in this country for our products and our foreign accounts would show a balance. 

We became noncompetitive because the exchange rate between the dollar and other currencies has not changed with the changing competitive picture. After the war, Europe and Japan replaced their wartorn and bombed-out plants by modern, new automated ones. They did this largely with our foreign aid dollars and with a great deal of technical assistance from us. Consequently, they have made a great leap forward in productivity. Their unions did not demand that this productivity increase be matched by wage increases, and thus, the products of their factories became more competitive in world markets. 

During World War II and in subsequent years, we have poured more than $100 billion of inflationary money into our economy. As a result of this inflation, we have more than one worthless, "printing press" dollar for every good one.

After the war when consumer goods became available, there was $2 coming to the marketplace to buy a dollar's worth goods. Since the market couldn't tell the good dollar from the bad dollar, the price of goods was bid up until a dollar's worth of goods was selling at $2; in fact a little more, because the dollar is now worth only about 42 cents as compared to its prewar value.

1967 

The price of labor went up with, in fact a little faster than, the price of goods; and as a result, today American workers and American factories are no longer competitive in world markets. 

We see the real consequences of this when we turn our attention again to the basic exchange equation: GOLD GOODS

DOLLARS GOODS 

When foreigners exchange goods and services to us for our dollars, or get dollar gifts, normally they would exchange those dollars for goods and services from us. Through the process of inflation, the prices of our goods and services have more than doubled; but there is one economic good, gold, which is still priced at $35 an ounce where it was fixed in 1934.

Thus today, gold is the cheapest commodity we offer the world. It is not surprising, therefore, that foreigners who get dollars prefer to keep part of those dollars to exchange for gold. 

Of course, as we have seen, they don't actually have to exchange them for gold as long as the world has confidence that we will honor our obligation to furnish gold upon demand. By holding their dollar claims in the form of Treasury bills, they can collect interest until such time as they may choose to request gold.

Actually, there are two types of imbalance which are involved in our international finance relations. Since the dollar price of gold has remained fixed by Government and has not been able to adjust upward along with other prices, the dollar price of gold no longer represents its true value in terms of labor and capital to find, mine, and refine it. 

This disparity can be fixed only by a devaluation of the dollar or a long-term adjustment of all other prices downward. 

A more pertinent imbalance insofar as balance of payments is concerned is the exchange rates between the dollar and other currencies. 

The current exchange rates do not accurately reflect the relative value of the dollar with respect to other major currencies. If we do not remove this distortion by an appropriate adjustment in the exchange rates, we will be forced eventually to devalue the dollar. 77 

If the exchange rates were adjusted to be realistic, then our products would become competitive in world markets and we would earn back the dollars which foreigners obtain from us through trade, tourism and capital flow.

BASIC SOLUTION TO BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS PROBLEM 

We need to take three steps to attack the balance-of-payments problem at its base. First, we must drastically reduce our foreign aid program and the small part of it which might be continued should require that the dollars be spent in the United States.

939 The director of AID is trying to increase the fraction of foreign aid dollars which are spent in this country. It is generally assumed that if all the aid dollars were spent here, then there would be no influence on the international standing of the dollar. This is a mistaken notion. 

When aid dollars are spent here, the overall transaction consists essentially of the Government buying products from U.S. producers, paying for them from the Treasury, and shipping them overseas. If the Federal budget were balanced, such a transaction would consist of using taxes to furnish aid to other countries. It would reduce our standard of living by an equivalent amount, but it would not endanger our monetary system.

We do not and have not had a balanced budget. The aid dollars add to our deficit, and hence, contribute to monetary inflation. If we continue to erode the value of the dollar by monetizing debt, it is only a question of time before foreigners will lose confidence in the dollar and call for gold. When the fundamental economics is considered, it is clear that we cannot afford large grants of aid whether the dollars are spent here or not.

Secondly, we need to put an end to Federal deficits in order to reassure the foreigners that we have put a stop to monetary inflation in the United States. This will give them confidence that we will be able to avoid devaluing the dollar and lessen their likelihood of calling for gold. It is an absolute certainty that if we continue monetary inflation in this country, sooner or later we shall have to devalue the dollar. 

Finally, we need also to readjust the exchange rate of the dollar as between the currencies of the major industrial countries of the free world. Prior to World War I, exchange rates were set in an exchange market, much like a grain or stock market. The exchange rate between, for example the U.S. dollar and the British pound, was determined on a day to day basis by the supply and demand in exchange of the one for the other.

We no longer permit a free market to set the exchange rates. They are set by the International Monetary Fund. The present exchange rates for the dollar were set soon after World War II, before anyone could foresee the large and rapid increase in productivity in Europe and Japan. Because of this and divergent monetary policies here and overseas, the present exchange rates are unrealistic and overvalue the dollar.

So long as exchange rates do not accurately reflect the wage rates times productivity of the different countries balance-of-payments problems will be chronic.

SUMMARY 

For too long we have been satisfied with a superficial look at the balance-of-payments problem. The situation is now so series that we can no longer afford to delude ourselves. We must adjust our policies to match the fundamentals of the situation. 

An examination of the fundamentals of economic exchange and monetary policy makes it clear that we cannot afford to continue our massive foreign aid program. Our taxpayers already are burdened with a Government debt that is about $100 billion larger than that of all the other countries of the free world together. 77-470-67-pt. 5—3

1967 

If we continue our profligate giving, we shall hasten, if not actually precipitate, a world liquidity crisis. This will have dire consequence both for us and the free world. First of all, it would certainly disrupt the U.S. economy and result in the most severe setback our economy has seen since the 1930's. This would shake the confidence of the rest of the free world in our enterprise system. Other peoples would be skeptical of an economic system plagued with such difficult problems..

In the postwar years, the dollar has become an important reserve currency. In a sense, we have become the bankers of the world. In the face of this circumstance there will be serious consequences if respect for the dollar is lost. We will lose more than our position as world banker; we will forfeit our leadership, politically and ideologically as well.

In the face of these consequences, we dare no longer postpone a substantial cut in foreign aid authorizations. In fact, the continued gifts from funds already authorized but not yet distributed may be enough to precipitate a crisis without further authorizations. It is time to adjust policy to reality, and stop or drastically reduce aid authorizations.

Mr. WHALLEY. About spending. 

General FELLERS. I think this year we could balance our budget by making no appropriation for foreign aid. There is probably $15 billion in the pipeline that is unexpended. I would certainly think that there could be a carryover of spending for the foreign aid program and no new appropriation this year, which would help tremendously on the appropriations.

Mr. WHALLEY. Each year we have a wage-price spiral which pretty much puts us out of competition with the rest of the world. Would it be better to try to hold wages in some way and bring prices down, which would keep us competitive with other nations and also keep the 30 million people on social security and other forms of retirement in the market?

Dr. LLOYD. Mr. Congressman, in all recorded history whenever paper money is put into circulation as for example by monetizing Federal debt, there is no known way of keeping prices and wages down. 

Even when black marketeers have been faced with a death penalty they succeed in taking place. The only way to get this problem is to cut out the monetization of Federal debt.

Mr. WHALLEY. We keep thinking we are in good shape as far as imports and exports are concerned. Do you think it would be well to also base the amounts on the hours of production or the hours of productivity that goes into the exports or imports instead of just the total dollar volume?

In other words, if Japanese wages are $50 a month, and we receive $100 million in imports for example from them and we export $100 million to them, at our wages of say $3 an hour, wouldn't it be well also to consider the quantity of products that we are getting?

Dr. LLOYD. The marketplace, if it is free to adjust currency exchange rate will adjust so that the wage rate times the productivity in one country will balance out the wage rate times productivity in another country. If the exchange rate is not free to adjust to these changes, the wage rate times productivity, you see, then we end up with the imbalance.

Mr. WHALLEY. The productivity in Japan, West Germany, and the other nations is just as great as it is in our country apparently due to the fact that they have just as modern plants as we have and in some cases even more so.

Getting back to the gold situation, does anyone know the cost of mining an ounce of gold today?

945 1 1 Dr. LLOYD. That will depend on the particular mine. In South 

Africa presumably at the wage rate they are paying with the highyielding ores they have, they are making a return, maybe a satisfactory return at present prices. The reports are that the Russians are mining gold and it is costing them about $67 an ounce, almost twice the market value of it in the free world. There is essentially no gold mined in the United States any more because the cost of mining it is so high that $35 an ounce doesn't make it worthwhile.

Mr. WHALLEY. General de Gaulle would like to double the price of gold. Do you think he might persuade other people to raise the price to say $70 an ounce ?

Dr. LLOYD. I doubt he can succeed in getting other people to do this until or unless we take a move. As long as we will supply gold at $35 an ounce, nobody else can raise the price. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Is there a new U.S. policy which we are going to put into effect or refusing to sell gold at the world price of $35 an ounce?

Dr. LLOYD. This is being discussed. 

Mr. WHALLEY. What effect would that have if the world found out we have refused to sell gold for dollars at $35 an ounce? 

Dr. LLOYD. The first effect would be to announce to the world we were insolvent in our international accounts. The dollar would slip with respect to other currencies. No longer would the European countries accept the dollar at $35 an ounce. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, at the start of this discussion you seemed to minimize the statement made by the gentleman from Indiana, Mr. Adair, with respect to the demonstration that he spoke of. Mr. GROSS. A few days ago a 15,000-person demonstration occurred in Paris, American flags were dragged through the streets and burned and the police apparently did little or nothing about it. This is in 

France where, for all the billions we poured into that country, we ought to be getting a far different reception. We are not, and I don't minimize what is happening. I think these demonstrations that are increasing in foreign countries symbolize the fact that we haven't bought much of anything with the billions upon billions that we have spewed out in foreign aid.

I want to commend you gentlemen for your excellent statements, all of you. I am particularly interested in the fact that you spoke of the differential in building ships in foreign yards. We went over and bombed out the shipyards in World War II in Germany and in Japan. 

Then we turned around and used various forms of aid, and various devices to rebuild their yards. We built them new, modern, automated yards.

Today Congress is called upon to subsidize, I believe the differential, based upon Japan is 55 percent, the building of ships in American yards which are antiquated and labor costs are higher. 

This is the way our money has been going in foreign aid and then we run into this competition, hopeless competition for American shipbuilders. The reason why we subsidize, of course, is to employ American labor. On no other basis can we build ships in American yards except to go to the taxpayers and get the money to do it. It is just one of the byproducts of what we have gone through in this fantasy of foreign aid. I don't want to continue it.

You gentlemen have made, I say again, excellent statements. It is refreshing to have you come before this committee with a new breath of air because all I have heard and all we hear, with the exception of you gentlemen, and one or two others, is support for this program that has cost the taxpayers of this country so dearly. 

I might add that on top of rebuilding German shipyards, helping them to rebuild their automated yards, the Germans have today in the Federal Reserve Bank vaults in Manhattan $4,300 million of gold stashed away in this country. France has $5,200 million of gold in the 

Federal Reserve vaults. The central banks of foreign countries and foreign governments have more money in the Federal Reserve vaults in New York City today than the U.S. Government can lay claim to in Fort Knox and in the Treasury vaults, the assay offices around the country.

949 This is what we have gotten into in part with this foreign aid program. I agree with you there isn't any reason why, with the ability to deobligate, reobligate, transfer money, so on and so forth, we shouldn't go to the foreign aid pipeline, cut this new money program out entirely, go to the pipeline phase this program out, get rid of it and save the hides of the American taxpayers. 

Dr. GROSECLOSE. Mr. Congressman, could I take this occasion to respond to a question raised by the chairman earlier as to whether we had made appearances before other committees that have charge over certain aspects of foreign spending which properly should be considered by this committee.

We have where we have been able to. The funds of the committee are limited; it is a small committee, not highly financed; it is difficult to keep track because a lot of things are running around. Last week there were hearings before the House Banking and Currency Committee on an authorization for increased funds to I believe the Fund for Special Operations of the Inter-American Development Bank. 

Those hearings were held before we were aware of them. We had little opportunity to present a statement. Dr. LLOYD. In the case of Dow Chemical Co.- 

Mr. MURPHY. Any company.

Dr. LLOYD. Let me first mention a specific case. In our case our net return from export of goods and services far exceeds any capital outflow in the case of Dow. In the case of the total companies, U.S. companies since 1950, the minimum year has been a net positive inflow of dollars against capital outflow of the minimum is about $500 million and the maximum is something over a billion, except for one year, 1957, when there was a negative, more outflow than inflow in that one year. 

Mr. MURPHY. Does this operation affect unemployment in this country?

1967 

Dr. LLOYD. Do you mean the export?

Mr. MURPHY. I mean the fact of operating on foreign soils instead of operating in the United States? 

Dr. LLOYD. No, I wouldn't say so because we are either exporting goods made with American labor to foreign countries or operating plants there which with their labor are selling to their citizens in which case the only impact on the home company is earnings brought back which then can sustain expansion and good wages here at home. 

Mr. MURPHY. If you had that operation in the United States instead of a foreign country you definitely would have to employ Americans, would you not?

Dr. LLOYD. Yes; but we probably wouldn't be able to sell much of the product in the foreign market. We find that practically every country around the world as soon as we can establish a-justify a small plant to produce something that we can sell not only that product but many of the other products that we can export because then the natives think of it as a local business and they are more inclined to buy than they are to buy from the United States directly.

The members of these organizations share the view of one ambassador to the United Nations who said recently, "It is UNICEF's duty and privilege to keep children before the conscience of mankind".

THE FIRST 20 YEARS Last December, UNICEF celebrated its 20th birthday. On December 9, 1966, the members of the UN's Third Committee, which is concerned with UNICEF's work, met to evaluate and to pay tribute to UNICEF for its accomplishments during the two decades of its existence. After listening to the words of praise from a number of the delegates present, Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Michael Comay, was moved to observe: "UNICEF's remarkable achievements could be doubled and trebled if the tributes to it could be converted into negotiable currencies, and the currencies converted into more training programs, equipment and national planning for the greatest of all national resources-each country's babies and children".

955 UNICEF's Executive Director, Mr. Henry R. Labouisse, considers the occasion of the 20th birthday an appropriate time to review highlights in the history of the organization, to examine what has been accomplished, and, most of all, to explore the needs and possibilities for the future. As he sees the purpose of this vital agency of the United Nations, "There are two main themes characterizing its work: the humanitarian, predominant from the beginning, and, of course, ever-present; and, secondly, the development of human resources, a prerequisite to economic and social development". 

From the beginning, members of our organizations have been deeply moved by the humanitarian appeal of a sick, hungry, and helpless child. The symbol of the child with the cup of milk established UNICEF's image as an emergency feeding program which, in large measure it was, in the aftermath of World War II. Gradually over the years, however, the broader objective, the development of human resources, has gained increasing recognition as the foundation on which sound economic and social development can take place. Unless the majority of the children of a country can have the opportunity to develop into strong, healthy and educated citizens ready, each within the limits of his own ability, to make his contribution to the society in which he lives, that country cannot benefit fully from any amount of outside financial and technical aid, no matter how massive in quantity.

The recognition of this basic principle is reflected in the new direction of the U.S. bilateral aid programs. More and more insistence is being placed on the criterion of self-help, of matching within the country the external aid received. 

We should like to suggest again that UNICEF's success in accomplishing so much good for so many children with such small amounts of money has been due in large measure to the fact that UNICEF aid has always required that the assisted country should contribute an amount in goods and services equivalent to the external aid received. It has stressed the importance of self-help. Also, this requirement of matching has generated additional assistance to UNICEF projects at a ratio, on the average, of $2.50 for every UNICEF dollar. 

UNICEF'S ACCOMPLISHMENTS 

A few dramatic statistics will illustrate UNICEF's impressive success story and remind us again of what has been made possible with very modest resources. 

Emergency aid to 13 countries. During the winter of 1947-48, UNICEF gave 

4 million children and mothers a meal a day. To war-devastated countries in 

Europe it provided clothing, medicines, soap, lard, blankets, skim and powered milk. In 1950 relief operations in Europe ended. While emergency aid is today only a small part of its work, UNICEF has provided blankets, clothing, milk and other foods, and medical supplies to child-victims of earthquakes, floods, typhoons, epidemics, famine in 50 countries. 

Permanent health services in 122 countries.—UNICEF has helped to establish over 33,000 health centers serving more than 100 million people. Services have included health care to mothers before, during and after the birth of their babies, regular health examinations and treatment of infants and young children, nutrition and health education for the mothers. UNICEF has provided over 1,500 training institutions for medical workers and over 61,000 stipends and fellowships for health workers, nurses, sanitation workers and other health personnel. It has helped to establish vaccine-production factories in 22 countries to combat some of the major communicable diseases affecting children. It has assisted sanitation projects (providing safe water, improving plumbing and sewage facilities, and aiding health education) to reduce infant dysentary, typhoid fever and cholera in 65 countries. It has helped to provide programs for care and rehabilitation of blind and orthopedically handicapped children. 

Control of communicable diseases. More than 2 million persons have been treated for leprosy in 41 countries. In the campaign against trachoma (a disease usually contracted in infancy) 40 million persons have been given eye examinations; over 22 million have been treated for trachoma and over 8 million have been treated for conjunctivitis. In cooperation with WHO and other agencies, UNICEF is helping in the struggle to eradicate malaria all over the world. 

It has aided projects in 60 countries. In one year alone, over 36 million persons were protected from the disease by UNICEF supplies. Here again the highest death rate is found among children, accounting for 10-15% of all infant deaths. 

Already a reduction of many millions of cases has been accomplished. Tuberculosis, another affliction to which children are especially susceptible, has been at- 77-470-67-pt. 54

1967 

tacked in 88 countries, where over 200 million children and young people have been vaccinated with BCG vaccine. UNICEF aid has gone to yaws campaigns in 

52 countries; 350 million persons have been examined and more than 43 million have been treated.

The fight against hunger and malnutrition in 87 countries. The main programs which UNICEF has assisted to improve child nutrition are: child feeding; the distribution of milk and vitamins; applied nutrition; aid for over 4,500 school gardens or canteens; fish culture, poultry and small animal raising; milk conservation: UNICEF has equipped over 200 milk processing plants in 41 countries. New protective protein-rich foods have been developed, tested and processed thru 10 projects in 6 countries. 

The campaign against ignorance and illiteracy in over 60 countries.-UNICEF has helped to equip over 7,000 schools and teacher training institutes and over 300 vocational training institutions. 

In 1966 alone, UNICEF assistance was reaching children in 119 countries. 

THE CONTINUING NEEDS OF CHILDREN 

Ambassador Goldberg commented at the meeting of the Third Committee last December 9 that he regretted the fact that the word "emergency" has been removed from the name of the United Nations Children's Fund because it is his view that whenever a child is starving, or malnourished, or sick, or neglected, an emergency exists. A child in need is always an emergency. He should be able to receive the necessary care. So long as the survival of millions of children is threatened by starvation, malnutrition, sickness and illiteracy, an emergency will continue to exist and efforts must be made to meet it. 

Most Americans think of food deprivation only in terms of hunger. Malnutrition, a diet lacking in the proper balance, is, like hunger, largely rooted in poverty. Evidence is accumulating that malnutrition in the first three years of life, when the human brain grows rapidly to reach 80% of adult size, may permanently impair intelligence. This evidence was discussed early in March 1967, at a conference held in Cambridge, Mass., sponsored by the Nutrition Foundation of New York and the Department of Nutrition and Food Science of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and aided by a Ford Foundation grant. The conference heard estimates that from 300-350 million children under the age of six are suffering from malnutrition. This threat to child development could mean that more than half of the 90 million babies born each year may be running the risk of permanent retardation solely from malnutrition. Furthermore it has been estimated that 30,000 children die every single day-of hunger or disease that could, in so many cases, have been prevented. The challenge to UNICEF in this field is clear.

To break out of the age-old cycle of ignorance-disease-poverty, better education is essential. Training in child care for the mothers can teach them how to protect their families from many of the debilitating scourges of the past. 

Teachers, practical nurses, and sanitarians need assistance in order to learn how to help their people. One teacher can inspire hundreds of mothers to create a better life for her family; the benefits are incalculable that can result from a stipend granted to a potential teacher to make possible such training. Small grants provided through UNICEF assistance can offer this important catalyst to a better standard of living.

Beyond the basic training for mothers, however, is the great need for education for the oncoming generations of children. Half of the children in the developing countries never go to school. Of those who do, only one out of three are able to complete the elementary grades. Here is another area where the developing countries are requesting UNICEF's help-for training stipends, for even the simple tools of learning such as pencils, crayons, etc. Much remains to be done. 

UNICEF'S TARGET BUDGET 

The delegates to the Executive Board meeting of UNICEF in Addis Ababa last May adopted a target budget of $50 million to be reached by the end of the UN's Development Decade. Last year UNICEF's income was $35 million. The higher amount is by no means a measure of the total needs of children but there was warm support among representatives for the target and UNICEF's Executive Director regards $50 million as an amount that can be used immediately and most effectively. UNICEF's Executive Board sees so clearly how a small amount of money can go a long, long way. In fact, one UN official has said that the most

957 important contribution of all economic and social develpment is the idea itselfthe opportunity to show people what is possible, what they can do to help themselves. This does not cost very much but viewed against the needs of nearly one billion children, even a target of $50 million is modest indeed. 

The first government to make a contribution to UNICEF was the United States. The amount was $15 million; the year, 1947. We are proud of our country's leadership in the beginning and our continued support of the Children's Fund and its work in aiding children, not only as a humanitarian gesture but also as sound economic policy. However, when there remain hungry, malnourished, sick and illiterate children and young people, the challenge will have to be met. Our organizations believe that it is again time for our country and this 

Congress to reaffirm its dedication to the worth of young people, not only at home but throughout the world, and to assert its leadership in this continuing struggle to save the children.

For the past 8 years, the contribution to UNICEF by the United States has remained at the same amount: $12 million. The Department of State has again recommended that same figure, subject to a matching ratio of 40 percent, for Fiscal 1968. We support the State Department's request reluctantly, accepting the estimates of the experts that other countries may be unable in the year ahead to increase their own contributions to the Children's Fund sufficiently to permit a substantial increase by the United States above the $12 million on the basis of matching at 40 percent. So far this year, the governments of France, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland and Korea, among others, have announced increased con tributions to UNICEF's Central Account. Total Government contributions to 

UNICEF have increased slowly but steadily over the past few years. 

In the expectation that this trend will continue, our organizations request this Committee to authorize and direct the Executive Branch to recommend an increase in the U.S. contribution to UNICEF next year on the established matching basis. This will enable the United States to match the higher contributions anticipated to be forthcoming from other governments in the years ahead and serve as an incentive to them as well, in the effort to meet the target budget of $50 million for the world's children in 1970. Since it does not appear possible this year, then certainly next year, it is our hope that the United States contribution can once again reach the amount of $15 million which was contributed in 1947.
