STATEMENT OF MRS. THOMAS KOUZES, MEMBER OF THE PTA LEG- ISLATION INFORMATION COMMITTEE, PRESENTING STATEMENT FOR MRS. EDWARD F. RYAN, CHAIRMAN OF NATIONAL PTA COM- MITTEE ON LEGISLATION, NATIONAL CONGRESS OF PARENTS AND TEACHERS Mrs. KOUZES. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee: 

I am Mrs. Thomas Kouzes, member of the legislation information committee of the National Congress of Parents and Teachersnational PTA.

On behalf of our membership, we wish to reaffirm our established policy of support for UNICEF-United Nations Children's Fundand particularly to offer support of the recommended appropriation of $12 million as the U.S. Government's contribution to the UNICEF program for fiscal 1968. But also we continue to urge, and look forward to, an increased appropriation for this worthy program as it extends its invaluable assistance to millions of children and youth. 

Since the inception of UNICEF in December 1946 to provide emergency assistance to needy children in Europe, the National Congress of Parents and Teachers has consistently supported this program. 

Our organization comprises more than 11 million memberships in 50 States, in the District of Columbia, and in the American overseas dependents schools. It has been dedicated since its beginning, in 

1897, to the health, education, and welfare of American children. 

It has always been in the forefront in encouraging the development of UNICEF into a permanent organization concerned with the health and welfare of all children in the world. 

In 1961, at the request of the executive board of UNICEF, and in cooperation with many governments and agencies of the United Nations, a world survey of the needs of children was undertaken on a global scale. The needs studied in this survey are overwhelming. 

They are further compounded by their interrelationship and their cumulative effects. Poverty entails ignorance, one of the causes of malnutrition; malnutrition brings disease, which in turn produces poverty. This vicious circle is fearsome in its consequences because the lives it threatens are already weakened ones. 

In our world today, there are approximately 1 billion children, and three out of four of them live in the "developing" countries.

963 These countries, struggling to achieve an economic status somewhat comparable to industrially advanced ones, have 600 million children suffering from hunger, disease, or lack of education, and most frequently from all three.

UNICEF has been in the forefront of the fight for the preservation of the world's greatest resource-its children. From its small beginnings in 1946, it has brought lifesaving aid to millions of children and mothers.

Today, the first babies helped by UNICEF are celebrating their 

21st birthday. This new generation of healthier and better prepared young adults are stepping into the adult world because mankind 21 years ago marked a new dimension in civilization, when it recognized man's united responsibility for all children, everywhere. 

A suffering child is more than a heartbreaking fact; it means a serious loss of strength for a country that is still poor. An illiterate child is not only deplorable in our modern world, it means the loss of a potential leader or teacher for a country that cannot afford that loss. 

To alleviate the present misery of a child or mother is one area of work for UNICEF, but its work goes deeper as it encourages and stimulates economic and social progress that will prevent such misery. 

In this area, the work of UNICEF has been indeed spectacular, within the limitations of its budget. The UNICEF program has always been conducted in the best tradition of "self-help" and has been described as a poineer in this emphasis. 

In recent years the average contribution by each country aided was $2.50 in services, materials, and funds for every dollar of UNICEF money spent. Because of insufficient funds, however, many worthwhile projects could not be considered, and it would seem that an increase in our contribution would be justified, particularly because of the population explosion and UNICEF's dramatic impact for good. 

For the past 8 years, however, our Government has recommended that our contribution be $12 million, on the basis of the State Department's expert advice that pledges made or anticipated from other governments cannot be raised to match more than $12 million-at 40 percent.

The general upward trend does continue, however, with Sweden's spectacular increase last year of 50 percent. The United States is

UNICEF's largest contributor in dollar total, but it is not at all its largest contributor per capita. We rank, in fact, eighth: Sweden is first, with 19 cents per capita; Norway, 12 cents; Denmark, 9 cents; 

Monaco, 8.8 cents; Liechtenstein, 7.9 cents; New Zealand, 7.7 cents; 

Switzerland, 7.3 cents; United States, 6 cents.

In these years of service since 1946, UNICEF has treated approximately 22 million cases of trachoma, more than 2 million cases of leprosy, and 43 million cases of yaws; and has given more than 200 million vaccinations for TB. From vast sections of the world, it has helped eradicate malaria (described by experts as the world's most costly disease because it not only kills and incapacitates man, but ruins the land for habitation). It has established and equipped more than 

33,000 maternal and child health centers and subcenters. It has provided scholarships and training allotments to thousands of nurses and auxiliary health and social workers.

1967 

The consequences for good of this care and training is incalculable. 

These children are the potential leaders of tomorrow. These are the children who will work alongside our own children as adults in an increasingly interdependent world.

It is a sad commentary on our world to note that UNICEF helps millions of mothers and children each year with less money than the governments of the world spend on armaments in less than 2 hours of a single day. Would that we could devote more of our money and talents to solving these health, poverty, and education needs. 

With an awareness of our country's leadership in building this better world for our heirs, that they may grow and live in peace, we are especially grateful for this committee's consideration of this important item. 

Thank you very much. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mrs. Kouzes, for a very interesting statement. I am sure the committee will go into the figures submitted by the State Department this year relating to our contributions to 

UNICEF to see if our contribution is adequate.

In my long service on this committee we have not been concerned so much with holding down our contribution or fixing a limit of $12 million for UNICEF, but whether or not the other nations of the world will match our contribution. You have given some indication here that some countries such as Sweden and others may be willing to increase their contributions. I for one would be glad to vote for more money for UNICEF if the other countries would come through with matching contributions so as to bring the budget up to $50 mil lion by 1970. 

Mrs. KOUZES. We appreciate that very much. We understand the problem involved.

I would like to make the following comments about this statement by Dr. Lloyd: 

1. With one exception, the table does not represent data reported by A.I.D 

The one exception is that the first column sets forth figures that are in a report- 

U.S. Overseas Loans and Grants, and Assistance from International Organiza tions-prepared for the Foreign Affairs Committee by A.I.D. The figures in that column, however, do not represent A.I.D. grants and loans, but the total of all 

U.S. overseas grants and loans under the A.I.D. program, the military assistance program, the Food for Peace program, the Social Progress Trust Fund, other U.S. economic programs and Export-Import Bank long-term loans. 

2. The figures in the second column are the same ones that appear in the 

June, 1966 and March, 1967 issues of the Survey of Current Business, published by the Department of Commerce, on line 28 of Table 5. To compare the figures in this column, as Dr. Lloyd does, with the figures in the first column is misleading for a number of reasons The figures do not represent exports of goods and services but exports of goods only. Data on services are on line 29 of the same Commerce Department table.

The figures are on an expenditure basis, whereas the figures in the first column are on a commitment basis.

The figures in the second column exclude all military assistance, almost all of which is, of course, procured in the United States. The first column includes military assistance.

The effect of these three errors is to lower sharply the percentages that appear in the third column.

For these reasons the conclusion that Dr. Lloyd reaches that less than half of A.I.D. funds are expended in the U.S. is a false conclusion. In fact, it is expected that in FY 1968 87% of all A.I.D. expenditures (good and services) will be made in the United States and that 97% of commodity expenditures will be made in the United States. 

Further, you may recall that last year Congressman Morse asked Secretary

Rusk what portion of foreign assistance funds, other than those appropriated

1967

STATEMENT OF GEN. WILLIAM H. DRAPER, JR., NATIONAL CHAIR- MAN, POPULATION CRISIS COMMITTEE, AND VICE CHAIRMAN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD/WORLD POPULATION General DRAPER.  

Mr. Chairman, and members of the Foreign Affairs Committee: 

My name is William H. Draper, Jr. I am national chairman of the Population Crisis Committee and serve as vice chairman of 

Planned Parenthood/World Population. 

I am here this morning to urge your committee, in considering the foreign aid program, to deal with the world's population problem as a matter of the highest importance and priority. 

In 1946 I appeared before your committee to ask for food appropriations desperately needed for Germany. These were granted, and they saved Germany from starvation that critical winter of 1946-47. 

A year or two later I was one of those appearing to request Marshall plan approval. Favorable congressional action paved the way for the reconstruction of Europe. 

In 1959 your committee invited me to explain the recommendations made by President Eisenhower's Committee on Foreign Aid, of which 967

1967 

1 I had the honor to be chairman. Our Committee of 10 members ¹ recommended unanimously that the U.S. Government include, as part of its economic aid program, assistance in voluntary birth control to countries requesting such help. Only now-in 1967-nearly 8 years later, is such assistance in population matters getting underway on any appreciable scale. Even this year the Administrator reports that less than $10 million of the $2 or $3 billion total economic aid program will be used for birth control purposes.

I have always strongly supported our foreign aid program and still do. But since making our 1959 report I have gradually become convinced that unless and until the population explosion now erupting in Asia, Africa, and Latin America is brought under control, our entire economic aid program is doomed to failure. Our basic and very worthy objective is to help the poorer nations of the world in their efforts to raise their per capita standard of living so that their people can participate in at least some of the material blessings we now enjoy. 

Unfortunately this is proving to be impossible. Rapid population growth is offsetting increased economic resources almost everywhere. 

Failure to satisfy the revolution of rising expectations is already sowing the seeds of discontent in many countries. 

During the past year I have visited 18 different countries, most of them in Africa and Latin America. I have seen many facets of the problem at first hand, and have talked with government officials in many countries. In Egypt they told me that the Aswan Dam would add one-quarter to Egypt's productive land and to its food production by 1970, but that during its 10 years of construction Egypt's population will have increased by one-third, with no per capita gain. 

In the past 6 years world food production has been falling far behind population growth. Only the millions of tons of surplus food accumulated here in the United States before 1960, and since distributed as food for peace, have so far prevented millions of people in many countries from dying of starvation.

We shipped more than 8 million tons of grain last year to India alone-one-quarter of our entire wheat crop. In spite of comparable shipments so far this year, thousands are reported actually dving of famine in India today. A fortnight ago, India's Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi appealed to her own people to share what food they have and stated publicly that millions are now threatened. 

Drought has brought on the crisis earlier, but the basic cause is the 1 million additional Indian mouths to be fed each month. India's population is increasing more than 12 million persons a year, and its food production has not kept pace. 

Two of the most knowledgeable agricultural statesmen in the world today, Dr. Binay Sen, Director-General of the Food and Agriculture 

Organization of the United Nations, and Orville Freeman, our own

Secretary of Agriculture, have stated publicly that catastrophe lies ahead if present trends continue-that starvation in many countries is 

1 Membership of President Eisenhower's 1959 Committee on Foreign Aid, which unani mously recommended population assistance when requested : William H. Draper, Jr., chairman; Dillon Anderson, former Coordinator of the National Security Council; Joseph M.

969 inevitable unless the developing countries, in addition to growing more food, adopt and practice massive birth control. Speaking before the 

International Eucharistic Congress held in Bombay in 1964, Dr. 

Sen courageously asked:mode 

Can we a any more turn our faces away from the concept of family planning when the alternative is starvation and death? 

Several years ago, Dr. Raymond Ewell of New York State University, who will testify later this morning, long a student of food and fertilizer trends, predicted flatly:

The world is on the threshold of the biggest famine in history. 

Famine in India, Pakistan and Communist China by the early 1970's, he believes, would spread to Indonesia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, and Brazil a few years later. By 1980, if present trends continue, he predicts that most of the other countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin 

America will be starving.

He points out the basic reason the population in those three developing continents will increase between 1960 and 1980 more than 1,300 million people, while ever since 1960 the overall production of food in those three continents on a per capita basis has been declining. 

I do not know anyone who seriously disputes Dr. Ewell's predictions, if present trends are permitted to continue. I have here an advance copy of a new book, "Famine 1975-Who Will Survive?", by

William and Paul Paddock, which I will leave with the committee, and which documents in detail the truly desperate world picture now unfolding. The authors suggest writing off India as hopeless. I would rather we increase substantially our assistance to India in family planning so that their own efforts may succeed. 

Here also is a study by Dr. Lester Brown, now an Administrator in the Department of Agriculture, entitled "Increasing World Food Output" which proves that developing countries have been unable to increase per-acre food production more than about 1 percent a year. So countries that increase their population 2 percent to 3 percent will never be able to feed their people. 

Saving Germany from starvation after World War II was important. Helping Europe to recover was also important. The United 

States met both emergencies with statesmanlike resolve and great success.

But today's crisis-threatening famine to three continents-transcends by far the postwar dangers of two decades ago. Again in our own enlightened self-interest we must rise to the challenge. We must meet this new emergency. The space race, the cold war, even Vietnam, will fade into comparative insignificance when two-thirds of the world is starving.

Everyone favors helping hungry nations to grow more food. There is no opposition to this half of the solution. AID has 1,100 people working in the food help area. The funds provided are almost unlimited.

It is the effort to reduce the rate of population growth that has been controversial-that must be bolstered-and quickly. AID has just increased the personnel ceiling for its population division-but it is still only 28 people compared to 1,100.

And AID is projecting expenditures of only $20 million this coming year in the population area-a pittance compared to the hundreds of

1967 

millions in food aid-and to the $2 or $3 billions in the total aid program. How can any of our aid program succeed while the population explosion threatens survival in many nations?

So far the private organizations have been carrying the load almost singlehandedly in family planning research and action programs at home and abroad. The Rockefeller Foundation began its work in the mid-1930's. The Ford Foundation has committed nearly $80 million in this field. Research financed largely by the Population Council, with an annual budget of $8 million, has found acceptable methods to control conception and so to restore the balance between birth and death, if they are used sufficiently and almost universally. 

Planned Parenthood affiliates and supporters have established many hundreds of clinics throughout the world. They have bombarded the public and the government with facts and figures so that few today deny that a critical world situation exists. In fact, the Gallup polls and hearings by this and other committees make clear that a national consensus has been reached and that this issue is no longer controversial. 

A large majority in every religious group favors and actually practices family planning.

Now more than a dozen governments have adopted national population control programs. Only governments are powerful enough, broadly based enough, and rich enough to furnish the information and provide the facilities on the scale needed. 

I believe that now our own government in the cause of humanity and its own enlightened self-interest, should accord the highest priority to the world population problem and emphasize this priority throughout our foreign aid program. AID should recruit a large and able staff and actively develop a program of sufficient size to help the developing world deal with the issue effectively.

We must accept the fact that this will cost real money, in the neighborhood of the $100 million annually already recommended by Richard Gardner's Committee on Population at the White House Conference on International Cooperation. Dr. Gardner will speak later to the committee. This cannot happen overnight, nor without careful forward planning. But a start has been made and AID needs the resources to follow through on a larger scale.

As you know, President Johnson has said that $5 in population control is worth, if it is effectively used, $100 in economic development. 

On this basis $100 million a year spent for population should match in per capita benefits our entire economic aid program of some $2 billion. 

In a sense, this is true, but, of course, both are needed-development funds to raise more food and the general standard of living, and family planning funds to keep the population explosion in check. 

Last year's foreign aid bill specifically authorized AID to provide needed medical supplies-contraceptives.

Therefore, I believe that the United States should encourage the use of birth control pills by making supplies available to any country wishing such a program at the lowest price and even free if necessary. 

The Population Council already makes free intrauterine devices available to certain countries. Also with our assistance, the contraceptive most used in the United States-birth control pills-could be manufactured in the various countries. Then the cost could be greatly reduced. If women in the developing countries used oral contraceptives

971 in the same proportion that American women already do, then the impact on world population growth would be substantial, and the cost nearly $100 million a year-would be multiplied many times over in benefits to health, per capita income, and economic development to say nothing of closing the famine gap. 

There is no time for delay. It will take years for the most successful programs to bring birth rates back into balance we must start now. 

I plead for priority-the highest priority for our Government's assistance to voluntary family planning programs in the developing countries. Dlrow off at ipomo 

A Senate amendment introduced by some 20 Senators would increase the appropriations available for this purpose to $50 million a year. I hope this committee and the Congress will approve. This, itself, is only a start-if the world's rate of population increase is to be brought down quickly. India alone has budgeted $300 million for this purpose during the current 5-year plan-$60 million a year. Can we do less?

STATEMENT OF DR. RICHARD N. GARDNER, PROFESSOR OF INTER- NATIONAL LAW AND ORGANIZATION, COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY, NEW YORK Dr. GARDNER.  

I have had the privilege, Mr. Chairman, of appearing before you many times in an official capacity. This is my first appearance before you in a private capacity. I am grateful for the opportunity. 

I want to say, too, what a privilege it is to be appearing here today with General Draper, who has done perhaps more than any other American to call attention to this important problem. 

This is a subject in which I was deeply involved during my service from 1961 to 1965 as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs. In December 1962, before the General 

Assembly of the United Nations, I was privileged to make the first offer of assistance on behalf of the U.S. Government to family planning programs overseas. In 1965 I was chairman of the Committee on 

Population which presented recommendations for further U.S. Government action to President Johnson's White House Conference on 

International Cooperation. 

I can sum up my message today very briefly: Although the U.S. 

Government is finally on record in support of voluntary family planning both here and abroad, its actual programs are still grossly inadequate when measured against the problem to be solved. To put it bluntly, the ratio of talk to action is far too high. As long as this continues to be the case, our foreign aid program is doomed to fail in its primary purpose the achievement of living standards in the lessdeveloped countries compatible with minimum human dignity. 

We hear a great deal these days about the "aid gap" and the "trade gap" and the "food gap." But none of these gaps can be closed unless we reduce the "family planning gap" the gap between the number of married women who now have access to modern birth control tech- 77-470-67-pt. 5- -5 

---

1967 

niques and the number that would make use of them if given the opportunity. mong noit hugoy When I began to prepare this testimony it occurred to me that you might like to have a rough estimate of the size of the world's family planning gap and the cost of closing it. Strange as it may seem, could not find these estimates in the available literature. With the help of a group of experts, I have come up with some figures, very rough approximations, which I shall present in detail later on. But to set the stage for our discussion, let me give you the principal conclusions:

There are 225 million married women in the world today who are subject to unwanted pregnancies; 

150 million of these women are outside of Communist China; 

These 150 million women have 37.5 million children each year;

These children represent 39 percent of the children being born in the world outside of Communist China; andonin sibat 

The cost of eliminating these unwanted pregnancies would be $2.1 billion annually.

Obviously, nothing like this $2.1 billion a year could be spent effectively now or in the immediate future. I simply present these figures to indicate the magnitude of the job ahead and to measure the adequacy of the $9 million being spent by the Agency for International Development on population control in the present fiscal year-a sum, by the way, which represents less than four-tenths of 1 percent of our total foreign aid expenditures.

My statement today will be divided into three main parts: the basic principles which should govern U.S. policy; estimates of the family planning gap; and specific recommendations for expanding U.S. efforts to reduce this gap through bilateral and multilateral cooperation. 

Let me suggest the following basic principles which should guide the United States in dealing with this critical world problem: 

First: We should be concerned with the quality of life. 

The central objective of U.S. policy at home and abroad should be to promote the welfare and dignity of the individual human being. We must concern ourselves not just with aggregate statistics, but with the progress made in assuring each person a full and satisfactory life. This means not merely adequate levels of personal consumption, including food and housing, health and education, but the satisfaction of those political, cultural, and spiritual needs that are fundamental to all men. 

The problems arising from present rates of population growth are not limited to the avoidance of famine and the achievement of increases in per capita income important as those problems undoubtedly are. 

If the condition of the individual and not gross statistics, is to be the measure of our progress, we must be concerned with the broader implications of population trends. So long as we are concerned with the quality of life, we have no choice but to be concerned with the quantity of life.

Second: We should seek the maximum dissemination of knowledge. 

It has been estimated that at least two out of every three persons in the world as a whole, and about nine out of 10 in the less developed countries, are without modern family planning information and services. We should seek to make information and services available to all these persons who wish to have them. If we do this, we will eliminate a particularly objectionable form of discrimination presently existing

OF 

973 in the world today--discrimination against persons who are denied family planning information and services by virtue of limited educational, economic, or other circumstances. 

Third: We should support freedom of choice.

Freedom to limit family size to the number of children wanted is a basic human right. Our aim should be to enable every couple to determine the family size it wants by means of its own choosing. Once adequate family planning information and services are available, individuals will be in a position to make decisions in the light of their own religious, ethical, cultural, and economic circumstances. 

If we wish to make a success of planning, time is of the essence. The rate of world population growth the essence. The rateogram of voluntary family is so great its consequences are so grave-that this may be the last generation which has the opportunity to limit population growth on the basis of free choice. If we do not make voluntary family planning possible in this generation we may make compulsory family planning inevitable in some parts of the world in future generations. Such an outcome would be incompatible with the values of a free society and tragic in its consequences for the human race. 

Fourth: Family planning begins at home. 

Our policy for dealing with population growth must be applied consistently at home and abroad. We should not ask other countries to do things we are not prepared to do ourselves. We should not give the impression that we are in favor of limiting the population growth of other peoples but not that of the American people. 

We must practice what we preach if our words are to carry weight overseas and if our efforts overseas are not to be misunderstood. We can set an international example for other countries by making family planning information and services fully available to persons within the United States, with the understanding that there be no coercion and that in tax-supported facilities there be full freedom of choice of methods to be used in regulating pregnancy. 

Of course, the principal reason for accelerating our domestic family planning programs has to do with the value of those programs in our own society. If it is good for Asian and African and Latin American women to be freed from the scourge of unwanted pregnancy, it is equally good for American women. Therefore, I strongly support the bills S. 1503 and H.R. 8461 introduced by Senator Joseph Tydings and 

Congressman Samuel Friedel, respectively, of Maryland, to increase voluntary family planning services in the United States.)

Fifth: U.S. assistance to another country should be solely at the request of that country.

HOT În family planning assistance, as in other types of assistance, the United States can only act with the consent and cooperation of the other country concerned. It is significant that the first call for international assistance in support of family planning came from the Asian countries in the Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East. If international cooperation in family planning is to become a reality, it must originate in the needs and demands of the countries concerned. 

Sixth: The principal responsibility for implementing programs of family planning in foreign countries must be taken by the people of those countries themselves.

In this area of foreign assistance, as in every other, we can only help people to help themselves. Our aid and advice in family planning can

1967 

be an important supplement to domestic efforts, but it is bound to fail if those efforts are inadequate. The basic commitment in terms of policy and leadership and money and trained people must come from within the country concerned. 

Modern forms of family planning are not going to be brought to Indian peasants by social workers from New York. People will only accept and apply strange and new methods of family planning if they are strongly endorsed by their own Government and presented by individuals they trust and understand. 

Seventh: Family planning is not a substitute for foreign aid-what is needed is more of both. 

I respectfully suggest, Mr. Chairman, that nothing could be more harmful to the acceptance of family planning overseas-nor more certain to frustrate the objectives of both family planning and foreign aid-than to suggest that the former is a substitute for the latter. In my judgment, we need more of both. 

Unfortunately, some people think of family planning as essentially a mechanical problem, to be solved by means of some technological miracle. But as Dr. Frank Notestein, president of the Population 

Council, recently noted:

If, by a miracle, we learned how to make prayer an effective means of contraception we would not have the organizational and educational machinery to make very efficient use of the discovery.

To bring modern methods of family planning to vast rural populations requires a network of health and social services which does not exist in most of the countries concerned. It requires administrators, communication specialists, doctors and paramedical personnel, vehicles, dispensaries, medical implements, communication equipment-as well as pills and intrauterine devices. Moreover, the acceptance of family planning will be facilitated if it is not a separate program but rather one element in a total package of services of maternal and child care. 

A woman is likely to be interested in the pill or the IUCD when it is explained to her by the same health worker who has delivered her child.

Going one step further, I simply must state my view that the present level of the foreign aid program is simply not adequate to carry out its proclaimed objectives. To put it bluntly, the international war on poverty is now being lost. In the decade of the 1960's-a decade hopefully designated as the "decade of development" by the United Nations the average annual increase in gross national product of the poor countries has been little more than 4 percent. With rates of population growth in most of these averaging 2 or 3 percent, there has been only a 1 or 2 percent average annual increase in individual living standards.

Indeed, the average rate of increase in per capita income in the 1960's, in the less developed countries, has actually been lower than in the decade of the 1950's.

The time has come to escalate the international war on poverty. We should do this through new forms of international cooperation and an entirely new level of effort on the part of both developed and less developed countries. 

To this end I venture the following proposal:

This June marks the 20th anniversary of General Marshall's famous speech at Harvard which launched the Marshall plan. This anniver-

975 3 sary is an appropriate time for the country which initiated the Marshall plan and the countries which were its principal beneficiaries to launch a new Marshall plan for the benefit of the less developed countries.

The United Nations and other bodies have recommended an aid effort by the developed countries equivalent to 1 percent of their gross national product. Despite rapid economic growth in the industrialized countries during the last few years, their foreign aid efforts have not expanded; as a result, according to U.N. estimates, foreign aid as a proportion of GNP has slipped from 0.83 percent in 1961 to 0.69 percent in 1965.

This trend can and must be reversed. 

The heads of state of the Western industrialized countries should meet on the Marshall plan anniversary-or at a suitable time thereafter-to chart a program of progressive escalation of their foreign aid efforts. The objective should be achievement of the 1-percent target by 1975. This would mean a doubling by that date of the total foreign aid effort of the United States and other countries, in view of their present rates of economic growth.

Eighth: U.S. assistance in the field of population should be related to the maximum possible extent to the work of multilateral agencies, particularly the relevant agencies of the United Nations. 

U.S. assistance to other countries is often more effective when it is related to the work of multilateral agencies. This is particularly true in a field like family planning. Through multilateral cooperation we can share responsibility for action with other countries and promote a broad consensus on the nature of the population problem and what ought to be done about it. It is particularly important that family planning not become a cold war issue involving political ideologies, or a subject of disagreement between racial groups. 

In our cooperative efforts with other countries, we should place the greatest possible reliance on the United Nations Secretariat, the United Nations development program, the United Nations Children's Fund, the World Health Organization, UNESCO, and the UN Regional 

Economic Commissions. We should also work through the institutions of the Alliance for Progress, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, and various aid consortia such as the ones chaired by the World Bank for India and Pakistan. 

I come to the second part of my testimony, Mr. Chairman, the family planning gap.

As I mentioned earlier, it occurred to me when I received your kind invitation to appear today that you would be interested in some statistics on this problem, even if they were only rough approximations. I emphasize, Mr. Chairman, they are very rough approximations.

There are about 225 million married women in the world currently exposed to the risk of unwanted pregnancy. About 10 million of these live in developed countries, and about 215 million in less developed countries.

How these figures are arrived at is explained in attachment 1 at the end of this statement. The first column shows world population at 

3,285 million. The second column shows that 43 percent of this total are in the main childbearing ve 15-44, giving a total of 1,413 million people in this category, of which about 707 million are women.

1967 

Column 5 shows the estimate that 80 percent of these women are married, which leaves the 566 million married women in the childbearing years shown in column 6. 

As the explanatory note (g) for column 7 indicates, Mr. Chairman, this is on the basis of field work and samples and statistical information gained from experience in countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, and India. It is estimated that 20 percent of the women in the underdeveloped world are sterile or subfecund, currently using contraceptives, or have an absent husband, and that another 30 percent are pregnant, lactating, or want a child. This means there is a total of 

50 percent not exposed to risk of unwanted pregnancy, leaving 50 percent who are exposed to this risk; 50 percent of the 566-million total in column 6 gives the rounded off figure in column 7 of 225 million women in the world exposed to the risk of unwanted pregnancy. 

The next two lines of columns 6 and 7 show the subtotal for the developed and less developed countries respectively: In the developed countries, there are 100 million married women in the childbearing years, of whom 10 million are exposed to the risk of unwanted preg nancy; in the less developed world, 466 million of these women, of which 215 million are exposed to the risk of unwanted pregnancy. 

Further down we see the appropriate subtotals for the different regions of the world. The last line shows the total for the less developed countries excluding China. You will note that there are 140 million married women in the less developed countries, outside of 

Communist China, exposed to the risk of unwanted pregnancy. Together with the 10 million women exposed to unwanted pregnancy in the developed countries, this adds up to a grand total of 150 million such women in the world as a whole, outside of Communist China. 

Attachment 2 shows the cost and consequences of eliminating unwanted pregnancies in the world. It first shows the average cost of applying family planning methods in South Korea. A variety of presently available methods were applied there and the average cost per capita (that is, per man or woman using them) was $5.14. This figure is doubled to about $10 per capita in order to be applicable to the less developed countries as a whole, since they are much less advanced on the average than Korea in such relevant areas as education, administration, and health services.

A further increase of 40 percent has to be made in the estimate to allow for normal attrition. Experience has shown that many men or women discontinue use of the particular device, necessitating a duplication of the initial expenditure. This brings the estimated cost to $14 to provide an acceptor with 1 year's protection against pregnancy. Tourret 

Now, we turn to the figures derived from attachment 1-225 million married women subject to the risk of unwanted pregnancy in the world as a whole, of whom 150 million are outside Communist China. 

Most of these women are among the older married women, since under assumption (g) in attachment 1 we allowed for those wanting another child. With this in mind, we assume 1 in 4 of these women gives birth to a child each year. This assumption again is based on fieldwork and attitude studies and experience. This means a total of 37.5 million births per year which are unwanted.

Since the total number of births in the world outside Communist China is 95 million per year, this means that 39 percent of the children

977 being born outside of Communist China are unwanted, in the sense that they would not have been born had their mothers been given access to modern family planning methods. This number, by the way, would be even higher but for widespread and increasing resort to abortion. As protection against unwanted pregnancy can be provided, abortion can be progressively reduced. musiq viina)

To estimate the cost of eliminating this total of 37.5 million unwanted births per year, we multiply the 150 million women by the $14 estimated to be necessary to provide 1 year's protection against pregnancy and arrive at the total of $2.1 billion as the sum necessary per year to fill the family planning gap outside Communist China. 

This figure would be something like $3 billion if mainland China were included.

Titto brow 

The table at the bottom of attachment 2 shows what would happen to the world's vital statistics if the family planning gap were closed in this way. The present figures per thousand are birth rate, 36; death rate, 15; net increase, 21. Without unwanted births outside Communist 

China the new figures per thousand would be birth rate, 25; death rate, 15; net increase, 10. In other words, the elimination of unwanted births outside Communist China would reduce annual population growth from the present level to 2.1 to 1 percent.

Note that the 1 percent figure applies to the world as a whole, and still assumes high birth rates in China. The elimination of the 37.5 million unwanted births outside China would reduce the annual increase in population in the less developed world outside Communist China to one-half percent. Assuming the continuation of present death rates, population growth in the less developed countries outside Communist China can be reduced to 1 percent at one-half the annual cost estimated above or about $1 billion per year. 

So far we have made no distinction between countries with official policies favoring or permitting family planning programs nor countries without such policies. Attachment 3 provides the estimate of $1.05 billion as the cost of eliminating unwanted pregnancy in countries which have such policies. Obviously, nothing can be spent in countries which do not permit family planning programs to be established. 

The $1.05 billion figure breaks down into $921 million for south and east Asia outside of Communist China, $76 million for Africa, and $53 million in Latin America. og som

Attachment 4 shows the cost of eliminating unwanted pregnancy in three large countries of Southeast Asia. It shows the estimates of $616 million for India, $126 million for Pakistan, and $140 million for 

Indonesia. 

To sum up this part of my statement: It is estimated that, excluding 

Communist China, it would take approximately $1 billion to eliminate all unwanted pregnancy in all countries which have or tolerate birth control programs. I cannot imagine any other use for $1 billion which would do more to relieve the suffering of so many human beings and bring greater benefits to the human race as a whole. alt opomen 

When the day comes when we can use on for this purpose $1 effectively, we will not only alleviate suffering for millions of people; we will save their governments additional billions in food, education, housing, health, and other costs. Most important of all, we will eliminate something more dangerous in its long-term consequences for civilization than even the hydrogen bomb the production of millions

FOREIGN, ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1967 

of unwanted children destined to grow up in the world without adequate parental care or adequate opportunities for a decent life. 

It is obvious, of course, that the bottleneck is not just money. We could not spend $1 billion next year for this purpose even if we and the countries concerned made the sum available. In addition to lack of funds, family planning programs are impeded by the absence of administrative capacity, the absence of trained personnel, the absence of communications techniques, and, perhaps most fundamentally, the absence of the necessary sense of urgency and the necessary will to get on with the job. Nonetheless, these rough estimates may serve as target figures indicating the direction in which we and other countries will have to go to deal with what President Johnson has described as "humanity's greatest challenge *** second only to the search for peace."

I come finally to the third and last part of my statement, proposals for action.

In the light of the family planning gap, its grave consequences for humanity, and the probable costs of closing it, how adequate is present 

U.S. Government policy? What more needs to be done?

Until December 1962, the U.S. Government had no policy on this subject; or perhaps it might be more accurate to say that we had a policy against U.S. Government involvement in family planning programs at home or abroad. Our AID missions were under instructions which prevented them from providing aid or advice of any kind in this field, in line with President Eisenhower's 1959 statement that: 

I cannot imagine anything more emphatically a subject that is not a proper political or governmental activity or function or responsibility. 

As you know, President Eisenhower has since completely changed his view.

In December 1962, in a speech which was approved by the late President Kennedy, I told the United Nations General Assembly that the United States was now willing to "help other countries, upon request, to find potential sources of information and assistance on ways and means of dealing with population problems." Shortly thereafter, new instructions were issued to AID missions overseas citing this statement as the new basis of policy. President Kennedy, in April 1963, confirmed the new policy in response to a press conference question, declaring that we need to "know more about the whole reproductive cycle" and that this knowledge should then "be made more available to the world."

Some 2 years later, on March 3, 1965, AID issued an instruction to all its overseas missions providing a detailed mandate to respond affirmatively to requests for technical, financial, and commodity assistance in support of family planning programs. This instruction noted, however, that AID would not consider requests for contraceptive devices or equipment for their manufacture. In his testimony before this committee on April 5 of this year, AID Administrator William Gaud announced that this last qualification would at last be removed. 

President Johnson's strong leadership on this issue has been a vital element in the rapid progress that has been made in developing a new U.S. population policy. In his state of the Union message of January 

1965 President Johnson declared: 1/2 ton reifte bing

I will seek new ways to use our knowledge to help deal with the explosion in world population and the growing scarcity in world resources.

979 Since then the President has made at least 30 statements reiterating his concern with domestic and foreign population problems. 

The shift in Government policy on family planning has been reflected in forward-looking policy guidelines issued by the Office of 

Economic Opportunity, the Department of Health, Education, and 

Welfare, and the Agency for International Development. Fifty Members of the Congress (16 House Members and 34 Senators) have sponsored or cosponsored legislation that would expand Government support for family planning, thus providing exceptionally broad political and georgraphical support for action in this field. In the 89th Congress five different pieces of legislation were enacted which in one way or another expanded the authority or activities of executives agencies. 

These included the Food for Peace Act, the Foreign Assistance Act, OEO authorizing legislation, the Labor-HEW appropriation, and the 

Comprehensive Health Planning Act. 

1 Yet despite the increasing urgency of the population problem and the growing support in the Congress and throughout the country for more vigorous programs to deal with it, the fact remains that our foreign assistance program has barely touched this vital aspect of economic and human development. In this fiscal year, AID programed less than $9 million for activities relating to population. 

Much of that $9 million was used for academic studies, statistical studies, and attitude studies-studies which are extremely useful but which do not in themselves increase the availability of family planning information or techniques for those who desire them. AID has provided a significant amount of aid going beyond studies only in Turkey in the form of jeeps for family planning workers and support for an educational effort. That single program in Turkey accounts for more than one-third of AID's fiscal year 1967 population budget ($3.5 million out of $8.9 million).

For fiscal year 1968 AID is, I am told, budgeting a total of about $20 million for assistance in voluntary family planning programs. In my judgment, this amount is inadequate. It is only slightly more than the annual budget of a single voluntary organization, Planned Parenhood-World Population, which operates in the United States alone and depends very heavily on private contributions. In India the current 5-year plan allots $306 million over 5 years for population, or an average of $61 million per year. 

A dozen other countries have adopted national family planning programs with services included as a basic element of national health activities and with budgets ranging from many millions to a few thousand dollars.

In more than 50 countries, private voluntary groups, affiliated with the International Planned Parenthood Federation, are pressing locally for more vigorous action. In almost every case, public or private, lack of funds is a major obstacle in expanding programs-programs which are popular, beneficial from a health point of view, and extremely important to overall economic objectively a population explosion but a We are witnessing today not family planning revolution. For the first time in history there is concrete evidence that nations and peoples throughout most of the world not only accept the need for family planning programs but desire that family planning services be made available to them. For muik notxA

1967 

the first time in history we have the technical means to implement family planning progress the pill, the intrauterine contraceptive device, and other methods.

Moreover, research now underway suggests that reliance on a contraceptive pill which must be taken daily or an intrauterine device which is presently unsatisfactory to 25 out of 100 users will some day be of only historical interest-mere shadows reflecting the dim dark ages in the history of family planning. Already researchers have had success with an injectable contraceptive that provides long-standing immunity from pregnancy.

It is clear that the problems facing the less developed countries in the field of family planning are neither problems of resistance to contraception nor lack of imagination on the part of family planning experts. The major problems are insufficient funds, weak administration, and inadequate personnel. 

Unless the United States is willing to give considerably more support than it has in the past to these programs, the organizational and educational machinery necessary to reduce birth rates in the less developed regions of the world will never materialize. To reduce the birth rate in India, for example, to a point where economic growth becomes meaningful, the Government of India in the next decade must encourage over 50 million couples to practice family planning. 

When you remember that India has over 375 million people who can't read, 550,000 separate villages, and only 3.5 million Indian couples now practicing family planning, it becomes obvious that the challenge which the Indian Government has accepted cannot be met without full U.S. support. 

Well organized and effective nationwide family planning programs must be developed in the less developed countries of the world beginning now. Without them the new technological developments which have simplified and will further simplify contraception will be meaningless for these countries. And such programs will not develop unless the United States greatly expands its presently minuscule financial assistance for this purpose.

981 Dr. GARDNER. I have with me today the report which our committee presented to President Johnson at the White House Conference in December 1965. With the permission of the chairman, I should like to have it included in the record at the conclusion of my statement.

Mr. GARDNER. The key recommendation of our committee was the following: ཨཱ 5. That the U.S. Government be prepared to make available upon request up to $100 million a year over the next three years to help other countries implement programs of family planning and strengthen national health and social services necessary for the support of family planning programs. 

The Committee on Population is no longer in existence, and I have no mandate to speak for its members today. However, I believe they share my deep gratitude at the introduction by Senator William Fulbright of Arkansas, with 18 cosponsors, of S. 1264. Both Senator Fulbright and Senator Charles Percy of Illinois, in presenting the bill, specifically cited this key recommendation of our committee, and their bill would substantially implement it. 

I hope the Fulbright bill will be approved as an amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act. It authorizes the appropriation of $50 million per year for 3 years plus available foreign currencies for use in support of voluntary family planning programs in friendly foreign nations. This support would be available, under procedures to insure that no coercion is involved to foreign governments, U.N. specialized agencies, U.S. and foreign nonprofit organizations, universities, hospitals, accredited health institutions, and voluntary health or other qualified organizations. It would cover a wide variety of action including demographic studies, medical and psychological research, personnel training, instruction and staffing of clinics and rural health centers, training for doctors, manufacture of medical supplies, dissemination of family planning information and provisions for medical assistance. and supplies to individuals who desire such assistance. 

It would be a major step forward, in my view, if this committee would give its support to legislation along the lines proposed by 

Senator Fulbright, as an amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act. 

While we should not make family planning a condition of eligibility for receiving foreign aid, it is certainly appropriate that we seek to influence policy by earmarking a certain portion of aid for family planning and saying in effect, "you don't have to use it, but there it is if you want it."

There are some who may say that $100 million or even $50 million plus available counterpart funds would be too much more than could usefully be spent. I would strongly contest that view, While this might have been true a few years ago, it is not true today when many foreign governments are getting family planning programs underway. Once it is known that AID has substantially increased funds available to assist local family planning efforts, uses for the money will be found. 

I have prepared an illustrative 1-year budget showing how the $100 million recommended by our Committee on Population might usefully be spent. This budget, shown in attachment 5, includes $20 million for training, $6 million for additional AID staff, $10 million for demonstration projects, $10 million for information programs, $15 million for commodities (including equipment, transportation, and supplies),

1967 

$11 million for research and evaluation, $8 million for private nonprofit organizations and $20 million for U.N. and international organization programs. Broken down geographically it shows $42 million for Asia, $26 million for Africa, $19 million for Latin America, and $13 million for supporting assistance, training, and the like in the 

United States, including U.N. headquarters.

Let me say a special word about three of the categories of assistance noted in this table. The first is the $15-million category for commodities (equipment, transportation, and supplies). This category would include the purchase of contraceptive devices themselves where this is regarded as necessary for the achievement of effective programs. 

The Fulbright bill would explicitly authorize the use of AID funds for the purchase or manufacture of such supplies a use which Mr. 

Gaud has now indicated is regarded as appropriate by AID. This type of expenditure may be increasingly necessary as foreign countries move out of the planning stage into large-scale implementation of programs. It is likely to be required now that experience has demonstrated that the pill will play a major part in birth control programs along with the IUCD. Since the pill is more expensive, there may be occasions when the U.S. Government will need to provide financial assistance to help make it available. A year's supply of pills for a woman in a less developed country costs $1.50 to $2, compared to 22 cents for an IUCD.

The second category is financial support for private agencies. One of the great strengths of our country is our ability to work through nongovernmental organizations. In the field which concerns us here, invaluable work has been done by the Ford and Rockefeller Foundations, the Population Council, and Planned Parenthood/World Population and its international affiliate, the International Planned Parenthood Federation, not to mention other organizations. Such private agencies can often carry on informational activities, research, and pilot projects better than Government. It is clearly in our national interest to make Government funds available to such organizations where they are in need of assistance. So far AID has made grants of only $400,000 to private agencies. The proposed figure of $8 million a year would be in line with the enlarged scope which should be afforded to private institutions in this field. 

The third category of assistance is to the United Nations and international agencies. There are, as I suggested earlier, important reasons why we should work to the greatest possible extent through multilateral channels.

In the last 5 years the United Nations system, like the United States, has begun to develop an affirmative policy on the world population problem.

The 1966 session of the U.N. General Assembly passed without objection a resolution calling on U.N. agencies to "assist, when requested, in further developing and strengthening national and regional facilities for training, research, information, and advisory services in the field of population." 

The U.N. Population Commission has drawn up an ambitious 

5-year plan of action.

The Population Branch at U.N. Headquarters has been strengthened and raised to the level of a Division.

983 

The World Health Assembly has authorized the Director Gen eral of WHO to offer advisory services on the medical aspects of population. 

The General Conference of UNESCO has called for research by the agency in education and communication related to family planning. 

The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) has approved major projects in India and Pakistan which will offer family planning services in clinics providing maternal and child care. 

The U.N. regional commissions and their regional demographic and training centers have expanded their facilities, and the Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East (ECAFE) has established a center in Bangkok to assist countries in the actual implementation of family planning programs. 

A subgroup of the Administrative Committee on Coordination has been established to coordinate the activities of U.N. agencies in the population field. 

Like the U.S. Government, however, the United Nations has been slow to translate policy into program. Of the $120 million U.N. budget for 1966 only $1.8 million is devoted to population work-and even this sum is mainly for research and training related to statistics, demography, and the economic aspects of population growth. Various U.N. agencies are spending small additional sums for population work, but except for the two UNICEF projects totaling $800,000 there is very little by way of actual implementation of family planning programs. 

The U.N.'s role in direct support of family planning will continue to be very limited, in all probability, unless we and others take a new initiative. 

I therefore propose the establishment of a world population program to enlarge U.N. efforts in the field of population. The United 

States should offer $20 million annually for such a program and encourage contributions from as many other countries as possible. 

The world population program could help to expand the research and training programs now underway at U.N. headquarters, in the regional commissions, and in specialized agencies; but most of the money should be used for field operations in direct support of national family planning efforts. With the help of the world population program, the U.N. could undertake pilot or demonstration projects to get national or regional programs underway. Interdisciplinary teams drawn from different U.N. agencies including doctors, administrators, communications specialists, economists, demographers-could work in model areas with host government personnel. Aided by advice and training from the U.N. on the organization, administration, execution, and evaluation of programs, the host countries could gradually learn to carry forward nationwide programs through their own efforts. 

I would like to see the world population program administered by the Secretary General of the U.N., perhaps through the Administrator of the U.N. development program. The various U.N. agencies like 

UNICEF, WHO, and the regional centers would be given funds to execute specific projects, but a centralized budget and administration at U.N. headquarters would encourage more effective teamwork in regional and country programs.

1967 

If an efficient arrangement of this kind cannot be worked out, we may need to establish the world population program outside the U.N. and have the participating countries make contributions directly to individual U.N. or other multilateral agencies. To provide maximum flexibility, the present reference in the Fulbright bill to "United Nations specialized agencies" should be changed to "United Nations agencies and programs, other multilateral programs," and so forth. 

There is, I recognize, a general policy in the State Department and Budget Bureau against establishing new voluntary programs in the U.N. system. As a general rule this is sound, but exceptions are justified when they are necessary to do a particular job which we want to see done. We recognized the need for such exceptions, as this committee recalls in launching a separate voluntary program in WHO for malaria eradication, and in 1963 we made a voluntary contribution of $500,000 to launch a WHO research program related to family planning. This latter investment facilitated important studies by WHO scientific groups which have helped to encourage the international acceptability, from a medical point of view, of the pill and the I.U.C.D. 

A new voluntary program is now a necessity if the U.N. system is to be effective in the field of family planning. As a practical matter, it will not be possible to get sufficient funds in the U.N. budget or in 

U.N. agency budgets for family planning in competition with other activities. 

The Director General of WHO has already warned against diverting funds for WHO's customary activities to family planning efforts. 

Moreover, and this I submit is the real point, since certain countries have reservations about the use of their money for family planning, it is best to have a separate fund for this purpose for those who are prepared to contribute.

I earnestly hope the United Nations may prove adequate to this challenge. In the long run, it could prove to be the Organization's most vital contribution to human welfare second only to keeping the peace. 

On a matter of such transcendent importance to humanity as a wholewhere international cooperation is such an obvious necessity-the United Nations should be at the very center of the picture. 

In addition to the U.N., we should explore the possibility of involving the international consortia for India, Pakistan, and Turkey in assisting these countries with their family planning programs. Each of these countries has initiated nationwide family planning programs, but there are great shortages of trained family planning personnel and individuals capable of training doctors and paramedical personnel in family planning techniques. The consortia members should consider the feasibility of creating a doctor pool which India, Pakistan, and Turkey could draw upon for family planning assistance. The trainers of medical personnel could be made available directly to these countries or through U.N. or WHO auspices. 

I urge you to give careful consideration to the importance of the world population problem and particularly to the urgent need for increased family planning programs in developing nations which receive the principal share of U.S. assistance. A substantial investment now

985 in voluntary family planning can return a tremendous dividend not merely in economic terms, as General Draper has so eloquently pointed out increased per capita income or larger capital investment but also in the human elements of health, family stability, and individual betterment which are the long-run objectives of our foreign aid program. 

The time has come to provide the muscle for programs which have been receiving lipservice but which are still without the financial resources to make a real impact. I believe the Fulbright bill and some of the measures I have suggested would be steps in the right direction.
