And the second is that- The President has determined that neither such payment or contribution nor any other payment or contribution from the United States will be used for any program or activity which is contrary to the policies of the United States. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I am trying to confine myself to subparagraph (1). 

Mr. BENNETT. So far as I know there is no great need for No. 1. It was put in by the drafters. They thought it was needed. I am not scholar enough to know why it was needed. I don't see any great ideological thing to be accomplished by (1). There must have been a reason for it because the drafters put it in. 

They knew my objective, and they drafted the legislation after many criticisms of what I had drafted. If it is not necessary, I have no great feeling about that. It says you are not supposed to spend money until it is needed. I think that is a sound idea. If you object to that, I don't have objection to striking it. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. It doesn't say the U.N. is not to spend it until it is needed, it says that the United States is not to make any contribution-

STATEMENT OF HON. JACK MILLER, U.S. SENATOR FROM THE STATE OF IOWA 

Senator MILLER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. May I say that the harmony and unanimity as just displayed during the previous testimony on the part of members of this committee makes a Member of the Senate feel very much at home.

1967 

Never before in history has any nation committed so much of its resources to the well-being of other nations in the family of nations as has the United States. While it may be said that no other nation has been so well able to do so, the fact remains that since 1945 the people of the United States have taken from their pocketbooks tax payments amounting to $123 billion for foreign aid to help the people of other nations, and this does not include nearly $3 billion additional in payments to the United Nations. There was no legal basis for this commitment. It was a commitment from the hearts of our people. And long before the Marshall plan, that commitment was demonstrated by millions of our citizens in helping less fortunate people in other lands through lend-lease and foreign missionary activities. Foreign aid has been a natural development in keeping with our national character.

At the same time, our foreign aid program has been a major instrument of our foreign policy. Ultimately this policy is directed at a more orderly and peaceful world. To the extent that our foreign aid programs have furthered this objective, they have been consistent with our foreign policy. To the extent that they have failed to promote a more orderly and peaceful world, they have been inconsistent with our foreign policy. Bearing this in mind, it would be foolhardy if we were not to establish priorities among the nations being considered for foreign aid, and if we were not to attach political and economic strings to our foreign aid programs which would provide reasonable assurance that they would contribute to a more orderly and peaceful world.

Requirements of self-help and internal reform, such as those which characterize the program and administration of the Alliance for Progress, are perfectly natural and logical. For example, if we attach a string to foreign aid to one of the Latin American nations in the form of a requirement that its government do a better job of collecting taxes owed by its people, there are some who might say that the United States is becoming a tax collector. In reality, however, we are merely taking the precaution that our foreign aid will promote the self-help and internal reform needed to assure that the recipient nation will be more responsive to the needs of its people; and this, in turn, will lay a foundation for a more orderly and peaceful world. 

Our foreign policy has long been to support the United Nations as an organization which has the potential-if the principles of its charter are adhered to-of helping secure a more orderly and peaceful world. The financial assistance the United States has provided the 

United Nations and its specialized agencies clearly demonstrates this support. 

For fiscal year 1967, the United States will contribute a record $233 million for this purpose, which will bring our total support since the inception of the U.N. to $2.9 billion.

This is nearly one-half the $6 billion expended by the U.N. during this period. During the current fiscal year, the United States will be paying approximately 30 percent of the cost of the United Nations and its 11 specialized agencies, nearly 40 percent of the Cyprus and Middle East peacekeeping forces, 40 percent of the U.N. development program and the Children's Fund, and up to 70 percent of special relief programs. In addition, we have purchased some $76.2 million of 

United Nations bonds under authority extended by the Congress to

1035 purchase 50 percent of the subscriptions made under a $200 million U.N. bond issue designed to relieve a serious financial crisis in the U.N. 

Notwithstanding the strong support of the United States, the United Nations has been in a worsening financial position as a result of the failure of member nations to pay their dues and assessments. 

As of December 31, 1966, delinquencies in the regular budget and the Congo and Middle East peacekeeping operations totaled over $167 million.

Of the 117 members of the United Nations, 108 were delinquent in one form or another as of last February 8. Of these, 96 received foreign aid from the United States, and their combined arrearages amounted to $65 million. The Soviet Union was delinquent in excess of $76 million and other Eastern bloc nations (including Poland) were delinquent in excess of $27 million. It is apparent that the Soviet Union and its bloc must_bear the primary responsibility for the financial crisis in the U.N. However, it should not be overlooked that there are 

96 members of the United Nations which have been receiving foreign aid from us and which, by their very numbers as well as total combined arrearages of $65 million, contribute materially to the crisis. 

One might well ask the question whether, if the 96 nations receiving our foreign aid were reasonably current in their dues and assessments, the weight of world opinion would not long ago have persuaded the Soviet Union and the other members of its bloc to pay up their delinquencies.

There seems to be an inconsistency between our foreign aid programs and our foreign policy with respect to the United Nations. It would seem that one of the first requirements for eligibility to receive our foreign aid should be that the recipient nation is supporting the United Nations. Instead, it almost appears that one of our guidelines is that the recipient nation be contributing to the financial crisis of the U.N. by failing to pay its dues and assessments. At least this is the way it has worked out. Something should be done about it. 

Each year since 1961, when I first became alarmed over the situation, I have offered an amendment designed to do something about it. 

Last year the Senate adopted my amendment, but it was dropped in conference. It had not previously been presented to the House, and I doubt that the House conferees understood the amendment or how deeply serious has been the inconsistency between our foreign aid programs and our foreign policy in support of the United Nations. That is why I am here today.

The amendment which I would propose to the foreign aid bill before this committee is as follows: ཙཱ,། In the case of the government of any nation which is more than 1 year in arrears in its payment of any assessment by the United Nations for regular budget or for peace and security operations, assistance under the provisions of this Act may nevertheless be furnished upon a determination by the President that the particular assistance to be furnished is essential to the national interest of the United States and transmittal by him of a report to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate and the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives setting forth the assurance given by the government concerned of paying (independently of such assistance) all of its arrearages and of placing its payments of such assessments on a current basis, or an explanation of the unusual and exceptional circumstances which render it economically incapable of giving such assurance. 

It may be observed that the amendment would affect only those nations to which we propose to extend foreign aid if they are over 77-470-67-pt. 5-

1967 

1 year behind in the payment of their dues and assessments; and it would not affect those if there is a determination by the President, that, notwithstanding their delinquency, it is essential to the national interest of the United States to nevertheless extend its foreign aid. 

In such a case, the President would transmit a report to the two appropriate committees of the Congress setting forth the assurance of the recipient country that it would pay up its arrearages and keep current in its payments; or, in lieu of this, an explanation would be required of the unusual and exceptional circumstances which render it economically incapable of giving such assurance. The Republic of 

China would seem to be a country to which military assistance should be furnished in our own national interest; and there are, I am sure we would agree, unusual circumstances making it incapable of giving the assurance of meeting its delinquencies at this time-not the least of which is that its share of the U.N. budget has continued at approximately the same percentage since it became a charter member of the United Nations, although such percentage is most unrealistic when related to the economy of Taiwan. In any event, it would be for the 

President to make the determination when exceptions are to be made. 

The amendment squares with the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice rendered July 20, 1962, on the question put to it by the General Assembly of the United Nations in resolution 1731 (XVI) of December 20, 1961, whether expenditures authorized by the General Assembly relating to United Nations peacekeeping operations in the Congo and Middle East constituted "expenses of the Organization" within the meaning of article 17, paragraph 2, of the charter, to be apportioned in accordance with the power granted the General Assembly by article 19, paragraph 2. My amendment further squares with resolution 1854 (XVII) of the General Assembly accepting this advisory opinion. Both the regular dues and the assessments for peacekeeping operations are taken into account in determining whether a country is in arrears. 

It is true that article 19 provides that a member of the United Nations over 2 years in arrears shall have no vote in the General Assembly; whereas under my amendment, over 1 year in arrears would trigger the possible loss of our foreign aid. But I can see no necessary correlation between the two situations. 

My amendment has nothing to do with eligibility to vote. It is designed merely to persuade our foreign aid recipients to become reasonably current in their payments to the United Nations, and I suggest that more than 1 year in arrears is serious enough to warrant concern. 

Arrearages beyond 1 year cause the United Nations to have to look to other members for assistance to help make up the deficiency in funds.

There should be no hardship occasioned to any country genuinely in support of the United Nations, especially when we consider the discretion provided the President. When considered in relation to the amount of our foreign aid, the burden of paying up the delinquencies is in the case of most delinquent countries-insignificant. I would invite the attention of the committee to exhibit 1, near the end of my table. 

The table included as exhibit 1 to this statement illustrates the truth of this statement. Afghanistan's total arrearages as of December 31,

1037 1966, came to $122,297; but her arrearages in excess of 1 year amounted to only $64,748. During fiscal 1966, we furnished over $40.4 million in foreign aid.

Argentina's arrearages in excess of 1 year amounted to $1,466,619; but during fiscal 1966 we furnished her $44.9 million in foreign aid. 

And practically all of the 56 countries listed, which are receiving our foreign aid and are more than 1 year in arrears, have been the recipients of foreign aid for far in excess of what it would take to bring their payments reasonably current. 

If I may invite the committee's attention to the next exhibit, exhibit 2. A breakdown of the arrearages by account is set forth in exhibit 

2; and it will be noted that there are 35 of the countries receiving our foreign aid which are more than 1 year behind in the payment of just their regular dues. In exhibit 3, you will find that the number of member nations which have lost their right to vote under article 19 has risen to 32, of which 21 are receiving foreign aid from the United 

States. 

The situation has been worsening. When my amendment was first offered in the Senate on April 5, 1962, there were only 25 nations receiving our foreign aid which were more than 1 year delinquent. 

On November 12, 1963, when the amendment was next offered, the number had risen to 35. 

When it was next offered on August 10, 1964, the number was up to 41.

On June 8, 1965, I pointed out at the time the amendment was offered that there were 46 nations subject to the amendment. 

On April 27, 1966, when I appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the number was still 46. Today, as I have already pointed out, it is up to 56. And, bear in mind, there are another 40 of our foreign aid recipients which, though not over 1 year in arrears, are in arrears in one way or another. 

I believe I can safely predict that, until we correlate our foreign aid programs with our foreign policy in support of the United Nations, bad as things are today, they will grow even worse. Those nations which are keeping current in their payments, and Israel is an example, will be encouraged to become delinquent, for they see us extending foreign aid without distinction between themselves and delinquent nations.

Those nations less than 1 year in arrears will be encouraged to become even more delinquent, for they see us extending foreign aid without distinction between themselves and those more than 1 year in arrears.

I know this committee wishes to see the United Nations succeed. 

That organization was born in San Francisco after World War II with a charter which is a great statement of moral principles. It was never intended to exist as a mere debating society. It was intended to be a great moral force for world peace; and, hopefully, to have the capability of serving the end of world peace through law. But it cannot do this if it dies because of the failure of its members to pay their justly assessed dues and assessments. Nor will the organization achieve its goals if so many of its members pay lip service to the charter and let some other nations pay the bill, assuming that enough nations might be found to do so. There must be a commitment by every member to the charter.

1967 

The Congress has an opportunity to reverse the trend-not by appropriating more money to make up the deficiencies of other nations, but simply by gearing our foreign aid programs into our foreign policy. My amendment will do this, and I close with the suggestion that it is worth a try. The stake is very high-a viable United Nations serving the cause of a more orderly and peaceful world. Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Senator Miller. 

Senator Miller, we certainly appreciate your taking your time to come over here and explain your amendment. I think your objectives are right. As a conferee last year, I can tell you that this was an amendment that the House conferees were totally unfamiliar with. Today you have explained your amendment in detail and it now carries much more weight with me as a prospective conferee than it did last year, when I knew nothing about your proposal. 

I have the conference print in front of me. The executive doesn't make too strong a case against your amendment except to say it would put the U.S. Government in business as a collection agency for the U.N.

Do you believe it would put us in that position, that the U.S. Government, through the AID program, would be in the position of being a collection agency?

Senator MILLER. I am familiar with that argument. I think it is specious on its face. I have already pointed out in my testimony that

1041 in the case of the Alliance for Progress we have laid down the guidelines for some of the Latin American countries that they institute internal reform, do a better job of collecting the taxes from the people who owe them in their countries. I have never heard on the Senate floor any criticism of the Alliance for Progress program in terms that we are becoming a tax collector for that particular nation. We are not collecting anything. We are merely discriminating in the use of our foreign aid.

We are laying down as a guideline the proposition that recipients of our foreign aid should meet the requirement of supporting the United Nations. I think that is essential. If there is any overriding string that ought to be attached to extending our foreign aid as long as our national policy is to support the United Nations for the purpose of obtaining a more orderly and peaceful world, then it ought to be a basic requirement that the recipients of our foreign aid be in support of the 

United Nations, not by lipservice, but by deed.

Chairman MORGAN. Your amendment in no way helps to collect the amounts that the large countries owe the U.N. because we don't give them any foreign aid? 

Senator MILLER. I would suggest this: I raise the question in my statement that we might well conclude that if all of these 96 recipients of our foreign aid were current in their payments that, by their very numbers, there would be a force of world opinion which I don't believe the Soviet Union and its bloc could ignore. I like to think that the force of world opinion, all of these 96 recipients of our foreign aid being current in their dues and assessments would have a profound influence on the Soviet Union and its bloc and might well encourage them to become current and stop trying to ruin the United Nations by refusing to meet their properly assessed dues and assessments. 

I think this lays the foundation for world opinion which could achieve the results which we cannot achieve because we are not extending foreign aid to any of those nations with the exception of Poland and a small amount to France.

Chairman MORGAN. Senator, according to this conference print of 

December 31, 1965, which is what we used last year when we made the decision on your amendment, 62 members of the U.N. owed the U.N. about $124 million on 1964 and prior year assessments. 1043 earlier to the chairman, this is specious. We are putting pressure on people to pay. There is an entire difference there.

Then I add further, take the poorest nation you have, the one least able to pay, and compare the amount that they owe to the amount of our foreign aid for just the last fiscal year, not cumulative of previous years, just the last fiscal year, and it is almost insignificant. 

Then finally my amendment provides for discretion on the part of the President to make a determination that it is essential to our national interest to nevertheless furnish foreign aid if a nation is not paying, but then he has to send a report over to your committee setting forth the assurance, if any, that that country has given, that it is going to make those payments or the economic conditions, the special conditions which make it impossible to do so. 

I think it is a most reasonably drawn amendment. I recognize that 

Mr. Gross, my colleague from Iowa has some concern about the use of this phrase "in the national interest." My amendment is designed to meet that objection by requiring that it be essential to the national interest.

STATEMENT OF PROF. JAMES SHELDON, COUNCIL FOR CHRISTIAN SOCIAL ACTION, UNITED CHURCH OF CHRIST 

Mr. SHELDON. My name is James Sheldon. I appear here on behalf of the Council for Christian Social Action of the United Church of Christ. I am a member of the international relations committee of the council and have also served for 5 years as chairman of the Committee on Christian Social Action of the New York State Conference of the United Church of Christ.

The Council for Christian Social Action is an official agency of the United Church of Christ, governed by a board of 27 men and women who are elected by the general synod of the denomination. 

It maintains offices in New York and Washington. 

The United Church of Christ was formed in 1957 by the merger of the General Council of the Congregational Christian Churches and the Evangelical and Reformed Church. Its membership totals more than 2 million persons.

I do not presume to speak for every one of our churches or every one of our members. I do, however, reflect positions which have been formally voted by the general synod, which in turn consists of publicly elected delegates from our churches and conferences in every 

State of the Union.

The Council for Christian Social Action is charged with the legal responsibility of carrying out and developing policy positions taken by the elected members of the general synod. 

I therefore begin by quoting from formal statements adopted by the general synod. At its meeting in July 1961 the synod declared: 

In the crucially important matter of world economic and social development, the United States has not been inactive. But our response still lacks the positive and energetic quality clearly demanded both by the need and by our national resources and traditions. For too many Americans the question still is how little we can do, or how soon we can be relieved of the "burden" ***. We should instead, rejoice in the great new opportunity to help build better foundations for free and peaceful societies throughout the world, and to aid in providing a better life for people hitherto tragically underprivileged.

1053 At its 1965 meeting the synod again emphasized the importance of overseas aid and development, and said:

The General Synod recognizes that our government, agencies and individual Americans have a supreme opportunity and obligation to assist developing nations to realize their own goals. Assistance in the scientific and technological areas should be geared to the felt needs and the aspirations of people themselves. 

Aid should be extended in such fields as population control programs, improved education, increased trade and the stabilizing of social structures. 

These, Mr. Chairman, are basic positions our denomination adopted through its elected delegates. 

So important does the United Church of Christ consider this issue that we have established in Washington a special office on foreign aid and development, for the purpose of more fully and adequately interpreting this subject to our churches and their members, and for maintaining a continuous relationship between the United Church and the many governmental agencies concerned. 

As director of this important project, we have chosen the Reverend L. Maynard Catchings, a man who has had a long personal experience abroad in dealing with many of the issues involved in developing countries. For 5 years he was in Singapore and Malaysia where he was in charge of the training of YMCA secretaries and other youth leaders. He conducted leadership institutes in six other countries of 

Southeast Asia, and later, he headed the Singapore American School, whose enrollment included some 22 nationalities. He was also a con sultant to the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Singapore. 

He returned home in the fall of last year, and now directs our newly established office of international development. 

It gives me real pleasure to introduce the Reverend Catchings to your committee today.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the action of the United Church of 

Christ in establishing this special office on foreign aid and development speaks for itself more loudly than any other arguments that I may be able to provide for you this morning. Ours is a democratically controlled church and when a budget is voted for such a purpose you can take it as definite proof that the denomination really has its heart in the cause.

Although this office is at present budgeted entirely by the United Church of Christ, it has from the beginning been established as a joint endeavor along with several other participating denominationsand under an arrangement recently completed, it will also serve as an integral arm of the National Council of Churches. 

I come now to the immediate proposals that are before your committee.

We strongly support the statement of President Lyndon B. Johnson in his message to you. He declared that: "In the long run, the wealthy nations cannot survive as islands of abundance in a world of hunger, sickness, and despair."

We emphatically support those portions of his message having to do with the importance of self-help, multilateralism, regionalism, and emphasis upon the key sectors of agriculture, health, and education. 

We are disturbed, however, by what appears to be a reduction in the total volume of America's commitment to this great purpose of world development.

1967 

As the costs of international development have mounted, the Executive has proposed and the Congress has voted successive decreases in the American contribution. During the Marshall plan (1948-53), the 

United States gave 2 percent of its gross national product as economic grants for European reconstruction. By contrast, the United States in 

1967 was providing only 0.3 to 0.4 percent to all of Asia, Africa, and 

Latin America, primarily for loans rather than grants. 

It is true that aid to Europe and economic and technical assistance to the developing nations have called forth unprecedented funds from the U.S. Government and have made substantial contributions to human welfare. Yet it is also true that disillusionment and apathy have overtaken U.S. development policy at the very time that the wisdom of experience is ripening, the fruits of scientific study are becoming genuinely significant, and the opportunities for acceleration in development are rising.

It is particularly unfortunate that the shrinking of American vision and support comes at a time when bitterness and despair are growing in the poorer nations.

To make our position precisely clear, the Council for Christian Social Action has declared that in its opinion an adequate aid and development program should require the allocation of at least 1 percent of the Nation's gross national product for governmental assistance, and a total public and private allocation of at least 2 percent of the GNP. 

This is an amount considerably in excess of the total written into the proposals presently before you.

We do not, however, think that it is an excessive amount. 

I happen to come from the former Congregational section of our merged United Church-and as many members of this committee know, New England Congregationalists are not notoriously careless with money. In fact, the term "Yankee parsimony" has sometimes been critically used against us.

In short, there are two imperatives which compel us, with about equal force, to support an adequate and enlarged program for foreign aid and development.

One of these two imperatives is religious, and the other is economic. 

It is unconscionable for a nation, wealthier than any other which God has permitted to exist, not to do what it can to help mitigate starvation and suffering. When we know that an injection of penicillin will change the life of a child in Malaysia from a short existence of misery and nonproductivity into a full existence of health and production, we cannot stand by and not provide the help needed. 

The traditions of the American Nation, and the commands we find written in the Bible, answer that question for us, and answer it categorically.

Now, there are many cases where it is easier to preach about a subject or make campaign speeches about a subject, than it is to take practical action.

But the matter before you today is one of those rare instances where what we ought to do, for reasons of morality and humanity, is so obviously what we also need to do for reasons of sound economy, that I cannot see why there should be much doubt about the matter. 

Perhaps the difficulty is traceable to some person who had too great an affinity for acronyms, and cut down the full name of the

1055 

FERM 

-0 

Agency for International Development into the single word "AID."

To be sure, aid is involved: but equally important is the fact that through this Agency-more than any other-America is making her investment in the future of the world. 

I recall saying to this committee in a previous hearing that foreign development is the process through which we push forward the American frontier in our day-and I do not say this in a chauvinistic or ungenerous spirit. Just as our ancestors, when they heard of the vast unsettled plains of our Middle West, felt that it was up to them to make those plains productive, so must we feel now that it is up to us to make productive the fertile plateaus of Nigeria, to develop the fisheries that abound off the shores of Ceylon, to find ways of raising more and bigger potatoes in the highlands of Peru and Bolivia, and :so on.

It is a truism to say that the world is getting smaller-but that is a fact which we must again and again realize. It was borne home to me in a very special way when I was in Saigon, recording tapes for radio broadcast in New York. I could say, "This is James Sheldon, speaking on Friday night in Saigon"-and thanks to modern jets, my tape would be back in New York in time to be broadcast there on the very same Friday night. Of course, the international date line had intervened.

Our country's business in the decade ahead will be closer to the farmers of Nigeria, the fishermen of Ceylon, and the potato-growing Indians of the South American alto plano, than was ever the case with my New England ancestors when they were doing business with Virginian plantation owners, in the days of the American Revolution. 

In short, the Agency for International Development is the means through which we push forward the frontier of America in our day, both spiritually and economically. The extent to which we succeed in this task will determine much of the future shape of the world, and will certainly determine the limits of our influence and trading. 

This is therefore a project in which we ought to invest not the least that we can get by with, but the most that we can possibly afford-because it will determine the future not only of our neighbors, but also of ourselves, and of our children. 

This is the one basic point which we have come to present before you today.

It combines both idealism and hardheaded business, and the two together make a weapon which, once taken up, can never fail. 

So much for general matters. I am directed also to present a few specific observations on the bill before you.

We strongly urge that the element of self-help be built into our future development programs wherever at all possible. As President 

Kennedy said:

To those peoples in the huts and villages of half the globe, struggling to break the bonds of mass misery, we pledge our best efforts to help them help themselves, for whatever period is required.

I shall never forget watching poor farmers in Haiti manufacture mud bricks under the direction of one of our Point 4 specialists, for the purpose of building schoolrooms in their villages. The only aid that we were extending was a little technical advice, and the people were doing the rest. now To tom bre TEROLI

1967 

This particular project was not very successful-and that is the reason I cite it here. It was a case of too little and too late, because before the program had had an opportunity to take hold, the whole structure of Haitian society was seized upon by one of the most cruel dictators alive in the world today.

I have often wondered what would have been the situation in Haiti had we helped those farmers to build their schoolhouses a generation earlier, and I think it is a safe conclusion that had we done so, our State Department would not be burdened today with one of the more worrisome situations in our hemisphere relations. 

The type of program that can be carried on through self-help technicians not only represents the best investment, but it also tends to involve more and more people who must operate its facilities in the future, and they will do a better job for having had a part in the operation from the beginning.

Although it is not a part of this particular bill, your committee will, I know, consider the whole development program in relationship to our global trade and commodity policies. This is just another aspect of that New England parsimony that I spoke about a minute ago. It does no good to increase the coffee production of a country beyond what the market can absorb, or to develop a sound agriculture in a country and then erect fiscal policies which will upset its currency. 

I remember changing a hundred-dollar bill for more than a million bolivianos one day in Bolivia. Obviously, in such a condition of inflation, development funds invested by the one hand were being taken away by poor fiscal policies resulting from actions by the other hand. 

We hope and strongly urge that this question of world development will not be considered finished once you have completed the bill that is now before you. It is absolutely necessary to think of the problems of development in the closest association with problems of world trade and finance.

There is one aspect of this bill, however, which does impinge directly on this subject; namely, the sections having to do with the making of loans. Sometimes I believe we have handled our international loans as if we were in the pawnshop business rather than the international banking business-and that is no reflection upon either of those occupations. There is no sense in making a development loan unless it is made under such terms and over such a period of time that the results sought may reasonably be achieved. I therefore suggest the reasonable scaling down of many of our provisions for interest and return schedules on international development loans. 

In some cases, indeed, we should regard these loans as permanent investments, on which we shall gain our return not in terms of specific repayment but in terms of vastly increased business and security. 

A good deal has been said about the use of development funds as a means of influencing the attitude of other nations toward the United States; and as a corollary of this, about the question of labeling our material aid.

We do not believe that it is worthwhile to appropriate several billion dollars in order to get other people to give us thanks. I can think of no purpose for which I would less wish to pay taxes. The utility of investment in foreign development is to be judged in terms of results, and not of words; and in many cases the results may be vague, or visible only in the somewhat distant future.

1057 I have in mind, for example, an antimalaria project which I once visited in Vietnam. About 1,500 Vietnamese, under the direction of a military physician named General Oai, were engaged in spraying the thatched roofs and walls of huts and houses in malaria-infested regions. In one Province they had already reduced the incidence of malaria from more than 50 percent to less than 15 percent. 

They were using little over-the-shoulder spray guns, such as my father used to use to destroy insects in our apple orchard. Now the reason that I think of this project today is the following: I saw a warehouse containing a great number of these spray guns, through which the Vietcong had shot bullet holes. They were not at that time shooting at the men in the project, but were trying to stop the project by destroying the sprayers.

I tried to figure out why there should exist this strange alliance between the mosquitoes and the Vietcong. The answer was fairly clear: 

When the incidence of malaria had been cut down from 50 to 15 percent, the productivity of the Province rose by at least a third, and the happiness of every family was increased. 

In short, killing the mosquitoes was helping to lay the foundations of a free and prosperous government. And that was the very reason which prompted the Vietcong to enter that particular war on the side of the mosquitoes.

Now it is obvious that in such a situation we do not need to worry about having every spray gun labeled "A Gift From the United States."

What we are trying to do there is to build a workable society, constructed by the hands of the people themselves. 

In this illustration I have also indicated another major reason for increased appropriations for international development purposes. 

When people are more productive, there is a better opportunity for education, and there are greater obstacles in the way of those forces who would like to set up communism or other kinds of dictatorship. 

The effectiveness of development as a bulwark of democracy in the world depends upon the success of projects such as this one I have been talking about.

The same kind of thinking ought also to govern us in deciding what to do about development funds for countries with whose governmental policies we do not totally agree. 

There we must not ask the question: "Is this country safely on our side?" but instead we must ask the more important question: "Is there a possibility that if the people of this country have a better life, they may come to be on our side?"

An exception would arise, of course, when a nation is engaged in making war—or overtly threatening war-against another nation to which the United States extends assistance, or with which we are at peace. In such a situation, economic implements would no longer be effective, and ought to be discontinued. 

I do, however, believe that we would be wise to give up the idea of limiting our aid to a narrow circle of any particular number of countries, limited by specific provisions in the bill. There are many new and small nations where a mere "drop in the bucket" may bring bigger future results than a vastly larger expenditure in older situations.

1967 

Finally, Mr. Chairman, I want to pledge to you and to this committee the support of the instrumentalities of the United Church, in making our country's program of foreign aid and development the best program that it can possibly be. This is a matter very near to the central purposes of the United Church and we take our obligations in this regard very seriously.

STATEMENT OF HON. PAUL FINDLEY, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF ILLINOIS 

Mr. FINDLEY, Mr. Chairman, we had a very illuminating and I think helpful presentation by General Draper and three other witnesses earlier this week. They dealt with what I would call the population-food collision; to put the problem simply, the world population is growing at accelerating rates. America's ability to meet the world's food deficit is decreasing with terrifying speed. As William and Paul 

Paddock, authors of "Famine 1975" state, collision between exploding population and a static agriculture is imminent. This very day about 12,000 people will die of hunger in the world, and we have no reason but to expect that tomorrow another 12,000 and the day after that, still more.

The agonizing story will continue. This problem won't go away, in fact; it is getting worse all the time. A relatively easy way to grasp the enormity of the problem is to consider the rate of increase of the most prolific countries of the world, and taking these figures from the book by the Paddock brothers entitled "Famine 1975," and taking as the best year 1957, the year of the most recent available census, these are the years in which the populations of these countries will double -compared to 1957. 1063

1967

Vietnam__ Honduras_ Malaysia. Mexico... Mongolia. 1973 1974 1974 1975 1976 1977 1977 1977 1977 1978 1978 1979 1979 1979 1979 1979 1979 1980 Panama.. Philippines.. Brazil.

Mr. FINDLEY. They are apt to be conservative rather than on the high side. This population explosion can be explained because of a number of different dynamics. Perhaps the most striking and the least understood is the sharp decline in death rates. We think of the population explosion in terms of birth rates, but the factor that has caused the problem to be far more serious than birth rates has been the decline in death rates.

In Latin America, for example, the death rate per thousand declined from 19 in 1950 down to 12 in 1965, and going still lower. 

The Paddocks explain the population explosion by pointing to several population "dynamics": 

1. The death rate has dropped sharply with the effectiveness and widespread acceptance of modern-day medicine. 

Below is a table from "Famine, 1975" showing the declining death rates in less developed countries. 

Falling death rates in the hungry world World. Asia..

Africa 

Latin America.. [Per thousand] 

1935 000 1950 1965 1980 25 19 16 12.7 33 23 20 13 27 23 18 19 12 8.2 

2. A larger proportion of the people in this world are young and capable of having children. In Latin America there will be 60 percent more marriages in 1975, than in 1967. 

3. Ten years ago the maximum birth rate possible was believed to be 45 per thousand. Today the birth rate has increased to as high as 50 per thousand. There are a combination of reasons for this statistic such as health and as just mentioned a higher percentage of young people within most societies.

The agriculture side of the picture is equally bleak. Nations that prior to World War II were major exporters of grain now import food to survive.

1065 Until a decade ago the world was increasing food production somewhat faster than the number of mouths to be fed. This was managed largely by utilizing new land. It was just about that time when this virgin land ran low. B. R. Sen, Director General of FAO, summed up the situation in a 1965 statement to Ministers and Secretaries of Agriculture throughout the world. "The stark fact is that it is now no less than 7 years since there was any appreciable increase in food production per head of world's population. These have been 7 very lean years for the developing countries. The world food situation is now more precarious than at any time since the period of acute shortage immediately after the second World War".

The plain fact is that the stork has passed the plow. 

Beginning in 1963 FAO has issued regular statements that the world's population is growing 1 percent faster than its food production. In 1966 world population grew by 70 million, but there was no increase in agricultural production according to an FAO study. In 

Africa, Asia and Latin America per capita food production last year actually dropped so that there was 4 to 5 percent less food available for each person in those hungry areas than the previous year. 

Recent data developed by the Agriculture Department reveals that corn yields per acre in Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador were higher in the 4-year period 1955-59 than in 1961-63. In Brazil both wheat and corn per acre yields were higher in 1935-39 than in 1955–60. 

Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the food production story is that what increases in food production have occurred in the developed countries can be attributed almost entirely to putting into production land which was previously unused. Since World War II, four-fifths of the agriculture production in the undeveloped nations has resulted not from the use of fertilizers or other new technology but from putting new land into production. It was nothing more than extending traditional farming methods into submarginal land. 

But by 1958 most of the unused, submarginal land which would be brought into production even on a forced, substandard basis was being farmed. 

Thus, with no new technology and no new marginal land available the race between food production and mouths to be fed-the race which until then agriculture had at least been keeping up with-now is being lost.

New food developments may eventually meet the problems. But synthetic foods, food from the ocean, or dramatic agricultural research are long-range answers. Needs are immediate. Very soon we will face widespread famines in many parts of the world. 

I would like to discuss several amendments and a different approach to foreign aid which I would hope the committee would give some consideration to. This program could be transformed into an effective instrument for worldwide self-help and food production and population control. 

The population explosion is already causing widespread famine in India and within a decade as these figures I earlier cited show, millions of people there and in other countries will die of starvation unless broad and effective measures are taken quickly to improve food production and population control. The time for moralizing and academic discussion of these questions I feel is past, and the time for action is here.

1967 

To me the single most important item of business before the 90th Congress is to inaugurate an effective worldwide program to avert famine. Therefore I suggest that we not only redirect the foreign assistance program, but even give it a new name. 

The name that I would suggest would be famine prevention, which would reflect the new targeting of the program to these related twin problems. The amendments I suggest for your consideration, and you will find the text of the amendments I am sure before you, the first amendment would require annual achievement targets in food production and population control for each country receiving aid. Yearend reports to Congress on how well each measures up. This is quite a change from the present approach on either of these problems. It has been felt with some justification that population control is too delicate a matter to talk about in specific statistics or objectives or targets. But if the future is as I see it, and I believe it to be, we simply have to set aside some of the sensitivities that we have recognized in the past and try to get on with a program which is realistic and effective.

The suggestion I present here on establishing annual achievement targets including production and population control, is only a first step. Maybe it will do the job; maybe it won't. At least it would be a reasonable and moderate starting point and after a year or two of experience we could then review its effectiveness and decide whether it was adequate for a continuing basis. 

The second suggestion I have in the way of an amendment is to require that programs related to food production and population control get a first claim on all funds of the foreign assistance program or as I would say it, the famine prevention program. This would take the form of a provision in the general authority of the Foreign Assistance Act which would require that the President certify before he authorizes any moneys for programs not related to population and food control that these moneys cannot be utilized effectively for these purposes. This would require indeed that population control and food production have No. 1 priority and first claim on all resources of the program. The amendment allows the President adequate discretion. He can determine whether projects are related to food production and population control. However, the amendment will require that he review critically the authorized expenditure to determine whether the moneys can be utilized fully for food production and population control. This amendment will insure that other less-essential programs will not compete with what must be our principal priorities in the developing nations.

I have another suggestion which is patterned after an amendment which was made a part of Public Law 480 last year. Under it some 

U.S.-owned local currencies which are piling up at an astonishing rate in what are called the excess currency countries would be made available for use under U.S. supervision to guarantee credit, to encourage risk taking in private enterprise on the part of local business interests whether they be farmers or involved in population control activities or other enterprises. These U.S.-owned local currencies which are now lying idle, doing no one any good, which cannot be spent outside the country, would be made available for use to stimulate what

1067 might be called the entrepreneurial class in those countries, which I am sure we would all agree is the great hope of the developing countries.

The text of the language that you have before you on this amendment is taken almost verbatim from the language which is a part of the Public Law 480 program. The reason that two different approaches to this are necessary is that the Public Law 480 amendment dealt only with the currencies that were accumulating as a result of Public Law 480 transactions of the past. The currencies which would be freed by means of this amendment are those which have accumulated in these excess currency countries as a result of payback in local currencies as distinguished between dollars from AID loans in past years. 

You are aware I am sure that under present law economic loans have to be repaid in dollars, but before this requirement became effective quite a number of loans were made and they are being paid off now in local currencies. They are owned by the United States, but are simply excess currencies that are not being utilized. 

My proposal is that these local currencies be made available to encourage private enterprise risk taking in the underdeveloped countries. Already in the Foreign Assistance Act is provision for guarantee with dollars of risk taking by U.S. investors in these countries, and an even more laudable objective from their standpoint as well as from ours is to encourage risk taking on the part of local interests. 

The use would normally be to make loans. The President would be authorized, however, to guarantee other financing, loan or equity, for private businesses. This amendment would be a significant measure to encourage risk taking, strengthen the private market plan, and establish local entrepreneurs.

Priority in use would be to increase the availability of financing for farmers as well as enterprises processing, distributing, storing, and marketing food, for family planning enterprises and other enterprises. 

The funds for all of this would be excess foreign currencies that are now accruing under prior foreign aid loans and which now are not being fully utilized. The United States needs and uses for those excess currencies have already been met. 

Those excess currencies are not the same as dollars. Their use would be to finance goods and services produced locally. There is a continuing demand for local currency credit resources among private businesses, particularly among the development banks lending to private businesses. 

This kind of use has generally been agreed to be the countries concerned. Thus this program could be started without the necessity of seeking new agreements by the local governments. 

The Indian fellow who has some money to invest, risk, we want to encourage him to invest it and risk it in his own territory, hopefully in food production so they can build their own marketplace system.

National Advisory Committee on Self-Help to recommend to the President not later than January 1 of next year, for transmittal immediately to Congress, recommendations in regard to establishing an agricultural research and training center in each of the three major tropical regions in Latin America, Africa, and Asia. We have done tremendous wonders in agricultural research in the temperate zones, but I learned, partly from my experience on the House Agriculture Committee the last 6 years, that this research and study and development of agricultural food production techniques has not been applied to the tropical regions.

In those regions, ironically, the position of agricultural specialist or farm manager is not upgraded as it should be. There is a tendency on the part of those seeking higher education to go into the humanities, into the professions, rather than into agriculture. I think the time has come for us to study the possibility at least of establishing adequate centers for research and training in agriculture in these three major tropical regions.

My final amendment in regard to food production and population control would be similar to the one offered in the Senate. In this case 

I would stipulate that not less than $75 million of the resources earmarked by this year's authorization be for population control projects, including research. 

I have also an amendment which is not directly related to food production and population control, but I believe is of great importance to us as a nation. It would encourage, I believe, the maintenance and development of basic freedoms in the countries that receive aid. Under it the National Advisory Committee on Self-Help, which is already provided by law would be required to report annually to the Congress on the status of these basic freedoms in each of the countries receiving aid, and the freedoms I have in mind are those set forth in the U.N. 

Declaration of Human Rights, to which virtually every nation on earth has subscribed, and these are freedom of the press, speech, assembly, worship, security of the person, and freedom from arbitrary arrest in each country.

I placed in the Congressional Record not long ago a table listing the countries of Africa and Latin America and rating press freedom in

1069 each of these. It is not my rating, it is a rating provided by a professional organization reported in the Journalism Quarterly. The Missouri School of Journalism now has a worldwide institute on world freedom. It is in the process of rating press freedom in various countries.

I was shocked to notice the press freedom or press control from country to country in Africa and Latin America. They range so widely there seems to be no rhyme or reason to it. It occurs to me by showing our interest in basic freedoms as a part of this program, not by establishing the establishment of freedoms as a firm, fixed requirement for aid, but showing our interest in them requiring annual reporting on the status of these freedoms, we could perhaps tend to level these things up in the right direction.

I have one final suggestion. I hope before too long we will find it possible to make the food-for-peace program, Public Law 480, a part of the, hopefully, famine program that I suggest you will recall, I am sure, I suggested we change this into a famine prevention program. I submit as a part of my remarks the complete text of my amendments. (The amendments are as follow:)

Section 209 (which deals with the National Advisory Committee on Self-Help): (d) The Committee shall establish as soon as possible and yearly thereafter, for each recipient country minimum achievement targets in food production and population control, and shall determine annually the level of achievements in food production and population control and their relation to the targets previously established for the year for each recipient country. The committee shall report promptly achievement target details and determinations of levels achieved to the President for transmittal within 30 days to the Congress. (e) In order to encourage the maintenance and development of these basic freedoms freedom of press, speech, assembly, worship, security of person and freedom from arbitrary arrest, the Committee is directed to report annually to the President for transmittal within 30 days to the Congress on the status of each of these freedoms in each recipient country indicating changes which may have occurred in the preceding year. (f) Not later than January 1, 1968 the Committee is directed to report to the President for transmittal to the Congress within 30 days recommendations in regard to establishing an agricultural research and training center in each of the three major tropical regions-Latin America, Africa and Asia. In developing its recommendations the Committee is directed to consult with the Department of Agriculture, Land-Grant Colleges of Agriculture, and other appropriate institutions. 

Subsection (b) of Section 211 (General Authority) is amended by adding the following language:

The President shall certify that monies obligated for any purpose not involved, directly or indirectly, in food production and population control cannot be effectively utilized for the latter 2 purposes.

Section 612 (which relates to the use of foreign currencies) is amended by adding thereto a new subsection as follows: (d) Notwithstanding Section 1415 of the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1953, excess foreign currencies, as defined in subsection (b) may be available, in addition to funds otherwise available, to encourage the establishment, improvement or expansion of private enterprise in friendly less developed countries. Priority shall be given to enterprises designed to promote, increase, or improve food production, processing, distribution, storing, marketing and enterprises related to population control. The President may make loans or guaranties with such currencies on such terms and conditions as he may deem appropriat? in the circumstances. There was no investment in food production, self-help on the part of India until I believe about 2 years ago.

It is quite plain to agricultural economists that India can feed its present population adequately without any problem if it will use the right techniques. It can feed twice the population. It has the right soil and ample water to do this. It has to break loose from the methods and habits of the past.

STATEMENT OF HON. ANDREW J. BIEMILLER, DIRECTOR, DEPART- MENT OF LEGISLATION, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF LABOR AND CONGRESS OF INDUSTRIAL ORGANIZATIONS Mr. BIEMILLER.  

Mr. Chairman, my name is Andrew J. Biemiller. I am director of the Department of Legislation of the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations. I am here today to reiterate the support of the AFL-CIO for our Nation's foreign aid program in general and to express our support for the foreign aid authorization legislation proposed by President Johnson for fiscal 1968. 

The AFL-CIO executive council on February 26, 1967, declared: 

In the present international situation, overseas aid is an indispensable part of our nation's foreign policy for preserving world peace, promoting freedom and fostering economic progress based on social justice. 

In this recognition, the AFL-CIO urges Congress to give prompt and overwhelming support to President Johnson's proposal for $3.1 billion in new funds for 1968 foreign aid.

The President reflects the viewpoint of the overwhelming majority of the American people in calling on the countries devoted to peace, democracy and human well-being for maximum cooperation in helping the developing nations achieve freedom from hunger, tyranny and war. Such concerted efforts would be a boon to all mankind and additionally they would strengthen the recipient nations' social base against subversion by Communists and other reactionary forces and thus tend to discourage aggressive adventurers endangering world peace. 

The Executive Council rejects the notion that the Foreign Aid program is a wasteful give-away or policy of futile philanthropy. Though comparatively prosperous, our own country has a better chance of attaining broadly-based stable prosperity in a peaceful world not weighed down by impoverishment, ignorance, illness and dictatorship.

The current economic aid request of $3.1 billion amounts to only one-third of 1 percent of our gross national product. This is in sharp contrast to our foreign aid program in the late 1940's. In 1949, we were putting 1.5 percent of our GNP into foreign aid-almost five times the proportion of our GNP that we are now putting into foreign aid. 

The AFL-CIO executive council has declared that this Nation should have "an annual foreign aid authorization at least equal to 1 percent of the gross national product." The executive council says that: 

An authorization of 1 percent of GNP would be a realistic response to the President's admonition that "in the long run, the wealthy nations cannot survive on islands of abundance in a world of hunger, sickness, and despair." 

As the executive council points out:

Aid to the new nations is a more complex and difficult process. It will take longer to realize the fruits of our assistance programs and to attain decisive results in the industrially underdeveloped areas. It takes more time, effort and

1967 

greater outside assistance to help the emerging nations develop the necessary modern social, economic and cultural changes and institutions. 

There is no other way to help these peoples achieve industrialization and modernization without repeating the tragic cost in human exploitation and degradation incurred by the industrial revolution in western Europe and by the forced industrialization and collectivization in the Communist countries. 

The AFL-CIO has always insisted that our country's AID program should be directed and administered in such a way as to help the growth of democratic institutions, like free trade unions and cooperatives, in the less developed countries.

We are proud of the role the AFL-CIO and organizations like the American 

Institute for Free Labor Development and the African-American Labor Center have played in this work and we intend that it shall be continued and expanded. 

We would like to mention some of the specific activities and accomplishments of the AIFLD and the AALC. 

In Latin America the AIFLD, since 1961, has supported several thousand educational courses in trade unionism and more than 100 social projects to strengthen free trade unions so that they can better represent the interests of the workers. 

More than 500 Latin American labor leaders have graduated from the advanced training school in Front Royal, Va., during the past 5 years.

More than 60,000 trade unionists have graduated from evening, weekend, and month-long courses given at AIFLD centers in Latin America.

A new AIFLD program-training in labor economics at the graduate school level in the United States-recently graduated 15 Latin American trade unionists who will set up research offices and training programs in their own unions in Latin America. 

The effectiveness of this AIFLD education program can best be judged by the number of graduates who stay in the labor movement after their training. More than 80 percent of these trade unionists are still actively working to preserve free, democratic trade unions in Latin American countries and in English-speaking Caribbean countries. 

Social projects such as housing, credit, and savings associations, vocational schools, and medical facilities strengthen free trade unions by showing progress attainable through unionism. In 5 years, about 

7,500 housing units have been completed with a total financing of over $34 million. AIFLD has plans for more than 6,000 more units in nine countries.

In Peru, a worker's savings and loan association has attracted more than 7,800 depositors and $2 million in savings in 3 years of operation. 

These savings have helped finance about 500 homes. 

AIFLD is active also in rural areas working with "campesino" unions in northern Brazil, Central America, Colombia, and many other countries. Three rural service centers have been built in Brazil and one is being developed in Colombia. These centers are focal points for community action, vocational instruction, union activities, health services, and literary training.

Success with AIFLD in Latin America encouraged the AFL-CIO to start a similar effort for Africa. In 1965 the African-American 

Labor Center was established by the AFL-CIO. 

We are fully aware that the social and economic problems of workers and unions in the newly emerging countries of Africa are quite different from South America, but our objective is the same-

1083 =1 the development of a strong free democratic labor movement as a vital force for social, economical, and political development. 

The AALC, still in its infancy, is helping workers in 13 different African countries. AALC projects include job training and education for workers, medical clinics, cooperatives, and housing. 

We believe the AALC is making an urgently needed contribution to the development of free democratic trade unionism in Africa in a manner parallel to the AIFLD operation. We urge the strong support of this committee for both these programs. 

These two programs fully accord with the intent of title IX of the 

Foreign Assistance Act. This title calls for "Utilization of Democratic 

Institutions in Development." The importance of Latin American and African labor unions and labor leadership cannot be downgraded or underestimated. This view lies behind our support for the African- 

American Labor Center and for AIFLD. But obviously the AIFLD and the AALC need expanding AID support. 

For this reason we regret that the portion of AID technical cooperation funds going to labor projects has been so small. Figures now available for fiscal 1966 show a decline in the share of worldwide technical assistance grants for labor projects from 1.8 percent in fiscal 1965 down to 1.32 percent in fiscal 1966.

In Latin America, labor projects received only 4.6 percent of technical assistance grants in 1965 and 1966. In Africa, labor projects received a mere 0.6 percent of the technical assistance grants. This very low percentage indicates a lack of appreciation of the role of labor in Africa today.

We believe the allocation of AID technical assistance funds should reflect the importance of labor unions in Latin America and Africa. 

Therefore, we urge this committee to direct AID to allocate a larger share of its technical assistance funds for labor projects. 

Last year your committee declared that "the portion of technical assistance going to labor is small in proportion to the role it is generally agreed labor must play in democratic development." The portion is still too low. We hope this committee will again express its view to AID on this subject.

The President has requested a worldwide technical assistace authorization of $243 million for fiscal 1968 with $100 million for Latin America and $91 million for Africa. In line with our support for technical assistance generally and for labor projects financed with technical assistance funds, we urge this committee to approve the full amount requested by the President for technical assistance. 

In connection with Africa, the "labor impact fund," is essential to AALC work in Africa. This fund, which consists of contributions by 

AID, as well as by the AFL-CIO, enables the AALC to implement projects throughout Africa with only the ambassador's or mission director's approval, and without the necessity for time-consuming redtape. At present, this fund is completely committed and we request the committee to instruct AID to increase its size in order to permit an expanded use of this excellent mechanism. 

A similar and equally important aspect of our foreign assistance program which has not received sufficient attention by AID is the Special 

Development Activities Fund administered by every AID mission 

77-470-67-pt. 5- -12

1967 

director. The money in this fund, which is supported solely by AID, is channeled directly to private groups in developing countries. It gives us a chance to provide an immediate demonstration of programs while greater and more time-consuming projects are in the mill. Your committee strongly supported this fund last year, and we urge that you again emphasize the high potential of these projects. 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me repeat a point we have made before to this committee. As our AFL-CIO executive committee has said: 

Over the years, some mistakes have been made in conceiving AID programs and administering them. Experience has to be gained and errors have to be corrected. 

The AID program now proposed by the President has had the advantage of two decades of experience behind it-experience under Republican and Democratic 

Administrations. 

On this basis, the Executive Council welcomes the President's proposal "to provide the continuity needed for sound management" by requesting "authorizations covering two years".

Let me make it clear that we strongly support longer authorization of funds. Indeed, we believe a 5-year authorization is reasonable and desirable. We urge that this committee approve at least a 2-year authorization for our foreign aid program. 

We also support the President's request for authorization to establish a "National Advisory Committee on Self Help" which will consist of members from both parties, from the business community, from labor, form universities, and from other walks of life. We believe such a committee can make a valuable contribution to our foreign aid program.

To us, the administration's foreign aid proposals appear very sound, and therefore we urge passage of the 1967 Foreign Assistance Act. We are ready to do our part in the aid program, and the specific recommendations we have made in this testimony, if adopted, will allow us to act more effectively in our particular portion of this total effort which is so vital to the progress of the developing areas and the peace of mankind. 

Mr. Chairman, I respectfully request that the AFL-CIO Executive

Council statement of February 26, 1967, "Overseas Aid," be included in the record at the conclusion of my testimony. I thank you for this opportunity to present the views of the AFL-CIO.

(The statement referred to above follows:) STATEMENT BY THE AFL-CIO EXECUTIVE COUNCIL ON OVERSEAS AID, FEBRUARY 26, 1967, BAL HARBOUR, FLA. 

In the present international situation, overseas aid is an indispensable part of our nation's foreign policy for preserving world peace, promoting freedom and fostering economic progress based on social justice. 

In this recognition, the AFL-CIO urges Congress to give prompt and overwhelming support to President Johnson's proposal for $3.1 billion in new funds for 1968 foreign aid.

The President reflects the viewpoint of the overwhelming majority of the American people in calling on the countries devoted to peace, democracy and human well-being for maximum cooperation in helping the developing nations achieve freedom from hunger, tyranny and war. Such concerted efforts would be a boon to all mankind and additionally they would strengthen the recipient

1085 11 nations' social base against subversion by Communists and other reactionary forces and thus tend to discourage aggressive adventurers endangering world peace. 

The Executive Council rejects the notion that the Foreign Aid program is a wasteful give-away or policy of futile philanthropy. Though comparatively prosperous, our own country has a better chance of attaining broadly-based stable prosperity in a peaceful world not weighed down by improverishment, ignorance, illness and dictatorship.

Moreover, our country's foreign aid program should be judged on the basis of what it has prevented, as well as on what it has performed. 

The world would be far different today if we had not aided free Europe and Japan, Israel and India, Jordan, Brazil and the Republic of China, Kenya and Korea, Chile and the Dominican Republic, among others. No one can deny that, if left unaided, the developing countries would have been endangered by explosive squalor and chaos which could only have provided fuel for more wars. 

Instead, today, western Europe, Canada, and Japan have been giving about $2 billion a year in aid to the developing countries to achieve social and economic progress. While we believe they should provide more aid, what they are doing confirms the essential effectiveness of our country's foreign assistance program. 

The increased assistance rendered by nations we once helped accounts, in some measure, for the decline of our aid burden in recent years. When the 

Marshall Plan was started, our economic aid constituted 2% of our gross national product. Then, 11.5% of our Federal budget was earmarked for foreign aid. In contrast, for the year 1965, our overseas economic assistance took only three-tenths of one percent of our GNP and but 2% of our Federal budget. And, as President Johnson has pointed out, "the combined value of our economic and food aid is less than seven-tenths of one percent of our national income." 

The Executive Council has often called for an annual foreign aid authorization at least equal to one percent of the gross national product. We reaffirm this proposal. An authorization of one percent of GNP would be a realistic response to the President's admonition that "in the long run, the wealthy nations cannot survive on islands of abundance in a world of hunger, sickness and despair." 

It is in our own national interest to do everything to reduce the gap between the richer and the poor nations by aiding the latter's industrial development and enhancing their prosperity.

The net outflow of dollars attributable to AID has hardly affected our balance of payments deficit and was far more than compensated for by the AID program's stimulus to exports and jobs. 

No doubt, aid to the new nations is a more complex and diffcult process. It will take longer to realize the fruits of our assistance programs and to attain decisive results in the industrially under-developed areas. It takes more time, effort and greater outside assistance to help the emerging nations develop the necessary modern social, economic and cultural changes and institutions. 

There is no other way to help these peoples achieve industrialization and modernization without repeating the tragic cost in human exploitation and degradation incurred by the industrial revolution in western Europe and by the forced industrialization and collectivization in the Communist countries. 

Over the years, some mistakes have been made in conceiving AID programs and administering them. Experience has to be gained and errors have to be -corrected. The AID program now proposed by the President has the advantage of two decades of experience behind it-experience under Republican and Democratic administrations. 

On this basis, the Executive Council welcomes the President's proposal "to provide the continuity needed for sound management" by requesting "authorizations covering two years." 

We likewise support the President in his emphasis that "the development job is primarily the responsibility of the developing countries themselves." AID will be increasingly geared to helping nations help themselves. 

Thus, every nation aided by the United States would be required to provide the major portion of the resources required for the development. Today, India and Turkey finance more than 75% their development programs from their -own resources. Recipient countries would be required to show that they are improving their own agricultural output before they can be eligible for American aid.

1967 

Furthermore, U.S. AID dollars are now seldom given directly to foreign governments. Most of current American AID involves the financing of U.S. goods and services for specific projects. Their feasibilities and priorities are carefully considered in advance. In the fiscal year 1965, more than 90% of the 

AID-financed commodities were purchased from American firms. Over $80 million were paid U.S. shipping lines for transporting these cargoes. In the coming year, well over 85% of AID expenditures will be for purchasing American goods and services. This compares with but 42% in 1960. 

The AFL-CIO has always insisted that our country's AID program should be directed and administered in such a way as to help the growth of democratic institutions, like free trade unions and cooperatives, in the less developed countries. 

We are proud of the role the AFL-CIO and organizations like the American 

Institute for Free Labor Development and the African-American Labor Center have played in this work and we intend that it shall be continued and expanded. 

We have persistently sought to have U.S. AID efforts geared to improving the living standards of the people, no less than to advancing their rate of national economic growth. In this spirit, American labor has actively championed agricultural reforms, better working conditions, higher educational levels, improved health and social projects. 

We heartily approve the President's request for authorization "to establish a National Advisory Committee on Self Help" which will "consist of members from both parties, from the business community, from labor, from universities and from other walks of life."

It would be wrong to approach foreign aid in a narrow business sense. Our humanitarian traditions, democratic heritage and our deep concern for the kind of world in which our children will live do not permit the American people to revert to any policy, like scuttling foreign aid, which would-in effect-be isolationist. We help others not because we seek their gratitude. We help others because our highest ideals and most vital interests require a world free from tyranny, poverty and war.

The Executive Council rejects as baseless the notion that "we give to conquer." 

We likewise repudiate as outright slander the contention of those who brand our country's AID effort merely as "an instrument of cold war" or "national charity."

Between 1945-1960, our country pumped in about $22 billion as aid to developing nations. In the past 12 years, the U.S. has distributed $15.5 billion in surplus food around the world. Our country has given thirty times as much aid to other countries as all the Communist nations put together. Here is no “arrogance of power."

America has neither sought nor acquired a foot of foreign soil in return. The 

American people can be justly proud that no other nation in history has done as much for safeguarding and strengthening freedom and assisting economic progress based on social justice. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you for your statement, Mr. Biemiller. Let me, at this time, express my congratulations to the AIFLD and the AALC in their activities in Latin America and Africa. Concerning your request that this committee again express its views to AID on the small amount of assistance going to labor, I can assure you as one member of this committee I agree and I will pursue the matter and insist that more assistance does go to labor projects.
