STATEMENT OF DEAN CLOWES, DEPUTY DIRECTOR, AFRICAN- AMERICAN LABOR CENTER 

Mr. CLOWES. The African-American Labor Center works in cooperation with the trade unions in the different African countries as well as in conjunction with the governments of those countries. 

Mrs. BOLTON. May I interrupt. If the trade union doesn't exist, then what?

Mr. CLOWES. We work with the Ministries of Labor in those countries, hoping to be able to eventually develop trade unions. Our programs are basically in the fields of trade union education, vocational training, cooperatives, medical clinics, and housing. We have in Kenya a tailoring school and are for the first time training Kenyans in the process of manufacturing dresses, suits, and clothing. This particular project is supported by the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union which has put up most of the money for the development of the project. The director of the school is a designer who comes from the garment industry in New York.

In Nigeria we are developing with the Drivers' Union of that country a program to train workers to handle and maintain heavy equipment and also to drive and care for their vehicles. In this program we have received a gift of equipment from Esso Standard. They have given us trucks and other heavy equipment to be used in training. 

They have also agreed to employ the people who graduate from this driver training school. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Do they have enough roads?

1967 

Mr. CLOWES. There is need for improved highways in Nigeria. The government is presently building additional highways. You must recognize that one of the chief methods of transport is the over-theroad vehicle.

We also are developing a number of educational programs particularly in Ghana, the Congo, and Nigeria, all very critical areas of Africa. We hope to be able to develop enlightened, trained union people who will not only be interested in the development of democratic unions but also in the economic development of their own countries.

We are planning in September to convene a general conference on economic development in Africa where we will invite as participants the major leaders of the African trade unions- 

Mrs. BOLTON. That will be where?

Mr. CLOWES. It will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. What we hope to do is develop trade union leaders who can make a contribution in their own country and also a contribution to Africa in economic development instead of having only government officials and industry leaders responsible for this activity. We feel the trade unions have a major role to play in economic development. 

We hope to be able to train people for this purpose. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Do you have any training for women?

Mr. CLOWES. Yes, we are presently developing a program in 

Ethiopia. Many of the young women who are coming from the rural areas into the major industrial cities are in need of a program of urbanization education in order to understand their new role. 

We are working with the women and the trade unions in Ethiopia to this end.

Mrs. BOLTON. Are the men willing to relinquish their feet on the machines?

Mr. CLOWES. This is happening, especially in the textile industry. 

Mrs. BOLTON. That has been their job, hasn't it? 

Mr. CLOWES. That is right. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you very much.

Mr. DOHERTY. Congressman Selden, I appreciate your compliment with regard to the work that we are doing in that very difficult area. 

As you know, the northeast part of Brazil is a particularly depressed area. They have suffered from drought, poor soil conditions and overpopulation and underemployment for many years. 

From a political point of view it has also been distressed and this was the reason that a few years ago, this was where the Communist movement was able to arm and train Communist leaders in the field

1089 of guerrilla activity. We were particularly interested in trying to reorient these groups that were paramilitary operations into a more positive trade union movement that would accomplish real progress in behalf of the workers.

We were able to convince the chief of the AID mission of a "campesino service center" concept that we had evolved going out into the hinterlands in three rural areas. The idea of these centers was to build a structure which would be very functional in purpose at a minimum cost. They range between $40,000 and $60,000 in their cost. The centers not only accommodate the unions in terms of giving them places to have meetings, but also to have trade union training classes and to help in terms of their problems with the agricultural situation. 

We have been able to go into these centers and help them develop marketing cooperatives, producer cooperatives. We are able to help them increase their own skills.

Mrs. Bolton may be interested that Mr. Dubinsky made sewing machines available so we could take the women of the community to teach them to make better clothes for their children. The women are now participating more in the community than they had in that particular area before. One of the important aspects of our work in literacy training. We found these people could not be good union people and good farmers unless they could read and write.

In cooperation with a Lutheran organization we have been able to get literacy training going in all three centers. The effect of our work has been that the leaders of the rural unions have publicly stated, as well as a Catholic priest who has cooperated with these unions, Father Crespo, that had it not been for the centers, the federation would probably have gone under during the past 2 years.

AID thinks it has been a worthwhile effort, and they have allocated local currency to have us build three new centers. We have representatives in three new northeastern States putting together the ingredients to get the centers going. We think it is important in the trade union, agricultural development and in the democratic political development of that region. 

Mr. SELDEN. I might tell you that I ran into one of the leaders in that particular labor center who had come to the United States on a grant of some type. He did not speak English, only Portuguese. When he arrived in New York, through some mixup, he was not met. 

He spent the night in the airport, and the next morning a policeman put him back on a plane and he went back to Recife. Although he is still a very ardent supporter of the United States, this might not be true of everyone who received similar treatment. Consequently, I think it might be a good idea, perhaps it could come through the labor organization, to meet these groups when they come up. Had there been such an arrangement, this would not have occurred. I hope we can get the gentleman back to the United States.

Mr. DOHERTY. I would hope to be able to claim with a great deal of certitude that this gentleman did not belong to our organization. We make great effort that all our visitors from Latin America are met at the port of entry. I therefore don't think this was our situation. 

I agree with you that they should have a warm welcome in our country.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. 

Mr. Biemiller, what has labor done so far to induce private industry to go into these underdeveloped countries, if anything? 

Mr. DOHERTY. Insofar as Latin America is concerned, currently the American labor movement along with Latin American labor leaders is serving on the private sector committee of the Common Market with the view toward implementing decisions that were made in Punta del Este with regard to a Latin American Common Market. We strongly feel that, in addition to government investment in the area, there has to be steadily increasing private investment if the Common Market and the whole market concept of creating greater purchasing power is to be successfully carried out in Latin America. 

We are trying to do everything possible in order to solve some of the labor problems that result from the need for greater investment, labor mobility, labor training, labor redundancy-the problems that are always present in the labor movement when automation and modernization of industry and the amalgamation of different industrial enterprises take place.

AID program to date is its failure to strengthen title 9 in a much more creative way to tailor political institutions to the realities and relevancies of the true situation in these underdeveloped countries. I think it is a very challenging thing for us to do because we have left them with a legacy of colonial governments, the French, British, ideally 77-470 0-67-pt. 5-13

1967 

suited politically for a colonial empire, but hardly the answer as we see, given the political instability of the last 8 years in Africa, and longer in Latin America, to effectively catapault these countries into the modern age with a minimum of political chaos. I would be interested in your observations as to whether we have been negligent in this regard. It seems to me that we have not designed and given enough tough-minded thought to creating political institutions which are suitable and genuinely and effectively accommodating the complex environments in which we are trying to operate. A Westminster model is nice for England, but what are we going to do with these countries in terms of effectively establishing political institutions which do give expression to the incredible tribal situations that exist there. 

It seems to me that when we try and superimpose some of these systems just out of national pride on these people, that they might work for a time because they have nothing else to hold onto in terms of national political institutions, but clearly the frustrations, both in implementation and limited manpower skills of the complex requirements of parliamentary government and more importantly, the inappropriateness oftentimes of these systems to the real problems of their constituencies, makes them totally unsuitable. 

We talk about the instability of Nigeria. What kind of instability will we have in Kenya when Kenyatta goes? It is stable today because we have a chief figure who is able to do something that nobody has been able to do before and that is work with these various tribes in the political spectrum there.

Will there be another strong man capable of that? I would be interested in your comments.

Mr. CLOWES. I think one of the principal roles that an organization like the African-American Labor Center can serve is to work with organizations within the country that transcend tribal and regional attitudes.

In Nigeria, for example, the trade union movement is the one organization that embraces people from all tribes and membership and participation from all of the regional sectors. This transcends tribal and regional ties. 

In Kenya the trade union movement has a very real role to play in making certain that there aren't further uprisings when and if there is a change in government. The trade unions working together with responsible political leaders can play a major role in maintaining national unity. 

Another good example as to the responsibility of the trade unions and the role they can play, is in the Congo where at the present time the trade union leadership of that country is serving on the board of the large copper operation in Katanga. 

It is this kind of attitude and this kind of role that the trade union can play to help unify their country. Getting back to your first point, the project that Congressman Gross was referring to is a project that is being funded by AID to some other organization and not through the African-American Labor Center.

Mr. CULVER. I couldn't care less where it is funded. I am grateful you have had $375,000 to apply to this. If we have able people working on this problem, the kind of information that they make available to our country might well lead to certain recommendations, both in Africa, as well as our own, that can be useful in terms of increasing the prospects for political stability.

1101 My real question to you is, based on your personal experience, whether or not you feel that our AID program has been negligent in terms of taking all the various alleged political science talent we have in this country and letting somebody write some rather creative and imaginative Ph. D. thesis on some of these countries as to how we can recommend the establishment of political institutions more effectively designed to bring about successful democratic institutions in an African context.

Mr. CLOWES. I don't think we are doing enough in this field. 

Mr. BIEMILLER. May I add on this point, Mr. O'Hara will recall, and I think this is the kind of thing we need more of, we recently brought to see Mr. O'Hara a Mr. Benton who is the Secretary General of the Trade Union Congress of Ghana who has written a very interesting book which I will supply members of the committee with on the overthrow of Nkrumah.

Mr. Benton was one of those who was in the government and ousted and is now the head of the Trade Union Congress. He was in this country doing just the reverse of what you are talking about. I am not belittling what you are saying; he was studying our institutions. to see how they could be adapted, if there was any basis for adaptation. 

He is on a committee of eight writing the new constitution of Ghana. There is a very serious effort being made here to study this kind of problem. As I recall, he told us in about 6 months from now that report has to be made. I think the more interchange of this kind we can have I sat down with him after he had been visiting around with Members of the House and Senate and watching some hearings and so on and he expressed a great deal of interest. 

He pointed out the point you are making that we just can't copy blindly what the British have used or the Americans have used. 

He commented on the tribal problems in Ghana, which exist there as you know, as well as in other countries. One interesting little sidelight, he told us as to how partly they are solving tribal problems in Ghana. They are maintaining their system of polygamy, in trying to see to it that a man's wives come from different tribes. 

They think this may have some effect on eventually helping to straighten out the tribal problems they have there. I quite agree, Mr. 

Culver, we have not paid sufficient attention to this idea that we can just blindly superimpose either the British or our institutions in Africa. 

I think that the African trade union leaders are quite cognizant of the fact and are trying to figure out new systems that will be adaptable to their own countries. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The time of the gentleman has expired. 

Mr. Buchanan.

Mr. BUCHANAN.  

Mr. Biemiller, what would be the position of the AFL-CIO on the use of AID funds for the development of heavy industry in developing countries such as, say, steel and textile in India or Latin America? generalization? 

Mr. BIEMILLER. I think there is no that can be made on that. I think it is purely you have to judge each question on its merits. We don't think there is any basic policy that can be laid down here.

Mr. BUCHANAN. That is very temperate in light of the fact that the livelihood of many of the members of the AFL-CIO is affected by low wage area foreign competition. For this reason, along with concern for the welfare of developing countries and people, I certainly want to join in the commendation of your efforts toward the development of free democratic labor movement in these various countries.

It seems to me it is very important not only to them but to us that wage standards and employment conditions shall be such in time in these developing countries that the competition, which we are not afraid of so long as it is fair, can be fair to our own working people. 

Certainly you would be commended for your efforts not only from their point of view but from ours. 

Mr. BIEMILLER. We feel this whole program is a two-way street, the United States has a great deal to gain from these programs as well as the developing countries. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. It has been a vital and an essential part of the development of our free society and of the fact that Karl Marx's dark predictions have been turned upside down in the United States since we have had the labor movement in this country.

AFRICAN-AMERICAN LABOR CENTER

1967 

Foreword

HE African-American Labor Center got underway in early 1965 under AFL-CIO sponsorship. It is based on the belief that African trade unions, while engaged in the usual tasks of representing their workers, also have a major role in the development of their country and in the building of free and democratic nations. It is in this spirit that the AALC concentrates on developing projects of economic and social importance in the countries of Africa, on the invitation and advice of the trade unions and with the cooperation of their national governments. 

It is our intention to specialize in five major areas of activity: • Vocational Training • Workers Education Cooperatives • Medical Clinics Housing The major purpose in publishing this brochure is to set out as clearly and succinctly as possible, the sources of our income and its uses. At the same time, we wish to emphasize the absolute and complete independence of the African-American Labor Center as to policies, activities and staff. The Board of Directors, under the chairmanship of George Meany, is drawn entirely from the Executive Council of the AFL-CIO. 

All basic policy decisions are subject to their control and supervision. 

As will be noted under projected activities our emphasis in the immediate future will be on regional projects but national projects of merit will still be considered. We are proud of our modest achievements of the past but expect to grow with the new nations of Africa, which are still in the very infancy of their existence. For Africa and the A.A.L.C., it is only the beginning. April 25, 1967 

IRVING BROWN 

Executive Director

Mr. ZABLOCKI. It is indeed a great pleasure to welcome Mrs. William M. Christopherson, chairman, Foreign Policy Committee, League of Women Voters of the United States.

The patience of the ladies is unending. We apologize for keeping you waiting so long. 

You have a prepared statement. You may proceed.

STATEMENT OF MRS. WILLIAM M. CHRISTOPHERSON, CHAIRMAN, FOREIGN POLICY COMMITTEE, LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF THE UNITED STATES 

I am Kathryn Christopherson, first vice president of the League of

Women Voters of the United States and chairman of the national board's foreign policy committee. The league has more than 145,000 members in over 1,200 local leagues in 50 States, Puerto Rico, and the District of Columbia. We are a volunteer citizens organization in the field of government on local, State, and national issues. 

I recognize that most members of this committee are familiar with the League of Women Voters long-standing support for adequate programs of economic assistance. Therefore, it would appear unnecessary to dwell on the league's conviction that exerting leadership to develop a viable world economy is unquestionably in this country's national interest. By the same token, I need not reiterate our conviction that the less-developed nations must give ample capital and technical assistance to supplement their own material and human resources if they are to reap the benefits of an expanding world economy. 

Foreign aid has become such an integral part of American foreign policy that it is easy to forget how recently it began. Although there were sporadic programs prior to the Marshall plan the year 1947 really marked the beginning of foreign aid. Its great success in Europe inspired the application of the same measures to the problems of the less-developed countries in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. However, these nations for the most part lacked the political institutions and economic structures which existed in Western Europe. So it was essential to work out in recent years new techniques for situations vastly different.

The problems of development are monumental but they are not insuperable. To break free from the vicious cycle of poverty, a country must simultaneously industrialize, develop its agricultural base, raise the general standard of living, educate its people in the social and political techniques of modern living, and combat the threat of population pressures. In a way these are all things which over time. we have learned to do, but I rather doubt that any of us in this room really understand quite how or quite why. In order to grow, the lessdeveloped countries must import capital goods and other materials not available from their own resources. They cannot increase their exports without further economic development. They cannot limit imports without stifling industrialization, and without paying the price for uneconomical substitute industries. 

Try as they may, there is a gap between income and expenditures which can be filled only by foreign assistance. While aid funds provide a very small portion of the investment needed for development, in many cases outside aid makes the difference between success or failure. 

Outside aid is the small but vital asset which enables these nations to progress toward their goals.

1117 The league believes that much progress has been made in the U.S. development aid programs, especially since the passage of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 which has served to place our assistance to the developing countries on a sounder footing. 

I proposed to focus my remarks today on the principles, purposes, and criteria of development aid which are set forth in the authorizing legislation under your review, to comment briefly on those specific programs in which the league has an interest, and finally, to explain the importance we attach to the 2-year authorization. 

POLICY AND CRITERIA 

We welcome the succinct restatement of policy which sharpens our country's interest and objectives in economic development and reflects what has been learned over the last decade. This statement, plus the section on the purpose of development assistance, lays down broad definitions. These go far beyond a narrow emphasis on economic "takeoff" which has sometimes characterized policy statements in the past. 

In commenting on the language of the legislation, I would also like to point out some of the emphases we believe to be vital: 

First is the clear concern for the fundamental health, education, and nutrition of the people of these countries. It is important that the legislation include, as it does, recognition of food population ratios as a key factor to progress on this front. 

Second, is the importance placed on self-help criteria which call for reform and growth of political and social institutions in the developing countries. As volunteers, we are particularly pleased to note that these criteria stress the key role of citizens in those countries in their own development process. We take pride that the Overseas Education 

Fund of the League of Women Voters has been actively involved in training women leaders for citizen participation in Latin America. 

A third is the increased emphasis on rectifying the past sad neglect of the agricultural sectors in most developing nations. Impatient people no longer accept hunger as inevitable. But unless these countries raise their own level of food production, the world's supplies on a per capita basis will soon fail to be sufficient. We can and must help these countries learn how to produce more, but they alone can and in fact must employ new techniques to this end. We agree with the administration that money spent for this purpose is of the highest priority. 

Fourth, we commend the increasing priority placed on multilateral and regional arrangements, both in the giving and utilization of economic assistance. The growing use of consortia, consultative groups, and resources of the development banks, has added much to the effectiveness and efficiency of development efforts. 

At the same time we must be realistic. Although the interdependence of nations is a hallmark of our shrinking world, many of these countries are still in the process of building national identities. It may prove difficult in the immediate future to overcome their current preoccupation with nation-building even though effective development may require regional economic integration. 

Fifth, the league recognizes that assistance must be supplied "in a manner consistent with the other efforts of the United States to improve its balance-of-payments position". But we hope that the need for increased international liquidity can be squarely met and that this country will continue to work for needed international monetary reforms. Over the long run, we also hope that alleviation of the pressures

196.7 

on the U.S. balance-of-payments will make it possible to eliminate this country's "tied loans" policy.

Finally, we applaud the overall emphasis on self-help contained in the criteria. We believe that a National Advisory Committee for Self- 

Help could provide an important way to determine the extent to which leadership in the aid-receiving countries is being more effectively focused on agricultural development, fiscal responsibility, a wise allocation of resources, and manpower training, as well as basic social and political reforms.

With reference to the specific programs which the league commends the leadership which you and your committee gave in obtaining approval by the Congress of the 3-year authorization of Development Loans and the Alliance for Progress last year. Since they are so authorized, we will not take time to comment on them now. We do urge you to approve the 2-year authorization and the total amounts requested for technical assistance, survey of investment opportunities, and contributions to international organizations. 

TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE 

The league has great confidence in programs of technical assistance since they successfully got under way in the late forties. These programs are designed to help the people of less developed countries learn to utilize the resources at hand more effectively and more productively. 

But another equally important-though somewhat subtler-result of technical assistance is the change that occurs in the individual's attitude toward himself and his role in development. 

For the first time he may see himself as the controlling factor in a pattern of positive change, no longer bound by tradition or circumstance blocking his growth. Instead, he welcomes new and far more efficient ways to farm, to transport, and to build. Although too little is known about how to generate human energies, we do know that such energies are basic to self-sustaining growth and needed reforms. Would you prefer that we put it off until later. I feel we may have entered- 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Some of the members will be coming back.

Mrs. CHRISTOPHERSON. I suddenly realized that you have had an opportunity to read it and I could have started by saying would you question me. I will continue.

As productive channels for change, the U.S. voluntary organizations are responding with increasing effectiveness to requests to share with the people of the developing countries their unique experience in institution-building. Leaders from cooperatives, saving and loan associations, labor unions, and many other organizations are now advising their counterparts in the developing countries. The league applauds this expanding involvement of the U.S. private sector in the economic development process overseas. In their close working relationship with indigenous groups these organizations can do much to help replace resignation and despair with hope and optimism.

PRIVATE INVESTMENT 

We are also interested in the potential contribution to development which can be made through the medium of private investment, both foreign and domestic. The investment opportunity surveys, the investment guarantees, and the establishment of the new Office of Private

1119 Resources are basic to this program. We note that the criteria for selfhelp include creation of "a favorable climate for private enterprise and investment." Certainly this is a basic part of the development program. 

Private investment must be the partner of public investment, with development itself the ultimate goal. Even when the economic systems of the developing countries create difficulties for U.S. private investment, we would expect the United States to continue its efforts to make such investment possible. In India, for instance, a deep reservoir of patience is needed. The successful conclusion of negotiations to construct low-cost fertilizer plants has proved to be an arduous taskthough it is essential. We hope that Congress will encourage a patient approach. 

INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS AND PROGRAMS 

The league supports the full request proposed for "international organizations" to cover the U.S. voluntary contributions to such programs as the U.N. development program (UNDP). It would appear that the work of UNDP, following the merger of the special fund and the expanded technical assistance program, has brought increased efficiency to U.N. preinvestment and technical cooperation projects. The ongoing review of all U.N. development by the Special Committee on 

Coordination of the Economic and Social Council also gives evidence of a growing emphasis on coordination of its full range of development efforts. We consider it essential that the United States continue to take the lead in increasing contributions to such international channels. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you will suspend, we will recess and come back.

Mrs. CHRISTOPHERSON. We understand. 

(Short recess taken.) 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The committee will come to order. 

Mrs. Christopherson, if you will, please resume your statement.

TWO-YEAR AUTHORIZATION 

Mrs. CHRISTOPHERSON. Now, I should like to place the league's interest in multiyear authorizations in perspective. Surely the countries which qualify for cur aid need the assurance which long-range authorization of all categories of development assistance would help provide. In addition, we are concerned that annual authorizations require of those who administer the programs too much time for explanation and defense which might be better spent in improving performance. We are, however, equally-perhaps more concerned with the advantages which could come to the American people if Congress were to be freed from a yearly review of requests. 

Long-range authorization could provide an opportunity for Congress to focus on particular countries and/or areas of the less developed world, perhaps in alternate years. By scrutinizing the multiple factors in development and the widely varying needs, problems, and methods of these countries, Congress could make a contribution to public education which no other institution-not the administration, not the universities, not the commercial and industrial world-could supply. 

We believe that annual reviews have dulled rather than sharpened the interest of Congress, to say nothing of the American public, in the problems and prospects of aid. In our judgment, continuous scrutiny has failed to reveal why progress in development has been slow and halting. Also, we believe, too much attention has been given to error,

1967 

too little to success. Annual reviews have also failed to reveal the complexity intrinsic to moving underdeveloped economies into the modern world. In short, Congress has had too little time to spend on the kinds of broad inquiries which stimulate new perspectives and initiatives. 

If long-range authorization is approved, may we also suggest three areas on which we believe congressional inquiries might profitably focus: (1) What are the objectives of development aid? What is the magnitude of outside aid needed by the less developed countries? How much and what kinds of aid can they actually absorb? How can their absorptive capacities be increased? To what extent can more aid be made available from the United States and other developed countries? 

How adequate are the methods currently utilized? (2) What have we learned from both successes and failures over the past two decades? The United States has become increasingly involved in a profound revolution of traditional societies-in the not inconsiderable effort to manage progress without violence. This is no inglorious adventure, yet the tremendous excitement of this unique challenge has failed to reach the public at large. Findings in the field and in research undertaken by our universities pile up in mimeographed reports or at best circulate in a small circle of experts directly involved in development programs. The recommendations of those engaged in research and those at work on the development front need to be seen in high relief. (3) What are the major implications that trade policies and practices have for development aid? The complicated interrelationship of aid and trade is the third major aspect of development which needs to be explored and communicated to the public. There is minimal awareness of the extent to and ways in which trading patterns, policies, and practices of both the developed and the developing countries stimulate or impede economic expansion and diversification. The less developed countries, through the mechanism of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development, are pressing their claims on the world market. Adjustments are inevitable. A major investigation needs to be undertaken soon as part of the overall review of world trade patterns which can be expected to follow completion of the Kennedy round of GATT trade negotiations. 

In closing I should like to comment on the recent levels of aid. It is disturbing to note that in real terms the United States has been falling behind in its support of long-term foreign assistance. While technical difficulties are encountered in measuring the flow of resources from the developed to the developing countries, America is falling short of the one percent GNP goal, no matter how it is figured. 

Further, the gap between the economic growth of the developed and the developing countries-in rates as well as in real terms-is widening. This trend must be reversed. The heritage and the traditions of the 

United States-indeed, our Nation's history-can be seen as a record of narrowing the gap between rich and poor. Approval of the full authorization would clearly indicate that American commitment to this tradition is unequivocal. 

The league is confident that foreign aid can work because it has worked. 

This fact does not alter our awareness of hard-core problems still to be solved. We know solutions will not be reached in the decade of the

1121 sixties, not even in the seventies. The most hopeful projections do not so much as hint that many countries in a century will equal American standards of growth and affluence. Too often people tend to be critical of the less developed countries' demands and expectations. Annoyed with their inability to match the pace set by European nations under the Marshall plan, America has at times seemed impatient and shockingly unrealistic in its optimism. With greater knowledge of the intricate complexity of development, the entire country would be more realistic in its expectations and so rightly proud of its contributions. 

In short, we think the program as outlined this year is a good one. 

We like the emphasis on multilateral aid and on regionalism. We support the various self-help measures which are included. We believe that the emphasis on health, education, nutrition, agricultural development, and social and political responsibility as major goals are the right ones. If it is in the national interest of the United States to contribute to development, and we believe it is, then the very minimum requests included in this year's foreign assistance bill should be authorized in full, and for the 2-year period.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Frelinghuysen. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

I should like to commend Mrs. Christopherson for her statement and say as a member of the fan club of the League of Women Voters, I of course am aware of the fact that you are acute observers of the congressional scene. For that reason I appreciate your comments on this 

2-year authorization which you seem to advocate primarily on the basis that you are sympathetic to our problems, and you want to see us improve our performance. 

I wonder how valid these arguments are? You suggest, for instance, that we need a sabbatical every other year in order to develop a broad inquiry in order to stimulate initiatives. I would certainly think we could do that without taking a year off every other year. 

You suggest also that in order to provide us with an opportunity to focus on particular countries, we need a year off every other year. 

Surely there is nothing to keep us from focusing on particular countries or areas, even with an annual authorization. 

You suggest the executive branch needs time off every other year because they now have to devote too much time for explanation and defense. Surely you realize that the explanation and defense will still go on in an annual basis in the Appropriations Committee. I would guess there is more criticism, there are more problems and more time wasted through the annual appropriation process than in the authorization process, and yet nobody really would suggest that the Appropriations Committee should give up its jurisdiction. 

Quite logically our committee should move slowly, unless there is some solid reason for giving up our jurisdiction. If we were free every other year we might spend our time focusing on this or that, but the devil might find work for idle hands, and we might come up with more searching criticism, and even more negative attitudes, and not positive attitudes.

You may be optimistic about how we would spend the time when we were not examining an authorization bill. You are hopeful it will lead to more understanding about the nature of developing countries, and the nature of our obligations to those countries. I don't think a 2-year authorization is necessarily going to resolve the problem of lack of public understanding, and a lack of congressional understanding. 

It is my fear that we may get into even deeper water. I say this as a friend of the aid program, and one who would like to see it expanded and improved. I am not at all sure there is much to be gained on the part of any of the participants in this process. 

You suggested that the recipients need the assurance that longrange authorization of all categories of aid would help provide. I would guess they have pretty good assurance already that we are not going to forget them altogether. They are sophisticated enough to know that a simple authorization for a long period provides them with no assurance at all. The Senate of the United States last month was slapping the President in the face when he asked for a kind of informal assurance that Congress was going to continue interest in Latin America. It was not that we would not be sympathetic to a formal request from the executive, but the Senate didn't want to commit itself in any concrete way before knowing more about the nature of the obligation the executive might present. 

I think you are exaggerating the benefits to be gained by the longterm authorization. The so-called long-term 2-year authorization is

1125 neither long term nor short. It is neither fish nor fowl, in my book, and makes no sense at all.

I think the best way the foreign aid program can be kept under control is to have both the authorization and the appropriation on an annual basis. This may be a hit-or-miss method, and you may be right in pointing the finger at areas that we have neglected, but I doubt very much whether a change in the authorization approach is going to change the habits of Congress, either in neglecting certain areas, or giving too much attention to the so-called negative aspects of foreign aid. 

This is perhaps a long way of saying I have no questions of you. I certainly admire your basic approach to this. However, as a member of the committee, I feel obligated to argue with you as to the advisability of a 2-year authorization program.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF PENNSYLVANIA, 

Philadelphia, Pa., April 25, 1967.

Chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR CONGRESSMAN MORGAN: The League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania urges you to do everything within your power to see that your Committee reports without weakening amendments the Foreign Assistance Act of 1967, H.R. 7099. 

We congratulate you on introducing this bill and we trust that you and its other sponsors will be able to steer it successfully through the House. 

It is especially important that the 1967 Act be passed because, in amending the 1961 Act, it states in clear language the objectives, standards and program techniques of foreign assistance, codifying experience gathered since initial pas sage of the 1961 Act. We are pleased that the 1967 Act omits the limitation authorized in 1966 on the number of countries to which U.S. aid could be given and that it succinctly restates the reasons for U.S. commitment to assist the develop ing countries. We are in agreement with the aid policies as stated in the bill, and believe that it goes far in providing the continuity needed for sound management by proposing a 2-year authorization for all the foreign aid programs not now on a long term authorization. The six guiding principles of the Act of 1967. under the subjects of: self-help, multilateralism and burden-sharing; regionalism; agriculture, health and education; balance of payments; and efficient administration are in accord with the position which the League of Women Voters holds in support of sound and adequate aid programs. 

It is feared by some legislators and news analysts that concern over spending in Vietnam and legislative priorities has encouraged public apathy over foreign aid programs. We do not believe that the public is apathetic and we want to assure you that the members of the League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania are in favor of the Act and that our current program is geared to help citizens throughout all our Congressional Districts understand the provisions of the proposed legislation.

We hope that our representatives in Washington will do their best to let the public know how much we need this peaceful form of national defense! Sincerely, 

(Signed) Josephine W. Farlow Mrs. ROBERT E. FARLOW, President.

MONDAY, MAY 15, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.O.

This committee met at 10:20 a.m. in room 2172, Rayburn House 

Office Building, Hon. Clement J. Zablocki presiding. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The committee will come to order.

We will have a continuation of the hearings on H.R. 7099. 

The witnesses this morning are Gen. William H. Draper, Jr., Richard N. Gardner, Dr. Louis K. Dupre, Dr. Raymond Ewell 

Dr. 

General DRAPER. Dr. Ewell is probably on a plane and unable to land at the airport. We took the liberty, in view of some of the questions, to ask Dr. Sheldon Segal of the Population Council, who is in charge of their biomedical research, to attend, but I think he also is on a plane unable to land. 

We are prepared to go right ahead, sir.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. General, you do have the answers to the questions that I asked for?

STATEMENT OF GEN. WILLIAM H. DRAPER, JR., NATIONAL CHAIR- MAN, POPULATION CRISIS COMMITTEE, AND VICE CHAIRMAN, PLANNED PARENTHOOD/WORLD POPULATION 

General DRAPER. Yes, sir. There were several questions raised. I first would like to reply to Mrs. Bolton's question she asked about the various research studies going on. Here is a listing of them which 

I will submit for the committee.

In addition, the Ford Foundation- 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. These are research studies by whom?

General DRAPER. This is a report by the National Institute of Child 

Health and Human Development, a survey of current research on fertility, sterility, and population dynamics. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Mr. Chairman, may I say I was appalled at the size of that, which has many, many organizations listed. I would like to have it in the record if the committee feels that it would be of important interest.

General DRAPER. I don't think you would want to print it in full in the hearing but you might want to keep it with the records of the committee. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Are any of those research foundations or organizations under contract with the Government? 

General DRAPER. Many of them, not all. Some are privately financed. 1127

1967 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Maybe we ought to have it in the record to see how much of our tax dollar goes for this purpose. 

General DRAPER. The Ford Foundation program for 1966 which I 

will also leave, shows how much more private organizations are doing so far than the Government. The listing here shows that last year $21 million was granted by the Ford Foundation. It lists about 50 universities here and abroad which are carrying on research and training and advanced programs of various kinds. It includes the contribution by the Ford Foundation to the new International Institute for the Study of Human Reproduction at Columbia and also a contribution to the 

Population Council.

Compared with what the Government is doing now through NIH in research, which I believe is in the order of only $3 or $4 million a year, this report indicates another need, but on the domestic side rather than what concerns this committee particularly. (The documents referred to may be found in the files of the committee.)

General DRAPER. A question was asked by Mrs. Bolton on oral contraceptives and the various risks or side effects. Here is a statement put out only last month by the Food and Drug Administration. I will quote a line from it. This is Dr. Goddard, the Commissioner, speaking: "All the information now available on oral contraceptives demonstrates that the benefits of use far outweigh the risks," Dr. Goddard said, "but there is still a need to build a bigger bank of reports on these drugs," he adds.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. General, is that the report that lists some of the side effects that could be anticipated if the medications are not properly administered or if the recipient of the pill has not had a thorough medical examination after the use of the pill?

General DRAPER. I don't know if he said that, but the full text of his remarks is here, going into the question of the latest statistics on the Nation's birth rate and considering what the Food and Drug Administration is doing and how it assesses the whole problem. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I do have a report from the Food and Drug Administration which does list these, and I think it should follow if your report does not include that.

General DRAPER. It should be included. 

Here is a report August 1 of last year by the Advisory Committee on Obstetrics and Gynecology of the Food and Drug Administration. 

This is the complete report which provides figures and methods of administration. That is in the record.

One question Mrs. Bolton asked was about multiple births that may occur after taking oral contraceptives. I understand that multiple births have resulted from another drug that is completely different from and should not be confused with the contraceptive pills. I refer to a fertility drug which is called clomiphene. It is used sometimes to induce ovulation so as to help women who are infertile to become fertile. In inducing ovulation, it occasionally causes more than one egg to be released and this can result in multiple pregnancies. As far as the contraceptive pills are concerned, they have never been known to cause multiple births, and, indeed there is no evidence, either experimental or clinical, to suggest that this possibility exists. 

You asked me about contributions to the Committee, I believe. I have looked into that. You asked whether there had been contribution by

1129 drug or chemical concerns. There have not. There are only two contributions which might even be remotely related. One, there have been contributions by the president of the Du Pont Co., which is a chemical company. To my knowledge, Du Pont has nothing to do with making pills or any kinds of contraceptives. In fact, of the six or seven companies that make oral contraceptives, not one has made any contribution.

One foundation has made contributions to the Hugh Moore Fund which in turn has made contributions to our Committee-Hugh Moore, you know, was one of the leaders in this whole movement for many years-I refer to the Sunnen Foundation in St. Louis. The 

Sunnen Co., which I suppose furnishes the money, is in the automobile parts business. Mr. Sunnen has financed a large part of the family planning programs in Puerto Rico and some in Mexico. His company, as a sideline in order to help in the population problem, has been making a contraceptive foam called Emko.

Except for that possible indirect relationship there have been no contributions from drug companies or contraceptive manufacturers. 

I do not want to indicate, however, that I feel it would be wrong to receive such contributions because anyone in that business like any other American citizen has the right to contribute to a cause like this. 

Were there any other questions that I left unanswered? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mrs. Bolton, do you have any questions? 

Mrs. BOLTON. I don't think so, thank you.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS.  

Mr. Draper, on page 3 of your statement you say "As you know,

President Johnson has said that $5 in population control is worth $100 in economic development."

Do you have any knowledge of where the President gets the specifics to back up this kind of statement? 

General DRAPER. Yes, sir; Stephen Enke is an economist who has made a great many studies along these lines comparing the economic impact of birth control programs and the impact that comes from the aid program and capital investment. Actually in his studies, which covered a number of developing countries, he arrived at figures that were even more startling than President Johnson's. I believe that he found that $1 spent for birth control would equal in effectiveness, $100 spent for economic development. 

I do not go that far. I have been involved in the economic aid program in many countries myself in past years. When our Committee appointed by President Eisenhower visited a great many countries, we went into the very question that you are asking. We did not have any ratio of 5 to 100 or 1 to 100 but we did find that in nearly every developing country that was experiencing rapid population growth, that population growth was adversely affecting economic development. As you get a larger proportion of the population under 18, these children have to be fed, and clothed, and housed. It takes a greater amount of the country's production for consumer goods than it otherwise would and leaves far less to be used for building factories or growing more food or meeting other economic goals. 

Mr. GROSS. There still seems to be implicit in your answer some difference of opinion as to the amounts as stipulated by the statement of the President.

1967 

Mr. Gardner, on page 5 of your statement you say:

We must practice what we preach if our words are to carry weight overseas and if our efforts overseas are not to be misunderstood. 

Again on the same page you say:

U.S. assistance to another country should be solely at the request of that country. 

Beautiful statements. I wish they might apply to the whole handout program and had applied throughout the years to the whole handout program. I imagine that once you get geared up with this program you will be putting pressure on countries to join in. 

On page 19 of your statement you say: sough

It authorizes the appropriation of $50 million per year for three years plus available foreign currencies for use in support of voluntary family planning programs in friendly foreign nations.

What do you suggest will be the total bill when you use country currencies in addition to the amounts you asked for from Congress on a direct appropriation basis?

STATEMENT OF DR. RICHARD N. GARDNER, PROFESSOR OF INTER- NATIONAL LAW AND ORGANIZATION, COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY, NEW YORK 

Dr. GARDNER. The Fulbright bill doesn't give any amount in terms of local currency. It just gives the $50 million of dollar appropriations. 

My estimate is shown in the attachment 5; that is to say, an estimate of about $50 million in local currencies that could be usefully employed in addition to the $50 million mentioned in the Fulbright bill. 

Mr. GROSS. How much did you say?

Dr. GARDNER. $50 million a year in counterpart funds, local currencies, together with the $50 million specified in the Fulbright bill of dollar appropriations for a total of $100 million a year. 

Mr. GROSS. On page 20 you say "Once it is known that AID has substantially increased funds available to assist local family planning efforts, uses for the money will be found." ban I don't think anyone in this room will quarrel with you, that if the money is put up, it will be spent. This sort of runs counter to your previous statements with respect to the restriction-that we won't go into a country and promote business. Yes, I am very much intrigued by your statement-just give us the money and we will spent it-because that is one of the things that this Government does best-just give us the money and we will be real sure to get rid of it. 

Dr. GARDNER. My purpose was simply to say that everything has to be done with the consent of the host government. I stand by that. 

On the other hand, I think if the host government knows that we take this problem seriously, as manifested by an appropriation for this purpose, it will accelerate its own efforts and draw on our support. I see no inconsistency between the two statements. 

Mr. GROSS. Has the Turkish Government got those 1,400 jeeps for family planning, and if so, are they in operation? And how many people does it take to man the 1,400 jeeps to fan out over Turkey? 

Dr. GARDNER. I am not informed on that. The

Mr. GROSS. One of you mentioned in your statement that the purchase of the 1,400 jeeps by AID was for family planning purposes.

1131 General DRAPER. I believe the loan for those jeeps was only approved about 2 or 3 months ago. I presume they are not all in operation. 

Mr. GROSS. I will be interested to know whether the jeeps wind up in the Turkish Army or whether they are used for family planning.

 Gen. WILLIAM H. DRAPER, Jr., DEPARTMENT OF STATE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, 

Washington, D.C., June 7, 1967.

National Chairman, Population Crisis Committee, 

Washington, D.O. 

DEAR GENERAL DRAPER: In answer to your inquiry, an A.I.D. loan agreement with the Government of Turkey to provide support for the Family Planning Program in that country was signed on October 4, 1966. Under the terms of this agreement, funds to a maximum of $3,600,000 will be provided to cover dollar costs of: (1) The purchase and import of up to 1,400 one-quarter ton jeep type vehicles or component parts thereof (for local assembly) for use in Turkey's family planning program and general rural health programs; (2) The provision of technical services and purchase of shop equipment to improve and extend the Ministry of Health's capability for maintenance and repair of the vehicles; and (3) The provision of communications media technical services and educational materials in connection with the Family Planning Program. 

Under the terms of the loan agreement, the vehicles will be provided only to health centers which are staffed with personnel trained in family planning or are scheduled to receive such trained personnel within six months. Other prerequisites are the availability of improved vehicle maintenance and repair, and a sound program for technical services and materials for family planning education. 

To ensure that the conditions are adhered to, several members of the U.S. 

AID Mission staff in Ankara will provide the necessary supervision. 

The first group of 350 vehicles should start arriving in Turkey during the first half of the calendar year, 1968. In the meantime, the several stringent, but necessary, requirements noted above must be met. So far 360 doctors have completed family planning training courses, and over 350 more will receive similar instruction before March. Proposals for American engineering services to supervise the maintenance of the vehicles are being submitted to the Ministry of Health. Furthermore, a list of equipment to be used in producing educational materials is being compiled prior to procurement. 

Regarding the people to man these jeeps, no precise figure can be given, because the services of persons in several fields will be required, including drivers, physicians, nurses, paramedical personnel and maintenance men. Sincerely,

GEORGE CONTIS, M.D., 

Medical Officer (Population), Bureau for Near East and South Asia.

I am not informed.

Dr. GARDNER. I am not aware of any money that has been spent for this purpose. 

General DRAPER. I am sure there is not.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Rosenthal. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. General Draper, are there other technically ad vanced countries participating in this effort? 

General DRAPER. Yes. About a year and a half ago in the latter part of 1965, at the time the International Planned Parenthood Federation was carrying on efforts to raise private money-and did raise $3 or $4 million for work in the developing countries-the Swedish Government made a grant to the International Planned Parenthood Federation for general budgetary work in 1966 of $386,000. They repeated that grant for this year.

The Dutch Government, the Norwegian Government, and the Danish Government all made contributions to International Planned Parenthood early this year to defray part of the expenses of the Eighth 

World Conference of International Planned Parenthood held in Chile last month. At the Conference itself the British Government, through 

Lord Caradon, their delegate to the United Nations, announced that the British Government was making a grant each year for the next 4 years, to International Planned Parenthood.

All of these Governments have recognized the unique role that the association plays, with Mexicans in Mexico, Indians in India, and Americans in the United States all endeavoring to set up pilot birth control programs and to carry on educational programs on the dangers of the population explosion and the need for private and governmental assistance.

Mr. ROSENTHAL. In addition to giving money, are they disseminating technical know-how?

General DRAPER. Yes. The Swedish Government has taken the lead in that direction. It has helped the Pakistani Government, the Tunisian Government, and two or three others in technical assistance in family planning. The Swedes have carried on a program that has been very enlightened. They have led the world. 

They started before our own Government, I believe. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. How do you assess general public attitudes on this subject in the United States, and what, if anything, do you intend to do about it?

General DRAPER. I personally have not had anything to do with assessing public attitudes. The various people that do this work- 

Gallup and Elmer Roper and others have from time to time taken polls over the last 5 or 10 years. These polls have indicated a continually increasing interest and understanding toward the problem. 

The very large majority of the public, including all religions, are favorable to, No. 1, our Government, supporting family planning at home, and No. 2, our Government assisting other countries, on request, for voluntary family planning programs. The studies also show that a large majority of our own couples, including, again, all religions, are actually practicing family planning themselves and approve of it.

1133 3 Finally, they show that a large majority approve the actions of our Government in the last 2 years in assisting State and other health programs that provide family planning, including the war on poverty. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. I was thinking in terms of the testimony today and the recommendations you made insofar as the bill we have under consideration, in addition to what you said, that if you want Congress to take the lead in this area, that it would seem to me from the political point of view there has to be a considerable interest on behalf of the public, that the public should generally match our level of interest. 

General DRAPER. I believe the great majority of the public are convinced. I would think that, frankly, the public has been ahead of the 

Congress and the Congress has been ahead of the administration, except for President Johnson's statements.

Mr. ROSENTHAL.  

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Morse. 

Mr. MORSE. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

General, I am sorry I wasn't here Tuesday when you were before the committee. I have just now had a chance to read your statement and a little of Mr. Gardner's statement. 

Would you advise the committee as to the specific proposal you have in mind I presume it involves the authorization of money, but to just what kinds of programs would you think this money should be allotted? 

General DRAPER. Thank you very much, Mr. Morse. My general approach has been to draw the attention of this most important committee of the House of Representatives to the vital necessity of our Government giving priority and urgency to the measures that have already been approved in principle by the Congress and by the administration. I realize that a great Government like our own has to contend with tremendous inertia, that a new problem simply cannot elbow all the other programs out of the way in a hurry. A new program does take time to develop. 

The unfortunate fact of life in this particular issue is that each day sees the problem getting worse in so many developing countries, particularly India this year with its actual starvation. My whole plea is not at the moment for any specific legislation-although there is legislation that I indicated I hoped the committee would approve-but rather it is to draw the attention of the Congress, which holds the purse strings and sets the policy, to a menace which in my opinion is threatening the prosperity and future peace of the world even our own life here will be threatened eventually. 

The death rate and the birth rate are now badly out of balance because of the very humanitarian medical miracles that American and other scientists have brought to the world in the last 20 or 30 years. It is a development in human history that has probably never been paralleled. From the time of Christ, when there were estimated to be about one-quarter of a billion people, it took 1,650 years to double the world's population to half a billion. Then it took about 200 years to double it again, to 1 billion in about 1850, then about 80 years to reach the second billion in 1930. Now we stand with 3.3 billion people. What is more, the present rate of growth is such that, if it continues, these 3 billion will double again in only 33 years, by the end of this century. 

We are facing an impossible situation. Starvation will intervene; nature will take over. In the meantime the question is man. Man is

196.7 

the only member of the animal world that can consciously control his fertility. Man alone has the mental ability and willpower, if he will use it, to control his destiny.

I urgently plead that this committee give the subject the consideration and priority that I believe it deserves. 

Mr. MORSE. May I ask Dr. Gardner to speak to that? 

Dr. GARDNER. I tried to say in my statement last week that there is a big gap between policy and program in this very important field. 

Our Government at long last has a policy of being willing to help other countries. But the policy is not yet being implemented in a substantial way.

My own hope would be that the Congress of the United States could give a mandate to the Agency for International Development to get on with this job in a much bigger way than has so far been the case. That is why I welcome the introduction of the Fulbright bill. I realize similar legislation is not before the House. It seems to me that its proposal of $50 million a year is the very least that should be appropriated for this purpose in view of what General Draper and others have said.

I also feel, Congressman, that the United Nations has been very slow in getting started with this. One of the central recommendations in my testimony was and is that we work to the greatest possible extent through the United Nations agencies, because I very much fear that, if we try to do this job unilaterally, or even bilaterally, we will be subject to charges by nationalists or Communists or people who wish us no well in the world, that we have some ulterior motive. 

The more we can associate ourselves with other countries through the United Nations, the better off I believe we will be, the more conviction this program will carry for the host government and its people. 

Mr. MORSE. Åre either of you familiar with the studies Dr. Szego has done on the application of systems techniques to the world food and population problems? 

General DRAPER. I have talked to him about them and I believe he has had some conversation with some of the Government departments, trying to get them interested in funding that kind of research. 

It is a very difficult thing to approach through systems research because it involves the individual motives and actions of billions of people.

Mr. MORSE. Dr. Gardner, I have been told, although I don't have any personal experience, there has been strong opposition to population control efforts in the United States among the more militant civil rights people on the alleged theory that the effort is being made in order to insure the continuation of a white dominated society. Is that the same sort of syndrome that you refer to 

Dr. GARDNER. Yes, there is unfortunately a feeling in some quarters that the way to increase racial power is through unregulated fertility. 

I think this is a tragically mistaken view. It is interesting historically that many of the national leaders of our time, I think this was true even of Nehru in his early years, have thought that rapid population growth served the interests of their people and their countries.

(The address referred to follows:) FAMILY PLANNING A SPECIAL AND URGENT CONCERN 

(Response by the Reverend Martin Luther King, Jr.

, on receiving the Margaret 

Sanger Award in Human Rights, May 5, 1966, at the 50th Anniversary Banquet of Planned Parenthood/World Population, Washington, D.C.) 

Recently, the Press has been filled with reports of sightings of flying saucers. 

While we need not give credence to these stories, they allow our imagination to speculate on how visitors from outer space would judge us. I am afraid they would be stupified at our conduct. They would observe that for death planning we spend billions to create engines and strategies for war. They would also observe that we spend millions to prevent death by disease and other causes. 

Finally they would observe that we spend paltry sums for population planning, even though its spontaneous growth is an urgent threat to life on our planet. 

Our visitors from outer space could be forgiven if they reported home that our planet is inhabited by a race of insane men whose future is bleak and uncertain.

There is no human circumstance more tragic than the persisting existence of a harmful condition for which a remedy is readily available. Family Planning, to relate population to world resources, is possible, practical and necessary. 

Unlike plagues of the dark ages or contemporary diseases we do not yet understand, the modern plague of overpopulation is soluble by means we have discovered and with resources we possess. 

What is lacking is not sufficient knowledge of the solution but universal consciousness of the gravity of the problem and education of the billions who are its victims.

It is easier for a Negro to understand a social paradox because he has lived so long with evils that could be eradicated but were perpetuated by indifference or ignorance. The Negro finally had to devise unique methods to deal with his problem and perhaps the measure of success he is realizing can be an inspiration to others coping with tenacious social problems. 

In our struggle for equality we were confronted with the reality that many millions of people were essentially ignorant of our conditions or refused to face unpleasant truths. The hard core bigot was merely one of our adversaries. The millions who were blind to our plight had to be compelled to face the social evil their indifference permitted to flourish. 

After centuries of relative silence and enforced acceptance we adapted a technique of exposing the problem by direct and dramatic methods. We had confidence that when we awakened the nation to the immorality and evil of inequality there would be an upsurge of conscience followed by remedial action. 

We knew that there were solutions and that the majority of the nation were ready for them. Yet we also knew that the existence of solutions would not automatically operate to alter conditions. We had to organize, not only arguments but people in the millions for action. Finally we had to be prepared to accept all the consequences involved in dramatizing our grievances in the unique style we had devised.

There is a striking kinship between our movement and Margaret Sanger's early efforts. She, like we, saw the horrifying conditions of ghetto life. Like we, she knew that all of society is poisoned by cancerous slums. Like we, she was a direct actionist-a nonviolent resistor. She was willing to accept scorn and abuse until the truth she saw was revealed to the millions. At the turn of the century she went into the slums and set up a birth control clinic, and for this deed she went to jail because she was violating an unjust law. Yet the years has justified her actions. She launched a movement which is obeying a higher law to preserve human life under humane conditions. Margaret Sanger had to commit what was then called a crime in order to enrich humanity, and today we honor her courage and vision; for without them there would have been no beginning.

1967 

Our sure beginning in the struggle for equality by nonviolent direct action may not have been so resolute without the tradition established by Margaret Sanger and people like her. Negroes have no mere academic nor ordinary interest in family planning. They have a special and urgent concern. 

Recently the subject of Negro family life has received extensive attention. 

Unfortunately, studies have overemphasized the problem of the Negro male ego and almost entirely ignored the most serious element-Negro migration. During the past half century Negroes have migrated on a massive scale, transplanting millions from rural communities to crammed urban ghettoes. In their migration, as with all migrants, they carried with them the folkways of the countryside into an inhospitable city slum. The size of family that may have been appropriate and tolerable on a manually cultivated farm was carried over to the jammed streets of the ghetto. In all respects Negroes were atomized, neglected and discriminated against. Yet, the worst omission was the absence of institutions to acclimate them to their new environment. Margaret Sanger, who offered an important institutional remedy, was unfortunately ignored by social and political leaders in this period. In consequence, Negro folkways in family size persisted. The problem was compounded when unrestrained exploitation and discrimination accented the bewilderment of the newcomer, and high rates of illegitimacy and fragile family relationships resulted. For the Negro, therefore, intelligent guides of family planning are a profoundly important ingredient in his quest for security and a decent life. There are mountainous obstacles still separating Negroes from a normal existence. Yet one element in stabilizing his life would be an understanding of and easy access to the means to develop a family related in size to his community environment and to the income potential he can command. 

This is not to suggest that the Negro will solve all his problems through Planned Parenthood. His problems are far more complex, encompassing economic security, education, freedom from discrimination, decent housing and access to culture. Yet if family planning is sensible it can facilitate or at least not be an obstacle to the solution of the many profound problems that plague him. 

The Negro constitutes half the poor of the nation. Like all poor, Negro and white, they have many unwanted children. This is a cruel evil they urgently need to control. There is scarcely anything more tragic in human life than a child who is not wanted. That which should be a blessing becomes a curse for parent and child. There is nothing inherent in the Negro mentality which creates this condition. Their poverty causes it. When Negroes have been able to ascend economically, statistics reveal they plan their families with even greater care than whites. Negroes of higher economic and educational status actually have fewer children than white families in the same circumstances. 

Some commentators point out that with present birth rates it will not be long before Negroes are a majority in many of the major cities of the nation. As a consequence, they can be expected to take political control, and many people are apprehensive at this prospect. Negroes do not seek political control by this means. 

They seek only what they are entitled to and do not wish for domination purchased at a cost of human misery. Negroes were once bred by slave owners to be sold as merchandise. They do not welcome any solution which involves population breeding as a weapon. They are instinctively sympathetic to all who offer methods that will improve their lives and offer them fair opportunity to develop and advance as all other people in our society. 

For these reasons we are natural allies of those who seek to inject any form of planning in our society that enriches life and guarantees the right to exist in freedom and dignity.

For these constructive movements we are prepared to give our energies and consistent support; because in the need for family planning, Negro and white have a common bond; and together we can and should unite our strength for the wise preservation, not of races in general, but of the one race we all constitute the human race.

 [From the U.S. Food and Drug Administration] ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE LABELING Guide Lines: (Revised October 24, 1966) Chemistry. This should include Generic Name, amount, Chemical Name and the structural formula of each active ingredient. 

Mechanism of Action.—1. Gonadotrophin suppression. · 

Indications. The Obstetrics and Gynecology Advisory Committee considered the following indications acceptable: contraception, endometriosis, and hypermenorrhea. These indications may be used in the labeling when efficacy has been demonstrated in each case. Any other claims will be evaluated on the basis of efficacy data available to support each. 

Contraindications 1. Patients with thrombophlebitis or with a history of thrombophlebitis or pulmonary embolism. 

2. Liver dysfunction or disease. 

3. Patients with known or suspected carcinoma of the breast or genital organs. 

4. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding. Warnings 1. Discontinue medication pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, or if there is a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine. If examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions, medication should be withdrawn. 

2. Since the safety of in pregnancy has not been demonstrated, it is recommended that for any patient who has missed two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing the contraceptive regimen. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule the possibility of pregnancy should be considered at the time of the 1st missed period. 

3. Detectable amounts of the active ingredients in oral contraceptives have been identified in the milk of mothers receiving these drugs. The significance of this dose to the infant has not been determined. Precautions 1. The pretreatment physical examination should include special reference to breast and pelvic organs, as well as a Papanicolau smear. 

2. Endocrine and possibly liver function tests may be affected by treatment with Therefore, if such tests are abnormal in a patient taking it is recommended that they be repeated after the drug has been withdrawn for 2 months. 

3. Under the influence of estrogen-progestogen preparations, pre-existing fibroids may increase in size. 

4. Because these agents may cause some degree of fluid retention, conditions which might be influenced by this factor, such as epilepsy, migraine, asthma, cardiac or renal dysfunction, require careful observation. 

5. Although a cause and effect relationship has not been established should be used with caution in patients with a history of cerebrovascular accident. 

6. In relation to breakthrough bleeding, and as in all cases of irregular bleeding per vaginum, nonfunctional causes should be borne in mind. In cases of undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, adequate diagnostic measures are indicated. 

7. Patients with a history of psychic depression should be carefully observed and the drug discontinued if the depression recurs to a serious degree. 

8. Any possible influence of prolonged therapy on pituitary, ovarian, adrenal, hepatic or uterine function awaits further study. 

9. A decrease in glucose tolerance has been observed in a small percentage of patients on oral contraceptives. The mechanism of this decrease is obscure. 

For this reason, diabetic patients should be carefully observed while receiving therapy.

10. Because of the occasional occurence of thrombophlebitis and pulmonary embolism in patients taking oral contraceptives the physician should be alert to the earliest manifestations of the disease. A cause and effect relationship has not been demonstrated. 

11. Because of the effects of estrogens on epiphyseal closure, should be used judiciously in young patients in whom bone growth is not complete. 

12. The age of the patient constitutes no absolute limiting factor, although treatment withmay mask the onset of the climacteric. 

13. The pathologist should be advised of specimens are submitted. therapy when relevant
