STATEMENT OF DR. SHELDON SEGAL, DIRECTOR, BIOMEDICAL DIVISION, POPULATION COUNCIL OF NEW YORK 

Dr. SEGAL. Mrs. Bolton, if I understand correctly-and I apologize for not having been here earlier when you initiated the discussionyou are concerned with what would be the effect of administering these combinations of estrogens and progestins on the bone growth of young girls- 

Mrs. BOLTON. The condition of the bone. 

Dr. SEGAL. And other aspects- 

Mrs. BOLTON. And boys.

Dr. SEGAL. I think there is no question but that estrogen which is one of the components of oral contraception can affect the growth plates of bones in growing young girls. This is true whether the estrogen is provided from the external source or is provided by the ovary itself. In the normal course of physiologic development when a young girl reaches the age of the menarche her own ovary starts to produce estrogen. This is one of the reasons for the stopping of bone growth. 

This is why some women are shorter than others; their ovaries start functioning at different times in relation to completion of bone growth. 

It is very unlikely that the compound would be given for contraceptive purposes prior to the time that ovarian function has begun. So I would see no likelihood of affecting bone growth by the administration of estrogens with progestins over and beyond what had already occurred normally as a result of the girl's reaching the menarche. 

I think nevertheless the Food and Drug Administration has been very wise in including the warning pertaining to the use of these substances in young girls in the labeling requirements they have established for these substances because oral progestin and estrogen combinations are used for a variety of things in addition to oral contraception.

My point, however, is that if a young lady is requiring this type of therapy for contraceptive purposes she has already had enough normal estrogen production to have essentially done whatever these estrogens will do to her bones. As far as bone pathology is concerned, if anything, estrogens are beneficial for preventing osteoporosis, a condition associated with a lack of estrogenic hormones. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you.

We are still restricting the wheat acreage, are we not, in this country?

1967 STATEMENT OF DR. LOUIS K. DUPRE, PROFESSOR OF PHILOSOPHY, GEORGETOWN UNIVERSITY, AND MEMBER OF THE EXECUTIVE BOARD, CATHOLIC COMMITTEE ON POPULATION AND GOVERN- MENT POLICY 

Dr. DUPRE. I only want to use this opportunity perhaps to point out that the position which was presented as being the position of the entire church is by no means the position of the Catholic Church. If I may use 2 more minutes of your time, I would read to you the position that is taken by the Dutch hierarchy, all the bishops of Holland speaking authoritatively, in their official catechism. May I read it, Mr. 

Chairman ? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you will.

Dr. DUPRE. This is their position: 

Human procreation is not a lot that befalls a family without planning. Children must be brought into the world in conscious love. Health, housing, personality structure and many other factors determine each couple's decision about the size of their family. No one else can make this decision in their place. 

One consideration of a more general nature is that one family must not expand beyond the responsibility which one owes the family itself and the world. It would be erroneous, however, to define this responsibility in mathematical terms valid for each couple. 

There are, as everyone knows today, several methods to achieve birth regulation. They all converge in an attempt to enable a man and a woman to have sexual intercourse without the risk of conception. In its Constitution on the 

Church and the World the last Council made no pronouncement about any of these methods as such. This position differs from the one taken thirty years ago by Pius XI and maintained by his successor. We perceive here a clear development within the Church, a development which is also taking place outside the Church.

Today we know more about the processes active in the conception of a human being. As a result, man can now more freely control his fertility. Moreover, today there is a definite awareness of sexuality as an independent value. Sexuality and fertility are seen more and more as values united in one living totality, rather than as realities coordinated to each other in an end-means relation. 

Are all methods of birth regulation equal for the Christian conscience? The 

Council has not answered this question. But the Council appeals to the conscience of all married people to investigate whether the practices do full justice to the great personal values that are expressed in sexual intercourse. It is prudent also, in these matters to consult a doctor who can take into account the great variety of circumstances and who can judge what is medically advisable. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Thank you, Doctor.

Dr. DUPRE. May I point out, Mr. Fulton, the apostolic delegate is no authority whatsoever for other bishops. Each bishop in the Catholic 

Church is his own bishop and the bishop of his own diocese. There is, of course, as you know within the Catholic Church a supreme authority which consists of the collegium of all the bishops together and of the Pope and the bishops, but the apostolic delegate as such has no authority.

I am sure his opinions are worth listening to, but they have no authority either for Catholicism in America nor for any other brand of Catholicism.

STATEMENT OF RODNEY H. CLURMAN, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, WORLD FOOD AND POPULATION CRISIS COMMITTEE 

Mr. CLURMAN. First I want to thank you for receiving me on such short notice. Senator Jack Miller, who has been interested in our work, suggested last week that I attempt to place what we are doing before this committee.

I want to thank General Draper for his advice and I am pleased to be able to appear before such a distinguished group and particularly my old friend Dick Gardner, who I think has probably more than any other single person both in and out of Government advanced the cause that is being discussed here for the last several years both in his work in the State Department and in the U.N. 

I am executive secretary of the World Food & Population Crisis 

Committee which is endeavoring to provide aid to the stricken areas of northern India. We are totally committed to the goal that the problem of food and population control in the developing nations can be met through education and development of industry, and through increasing research and implementation of programs in these crucial areas. Our committee is working directly with the government of the 

State of Bihar and with the voluntary agencies, including CARE, UNICEF, AFPRO OXFAM, the Bishops Relief Committee, the 

Bihar Relief Committee, and other groups in the field. 

The facts of the terrible tragedy in northern India have been stated graphically many times. The latest information received indicates that a million people will die in Bihar this year. There is little or no hope that food can be produced within the area in the months ahead. The 

U.S. Government recently allocated $25 million for CARE for use in 

Bihar, and we feel it unfortunate that this money was held up so long. 

It is our understanding that there will shortly be additional allocations for food grains.

The World Bank consortium is also contributing, and it is our further understanding that the nonconsortium countries are being asked to contribute. The current crisis cannot be met by the normal pipeline food grains. I have a letter from Mr. Douglas Heck, country officer for 

India, Department of State, outlining the immediate needs as determined by our committee and the highly qualified experts who have given us their time and energy.

In brief, these are the immediate needs that we see : 

1. Well-drilling equipment with the necessary pumps and pipes, and maintenance and operational personnel. 

2. Medical supplies. Dr. Joseph Alter's most recent report, which presents a terrifying picture of almost every known kind of pestilence. 

Critical at the moment are cholera vaccine and the means for distrib-

1159 uting it among the 52 million people in Bihar. Dr. Howard Rusk has told us that while vaccination against cholera should be undertaken, it is not known whether at this lowered state of resistance it will have the necesary effect.

Smallpox and general medicines are needed. Dr. Alter has provided complete lists, which have been circulated to the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association and to individual drug companies. We have consulted with public health officials and a program of paramedical personnel is being organized to help with the enormous task of vaccinating 52 million people, in a state where the availability of medical help is virtually nil. 

3. Food. While any and all types of food continue to hold the highest priority in the months to come, the immediate need is for the sustenance of life. CARE, UNICEF, and other organizations including the Bihar Relief Committee are feeding an estimated 8 million the only daily meal they have. It consists of grain mixed with whatever water is available, but much of the water is contaminated. The current figure on numbers of people in badly affected areas is 30 million. The voluntary agencies are doing a monumental task under the most difficult circumstances. CARE has thrown virtually its entire staff into the 

Bihar operation. UNICEF has increased its efforts significantly. 

I would like at this point to read a portion of a letter received from the head of Freres des Hommes which will give you some idea of the extraordinarily difficult circumstances under which those in the field must work. [Reading:] 

The boys of the well-digging group were nearly killed a month ago. They were driven (and happily not driving) to Bihar and the man of AFPRO (Action for Food Production) who was driving had an accident and killed a man driving his chariot and buffalo. They were surrounded in three minutes by a howling mob who tried to kill them. The most badly hurt was Dave Henry, a charming

Scots boy of 22, son of a surgeon of Aberdeen who being very badly hurt thought that the only way not to be killed was to look dead, which he did, and they thought he was dead and left him and he escaped. He was in the hospital and at one moment thought that it was less dangerous to go back to feed the children in the towns but his health coming back his spirit came back too and he decided to go on with the well-digging program.

They are starting in Bihar helping the Indians a program of digging one hundred wells. 

Jayaprakash Narayan, who heads the Bihar Relief Committee, has mobilized a dramatic people-to-people effort. Mr. Narayan's workers can provide, for only $250 per month, enough food for 1,000 people. 

Bihar has received contributions from all over the world. The Dutch and Canadian Governments have airlifted heavy well-drilling equipment to Bihar. AFPRO, a unique ecumenical church organization, has mobilized volunteers and equipment from all over the world and is concentrating its efforts in the well-drilling area. This, then, is a statement of what is being done.

We wish to indicate our distress at the position of the U.S. Government with regard to our Committee's efforts. On return from our trip to Bihar in December 1966, a trip undertaken at the request of Mr. 

John Taylor, a Quaker living in Bihar and working with the Ford

Foundation, we submitted recommendations to the Department of State, saying that unless action were taken immediately, millions of lives would be in grave danger. The Department's position was then

1967 

and has remained that until such time as a calamitous visitation was declared, they would not authorize the American air carriers to give free transport to emergency material.

There was not then, nor can there be now, any question but that this is a calamitous visitation. Anyone who has recently been to Bihar can attest to that. One argument advanced by the Department of State has been that Ambassador Bowles had not made the kind of requests we made. That is incorrect.

David Lubbock, of Edzell, Scotland, and John Taylor, Dr. Alter, and I on each of our trips met constantly with the Ambassador's staff assigned to the Bihar relief problem. Ambassador Bowles utilized his emergency $25,000 to buy well-drilling equipment for Bihar. This equipment sat at J.F.K. Airport for 6 weeks while AID and the Government of India argued who would pay for shipment. It was only after direct intervention by our Committee that they were shipped. 

The State Department's position has been that until such time as a formal request is received from the Central Government of India it cannot respond. The members of the Committee are individuals and feel that the Government's refusal to permit us to help is wrong. The 

Government of India directly requested smallpox vaccine last week, and 10 million units were immediately shipped. Dr. Alter has informed us that it is not apt to reach Bihar, as it was sent by our Government to New Delhi. The current political situation there is at best chaotic. The Congress Party was defeated in the recent Bihar election, and the new government is trying desperately to cope with the worst situation of its kind in this century. The Prime Minister, Mrs. Gandhi, after a recent trip to the Gaya district, one of the worst affected areas, declared in moving tones that this was a terrible tragedy.

I talked with her briefly after this trip and she was deeply affected. 

The State Government of Bihar declared 2 weeks ago a state of famine. 

There are now efforts underway to get the Central Government to ask for help. However, while Washington and New Delhi negotiate, the smallpox and cholera rage on. David Ben-Gurion, a member of our 

Committee, has written saying that although India did not recognize his government, he wanted to do all he could to help the people of India. 

His Royal Highness Prince Philip, has indicated that he would in every way possible encourage his government to help, and British Minister of Defense Denis Healey has been most helpful. Mr. J. J. 

Singh, a distinguished Indian who lived in this country for 35 years and is on this Committee, is attempting to mobilize his countrymen, who are perhaps most at fault for permitting this condition to exist. 

We have had letters and conversations with leaders in every walk of American life, many of whom serve on our Committee and an equally large number who serve informally. All have said that the crucial need is to get the U.S. Government behind this effort. 

Many Members of Congress, including the Speaker of the House, Congressmen Ottinger, Poage, Reid, Rumsfeld and Ryan; and Senators Brooke, Gruening, Javits, Edward and Robert Kennedy, Miller.

Percy and Ribicoff, have written in support. Many members of the administration, including the Vice President, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Labor, the Director of the USIA, the Under-

1161 

Secretary of State for Political Affairs, Eugene Rostow, members of the White House staff, and distinguished journalists from all over the world have indicated their genuine personal concern in the current crisis. 

We have had direct conversations with the Office of the Secretary of State for Vatican Affairs in Rome and similar discussions with religious leaders of every denomination. 

There are two major points in the Department of State refusal which need discussion and clarity. 

1. Each Member of Congress who has written on our behalf has received the same letter from William J. Macomber, Assistant Secre tary of State for Congressional Relations. The response of Mr. Ma comber's office, when asked repeatedly how such a statement could be made in the face of overwhelming evidence to the contrary was that Mr. Macomber is not responsible for what he signs. I find it impossible to understand what "responsible" means. 

2. On our third trip to Bihar we discovered quite by accident that

AID had, as part of a technical assistance contract, arranged with Peat-Marwick, a highly competent Boston-based consulting firm, to plan a disaster relief coordination center for Bihar. The total cost of the project was probably upwards of three-quarters of a million, of which an undetermined amount was spent on the center design. 

The center has been set up, and it is now a pleasant office with the usual cardex files, maps, et cetera, and stands not 50 yards from where the Ministers of the State of Bihar begged our help. At this time the center is useless; implementation was not a part of the contract. 

John Taylor, Dr. Alter, Mr. Lubbock and I, upon discovering the center, asked what it was, and were told that it was "just Washington doing some kind of study." Our Committee immediately wrote Mr. 

William Gaud of AID asking if we would be permitted to implement the center under contract to AID. We gave assurances that the most highly qualified personnel would be utilized, and that our plan of coordination had been discussed with all the agencies involved as well as with some of the best coordinators in the world. Mr. Gaud's answer, not unexpectedly, was "No." Although we have since had some indication that this may be reappraised, it is our feeling that the members of this congressional committee should examine the facts at once. 

Finally, our Committee submits the following recommendations for immediate implementation by the Congress: 

1. A resolution calling on the President, Secretaries of Defense and Health, Education, and Welfare, and Agriculture to examine the needs as set forth and recommend immediate steps. 

2. An allocation of $20 million in Public Law 480 funds for the purchase of desperately needed relief supplies. Half of this money could be in immediately available rupees now in India. 

3. A resolution of concern by the Members of Congress for the unfortunate people of Bihar, and pledging collectively and individually a continuing concern. 

Thank you.

STATEMENT OF DENNIS I. GOULD, REPRESENTING THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. GOULD. I am Dennis I. Gould, a builder in Miami, Fla. I appear here today as the vice chairman of the international housing committee and as a representative of the National Association of Home 

Builders of the United States (NAHB). 

With me here today are Edmund N. Wise, our counsel for international housing affairs and our legislative counsel, Joseph B. Mc- 

Grath. 

The National Association of Home Builders is the trade association of the domestic homebuilding industry with 45,000 members organized in 424 local and State affiliated associations in all 50 States, in Puerto 

Rico, the Virgin Islands, and the District of Columbia.

Our association for over a decade has had an international housing committee. This is only one expression of our very deep and abiding conviction that the native industrial talents and accomplishments of the homebuilding industry in the United States ought to be made available for the benefit of the less-developed countries. We believe, like the 

Congress, that we have a major responsibility to carry out in this regard and that for those builders who are willing to venture into a project in foreign lands, there may also be an opportunity for economic gain. NAHB POLICY STATEMENT INTERNATIONAL HOUSING 

The basis of NAHB's interest in international housing is the belief that home ownership promotes stable democratic governments and is a force for freedom and world peace. NAHB policy in regard to international housing is aimed at assisting government and private programs which help developing nations produce better housing, and at encouraging and promoting the concept of private home ownership abroad. The Foreign Assistance Act of 1967 should include homeownership and decent housing as one of the first objectives of foreign assistance. 

This policy is being promoted by the admission to NAHB of international affiliates, by NAHB's participation in the activities of the U.N. Committee on 

Housing, Building and Planning, and by participating in the activites of the 

Internatonal Union of Building Centers. 

NAHB endeavors to maintain close cooperation with United States manufacturers who have domestic and overseas plants that provide home building components.

Individual NAHB members, in partnership with nationals of other countries, have made a major contribution to the development and expansion of private enterprise home building industries abroad.

The NAHB feels that U.S. controlled funds overseas should be put to more effective use to provide home ownership through private enterprise. NAHB policy supports the Congressional action which strongly urged that U.S. controlled foreign currencies in each respective country be used for community development and owner-occupied housing, in which experienced private enterprise United State builders are the investment sponsors. 

NAHB has cooperated with the Executive and Legislative branches of our government, to encourage the development of insured mortgage systems abroad and the development of thrift institutions as long-range tools leading to home ownership. As the first step in providing tools and the mechanics for a sound long-term mortgage credit system, NAHB is willing to counsel with builders in other nations in the preparation and enactment of legislation to establish a system of mortgage insurance.

NAHB policy also declares that the housing investment guaranty program of the Agency for International Development should be continued, given a higher priority, and expanded to include qualified Free World countries. The appropriate government agencies should utilize the entire amounts of guaranty authorization for the housing investment guaranty program both for Latin America under Section 224 and for the entire free world under Section 221 of the Foreign Assistance 

Act. 

Mr. GOULD. The NAHB has testified before the Foreign Affairs 

Committee each time the Foreign Assistance Act of 1981 and its amendments have been considered. The association has a particular interest in sections 221 and 224 of the act which cover investment guarantees for housing. In fact, we were involved in the initial request for these sections to be included in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

We commend the committee for its consistent support of these two sections of the act. We are firmly convinced that the system of private mortgage financing and housing production-as it has been so successfully created in the United States resting as it does on the entrepreneurial initiative of builders and developers and coupled with a strong reliance on personal ownership of property including a home has a really meaningful role to play in aiding the economic growth of countries less developed than our own. For these developing countries, the provisions of sections 221 and 224 of the act make possible a real effort on our part to translate American experience into comparable examples abroad.

1171 

RECOMMENDATIONS 

This year our testimony before this committee is directed to the following points, two of which are related to the legislation now before you and others which are recommendations relating to administration of the program generally: 

1. Housing should be included as one of "the first objects of foreign assistance" under the statement of policy as set forth in H.R. 7099. 

2. The authorization of guarantee authority for use under section 

224 (b)1 should be increased by $50 million in H.R. 7099, which presently contains no increase. 

3. We believe the committee should direct the Agency for International Development (AID) to utilize fully and expeditiously its available guarantee authority under section 221(b)2. 

4. In the operation of the program under section 224 we feel that sales price limitations should be dependent upon market conditions in the selected Latin American countries and cities, and should not be subject to a general and arbitrary sales price ceiling, as presently proposed ($7,500). 

5. In the housing guarantee program generally, we object to the current policy of a complete prohibition of guarantees for construction financing; we think there are cases where such guarantees may be necessary and appropriate, and they should be available. 

6. We believe there is a real need for improvement in the processing of guarantee applications, and a need for a study of the entire program so that it may be evaluated in all of its aspects, including problems and accomplishments both here and overseas. We are sure, however, that these accomplishments will far outweigh the problems and NAHB would be pleased to aid in the study. We also hope members of the committee may have an opportunity in the near future to see at first hand many of these problems and accomplishments at the various project sites in Latin America. 

HOUSING AS A PRIME GOAL 

The amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act introduced this year have placed primary emphasis, as the first objectives of assistance, on three major areas: sufficient food, good health, and better educational opportunities. Included among lesser goals of the program is assistance for programs of urban development. NAHB agrees that these first objects of assistance are essential and should have the first order of priority. However, it is also our belief that decent shelter is of equal significance in the developing countries and, for this reason, we urge the Congress to include housing as one of the first objectives of foreign assistance in addition to the other three goals. For this purpose, H.R. 

7099 should be amended under section 101 at line 17, page 3, in order to add appropriate language emphasizing the importance of decent shelter. Our suggestion for such language is included in attachment 2 to this statement.

THE ROLE OF INVESTMENT GUARANTEES 

The investment guarantee program is an excellent means to provide U.S. assistance on a private basis and without appropriated funds.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT. OF 1967! 

There is no doubt that in the long run the less-developed countries are going to be required to marshal their own resources to provide housing for their people. It is evident that direct loans, either from the AID or from the Inter-American Development Bank, are now required to assist these governments in their public housing programs for low-income housing. However, until that time arises when sufficient resources are available on a private basis to finance housing for middle-income families, the housing guarantee program can provide the vehicle to meet the housing problem of those individuals who can afford to meet monthly amortization costs.

The housing investment guarantee program was developed from the basic premise that U.S. homebuilders could, through private resources, provide housing in the middle-income areas and at the same time demonstrate their techniques for building, financing, and marketing, as well as project planning. Mr. Herbert Salzman, the recently appointed Assistant Administrator for the Office of Private Resources in AID, testified before your committee that it is the policy of AID to use its credit before it uses its cash; in other words, use should be made of guarantees prior to making loans. 

SECTION 221(b) 2 

Section 221(b)2 of the act includes the provision for guarantees of privately developed housing projects as well as guarantees for other types of projects throughout the developing countries of the world. 

As section 224 of the act specifically provides for housing guarantee projects in Latin America, section 221 housing guarantees are directed at those areas of the world other than Latin America. However, of the three other AID regions, only the African region has attempted on any scale to develop this program for housing, and, even in this region, only one project is under construction. 

AID has proposed that the total existing authority of $375 million under section 221 be increased to $575 million although a proportional increase for the amount set aside for housing guarantees is not being requested. This authority would remain at $160 million, as was established by the Congress in last year's act.

The NAHB is not requesting an increase in the amount set aside for housing, although we believe there should be some increase, because the Agency to date has utilized less than 20 percent of the available authorization in firm contracts. This is despite the fact that Congress has yearly been authorizing additional amounts for the housing guarantee program. Of the $160 million of authority available under section 221 for housing guarantees, for example, only $50 million has been programed for use by AID.

We, therefore, feel that Congress should direct the Agency to develop more projects this year under this section of the act in all of the three regions in which it may operate. We think AID should institute the housing guarantee program in the Near East-South Asia area and expand it in the Far East area. 

During the past 2 weeks, AID and HUD have been jointly sponsoring in Honolulu a Pacific Conference on Urban Growth. They have gathered together housing officials from countries throughout the Far East in order to participate in a program to discuss methods of reliev

1173 ing the pressures on urban growth. At the very least, AID could program more of its guarantee authority, which does not require appropriations, to assist in relieving these problems and to provide an example of the type of housing that may be provided on a privately financed basis. At the present time there are only two projects for a total of $10 million that have been committed in the Far East area. 

The Agency should initiate the use of the $110 million of authority in these three regions that Congress has made available for the last 3 years and has been sitting idle.

SECTION 224-LATIN AMERICAN HOUSING GUARANTEES 

The initial efforts in the housing guarantee program were made in Latin America. The program was expanded each year from an initial $10 million to the present authority of $450 million. Last year Congress expanded the authority from $400 million to $450 million and provided that this additional $50 million be utilized for pilot or demonstration private housing projects under section 224(b)1. In its report last year this committee stated that:

The principal purpose of these amendments to the act is to assure that the guaranty program will continue to support private housing projects demonstrating U.S. techniques for building, financing, and marketing privately developed housing . . . It continues to be the position of this Committee that housing projects of this nature make substantial contributions to economic development and immediate impact upon social conditions by alleviating housing shortages. 

Therefore, the committee insists, as it did last year, upon the continuation of these self-liquidating pilot or demonstration projects. 

The committee went on to say that- Sufficient authorization is available and the committee expects it to be fully utilized for those purposes for which the committee expressly made it available. 

This last sentence points up the problem concerning the operations of the guarantee program. Although AID is attempting now to carry out the directions of Congress, great time delays have handicapped this effort. For instance, although the Foreign Assistance Act of 1966 was enacted early last fall, the Agency is only now prepared to announce its program to carry out the 1966 act. And it is very possible that it will take another year to carry out these aims. Since the inception of the program in early 1962, less than $150 million of guarantee authority is under contract of the $450 million authorized and less than $75 million is actually outstanding for homes constructed. 

We stress again that we believe many significant accomplishments have been attained under the program. However, the many delays in developing it have hidden those accomplishments behind a facade of administrative problems which have created manifold frustrations for those attempting to use the program. For this reason, NAHB believes, as I mentioned earlier, that a thorough evaluation of the program is in order and we are prepared to take an active role in this study. There should be an opportunity to observe the projects already constructed and to analyze the operating problems within the program. NAHB would be pleased to aid in this effort and we hope that by this time next year a long-range assessment of the program may be made by this committee. In the meantime, as we mentioned before, we would hope that some members of this committee will have an opportunity during this session to travel in Latin America so they

1967 

might see some of the accomplishments at firsthand on the construction sites. 

AN INCREASE IN GUARANTEE AUTHORITY 

With respect to the renewed program under section 224 (b) 1, we believe that the program should be increased by $50 million of authority to permit a program of $100 million to be undertaken. Section 

104 of H.R. 7099 should be amended at line 1, page 14, by inserting the appropriate language to increase the amount of guarantee authority. 

A suggested amendment is included in attachment 2 to this statement. 

The long delay in preparing and publishing the regulations under which the program will operate has already taken place. Therefore, the additional authority, which we recommend, would permit the development of a sufficient number of housing projects to be carried out over the next 2 years. With more authority, more projects could be developed during this period. This will make up for the time lost during the past year in creating the guidelines. 

OPERATIONAL POLICIES AND PROCEDURES 

There are two matters of operational policy and procedure which we wish to call to your attention. Before discussing them briefly with you, however, I would like to emphasize that we feel we have received close cooperation from AID officials in working out the guidelines to be used for the renewal of the guarantee program under section 224 (b) 1. 

MARKET CONSIDERATION AND SALES PRICE LIMITATIONS 

The AID has established arbitrary sales price limitations for housing constructed under the section 224 guarantee program. We have no objection to establishing some type of limitations, as the program is directed at middle-income housing and should not provide luxury housing. However, we do not think it is reasonable to apply an arbitrary sales price limit (now set at $7,500) to all countries and cities of 

Latin America.

Sales prices should reflect the market conditions for middle-income housing in the various cities and countries of Latin America. NAHB last year recommended that housing sales price limits be established dependent upon the particular market conditions of each country or city. AID has maintained that it is difficult to establish such limits. If it will be helpful, we are willing to assist in an economic study of selected cities and countries in Latin America to ascertain the appropriate middle-income housing market within which the housing guarantee program should operate. But we strongly object to the current policy of a single fixed ceiling. 

GUARANTEES FOR CONSTRUCTION FINANCING 

It has been the AID policy, with some exceptions, to prohibit guarantees of construction financing. The language of the Foreign Assistance Act does not include any such prohibitions. 

The argument of AID is that by permitting construction guarantees the problems of administration would be greatly increased and, fur-

1175 ther, that such guarantees are really not required by the majority of responsible builders in order to carry out a housing project in Latin America.

Yet, our experience has shown that because construction financing guarantees were not available there have been projects otherwise fully developed which have been seriously slowed down and delayed. Furthermore, there are cases when funds for construction financing are not available from either U.S. sources or sources within the country in which the project is to be constructed. In many cases, also, the cost for construction financing is so high that the cost of the housing is increased significantly. There are also instances when a U.S.-lending institution will refuse to lend non-guaranteed funds in a particular country without demands for security from builders which are unreasonable or unobtainable, or both.

These are the cases to which our request is directed. Since the legislation already permits the guarantee of construction financing, we urge the Congress to direct AID to revise its policy and procedure so as to grant guarantees for construction financing in those cases where capable sponsors are otherwise unable to secure construction financing. 

CONCLUSION 

NAHB wishes again to extend our appreciation to the members of this committee for so strongly supporting this housing guarantee program since its inception. We have presented our suggestions in order that the program may be improved and strengthened. 

We believe that this program has great potential. Our interest and confidence in its future prompts our appearance here again before this committee and we hope that you will accept our recommendations for its improvement. Thank you for this opportunity to present our views today.

I have attached a copy of our recommendations to H.R. 7099, which we should like to have included as a part of the record.

STATEMENT OF HON. THORSTEN V. KALIJARVI, REPRESENTING THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES Mr. KALIJARVI. I am Thorsten V. Kalijarvi, lecturer on interna tional affairs and dean at Cape Cod Community College. I have the honor to present the views of the Chamber of Commerce of the United States on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1967. As the committee knows, the chamber is composed of some 3,700 organization members and more than 32,000 business members representing an underlying membership of more than 4,600,000 individuals and firms. Accompanying me this morning are John C. L. Donaldson and John R. Gilbert of the chamber's international group staff. 

I serve on the national chamber's international committee and also work with its special advisory panel on foreign trade policy, specializing in those areas that relate to the economic development of emerging countries. The committee may also wish its record to show that since 

1947, I have been concerned professionally and at times first hand officially with our aid programs and with the problems of economic development abroad, as a member of the Legislative Reference Service and the staff of the Foreign Relations Committee, as an Assistant Secretary and as Acting Deputy Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, as U.S. Ambassador to El Salvador, and as a professor of international and public affairs. 

This year, as in the past, the chamber supports the proposed program on foreign aid as an instrument of U.S. foreign policy to strengthen the United States and other nations of the free world through responsible political freedom, social progress, and individual endeavor. In this context the chamber wishes to emphasize that it: 

Continues to support a balanced foreign assistance program geared to the type of long-range development that places primary emphasis on the effective use of private resources in furthering foreign assistance objectives, and Encourages the reduction of Government programs as they lay the groundwork-roads, dams, schools, and other public facilities for private resources to move the economic development process in the direction of self-supporting economies. 

FOREIGN AID IN REVIEW 

While the chamber draws a distinction between military and economic assistance, we wish to devote our formal statement to the consideration of economic assistance and more particularly to the role private enterprise can and should play in the implementation of programs of economic assistance.

The national chamber appreciates the national preoccupation with the situation in Vietnam. While we do not intend to discuss the military aspects of the conflict, let the record show that the chamber sup-

1191 ports the U.S. Government's policy of resisting Communist domination in Southeast Asia and urges more effective action by our allies and international organizations in sharing responsibilities in that area of the world. وا This morning, however, we are primarily concerned with what has been called the other war or the quiet war in Veitnam. This struggle involves the economic survival and the orderly development of that country-objectives which are receiving increasing attention. The magnitude of the task and its difficulties are slowly being revealed. 

It appears that the road ahead may be long. Not only are the efforts of our Government required to accomplish the task, but the chamber believes that material help can and should be mustered to help. 

The chamber urges this committee to encourage the U.S. Government to foster regional economic development in Southeast Asia, using private enterprise to the fullest extent as important aids to orderly economic development.

The President in his message of February 9 and H.R. 7099 place primary emphasis on six guiding principles-namely, self-help; multilateralism, regionalism, agriculture, health and education; balance of payments; and efficient AID administration. The overriding emphasis in this six-point program is on self-help. Last year, Mr. John O. 

Teeter, the chamber's witness, testified at length on this point and recommended that the program then under review place the recipient countries as quickly as possible in the position of solving their own problems. The national chamber continues to point out that self-help efforts through private initiative and the criteria proposed in section 208 of the bill are the driving forces that motivate emerging countries to develop, on their own terms, human and natural resources to solve their own problems.

H.R. 7099 as presently drafted would provide stronger emphasis on the use of private resources for economic development. These proposals in addition to self-help, already mentioned, include emphasis on the development of agricultural technology and productivity, and investment surveys and guaranty provisions designed to induce more private enterprise input into economic development. If these proposals are adopted and succeed, they should Government expenditure for aid and to tribute to the reduction in the stimulation of economic development. We hope this committee will give is fullest support to the implementation of programs designed to produce the desired results.

A concerted effort is being made by AID to involve more private enterprise in the continuing struggle to assist developing countries attain the position where they can fulfill their own national objectives. 

We are pleased that AID has established a new Office of Private Resources and a Private Investment Center to assist business, voluntary and nonprofit organizations in their efforts to improve conditions in developing countries which will support an expansion of private conditions in developing countries which will support an expansion of private economic activity. I will refer later to the International Private Investment Advisory Council in whose recent establishment AID which was instrumental and about which you will be hearing more after its first meeting some time next month.

1967 

In reference to the National Advisory Committee on Self-Help, we urge that the coordination of foreign economic policy and programs at all U.S. Government levels be given the highest priority if such a committee is established. The expansion of foreign assistance programs to increase responsibility for food, health, and education in various Government agencies emphasizes the immediate need to coordinate these programs if we are to implement effectively our foreign policies.

FUNDS FOR DEVELOPMENT 

As to the last of the six guiding principles of the bill; namely, efficient AID administraion, the chamber has consistently held the view that an integral part of the accomplishment of our aid objective lies in an efficient administration of the aid programs. The chamber continues to support the principle that foreign aid administration must be continuously improved in order to yield budgetary sarings. At the same time, it recognizes that administrative efficiency alone will not reduce the costs of our programs. The present requests of the administration reflect population increases in the world and mounting food needs. More food resources are required, but these must be supplied on a more equitable sharing of worldwide assistance to the developing countries. Demands for funds will increase as populations increase and as developing countries reach the point where they can effectively absorb assistance that can pave the way toward balanced development. 

With this background the chamber's foreign assistance task force and international committee reviewed the President's request for an authorized $3.1 billion economic and military aid program, and the fiscal year 1967 appropriations. These groups then presented their recommendations to the chamber's board of directors as a basis for positions on aid.

Economic assistance activities should, in general, not be expanded. 

Exceptions may be justified regarding amounts required for Vietnam supporting assistance, development loans, and technical cooperation and development grants. 

Based on this approach, the national chamber recommends a reduction of at least $70.3 million in the funds requested for economic assistance. This means that not more than $2.46 billion should be authorized for fiscal year 1968 economic assistance. 

No position is taken by the national chamber on the request for military aid outside of Vietnam because classified documentation and materials are not available to chamber members. 

Primary emphasis and support is placed by the national chamber on development loan programs because these are the programs through which a major part of private sector development is stimulated.

Although H.R. 7099 does not contain authorizations for the Inter- 

American Development Bank and the International Development As sociation, the impact of programs financed by these organizations is of direct concern to this committee. In general the national chamber supports the concept of multilateral aid provided by the IDB and IDA. Multilateral development financing and technical assistance should be emphasized as an essential instrument of U.S. foreign

1193 policy. We are encouraged that efforts are being made by both of these organizations to make burden sharing a reality in the scaling of contributions to the respective organizations. Pin We are aware of the President's Latin American message request for sizable resources-quoted by the press at $1.5 billion-for Latin American development. The national chamber applauds the President's emphasis on increased trade, agricultural productivity, and self-help. 

The chamber's view is that the North American business community can and should fulfill an increasing role in providing commercial, technical and entrepreneurial support for hemispheric economic and social progress. Emphasis on this role, we hope and believe, will ultimately reduce the need for public funds. 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

Earlier I referred to the establishment of the International Private Investment Advisory Council which was actively supported by the national chamber and brought into legislation through the leadership of Representative F. Bradford Morse and Senator Jacob Javits. The 

Chamber of Commerce of the United States is a member of the Council, in addition to five other business associations. We do not expect overnight miracles from this Council. But we do wish to register with the committee our view that an important liaison has been established between the U.S. Government and the business community. It is the business community's intention to cultivate this relationship. 

We do not consider the Council as just another group to study the aid program. We see the Council as a working group that can stimulate and monitor the implementation of such objectives as: (1) incentives to private investment; (2) regulation of AID-financed exports; (3) recruitment of businessmen as AID mission industry officers; and (4) guidelines for the use of cost-plus incentive fees on Government contracts. 

One of the concepts with which the Council should concern itself is joint ventures. The national chamber supports foreign business participation, where feasible, as a means of meeting nationalistic concerns. 

Another area of Council activity should be refinement of "build, amortize, and sell" arrangements under which U.S. investment provides initial capital and longer term management. Reference to both of these concepts is included in the attached "Statement in Furtherance of Policies on Mutual Security" as approved by the national chamber's board of directors last February.

The Council should consider development of a more precise definition of the actual requirements of U.S. business in the developing countries. The phrase "better business climate" needs to be refined. 

The Council should concern itself with such questions as: 

What does it take to attract private foreign investment in needed amounts? 

Are incentives decisive in whether or not to invest? 

Do local markets need protection, and if so, to what degree?

The Council should also concern itself with the terms under which U.S. business is acceptable in the developing countries. These terms can be developed best through AID and business liaison. In addition, a better U.S. business understanding is needed of operating conditions

1967) 

it faces in developing markets, and what can and should be done to overcome or adapt to these situations. 

AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT AND POPULATION GROWTH 

A great deal of attention has been given in the last few months to the field of agri-business as the turnkey to improved agricultural techniques that can provide more and more nourishing food for the hungry people around the world. Several chamber member firms are already involved in the systems development of production and marketing procedures, on a regional systems development of production and marketing procedures, on a regional basis, as an integral part of economic development. We are confident that this expertise will play a valuable role in efforts to win the war on hunger. 

AID statistics show that developing countries now have an annual food deficit of 16 million tons of grain, and that this deficit is expected to multiply rapidly as populations increase. These statistics also point out that over one-half of the U.S. reserve cropland is being returned to production to help alleviate this problem. 

The national chamber generally supports the objectives of the war on hunger. At the same time, the chamber urges that guidelines to implement food programs referred to in section 207 of the bill place greater emphasis on the use of private capital, free market transactions, and the resources of private enterprises and organizations to assistant the developing countries toward self-sufficiency and active competitiveness in world trade.

Every effort should be made to reinvest local currencies generated from Public Law 480 food sales in agricultural development. The national chamber reiterates its position that relief provided by Public Law 480 programs is a temporary measure. A condition of this type of assistance should be the improvement of agricultural techniques and productivity.

Proposals for voluntary family planning should be given appropriate consideration. The national chamber has stated that funds should be provided to encourage such voluntary programs when such funds are requested by the developing countries. 

PRIVATE ENTERPRISE AND FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

Several programs already authorized in the Foreign Assistance Act are designed to stimulate U.S. and foreign private investment in the developing countries. These include investment surveys, investment guarantees, and housing guarantees in Latin America. The national chamber supports the incentive concept embodied in the investment survey program as an approach for building an economic and political framework in which the profit motive can operate at full potential. 

Section 104 of H.R. 7099 extends the coverage of specific risk investment guarantees that result from civil strife. This provision would eradicate much of the uncertainty in the minds of investors as to what risks are covered by investment guarantees. The national chamber supports this amendment with the understanding that recourse to coverage by private insurance firms be exhausted prior to applying to 

AID.

1195 Section 104 also provides a separate guarantee authority, to be determined by the President, extending to 50 percent of any loss of equity investment. We understand that the amount of a guarantee coverage outstanding would be charged against the overall specific risk guarantee ceiling and would be limited to $125 million. This provision would seem to hold promise as an effective inducement to more private investment in the developing countries. 

The national chamber supports extended risk guarantees, that protect against commercial loss for which private insurance is unavailable, as desirable incentives for expanded invstment. 

CONGRESSIONAL AND PUBLIC ATTITUDES TOWARD THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

PROGRAM Several Presidents and Congresses, without reference to party, have endorsed the foreign assistance program as a necessary arm of U.S. foreign policy. Foreign aid has been and should continue to be a nonpartisan issue. That has been our approach at all times. We are of the firm conviction that this is the sound approach for business, for government, and for the American people. The current bill should be deliberated and framed on the merits or demerits of foreign assistance programs. Foreign assistance will continue for some time to be one of the responsibilities of the United States in its role as leader of the free world. Even if we wished to terminate it today, we could not do so without serious national and international consequences. Whether this responsibility be called foreign aid or bilateral and multilateral assistance programs makes little difference in the final analysis. 

The need for increased financial and technical assistance to developing countries has been amply publicized. The United States has heeded this call and will continue to be called upon for such assistance. It is gratifying to see that 31 of our 50 State governments now conduct active technical assistance programs with the less developed countries. 

In setting priorities for foreign assistance programs, we believe it to be most important to follow an orderly procedure. Congress can help immensely in this matter. We urge this committee to keep its sights on underlying needs. First priority should be given to such basic needs as agriculture, health, education, and technical assistance including management training. After these needs have been addressed and the seed has taken root is the time for second priorities; namely, emphasis on heavier industries and larger scale projects that will assist developing countries in meeting their desire for industrialization. We repeat in this connection our testimony of last year; namely, that multiyear authorizations are desirable to accomplish this type of long-range development. 

Today, we see in Europe the emergence of a fear that a widening gap of technology threatens to leave Europe behind us in economic matters as the United States moves at an accelerating pace into the world of computers, communications, space, and related fields of technology. The need to compete for industrial power in the world will have an even greater impact in time on the emerging countries as they achieve economic development. Private enterprise programs will be needed to train and retrain foreign nationals as specialists. Simul-

1967 

taneously, such training should also lead to the profits that can command the technology desired. 

Inescapably, there is duplication of effort by the emerging countries as they experience the economic development process. As the demand for financial and technical assistance by developing countries grows, it is clear that the United States cannot meet the needs alone. The chamber endorses and encourages the regional approach to development-as spelled out in section 210 of H.R. 7099. As the committee knows, substantial beginnings toward regionalism have been made. for example in the Inter-American Development Bank, the Asian and African Development Banks, and in the proposed merger of the Central American Common Market and the Latin American Free Trade Association to mention only a few. But these are only a start. Concerted efforts should be undertaken to encourage joint development of transportation, communication, and power facilities on a regional basis. 

CONCLUSION 

A combination of the practical overseas business experience of U.S. chamber members and information gathered by the chamber's membership during reviews of the foreign assistance programs with AID shows that those countries which are developing most rapidly are those where investment, public policy and external assistance have worked together to bring private initiative into play. Examples of such economic development are seen in Taiwan, Korea, Greece, Israel, Pakistan, and lately, Brazil.

The national chamber has consistently supported foreign assistance as an important element of U.S. foreign policy, as a humanitarian obligation, and as a means of developing the business community's own self-interest. The foreign assistance program has benefited business in general. In fiscal year 1966, exports of U.S. goods and services financed under economic aid programs totaled over $1.1 billion. This results from the fact that 90 percent of economic aid funds are tied to purchases in the United States.

The foreign assistance program has also created several hundred thousand American jobs and opened markets for American business and industry throughout the world. 

In our economic system, profit is an important driving force. If private enterprise is to be encouraged to increase its contributions to economic development, the profit motive must continue to be allowed free play at home and abroad. The development of human resources is a vital part of foreign assistance. Without cultivation of such human elements as man's ability to improve his own lot, our foreign assistance couched in our way of life will have failed one of its major goals. 

To this end, the business community favors increased emphasis on the use of private resources in furthering foreign assistance objectives and on the reduction of government programs after confidence and such infrastructure projects as ports and roads have been established to support the expansion of private economic activity within the free market system.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I request that the attachment to my statement be made part of the official records of your hearings.

(The attachment is as follows:) STATEMENT IN FURTHERANCE OF POLICIES ON MUTUAL SECURITY I. BASIC CHAMBER POSITION ON FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

A. Foreign aid as a means toward foreign economic and social development continues to be a proper element of U.S. foreign policy. Its objectives and principles have long been endorsed by the Chamber. 

B. Refinement of the program must provide an effective base for the exercise of private enterprise and initiative in foreign economic and social development. 

C. Program objectives should be continually clarified as they relate to U.S. foreign policy and to U.S. and foreign private enterprise. 

II. CHAMBER PROGRAM PROPOSALS 

A. Long-range economic planning and development must be emphasized. To accomplish this goal, multi-year authorizations are desirable. 

Although long-term aid investment seldom has a dramatic impact, in general it can yield far higher returns than short-term "gimmicks." Economic planning need not mean a government "planned economy" in underdeveloped countries. 

Recent efforts at country development planning have shown the need for private foreign investment. Foreign economic development programs must place increased reliance on private resources, and reduce government programs after these programs have served their catalytic purpose. 

Private enterprise and government should cooperate in their efforts to locate opportunities for the development of free and viable economies that can improve local conditions and provide markets for U.S. goods and services. In particular, foreign participation should be encouraged when feasible as a means of meeting nationalistic concerns. In negotiating such arrangements, business efforts to conclude equitable agreements should be fully supported by the U.S. Government. 

Where appropriate, "build, amortize and sell" arrangements under which U.S. investment provides initial capital and longer-term management should be explored. 

The expertise and future recommendations of the International Private Investment Advisory Council on Foreign Aid should be fully utilized and implemented. 

B. Government incentives to U.S. private foreign investment serve a useful purpose. But a more positive approach is imperative, centering around the need to build an economic and political framework in which the profit motive can operate at full potential. Priority must be given to removal of disincentives that discourage private investment. Certain provisions in the Revenue Act of 1962 on taxation of foreign income are punitive and self-defeating. International antitrust standards and an international patent system should also be developed. 

International principles relating to the rights and responsibilities of private foreign investment should be clarified. A multilateral system of investment guarantees could contribute to such clarification. 

The United States should suspend foreign assistance to any nation that takes discriminatory or confiscatory action against U.S. private investment in such nation without taking appropriate steps to discharge its obligations under international law including prompt and full compensation or relief. Courts in the 

United States should determine and apply principles of international law in appropriate cases to encourage the develoment of an international legal system that will contribute to the improvement of the investment climate, and the protection of private property abroad. 

C. Development loans should receive priority. The trend towards government lending to, and for the express development of, private institutions and organizations should be accelerated. Terms of development loans should take into consideration the overall debt management position of recipient countries. 

D. A limited program of military assistance to selected allies is essential to free world security. Military assistance should be held to a minimum, particularly in Western Europe and Latin America. The cost to the United States of such assistance should be accountable to the Department of Defense. 、,ཟླ་་།།

1967 

E. Multilateral development financing and technical assistance should be em phasized as an essential instrument of U.S. foreign policy. In many instances, this approach is more practical and effective than the bilateral approach. Private international consortia should be utilized to the fullest extent possible. 

Congress and the Administration should continue to place major emphasis on U.S. participation in international institutions, including regional development banks, provided the United States has voting rights commensurate to its contributions. Such programs must assign a major role to the private sectors of both donor and recipient nations, and the administrative cost of such programs must be equitably shared by the respective national governments. The Chamber recognizes a continuing need for a substantial U.S. bilateral program until acceptable multilateral programs are developed. 

F. The Administration must apply great selectivity in choosing which nations and projects are to be aided from among ever-increasing requests for assistance. 

Assistance must be based on results. 

Emphasis must be placed on technical assistance programs that can put aid recipients in the position of solving their own problems. 

G. The Food for Freedom Program, including P.L. 480, Title II, serves in gen eral the best interests of U.S. foreign policy. Relief provided by P.L. 480 programs is a temporary measure. A condition of this type of assistance should be the improvement of agricultural techniques and productivity. Funds should be provided to encourage voluntary birth control programs when such funds are requested by less-developed countries. 

U.S.-owned local currencies should be used where available to finance investment surveys and the development of vocational training facilities. 

H. The Alliance for Progress must be moved forward along the sound lines recommended by its Inter-American Committee (CIAP). A broader concept of the Alliance should be developed by encouraging other members to contribute appropriate financial and technical assistance for Latin American development. 

The objectives of the Alliance must be realistically determined with emphasis on regional market integration and the availability of external resources. 

Alliance programs must create a stable atmosphere in which private investment and initiative, local and foreign, can operate beneficially. 

I. The aid task must be justly shared. The United States should continue to enlist greater cooperation from other industrialized nations in assisting less developed countries. The Development Assistance Committee of the OECD has an important duty as an instrument to serve this purpose. 

J. Effective foreign assistance programs can be implemented only by competent personnel. Private enterprise urges, and is willing to cooperate with AID in, the maintenance of such standards. The administrators of the program must have the legislative authority to improve the quality and reduce the number of AID personnel, both domestic and overseas.

NATIONAL CHAMBER POLICY ON BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

In its role as an international banker, the proper posture of the United States is one of confidence and strength. The U.S. should so conduct its affairs as to command trust and respect in the monetary sphere without compromising other U.S. national and international objectives. 

Domestic and international policies and actions should be weighed carefully to encourage constructive measures, consonant with our traditional principles of freedom, to prevent erosion in our payments position. To this end, it is imperative that sound fiscal and monetary policies be followed, with shifting emphasis as the situation may require. 

Particular effort must be made to avoid restrictive measures, particularly affecting the free flow of trade and capital, which could become entrenched and have undesirable long-term implications. 

Mr. TAFT. In section 201 (b) of the act there is limited to 10 the number of countries that can receive development loans. Do you have an opinion as to whether or not this is good policy? 

Mr. KALIJARVI. Selectivity in giving assistance is, of course, a goal that should be continually refined. The U.S. chamber has stated that assistance must be based on results and that emphasis must be placed

1209 on technical assistance programs that can put aid recipients in the position of solving their own problems. 

Development loans should receive priority in foreign assistance and the terms of these loans should take into consideration the overall debt management position of respective countries. If the Congress feels that limitation should be placed on the number of countries which receive development loans in any fiscal year, provision should be made that the limitation is placed only as far as government-to-government aid programs are concerned and not as a limitation as far as American private enterprise is concerned. The chamber position on the whole aid program is that it must be refined to provide an effective base for the exercise of private enterprise and initiative in foreign social and economic development.

Mr. DONALDSON. This position would exempt from a country limitation, for example, the authority for direct-dollar financing for American private companies.
