STATEMENT IN SUPPORT OF H.R. 7099, , BY NATIONAL COUNCIL OF JEWISH WOMEN, INC., NEW YORK, N.Y. 

The National Council of Jewish Women's support of the Foreign Assistance Act dates back to the program's inception as the Marshall Plan in 1948 and has been reaffirmed in the ensuing years, most recently at our Biennial Convention held in Atlanta in April. It has its basis in two of our Organization's major interests, first, our concern with the disadvantaged everywhere, reflected in our service projects at home and our overseas projects in Israel-and second, the belief expressed in our resolutions that conditions for peace depend on free institutions, self-determination and social and economic progress. 

In the past, our testimony before the appropriate Congressional Committees on behalf of Foreign Aid, has emphasized: careful consideration of the needs and potentials of recipient countries, long-term authorization with yearly review of appropriations, channelling aid through multilateral institutions, strong family planning programs and the increased participation of the private sector. 

In reviewing this year's proposed Foreign Assistance Act with our delegates in Atlanta, it occurred to us that the great pitfall in presenting it to an informed audience, was not in oversimplifying an admittedly complex program, but in allowing a highly sophisticated approach to Foreign Affairs to make us overlook the obvious-the "obvious", in this case being the one constant element of Foreign Aid-our effort to assist other countries in maintaining their independence and be self-supporting.

As we re-examined the general aspects of the program, it was clear to us that the "constant" was there, the changes occurring only in methods and administration. As a matter of fact, these changes reflect variations of emphasis rather than complete innovations. Multi-lateralism, self-help, regional and intra-national cohesion, concern with agriculture health and education, are all terms we have encountered and supported in the past. We indicated that the financial give-away approach had been realistically discarded in favor of a social economic development program based on matching efforts. Requirements for Aid had been tightened, administrative offices consolidated. But the "constant" remained.

1967 

We pointed out to our delegates that the geographical scope of the program would be more restricted. A realistic appraisal of individual needs is serving as a guide line in determining where Aid can be most effective. There is a growing recognition that we are now dealing with a number of complex and dissimilar situations, each calling for their own particular solution. The immediate security problems of South East Asia, for example, require a different consideration, then the political development of Africa or the long-term development plans of Latin America.

We noted also that it was the proposed program's intention to concentrate a high percentage of each regional allocation in a smaller number of countries. 

We cited East Asia, as a case in point, where of an allocation of 812 million dollars, it is proposed to use 650 million in Viet Nam, Laos and Thailand. We stressed the fact that the war in Viet-Nam and the military expenditures involved therein, have unfortunately overshadowed the economic assistance program which has been in effect in that region for some time; that a large number of 

AID technicians are working under extremely hazardous conditions training teachers and doctors, providing textbooks and advising in the field of agriculture, transportation and public administration; and that the proposed Foreign 

Assistance Act intends to continue this program, to help begin the task of reconstruction and to alleviate some of the immediate needs resulting from the war. 

In reporting on the economic aspects of the program, we reiterated the fact that the proposed 2.5 billion dollars represent 7/10th of 1% of our Gross National 

Product, far less than the 2% of our G.N.P. spent on the Marshall Plan, and that 

90% of these funds never leave the United States. We also repeated our desire to see a two year authorization as requested by the President, for the same reasons that we had favored long-term authorization with yearly reviews in the past. 

Finally, we reminded our delegates that prior to reconsidering their positions on Foreign Aid, and, in addition to examining all the facts mentioned above, that they should not overlook the "constant" èlement within the program: that is, the 'basic concept behind foreign aid, the concept which gives validity to all of America's efforts in the disadvantaged parts of the world; the same concept which this Organization has supported for the last nineteen years; that, although 

Foreign Aid is a major part of our foreign policy, it is first and foremost a humanitarian program designed to serve the same purpose and inspired by the same logic which has propelled the original Marshall Plan, the Peace Corps, and the War on Poverty, the Civil Rights and equal opportunity programs at home. 

Individual world needs may change; our foreign policy may change, our image abroad may change; but the need for humanitarian assistance remains the same. 

This is the aspect of our Foreign Aid program which requires no updating and no revamping.

In conclusion, the 1967 National Convention of the National Council of Jewish Women has charged this Organization to express its support for the Foreign Assistance Act of 1967 and to urge this Committee to give its favorable consideration to the bill. 

INTERFAITH STATEMENT ON FOREIGN AID 

Presented by Department of International Affairs, National Council of Churches, Washington, D.C.; Social Action Department, U.S. Catholic Conference, Wash. 

ington; Commission on Social Action of Reform Judaism, Washington, D.C. 

We wish to thank the Committee for the opportunity of appearing before you today to testify in support of the economic assistance portion of the Foreign Aid 

Bill (H.R. 7099).

There is much in our Judeo-Christian tradition to substantiate such a stand. 

The wealth of nations is in part at least the product of natural resources which have been created by God. As the Psalmist has declared, "The Earth is the 

Lord's and the fullness thereof." Therefore, it is man's obligation to use God's gifts responsibly and for the benefit of his fellow man. The existence of human want in time of duress is a tragedy, but the persistence of want in time of prosperity is morally intolerable. The major faiths consider foreign aid to be a direct application of religious teachings urging concern for the welfare of all people and the pursuit of a just and peaceful world.

The seriousness of our concern is evidenced by the fact that all of our policymaking bodies have had these issues high on the agendas of their recent meetings

1211 and numerous statements concerning them have been made. Pertinent excerpts from some of these statements are attached as an appendix to this testimony. 

STRONGLY FAVOR A FOREIGN AID PROGRAM 

There has been considerable response to world need by our members as witnessed by the sizable humanitarian programs carried on by our various religious organizations. However, as the attached statements show, there is a growing recognition that only a massive government effort can be sufficient for the task of long range development. Therefore, we strongly favor giving assistance to the nations which have yet to bring their economies into the mainstream of modern economic life and which are not yet equipped to provide adequately for the subsistance of their peoples. This should be done on the basis of their need and their ability to use help effectively. 

While firmly believing that humanitarian concern is a strong enough imperative for this program, we realize that there are areas of national interest that are also served. We therefore concur wtih the Congress in its statement of the purpose of the bill "that freedom, security and prosperity of the U.S. are best preserved in a community of prospering nations." We believe that a true expression of our sense of freedom, justice and compassion will in a very real sense contribute to our national security but we do not want this to be construed to mean that we favor the use of our aid program at any time as an instrument of the cold war.

We would not wish to see development plans that have long range significance thwarted by temporary set-backs in local political situations. 

DEPLORE INADEQUACY OF FUNDS 

We commend the drafters of the bill on many phases of the program they propose, realizing that it has been admittedly pared down and altered to meet what they assumed to be the political climate at the present time. We deeply regret, however, that they did not see fit to lay before the Congress and the American people a bill that would more accurately show what we, and we believe what most of the authorities in the field, believe to be the full extent of the commitment that we should be called upon to make at this time. 

In spite of our growing GNP the level of our aid seems to have reached a plateau and now nowhere reaches the 1% of GNP that is conservatively estimated as the minimum amount necessary from government sources. This is particularly deplorable since it comes at a time when not only the needs of the developing nations are increasing but at a time when their capacity to plan and to make effective use of assistance is also growing rapidly. If we do not take the initiative and go ahead now we will lose much of the ground that has been gained.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES INVOLVED IN THE DIRECTION OF THE PROGRAM 

We are aware that the effort to help other peoples in their development is a relatively new effort and that many of the programs are still in the experimental stage. There have been some mistakes in the past and, if we are to continue to explore creatively for new ways of addressing ourselves to the problems presented by the developing countries-and there will be some in the future we must not be led into the trap of expecting too much too soon, nor of expecting more "progress" in remote places and alien cultures for our money than we do at home.

We do feel that there has been great progress over the past twenty years and we are pleased to see an effort to incorporate some of the experience so gained into guidelines to make our future endeavors more fruitful, such as: 

1. Support Self-Help Principles. We support the principle of self-help from the point of view that development is most effective when governments and individuals join in the effort to determine their own destiny and to assume responsibility for their own betterment. The continued emphasis on building institutions that actually involve people in their own progress such as educational, research and extension programs, cooperatives, labor unions, improved local governments, etc., as set forth in Title 9 of the bill is a realistic effort to build programs that will have continuity and selfsustaining momentum. 

Whereas effective progress requires standards of performance and sometimes reforms and changes of policy in a recipient country, as set forth in the self-help

1967 

criteria, we would emphasize that care should be taken that we do not impose our own values on others.

It is important that we do not take the stance of bearing the whole world's burdens; thus we should be more vocal in recognizing in our discussions and publicity the very real contributions to selfimprovement that are now being made by the developing countries themselves. We must continue to encourage their efforts in this direction, realizing nevertheless that our role in supplying the necessary technical assistance and foreign exchange plays a vital part. 

It is our hope that the National Advisory Committee provided for in the bill will make use of the valuable experience and background of many of our private citizens and will be helpful in objectively evaluating self-help performance. 

2. Commend Multilateralism.-We commend the approach toward giving a larger proportion of our aid through mutlilateral channels, realizing the many advantages that it gives, such as; preserving the dignity of the recipient, freedom from the suspicion of political motives and involvements and the ability to be firmer in demands for better performance, etc. 

However, knowing how great the needs will be in the years to come and realizing that our position of exceptional wealth calls us to bear an extremely large part of that burden, we must accept the fact that we will have to maintain a U.S. aid program for some time and as we do this we must work in the direction of continually improving its quality and nature. We must, in conducting our aid program seek for ways that will negate the disadvantages and dangers of a bi-lateral relationship. Among other things, new schemes for multilateral receiving and the wider use of multinational advisory committees and consultative groups should be employed.

A facet of multilateralism is to be recognized in the regional approach wherein assistance may be given to contiguous countries through a mutually helpful regional project. Such projects have the advantage of encouraging several conntries to come together to discuss their mutual welfare. 

3. Favor Emphasis on Health, Education and Agriculture.-We sympathize with the longings of people in the new and developing countries for the attainment of equal status in the modern industrialized world and the need for their leaders to give them visible symbols to that effect. We also feel it to be increas ingly important that they be assisted in their efforts to come to grips with their basic problems involving the hard work of building a strong agricultural base for their economy and the development of dynamic and humanly responsive social economic processes and institutions.

We support the "War on Hunger". It is time for an intensive effort to help other nations increase their own food supplies and we feel that a substantial increase in the programs of technical assistance in agriculture and in the production and distribution of agricultural supplies is essential at this time. 

We recognize the seriousness of the problems encountered when 40 percent or more of a population is under 15 years of age and realize the great strain that this places on the educational facilities. We urge maximum assistance to these countries in their efforts to educate their populace to meet the mannower needs of modernization as well as to allow humans to develop their potentials. 

4. Favor Long Term Planning and Removal of Limitation on Number of Coun tries Assisted.—Recognizing that economic assistance to developing countries is a long time proposition and that we must be involved for whatever period is required, we endorse the request for at least a two year authorization now and for longer range authorization and appropriations in the future. This will allow the administrators of the program to plan ahead and to utilize flexibility in management and re-adaptation as conditions change and new learnings are discovered. 

A suitable check on such long term authorization can be provided by a competent citizens' and Congressional review committee.

In view of the rapidly changing conditions and situations in the world we urge that no arbitrary limitations be placed on the number of countries to which the U.S. may render assistance. Each country's program, in the light of our resources, should be judged on its own merits and in regard to the self-help standards. In this connection the program must be allowed adequate funds for development loans and technical assistance. 

5. Support Mobilization of Private Industry.-We support the continued effort to mobilize private industry as a partner in the development process. As countries that are most likely to be torn by civil strife are often the ones most needing outside investment, the inclusion of such losses under risk investment guarantees under Title III should give added encouragement to the movement of capital into some areas not yet considered safe.

1213 

CONCLUSION 

In conclusion let us say that we favor the passage of this bill without any amendments that would in any way limit the effectiveness of this program for sound development purposes. We would consider any cut in the funds requested as disastrous. We would, instead, favor increased appropriations. 

The times call desperately for a response to the challenge of development that is worthy of the ideals, compassion and common sense of the American people.

From Statement Adopted by the General Board of the National Council of 

Churches of Christ in the U.S.A., February 24, 1966 "Many factors have created a 'revolution of rising expectations.' These expectations are being widely frustrated by slow processes of economic development, by exploding population and by the policies which some developed and developing nations pursue to realize their interests. On the one hand, economic interdependence steadily increases; on the other hand, the gap between rich and poor nations grows steadily more evident and may well produce the deepest conflicts of the future. In the light of this situation the United States has a major economic responsibility to continue to cooperate with other nations in programs of economic development and to do so in relation to the developing nations' growing needs and our growing capacities."

These facts have caused every informed and concerned person to issue warning after warning: this inequity, this injustice is brewing a human trouble that will dwarf our present difficulties." 

From World Council of Churches' "Church and Society Conference," Geneva 1966 "Recognizing that many channels for the transfer of capital, skill, and knowledge are available to help the developing nations in their efforts, churches every where should do their utmost to "a. contribute generously through direct personal service and financial resources; "b. urge their fellow-citizens and governments to increase their contributions to developmental aid, as indicated in the report; preferably through international channels, at non-commercial interest rates and on non-commercial terms; "c. make every effort to put these contributions to maximum use in the interest of the long-term needs and objectives of the recipient churches and nations."

A planned programme is of course better and more effective than occasional aid left to individual good will. It presupposes, as We said above, careful study, the selection of ends and the choice of means, as well as a reorganization of efforts to meet the needs of the present and the demands of the foreseeable future. More important, a concerted plan has advantages that go beyond the field of economic growth and social progress; for in addition it gives significance and value to the work undertaken. While shaping the world it sets a higher value on man" (p. 50).

STATEMENT OF AARON SCHEINFELD, CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD, MANPOWER, INC., CHICAGO, ILL. 

ܐ ܂ 

WWW THE SCHEINFELD "BUILD-SELL" PROPOSAL A Plan for Accelerating the Flow of Private Capital Into Developing Countries SUMMARY I. Objectives of the "Build-Sell" Proposal 

The principal objective of this proposal is to accelerate the flow of private capital into developing countries by extending the use of the build-sell technique, in which U.S. investors-with or without the initial participation of local investors will build, operate, and after an appropriate period of time, offer their investments for sale to the local private sector. 

II. Purposes of the “Build-Sell” Proposal 

A. To make investments in developing countries more attractive to the U.S. private sector, and less subject to expropriation, harassments, discriminatory foreign taxation, and other impediments;

B. To stimulate the development of an indigenous private sector, and to broaden the base of private business ownership in many developing countries; 

C. To brighten the image of capitalism where it is most needed, and to present the United States as a nation which is interested in and concerned for the welfare of local populations, and the development and encouragement of the local private sector; and

D. To help create companies that will be good customers of U.S. firms abroad, either as users of these products or services in their own local operations, or as marketers and distributors of these products or services. 

III. Elements of the Proposal 

Under this proposal, the U.S. Government through the Foreign Assistance 

Program would assist U.S. private investors including cooperatives, to participate in the program through loans, technical assistance grants and investment guarantees. The proposed amendments to PL 87-195 authorize $75,000,000 in Development Loan Funds, $500,000 in Development Grant Funds, and up to $100,000,000 in Investment Guarantees for use in this program. To be eligible, the U.S. Investor must: 

Agree to invest in programs related to the development of agricultural #stand marine resources including those which are basic to the development of the above; 

Be willing to sell or offer for sale his equity interest in the overseas facility after a specified length of time; 

Be willing to accept a price for his equity interest based upon an agreedupon price formula; and 

Have a demonstrated capacity to carry out the proposed project. 

The loans offered to the U.S. investor by the U.S. Government would be longterm and low-interest, and would be accompanied by certain tax concessions on the part of both the U.S. and the Host Governments. 

IV. Focus on the War on Hunger 

The investments supported by AID under this plan would relate to the development of agricultural and marine resources, including processing and distribution, and industries basic to the development of the resoures above. It could, in the spirit of self-help, be an integral part of the War on Hunger. 

V. Balance of Payments Implications phon 

It is likely that firms set up in the developing countries would become increasingly good customers for U.S. goods and services because of the U.S. equipment and technical help which will be involved. It is also likely that some of the projects undertaken will result in the direct creation of marketing outlets for U.S. firms. 

VI. Coordination With Other Institutions 

The instrument by which the loan is made to the investor group by the U.S. 

Government will also spell out certain relationships between the project and other institutions. Fair wage and price standards must be enforced throughout

1967 

the project, arrangements for the sale and evaluation of the sale price must be conducted smoothly, and disputes arising during the project period must be resolved. It may be in some instances that AID will undertake this function. It may also be that some local institution in the Host Country will perform it. Specific projects in specific countries may want to take advantage of newly formed Joint Commissions on Rural Development, and for disputes within its jurisdiction, the 

International Center for the Settlement of Investment Disputes. 

VII. Specific Steps to Implementation 

Initially, the "Build-Sell" technique might be begun in countries which have signed specific and extended risk guarantee agreements with the U.S. Government and which indicate a willingness to participate. 

There are companies such as Nebraska Consolidated Mills, Omaha, and International Rural Development Corporation, which are already practicing "Build- Sell." Our preliminary conversations with certain responsible U.S. corporations indicate that this kind of plan would indeed accelerate the flow of private capital into developing countries. 

This program could be of immeasurable assistance in building the image of the United States abroad as a nation which cares for the development of indigenous free enterprise. The United States can offer this program to U.S. inve tors with the sure knowledge that its very existence will change the attitude which many countries have now toward the private sector. U.S. investors will find that they can make profits abroad and still retain the positive healthy and enthusiastic cooperation of local citizens and local governments. 

STATEMENT BY AARON SCHEINFELD A Plan for Accelerating the Flow of Private Capital Into Developing Countries 

Most of us feel that freedom is the element which distinguishes the United States from many other countries. In freedom, especially freedom in business and commerce, we have built this vast land and made it great. Our free enterprise system, although it is certainly not what it was in 1870, is still a vital moving force.

U.S. government aid to the developing countries, in its present form, has not brought us the results we hoped for. Our aid to some of the developing countries has brought us no thanks-only curses. In these cases they have neutralized themselves against us, and have refused to swallow the democratizing pill we have put in their mouths.

I find it rather paradoxical that under our present foreign aid program many millions of dollars are given to the governments of the recipient countries, and with these funds, coming from the U.S. taxpayer, government-owned industries are established. It should be the principal aim of our foreign aid program to persuade these recipient countries to increase the degrees of freedom they offer their citizens, especially to encourage free enterprise as the best form of economic organization. If these countries want to experiment with state socialism, they are going to find that it is a rather disappointing engine of economic growth. It takes freedom to loose man's energies and talents. Russia itself has learned this lesson.

A NEW APPROACH IS NEEDED 

Therefore, the time has come for an encouraging and more dramatic formula for our foreign aid and for our private investment program. Such a formula should mark the beginning of the development of a middle class emerging first from the establishment of basic industries, then to heavy industries, and then eventually to consumer goods. 

We must plant within the recipient countries the missing ingredients of private local initiative without which nothing further will happen in the direction of their economic development. This can only be done if we help the nationals of these countries create their own enterprises. 

Communism in these developing countries is gaining headway. I understand they have found a Castro-type training camp deep in the interior of Bolivia, and I wonder how many of these camps they have not found. Communism can only be avoided when the people of these countries have a stake in their own prosperity. It can only be avoided when indigenous private capitalism is encouraged to flourish.

1217 Our foreign aid program has not accomplished enough in this regard. If a successful effort is to be made, a coalition and coordination of efforts is necessary between government and business in this country and elsewhere in the free industrially-developed world, and their counterparts in the developing countries. 

IMPLICATIONS OF THE COMING WORLD FAMINE 

The world, according to some, is on the threshold of the biggest famine in history. The populations of Asia, Africa and Latin America are now growing at the rates of 2.5%, 2.5% and 2.9% per year respectively. These are the highest growth rates in history, and the rates of growth are still increasing. The production of food in Asia, Africa and Latin America has remained approximately constant for the past 3 or 4 years. This situation seems to bear out the Malthusian pessimism after 170 years.

The fact that the stork is winning the race with the plow, and that the famine which we see already in India is predicted to spread throughout the world, makes the problem all the more immediate. Some say that the problem of feeding an overpopulated world will turn out to be the most important single problem of our century.

Alarmists see the famine as a dagger pointed at the heart of the American Society, the American way of life. They do not see how we can long survive as an island of prosperity in a sea of famine and despair. Even conservative Americans are alive to the deep human problem involved in famine and malnutrition, and are concerned over the recent research findings linking malnutrition in preschool children to permanent mental retardation. 

And yet the solution to this problem must come from within, not from the United States. We cannot be the breadbasket of the world. We have heard this many times. If the problem is to be solved, local initiative and self-help must be encouraged. 

DETAILS OF THE PROPOSAL 

What we are proposing is very simple. Indeed it has been put to use by several firms already, and in at least one case, with the assistance of AID. We suggest that the U.S. Government, through the Foreign Assistance Program, assist U.S. investors, including cooperatives, to make investments abroad under an agreement by which they would bind themselves to offer their equity interests for sale to local nationals at an agreed-upon future date. 

The suggested changes in PL 87-195 authorize the President to set aside $75,000,000 in Development Loan Funds, $500,000 in Development Grant Funds, and up to $100,000,000 in Investment Guarantees for use in this program. To be eligible for assistance under this section, the U.S. investor must: 

Agree to invest in programs related to the development of agricultural and marine resources, including those which are basic to the development of the above; 

Be willing to sell or offer for sale his equity interest in the overseas facility after a specified length of time; 

Be willing to accept a price for his equity interest based upon an agreedupon price formula; and 

Have a demonstrated capacity to carry out the proposed project. 

Private industry, under this plan, would be offered long term loans at low interest rates. The amount of the loan could be up to 75% of the dollar requirements of the project. Local currencies can in some instances be made available. We strongly recommend that, at least as far as the American parent company is concerned, these loans should not require the parent company's guarantee, and could be made without recourse.

In addition to the long-term loan, I would urge that tax concessions be offered to the investors by both U.S. and foreign governments. An example of this kind of tax concession is found in the Western Hemisphere Act, under which investments within the Western Hemisphere receive favored treatment. 

The loan could be repaid by the investors under an amortization plan related to earnings. It is possible that 50% of the after-tax profits could be earmarked for amortization of the loan. 

The loan agreement by which the loan funds were provided to the project might be a three or four part agreement as follows:

The investor group would undertake to put up the equity required and to repay the loan; 77-470-67-pt. 6- -7

1967 

The U.S. Government would agree to make a long-term low-interest loan to the investor group;

The local government would agree to convert local currency into dollars according to the amortization schedule; and 

A separate organization, perhaps a local body, or perhaps a bi- or international organization might undertake: 

To enforce fair wages, prices and working conditions in the project; 

To monitor and assist in the development and training of the human resources involved; and 

See to it that the sale to local nationals went off smoothly. 

In some cases this monitoring organization mentioned above could be AID. 

Specific projects in specific countries may want to take advantage of the Joint Commissions on Rural Development, which are bi-national commissions authorized to formulate and carry out rural development programs, and which were authorized under Chapter 7 of PL 87-195 added in 1966. It may be that these 

Joint Commissions, when operating, can assist in identifying and evaluating the feasibility of projects in the rural sector, or can assist in monitoring the agree ment or perhaps arbitrating disputes. Also of assistance in arbitration within its jurisdiction would be the new International Center for the Settlement of Investment Disputes set up at the World Bank. 

We would hope that during the period of time before the sale to local nationals, the wages paid to both blue and white collar workers would contribute to the development of a middle class. This factor will probably be one of the most significant elements in the program. It is not until this class is well-established that we will find significant popular support for free enterprise. Conformity throughout the period to fair wage and price standards is essential to the development of this middle class.

SALE TO LOCAL NATIONALS AFTER 25 YEARS 

When the agreed-upon time arrives for the sale of the productive facilities the question often arises whether or not there will be any local nationals ready to buy. I think the likelihood is that there will be. There are a number of possibilities:

A responsible group of local nationals can refinance the loan with (1) the financial organization that originally backed the venture, or (2) a local financial organization such as a development bank which has access to dollars, or (3) a public international source such as IFC or IDB; 

Local nationals might purchase only enough equity to control the corporation, but not take 100%;

Local nationals might form a corporation and float a share issue either in that capital market or elsewhere; or

U.S. investors might accept bonds issued by the local company in part payment.

The experience in forming the capital of the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank is a case in point. Nigerian law requires that such an institution be 51% owned by Nigerians, yet local Nigerians did not have sufficient capital to purchase this amount of stock. So the International Finance Corporation pur chased 49% and the local Nigerians 2%, with the IFC portion held by them under a trust agreement which stipulated gradual sell-off to local Nigerians. The re maining 49% of the shares were bought by international investment banks and Edge Act companies in New York, London and Paris. 

WILL U.S. INVESTORS ADOPT THIS PLAN? 

We have already begun some preliminary inquiries with responsible U.S. cor. porations to find out whether this approach would be appealing to them, and we are delighted with the response. We think that many firms are going to adopt this technique in order to provide themselves with an outlet for their products in developing market areas, or with a source of supply for an important ingredi ent for their own production process. Other firms will go abroad under this ar rangement because they anticipate making a profit. Still others will catch the vision of the future and see that unless we stimulate free enterprise at the local level abroad, we may place our own system in jeopardy. 

No firm wants to build competitors. Yet after the World War II. we poured millions of dollars into war-torn Europe to help rebuild her industry, and we have enjoyed a tremendous trade and investment boom in this area. I would

1219 also like to point out that the healthy prosperity that Europe has enjoyed since the days of the Marshall Plan is one of the principal reasons why Communism hasn't been able to increase its hold on the minds of Europeans. 

CONCLUSION 

I have been noticing that there is a growing awareness on the part of the American People that we are engaged in a War on Hunger. All those who have had military experience know that a Declaration of War doesn't by any means ensure a victory.

We can win that war only if we trigger the local initiative and energies of the people living in the developing countries themselves. Trying to sustain the world with U.S. surplus production has proved to be an illusion. The possibility that U.S. firms can assist with perpetually-owned direct investments offers only limited hope for progress. What is needed is a program which offers the prospect that free enterprise can indeed be "home-grown."

THE SCHEINFELD "BUILD-SELL" PROPOSAL SOME KEY QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS 

Q. Why do we need a proposal like this? Haven't we enough tools in AID right now?

A. Free enterprise is in trouble in many parts of the world because it is associated with "foreigners" or with the wealthy few. This proposal seeks to enlist the wider involvement of the U.S. private sector as well as stimulate the growth of indigenous free enterprise.

The fact is that AID has the authority to fund projects such as these even now. 

This proposal would give formal recognition to the "build-sell" idea, and would earmark specific funds for use in the effort. This action should give the idea the boost it needs to be a powerful weapon in the war on hunger. 

Q. Is there any evidence that U.S. investors are willing to invest abroad under such an arrangement?

A. Yes. Several firms have already entered into such arrangements. 

Many firms are going to adopt this technique in order to provide themselves with an outlet for their products, or with a source of supply for an important ingredient for their own production process. Other firms will go abroad under this arrangement because they anticipate making a profit. 

Other firms may catch the vision of the future and see that unless we stimulate free enterprise at the local level abroad, we may place our own system in jeopardy.

Q. Wouldn't U.S. firms be building competition for themselves? 

A. The primary purpose of the Build-Sell plan is to encourage investment in developing nations by those U.S. manufacturing firms whose sales, or source of raw material supplies, will be improved by this investment. The plan also is intended to encourage investment by financial interests which seek attractive opportunities for foreign investment under conditions that will prevent or minimize the risk of expropriation or harassment.

Of course, the plan should not be considered as preventing the creation of duplicate and competitive facilities by any U.S. manufacturing firm that wishes to do so, but this would not be its primary thrust. There may be many situations in which the creation by one company of duplicate facilities in a foreign country would offer little or no competition to the domestic plant. 

Q. Why should this "build-sell” proposal be limited to industries related to the development of agricultural and marine resources? 

A. This is a very broad area, and includes industries that are basic to the development of these resources. The reason that this field has been selected is because without a doubt the War on Hunger is the most critical battleground of our time.

Q. What is the profit incentive for U.S. investors to participate in this program? 

A. Assurance of a hospitable environment for their investment. 

A subsidy program in which the U.S. Government would lend a large part (up to 75%) of the dollars required, and also where available, local currency;

1967 

A return of capital, with capital gains, through the sale of the enterprise after a specified number of years using a sales-price formula related to profits; and 

Possibility of continued income through a royalty arrangement. 

Q. Can local citizens from the developing countries participate from the beginning?

A. Certainly. In many countries, local laws require local participation in the equity of the enterprise. 

Q. Why does it make good sense to suggest ownership and control by the parent firm for the first few years?

A. If the parent firm had only a minority of the shares, there may be a lack of control needed to assure good management and thus the success of the enterprise. 

Q. Do you see this plan as a weapon against global communism?

A. Developing countries are casting about for economic and business institutions which can propel them into the Twentieth Century. Private enterprise is losing ground to socialism in many countries because it has not accomplished vital social and economic obectives. This plan could help turn the tide. 

Q. Will it be possible to agree on a sales price!

A. Admittedly, the problem of arriving at a fair valuation is a problem, but no more so than the sale of any business property in this country or elsewhere. 

Q. How is the selling price calculated?

A. The selling price might, for example, be based upon five times the annual profit before taxes averaged over a five year period prior to termination, or book value, whichever is higher.

In addition to the selling price the plan provides for a royalty of from 2% to 5% of sales, depending on the product involved, to be paid for a period of 10 years or longer following the sale of the business. The length of the royalty period would vary depending upon the technical capability of the parent firm and the flow of new ideas relating to the product. 

Q. What happens if at the end of the period there are not enough buyers!

A. Then what can be sold at the agreed-upon price will be sold. The offer for the sale of the remaining equity is then to be made every 5 years thereafter, or at shorter intervals at the option of the seller. 

Q. How will the U.S. investor repatriate his funds!

A. This again, like the calculation of the selling-price, ought to be faced in advance. Present devices for assuring U.S. investors of convertibility may be used here with or without modification.

Add the following language to the existing text: "The Congress specifically recognizes the tremendous threat to world peace and security posed by the existence of famine in the world, and also the need in many countries for a stronger, more broadly-based indigenous private enterprise community. Congress therefore declares that in the administration of programs of assistance under this act emphasis shall be given to programs related to the development of agricultural and marine resources, including those that are basic to the development of the above, which plan from the beginning for eventual ownership of the productive activity by the indigenous private enterprise community, including producer and consumer cooperatives. "Experience has taught that there is a resistance in developing countries to the development of facilities by foreign nationals because of the perpetual foreign ownership of these facilities. Such resistance has manifested itself in some cases in expropriation, harassment and sabotage. It is the intent of Congress that the program provided herein (sections 207, 218 and 225) will help overcome such resistance by affording the nationals of the developing countries an opportunity to acquire permanent ownership of such facilities. It is further the desire of 

Congress that the use of this authority should be extended to U.S. Companies

BIOGRAPHY OF AARON SCHEINFELD, CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD, MANPOWER, INC., PRESIDENT, SALESPOWER DIVISION, CHICAGO, ILL. 

A successful tax and corporation attorney, from 1923 to 1956, Aaron Scheinfeld was co-founder with his law partner, Elmer Winter, of Manpower, Inc., Milwaukee, Wis., the world's largest comprehensive business service and employer of short-term personnel. 

Born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1899, Mr. Scheinfeld holds Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Laws degrees from the University of Wisconsin. He began the practice of law as counsel for a number of insurance companies. In 1936, he and 

Winter formed the law partnership of Scheinfeld and Winter. 

Mr. Scheinfeld serves both as Chairman of the Board of Manpower, Inc. and as President of Salespower, its international marketing division, which provides a broad spectrum of marketing services to a wide variety of clients.

1967 

Manpower's annual dollar volume is currently in excess of $122,000,000. The company operates 530 offices throughout the world, including major cities in Europe, Canada, Asia, Latin America, Africa and Australia. Manpower serves annually more than 150,000 companies and governments, providing over 47,- 000,000 man-hours of employment annually for some 315,000 men and women. 

Mr. Scheinfeld is a member of the national executive committee of the Council for Equal Business Opportunity, Small Business Administration. He also is a founding member of the Center for the Study of Democratic Institutions, Santa Barbara, Calif., and has served as director of many private business corporations. 

Mr. Scheinfeld is a director of the Council for the Study of Mankind; a member of the Population Crisis Committee; a member of the National Foreign

STATEMENT OF W. B. HICKS, JR., EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, LIBERTY LOBBY, WASHINGTON, D.C. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the Committee, the following represents the views of Liberty Lobby's 12.000 member Board of Policy, expressed on behalf of the 170,000 subscribers to our monthly legislative report, Liberty Letter.

Liberty Lobby is strongly opposed to H.R. 7099. This Nation's experience over the past two decades has proven beyond a doubt that the concept of foreign aid is wasteful, unnecessary, and self-defeating. 

The Administration, apparently in the belief that a never-ending outpouring of American wealth can substitute for a meaningful foreign policy, is asking for an additional authorization of almost two billion dollars for fiscal 1968. 

But the American people know better. Senator Fulbright has observed that the people would vote down the foreign aid program if they were given an oppor tunity to do so, which observation could not be disputed by anyone familiar with the current political scene.

For years, we have witnessed astronomical Administration requests for foreign aid funds, followed by lengthy Congressional debate, relatively small reductions, and the waste of billions of dollars of the American taxpayers' money on foreign aid. We believe the time has come to call a halt to this charade. If the 

Congress refuses to authorize any new funds, the Administration will still have at its disposal over $16,000,000 in funds already authorized, according to figures supplied by Rep. Otto Passman. This should be easily sufficient to wind up the program, and will allow our numerous international welfare clients ample notice that the gravy train is coming to the end of its run. 

It is clear that the billions of dollars we have spent on foreign aid during the course of this program have been of little, if any value to the security of the United States. This is so although national security is given as the excuse when irate taxpayers complain of the exorbitant sums being squandered. 

In 1959, President Eisenhower, in a message to Congress attempting to justify foreign aid, stated that as a result of it, "our friends among the free world nations make available to us for use of our forces 250 strategic bases, 5 million ground forces, 30,000 aircraft, and 2,500 vessels." If this rationale had any validity, this would seem to be an appropriate time for us to begin receiving a return on our foreign aid investment. 

But, with Americans dying daily in Vietnam, our grateful aid recipients are conspicuous by their absence. With the honorable exceptions of South Korea and Thailand, the nations which have accepted billions of American dollars refuse to give us any assistance in our bloody war against Communist aggression. And many of them not only refuse their assistance, but actually assist the enemy. Foreign leaders, supposedly made into friends of the United States by large doses of foreign aid, are so strongly opposed to our war effort in Vietnam that many of them actually refuse American soldiers permission to enter their countries on brief "rest and recreation" leave from the Vietnam front lines. 

Burma has received over $95 million in American foreign aid. Our sole return on this investment is U Thant, who has been performing as a virtual Soviet agent, most recently in the Mid-East crisis. Poland and Yugoslavia, both allies of North 

Vietnam have received $3 billion. France, demonstrating its gratitude for $9.438000,000 in American aid, more than has been given to any other country, constantly obstructs our war effort and draws down our gold reserve. North Vietnam could

1223 not survive, if it were not for supplies provided by ships belonging to nations which have been the recipients of our aid. 

At a recent meeting in New Delhi, the leaders of India, Yugoslavia, and the United Arab Republic adopted a manifesto demanding that the United States stop bombing North Vietnam and get out of South Vietnam. Between them, these three nations have been the recipients of almost $11 billion in American foreign aid. It is not clear how much more will be necessary to bring them around to civil behavior, if not friendship, toward the United States. 

Many of our aid recipients not only fail to show gratitude, but also fail to pay their bills to the United States. President Nasser of the United Arab Republic has abusively refused to repay $200 million in debts now owing, but has indicated that he might pay them if we extend him more credit. Since January 1965, when 

Congress refused to cut off aid to Nasser, he has received 83½ million dollars. 

According to reliable figures supplied by Rep. Otto Passman, total disbursements for foreign aid in the twenty year period ending December 31, 1965 amounted to $103 billion, not counting $39 billion in accumulated interest cost. 

Foreign aid thus accounts for a full one-third of our astronomical national debt. 

Rep. Passman estimates that, as of the end of 1966, foreign aid expenditures amounted to more than $152 billion. It is clear that this huge sum has not bought any substantial improvement in our national security, and that further expenditures along the same line will be wasteful and futile. 

The fact that the foreign aid program has failed in its purpose of securing allies and protecting American national security is sufficient reason for its termination. However, it is worth noting that, even from a humanitarian viewpoint, foreign aid has proven to be a total failure. The program has subsidized costly socialistic experiments in nations all over the world, thus retarding the growth of free enterprise and private capital, which is essential if the underdeveloped countries are ever to develop viable economies. India, for example, after receiving $7 billion in foreign aid, is today actually worse off than it was before the program began. The foreign aid program, by encouraging costly socialist industrialization projects, built for prestige rather than economic reasons, at the expense of food production, must share a good deal of the blame for the deplorable conditions existing in India today. 

Much American aid is consumed in wars between our aid recipients, and military and subversive adventures engaged in by them. India and Pakistan have diverted their American aid dollars, provided for defense against Communism and the development of their economies, to fighting each other. Tanzania, the recipient of almost $20 million in American aid, has set itself up as a Chinese Communist base for "wars of liberation" against the anti-Communist nations of 

Southern Africa.

In the Middle East, Israel and the United Arab Republic have each received around $1 billion in American aid, while other nations in the area have received smaller, but substantial sums. This money is used for constant military activity which has so disrupted the stability of the area that, at the present time, active military involvement by the United States is considered a possibility. Yet, as late as April 5 of this year, Secretary McNamara admitted that he was supplying, under the foreign aid program, "certain defensive weapons to selected countries in the area, including Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Jordan." 

It is difficult to understand how organizations and individuals who claim to favor peaceful solutions of international disputes can also favor the continuance of a program which so demonstrably encourages the aggressive ambitions of nations in every part of the world. 

It has been argued that termination of the foreign aid program would aid the Soviet Union by allowing it to step in with its own aid as we step out. The facts prove this contention to be completely without merit. Competent observers have reported the massive failure of the Soviet equivalent of our foreign aid program. The Soviet Union has made its gains throughout the world by subversion, not by giveaways. Indeed, if the Soviet Union were to attempt a massive foreign aid program on the same scale as ours, with the resultant damage to its own economy, the United States could only gain by it.

The claim is that the problem is not a military one but the pacification of and bringing of control and security to the hamlets is the vital area, 1225

1967 

and that we are not achieving success in this area and that this is really the key fact in the national effort at the present time.

STATEMENT OF HON. RUTHERFORD M. POATS, DEPUTY ADMINIS- TRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. POATS. I would like, if I may, to offer the opportunity to add to my comments to Mr. Habib, who has returned from a long period in Vietnam, and to Mr. Steadman or Admiral Heinz. I think all of us would agree that the essential task which has not been adequately performed is the task of village-by-village pacification for the purpose of bringing the village into a relationship of cooperation and mutual benefit with the Government, which essentially means with its district and provincial governments. 

The great limitation on success in that program has been the difficulty of providing adequate, full-time, day-and-night security for the hamlets which are the targets of the systematic program of pacification. The military forces have been strained to carry out other functions. [Security deletion.] There certainly has been weakness in the local leadership; that is to say, the hamlet chiefs have been the regular target of Vietcong assassination and terror in a constant effort over the years to break down local government, so that the leadership potential is thin in the hamlets. 

There were a succession of changes of government during 1963 through the first half of 1965, which stalled pacification. A number of starts, which were disappointing, were made in 1964-65, leading to a fresh start in early 1966 on the present conception. It took a good part of 1966 to get the present revolutionary development scheme well established. It is a conception which attempts to integrate the military, political, psychological, economic and social effort, with the province chief who works under the Minister of Revolutionary Development and tied in with the military authorities combined action plans for each designated hamlet.

By the end of calendar year 1966, 4,400 hamlets were listed by the Vietnamese Government as meeting several criteria which were the tests of whether they were succeeding in bringing about pacification. 

The target for 1967 was set at about an additional 1,100 hamlets to be brought to the status of meeting the criteria. This means that the government in place in the hamlet, having security established, is beginning the processes of rebuilding contact between the villager and his government, providing the basic social services such as schooling, and so on. This program is moving very slowly, partly for the reasons 

I enumerated as being basic to the whole effort and partly because of the difficulty of training cadre, the village workers, to perform this rather subtle task of changing the attitudes of the villagers, assuring them security, bringing about the kind of visible dramatic change that would alter belief in the outcome of the war and make a man willing to stick his neck out and fight for his cause against the kind of nighttime hit-and-run terrorism that the Vietcong have used. Some progress is being made. It is painfully slow.

1227 We have reason to expect during the course of this year that it will pick up momentum. We think the recent elections at the hamlet and village level will have an influence on the relationships of the people to government and the performance of government. 

We think the Chieu Hoi defection rate indicates the Vietcong on their side are having greater difficulty obtaining recruits or keeping recruits and that morale is a serious problem for them. We have reason to hope that the recent assignment accepted by the Army of Vietnam, the assignment of some [security deletion] combat battalions to the village level screening job, supplementing the Popular Forces and Regional Forces will add the kind of military muscle for day-and-night security that have often been lacking in the past. 

This process is moving along. However, it is often interrupted by main force requirements that divert ARVN. It is interrupted in parts of the 1st Corps now up near the DMZ because of the use by the North Vietnamese of major military units to conduct more conventional warfare and to harass and divert forces to defense. 

It is interrupted in parts of the country here and there from time to time because of changes in local leadership. We think the general trend line of applying more military muscle to this village level task is on the up and if we can get higher qualitative levels of actual performance by these security forces, then the program can move more rapidly. 

We think that General Thang, the leader of Revolutionary Development, is a most dynamic, activist leader, a man who has sound ideas and who is out and around every day visiting and correcting and peptalking and carrying on the effort to get the provincial and district level people into the act more effectively. How many additional hamlets will be secured, and whether it will move as fast as we hope and that is a conservative hope-remains to be seen. The reports of the first 3 months this year still show many of the same problems and show a lot of bugs that need to be cleaned out of the rural development cadre teams and how they operate, still show some lack of effectiveness on the part of hamlet chiefs in showing to the people that there is a change in the performance of government. 

We have a long way to go and it is a slow process. May I ask if others would like to add to that?

STATEMENT OF PHILIP HABIB, ACTING DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS 

Mr. HABIB. I would only add one thing to what you said and that is to dramatize for a moment the importance of the security aspect. I think it is related directly to what Congressman Monagan said. To say simply the problem is not a military one does not take into account the funadmental step that we all believe is necessary when we start, and that is the establishment of security, that without the establishment of security the concepts don't get a chance to work. 

In our experience there where security is properly established we have at least demonstrated to ourselves and to the people that the concepts are the correct concepts. At least we have the right kind of an organization, the right kind of personnel, and the right kind of inte-

1967 

gration of American military and civil and Vietnamese military and civil efforts. Our experience demonstrates, therefore, that we can assume the success of the concepts of revolutionary development or pacification provided that the security happens. it?

Mr. MONAGAN. You need more troops to provide the security; is that 

Mr. HABIB. Not necessarily, Mr. Congressman. I think one of the things that we determined early this year was by a restructuring of troops and a training of the troops, by bringing in the ARVN battalions to a closer relationship to local security that you would in effect be able to shift your military stance sufficiently to pay more attention to the development aspect of the problem. That is what Mr. 

Poats meant when he spoke of the assignment of [security deletion] battalions. Those battalions were put through a preliminary training course to reorient them to the requirements of revolutionary development [security deletion] and they are being followed up specifically by the teams as well as the other administrative and social services that the Government provides. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS.  Along the same line of Mr.

Monagan's question, is any real progress being made with respect to curbing thefts and the diversion of supplies? 

Mr. POATS. I think so, Mr. Gross. A number of things have been done. We don't have a new report. We are working on one now to attempt to produce some accurate figures on this matter. We made a study in the latter months of 1966, as you know, which showed that according to our best estimates, and they are nothing more than that at this point, about 5 to 6 percent of economic assistance supplies were either lost, stolen, damaged or diverted from their intended use. Some of this diversion is not entirely a dead loss, of course. It goes into other uses that have some economic benefit, but it is diverted one way or another.

We and the Vietnamese Government have since that time taken a number of additional steps to further tighten up the controls. The 

Vietnamese have a far more active inspection corps now which is out checking commodities. We have more people in the provinces following up on the actual use in village projects and so on. We are putting into our provincial warehouses an American supply clerk to actually handle the checking in and out the documentation. So we will have a paper trail that we can use to audit. We have auditors now out in the regions on a spot basis following up on any discrepancies that we find. 

Mr. GROSS. Does all of this mean a greater diversion of South Vietnamese troops from the battlefronts?

Mr. POATS. No, sir, this is being done by Americans or by third country employees of the AID mission or small groups of inspection teams under the direction of the Minister of Revolutionary Development.

Mr. GROSS. So it is your statement that that theft and the diversion of supplies from their intended use is being curbed; is this your statement?

Mr. POATS. That is my belief on the basis of the actions we have taken and on fragmentary reports. We do not yet have a complete

1229 summary comparable to the one that estimated the loss at 5 or 6 percent to confirm that.

Mr. GROSS. There are reports of inflation again accelerating in Vietnam. Is this true?

Mr. POATS. The rise in prices in Saigon in January and February and again in May is disturbingly high, yes. This is resulting entirely from the pressure on domestic production of rice, pork, charcoal, and chickens. In February there was a sharp increase in rice prices, not entirely an undesirable one I might say, resulting from fear of a shortage, which was actually a false fear, but the stock did get very low. 

The stock is now going up steadily and will be several months supply by the middle of the summer. 

The current price increase in May resulted partly from shortages in the flow of pork and chickens and charcoal to the Saigon market, in turn due partly to the continued withdrawal of Vietnamese from the transportation business and from the wholesaling business in those fields. Of course, this is complicated by the increased buying power in Saigon where you have full employment and a boom situation resulting from this heavy military spending.

STATEMENT OF RICHARD C. STEADMAN, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SEC- RETARY (FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS), OFFICE OF THE ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE FOR INTERNATIONAL SECURITY AFFAIRS 

Mr. STEADMAN. As Admiral Heinz says, the administrative control in the sense of the control of the funding and the administrative work of the ordering, physical ordering, responsibility for shipments, et cetera, will shift into the services. 

Mr. FRASER. Shift into what?

Mr. STEADMAN. The services, service funding. But the control over the size and content of the program will continue to be coordinated by the Office of Assistant Secretary of Defense for International

Security Affairs. He delegates it to me and I coordinate with the State 

Department and AID in the case of Laos and Thailand. 

Mr. FRASER. Suppose the Thai Government, for example, says they want 50 more fighters of some kind. This initially is looked at by the 

MAAG. They make an evaluation of the request and relate it to the other on-going activities. Where does the recommendation go?

Mr. STEADMAN. It will go to CINCPAC who will then forward it to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who will then forward it to us. 

Mr. FRASER. Is that different than it is today?

Mr. STEADMAN. No, it is the same flow today. However, if 50 were approved, Admiral Heinz would be involved in the administration and funding for procurement and the dispatch of these aircraft and

1233 fitting the dollar numbers into the total program sizes and his total 

MAP budget. 

Mr. FRASER. After the change, who will be? 

Mr. STEADMAN. From the money point of view, it will be the services. From the procurement point of view, it will be the services. From the point of view of policy control, it will remain as it is now. 

Mr. FRASER. So the only difference, the only operational difference here is the question of what budget the money is drawn against- Mr. STEADMAN. That is carried. 

Mr. FRASER. And the responsibility for placing the order and seeing that delivery is effected—that is transferred to the services? 

Mr. STEADMAN. Yes, and the ability to expedite from the logistics point of view will be altered. 

Mr. FRASER. Would you explain that one?

Mr. STEADMAN. They will then have the authorization to draw from, if approved, U.S. stocks in-country or in-area. 

Mr. FRASER. Which is authority that is now lacking? 

Mr. STEADMAN. Yes. 

Mr. FRASER. Why is that? 

Mr. STEADMAN. Why is the authority lacking? Because the procurement is done now through the military assistance channel. The material cannot be easily diverted to U.S. use and vice versa. 

Mr. FRASER. Can't you draw on stocks that are available in the area and transfer the necessary credit to the service involved?

Mr. STEADMAN. Let me transfer this back to Admiral Heinz who understands this far better than I do. 

Admiral HEINZ. At the present time the services have no authority to provide military assistance to [security deletion] Thailand. Therefore we have duplicate supply lines: There are U.S. supply lines going out to [security deletion] Thailand for U.S. forces as well as supply lines for MAP supported forces. When the authority is granted for the military departments to provide assistance to these two countries, the supply lines can be combined. Then the logistic processes are simplified. There will no longer be the requirement to keep everything fully separated as it is now. Of course we will still have to keep a record of the assistance provided to these two countries. ISA will still maintain policy control of the assistance that is provided. 

The Department of State will still have the same policy role relative to U.S. assistance but the logistic channel, the handling of supplies and equipment, will be simplified. 

Mr. FRASER. Do I understand what you are saying is that under the way it is presently administered you can draw down on inventories that are in the area that are held by the services? 

Admiral HEINZ. At the present time it is possible to do that if an order is given to the military department from the military assistance program to utilize service stocks. However, stocks are not maintained for the foreign forces by the services. The stocks that are maintained for U.S. forces are only of the size that is required for U.S. forces.

STATEMENT OF SAMUEL D. BERGER, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRE- TARY OF STATE FOR EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS 

Mr. BERGER. The elections are on June 8 for the Assembly. At the present time the Government has 110 members of the Assembly. [Security deletion.] They have a proportional representation bonus which goes to the different parties in terms of the outcome of the election itself.

Mr. DERWINSKI. Will the elections be reasonably free from charges of ballot-box stuffing?

Mr. BERGER. I don't think they will be free of charges. There are a lot of charges being circulated there all the time by the opposition. 

The debate that is taking place and the campaigning are quite free. 

It is reported in the press and quite actively. The charges that are being made against the Government are in many cases pretty strong. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. Both the Japanese Government and the Korean 

Government took a little heat internally when they negotiated their trade agreement. To what extent so far has their trade agreement helped the Korean economy, or has it?

Mr. BERGER. What they negotiated was a settlement of outstanding claims rather than a trade agreement which is a separate part. That settlement called for $300 million in grants over a period of 10 years at the rate of about $30 million a year in settlement of claims as well as $200 million government-to-government grant and $300 million in private loans. This comes to about $80 million a year roughly. 

During the first year they have already drawn on this and are doing quite well. They regarded this settlement as of great importance to 

Korea as well as Japan-to Korea because Japan is a next door neighbor with which they have amicable relations. It is a natural source of trade for them and it is a natural market for them to sell to. 

We always felt that the settlement with Japan was essential for rapid economic progress. We have seen in the last year, as you know, considerable progress in all fields. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. To what extent has the participation of the Korean troops in Vietnam affected the tension with North Koreans; also, has this affected the South Korean economy? I am assuming that we are subsidizing their Vietnam participation, but indirectly does it have any complication?

Mr. BERGER. The Koreans took the position that they wanted to contribute something to Vietnam. It is in their interest, they said, to help defend Vietnam. They felt a moral obligation to repay the assistance that was given them- Mr. DERWINSKI. I am not quarreling with that. I am asking if there has been an adverse effect. 

Mr. BERGER. They take great pride in this step. In terms of adverse effect, I would say none in economic terms. There is very little additional drain on their resources. In terms of the reaction of the North 

Koreans it is quite possible what we are seeing now in these incidents on the DMZ may be an attempt by the North Koreans to unnerve the

1235 South Koreans to make them feel it was a mistake to have sent these troops there.

But it is not having that kind of effect in South Korea. They are well protected by their own forces on the DMZ as well as by ours. It is not having that kind of effect on the people there. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. Are any of you gentlemen, or anyone accompanying you, able to tell us of the inflation problem in North Vietnam as it affects either their rice costs, and to what extent are they suffering, hopefully, from the same effects that we have discussed here in South Vietnam?

Mr. POATS. The North Vietnamese of course have a controlled economy so the market prices don't reveal the degree of shortage of supplies. We do know they have had serious problems of shortage of grains and proteins. We know that they have had problems of movement of goods of course partly because of military action and partly because of a squeeze on POL availabilities in the country and the military demands on them. They do control prices through rationing through a system of neighborhood associations in which the Communist cadres are very active.

They have not had the degree of price instability that you would have in a free market. They have, however, had real shortages which will over time have an effect on morale. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. To what extent is the supply complication in South 

Vietnam being caused by the ability of the Vietcong to intercept shipments on the highways and in effect feed themselves? 

Mr. POATS. We think a good part of the reduction in the flow of rice from the delta area to the deficit areas of Vietnam results from the harassment by Vietcong along the line, harassment by armed Vietcong who make life perilous for the wholesaler and shipper. It has also been caused indirectly by the diversion of barges from the delta rice trade to the more secure trade of working in the port of Saigon where there has been a great demand for increased use of barges to handle the increased flow of goods through that port. 

There has been more serious interdiction of supplies in other parts of the country than in the delta. I recall for example that there have been several occasions when the Vietcong apparently had a policy of trying to starve out provincial towns. This didn't last very long and the South Vietnamese have been able to get out troops and break these blockades.

There was a period of 2 or 3 months when the shipment of vegetables from the Dalat area to Saigon was seriously interrupted and prices shot up during that period. This has subsequently been stopped. 

There is a good story lately on the opening of roads by the United States and Vietnamese and allied military forces. I think nearly 80 percent of the main roads are listed as daylight passable, which is something like twice as good as the situation was over a year ago. 

This should lead to a better flow of goods throughout the country. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. What about the railroad, Mr. Poats?

Mr. POATS. The railroad is not nearly that usable. Only about 400 kilometers are now being operated. Pieces of it are used. You can go some miles north of Saigon. There is a stretch from Dalat that is open, and portions of Qui Nhon, also runs all the way down to Nha Trang, a section around Cam Ranh Bay.

 ESTIMATED COST OF MAINTAINING U.S. FORCES IN KOREA, FISCAL YEAR 1966 

Accounting records are not maintained to reflect total costs on an area basis. 

Therefore, cost estimates are necessarily based upon the use of factors where accounting records do not exist. Utilizing available data, it is estimated that direct budgetary costs of maintaining U.S. Forces in Korea during fiscal year 

1966 was approximately $0.5 billion. This includes the direct costs of military personnel, operation and maintenance and military construction in Korea. Indirect logistic and administrative costs for support from sources outside Korea, and major procurement costs which cannot be reasonably identified with support of forces in Korea are not included in the $0.5 billion estimate.
