Mr. Culver. 

Mr. CULVER. 

Mr. Poats, since 1960, I believe we have had about five different mission directors in our Vietnam AID program. My question is, What efforts have been made within your department to insure a maximum continuity of valuable and useful experience from these changes in administration? It is my impression with each change we come in with a new scheme of operation and concept and I wonder if in each and every situation you have been throwing the baby out with the bath water and in fact starting all over?

Mr. POATS. The changes have been heavy and they have certainly slowed down the process of building on lessons learned. Each of these changes relates to particulars that simply cut across an obviously preferable policy of continuity. We hope we have there now a team of a number of very senior people who will be there for a longer haul. 

The changes that occurred in the past were at times often timed with changes of ambassadors. I hope we have stability there now although

1967 

it is obvious that in the organization to deal with the overall war effort we have had to make, recently, a number of changes of structure within the U.S. establishment which will undoubtedly bring to bear fresh ideas and viewpoints which are different from those of the past with respect to the pacification program. 

Mr. CULVER. Regardless of the justification for periodic change in the administration there which are clearly understandable, my question really goes to the point of whether or not we have any systematic way in your department to isolate those aspects of the pacification experience which have proved to be successful, albeit in a limited way, under previous administrations and are now effectively being cranked into any scheme that we are attempting to implement? For example, there was Gardner in 1960, Brent, 1962, Killen, 1964, Charles Mann, 1965, now Don MacDonald in 1967. What do we have operating today in this new approach that represents previous American experience, at least the limited effort there that proved to be effective and successful, or are we just jettisoning it all?

Mr. POATS. I think the most concrete case I could cite was a meeting in 1966 when we brought together people with great experience in pacification, from Washington agencies and Saigon. Out of this we drew a number of lessons learned. Similar meetings have been held with the Vietnamese who had been involved, particularly people like Colonel Chou, and General Thang. The result was a revised concept and approach of the rural development pacification scheme. Subsequent meetings were held which led to the decision last fall. 

Mr. CULVER. My point is that if you started the effort in 1960 and in 1966 we are having a meeting to try to determine what in the previous 6 years has been useful, and how to incorporate this into a more effective overall scheme we have certainly wasted much valuable time. 

I have talked to people who have served in these mission operations and one of the most frustrating problems over there is that whenever you turn around there is a change of order and a grand scheme. 

I wonder if we are too busy coming up with new ideas and having too little time to implement in a pragmatic way the experience of the past.

Mr. POATS. Yes; I think we have spent more time on planning than on implementation at the highest levels.

Mr. CULVER. About this Vietnam Bureau that Mr. Morse discussed with you briefly. I wonder are you doing a similar thing in the case of Thailand and Laos?

Mr. POATS. No. 

Mr. CULVER. Why not? Mr. POATS. The Vietnam program simply has a much different order of magnitude than the programs in Thailand and Laos. They are more conventional programs. They deal there with a much less fluid situation. You have a much smaller set of problems in commodity flows, logistics, and personnel. 

Mr. CULVER. The problem we are facing in northeast Thailand which by the reports has been deteriorating in the last 6 months, at least the genesis of that type of situation is almost exactly on all fours with the situation in Vietnam. I know one of the things in 

November of 1965, when we visited Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos, that was disturbing was in each of these situations, acknowledging

1241 the uniqueness of the environments, AID mission people trotted out the drawing board as to what their particular pacification plan was in these situations and there did not seem to be any coordination of approach or any similarity of operation. 

It seems to me that given the similarities in these environments and the nature of the problem which we are confronting that it would be very useful to have a far more coordinated and effective approach and program. I wonder if that is now being done before it is too late? 

Mr. POATS. So far as Thailand is concerned, the Ambassador is the coordinator and he is very active in it. His special assistant for counterinsurgency served for several years in Vietnam and is trying to apply those lessons he experienced. 

Mr. CULVER. In the Washington office are we trying to coordinate our experience and trying to develop some continuity for the approach and implementation of our aid effort in Southeast Asia generally speaking to the extent it is valid to do so? 

Mr. POATS. I am sure you appreciate that the problem in Thailand, while it has some worrisome patterns that could suggest a repetition of Vietnam, is quite different from Vietnam in the sense that you do have a long-established central government. You do have much more advanced capacity to communicate, to manage programs in northeast Thailand, than you had in Vietnam.

Mr. CULVER. Those factors you are suggesting do not necessarily mean we should have a different program if we are dealing essentially with the same type of Communist infiltration and insurgency posed in Vietnam.

Mr. POATS. The main thing we are trying to do in northeast Thailand is quite similar in the general sense of what we have been trying to do in the pacification program in Vietnam; that is, improve or strengthen links between the government and the people based on mutual benefit and respect. We have attempted to induce and accelerate the pace of establishing of local government that can function in that way. That is what our program is all about. 

Mr. CULVER. I just wonder whether or not we are using the experience in these other areas as effectively as possible and I have not been convinced we are. Mr. POATS. We do transfer a number of our people from Vietnam to Thailand and Laos. I can cite any number of cases in which this has happened. I mentioned the man in Thailand who is working for the Ambassador. The No. 2 man in our program office in Thailand was formerly in Vietnam.  THE INTERAGENCY REGIONAL GROUP (IRG) 

The President, on March 4, 1966, established a permanent interdepartinental committee, the Senior Interdepartmental Group (SIG), to assist the Secretary of State in the direction and coordination of interdepartmental policy and activities overseas. The Under Secretary of State was designated executive chairman, with authority and responsibility to make final decisions on all matters coming before the committee (subject to the right of any member to appeal his decision to higher authority); regular members of the Senior Interdepartmental Group are the 

Deputy Secretary of Defense, the Administrator for AID, the Director of CIA, the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Director of USIA, and the Special As sistant to the President for National Security Affairs. 

Beneath the Secretary of State and the Senior Interdepartmental Group, the 

President created Interagency Regional Groups for Africa, East Asia, Europe 

Near East-South Asia, and Latin America.

The regional Assistant Secretaries of State, serving as Executive Chairman, occupy focal positions in the channel of responsibility for overall direction, coordination, and supervision of interdepartmental matters in their regions. Other members of the committee are the regional heads from AID, the Defense Department, the CIA, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the USIA and a representative of the 

Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs. The major volume of policy analysis and decisions has been resolved at this level, leaving the Senior Interdepartmental Group only the major problems.

Mr. BUCHANAN.  

Mr. Poats, on April 4 you stated that AID commercial import financing for economic stabilization was expected to decline. You have partially answered this in answer to Mr. Gross.

Mr. POATS. I think we will not have to spend more; but I think there will be a revival of the import licensing demand, largely financed by the Vietnamese National Bank rather than by AID, taking advantage of the Government of Vietnam's growing foreign exchange earnings from the sale of piasters to U.S. military contractors and troops, and so on. The inflation that we discussed a moment ago was, as I noted, primarily on domestic consumable goods. So far as goods imported from abroad are concerned, there has been remarkable price stability since the devaluation last summer. The line is steady. Despite the enormous pressures for inflation in Vietnam, particularly in Saigon, you will note if you look at the chart that the price levels now only are about 30 percent higher than they were last summer, 10 months ago. That is inflation.

But it is nothing like the 2,400-percent inflation we had in the Korean war.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Hamilton. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Poats, I have been reading some newspaper articles that disturb me a great deal about the pacification program. 

A Christian Science Monitor reporter not long ago came back and said the pacification program was about to collapse. The New York 

Times had an article in which it said it was in trouble. 

Your response a while ago in response to questions was not too optimistic. You said some progress had been made. You also mentioned it had been reorganized in early 1966. If that is correct, shouldn't we be seeing some real progress about now?

Mr. POATS. I expected more progress than we have seen. I thought that the targets that General Thang developed with help from our people from several Government agencies-not just AID, of course-

1967 

was rather conservative for 1966. Then came the Buddhist struggle movement in the I Corps which set the program back in that area. 

Then came some problems of properly indoctrinating the province chiefs and district chiefs to effectively use the rural development and cadre, and a number of other problems. I mentioned the security problem which is basic and continues. These have slowed it down. 

One test of how it is doing, I would suppose, would be the cases in which elections could be held securely and with a big turnout. This spring there were or will soon be elections in 4,612 hamlets and 984 village council elections. In the summer and fall they are scheduled to have more, both in villages and hamlets, raising the total numbers in each case of elected governments to just about half of the total throughout the country, or over 1,200 villages and over 6,000 hamlets. 

Mr. HAMILTON. You mention that we expected to pacify 1,100 villages in 1967.

Mr. POATS. Hamlets. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Are we on target? How many have we actually pacified in 1967?

Mr. POATS. We are behind target. I don't have the figures. 

Mr. HAMILTON. How far behind are we?

Mr. POATS. One of the difficulties in answering is that we have not been satisfied with the present reporting system. We have tried-here again when I say "we" I mean the whole U.S. Establishment which is now for this purpose headed by General Westmoreland-and have tried to establish a hamlet evaluation reporting system which would be more objective, answering for each of six categories a number of specific criteria questions.

This is being done by the MACV subsector people in each district. 

The first reports showed a lot of bugs in the system, and a lot of subjectivity in one part of the country to another. They are trying to fix that now.

At the moment we don't have a report that can be racked up against the Vietnamese figures to see how well we actually are doing. We should have it this month, I think. 

Mr. HAMILTON. If you are not able to tell us how many villages or hamlets have been pacified since the beginning of this year- Mr. POATS. The best I can say is that at the beginning of the year there were 4,400 hamlets listed as meeting the rural development criteria. Elections were held in April through early June in 4,600. 

Whether the increase of 200 is a useful figure, I am not sure. 

Mr. HAMILTON. It wouldn't be greater than that, surely. 

Mr. POATS. I think you are right. I think it would not be greater than that.

Mr. HAMILTON. That means at best you have pacified 200 with a target of 1,100 this year. We are now five-twelfths in the year, so we are substantially behind target. 

Mr. POATS. There is great dependence upon the application of military resources for security, which is just coming on the line in May, with these ARVN battalions going into position. We also have an increase in the revolutionary development worker teams. They number about 30,000, organized in 500 teams going up to 800 teams by the end of the year. You will have an increasing capacity to produce results as

1245 the year progresses. We didn't expect to be at the halfway point at the middle of the year- Mr. HAMILTON. What is the practical effect now of the military taking over the pacification program? What changes does that bring about?

Mr. POATS. The practical immediate effect was to consolidate responsibility at the province, region, and Saigon level for both the military and civil sides of the job of advice and support by the Americans. It had no effect on the Vietnamese organization at all. It did not change the expected involvement of Americans or relationships between the Americans and the Vietnamese. It did not imply putting 

American troops into the job of pacification in the military screening sense any more than they have been. It did imply an effort to get more effective performance and a larger proportion of Vietnamese military resources to the pacification job. The method of going about this was to place responsibility for the success of the Vietnamese pacification effort to the extent that advisers and supporters can take that responsibility-in the U.S. corps commanders and through them and below them consolidated, combined military-civil units at province and district.

At Saigon there is added to the scheme Ambassador Komer as a deputy to General Westmoreland, and working full time on this problem of coordination, maximizing of the U.S. supporting effort in pacification. All of this, of course, is under Ambassador Bunker's direction.

We expect to see requirements for additional U.S. personnel at the lower echelons-more intense U.S. presence to be sure that things get done more rapidly at the province and district levels. We expect some of the new personnel will be supplied by the civilian agencies and some by the military. We don't expect any radical change in the program, or the doctrine, but a much closer coordination of militarycivil views and actions, perhaps some increase in the use of military resources for logistics in support of pacification and certainly more effective advisory and training work under General Abrams' direction in the use of the ARVN in pacification.

Mr. HAMILTON. I take it you wouldn't agree with any characterization of the pacification program that it was "in trouble" or "near collapse"?

Mr. POATS. Not near collapse. It is in trouble in that in any reasonable time frame of U.S. involvement in Vietnam pacification is the most worrisome in its slowness.

Mr. TAFT. Are U.S. agricultural advisers able to work effectively with the South Vietnamese considering the differences in their agriculture and our own and language differences, and might it not be helpful or are we bringing in advisers from other less developed countries?

Mr. POATS. We are doing both. We have 80 people from the Joint 

Commission for Rural Reconstruction of Taiwan in the agricultural program and have just signed a contract for 60 more to work in demonstration rice farming. The Americans have worked out remarkably well. They have to work through interpreters in some cases although we are giving them a short language training program. We have combined a language and tropical agriculture training program down at the University of Florida which has been turning out about 20 percent of agricultural extension people who go out and serve in the provinces. We borrowed people from the U.S. military who have had agricultural backgrounds and agriculture college degrees and even without language training they have done remarkably well.

Vietnam? I know this probably isn't in your area again.

That, of course, goes into foods that are acceptable to their diet. There is no indication that they will not be able to get the supplies of rice and other food grains that are required. Mr. HABIB. Yes.

Mr. POATS. They have had temporary shortages in some cities. 

Mr. HABIB. They have been shifting their diet. We know the ration of rice has been cut and they substitute wheat grains. 

Mr. ADAIR. Mr. Chairman. Mr. POATS. Yes, we have a contract arrangement on co-ops which does include what we call participant training with co-ops here in the United States but a bigger group of trainees in the agriculture field are agricultural employees who come here for a period of longer study in the universities.

Mr. ADAIR. Has that type of program been successful, in your opinion? Or is it too early to form an opinion?

1249 Mr. POATS. We can cite large membership in Vietnamese agricultural cooperatives, farmers associations and 4-H type clubs. But the co-ops have been starved for adequate funds; they have not had the kind of business management that they have had in Taiwan. They have had to take on emergency jobs of distributing seeds and fertilizer, and so on, diverting them from their usual type of function. 

They have new co-ops in the rural electric field now; new or expanded co-ops in the fisheries field; by numbers an impressive array of cooperative institutions. I think they need a great deal of strengthening. They need to have a ready source of low-cost capital loans. Of course, they need stability.

Korea. Could you give us a little more specific information? How is that $34 million being expended?

Mr. POATS. About $11 or $12 million is for distribution line extensions transmitting the Korea electric power system to more areas of the country. The balance is for the Yungnam powerplant which was in the book set for $22 million but is now reduced to $17.5 million. Mr. ADAIR. Now just to choose an item somewhat at random from the proposals, you propose about $20 million. I believe, for petrochemical loans out of the development loan fund?

1251 Mr. POATS. I don't think it will be that high. The program book was made up in January. The present outlook, I believe, is that there will be a smaller expansion of petrochemical borrowing from the United States than we predicted at that time. On the other hand, there is likely to be a larger demand for power, transportation, some other fields, and for small industries. The loans running through the Korean intermediate credit institutions, the KRB, and MIB, are moving more rapidly than we figured. These are for small industry projects, expansion of industry. We have advisers in those banks who are checking the loans they make with our funds. 

Mr. ADAIR. These are AID loans. How will they be made?

Mr. POATS. They are made to the Korean Government for relending to these two institutions on long term by us to the Korean Government and on intermediate terms by the Korean Government to these banks. The banks make the loans on terms appropriate to the project, on terms more favorable to the borrower than the commercial banks. 

Mr. ADAIR. We supply dollars?

Mr. POATS. We supply dollar letters of credit against tranches of these loans. The bank makes a subloan, as we call it, to a Korea private entrepreneur.

Mr. ADAIR. At what rate of interest is this package loan made? 

Mr. POATS. It has three steps. Our loan is made to the Korean Government as a whole on 40-year terms. The Korean Government reloans to the KRB for a 15-year term, at 5 percent. The KRB in turn makes loans to specific projects at 8 percent with maintenance of value. 

Mr. ADAIR. What interest does the Korean Government pay?

Mr. POATS. One percent during the grace period and 22 percent thereafter.

Mr. ADAIR. I thought you said the terms of the intermediate institution were a little more liberal?

Mr. POATS. They are 5 percent to the KRB-the bank gets a faster turnover of its capital. When the bank pays this loan back to the 

Government the payments go into a capital account for financing other industrial development in this same way. 

The Korean Government also loans won to these banks for their capital. Then the Korean bank, the KRB or MIB, makes a loan to the 

Korean company at terms more liberal than commercial banks which are 22 percent, I believe, basic interest. They make them at 8 to 12 percent, normally to a Korean business. 

Mr. ADAIR. The interest keeps escalating?

Mr. POATS. Yes; it is still well below the commercial rate in the country. So it is a favored instrument.

Mr. Ives tells me the commercial rate now is 26 percent from the commercial banks and no long term. This provides a long-term facility at what for Korea is liberal terms of lending. The profit differential between these long aid terms and the shorter terms charged by the KRB and MIB go into capitalizing these banks on the won side of their accounts. 

Mr. ADAIR. What is the $15 million program loan?

Mr. POATS. We made a program loan at the beginning of this fiscal year of $15 million to furnish primarily industrial raw materials and some spare parts for Korean industry.

1967 Mr. ADAIR. Purchased where? 

Mr. POATS. In the United States entirely. This is similar, you see, to the supporting assistance. What we are doing is phasing out grant supporting assistance and substituting on a smaller order of magnitude [security deletion] of program lending. This program loan is part of our package which includes supporting assistance and Public Law 480 under which we negotiate the annual stabilization agreement with the Korean Government, in which they set certain targets for themselves, and it becomes part of our international contract with them. When they do not meet any of the targets we reduce the amount of our loan. We cut off $22 million of this $15 million program loan the first of this year because they did not meet one of the quantified targets of the stabilization program. In this way we build discipline into the system of carrying out this orderly stabilization development scheme.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

DEPARTMENT OF STATE, 

Washington, June 2, 1967. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: Some of the testimony before your Committee on this year's Foreign Assistance Act called into question the present structure of the foreign aid program on the grounds that it has an adverse effect on the U.S. balance of payments and recommended certain changes in the Foreign Assist ance Act. I thought it would be helpful to provide you with my views on this testimony for use during the Committee's deliberation on the Bill, or for inser tion into the record if you so desire. 

There is nothing unique about the effect of foreign aid on the balance of pay ments. If one wishes to characterize a transaction which increases foreigners' claims on United States resources as having an "adverse" effect, then United States private foreign investments, United States imports, expenditures of United States tourists abroad, in short anything that leads to an outflow of funds, also has an "adverse" effect on the balance of payments. 

Just as American business firms invest in factories abroad to enhance the enomic development of the foreign country while at the same time seeking to increase the income of their stockholders and employees, the American people are investing in the political and economic development of the less-developed countries through U.S. foreign aid expenditures. Both foreign investment and foreign aid lead to an outflow in the U.S. balance of payments. Both serve highpriority national objectives. That is why instead of cutting off United States foreign investment by imposing direct controls on capital movements the Gov

1253 ernment issued guidelines for a program of voluntary restraint on such investments. These guidelines have not eliminated the short-run "adverse" impact of foreign investment on the balance of payments but this short-run cost is considered to be outweighed by the benefits of preserving the freedom of American capital to seek profitable investment opportunities abroad. 

Similarly, we have restricted the less-developed countries' ability to use United States aid dollars by tying them to United States exports. Some "substitution" may take place (depending on what one considers a "normal" United States market share), although it is very difficult to demonstrate this in Latin America. Even if it could be demonstrated, however, the net outflow of funds which might be involved would be in the national interest if it meant achieving our foreign assistance goals. Proposals to restrict our loans to the dollar-cost of projects or other forms of super-tying would so diminish our ability to do our job as to spell failure for the foreign aid program. 

In any event, I believe that in the case of Latin America it can be demonstrated that U.S. assistance has not had an adverse effect on the U.S. balance of payments in recent years. The United States supplies 43 percent of the market in Latin America. Furthermore, it is necessary to realize that in recent years the 

United States has been earning healthy balance of payments surpluses with Latin America. During the period of the Alliance for Progress our balance of payments with Latin America has steadily improved from a deficit of $296 million in 1960 to surpluses of $170 million in 1965 and $361 million in 1966. 

Enclosed is a paper which sets forth our views on the balance of payments effect of U.S. assistance to Latin America. One of the witnesses before your 

Committee who appears to disagree with our analysis was Mr. N. R. Danielian, President of the International Economic Policy Association. I am also enclosing a statement which is a further discussion of the specific points which he raised in his testimony.

If you or the Committee require further assistance, I am sure that my successor will be glad to help. 

Sincerely yours,

LINCOLN GORDON, 

Assistant Secretary. 

(Enclosures 1. Paper, "U.S. Economic Assistance to Latin America and the U.S. Balance of Payments"; 2. Paper, "Comments on the Effects of Foreign Aid on U.S. Balance of Payments and Export Trade.") U.S. ECONOMIO ASSISTANCE TO LATIN AMERICA AND THE U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS 

1. This memorandum examines some questions relating to the proposal to increase U.S. financial support of Latin American efforts at development and economic integration. 

2. U.S. foreign aid disbursements could have a negative impact on the U.S. balance of payments if U.S. aid leaks away from the recipients to the surplus countries in Europe and to Japan or, more specifically, if U.S. aid merely substitutes for dollars which would normally be spent for U.S. exports and which are thus freed to pay for imports from third countries. 

3. In the case of Latin America, neither of these concerns is borne out by an examination of the data for recent years since aid-tying procedures have become more effective. 

4. An examination of the data indicates Latin America has not been using 

U.S. assistance and other earnings in the United States to finance net purchases or to service debt in other industrialized countries. 

5. Rather the data suggest that for three of the last four years Latin America has earned apparent surpluses with Europe and Japan; moreover in 1965 and 

1966, Latin America (including the IDB) has been in deficit with the United States (on the liquidity definition of the U.S. balance). 

6. In spite of a substantial increase in its total foreign exchange reserves in recent years, Latin America's holdings of gold have declined by $435 million since 1961. 

7. Since the beginning (1961) of the Alliance for Progress, the U.S. share of the Latin American market declined initially, but has subsequently been maintained, even when that market is defined to exclude imports financed by U.S. aid. 

Similar trends are apparent in those countries in which U.S. assistance is high.

1967 

8. Improved techniques for utilizing AID dollars which were put into effect by the largest aid recipients during the last two years appear to be helping to increase the U.S. market share in those countries. 

9. Judged by this recent experience, it should be possible to provide further 

U.S. economic assistance to Latin America in such a way as to safeguard the U.S. balance of payments. 

OVERALL BALANCE OF PAYMENTS WITH LATIN AMERICA 

10. The general concern that U.S. assistance leaks to other industrialized countries reflects an assumption that the less developed countries run a payments deficit with Europe and a payments surplus with the U.S. In Latin America. however, the trend in recent years has apparently been in the opposite direction: there has been an improvement in the U.S. balance of payments position on recorded transactions with the Latin American Republics (including the IDB). 

The U.S. deficits with Latin America declined from 1961 to 1964 and moved into surpluses in 1965 and 1966. This improvement and surplus accrued in a period of sharply increasing disbursements of AID assistance. At the same time, there was a marked improvement in Latin America's payments position with the rest of the world. Beginning in 1963 Latin America has gained substantial foreign exchange reserves through transactions other than those with the United States. Latin 

America earned large trade surpluses with Europe and Japan from 1962–65. Latin 

America, unlike Europe, has not been converting its increased dollar holdings into gold. In fact, since 1961, Latin America has sold $435 million worth of gold, with $200 million of the decline in the period since December 1962 when dollar holdings have been increasing. 

THE U.S. SHARE OF THE LATIN AMERICAN MARKET 

11. Of particular interest in considering the effects of aid to Latin America on the U.S. balance of payments is the United States share of Latin America's imports. During the Alliance for Progress, the U.S. share of the Latin American market initially fell, but has been relatively stable since 1961. However, to deter. mine whether a substitution of AID dollars for free dollars is actually taking place, we have prepared a statistical study which shows the year-to-year trend in the U.S. share of Latin American imports not financed by U.S. assistance. If imports financed by U.S. assistance dollars were substituting for "commercial" imports from the United States, the U.S. share of this residual market would decline. The data show that, after falling in the first year of the Alliance for 

Progress, the U.S. share of the non-aid-financed market was maintained throughout the period 1961-66 at about 38-39 per cent. The data also show that the U.S. share of the import market supplied by the industrialized countries (i.e., exclud ing the effect of intra-Latin American trade) after an initial fall, has improved slightly, rising from an average of about 48 per cent in 1961-64 to about 49 per cent in 1965-66. 

12. In countries which have received relatively large amounts of U.S. assistance-Brazil, Chile, and Colombia-the U.S. share of the non-aid-financed market has followed the same general pattern as in Latin America as a whole. Since the beginning of 1965, the State, Commerce, and Treasury Departments have worked together in developing significant innovations in the use of the AID dollars made available to these three countries to facilitate U.S. exports. The results of these measures are encouraging. The United States share of the market supplied by the industrialized countries in Brazil, Chile, and Colombia has increased from an average of 37 per cent in 1961-64 to 42 per cent in 1965-1966. 

AID PROGRAMS IN LATIN AMERICA AND THE U.S. BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS POSITION 

1. Some observers have suggested that there may be considerable scope for reducing the overall U.S. balance of payments deficit by reducing an assumed leakage of dollars to surplus countries through U.S. foreign aid disbursement. 

This suggestion reflects an assumption that the less developed areas run a payments deficit with Europe and a payments surplus with the U.S., taking into account U.S. aid flows. 

2. The principal purpose of this memorandum is to consider the validity of this concern in the specific case of U.S. AID assistance to Latin America by examining the balance of payments position of the Latin American Republics. 

The general conclusion is that Latin America is not a problem area in this regard.

1255 3. In the absence of regional payments statistics for Latin America (including the IDB), we have used Commerce Department data on the U.S. balance of payments and changes in Latin American gold and dollar holdings (Table 1). These data indicate that in recent years Latin America has had a liquidity payments deficit with the U.S. and an apparent payments surplus with other areas and international institutions. Thus, there has been a steady improvement in the 

U.S. balance of payments position with the Latin American Republics from a liquid deficit of $296 million in 1960 to surpluses of $170 million in 1965 and $361 million in 1966. This improvement and surplus, of course, occurred in a period of increasing AID disbursements. On the other hand, there was an apparent sharp improvement in Latin America's payments position with the rest of the world during this period. Since 1962, Latin America has gained $1,357 million in gold and dollars through transactions other than those recorded with the U.S., while it had lost $863 million through such transactions in the 

1960-1962 period. 

4. Part of the dollars earned by Latin America in third areas are in payment for Venezuelan crude exported to the Netherlands Antilles where it is refined and exported to the U.S. Such Venezuelan exports, estimated to have amounted to about $200 million per year, could be attributed to the U.S. balance of payments with Latin America. Such an attribution would leave $550 million of the increase due to surpluses with the rest of the world. 

5. These apparent payments surpluses with the rest of the world in turn reflect a drastic shift in Latin America's trading position with Europe and Japan. Table 2 shows that Latin America's trade accounts with these areas moved into surplus in 1962 and since then have stayed in surplus. Indeed, Latin 

America's imports from Europe and Japan were little larger in 1965 than in 1961, while its exports to Europe and Japan increased by one-third. 

6. This Latin American accumulation of gold and dollars since 1962 has not been used to convert dollar holdings into gold. In fact, Latin America's gold holdings have declined by $435 million since 1961, with $200 million of the decline in the period since December 1962 when dollar holdings have been increasing.

THE U.S. SHARE OF THE LATIN AMERICAN MARKET 

Of particular interest in considering the effect of aid to Latin America on the U.S. balance of payments is the United States' share of Latin America's imports. U.S. foreign aid disbursements might have a negative impact on our b/p if our aid does not contribute to increasing our exports to Latin America, i.e. if it "substitutes" for commercial purchases in the United States. The U.S. share of Latin America's total imports has been maintained in the range 43%- 45% since 1960. At the same time, the U.S. share of Latin America's imports from industrialized countries has fluctuated between 51 and 55%. This record has been realized during a period of growth of intra-Latin American trade, fostered by the integration process under way. 

The next question to be examined is whether there is any so-called "substitution" of aid dollars and if so whether it is significant. To determine whether substitution of AID dollars for free dollars actually takes place, we have prepared the attached statistical study which shows the year-to-year trend in the U.S. share of Latin American imports whose financing cannot be attributed to 

U.S. assistance. If imports financed by U.S. assistance dollars were substituting for "normal" or "commercial" imports from the United States, the U.S. share of this residual market would decline. To make a fully accurate comparison assistance from Europe and Japan should also be deducted, but such data are not available. Moreover, trade is subject to a wide variety of influences; one cannot assume that the U.S. share in the market in any one period would have been maintained in subsequent periods even in the absence of foreign aid. 

The data show that prior to the onset of the Alliance for Progress, there had in fact been a decline in the U.S. share of the Latin American market not financed by U.S. aid. An increase between 1960 and 1961 of $481 million in all forms of U.S. Government assistance to Latin America was associated with a drop in the U.S. share of the non-aid-financed market from 43% in 1960 to 38% in 1961. There was an absolute drop of $453 million in non-aid-financed imports from the United States. About 55% of the increase in U.S. aid between the two years was accounted for by Eximbank disbursements. 

The data show that, after falling in 1961, the U.S. share of the non-aidfinanced market was maintained throughout the period 1961-1966 at about 3839%. This maintenance of the U.S. share is all the more encouraging when it is considered that it occurred during a period when Eximbank loans—which provide credits to the ultimate purchaser of U.S. goods-were declining sharply and there was an increase in other forms of U.S. assistance. 

Data also has been prepared with respect to the U.S. share of the import market supplied by the industrialized countries. The U.S. share of this market has shown significant improvement, rising from an average of about 48% in 1961-64 to about 49% in 1965–66. The distinction between the industrial countries' import market and the total market is of interest in assessing the U.S. position because (a) these countries are our principal competitors, most of our balance of payments problem is with these countries, and we look to these countries to do more to assist the LDC's, and (b) as is to be expected as the process of integration unfolds, intra-Latin American trade has been increasing faster than the area's total imports in recent years.

1257 

THE U.S. SHARE IN INDIVIDUAL COUNTRIES 

It is legitimate to inquire how the U.S. share has fared in countries which have received relatively large amounts of U.S. assistance. Brazil, Chile, and 

Colombia have received over 50% of disbursements of U.S. economic assistance to Latin America during the past six years. The U.S. share of the market in these three countries has followed the same general pattern as Latin America as a whole. While in these countries the decline in the U.S. market-share between 1960 and 1961 was more pronounced, since 1961 the tendency has been for the U.S. share of total imports to remain within a relatively narrow range. 

In the last two years the U.S.'s competitive position in these countries has improved at the expense of Europe and Japan (see table below). This has been a period, it should be noted, in which the bulk of U.S. assistance has been in the form of program loans. 

Since the beginning of 1965, the State, Commerce, and Treasury Departments have worked together in developing significant innovations in the use of the AID dollars made available to these three countries to facilitate U.S. exports. The governments have conceded substantial cost advantages to selected commodity imports financed by AID dollars, such as the waiver of certain surcharges. Also, arrangements have been made to extend bank credit directly to the importer on favorable terms.

The results of these measures are encouraging. For the last two years, the increase in the U.S. share of the total import market supplied by the industrialized world in these three countries has been as follows: Brazil. Chile.

COMMENTS ON THE EFFECTS OF FOREIGN AID ON U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS, EXPORT TRADE, AND THE PROMOTION OF PRIVATE ENTERPRISE IN LATIN AMERICA BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

1. The statement is made that the United States has been in balance or surplus with Europe in recent years, but in deficit in its recorded transactions with Asia, Africa, South America, and international institutions. 

First, regarding the U.S. balance vis-a-vis Western Europe, it should be noted that the usual way of looking at the U.S. balance of payments by area is to consider the industrialized countries as a unit, and therefore to combine Japan with Western Europe. Our balance of payments with Western Europe and Japan¹ for the past four years has been as follows:

Western Europe and Japan... 

Total balance-of-payments deficit. 

[In millions of dollars] 1963 1964 1965 1966 -777 -2, 670 -956 -2,798 -462 -737 -1,337 -1,424 As we can see from the table, Western Europe and Japan accounted for half the deficit in 1966. Moreover, if we accept Dr. Danielian's point of view that the balance of payments deficit should include the proceeds from the sale 1 Defined as increases in foreign gold reserves and liquid dollar holdings through known transactions with U.S. (Table 9. Survey of Current Business, June 1966 and March 1967.)

1967 

of medium term U.S. Government securities to foreign governments and debt prepayments of foreign governments, the U.S. deficit with Western Europe and 

Japan becomes: 

19631964. 1965. 1966. Millions -$992 -959 -643 -1, 114 In contrast, the U.S. balance of payments with Latin America on recorded transactions has steadily improved, from a deficit of $296 million in 1960 to sizable surpluses in 1965 and 1966. Even when allowance is made for the 

Venezuelan crude content of U.S. petroleum imports from the Netherlands 

Antilles, the trend was the same and the U.S. was in surplus with Latin 

America during the two-year period of 1965-66. This improvement in the U.S. balance of payments position vis-a-vis Latin America took place during a period of increasing AID disbursements. 

On the other hand there was a sharp improvement in Latin America's payments position with the rest of the world during this period. Since 1962, Latin America has gained $1,357 million in gold and dollars through transactions other than those recorded with the U.S.

These surpluses with the rest of the world reflect a dramatic shift in Latin America's trading position with Europe and Japan. Since 1962 Latin America has had substantial trade surpluses with those areas. 

Latin America, unlike Europe and Japan, has not been converting its increased dollar holdings into gold. In fact, Latin America's gold holdings have declined by $435 million since 1961, with $200 million of the decline in the period since December 1962 when its dollar holdings have been increasing. 

2. Program Loans and Substitution.-The allegation is made that because program loans are available for general imports while project loans finance specific capital projects, there is a vast field for "substitution" under program lending which could be eliminated if loans were made only for the dollar costs of projects. 

In fact, program loans have been used in Latin America to improve the competitive position of U.S. exports. Over the past two years, techniques have been employed in Brazil, Chile, and Colombia to obtain cost advantages for U.S. exports financed by the program loans to these countries. This has been achieved by a number of methods, including exempting AID-financed imports from import surcharges and prior import deposits, extending short-term credit to importers of AID-financed goods, the liberalization of import restrictions, and use of positive lists of commodities elegible for AID-financing. These efforts appear to be having the desired results. The United States share of the market supplied by the industrialized countries-exclusive of imports which could be attributed to U.S. aid financing-rose from an average of 37 percent in 1961-64 to 42 percent in 1965-66. 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE AND U.S. TRADE 

Comparing the U.S. trade surplus with each less-developed country and the amount of aid to each country does not provide a meaningful answer to the bal ance-of-payments effect of aid. In the first place, our historic, private enterprise policies have been aimed at promoting the maximum degree of multilateralism in our trading and payments relationships on the sound principle that by multilateralism we get the maximum economic benefits from our foreign transactions, while bilateralism constricts trade and the benefits to be derived from it. 

The cost-of-aid analysis in the Danielian testimony is valid only if one accepts a shaky premise that the U.S. share of the Latin American market which ob tained in 1955-1960 would have been maintained into the indefinite future. Such an assumption flies in the face of experience and common sense. Trade patterns are subject to the myriad influences characteristic of the marketplace-competi tive pricing and quality, changes in tastes, aggressiveness of sales, credit terms, to mention a few. The Danielian testimony ignores the effect of the resurgence of the economies of Western Europe in the late fifties as a result of European reconstruction and the formation of the Common Market and the similar recovery and expansion of the Japanese economy. Thus, whereas the Danielian paper seems to argue that U.S. aid made possible the increase in the market share going to other areas, one could more easily argue that the flow of U.S. assistance

1263 prevented a worse erosion of the U.S. share. Neither conclusion, however, can be adduced without a detailed examination almost product-by-product and market-by-market of the various factors which affected the U.S. competitive position in the market.

In the meantime, the Agency cannot accept the Danielian hypothesis about extrapolated market-shares-and if the extrapolations are in question then tables 10 to 12 in the testimony, which purport to measure the "balance of payments cost of aid," are also questionable.

A more plausible explanation for the lower U.S. share in 1961-65 than in 

1956-60 is that this was a decline that had been in progress during the latter half of the fifties, reflecting the increasing competitive position of Europe and Japan. 

In fact, since the Alliance for Progress has gotten under way the U.S. share has been maintained at about 43 percent for the past six years. This is during a time when disbursements of AID loan assistance 2 and P.L. 480 sales has grown from $136 million (1961) to $672 million (1966). Where is the alleged substitution?

Even more striking is the performance of the U.S. in comparison to its principal industrial competitors in Europe and Japan. The U.S. share of the Latin 

American market supplied by industrial countries has actually risen from 52 percent in 1961-62 to 54 percent in 1965–66 (or from 51 percent to 53 percent if P.L. 480 sales are excluded). And even when U.S. assistance is deducted from total imports in order to measure the market share which cannot be attributed to U.S. assistance, the U.S. share rises from 47 percent in 1961-62 to about 49 percent in 1965–66.

Obviously, what has happened since the advent of the Alliance for Progress is that an increasing share of the Latin American market is going to intra-Latin trade, i.e., trade among the Latins themselves. The other side of the coin in this process is that the industrial countries' share has declined. But-and this is the important point-the U.S. has been able to protect its share and even increase it at the expense of the other industrial countries. 

OTHER COMMENTS ON MR. DANIELIAN'S RECOMMENDATIONS 

While the recommendations seem to have been stimulated by the desire to mitigate the effect of aid on the U.S. balance of payments, they also reflect concern about other aspects of program loans and about private enterprise promotion.

Program Loans.-Recommendation 8 proposes "that the U.S. aid program be reoriented from the existing line-of-credit basis to provide real resources-U.S. goods and technical services-for specific projects. 'Program' loans should be given only in emergency situations and not on a regular basis, and they should be taken out of the category of 'Development Loans' and placed in the President's contingency fund, which should be increased accordingly." 

Many points can be made about this recommendation, all of them leading to the conclusion that the proposed system would be unworkable: a) countries need capital and foreign exchange in a variety of forms to support their overall development efforts. Not all desirable activity can be translated into identifiable projects to be financed by external aid agencies. Much development, especially in the private sector, consists of numerous small investment not authorized or otherwise controlled by any public authority. To treat each of these as a project, and to apply the control procedures the external aid agencies have set up, would make an extremely unwieldly system. The foreign exchange provided by program loans and local-cost financing supplies immediately and directly those very imports needed by the private sector, and because of this, can give much greater stimulus to private sector development than dollar project loans; b) the goods and services supplied for investment are only one side of the foreign-aid coin. On the other side are the improvements in host country policies supported by the foreign aid. We find we can promote development more effectively by supporting country development policies and programs with overall and sector program loans than we can in providing funds to specific projects. 

Much of this direct support for effective country policies-including those that 2 We exclude grant and technical assistance from our studies on the basis that these funds largely purchase U.S. services that would not have been used in the absence of the technical assistance projects. 93

1967 

are crucial to the encouragement of private investment-would be lost if we were restricted to project loans only; c) the especially heavy need for institutional reform and development through agriculture and education projects (where local currency costs often predomi nate) makes participation of the foreign aid agencies in these areas particularly necessary, and sector loans often the most effective method; d) restricting non-project aid to the contingency fund category would create the erroneous impression that the primary function of non-project aid was to serve emergency or stop-gap needs. 

Aiding the Private Sector.-Recommendation 2 proposes "that Congress make clear that those provisions of Sections 202 and 252 which require that 50 per centum of the funds provided for Development Loans and the Alliance for Progress be used to encourage development through private enterprise must be used directly and exclusively for such purposes.” 

All our experience points to the conclusion that it is not economically or institutionally feasible to put half our aid funds directly into private enterprise investment. The aided countries need many other things besides industrial or commercial investment. The lack of basic infrastructure both physical-as in roads, and social-as in education, is a fundamental obstacle to the more rapid progress of economic development. 

The results of trying to apply this recommendation would be further reinforced if aid could be transferred only in the form of project imports. As mentioned above, relatively few direct small and medium-size private enterprise projects could be handled economically under present legal and administrative arrangements and requirements. Moreover, many smaller businesses need only access to foreign exchange for imports which they can afford to buy with their own funds. Program loans supply foreign exchange for such cases. Other businesses need capital for other purposes than to import equipment. All these needs are served by the intermediate credit institutions to which both foreign exchange and local currency sales proceeds of aid imports are loaned. For example, in 1965 and 1966, Alliance loans direct to private enterprise totalled $46 million. 

However, loans to intermediate credit institutions for relending to private enterprise exceeded $140 million. In addition, $505 million out of $525 million in non-project loans to governments went for imports by or destined for private enterprise. These proportions show vividly the relative feasibility of reaching 

Latin American private enterprise with the various forms of U.S. assistance. 

Finally, we are continuing to work out more effective ways of promoting U.S. exports and private enterprise. The 1967 Brazil program loan will contain a $40 million Investment/Import Stimulation Fund largely patterned after the successful $30 million Capital Goods Fund in the 1966 program loan. Financing will be for equipment imports for private enterprises and agricultural cooperatives. It will cover up to 90 percent of the CIF cost of imported equipmentlocal costs to be provided by the borrower, and will cover a period of 3 to 10 years. Of the total amount of the new loan, $30 million will be destined for the industrial sector and $10 million for the agricultural sector. While credit facilities are available to Brazilian enterprises to finance purchase of locally produced equipment and materials, there are very limited foreign supplier credits available for foreign equipment. All equipment to be imported under the 1967 

Fund will be of U.S. origin, because of the incentive provided by this credit facility, will have the effect of providing substantial additionality of U.S. exports.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE, 

Washington, June 1, 1967.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, 

​Chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, House of Representatives. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: During Secretary Rusk's appearance before your Committee on May 18, Congressman Fulton requested information concerning the blacklisting of ships going to North Viet-Nam.

The Maritime Administration maintains a "black-list" of ships calling at North Viet-Nam ports on or after January 25, 1966 in accordance with a directive approved by the President. Any vessel on this black list is forbidden from carrying United States Government-financed cargoes shipped from the United States. 

This list applies only to the particular ship and not to all ships owned and operated by the company. However, through a certification procedure, it is possible for the company owning such a ship to regain eligibility to carry such United States Government cargo by certifying that the ship in question, as well as all other ships controlled by the company, will no longer call at North Viet- Nam ports. Thus, if the company wishes to have the ship taken off the list, it must certify that none of its ships will go to North Viet-Nam. 

Virtually the only ships now going to North Viet-Nam are British flag ships owned by one Hong Kong company, Ocean Tramping Ltd., which is under the control of Communist Chinese interests. None of the ships owned by Ocean 

Tramping Ltd. visit the United States, or carry United States Governmentsponsored cargoes, nor, so far as we are aware, are they engaged in carrying commercial cargoes shipped by United States firms. A blacklisting of Ocean 

Tramping Ltd. would, therefore, have very little effect on the operations of this company.

If there is additional information which you believe we can furnish, please do not hesitate to let me know. 

Sincerely yours, WILLIAM B. MACOMBER, Jr., Assistant Secretary for Congressional Relations. 77-470-67-pt. 6-10

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE BILL OF 1967 TUESDAY, JUNE 6, 1967 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, Washington, D.C.

The committee meets this morning in executive session for a continuation of the hearings on H.R. 7099. Since the hearings on the foreign aid program were closed last week, several members of the committee thought that the situation in Nigeria required further study by the committee, so we have invited back today Hon. Joseph Palmer 

2d, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs.

Í think, Mr. Palmer, it would save time if you could give us a short statement on the present situation in Nigeria before we start to ask questions.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH PALMER 2D, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. PALMER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. As I know all members of the committee are aware, the very bitter and longstanding dispute between eastern Nigeria and the northern-dominated federal military government in Lagos came to a head on May 30 when the eastern region declared its independence as the "Republic of Biafra.” 

I believe we are all aware of the background to this-the various changes that have taken place in Nigeria beginning in January 1966, when the civilian government was overthrown, and then the events of mid-1966 when General Ironsi was replaced by General Gowon. 

The massacres of Ibos in northern Nigeria took place shortly thereafter.

Since then there has been very much of a polarization of the positions between the Ibos and the northerners. The western region of 

Nigeria, the Yoruba section, was caught somewhere in between the two antagonists. 

Mr. FULTON. Could we see that on the map?

Mr. PALMER. Yes. The eastern region of Nigeria is this section approximately in here south of the Benue River, which is the river shown here. The midwest is an area approximately in here. The western region is over in this area and the northern region is this vast area up here. 

Mr. FULTON. Would you please repeat your remarks now, having shown us the areas relating to what you have just said? 1267

1967 

Mr. PALMER. Fine. I indicated, Mr. Congressman, that the origins of this dispute go back to January 1966. 

Mr. FULTON. The geography, will you put that in context for us? 

You say the east and the center and the north, how are they joined now?

Mr. PALMER. The eastern region has now declared secession and is now ranged against the remaining sections of Nigeria, which remain under the Federal Government. In this situation the principal power base in what remains of the Federal Government is the large northern area with the west and midwest sort of caught between the two protagonists [security deletion]. The west and midwest are continuing to adhere to the Federation. General Gowon, who is head of the 

Federal Government, has declared the eastern secession is an act of rebellion which will be crushed. He has ordered a general mobilization within Nigeria and has warned shippers to stay out of eastern Nigerian waters and ports, although some practical accommodations are being made with that with respect to the movement of oil tankers into the port of Bonny in eastern Nigeria. He has also instituted a number of financial and economic measures against eastern Nigeria in an effort to bring the rebellion to an end. 

The eastern region has also mobilized. [Security deletion.] 

We, the British, and a large number of African states have strongly advised against the use of force. [Security deletion.] 

To some extent this advice does cause some resentment and strong feelings on both sides. It remains to be seen how effective the advice that we and others have given is on this subject. 

One of our primary concerns, of course, is the safety of approximately 7,500 Americans who are in the area. Thus far American lives and property have not been threatened, but the threats of force and the movement of troops that have taken place could unleash a train of events which would jeopardize American lives. 

It seems quite apparent to our Embassy and to us that the most likely danger of hostilities at the present time is in the area surrounding eastern Nigeria. It is for that reason that our Embassy has recommended and taken steps to bring about a phased evacuation of American nationals from the eastern region of Nigeria, from the midwest region which adjoins it, and from the southern part of northern Ni geria [security deletion]. 

Mr. ADAIR. Mr. Chairman, could I ask a question just at that point? 

When you said you fear, Mr. Palmer, violence around the eastern region, do you mean within it or in the territories adjacent to it? 

Mr. PALMER. I think, Congressman Adair, that our concern is that if there should be a penetration for example of eastern Nigeria [security deletion] we think that the entire area could become involved in hostilities.

Therefore we have started moving our people out of this general area first. Moving 7,500 Americans and of course many other nationalities from the country as a whole would put a tremendous strain on facilities. I would like to emphasize in this connection that the present evacuation is merely a matter of priority. The security situation is difficult in other parts of the country also, particularly in the area around Ibadan in western Nigeria, where there is considerable tension as the result of the fact that northern troops remain stationed there.

1269 The western Nigerian government has been pressing to have these 

We are watching that situation very carefully as well. As of this morning we had evacuated approximately 400 Americans from eastern Nigeria out of approximately 2,000 we have in that area. The airlift out of the region is continuing. I should make clear at this point we are only evacuating dependents, although others are of course free to go, and some undoubtedly will go.

As I indicated earlier, Mr. Chairman, we have been trying to use our influence in every way that we can toward a peaceful settlement of this problem. Others have as well. So far we would have to say for very obvious reasons that the prospects for the continuance of a united Nigeria have been dealt an extremely heavy blow by these events. 

Whether or not it will ever be possible within the foreseeable future to put it back together again I think remains a moot point. 

We have tried to conduct ourselves in this situation on just as evenhanded a basis as possible. I don't think it is any good trying to assess fault with respect to this. There are faults on both sides. It is a tragedy that things have not worked out as everyone had hoped. 

We do wish to maintain contact with all of the various elements. 

We do have extensive interests all over the country. Contrary to press reports that were put out in eastern Nigeria right after the declaration of independence, we have not recognized eastern Nigeria. But we are continuing our consulate there on a de facto basis.

 RECENT PRIVATE INVESTMENTS IN NIGERIA 

In providing information about private investors in Nigeria during the past three years it should be recognized that the uncertain political situation which has prevailed over most of the past eighteen months has caused a number of potential investors to defer their plans pending a clarification of the situation. 

Notwithstanding this recent caution, an impressive number of new investments have gone forward over approximately the past three year period. The greater part of the dollar amount of new investment has naturally been connected with activities of petroleum, exploration and production which require large capital injections. In addition to new companies in those activities, nearly fifty US firms providing equipment and services to the petroleum industry have been established in Nigeria, mostly near the oil fields in the East and Mid-West. 

New US investments have extended to a wide range of other activities, however. 

These have included production of plywood and veneer, textiles, paper bags, baked goods, cigarettes, asbestos and cement items, shrimp harvesting and processing, sewing machine assembly, costume jewelry, plastics, livestock feed, drugs and pharmaceuticals, dairy products, metal working, printing, ceramics, electric goods, detergents, and machine shop operation.

 AID GIVEN BY ROCKEFELLER AND FORD FOUNDATIONS AND COORDINATION WITH AID PROGRAM 

Since 1959 the Ford Foundation has made grants totaling approximately $18,000,000 to Nigeria. These funds have been used to support activities in agriculture, population, development planning and management, education and research. A.I.D. and Ford Foundation personnel consult frequently on the problems of assistance to Africa and on specific programs in Nigeria. In Nigeria

1967 

the Ford Foundation Representative and the A.I.D. staff maintain close relationships and cooperate in several projects, all of which are closely coordinated. 

In Northern Nigeria, A.I.D. and the Ford Fonudation are jointly assisting in the development of a teacher education program. At the University of Nigeria at Nsukka, the Ford Foundation provided funds to the Economic Development Institute for research projects. Through a contract with Michigan State University, A.I.D. has helped to establish and develop the program for the Institute as part of the assistance given to set up a university modeled on a U.S. land grant college approach.

At Ahmadu Bello University, the Ford Foundation has provided assistance to the Institute of Administration for the construction of buildings, expansion of the Library, and support for the Provincial Local Government Training Scheme. All of these assist the A.I.D.-supported program for the development of the Institute.

The Rockefeller Foundation has provided approximately $3,000,000 to Nigeria over the past seven years. These funds have been largely devoted to food crops improvement and to universities, mainly those at Ibadan and Ife. The funds provided universities have been used in the fields of agriculture, humanities and social science, including economics, medicine and nutrition. There are frequent discussions between A.I.D. and Rockefeller personnel in the U.S., and when representatives of the Foundation visit Nigeria they normally hold discussions with A.I.D. personnel.

"KORRY REPORT" 

In his speech of May 26, 1966 on the occasion of the anniversary of OAU, President Johnson stated: 

"I have instructed the Secretary of State and other American officials to review our own development policies and programs in Africa. We shall be seeking new ideas and advice from American scholars, businessmen, and experts concerned with Africa's problems. Our Ambassador to Ethiopia, Ed Korry, will be working full time in the weeks ahead to follow through these initiatives. We wish to discuss new cooperative approaches and ideas with African governments, as well as with other governments and international groups." 

Ambassador Korry directed a working group whose members from the State Department were Oliver Troxel, Director, Office of Research and Analysis for Africa, Bureau of Intelligence and Research, who has served in Ghana and Ethiopia, Philip Heller, who has served as Political Officer in Guinea, Kenya and Burundi, and Michael Ely, Financial Economist, Bureau of Economic Affairs.

Officers from A.I.D. were Carroll Hinman, Director, Office of Development Plan ning, Bureau for Africa, and Robert Smith, Associate Administrator for Program, Office of Program Coordination. In the course of the study, the team sought the views of a number of individuals and organizations in the categories mentioned by the President.

1275 The report, submitted to the President in August, 1966, had as its principal conclusions and recommendations vis-a-vis aid: 

Support of African development continues to be in the US national interest; 

African development will be a long-term, difficult and necessarily gradual effort requiring the fullest possible coordination of effort by the United States, the other countries now providing much larger amounts of aid, and international organizations, as well as the African countries and regional organizations; 

This coordination effort could be led best by an international organization, particularly the World Bank; 

The United States should concentrate its bilateral development support efforts in those countries where development prospects are good and where US aid can be most effective;

The United States should continue development assistance to other areas of Africa primarily by assisting regional and multinational efforts rather than through strictly bilateral programs; 

US development aid should emphasize agriculture and rural development, education, health and population, the private sector and infrastructure including transportation, power and communications; 

Procedural improvements are needed to achieve more effective use of assistance; 

The amount of US aid should increase gradually as the development of African institutions and the fulfillment of the Report's other recommendations provide growing opportunities for its more effective use. 

The recommendations were approved in principle by the President, who directed that a program of implementation be drawn up. The Secretary of 

State designated the Assistant Secretary for African Affairs to develop such a program, in coordination with A.I.D. and other interested agencies. This program is reflected in the Congressional Presentation materials for FY 1968. It should be noted that this action program also took into account the limitations on the number of countries that may receive aid as contained in the Foreign Assist ance Act of 1967. 

Differences of views concerning the Korry Report recommendations and the action program revolved chiefly around whether bilateral programs should phase out in favor of regional programs for a number of countries.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Nigeria, as I understand it, is the second State Department blowup of a showcase government in Africa. The State Department first tried to make Ghana a showcase. It blew up in the Department's collective face. And now Nigeria. Where is it proposed to set up another showcase government in Africa?

Mr. PALMER. Mr. Gross, I think that the situation in Nigeria for some time was promising. But I have always shied away myself from terms such as "showcase," because I believe it is unreal to imply perfection when you are talking about developing countries that are starting from a very low base and trying to build nations with many divergent elements and with slow institutional development, as well as boundary lines that were drawn arbitrarily-not in Africa but in Europe. I do not believe that any of these countries really can qualify as a showcase. However, some have been better than others. 

I think that the problems of building stability in these countries are going to be long term, and I therefore mistrust the term "showcase." 

I served for 31½ years in Nigeria. I never called it a showcase. I never regarded it as a showcase. I regarded it as a country that I thought had great potential and that I thought had hope. 

But the weaknesses that have come to the fore here have been known all along. They have been there beneath the surface. I think the history of all developing countries is that they all encounter great difficulties in building a nation. They all have setbacks. 

Mr. GROSS. We got quite a song and dance, Mr. Palmer, on the subject of Nigeria and its model government. Is the President or the State 

Department or both giving any thought to an economic boycott of eastern Nigeria which now seeks its independence?

Mr. CULVER.  

Mr. Secretary, I wonder if you would be good enough to comment, on what I feel is a very basic problem in our aid approach to Africa in the past 7 years. It seems to me that the situation in Nigeria is a classic problem of political instability that we are encountering to a greater or lesser extent throughout the continent. 

The thing that concerns me a great deal is the consequences of the colonial legacy imposing upon these very arbitrary geographic units a political framework and institutional structure which is totally unrelated to the genuine realities of the African environment, its tribal groupings, diversity of language, customs and animosities. We have in

1967 

the West something called democracy which in all of its manifestations in individual countries is markedly unique, yet when we talk about the African Continent in terms of "democracy," we talk about these inflexible straitjackets modeled on the Westminster system or French or whatever it is, which although ideally suitable for the administration of a colonial empire, are totally ill-conceived and totally unsatisfactory for the efficient and stable development of a nation state in the African Continent. If you agree with that premise, my question really is with all our efforts in economic assistance and with all our general recog nition that political stability is the sine qua non for any meaningful development, of a sustained nature, what are we doing in our aid efforts in cooperation with other Western powers and the African intellectual community to create and tailor political institutions based on the anthropological nature of the societies in which they are intended to work in order to develop an imaginative, creative order with fresh, new approach, something that politically fits their requirements. A Nigerian observer made a statement last week, that we have been cutting the man to fit the suit rather than the cloth to the man, and it seems to me this has been the agony in the last 7 years in Africa, and I see no hope for any sort of stable democratic development unless we address ourselves to this problem. 

Mr. PALMER. Mr. Congressman, let me say first of all that I entirely agree with you with respect to your analysis of the problem. I think one difficulty is that most of these independent states emerged in independence with an older generation who were very oriented toward the metropole, and not only that, but a lot of accommodations were made and a lot of institutional frameworks were accepted at the time, without a full realization of the implications and the lack of relevance to the African environment. In many cases they were accepted solely because this was the way to get independence. 

I agree with you very much, and I think one of the manifestations of instability in Africa now is that Africa is going through a period of experimentation, of institutional adaptation. What have we done? We haven't done enough. But we have taken certain steps. I don't want to impose too much on your time, since I know it is limited. If I could give one instance which I think is very relevant to what we are talking about, the University of Ibadan in western Nigeria when it first came into being was a British institution put down in Africa. Nigerians recognized this. Azikiwe recognized this. He had been educated in the United States. He said, "What we have to do here is bring to Nigeria some of the concepts of an American land grant university."
