PRESIDENTIAL AUTHORITY TO TERMINATE PUBLIC LAW 480 AND FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT AGREEMENT 

The President can terminate any and all assistance under P.L. 480 as well as under the Foreign Assistance Act. This would include the ability to halt or divert shipments of commodities. This right is provided for by standard language in the underlying assistance agreements. In the case of P.L. 480 agreements, standard language provides that the U.S. may terminate the financing, sale and delivery of commodities under the agreement if it determines that because of changed conditions such termination is necessary or desirable. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Are the recipient governments aware of this possibility?

Mr. KLEINE. The provision which makes possible termination is included in the basic understandings of project agreements or loan agreements that are pending, whether it is a grant or loan program.

1967 Mr. FINDLEY. I recall in particular a Public Law 480 transaction with the United Arab Republic a couple of years ago. Shipments were made under this program within a week or 10 days after Nasser had been very insulting in public remarks about the United States. 

I concluded from that that our Government felt dutybound to carry through with the completion of contracts even though developments might dictate otherwise.

Mr. KLEINE. I am not familiar with that particular case. But it might well have been a feeling of good faith rather than a legal necessity. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Good faith; yes.

Mr. KLEINE. I don't know what the circumstances were. There may have been the authority but a decision not to exercise the authority for other reasons.

Mr. FINDLEY. It occurs to me that it could be a desirable incentive for stability and constitutional processes in these countries if the heads of the governments realized that our President might terminate all forms of aid instantly in case things went bad. I question whether the governments are fully aware of this possibility in view of our lack of action in this direction up to now. 

Mr. PALMER. I am not sure myself, Mr. Congressman, in the sort of emotional situations you have here whether this would have that effect. 

In fact, I think it could very well have the opposite effect, of destroying the basis that you maintained for a relationship. I think it probably would be resented, and I am not sure would be in our longer term interest.

Mr. FINDLEY. I am not suggesting that this action would necessarily be taken. But are you suggesting that such a provision in contracts, a universal provision in the basic legislation would make aid unacceptable to these governments?

Mr. PALMER. Let me say that I think that simply in the case of 

Nigeria that they are and have been all along very much aware that what we can contribute to the development of Nigeria is very heavily dependent upon the circumstances in which we have to work there. 

Of course this is a program that originally was based on the maintenance of the unity of the country. 

I think they do understand in a genal way that aid might be able to continue that the resources we would feel justified in putting in, in terms of the conditions that exist there, is dependent upon the general situation.

Mr. FINDLEY. Mr. Secretary, do you recall any specific efforts in the last year or so to encourage press freedom and freedom of speech in individual countries in Africa?

Mr. PALMER. I think this is a subject that our ambassadors constantly bear in mind and have talked about to governments. I would like to say off the record if I may- (Discussion off the record.)

Mr. FINDLEY. As you may know I am suggesting an amendment which would call for an annual reporting on the status of individual freedoms in the countries which we have foreign assistance in and that is why I ask that. May I ask Admiral Heinz if he would comment on the practicality of sending the U.S. 6th Fleet to the war zones as a flotilla of mercy with the announced purpose of evacuating the aged,

1293 el infirm, children, mothers, people of that sort, and thus establish a position near the war zone? Would this present serious difficulties that you would care to comment on?

Admiral HEINZ. I can only comment from having served in the 6th 

Fleet in the past. All the ships have a capability of taking care of evacuees. The main way of handling them would be by helicopter or by boat. If by boat, you would have to get in closer. The amphibious force has a capability, the carriers have some capability, but it would not be too large because there are not extra spaces on the ships. In almost every case of a crisis the ships always review their evacuation plans to see what they can do or may have to do to take care of people in such a contingency. So that evacuation of people, taking care of people, is always a contingency you are planning for. 

Mr. FINDLEY.  

Chairman MORGAN. Any further questions? 

Mr. Palmer, Mrs. Bolton left a series of questions here and she has checked off the ones she has asked and she want to know if your people would prepare answers to the rest of the questions and submit them for the record.

Mr. PALMER. We will be happy to. (The questions referred to and the answers thereto follow :) 

ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS BY MRS. BOLTON 

Question: Are the British evacuating their personnel?

Answer: The British are undertaking partial evacuation measures very similar to our own. They have taken over sponsorship of the DC-6 shuttle airlift from 

Port Harcourt to Lagos which was formerly under American direction. They are also chartering additional aircraft because of the greater number of UK citizens in Eastern Nigeria. 

Question: Is Biafra self-sufficient? Does it produce enough food? Is it dependent on commodities from other nations? What are the prospects for requests for aid coming to us from Biafra in the near future?

Answer: [Security deletion.] In addition to immense petroleum resources and oil palm products, the East has an energetic and competent civil service, a fairly well-developed infrastructure, a small but growing industrial sector, and a population of over 12 million.

The Eastern Region depends upon imports to meet its needs for most manufactured goods. In view of the East's high population density the agricultural sector could have increasing difficulty in future decades in supplying a rapidly growing population. At present, however, food stocks are sufficient to enable the 

East to survive at a somewhat austere level until September, when a greatly enlarged yam crop will be harvested. For protein intake the East could fall back on goats, sheep and poultry, supplemented by fish landings. 

[Security deletion.] 

Question: Does the U.S. have any official communication with Biafra? If so, what?

Answer: The U.S. maintains a Consulate in Enugu under authority originally granted by the Nigerian Government under Prime Minister Balewa and continued by its successors. The Consulate is responsible for normal consular functions, including the welfare and protection of American citizens and the protection of American property. In the discharge of these duties, the Consulate is naturally in touch with de facto local authorities. 

Prevailing legal doctrine is that recognition of a new state is a matter of intention by the recognizing state. The United States will therefore not "inadvertently" recognize a new state in Eastern Nigeria. Furthermore, there is no inconsistency in our continuing to provide normal consular services in the East while we continue to recognize the Federal Military Government as the Government of Nigeria. As you know, we continue to maintain a post in Rhodesia although we do not recognize the Smith Regime.

1967 

Question: Before the secession, how much did the Eastern. region contribute to the nation (economically, in civil service, etc.)? Can the remainder of Nigeria get along without Biafra?

Answer: Under the combined Federal-Regional budgetary system that has been in effect in Nigeria, the Federal government collected various taxes and revenues in all regions. A portion was retained for central government expenditures and a portion was allocated by the central government to the regions for and without regard to the their budgets, according to a formula based omated that [security deletion] region in which it was collected. It has been in annual revenues derived from Eastern Nigeria has been distributed to other regions. The East has also contributed people and skills, as well as materials and revenues. Easterners have made up a disproportionate share of personnel of the 

Federal civil service and various statutory agencies such as the Railway Corporation. Easterners have also been prominent in commerce and education in the other Regions of Nigeria. 

The withdrawal of Easterners from the remainder of Nigeria in recent months has not had as serious an impact on the economy as many had feared. The Federal civil service, the railways, the electricity corporation, etc. continue to function, though at a somewhat reduced rate of efficiency. Thus, the remainder of 

Nigeria has so far been able to get along without the East. Whether Nigeria can resume its former rate of economic development, however, will depend mainly upon its ability to regain political stability and to retain its identity as an economic unit. 

Question: Can General Gowon enforce the embargo against Biafra? Is he successfully commanding the troops of the 3 other regions does he really have their support? 

Answer: [Security deletion]. The Federal Military Government has already made an exception for oil tankers, which are allowed to load in the East provided they first call at Lagos to be inspected. 

The Federal navy, which has available a destroyer escort, two mine sweepers, and several large patrol-craft, could provide limited support for the blockade. 

[Security deletion.] 

General Gowon has the respect and loyalty of soldiers from the Middle Belt of Northern Nigeria, who account for over half of the army personnel under Federal control. Although the deepest loyalties of Western and Mid-Western units extend to their own areas and peoples, it is the Northern troops who dominate the Federal armies.

The stresses and strains from political events of the past eighteen months have caused military discipline to deteriorate and have necessitated a reorganization of the Nigerian army to provide greater regional autonomy. [Security deletion.] 

Question: What aid adjustments do you forsee are necessary in our aid programs for Nigeria in the immediate future? 

Answer: [Security deletion.] Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, gentlemen.

Mr. ADAIR. Are the wheat shipments to India on schedule, gentlemen? Would you give us a rundown on that, or the grain shipments, generally, I guess that includes some corn too, doesn't it?

STATEMENT OF MAURICE J. WILLIAMS, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRA- ISTRATOR FOR NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. WILLIAMS. By and large the shipments have been on schedule. 

It is necessary, of course, to qualify any statement of that sort because of the closure of the Suez Canal.

Mr. ADAIR. That was going to be the second part of my question. 

So if you want to include that in your answer, if the Suez Canal is closed or remains closed for any appreciable period of time, what effect will that have?

Mr. WILLIAMS. It does affect the schedule of wheat deliveries. The effect of the closure of the Suez Canal is particularly great for those shipments that are underway and in the Mediterranean approaching the canal.

First of all someone must decide whether the ships turn around, or wait for the canal to open. Either way, the closure could delay arrivals in India considerably and would mean that the shipping schedules would be off. [Security deletion.] This is classified information, but generally [security deletion]. 

Mr. ADAIR. We are in executive session. 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes. I just wanted to note [security deletion].

Mr. ADAIR. What other nations are now providing India with foodstuffs? 

Mr. MURPHY. Would you yield? 

Mr. ADAIR. Yes. 

Mr. MURPHY. On the first point. 

Mr. ADAIR. Certainly. 

Mr. MURPHY. Mr. Handley, I understand that the freight rates have gone up and that the recipient country must pay the freight, is that correct? I understand that India is very fearful of the increase in cost?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, there are two increases in cost-the increase in cost for the longer distances that are involved, Mr. Murphy, and the increase in insurance.

Mr. MURPHY. The increase in costs took place before the United 

Arab Republic closed the Suez? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, freight rates have gone up generally.

1967 

Mr. MURPHY. I understand India called this to the attention of your department that this increase was going to be very difficult for them to pay.

Mr. WILLIAMS. It will impose an additional burden that they had not anticipated. They now pay the most of the freight, as you know, Mr. Murphy, on Public Law 480 sales. The United States pays the freight on shipments of donations.

Mr. MURPHY. I understand that. The Indian Government question is on the increase in freight rate, that it might be unable to be able to pay for the tonnage. The new rates will be prohibitive. 

Mr. WILLIAMS. It is, indeed, an added and unanticipated problem for them against their slim foreign exchange reserves. 

Mr. ADAIR. Had you finished, Bill? 

Mr. MURPHY. Yes. Thank you. Mr. ADAIR. On this question of food, Mr. Williams or Mr. Handley, either one, I was reading last night a paper that indicated there are between 200 and 250 million cattle or cows, perhaps both cows and bullocks, in India. Do you think that figure is about correct? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. It is about right.

Mr. ADAIR. Then in addition to that, when one is thinking about food supplies, the matter of pests and rodents which I am told consume 20 percent roughly of the food supply of India, would you agree with that figure?

Mr. WILLIAMS. I don't believe we really know what is consumed by pests and rodents. There have been various estimates made. Of course, the variable factor is how much is consumed in the field. That is anybody's guess. The problem that India is addressing is the consumption by pests and rodents of grain in storage is a problem that can be addressed by improving storage facilities and handling practices. 

Mr. ADAIR. This article again speculated that there were possiblefive rodents for every human being in India. Would you think that a likely figure? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. I do not know.

Mr. ADAIR. If you think about the cattle and the rodents and the monkeys, and my question is a very broad, general one, one India expect to feed her people and still follow her religion or her beliefs based upon mythology or whatever else which tends to protect those animals, or hard as it sounds, must we come to the point of view where we think that India someplace has to make a decision between feeding animals or feeding human beings?

Would you address yourself to that admittedly difficult question? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. It is a very difficult problem for India that you point out, Mr. Adair. Certainly they are not feeding rats consciously 

Mr. ADAIR. Not voluntarily, no, but based on mythology they do not kill rats generally, am I not correct in that?

Mr. WILLIAMS. They have an antirat campaign, and they are attempting to exterminate them. This is quite a different problem from the cattle, as I understand it. Exterminating rats is not an easy problem. It has been said that a rat population is a biological organism and that they reproduce back to the level of the grain supply. 

That is why India's main focus is on cutting off the access of rodents to stored grain. Experts have told us that just a simple matter such as the control of doors, of closing off effectively stored grain, will have a very real effect in cutting down the consumption of rodents.

1311 The problem with cattle is deep seated and religious. India is, however, changing. There are programs to pen up the cattle, keep them from foraging across the fields. Anyone who has been to India will have seen that these cattle are not overfed by any means. 

I think, in answer to your question, India believes the programs that it has underway in agriculture, particularly its policies of the last 2 years using new seeds, water and fertilizer-can make the country self-sufficient in food grains sometime in the early 1970's. This would mean a fairly dramatic annual increase in grain production, something like 5 percent a year.

The question of whether India can achieve that rate of increase over a sustained period is one that experts have not agreed on. Certainly yields in India today are very low. In these circumstances, the application of new technology-new seed varieties with fertilizer and water—which India is now aggressively pursuing, will have an effect on grain production and on food supply. 

India has to continue, of course, its programs of rodent control. 

Mr. ADAIR. There is much more, there is a great deal more that could be said on that, but my time has run out. Mr. Chairman, if I could ask just one final question, though. 

Will India's apparently gratuitous and, in the opinion of a good many people, unnecessary support of President Nasser have any bearing upon our rethinking of our aid program to that country? 

STATEMENT OF WILLIAM J. HANDLEY, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SEC- RETARY OF STATE FOR NEAR EASTERN AND SOUTH ASIAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. HANDLEY. Mr. Chairman, Mr. Adair, it seems to us that the main consideration really is what is going on in India, whether the democratic society that is India can function in that part of Asia. 

Even though there certainly seems to be strong bias on the part of India toward one side of this particular problem in the Near East, we should not be distracted by that. We should concentrate on doing what is necessary for this country, which has gone through four general elections, has a free press-which, incidentally, has taken issue with the Government of India on the very question that you have raisedhas so many universities, has a strong civil service, and has what the experts believe is a workable economic program. Under the circumstances, I think India deserves our support. 

I would not think that we would want to take a position that would handicap the people in India who are working so hard to make this a viable economy. If I may say a few things on the question of the COWS- Mr. ADAIR. If the Chairman will let us have another minute or two. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Adair, I will yield you my time. 

Mr. ADAIR. Thank you.

Mr. HANDLEY. There is another side to the cow picture. The cow does provide certain very definite benefits to the Indian economy. The cow and the bullock do provide power in certain- 

Mr. ADAIR. But rarely the cow, just the bullock.

Mr. HANDLEY. Sometimes the cow too. 

Mr. ADAIR. In Pakistan I guess the cow is so used.

1967 

Mr. HANDLEY. Secondly, there is a fair amount of fertilizer that is used which can be traced back to this animal. I would also like to mention that cow dung is used for fuel. It is an important source of fuel in the rural areas. When the cow dies, there is the leather that is made from the cow.

Mr. ADAIR. That is inferior in a good many cases because the animal isn't- Mr. HANDLEY. That is correct. I would also say, having lived in 

India a number of years, I really did not see too much evidence personally of cows being fed the kind of grain we are talking about. 

Usually the cows eat rubbish, and some of the grass along the sides of the road.

So I think perhaps the loss to the inefficient cows is perhaps not as great as some people think. There is also, strangely enough, a small amount of milk from some of these cows. So without going too far into the ecology of the cow in India, I think there is this positive side. 

For a foreign state to take a position on something as sensitive as this, I would think, would have a very disturbing effect in India and might have consequences which I don't think would be particularly useful. 

Mr. ADAIR. I would just say, Mr. Handley, speaking for myself now, that as you communicate with your friends in India, you could say that at least some of us in America don't appreciate the fact that their leaders go around making these anti-American and pro-Russian statements, and then look to us for supplies of various kinds. I think they could use a great deal better judgment in this respect. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Murphy. 

Mr. MURPHY. No questions. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Frelinghuysen. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Following up Mr. Adair's question, can I get any indication from any of you gentlemen as to why India is supporting the Arab cause if it professes to be nonalined? How can this be justified? 

Mr. HANDLEY. This, I suppose, goes back to India's interest in being very much involved in the developing world. Their support also goes back I suppose, to the fact that there is just one Israel, while there are many Arab countries. 

It also should be recognized that even though India does not have full diplomatic relations with Israel, they do have consular relations. 

There is a consul general in Bombay. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Becoming involved in the developing world by a gratuitous involvement like this, does result in antagonisms in the developed world which I would think India would be anxious to avoid if she is interested in her own national interest primarily. 

Getting to the broad problem of agriculture and food, the book says that future aid assistance will be closely related to further progress toward the achievement of production goals in agriculture and population control. This is on page 187. 

Have we ever made a thorough study of the need in India for food, and how this need can be met? Who has analyzed the nature of the problem, what the goals should be? Also, how do we determine what progress is being made toward those goals? 

Would we actually cut off assistance if we felt there was not progress toward certain goals?

1313 Mr. WILLIAMS. As to who analyzes objectives in agriculture, certainly the Indian Government projects goals. It develops analysis of its problems and the program to deal with these problems in the framework of its fourth 5-year plan and annual plan targets. 

The principal effort for the donor countries is by the World Bank. 

This institution has completed a very detailed report of the Indian economic programs, particularly focused on agriculture. The report comments on the adequacy of India's agricultural efforts, its policies and how realistic its targets for achievement in the years ahead are, as well as commenting on and evaluating the requirements for economic assistance.

There are other groups that also are engaged in analysis of this problem. I believe the Ford Foundation, and certainly the Agency for International Development itself, are engaged in making projections ahead and evaluating the adequacy of policies and programs in India.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. How much can we rely on what India says she can do? As I understand it, she said they can be self-sufficient in food grains by 1971. That is within 4 years. Is this a realistic goal in your opinion? Do you think this is a goal that can be met?

Mr. WILLIAMS. In our opinion we do not think it is a realistic goal. We are glad to see them strive toward a target of self-sufficiency as rapidly as possible, but we don't believe they will achieve it as quickly as they say. We hope we are wrong.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. How does the World Bank evaluation com pare with India's own evaluation of her problem?

Mr. WILLIAMS. They have seen enormous progress in India in the last 2 years.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. They have seen it? You mean we have seen it?

Mr. WILLIAMS. The World Bank in its report has pointed out and highlighted the enormous progress in economic policies affecting agriculture in India in the past 2 years. These policies are related to price incentives, dependence on the market, the importance of fertilizer and its use.

For example, 3 years ago India was importing $65 million worth of fertilizer. This coming year it will be importing some $300 million worth of fertilizer. At the same time its plans for expanding domestic production of fertilizer by more than 2 million tons additional by the end of this 5-year plan are proceeding fairly aggressively. Policies encouraging private investment in fertilizer plants have been adopted.

As a measure of the planned increased production, current production amounts to about 500,000 tons. The increases in fertilizer use, coupled with new seed varieties and with water, will have a very real effect in terms of increasing production. Our own estimates are that it is possible for India to approach self-sufficiency in food grain by the middle part of the next decade, but it is probably not likely in the early 1970's.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Is this roughly what the World Bank also envisages? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, that is my recollection, sir. 77-470-67-pt. 6- -13

1967 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. If I could ask about the fertilizer industry, I understand that Government policy has not been helpful in encouraging private business to get into this field, either in operating plants or in marketing fertilizer. You have indicated that some improvement has been made along those lines. How much has been done? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. That is correct. There is a very real change in Indian policy affecting private investment, particularly focused on fertilizer plants. This change took place some 18 months ago. 

The main features are the possibility of majority equity and control by foreign management in new fertilizer plants. That is a departure from previous policy. The company will have complete freedom to set its own price on fertilizer it produces and to establish distribution systems within India for a period of 7 years. 

This too is a very real departure from the previous public sector oriented approach to fertilizer production and distribution in India. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. What is being done in the area of irrigation? 

Is there much emphasis on providing adequate irrigation for these areas?

Mr. WILLIAMS. There are a number of irrigation projects affecting the main rivers. The Indian Government turned only recently to considering tapping through tube wells the very large subwater resources of the country. This of course could play an immensely important role in the future in giving assurance against drought, if you can create a secure water supply through tube well developement. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Is this something we are assisting them in or have they just begun to think it is a good idea? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. We have been assisting them in some of the initial planning.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Could you tell me whether you think, even if 

India does meet its objectives in the area of food production, that this is going to mean much? This is following up Mr. Adair's question. Is it going to mean much if they don't do something about the population situation, holding down the consumption of food to some degree, and also the problem of conservation of food through better rodent control. 

Mr. WILLIAMS. There is the serious problem of population expansion, growing at a rate of 2.5 percent, which means 12 million extra mouths a year. This is a very serious problem indeed, and one which the Indian Government is addressing in a quite aggressive family planning program. 

Again, the family planning policies of the last 2 years have changed dramatically over those of the earlier period. In 2 years, they have doubled the number of couples practicing family planning over the level achieved by their program during the prior 10 years. There are now 4 million participating couples using various family planning devices.

The main part of the program is based on use of the loop or the coil. but they are beginning the subsidized distribution on a wide scale of condoms, using established private distributors. Evaluation of the possible use of the pill is underway in India. They are not quite sure how it would fit in, or whether it meets their situation in the rural villages.

1315 Family planning is a State responsibility in India, and the Central Government has assured the States that it will subsidize costs to them of an expanded family planning program for the next 10 years. 

These subsidy costs being provided are very large indeed. 

Some $25 million in 1965-66, expanding to $50 million last year and $80 million in the current Indian fiscal year. 

The program will attempt to train enough workers to reach every village and carry the message of the importance of family planning and training in the techniques of family planning. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I thank you. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Roybal. 

Mr. ROYBAL. I would like to know how much money is actually spent by the United States in helping India with her family planning program?

Mr. WILLIAMS. At the present time the amount of money spent by the United States is very small. The problem has not been one of money as much as administration, organization, and primarily motivation. We have made it known to the Indian Government that we stand ready to help them in any way with financial resources. This might take the form of providing foreign exchange for vehicles. Our large program of assistance in financing Indian imports is an indirect support to the Indian family planning program, as components for vehicles to be assembled in India are included as a basic element of the imports we are helping to finance. 

The question of importing condoms is under review currently in India. An international tender has been published by India. We have indicated we would be willing to use loan funds to finance these or other devices. 

But our help so far has been limited to technical assistance. We have five advisers assisting India in the evaluation of program effectiveness and on the medical side of the program, and we have trained some participants in the States. 

Mr. ROYBAL. Are these programs actually executed along public health techniques in connection, for example, with a "well baby clinic" or some kind of public health project? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. The family planning program is, using public health services, public health techniques. A network of family planning centers is being established. All the doctors in India are being asked to undergo special instruction on the importance of family planning and on techniques of family planning. 

The curriculum of medical schools is being revised to give family planning a very prominent and important place. The same is true for the nursing schools. 

The public health service is fully engaged in this program in India. 

Mr. ROYBAL. I have one more question, Mr. Chairman. An American firm built the Trombay fertilizer plant which I understand is a successful operation. The Government of India wants to expand this plant with the help of the U.S. Government, but wants an Italian firm to do the work. Will you supply for the record all the information concerning the proposal of the Indian Government?

1967 

Mr. WILLIAMS. That question is before us currently, and I will be pleased to supply that information for the record, sir. (A classified memorandum was subsequently supplied in response to 

Mr. Roybal.)

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Whalley. 

Mr. Secretary, how will the [security deletion] million in nonproject aid be used?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Nonproject loans will finance imports into the economy of India. The importance in this case is to assure the effective use of existing capacity in India. We feel that the best investment in terms of the return on foreign exchange is to help the Indian Government assure that existing industrial capacity is used to the full, rather than to build new plants, new capital facilities whose capacity can only be used in part. This is the primary reason we emphasize nonproject aid in India's current situation. 

The specific commodities we envision financing are fertilizer-I have mentioned the importance of fertilizer to the achievement of India's agricultural objectives and the way in which they are seeking to expand imports of fertilizer threefold over the current period to a projected $300 million a year-fuel, largely lubricants for the economy; iron and steel products; nonferrous metals; sulfur, a raw material used in the production of fertilizer as you know, sir; machinery and equipment; and motor vehicles and parts. These are the major components that we propose to finance with the nonproject aid request for fiscal year 1968.

All of this is of course for procurement from the United States. 

Mr. WHALLEY. What effect has the recent elections for Parliament had on India's development plans? 

Mr. HANDLEY. I would say none, sir. The plan is a Central Government plan. Quite obviously the relationship between the Central Government and some of the State governments is going to be a little different from what it was in the past, since I believe about half the State governments of India are under the direction of the party, or a coalition of parties which is different from the Congress Party. There is the same Planning Minister in India today as before the election. 

I really don't see from the political standpoint that there will be any change here. If there is any change, I would think there would be a little more prodding from some of the State governments which are not in the Congress Party hands to get a little more action. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Does India have any minerals that they could develop? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. They have quite extensive deposits of iron ore, also coal. They may have substantial oil resources. Also phosphate deposits have recently been discovered. They are not very well endowed with nonferrous metals by current indications. I might say while dealing with their basic resources that their hydroelectric potential is very high. One of our loan projects involves trying to locate nonferrous metals through aerial surveys and ground followup. This is a major deficiency which affects their import- 

Mr. WHALLEY. Did you say they had good prospects for hydroelectric power?

1317 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, sir.

Mr. WHALLEY. What benefits did Great Britain get from holding 

India, or why did everyone want to get it in the old days? What did 

India have then that made it so desirable? Did it actually cost Britain to hold, or was there any benefits, or was it their management that made it work out OK?

Mr. WILLIAMS. I am not informed in detail. I have a general impression that there was a commercial advantage in trade, selling manufactured goods from Britain in return for raw materialsparticularly jute and other fibers and tea. There was a complementary trading relationship between Britain and some of her overseas possessions, of which India was a very major one. 

Mr. HANDLEY. We should add spices to that, sir. Spices were, I suppose, what attracted most people to India in the very early days, even before the British were there. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Thank you very much.

Chairman MORGAN. Mrs. Kelly. 

Mr. MURPHY. Pardon me, will you yield?

Mrs. KELLY. I yield. 

Mr. MURPHY. Tea is really their main product, is that correct, as far as foreign trade?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Tea is one of the major exports. 

Mr. MURPHY. That comes from Kerala, in the south?

Mr. WILLIAMS. No, the tea exports come from the north. 

Mr. MURPHY. I understand Kerala is the only state that is earning sufficient dollars?

Mr. WILLIAMS. No. West Bengal, through jute exports, earns substantial dollars. 

Mr. MURPHY. I understood tea is the major dollar earner.

Mr. WILLIAMS. Assam also is a major tea area in earning dollars. 

Mrs. KELLY. Is that all the time you needed, Mr. Murphy? 

Mr. MURPHY. Yes. 

Mrs. KELLY. Mr. Chairman, I have only one short question. Have we much local currency in these countries? What is our fund of local currency in India? Pakistan? Turkey?

Mr. WILLIAMS. The local currency accumulation as a result of the

Admiral HEINZ. India is getting its military equipment from a number of sources. To date they have signed arms agreements with the 

U.S.S.R., Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria on the Communist side. From the non-Communist countries they have gotten equipment from Australia, Belgium, Canada, Finland, France, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, as well as some equipment from the United States.

Admiral HEINZ. The agreements vary. I do not have all the details of the sales agreement. A significant increment is repaid in hard currency, and part is paid in rupees.

United States is the fact that they did nothing to help us in Korea, and they are doing nothing to help us in Vietnam. I think that is probably the best assessment of how they really feel toward us.

Mr. WILLIAMS. The debt service on loans to the United States is running about $60 million annually. 

Mr. GROSS. How about the same with other governments?

Mr. GROSS. You don't have a total?

Mr. GROSS. Are those loans by other foreign governments on more or less favorable terms than ours?

Mr. WILLIAMS. They are generally less favorable than the terms that the United States is providing, sir, but I should point out that in recent years the terms of other donor countries have been improving. 

The Canadians have been outstanding in this respect, softening their terms pretty much to those of IDA, and even going beyond in some cases in making grant capital assistance available for development. 

Canada also gives large amounts of food aid as gifts. 

The United Kingdom also has recently taken steps to improve its terms to developing countries like India. For example, on many of its loans it is now requiring no interest payments, only principal. 

Mr. GROSS. What about the international agencies, the World Bank, such institutions, was that included in the figure you gave me a moment ago?

Mr. WILLIAMS. No, sir, that was not included in the figure I gave you. 

The debt service on loans from the World Bank is $88.4 million and from IDA $3.4 million for 1966-67. That would be additional to the figure that I mentioned earlier.

Mr. GROSS. Do you think India will ever be able to meet its obligations with respect to these loans?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, sir. They do now, and over the long run I do believe they will continue to if they can sustain the development program that they have projected for themselves. It will take a while before India can get along on commercial term loans. 

I wouldn't want to say this is going to be done overnight. It is a matter of- 

Mr. GROSS. Say 40 years? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. I would think less than 40 years. I would say two decades, 15 to 20 years. The economy has been developing very rapidly. 

Investment has increased, almost doubling from the first 5-year period of the early fifties to the second 5-year period of the late fifties. Power supply has increased fourfold. 

Manufacturing output is going up at a rate of about 9 percent a year average over the last 5 years.

Agriculture, even though they haven't applied the new technology yet in terms of seed and fertilizer, has been increasing almost 3 percent a year. India has real problems. It is a large country, continental in

1321 scale, with a large population, but I believe that they will organize themselves and that they can manage this indebtedness. The indebtedness is now about 25 percent of their foreign exchange earnings. 

They are on the verge, it appears to me, of an increasingly vigorous and effective export program. That will make it possible to service this debt; yes, sir.

Mr. GROSS. Mr. Frelinghuysen asked you a while ago what studies, reviews, and so on, had been made with respect to agriculture in India, and I gained from the response of you gentlemen that there had been no study or studies of any serious nature. 

Mr. WILLIAMS. I am afraid my answer was deficient if I gave you that impression. There have been many studies. The World Bank, as I mentioned, has completed a study. The Ford Foundation is engaged in this. The U.S. Government and various agencies; for example, the Department of Agriculture, in addition to the Indian Government are deeply concerned and are studying and evaluating Indian performance and its prospects. 

Mr. GROSS. This book for last year shows $21 million in contracts, technical service contracts. There are a number of studies included.

You can't find out in a quick perusal of this book how many of the worldwide $45 million contracts have gone to India for various studies, reviews, call them what you want. I would think there would be a wealth of material with respect to agriculture in India and the problems relating to agriculture. 

I yield to the gentleman if he would like to ask a question. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I thank the gentleman. 

I simply wanted to ask how active is our Department of Agriculture in evaluating the problem of food production in India? In other words, have we directly put our agricultural experts to look at the problems and try to evaluate what might be done about them? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, sir; we have. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has been increasingly active, as you would expect it to be, given the size of our Public Law 480 program to India. They review not only the requirement in terms of the Public Law 480 shipments, but performance in production. Under the recent legislation, the U.S. Department of Agriculture and AID work very closely in assessing selfhelp performance in terms of effective policies in agriculture and the steps that India plans to take if it is to achieve the goals that it has laid out for itself. These self-help measures are a part of every single one of the agreements in Public Law 480 that we are now negotiating with India. These negotiations are not completed until we are satisfied that India is moving ahead with the policy reforms, whether it be fertilizer, water, or new techniques which it has adopted. These are the major changes that I mentioned have been taking place in Indian agricultural programs over the last 2 years. We also get help from the 

Department of Agriculture on water development problems and on price marketing problems.

Mr. GROSS. We have been hearing that they would be self-sufficient in food by 1971. Do you believe this?

Mr. WILLIAMS. No. sir; I do not. I think that is an admittedly ambitious target, but targets should be high. However, I do believe that with the programs underway, they can achieve food grain self-sufficiency by the mid-1970's.

Mr. BUCHANAN. I wonder if you would state what our plans are in the area of family planning, whether we are looking toward projecting a major program or assisting the Indian Government in conducting a major program in this area, exactly what our plans are in this regard? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. The Government of India has launched a major program, and we naturally feel that the responsibility and the initiative must rest with it. 

I outlined earlier the way in which this program has been expanded in the last 2 years particularly the expansion in budget allocation, in training, in reaching down through all the states, and the commitment of the Central Government that it would undertake to cover all financial expenses of the states for the next 10 years so the states can proceed to expand their effort with some confidence in the future. 

In other words, the Indian Government is itself placing a priority which says there is no real budgetary restraint on family planning programs. The amount of assistance that we are providing is currently not very large. Some five technicians are working with the 

Indians in evaluation and on the medical side. The Ford Foundation is very heavily engaged in assisting them in the evaluation of their efforts. We are offering training opportunities, and we stand ready to help them with any financing in foreign exchange that they may require for their family planning program. 

As yet we have not received a request from India. The foreign exchange expenditures are not the major part of the program. Rupees have been a major part, and this has been assured as a priority in their budget.

The problem is one of administration, education, getting motivation and understanding, along with the devices that will permit the expansion of the program, measured by the number of couples practicing family planning. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Since their Government is committed to this policy from what you have testified here and earlier and since we have the dark projections of what could happen regardless of what we do in other areas of aid if something is not done about the population explosion problem, what would be your reaction to us making that an item of priority, designating a specific amount of funds, or making this an area of emphasis in our own aid program and policy and doing what we can to stimulate more in this direction, rather than more or less plaving a supporting role and responding to what they do? 

Mr. WILLIAMS. I think we must continue to emphasize to the Indian 

Government the importance that we place on this program parallel to their efforts in food production and agriculture. I do not believe that earmarking specific amounts of funds is necessary, or indeed very useful as a means of placing this emphasis.

1323 My Agency does currently place the highest priority on family planning along with agricultural production. We are seeking means to bring this to the attention of other governments. It is, of course, a sensitive area. It is one they have to deal with themselves. But anything we can do to forcefully call their attention to our concern should be done.

Mr. BUCHANAN. Say if 50-as one proposal goes, $50 million be designated for this purpose, we have had testimony before this committee that there could be a need for as much as $100 million toward this purpose, if this was set aside, with some rather major share going to India in any logical breaking down of this money, since this is one of the really crucial countries and critical problems, would you say then that if the money were set aside and designated, you might have some difficulty deciding just exactly what to do with it?"

Mr. WILLIAMS. I think the sums that you mention would be excessive to the needs. I am speaking only in my understanding of India. 

I am not evaluating worldwide possibilities, I can't stress too strongly that it isn't foreign exchange that is required to move these programs forward. It is motivation and education. 

For instance, coils, which are the foundation of the Indian program, are not very costly and are produced in India. Importing condoms could become a significant foreign exchange cost, but I can't conceive of it reaching the levels that you have indicated. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Could we do more in the area of education, or do you think this wouldn't work?

Mr. WILLIAMS. I think that we could do more in the area of education. We are seeking ways in which to be helpful. You don't want to get in and take over the program. You don't want to step in and make it your program. You would find yourself running it. You couldn't do that anyway, and it isn't effective in the long run. 

So we are in an advisory, in a supporting role. I think that is the right role. I do feel we need to encourage, to prod, to stand ready, and to stress the importance that we place on family planning. It should be increasingly linked to the effectiveness of their agriculture programs and our food aid. As sensitive as the problem is, we must find ways to drive this home.

Mr. HANDLEY. May I say, in addition to what Mr. Williams has said, that obviously this is a major problem, but it can only really be solved by the Indians themselves. 

Motivation, education, are certainly all important. There are possibilities of legislation against a cultural background which should be thought of and the Indians are thinking of. For example, raising the marriage age. Some of the people who have studied this problem told me that if the marriage age could be raised-I think it is 14 or 15—to say 18 or 19 or 20, you would have an enormous impact and that wouldn't cost a penny.

This has to be understood, of course, against cultural backgrounds in which people do get married fairly early. The problem has all kinds of aspects to it.

Mr. BUCHANAN. That is the most delightful testimony I have heard this year. Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to yield to the gentleman from

1967 (The document referred to is as follows:) DEPARTMENT OF STATE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, 

Washington, D.C., June 6, 1967.

Hon. ROBERT TAFT, Jr., 

House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.

DEAR CONGRESSMAN TAFT: Thank you for your letter of May 25, 1967 request ing additional information about India and about our programs to promote the economic and social development of that country. I appreciated the opportunity which you afforded us the other day to explain in some greater detail our objectives in India and the programs which we have under way to achieve them. 

India now is at a critical juncture in its efforts to modernize its economy. 

Economic progress over the past 15 years has been impressive but too slow when measured against the needs of India's rapidly expanding population. For the past 15 years, Indian GNP growth has averaged about 4% a year. Industrial production rose an average of 6% a year. Agricultural production rose approximately 3% annually, but this increase represented only a slight advance in per capita food availabilities since population has been rising about 2.4% per annum. 

Domestic savings have risen from 5 to over 10% of GNP and investment from 5 to 14% of GNP in the last 15 years.

The new programs initiated by the Indian government over the past two years to improve agricultural production and to create a market-oriented economy hold out promise for a sharply increased rate of economic growth. Unfortunately, these promises have not yet been realized because of the disastrous effects of the second successive drought which has had serious repercussions throughout all sectors of the economy. Given a more normal monsoon this year, the present pessimistic outlook could be dramatically changed by a year from now. 

The hoped for improvements will continue to require Indian persistence on the new policy lines on which they are embarked, but also substantial amounts of external assistance to help finance the import of fertilizer and industrial goods needed to develop the economy. 

In reply to your specific questions, the purpose of the proposed non-project component of the proposed A.I.D. assistance for FY 1968 is to help India pay for general imports which are needed to maintain the momentum of the economy and to exploit more fully existing capacity for production both in agriculture and in industry. A large proportion will be needed to finance fertilizer, sulphur and other imported needs for agriculture. Items needed by industry include copper and other non-ferrous metals, pulp for paper manufacturing, chemicals and semifinished products for the manufacture of pharmaceutical and other chemical products. Spare parts and related equipment are needed to maintain power stations. Indian manufacturing facilities of trucks and tractors depend heavily on a continuing supply of components which are not manufactured in India. A substantial portion of industrial imports are needed by firms in which American companies have invested.

Table 1 shows the amounts that have been committed for program loans since FY 1962. The classified memorandum "FY 1968 Aid Level for India" handed to you recently explains that we had been able, because of the suspension of new aid commitments in 1965 and because of the timing of the announcement in June 1966 of India's economic reform program, to draw on FY 1966 funds to meet some of the requirements for FY 1967. As explained in the note, the amount of $132 million authorized in FY 1967 does not fully reflect the amount effectively available for expenditure in that year. The amount requested for FY 1968 will therefore permit A.I.D. to extend approximately the same amount of effective assistance in FY 1968 as in FY 1967 and will support the economic reform programs India adopted last summer. 

Table 2 provides a breakdown by major category of the goods which have been financed by A.I.D. under both program and project assistance from FY 1962 through FY 1966, the last year for which complete statistics are available. We expect that the range of commodities to be financed will be similar in FY 1967 and FY 1968, but that the amount of fertilizer will be sharply increased. 

Table 3 lists some of the more important projects for which A.I.D. has provided development loans in the past three years. The first five of these loans totalling $59.3 million have been extended to private firms in India manufacturing automotive equipment, ball bearings and power shovels. The Industrial Finance 

Corporation of India, which received a $10 million loan is a semi-public inter-

1327 mediate credit institution established for the purpose of extending medium term credit to permit the expansion of medium and small sized private enterprise. 

With one exception, there are no immediate plans to provide additional funds for any of the projects listed on Table 3 although we contemplate making loans in the future to support the expansion of Indian transportation and power generating facilities. We have under consideration, as shown on Table 4 a proposal for the further expansion of the Trombay Fertilizer Plant. 

I am attaching as Table 4 a list showing proposals for project assistance which are now in various stages of consideration. Some of these proposals are still in a very preliminary stage and it would be too early to determine whether and when the Agency would be prepared to approve them. The total under consideration exceeds the amount expected to be available for this purpose. 

Table 5 provides information on the rate of utilization of chemical fertilizer in India and projections for further expansion of fertilizer use. $300 million have been firmly budgeted for the import of fertilizer in the current year. This will assure the availability of chemical fertilizer in sufficient quantities to permit rapid expansion of use in the next crop year. By comparison, fertilizer imports in 1964-65 were about $65 million. 

Table 6 provides some basic data on the economy, including population change and average income per person expressed in a constant dollar figure. This table shows the steady but slow progress in per capita GNP and per capita food production until 1965 which reflects the first impact of the drought disaster which has struck India in the past two years. The table also shows that roughly 80% of India's investment and development effort has been financed from domestic resources. External aid has provided a critically needed 20%. 

There are a number of other indicators which provide clues to India's past progress and to her capacity to grow in the future. Since 1951 literacy has increased from 17% to 24% and school enrollment has tripled. The amount of power generated has increased by four fold; finished steel production has grown from one million tons to 4.5 million tons since 1951. Capacity has reached 5.6 million tons in 1966. 

Total investment during the Third Plan period from 1961 to 1966 is estimated at the equivalent of $21.4 billion. $8.5 billion of this amount-or roughly 40%was in the private sector, the balance in the public sector. 

Table 7 provides information on the amounts budgeted for family planning purposes and reflects the growing priority being assigned to this important area. 

Taking into account the relative size of the U.S. and Indian economies, the amount budgeted by India for family planning for the current year could be regarded as being roughly equivalent to $700 million program in the United States.

I hope that this additional material will help you to be persuaded of India's determination and capacity to make effective use of the assistance being provided by the United States. India's resolve to achieve self-sustaining growth, to maintain democratic processes, and to assure freedom and justice to her population, combine to make her a test case of possibly great influence in Asia. An economically strong India, assured of her position in the world and less dependent on outside support, could play an important moderating and constructive role in world affairs. 

Sincerely yours,

MAURICE J. WILLIAMS, 

Bureau for Near East and South Asia.

 BREAKDOWN OF USES OF NONPROJECT AID TO INDIA IN FISCAL YEAR 1968 

Last year the World Bank, as Chairman of the Aid-India Consortium, carried out a comprehensive review of India's economic situation and of its prospects. The Bank's report assesses the effectiveness of Indian policies in promoting economic growth and discusses additional self-help measures needed to accelerate the rate of economic and social progress. Special attention was focused on the need for increasing India's exports. The report also stressed the importance of vigorous execution of the new Indian program to expand agricul ture through greater use of production inputs and to improve the utilization of existing productive capacity through relaxation of import and other administrative controls. Family planning was identified as another area requiring im mediate attention and development of an aggressive program. 

We find ourselves in broad agreement with the Bank's conclusions and rec ommendations and we, as well as other country members of the Consortium have expressed this support at Consortium meetings and in direct conversations with the Indian Government. We also agree with the views of the Bank that India's aid requirements can best be met through the provision of nonproject aid. This form of aid has the flexibility needed to support India's import liberalization and other programs to reduce administrative controls over business decisions and to rely to a greater extent on the market mechanism. Nonproject aid also permits 

India to acquire the large amounts of fertilizer, pesticides, components for agri cultural machinery being assembled in India and other industrial inputs needed for the agricultural programs. India has reached a degree of industrialization where the need has declined for entire foreign financed projects, such as power plants, locomotive plants, automobile plants. Where large projects are needed, such as in the case of fertilizer, we are encouraging with some success the financing through private foreign investment rather than development loans. 

As Inida's industrial production increases, the need has grown, however, for general imports, such as raw materials, components, other semi-finished products, and spare parts.

As a result of its comprehensive analysis of India's economic development programs, the World Bank has concluded that India will require [security deletion] in nonproject assistance during the Indian fiscal year 1967/68 which began last April 1. Our own analyses conducted both by our Country Team in 

New Delhi and here in Washington supports the Bank's conclusions on this point. 

At the recent meeting of the India Consortium in April, the [security deletion] level of nonproject aid was accepted as a planinng figure by the members of the Consortium even though several members of the Consortium were unable (like the United States) to make firm pledges about the level of aid to be provided during the current Indian fiscal year. 

Last year the U.S. share of nonproject assistance provided by Consortium members was 42.4 percent. [Security deletion.]

The AID nonproject loans are expected to finance about 12 percent of India's nonfood imports during the current year. The precise composition of these im ports will of course depend upon the evolution of business conditions in India, on availability of goods in various markets, as well as on price and transporta tion factors. Based on past experience, on our estimates of development require ments, and on India's anticipated use of nonproject aid extended by others. we expect that fiscal year 1968 expenditures under nonproject loans (both existing loans not yet fully disbursed and nonproject loan assistance to be made available in fiscal year 1968) will be distributed as follows:

1967 

Mr. WILLIAMS. They hope to make 90 to 95 million tons of grain production this coming year. Their target for 1971 is 120 million tons.

Mr. FINDLEY. Have we made specific recommendations to the Gov ernment of India as to how that target of 120 million tons of wheat can be achieved by that date?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, sir. I think it is fair to say we have made recommendations on fertilizer, on seed and water. One of our recommendations, rather interestingly, has been to concentrate investment resources. There has been a tendency in India in the past, which is understandable given the federal political system of states, to pass around resources for increased production too evenly. Water often has been spread too thin as protection against drought rather than for maximum production. Consequently, they haven't gotten the high yields out of water availabilities. If one district gets seed, another district may get the fertilizer. There has been this effect in the past. 

The Indian Government is now attempting to concentrate these inputs, which are so closely related to each other if you are to get their full benefits in 32 million acres out of the 250 million acres of grain production in India.

Mr. PALMER. Coffee is their largest source of foreign exchange. It was formerly more than 50 percent of the total. They have moved to diversify their exports with the result that coffee is now less than 50 percent of their total.

1967 

conscripts. Since the illiteracy rate in Brazil is about 50 percent, at least half and probably more than half of the men that are inducted are not able to read and write. Also there is a requirement in the

The armed forces in Brazil perform not only the function of education but work in many other fields as well. They build roads and bridges. Mr. LANG. If I might answer that question, Mr. Congressman. You will recall the forces of both countries were largely equipped immediately after World War II with surplus and excess World War II equipment. The Argentine Government re ceived no military assistance until 1964. Since that time the bulk of the equipment has been in two fields, communications and transportation. 

We have not provided under military assistance the types of sophisticated military equipment that normally are associated with a modern army. As I said, the types of equipment for both Brazil and Argentina have been basically in the fields of communication and vehicles.

Going back 2 years, it compares with a 30-some percent rate of inflation in that same period. We find that the Brazilian Government has taken a number of steps, particularly in the agricultural sector. I would stress this because it brings a much better balance between the rural areas and urban areas. 

The previous discrimination which had existed against the rural areas has been largely corrected. Farm prices are much more attractive; a greater share of the country's resources is going to the agricultural area. This is beginning to show up in production. 

There are many serious problems in Brazil. I want to say nothing to give you the impression that we are sanguine about the situation. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. How does Brazil compare with other countries in Latin America with respect to its food sufficiency, and the rate of improvement in its agricultural production? Does it compare favorably or unfavorably?

Mr. PALMER. One of the proposals that we have in our fiscal year 

1968 program is what we call an agricultural sector loan in Brazil.

Mr. KUBISCII. I might add a word on the education side. There are problems at the elementary, secondary, and higher levels in Brazilian education and the U.S. AID mission is assisting in all three. The big problem is at the secondary level because primary education is free. 

Although half the people in Brazil are illiterate and efforts are made to build schools, train teachers, and so on, teaching materials, the problem is that if they complete primary school, the secondary school system is largely private and they have to pay to continue their education. These secondary schools are mostly religious schools or private independent institutions. At the higher education level we have contracts with a Midwest consortium of universities to help the Brazilian educators design modernization plans for the Brazilian university system.

We are working with Brazilians to help make improvements at all these levels. We have also worked with Brazil through Purdue University for 16 years in a successful project to establish what we might call here a land-grant college. The project involves training people in the field of agricutural economics, agronomy and other things, training Brazilians who use the knowledge that they have acquired to help improve agricultural techniques in Brazil.

Also, that U.S. Department of Agriculture here in the United States has a large number of technicians that have been sent to Brazil under a participating agency agreement. They are working with the Brazilians in many fields, including extension teaching.

 CAUSE FOR DELAY OF IMPORTS OF PARTS FOR CATERPILLAR TRACTORS AND GM TRUCKS 

In connection with the equipment at the Port in Vitoria noted by Congressman Gubser's constituent, we requested the U.S. AID Mission in Brazil to investigate the circumstances surrounding this case. The equipment was imported by the Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and financed under an A.I.D. community import loan. The importer is currently paying the storage charges. The unusual delay in removing this equipment from the post in Vitoria resulted from diffi culties with the local Brazilian Customs Office. These delays are not limited to 

A.I.D. financed commodities.

The Mission investigators visited the importer's office on May 4, 1967, and spoke to his superintendent. Mr. Joao e Beleza. The equipment amounts to ap proximately 130,000 kilos. comprising about 550 items which was off-loaded in 

Vitoria between June 23, 1966 and November 17, 1966. Mr. Beleza stated that there has been a recent change in Vitoria customs officials. The importer has met with these newly appointed officials and has resolved the principal problems which have delayed customs clearances. It is expected that the entire cargo will be cleared by June 30, 1967. Washington has requested the U.S. AID Mission to verify its actual clearance. 

Arrival accounting, controls and customs procedures under the commodity inport program are exercised by the Banco do Brazil. The Bank is a Governmentowned entity and also acts as the fiscal agent in administering the A.I.D. com-

1353 modity import loans. The USAID has recently instituted a number of procedures which should improve the early detection of any future problems. For example, the use of "Form Check Sheets" attached to appropriate Bill of Ladings which are sent to the Bank of Brazil for completion. The USAID evaluates the completed forms and when necessary takes appropriate action. Also, the USAID has now completed training its local Brazilian auditing staff to perform post audits and end-use observations. This should also increase the capacity of the USAID to monitor the commodity import program. 

Brazil with its huge geographical area has a number of widely scattered ports receiving goods from the U.S. The local administration of custom regulations varies from port to port which sometimes delays the release of commodities. In addition, buyers often find that prearranged sources of credit are not available when the commodities actually arrive. The importer is, therefore, unable to move the goods if private storage space is not available. The USAID is making every effort to ease the availability of credit thru direct loans to intermediate credit institutions and the allocation of Brazilian-owned counterpart for credit use.

Mr. MORSE. Would you define for the record the concepts of program loan, sector loan, and project loan? 

Mr. RICHARDSON. That is a difficult thing to do briefly, Mr. Congressman, but let me take a crack at it. 

A project loan is by definition the transference of real capital goods to a country, fixed in place, in order to achieve a particular output objective. A project loan in the power sector would provide the emplacement of a particular generator, for example. 

A program loan provides a commitment of resources to a recipient country in a more flexible, fungible form than a project loan would. 

[Security deletion.] 

A sector loan is more or less a combination of the two. It is analogous to a program loan in the sense that it provides a fungible command over dollars in order to buy a very wide array of commodities and capital equipment, but it is more like a project loan in the sense that it attempts to focus on a particiular sector of the economy of the recipient country in order to support certain policies and certain kinds of activities, such as an agricultural sector loan.

 IMPLEMENTATION OF TITLE IX IN BRAZIL PROGRAM 

Loans discussed below should be considered only as an illustrative list. There have been no commitments on the part of either the United States or the Government of Brazil to undertake these activities in fiscal year 1968. 

1. PROGRAM LOAN 

Application of currencies from the 1968 Program Loan have not yet been determined, but Title IX objectives will be considered in reaching final decisions for the allocation of these funds. 

2. AGRICULTURAL SECTOR LOAN 

The sector loan will serve to focus the attention of the federal government on food consumption requirements of all segments of the population and to stimulate increased federal-state-local partnership arrangements in planning and organizing programs for rural modernization. An attempt will be made to reach agreement with the Government of Brazil on the following matters: (a) Systematizing Government of Brazil evaluation and planning for national agricultural development, including the establishment of an adequate system for coordination and support of regional, state and local development entities aimed toward achieving established common goals and targets. Conditions for loans to municipios will include requirements for improved planning at the local level for specific needs and goals. It will be the responsibility of localities to make known their specific needs and to seek complementary technical services and financing from the national level through state level agencies. Local public and private groups and individuals will execute local plans related to national targets. (b) Continuation of presently established government policies which give incentives to individual farmer producers, especially price, credit and fertilizer incentives. (c) Commitment to provide adequate funds for the expanding operations of public and private agricultural credit institutions to ensure achievement of national goals, and the efficient allocation of these resources through state and local level agencies. 

3. EDUCATION SECTOR LOAN 

This is an attempt to increase productive relationships between federal and state governments by helping Brazil achieve its objectives of decentralizing the secondary education system. The proposed education sector loan envisages providing assistance to a number of Brazilian states to help them implement their state education plans. These plans are being developed by education committees in six different states using technical assistance provided by AID. It is planned that all education authorities in the states selected to participate in the loan program will be intimately involved in the preliminary discussions, planning and implementation of the program for their own state. 

4. AGRICULTURAL MARKETING AND STORAGE FACILITIES 

This is an attempt to encourage farmers to organize or expand cooperatives for productive purposes, to stimulate joint planning and increased communica tion between local private groups and governmental agencies, and to redirect the efforts and resources of federal and state agencies in order to better serve local organizations. Under this project an economic unit of farmers in one or more municipios (counties) may acquire financing for cooperative marketing facilities after presenting balanced plans for integrated agricultural development work. The "economic community" applying for a loan must demonstrate that plans have been made to meet related agricultural needs for production credit, farm supplies (seed, mineral supplements, equipment), necessary exten sion services or other technical assistance, and farm to market roads. To admin-

1359 ister the program the Brazilians are expanding operations of federal institutions such as the National Bank for Cooperatives which use state agencies as agents. 

Also, municipios will seek more and better advisory services from state agencies. 

5. FISHERIES IN THE NORTHEAST 

This project will provide economic opportunities to the underprivileged, but may not build formalized cooperatives in the first stage. The proposed loan will finance fishing gear and improved boats for fishermen working together in groups. It will also cover principal costs of cooperatively run processing, storage and transport facilities for fresh water and ocean fish. People who will be in charge of business operations in the project will need to be trained. Matching 

Brazilian contributions for the project will largely be in the form of labor and in-kind donations. 

6. FEEDER ROADS-MATO GROSSO 

This project attempts to foster on-going programs of community planning and action, particularly by requiring municipios to supply a considerable portion of the initial financial resources needed for public works. Cooperative local-state relationships will also be expanded. 

To stimulate communities to build or upgrade 3,000 to 5,000 miles of feeder roads in the western State of Mato Grosso, the proposed loan provides that the United States share 30 percent of construction costs when state and local organizations cover all remaining costs. U.S. financing will cover some equipment needs while Brazilians will provide for labor and other variable costs including equipment, supplies and professional services. The communities, in cooperation with the State, will organize to plan the locations, construction and financing of the road programs. Construction should be completed in two years, once equipment has arrived. Brazil now builds 2,641 miles of road annually, 825 miles of which are paved. 

7. [Security deletion.] 8. MALARIA ERADICATION 

This project has limited Title IX application in that it encourages useful federal-state cooperation to cope with a national health hazard. The federal government agency responsible for the Campaign for Malaria Eradication is presently decentralizing its operations to involve departments of health of state governments more actively in planning and carrying out eradication measures. 

Over 32 million people live in the five regions of Brazil covering the malarious areas of the country where the Campaign is being conducted. 

9. [Security deletion.] 10. FEASIBILITY STUDIES 

This effort responds to Foreign Assistance Act provisions calling for encouragement of private enterprise in developing countries, thereby contributing to objectives of Title IX. An additional loan is planned for the Fund for Financing 

Project and Program Studies (FINEP). This is a federal institution which makes it possible for private companies and state and federal groups to borrow money to finance feasibility studies and natural resource surveys. In addition to external financing, FINEP requires local contributions to feasibility studies, with financial agents covering 5 to 20 percent of each study and sub-borrowers covering 10 to 40 percent of each study. It is expected that participating Brazilian agencies and firms will cover an increasing share of the institutional costs of FINEP over the next few years. All investment studies financed by loan funds are performed by private consulting firms, 11. AGRICULTURAL DIVERSIFICATION 

This is an attempt to encourage development and expansion of private cooperative activity in a key farming region of Brazil, and to expand intergovernmental programs which lead to national economic integration. Farmers in the coffee states of Sao Paulo and Minas Gerais who are willing to work through cooperatives may apply for financing under this proposed loan project to increase production of non-traditional products such as feed grains, oil seeds or poultry. The United States may finance up to 60 percent of costs for marketing facilities provided that Brazilians cover thhe balance, and that cooperatives

1967 

themselves cover 22 percent of initial costs. To obtain financing for these marketing facilities, cooperatives will need to demonstrate how the area is capable of increasing food or feed production. They will make their case to expanding state level institutions which obtain funds from the federal government. In addition, the borrowers will be expected to raise any funds required for needed agricultural production inputs such as seed and equipment. 

The marketing facilities would be started by larger farmers who are able to help the cooperatives meet the financial requirements of the loans. In turn, the cooperatives will extend privileges to smaller farmers who may join as voting members. 

12. SUGAR DIVERSIFICATION 

Federal and state Brazilian agencies having responsibilities for the growth and welfare of the Northeast Sugar Zone are joining together to plan and administer an integrated area development program. Expanded private enterprise, increased job opportunities and formation of cooperatives are elements of the work which reflect Title IX objectives. The proposed loan will help launch in the coastal Sugar Zone of Northeast Brazil a five-year program for: (1) modernization of the sugar industry; (2) diversification of the economy and reform of the region's land ownership and use patterns; and (3) intensive development of the human resources of the rural area to meet new manpower needs. The 

Brazilian Government plans to provide support and economic incentives to cane and sugar producers to modernize the sugar industry in exchange for liberation of the land for agrarian reform purposes. Two federal agencies will administer programs to help install family farm units on liberated lands. Cooperatives will be formed to provide technical assistance, marketing and other services.

Bank. This circular expressly forbids “financial institutions in any way to apply or promote the application abroad of financial resources collected in Brazil."

This project is now underway. It is about a $70 or $80 million project. This project looks toward the creation of a fertilizer complex in Brazil that will supply all of Brazil's needs for the near-term future.

 THE USE OF FERTILIZER IN BRAZIL 

It is generally agreed that food production can be increased faster and cheaper by the proper use of fertilizer than in any other way. The IRI Research Institute is assisting Brazil to conduct research on the Campo Cerrado soils which cover 200 million acres of the country. This research has shown that, with proper fertilizer applications, corn yields are increased by 4,380 kg. per hectare with a 

59% return on investment. Soybeans gave a 1,740 kg. per hectare increase in yield and a 287% return on investment.

On September 29, 1966, a new AID loan for $20 million was signed with Brazil to finance fertilizer imports from the United States and to establish a revolving loan fund permitting farmers to obtain credit at reasonable rates for fertilizer purchases from distributors. The new loan supplements a previous $15 million loan for the same purposes authorized in 1964. In addition, the U.S. on November 21, 1966, signed a loan agreement with Brazil for $14.8 million to help finance a $70 million project for the production and distribution of nitrogen fertilizer to farmers. This project will result in a reduction of 30% in nitrogen fertilizer prices.

To induce farmers to close the food production gap. Brazil provides agricultural credits and a credit subsidy for the use of fertilizer on non-surplus food crops. As a further stimulant, the Government has removed price controls on most farm products. Under present conditions the expected return to farmers applying fertilizer is about 22 to 3 times the cost of the fertilizer. As a byproduct. the increased farm output yields new taxes. 

Brazil, like most underdeveloped countries, has been using little fertilizer per unit of area except on the comparatively few well managed commercial farms. 

As a means of comparison, the United States and Canada use 94 pounds per capita as against 8.9 pounds in Latin America.

Law 480 activity there? 

Mr. KUBISCH. That is a good question. The fact is that "breadbasket" was a poor choice of terms, because what Brazil cannot be is a "breadbasket" for wheat in the foreseeable future. Brazil has excellent pros pects, for example, of producing in large quantity rice, corn, potatoes, vegetable oils, coffee, sugar, soybeans and so on. Because of the location of Brazil it has been very difficult to develop strains of wheat that could grow in large quantity in Brazil except in the southernmost

 U.S. LOAN AND GRANT PROGRAMS FOR BRAZIL 

There are five U.S. programs for which the Congress enacts separate legislation to provide loans and grants to Brazil and other countries. The overwhelming majority of these are in the form of long-term dollar loans to Brazil. In fiscal year 

1966, the total provided through these channels to Brazil was $406.2 million, of which 80 percent was in the form of loans. With the exception of the Export- 

Import Bank, which may make loans to U.S. or Brazilian businessmen, all these loan moneys are repayable in dollars to the U.S. Treasury by the Government of Brazil.

In fiscal year 1967 the estimated amount of grant and loan funds to be made available through these five programs is [security deletion] of which [security deletion] or 79 percent will be in dollar loans.

Since the last authorization for milk was made in fiscal year 1966, none was made in fiscal year 1967. It is anticipated that an additional authorization for milk will be made in fiscal year 1968.
